three thousand of his followers with him.
junonia failed.
but the idea didn't:
the poor deserved land,
carthage's curse could be lifted.
caesar would refound it.
augustus would finish it.
the colony that failed
was just early.

the first political massacre 121 bce rome i walked the tiber the week three thousand of gaius gracchus's followers were strangled — the first political massacre, murder learned as policy, the river carrying the bodies. they killed gaius gracchus —
and then the senate passed the ultimate decree,
and three thousand of his followers
were strangled in prison.
i walked past the tiber that week.
the bodies — they threw them in the river,
like his brother's.
the first political massacre.
not a riot, not a brawl —
a systematic killing of the defeated,
ordered by the state.
roman politics had learned murder
as a policy.
the clubs of 133 became the nooses of 121.
the nooses would become the proscriptions,
the proscriptions the civil wars.
it started here:
three thousand strangled,
and the river carrying the bodies.

the music bureau 120 bce china i sat in village squares with a yuefu collector writing down farmers' songs — emperor wu's music bureau gathering the empire's voice, one song at a time, for two millennia. emperor wu founded the yuefu —
the music bureau —
to collect the songs of the people
from every province:
work songs, love songs, laments,
the empire's voice, gathered.
i traveled with a collector once.
we sat in village squares,
writing down what the farmers sang —
and the farmers were shy, then proud.
two thousand years later,
we still sing their songs.
the yuefu preserved the folk voice
of han china —
the empire listening to its people,
one song at a time.
every folk revival since
is an echo of the music bureau.

the battle of mobei 119 bce mongolia i rode the supply columns past the gobi to mobei — the han smashing the xiongnu on their own steppe, the victory that opened the silk road and quieted the north for a generation. the han armies went deep —
past the gobi, into the steppe itself —
and at mobei smashed the xiongnu:
the chanyu fleeing, the tribes scattered,
the northern threat broken for a generation.
i rode with the supply columns.
the desert crossing nearly killed us —
but wei qing and huo qubing
did what no chinese generals had done:
beat the nomads at their own game,
on their own ground.
the steppe went quiet.
the silk road opened.
china's greatest victory over the north —
won by marching into the desert
and refusing to come back
until it was over.

the wanderers from the north 113 bce europe i saw the cimbri and teutones spilling down from jutland — whole peoples migrating, wagons to the horizon — rome not yet understanding what was walking toward it. they came down from jutland —
the cimbri, the teutones,
whole peoples migrating:
warriors, women, children, wagons —
fleeing the sea, or hunger, or each other.
i saw the migration's front edge.
it stretched to the horizon.
rome had never seen anything like it.
the romans would learn to fear the name —
arausio was coming, the worst defeat since cannae.
but that year they were just wanderers,
looking for land,
and rome didn't understand
what was walking toward it.
migrations don't negotiate.
they just arrive.

the numidian jackal 112 bce africa i was in rome when jugurtha's bribes surfaced — the numidian jackal calling it "a city for sale" as he left — the joke about the senate that never stopped being true. jugurtha — king of numidia,
rome's "ally" —
murdered his rivals,
seized the whole kingdom,
and bribed roman senators
to look the other way.
i was in rome when the bribes surfaced.
the scandal stank.
jugurtha had bought the senate —
or rented it, which amounts to the same.
"venalis!" he said, leaving rome:
a city for sale, and soon to perish
if it finds a buyer.
the jackal knew rome's secret:
everything had a price,
including the senators.
rome would have to send marius
to do what bribes couldn't.
but jugurtha's joke —
a city for sale —
never stopped being funny.
because it never stopped being true.

the new man 111 bce rome i watched marius the farmer's son take the consulship — the new man whose army reforms would save rome and then, loyal to generals not republic, help kill it. marius — a farmer's son from arpinum,
no ancestors, no statues in the atrium —
ran for the consulship
on the soldiers' votes
and won.
the novus homo. the new man.
i watched him take office.
the nobles sneered.
the people cheered.
he would reform the army —
take the poor, the landless,
make them professionals, loyal to him —
and change rome forever.
the new man broke the old monopoly.
but his army, loyal to its general
instead of the republic,
would become the weapon
that killed the republic.
reforms have consequences.
his had legions.

the incense road 110 bce arabia i traveled with a frankincense caravan from yemen to gaza — a thousand swaying camels, the desert middlemen growing rich at every oasis, perfume worth its weight in gold. the caravans came up from yemen —
frankincense, myrrh,
the perfumes of the gods —
on camelback, through the desert,
to gaza and the mediterranean.
i traveled with a caravan once.
a thousand camels, swaying,
the drivers singing,
the desert middlemen growing rich
at every oasis.
the incense road:
the original luxury trade,
perfume worth its weight in gold,
temples from rome to babylon
burning arabian resin.
the desert bloomed with toll stations.
petra grew rich.
the middlemen always grow rich.
that is the one constant
of every trade route ever.

the fall of wiman's state 108 bce korea i walked the aftermath as han armies took wiman's capital — four centuries of chinese commanderies beginning in northern korea, the deep imprint of empire next door. han armies took the korean capital —
wiman's grandson's kingdom,
the adventurer's state —
and the north of the peninsula
became chinese commanderies.
i was there for the aftermath.
han officials, han laws, han taxes —
lelang and the other commanderies,
outposts of the empire
on foreign soil.
they lasted four hundred years.
four centuries of chinese rule
in northern korea —
leaving tombs, lacquerware, characters,
the deep imprint.
the adventurer's kingdom fell.
the empire's commanderies rose.
korea learned, under han rule,
what it meant to be next to china:
everything.

the disaster at arausio 105 bce rome i barely survived arausio — two roman armies annihilated by the cimbri, eighty thousand dead, the worst defeat since cannae, and rome bending its constitution to give marius command. two roman armies —
eighty thousand men, two consuls —
met the cimbri and teutones at arausio,
quarreled with each other instead of fighting together,
and were annihilated.
i survived it. barely.
the river ran red, they said.
the worst defeat since cannae —
some say worse.
rome panicked.
the gauls were coming.
marius was given command —
five consulships in a row,
the constitution bent to save the city.
arausio taught rome
what the wanderers from the north could do.
the lesson was written in eighty thousand dead.
rome never forgot it.
neither did the cimbri.

the second slave war 104 bce sicily i was in sicily for the second slave war — salvius's runaway army holding the hills for years — rome learning again that an economy built on chains must pay for their defense. the slaves rose again in sicily —
under salvius, a new king,
a new court, a new army of runaways.
i was on the island.
it was eunus all over again —
only bigger, better organized,
and rome was busy with the cimbri.
it took years to put down.
years of burning villas,
of slave armies in the hills,
of rome learning, again,
that an economy built on chains
has to pay for the chains' defense.
salvius died. the revolt died.
but the third one — spartacus —
was coming.
the slaves kept score.
rome kept winning.
the arithmetic never changed.

marius's mules 102 bce gaul i marched with marius's mules at aquae sextiae — the professional legions cutting down the teutones, italy saved, and the army learning loyalty to its general first. at aquae sextiae, marius's new legions —
his mules, they called them,
carrying their own packs, professional,
the poor made into soldiers —
met the teutones.
i marched with them.
the teutones came on in their thousands,
brave, huge, doomed.
the legions — drilled, disciplined —
cut them down like wheat.
a hundred thousand dead or captured, they said.
the women killed themselves
rather than be taken.
italy was saved.
marius was the savior.
the mules had proved themselves:
rome's new army —
professional, loyal, lethal —
and loyal to marius first.
that last part would matter.

the crows at vercellae 101 bce italy i watched the chained cimbri die where they stood at vercellae — the crows feasting, rome saved, and the city beginning to regret how much it owed its savior. the cimbri came last —
down into italy itself —
and marius met them at vercellae,
on a plain, in the dust and heat.
the cimbri tied their front ranks together
with chains — to not break, they said.
i watched the dust rise.
the legions advanced through it,
and the chained men died where they stood,
unable to run.
the crows feasted for days.
rome celebrated its savior
a little too much —
fifth consulship, honors, the title
of third founder of rome.
marius saved the city.
the city would regret
how much it owed him.
saviors collect debts.
this one collected in armies.

the machine in the wreck 100 bce aegean i dove the antikythera wreck and saw the bronze gears whole — the ancient computer that predicted eclipses, lost for two thousand years in a shipwreck. off antikythera, sponge divers found a wreck —
and in it, a lump of bronze,
corroded, unremarkable —
until the x-rays, two thousand years later.
gears. thirty-seven of them.
dials. pointers.
a machine that predicted eclipses,
tracked the planets,
the olympic games cycle —
a computer, two thousand years early.
i dove that wreck — in my way —
and saw it whole: the bronze gleaming,
the gears meshing.
the greeks built a computer
and the world forgot how.
it took two millennia
to catch up to a shipwreck.

the song on stone 100 bce greece i stood before the seikilos stone and read the oldest complete melody on earth — a widower's four lines on shining while you live, the song outlasting the singer's name. a widower carved it on his wife's tombstone —
the words, and above them,
the musical notation:
the seikilos epitaph,
the oldest complete melody on earth.
i stood before that stone.
"while you live, shine —
grieve not at all;
life is short,
and time demands its due."
four lines. a tune you can still play.
someone's grief, set to music,
carved in marble two thousand years ago —
and the song survived
when the singer's name barely did.
the oldest song we have
is about not grieving too long.
the widower knew.
shine while you live.

the city in the valley 100 bce mexico i walked among the first huts at teotihuacan — refugees gathering at the springs, unknowingly starting the greatest city of the ancient americas. refugees came down into the valley of mexico —
fleeing the volcano, the wars, the hunger —
and gathered around the springs of teotihuacan.
i walked among the first huts.
nobody knew what they were starting.
a grid. a plan. an avenue of the dead
that would run for miles.
teotihuacan would become
the greatest city of the ancient americas —
a hundred thousand people,
pyramids to the sun and moon.
it started with refugees
and springs.
cities always start with water
and people with nowhere else to go.

the lines in the desert 100 bce peru i walked the nazca lines — hummingbird, monkey, spider swept into the desert for the sky alone — two thousand years of wind unable to erase the prayer. on the nazca plain, they swept the dark stones aside —
revealing the pale earth beneath —
in lines, miles long:
a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider,
geometric gods only the sky could read.
i walked the lines.
from the ground, they're just cleared paths.
from above — from where i sometimes see —
they're a bestiary, a calendar, a prayer.
why? for the gods? for the water?
the desert keeps its reasons.
the lines are still there,
two thousand years of wind
unable to erase them.
someone drew for the sky,
and the sky, presumably,
was watching.

the bells of the rice gods 100 bce japan i stood before an unearthed dotaku — the great yayoi bronze bell, buried face-down, never rung — music for the rice gods in the silence they preferred. the yayoi craftsmen cast them —
dotaku, great bronze bells,
taller than a man,
decorated with scenes of the hunt, the harvest —
and they never rang them.
buried on hillsides, face down,
offerings to the rice gods.
i stood before one, unearthed —
the bronze green with age,
the decorations still sharp.
bells that never rang.
music for gods who listen
in silence.
the rice needed the gods' favor,
and the gods, apparently,
preferred their bells buried.
faith has its own acoustics.

the bronze drums 100 bce vietnam i heard a dong son bronze drum struck at a festival — the thunder rolling down the valley — bronze, music, and authority alloyed in ancient vietnam. the dong son smiths cast them —
towering bronze drums,
covered in stars, birds, feathered warriors,
the frog on top, the sun at the center —
and a chief's voice carried across the valleys
on their bronze thunder.
i heard one struck — once, at a festival.
the sound rolled down the valley
like weather.
the drums were power:
who owned the biggest drum
owned the loudest voice,
and the loudest voice ruled.
bronze, music, authority —
alloyed together
in the valleys of vietnam,
two thousand years ago.

the grand historian 100 bce china i visited the disgraced sima qian, writing through his punishment — the shiji, all china's history, the castrated historian out-writing the emperor who shamed him. sima qian — the grand historian —
defended a defeated general at court,
and the emperor had him castrated for it.
he lived. he chose to live —
to finish the work:
the shiji, the records of the grand historian,
the history of all china
from the yellow emperor to his own day.
i visited him in his disgrace.
he was writing. always writing.
one hundred and thirty chapters.
he finished it.
the punishment meant to silence him
produced the greatest history
china would ever have.
disgrace, endured for the sake of the record.
the historian's revenge:
he out-wrote the emperor.

the venus of milo 100 bce greece i saw the venus of milo whole, arms and all — but the world fell for the armless version: loss as a kind of completion, everyone finishing her in imagination. a sculptor on melos carved her —
aphrodite, the goddess of love,
larger than life, marble,
her arms lost to time
before she was ever found.
i saw her whole — in my way —
arms and all, whatever they held.
but the armless version is the one
the world fell for.
she was found in a farmer's field,
sold, shipped, displayed in the louvre —
and became the most famous statue on earth.
perfect anyway.
the missing arms made her universal:
everyone completes her
in their own imagination.
loss, it turns out,
can be a kind of completion.

the paper trail 100 bce china i held a damp sheet of han paper — hemp and bark pounded centuries before cai lun's fame — the everyday miracle every book since descends from. in han workshops, they pounded it:
hemp, bark, rags, old fishing nets —
soaked, beaten, spread on screens,
dried in the sun.
paper. sheets of it.
centuries before cai lun
would get the credit,
the han were already making it —
wrapping, writing, the everyday miracle.
i held a sheet, still damp.
rough. uneven. revolutionary.
everything written since —
every book, every newspaper,
this very collection —
descends from hemp pounded in a han workshop.
the paper trail starts here,
in vats of gray pulp,
two thousand years ago.

the king of kings 95 bce armenia i stood at tigranes' court — the king of kings ruling from caspian to mediterranean — the shining decade when the mountains ruled the lowlands. tigranes — tigranes the great —
built an empire from the caspian to the mediterranean:
armenia, syria, mesopotamia,
and took the old persian title:
king of kings.
i was at his court at tigranocerta.
the pomp was parthian, the ambition roman,
the king himself — shrewd, proud,
seventy and still conquering.
he called himself king of kings
while rome called itself the republic.
the titles would collide —
lucullus was coming, then pompey —
and the empire would shrink back to armenia.
but for a shining decade,
the mountains ruled the lowlands,
and tigranes was the greatest king
in the world.

the war of the allies 91 bce italy i marched in the social war — italians killing italians for citizenship — and watched rome win the war then grant the prize anyway: blood buying what petitions couldn't. rome's italian allies — the socii,
who had fought rome's wars for generations —
rose for citizenship.
roman citizenship. the vote. the rights.
rome refused. so they fought.
the social war — the war of the allies —
the bloodiest war rome ever fought in italy.
i marched in it. italians killing italians,
the same language, the same gods,
brothers in the legions now facing each other.
rome won the war —
and gave them the citizenship anyway.
the allies won by losing:
blood bought what petitions couldn't.
italy became roman —
not by conquest, but by admission.
the hardest-won citizenship
in history.

the poison king 89 bce pontus i dined with mithridates the poison king — twenty-two languages, daily doses of immunity — who made himself unkillable and then couldn't die when he wanted to. mithridates of pontus —
the poison king —
took a little poison every day,
building immunity, dose by dose,
so no assassin could kill him that way.
i dined at his court.
he spoke twenty-two languages.
he collected antidotes like jewels.
he plotted rome's ruin
with the patience of a man
who had made himself unkillable.
the daily poison worked — too well.
when he finally wanted to die,
the poison wouldn't take him.
he had to order a guard to run him through.
immunity has its price:
the man who couldn't be poisoned
couldn't poison himself either.

the night of knives 88 bce anatolia i was in ephesus for the asiatic vespers — eighty thousand romans killed in one night on mithridates' order — the night no roman ever forgave. the order went out across asia —
in every city, at the same hour:
kill every roman. every italian.
man, woman, child.
eighty thousand dead in one night.
i was in ephesus.
the screaming went on till dawn.
the asiatic vespers — the night of knives —
mithridates' answer to rome.
no roman would ever forgive it.
no roman ever did.
sulla's invasion, the wars, the proscriptions —
all of it flowed from that night.
eighty thousand throats cut
because a king in pontus
decided rome was a disease
and prescribed the knife.

the sack of athens 88 bce greece i walked sacked athens after sulla — the academy's groves cut for siege works, treasures shipped to rome — learning that culture does not protect you. sulla stormed athens —
the city of plato and aristotle,
of the parthenon and the academy —
and looted it.
i walked the streets afterward.
the walls were breached.
the treasures were gone —
shipped to rome, melted, sold.
the academy's groves were cut down
for siege works.
athens had sided with mithridates.
sulla made it pay.
the city survived — cities do —
but something broke that year:
the idea that culture protects you.
it doesn't.
the parthenon stood.
the academy's trees did not.
sulla taught the world:
even the school of hellas
is just another city to sack.

the heads on spears 87 bce rome i walked the forum past senators' heads on the rostra — marius and cinna's terror — rome learning to eat its own, one displayed head at a time. marius and cinna took rome —
the old lion, back for his seventh consulship,
mad, vengeful —
and the proscriptions began.
senators' heads on spears.
displayed on the rostra —
the forum's beaks, the speakers' platform —
where the heads of rome's enemies
had always been shown.
i walked the forum that winter.
the heads froze. the crowds stared.
marius died days later —
of age, of drink, of victory.
the heads stayed up.
cinna kept them there.
rome had learned a new political tool:
the displayed head.
sulla would industrialize it.
the republic was learning
to eat its own.

the death of wu 86 bce china i was at court when emperor wu died after fifty-four years — the martial emperor leaving a deathbed edict repenting his wars: larger and emptier, counting the cost at the end. emperor wu died —
fifty-four years on the throne,
the martial emperor,
who made china larger
and emptier than he found it.
i was at the court.
the wars — the xiongnu, korea, vietnam —
the expansion, the glory,
the taxes, the conscription,
the empty granaries.
he left an edict, they say —
repenting the wars, the waste.
the輪台 edict: no more expansion.
a dying emperor's apology
to his exhausted people.
fifty-four years.
larger and emptier.
the wheel-turning king's confession:
even emperors, at the end,
count the cost.

sulla's march 83 bce rome i watched sulla's legions march on rome — the first roman army turned on the capital itself — the taboo broken, the lesson the legions would never unlearn. sulla landed at brundisium —
with his legions, his veterans,
his proscription lists already drafted —
and marched on rome.
the first roman to turn an army
on rome itself.
i watched the column move north.
the soldiers knew what they were doing.
they did it anyway —
for sulla, for the loot, for the donative.
the republic's last taboo, broken:
the army as a political weapon,
aimed at the capital.
marius had seized rome.
sulla invaded it.
the difference mattered —
and didn't.
the legions had learned
they could take the city.
they would never unlearn it.

the lists of death 82 bce rome i read sulla's proscription lists in the forum — names added daily, murder made legal business — the republic's suicide note, posted for everyone to read. sulla posted the lists —
proscription: names on tablets
in the forum.
kill the named, take their property,
and it's legal.
i read the lists.
friends' names. neighbors' names.
added daily — the lists grew.
murder became a business:
the proscribed man's estate
went to the killer, the informer, the state.
thousands died.
rome's rich got richer.
sulla's veterans got farms.
the lists of death:
the republic's suicide note,
written in names,
posted in the forum
for everyone to read.

the young orator 80 bce rome i sat in court when twenty-six-year-old cicero defied sulla's regime to defend roscius — the young orator announcing himself with one brave speech. cicero — twenty-six, unknown,
a new man from arpinum like marius —
defended sextus roscius
against sulla's freedman chrysogonus,
who had proscribed the father
to steal the estate.
i sat in the court.
the young orator attacked the regime's favorite
at the height of the terror —
brave or reckless, no one was sure.
he won. roscius was acquitted.
cicero made his name in one speech —
and had to leave rome afterward,
for his health, they said.
for his safety, everyone knew.
the young orator had announced himself:
the voice of the republic,
at the moment the republic
needed a voice most.

the marble archive 78 bce rome i walked the marble corridors of the tabularium — rome's stone vault for its laws — the archive outlasting the republic it served, still standing, still saying remember. rome built the tabularium —
on the capitoline hill, overlooking the forum,
a great stone vault
for the laws, the decrees, the treaties.
i walked its corridors.
marble. order. permanence.
the republic's memory, in stone.
the laws would be safe here —
bronze and marble don't burn like paper.
the archive outlasted the republic
it was built to serve.
empires fall. archives remain.
the tabularium still stands —
its stones now hold a museum.
the laws it kept are dust.
the building kept the faith:
remember.

the pirate's prisoner 75 bce aegean i heard young caesar joke with his pirate captors about crucifying them — then do it: the ransom, the fleet, the crosses, and the laugh nobody found funny twenty years later. young julius caesar — twenty-five,
on his way to study in rhodes —
was kidnapped by pirates.
he charmed them. joked with them.
told them he'd have them all crucified —
they laughed.
the ransom was paid — fifty talents,
caesar insisted on more than they asked,
insulted at the low price.
then he raised a fleet,
hunted them down,
and crucified them —
all of them, as promised.
he cut their throats first,
a mercy, he said,
because they had treated him well.
i heard him tell the story later.
he laughed.
everyone laughed.
nobody was laughing
twenty years later.

the gladiators' revolt 73 bce italy i marched with spartacus's slave army — seventy men with kitchen knives grown to a hundred thousand — two years of rome terrified, ending with the fatal turn back from the alps. spartacus — a thracian, a soldier,
enslaved, trained to kill for sport —
broke out of the gladiator school at capua
with seventy men and kitchen knives.
i joined the march north — in my way.
the army grew: runaways, slaves,
the desperate, the brave —
a hundred thousand strong.
they beat every army rome sent.
for two years, spartacus —
the gladiator —
humiliated the republic.
he could have crossed the alps to freedom.
he turned back — why, no one knows.
pride? hope? the men's refusal to leave italy?
the revolt was doomed from that turn.
but for two years,
the slaves had an army,
a general, and a chance —
and rome was terrified.

the road of crosses 71 bce italy i walked the appian way past six thousand crucified rebels — crassus's warning in wood and flesh — and thought of the kitchen knives and the two years of freedom. crassus caught them at last —
spartacus dead in the battle,
his army destroyed —
and the survivors, six thousand,
were crucified along the appian way.
i walked that road.
six thousand crosses.
mile after mile.
men dying slowly in the italian sun,
a warning in wood and flesh.
the road of crosses:
rome's answer to the slave revolt.
it worked — no great slave war
ever rose again.
but i walked among the crosses,
and i thought of the kitchen knives,
the two years of freedom,
the gladiator who almost made it.
the crosses said: don't try.
the memory said: he tried.

the prosecutor 70 bce rome i sat through cicero's prosecution of the looting governor verres — the evidence so overwhelming he fled to exile — sicily cheering, rome noticing. cicero prosecuted verres —
the corrupt governor of sicily,
who had looted the island for three years:
the statues, the grain, the crucified roman citizen.
i sat through the trial.
cicero's evidence was overwhelming —
witnesses, documents, the works.
verres fled into exile
before the second session.
sicily cheered.
rome noticed.
the young orator was now the prosecutor —
the man who took down a governor.
the verrines made cicero's career.
they also made a point:
even in a corrupt republic,
a good prosecution
could still work.
sometimes.

the pirate war 67 bce mediterranean i sailed with pompey's pirate sweep — five hundred ships, three months, the whole mediterranean cleared — the twenty-nine-year-old making the sea rome's. the pirates owned the sea —
from spain to syria, they raided,
they kidnapped, they even cut rome's grain supply.
pompey got the command:
unlimited authority, five hundred ships.
three months.
that's all it took.
i sailed with the fleet —
the systematic sweep, west to east,
pirates hunted like vermin.
in three months, the mediterranean
was clear.
pompey settled the survivors as farmers —
clemency, the roman way, when it worked.
the pirate war: the fastest great campaign
in roman history.
pompey was twenty-nine.
the sea was rome's.
everyone knew whose it was.

the end of the poison king 66 bce pontus i heard the survivor's account — mithridates' poison failing at last, the guard's sword finishing the unkillable king in the crimea after thirty years of defying rome. pompey hunted him to the end of the world —
mithridates, the poison king,
fleeing to the crimea,
plotting still, at sixty-eight,
to invade italy itself.
his son rebelled. his army deserted.
he tried the poison —
it didn't work, of course.
the immunity held.
so he ordered his guard
to run him through.
i heard the account from a survivor.
the unkillable king,
killed by his own order.
pompey took the east.
the poison king's wars were over —
thirty years of defying rome,
ended in the crimea
by a guard's sword.
the poison worked.
the king didn't.

the province of syria 64 bce syria i was in antioch when pompey annexed the last seleucid remnant — three hundred years ending with a proclamation, rome reaching the euphrates. pompey annexed it —
the seleucid remnant, the last of alexander's eastern empire —
and syria became a roman province.
i was in antioch.
the last seleucid king — a boy, a puppet —
was set aside.
the eagles went up.
rome reached the euphrates.
the east's great hellenistic kingdom,
founded by seleucus, alexander's general,
ended with a roman governor
and a tax roll.
three hundred years of seleucids —
gone with a proclamation.
the province of syria:
rome's frontier with parthia,
the edge of the world,
administered, taxed, garrisoned.

the conspiracy 63 bce rome i sat in the senate for the catiline debate — cicero's thunder, the night vote for death without trial — the conspiracy crushed and the precedent haunting the republic. catiline — bankrupt noble, sulla's veteran —
plotted to burn rome,
kill the consuls,
seize the state.
cicero — consul that year —
unmasked him.
the speeches: "quo usque tandem abutere, catilina,
patientia nostra?"
how long, catiline, will you abuse our patience?
i sat in the senate for the final debate.
caesar argued mercy. cato argued death.
the senate voted death — in the night,
without trial.
the conspirators were strangled.
catiline died fighting in etruria.
cicero was hailed father of his country.
the conspiracy failed.
but the precedent — execution without trial,
voted in the night —
would haunt the republic
to its grave.

pompey in the temple 63 bce judea i stood outside while pompey entered the holy of holies and found it empty — the conqueror puzzled by a god with no statue, touching nothing, understanding nothing. pompey took jerusalem —
and walked into the temple,
into the holy of holies,
where no man but the high priest could go,
and only once a year.
he looked around.
he found it empty —
no statue, no image,
just the emptiness the jews called god.
i stood outside with the crowd.
the priests were horrified.
pompey was — puzzled, they say.
he touched nothing. he took nothing.
he just looked, and left.
the holy of holies, empty.
the conqueror, confused.
some gods don't need statues.
some conquerors don't understand
what they've conquered.

the three-headed monster 60 bce rome i heard of the secret handshake — caesar, pompey, crassus carving up the republic — cato's three-headed monster with one appetite, and the laws suddenly not mattering. they met in secret —
caesar, pompey, crassus —
and shook hands on it:
the first triumvirate.
caesar got the consulship.
pompey got his veterans' land.
crassus got his tax contracts.
the republic got carved up
like a dinner.
i heard about it afterward.
cato called it the three-headed monster.
he was right.
three men, dividing rome
in a private bargain.
the republic still had its senate,
its assemblies, its laws —
and none of it mattered anymore.
the monster had three heads
and one appetite.

the poet of lesbia 60 bce rome i watched catullus love and lose lesbia — a hundred poems of passion and rage — the young veronese inventing the broken heart in latin, still beating. catullus — young, brilliant, veronese —
fell in love with a married woman,
clodia, he called her lesbia,
and wrote her a hundred poems:
passion, jealousy, tenderness, rage.
i knew them both, slightly.
she was dazzling. he was doomed.
"odi et amo" — i hate and i love.
he invented the broken heart in latin —
the modern lover, two thousand years early:
the kisses counted by the thousand,
the sparrow dead, the door slammed.
lesbia married, cheated, discarded him.
the poems remained.
the most personal poetry rome ever produced —
a young man's heart, dissected in verse,
still beating.

the daily news 59 bce rome i read the acta diurna on the forum boards — caesar's daily news, the world's first newspaper: senate debates, omens, gladiatorial results, and the consul deciding what counted as news. caesar — consul, innovator —
ordered the senate's proceedings
and the city's news posted daily
in the forum: the acta diurna.
i read it on the boards.
senate debates. trials. births, deaths.
gladiatorial results. omens.
the world's first daily newspaper —
chalk on whitened boards,
copied by scribes, carried to the provinces.
caesar meant it as transparency.
it was also propaganda —
the news, edited by the state.
two thousand years of journalism
started here, in the forum,
with the consul deciding
what counted as news.

the helvetii turn back 58 bce gaul i watched the helvetii migration turn back at the rhone — the start of caesar's eight-year conquest of gaul, a nation wanting land and getting war instead. the helvetii — a whole nation migrating,
hundreds of thousands, wagons and cattle —
tried to cross roman territory.
caesar stopped them at the rhone,
then harried them, trapped them,
and sent the survivors home.
i watched the migration turn back.
it was the start of it all —
the conquest of gaul,
eight years, a million dead,
caesar's ladder to power.
the helvetii just wanted new land.
they got a war instead.
nations migrating, empires expanding —
when they meet, one of them breaks.
this time it was the migrants.
next time — it would be rome's turn
to learn about migrations.

the stone theater 55 bce rome i sat in pompey's stone theater — forty thousand seats, rome's first permanent playhouse — built for drama, remembered for the assassination at its foot. pompey built it —
rome's first permanent theater,
stone seats for forty thousand,
a temple to venus on top
(to make it religious, technically —
theaters were still scandalous).
i sat in those seats.
the stone was cool. the view was perfect.
greek plays, roman spectacles —
theater, at last, respectable.
it would stand for centuries.
caesar would be murdered
at its foot — in the senate house
attached to it.
the theater of pompey:
built for plays,
remembered for an assassination.

caesar crosses the channel 55 bce britain i landed with caesar's legions on britain's white-cliffed beaches — painted warriors, chariots, a raid not a conquest — but the eagles had seen the island and would be back. two legions, eighty ships —
caesar crossed to britain,
the white cliffs, the unknown island
at the edge of the world.
i landed with them.
the britons met us at the beach —
painted warriors, chariots,
screaming, brave.
we fought our way ashore.
marched inland a little.
took hostages.
then sailed home before winter.
it was a raid, not a conquest —
a reconnaissance in force.
but rome had set foot on britain.
the island would never be quite unknown again.
the eagles had seen the white cliffs.
they would be back.

the poem of atoms 55 bce rome i read lucretius by lamplight — atoms and void in latin hexameters, the universe explained without the priests' permission — the poem that would seed the renaissance. lucretius wrote it —
de rerum natura, on the nature of things:
six books of hexameters
on atoms and void,
epicurus singing in latin.
i read it by lamplight.
the universe: atoms, falling,
swerving, combining —
no gods needed, no fear of death,
just matter and motion.
he was mad, they said.
he killed himself, they said.
the poem survived —
buried, copied, found again,
to seed the renaissance.
atoms and void, in verse.
the universe explained
without permission from the priests.

the second landing 54 bce britain i marched with caesar to the thames — the second british landing, hostages and tribute promised — a paper victory that was really a promise rome would keep. caesar went back —
five legions this time, two thousand cavalry,
a real invasion force —
marched to the thames,
fought the british king cassivellaunus,
took hostages, tribute, promises.
i marched to the thames.
the river was wide, the britons brave,
the chariots terrifying —
and then winter came,
and caesar sailed home.
britain was "conquered" —
tribute promised, never quite paid.
a paper victory.
but the pattern was set:
rome would come back,
again and again,
until the island was a province.
the second landing was a promise.
rome keeps its promises.

the heads at carrhae 53 bce mesopotamia i stood in the testudo at carrhae while parthian arrows never stopped — crassus dead, the eagles lost, rome learning the fear of the east it would never forget. crassus — the richest man in rome,
hungry for military glory —
led seven legions into parthia.
the parthians met them at carrhae:
horse-archers, circling, shooting —
the parthian shot —
and the cataphracts, armored cavalry,
charging when the arrows had done their work.
i was with the column.
the arrows never stopped.
all day. the romans formed the testudo,
died anyway.
crassus was killed — molten gold
poured down his throat, they said,
for his greed.
twenty thousand dead.
ten thousand captured.
the eagles lost.
rome learned fear of the east —
and never forgot it.

the siege of alesia 52 bce gaul i walked caesar's double walls at alesia — besieging vercingetorix within, besieged by a quarter-million without — the masterpiece siege that ended free gaul. vercingetorix — the arvernian chief
who united gaul —
was trapped at alesia.
caesar built a wall around him.
then the gauls sent a relief army —
a quarter of a million, they said —
and caesar built a second wall,
facing outward.
two walls. one roman army
between them.
i walked both walls.
the relief army came.
caesar rode the lines,
reinforcing where they broke,
and the gauls broke instead —
both armies, inside and out.
vercingetorix surrendered —
rode out in his armor,
laid his weapons at caesar's feet.
gaul surrendered with him.
the masterpiece siege:
a roman army besieging and besieged,
winning both ways.

the last pharaoh 51 bce egypt i watched eighteen-year-old cleopatra's first procession — nine languages, a bankrupt beautiful kingdom — the last pharaoh, and anything still possible. she was eighteen.
cleopatra — the last of the ptolemies,
greek by blood, egyptian by throne —
took power in a bankrupt, beautiful kingdom.
i saw her first procession.
she spoke nine languages.
she was not the beauty of legend —
the coins show a strong nose, a firm chin —
but the mind, the voice, the presence.
the last pharaoh.
three hundred years of ptolemies
ending in an eighteen-year-old girl
who would charm caesar,
ensnare antony,
and lose to octavian.
but that year, she was just eighteen,
and the throne was hers,
and the nile still flowed,
and anything was possible.

the republic holds its breath 50 bce rome i spent that breath-held winter in rome — the senate ordering caesar to disband, both sides arming — the republic's last pause before the swords decided. the senate ordered it:
caesar must disband his army,
lay down his command,
come to rome as a private citizen.
everyone knew what that meant:
trial, exile, ruin.
caesar's enemies had waited years.
both sides armed.
pompey was given command.
caesar counted his legions.
i was in rome that winter.
the city held its breath.
the forum buzzed.
men made wills, hid money,
chose sides.
the republic's last moment —
the pause before the fall.
everyone could feel it:
the law had run out.
what came next
would be decided by swords.

the die is cast 49 bce italy i stood on the far bank at dawn and watched caesar cross the rubicon with the thirteenth — one river, one legion, one sentence: the die is cast, the republic ended. he crossed it at dawn —
the rubicon, the little river
that marked the boundary:
no general brings an army into italy.
caesar brought one legion —
the thirteenth —
and with it, the end of the republic.
"alea iacta est," he said.
the die is cast.
i stood on the far bank
and watched him cross.
one river. one legion. one sentence.
the law became whatever caesar said.
the senate fled. pompey fled.
rome — the city, the people —
waited to see what the die would show.
it showed caesar.
it would show caesar
for the rest of his life.

the field of pharsalus 48 bce greece i walked the field of pharsalus after caesar's veterans destroyed pompey's larger army in an afternoon — the republic dying not with a law but a cavalry charge. pompey had the bigger army —
forty-five thousand, the senate's best,
the republic's last hope.
caesar had twenty-two thousand veterans.
it took an afternoon.
caesar's third line — held back, fresh —
smashed pompey's cavalry,
then rolled up the flank.
i walked the field afterward.
fifteen thousand dead.
pompey fled — to egypt, to death.
the republic died on that thessalian plain —
not with a law, but with a cavalry charge.
caesar wept, they say,
over the dead.
maybe.
the field was quiet.
the republic was over.
the empire had an afternoon's work
left to do.

fire in the harbor 48 bce egypt i watched the alexandrian harbor burn — the warehouses, the scrolls, how many no one agrees — the greatest library's losses unknowable because the records burned too. in the alexandrian war —
caesar trapped in the palace,
the egyptians attacking —
he ordered the ships in the harbor burned.
the fire spread.
the warehouses caught.
and the scrolls — how many?
forty thousand? four hundred thousand?
no one agrees. no one ever will.
i watched the smoke rise over the harbor.
the library — or its annex, or the warehouses —
burning.
what was lost? we'll never know.
that's the hell of it.
the greatest library in history,
and we argue about how much burned
because the records burned too.
fire in the harbor.
knowledge in the smoke.

the queen's gambit 47 bce egypt i was in the palace the season cleopatra was carried to caesar in a carpet — the queen's gambit, betting everything on one audience and winning a kingdom in a night. she had herself smuggled in —
rolled in a carpet, they say,
carried past the guards
into caesar's rooms.
cleopatra. twenty-one.
facing the most powerful man alive,
betting everything on one audience.
she won.
caesar restored her to the throne —
with her brother-husband dead in the nile —
and egypt was hers.
i was in the palace that season.
the gambit worked because she understood
what generals don't:
power is personal.
a carpet, a conversation, a night —
and a kingdom changed hands.
the queen's gambit:
the boldest move on the board,
played with herself as the piece.

the last cato 46 bce africa i stood outside cato's room at utica while he tore out his stitches — the stoic choosing death over caesar's pardon, becoming the republic's saint in blood. at utica, after thapsus —
the republic's last army beaten —
cato the younger, the stoic,
read plato's dialogue on the soul,
then fell on his sword.
he botched it. the wound wasn't mortal.
his friends found him, stitched him —
and he tore the stitches out with his hands
and died.
rather than live under caesar.
rather than accept the pardon
he knew would come.
i stood outside his room.
the last cato became the republic's saint —
the man who chose death over submission,
the stoic ideal in blood.
caesar, they say, was furious:
"you grudged me the chance to pardon you."
even in death, cato denied him.

the triumphs 46 bce rome i watched from a rooftop as caesar paraded four triumphs in a month — gaul, egypt, pontus, africa — the city drunk on glory, nobody saying some were wars on fellow romans. four triumphs. one month.
gaul. egypt. pontus. africa —
caesar paraded them all through rome,
the captives in chains of gold,
the placards, the spoils,
the sheer overwhelming theater of it.
i watched from a rooftop.
vercingetorix — walked in the gallic triumph,
then strangled in the tullianum.
the gold, the elephants, the giraffe —
rome had never seen a giraffe.
"veni, vidi, vici" —
for the pontic triumph, the whole campaign
in three words.
four triumphs in a month.
the city was drunk on glory.
nobody noticed — or nobody said —
that the triumphs were all
for wars against fellow romans too.

the year of confusion 45 bce rome i lived through the 445-day year of confusion — caesar's calendar reform buying sixteen centuries of order with ninety extra days of chaos. the calendar was broken —
the priests had mismanaged the intercalations,
the seasons drifted, harvests came in the wrong months.
caesar fixed it:
one year of 445 days —
the year of confusion —
then the julian calendar:
365 days, leap year every four.
i lived through the longest year.
ninety extra days, inserted, endless.
the farmers were confused.
the priests were furious.
everyone was tired.
but the calendar worked.
it worked for sixteen hundred years.
the year of confusion bought
sixteen centuries of order.
time itself, reorganized
by a dictator with an astronomer.

the ides of march 44 bce rome i was in the portico for the ides of march — twenty-three daggers, caesar falling at pompey's statue — the assassination that proved daggers are not arguments. twenty-three daggers.
in pompey's theater — the senate meeting there —
the conspirators closed around him.
casca struck first. then all of them.
"et tu, brute?" — maybe he said it. maybe not.
i was in the portico.
the screaming. the blood on the marble.
caesar fell at the foot of pompey's statue —
the irony the gods must have savored.
twenty-three wounds.
the dictator was dead.
the republic — the conspirators thought —
was saved.
it wasn't.
rome fell into the abyss:
the funeral, the riot, the proscriptions,
the wars.
the ides of march solved nothing.
it just proved that daggers
are not arguments.

the heir 44 bce rome i watched nineteen-year-old octavian arrive in rome with nothing but caesar's name — underestimated by all, organizing, outwaiting — the climb to the top of the world beginning. he was nineteen.
octavian — caesar's great-nephew,
named heir in the will —
arrived in rome with nothing
but a name.
i watched him.
thin. sickly. polite.
everyone underestimated him —
antony laughed at him.
he didn't laugh back. he organized.
raised an army on caesar's name.
outmaneuvered the senate.
outwaited antony.
nineteen years old,
and he began the climb
to the top of the world.
the heir had nothing but a name —
and a name, it turned out,
was everything.

the lists return 43 bce rome i walked past cicero's head and hands nailed to the rostra — the triumvirs' proscriptions taking the republic's voice, the lists returned worse than sulla's. the triumvirs — octavian, antony, lepidus —
met on an island and made their bargain:
proscriptions, again.
the lists went up in the forum.
cicero was on them.
antony wanted him — the philippics,
the insults, never forgiven.
they caught him at his villa.
he told the slaves to set the litter down.
he didn't run.
his hands — the hands that wrote the philippics —
were cut off and nailed to the rostra,
with his head.
i walked past them.
the republic's voice, displayed
on the speakers' platform.
the lists had returned.
this time, they took the best of rome
with them.

the last republicans 42 bce greece i walked the field at philippi after brutus fell on his sword — the republic's cause dying with the last men who believed daggers could save it. at philippi, two battles —
brutus and cassius, the liberators,
against octavian and antony.
cassius died first —
misreading the battle, ordering his freedman
to kill him.
brutus held on, fought again,
lost again —
and fell on his sword,
held by his officer.
i walked the field after the second battle.
the republic's cause died with them —
the last men who believed
the old system could be saved by daggers.
it couldn't.
the republic died at philippi
the way it had lived at the end:
by the sword, for the sword,
of the sword.
the empire was next.
there was nothing else left.

the woman's speech 42 bce rome i heard hortensia shame the triumvirs in the forum — the women's protest against war taxes working: no taxation without representation, seventeen centuries early. the triumvirs taxed rome's richest women —
fourteen hundred of them, for the war funds —
and the women marched on the forum.
hortensia — the orator's daughter —
spoke for them.
i was there. she was magnificent:
why should we pay for a war
we had no part in declaring?
no taxation without representation —
seventeen centuries early.
the triumvirs backed down.
reduced the list. the tax shrank.
one speech, by a woman,
in the forum, to the masters of rome —
and it worked.
hortensia's words survived —
quoted, admired, the only woman's speech
from the republic we still have.
she spoke. they listened.

the meeting at tarsus 41 bce egypt i watched from the riverbank as cleopatra sailed to antony in a golden barge dressed as venus — deliberate perfect theater, and the rough soldier never stood a chance. she came up the cydnus river —
cleopatra, to meet antony at tarsus —
in a golden barge, with purple sails,
dressed as venus, with cupids fanning her.
i watched from the riverbank.
the whole city turned out.
antony — the rough soldier, the triumvir —
was lost.
it was theater. deliberate, perfect theater.
she knew antony loved spectacle.
she gave him the greatest spectacle
of his life.
the meeting at tarsus:
the alliance that would shape the east,
the love affair that would end
at actium.
it started with a golden barge
and a queen dressed as a goddess.
antony never stood a chance.

the poetess 40 bce rome i knew sulpicia's circle — the only roman woman poet surviving in her own hand — six short poems of forbidden love, a lamp in a dark room for two thousand years. sulpicia —
the only roman woman
whose poetry survives in her own hand —
wrote of forbidden love:
her cerinthus, the secrecy,
the longing, the defiance.
six short poems.
that's all we have.
i knew her circle slightly —
the elegant, dangerous world
of messalla's patronage.
her voice is direct, unadorned —
no mythology, no posturing,
just a woman writing what she felt.
the only roman woman's voice to survive.
six poems, two thousand years.
read them, and she lives —
briefly, brightly,
the way a lamp lives
in a dark room.

the shepherds' prophecy 40 bce rome i heard virgil's fourth eclogue read — the mysterious child who would bring the golden age — the prophecy readers have wondered over ever since. virgil — young, mantuan, unknown —
wrote his fourth eclogue:
a prophecy of a child to be born,
who would bring a golden age,
the iron race ending, the golden returning.
i heard it read.
the audience wondered: whose child?
pollio's? octavian's? antony's?
christians would later claim it
prophesied christ.
maybe. probably not.
but the poem's hope was real:
after the civil wars,
the longing for a golden age
was the most roman feeling of all.
a child. a prophecy. a hope.
readers have wondered ever after.

the poet of the farm 38 bce italy i read virgil's eclogues while italy bled — shepherds singing against the proscriptions — poetry as refuge, writing down what the wars were stealing. virgil's eclogues —
ten pastoral poems, shepherds singing,
while italy bled from the civil wars.
i read them in those years.
the contrast was the point:
the green fields, the piping shepherds,
against the proscriptions, the confiscations,
virgil's own farm seized
and given to a veteran.
poetry as refuge.
the shepherds sang of love and loss
while the real world burned.
but the eclogues aren't escapism —
they're the dream italy was fighting for:
the farm, the peace, the song.
the poet of the farm
wrote what the wars were stealing.

herod takes jerusalem 37 bce judea i watched herod storm jerusalem with roman legions — the builder-king's thirty-three-year reign beginning in blood and siegeworks, magnificent and terrible together. with roman legions at his back —
sosius's army, siege engines, the works —
herod stormed jerusalem
and took the throne.
i watched the siege.
the city held for months.
when it fell, herod restrained the romans —
barely — from sacking it.
thirty-three years he would reign:
the builder-king, the tyrant,
the temple, the fortresses,
the murders of his own family.
herod took jerusalem with rome's help
and held it with rome's permission.
the great builder-king's reign began
in blood and siegeworks —
as all his years would be:
magnificent and terrible,
together.

the first long count 36 bce mexico i watched maya scribes carve the earliest known long count date at chiapa de corzo — time measured from creation, numbers as art, while rome fought its civil wars. at chiapa de corzo, maya scribes carved it —
a date in the long count:
7.16.3.2.13 —
the earliest known,
a day counted from the mythic creation,
millennia deep.
i watched the carver work.
the glyphs were precise, beautiful —
numbers as art, time as architecture.
the long count:
the maya measuring time
from a creation four thousand years past,
forward into a future
they believed they could calculate.
the first long count date.
time, carved in stone,
at chiapa de corzo —
while rome fought its civil wars,
the maya were counting the days
since the world began.

the donations of alexandria 34 bce egypt i watched antony hand kingdoms to cleopatra's children in alexandria's gymnasium — the donations rome called treason, the ceremony that lost him the war of words first. antony — in alexandria, playing king —
handed out kingdoms:
to cleopatra's children,
to cleopatra herself —
the east, parceled like party favors.
i was in the gymnasium for the ceremony.
the children in royal dress.
the crowds cheering.
antony, the roman triumvir,
giving away roman territory
to a foreign queen's children.
rome called it treason.
octavian made it the centerpiece
of his propaganda:
antony has gone native.
antony gives rome away.
the donations of alexandria:
the ceremony that lost antony
the war of words —
and then the war.

the war of words 32 bce rome i sat in the senate while octavian read antony's stolen will aloud — the war of words won with documents, the vote for war on cleopatra, the ships next. octavian played his masterstroke:
he seized antony's will —
kept with the vestals, illegally taken —
and read it aloud in the senate.
the bequests to cleopatra's children.
the wish to be buried in alexandria.
rome heard it all.
i sat in that senate session.
the outrage was real — and manufactured,
both at once.
octavian was a genius at this:
the war of words,
fought with documents.
the senate voted war —
not on antony, but on cleopatra.
a neat fiction.
the war of words was over.
the war of ships was next.

the battle of actium 31 bce greece i watched from the shore as agrippa smashed antony's fleet at actium — cleopatra's sails fleeing, antony following, the roman world decided: one ruler, not two. agrippa — octavian's admiral, the real genius —
smashed antony and cleopatra's fleet at actium.
i watched from the shore.
the great ships — antony's floating fortresses —
outmaneuvered by agrippa's lighter vessels.
cleopatra's squadron fled —
sixty ships, sails up —
and antony followed her,
abandoning his fleet, his army, everything.
the east fell that day.
the last hellenistic kingdom's fleet,
broken on the ambracian gulf.
actium decided the roman world:
one ruler, not two.
octavian. augustus-to-be.
the republic's last war
ended with a queen's sails
disappearing over the horizon.

the asp and the dagger 30 bce egypt i was in alexandria the week antony fell on his sword and cleopatra died by her own hand — the ptolemies ending by choice in a mausoleum, egypt becoming rome's. antony fell on his sword —
botched it, died slowly,
in cleopatra's arms.
cleopatra — the last pharaoh —
died by her own hand.
the asp, they say. or poison.
she chose the manner, the moment,
the dignity.
i was in alexandria that week.
the city mourned.
octavian took egypt —
the richest prize of all,
the granary of rome.
the asp and the dagger:
the end of the ptolemies,
the end of hellenistic egypt,
the end of the republic's wars.
three hundred years of queens and kings —
over in a week,
in a mausoleum,
by choice.

the song of the soil 29 bce italy i read the georgics as they appeared — virgil teaching war-exhausted rome to love the plow — propaganda so beautiful it became scripture, the plow's greatest poet. virgil's georgics —
four books on farming:
the crops, the trees, the cattle, the bees —
written for a rome exhausted by war,
teaching romans to love the plow
after a generation of swords.
i read them as they came out.
the poetry is magnificent —
the bees! the plague of the cattle! —
but the purpose was political:
go back to the land, romans.
farm. rebuild.
maecenas commissioned them.
augustus approved.
the song of the soil:
propaganda so beautiful
it became scripture.
two thousand years of farmers
have read virgil.
the plow never had a better poet.

the first citizen 27 bce rome i watched octavian become augustus — the republic given back in form, the power kept in fact — the empire's magnificent mask, worn for five hundred years. octavian became augustus.
the settlement: he gave back the republic —
in form —
and kept the power —
in fact.
princeps. first citizen.
not king, not dictator —
just the first among equals,
who happened to control the armies,
the treasury, the provinces.
i was in rome for the ceremony.
the modesty was magnificent.
the power was absolute.
the republic became an empire
wearing a mask —
and the mask was so well made
that people wore it for five hundred years.
the first citizen:
the most successful fiction
in political history.

the one-eyed queen 25 bce nubia i traveled the nubian frontier where the one-eyed kandake amanirenas bloodied rome and forced augustus to treat — one of the few peoples to face the empire and walk away free. amanirenas — the kandake, queen of kush,
one-eyed, iron-willed —
bloodied a roman army in the south,
raided into egypt,
took captives, took statues.
rome sent petronius.
the romans pushed south, took napata —
but the queen kept fighting,
guerrilla war in the desert,
and augustus — the master of the world —
made a treaty.
i traveled the frontier.
the treaty held.
kush kept its independence —
one of the few peoples
to face rome and walk away free.
the one-eyed queen:
she looked at the empire
and didn't blink.

the odes 23 bce rome i drank with horace in maecenas's circle — the philippi veteran turned poet of wine and friendship — and read the odes: seize the day, two thousand years young. horace published them —
the odes, songs of wine and friendship,
of the briefness of life:
carpe diem, seize the day.
i drank with him once — maecenas's circle,
the sabine farm, the good years.
he was witty, weary, wise:
a republican turned augustan,
who had fought at philippi
and learned to live with the peace.
"exegi monumentum" —
i have finished a monument
more lasting than bronze.
he was right.
the odes: the most perfect poems
in latin, maybe in any language —
and all about the small things:
wine, friends, the fleeting hour.
seize the day.
two thousand years later, we still do.

the temple of marble 20 bce judea i walked the courts of herod's rebuilt temple — white marble and gold like a snow-covered mountain — the tyrant's wonder standing ninety years before rome's fire. herod rebuilt it —
the jerusalem temple,
in white stone and gold,
so vast, so bright,
they said it looked like a snow-covered mountain
from a distance.
i walked its courts.
the marble. the gold plate.
the great doors.
a wonder of the age —
built by a tyrant, for a god
he half-feared.
the rabbis said: whoever has not seen
herod's temple has never seen a beautiful building.
it stood for ninety years.
the romans would burn it.
but that year, it gleamed —
white stone, gold, the mountain of god
rebuilt by a murderer
who wanted to be remembered.
he is.

the poet of empire 19 bce rome i mourned virgil at brundisium — the aeneid unfinished, the dying wish to burn it overruled by augustus — the poet of empire saved from himself by the emperor. virgil died at brundisium —
fifty-one, on his way home from greece,
the aeneid unfinished.
his dying wish: burn it.
the twelve books, the epic of rome,
the work of eleven years —
destroy it, he said. it's not finished.
augustus refused.
the emperor overruled the poet.
i mourned him.
the aeneid survived —
became rome's bible, the middle ages' guide,
dante's master.
the poet of empire,
who wanted his empire's poem burned.
augustus knew better than virgil
what rome needed.
or maybe he just knew
what emperors need.

the art of love 16 bce rome i read ovid's amores as rome devoured them — the young poet teaching the city to flirt in elegiac couplets — augustus wanting morals, ovid wanting fun. ovid published the amores —
love poems, witty, erotic, shameless:
how to seduce, how to keep a lover,
the whole art of it
in elegiac couplets.
i read them — everyone did.
rome was scandalized and delighted.
the young poet was suddenly famous —
the bad boy of augustan letters.
the art of love would come later —
the manual that got him exiled.
but the amores were the start:
ovid teaching rome to flirt
in perfect verse.
augustus wanted moral renewal.
ovid wanted fun.
only one of them
would win the century.

the square house 16 bce france i stood before the maison carree at nimes — the perfect temple to augustus's heirs — rome's architectural perfection exported to gaul, still standing. at nemausus — nimes, in southern gaul —
they raised it: the maison carree,
the square house,
a perfect roman temple
to augustus's grandsons, the heirs.
i stood before it.
the columns. the proportions.
vitruvius made stone —
every line right, every ratio singing.
two thousand years later, it still stands —
the best-preserved roman temple
in the world.
tourists photograph it.
architects study it.
the square house:
rome's perfection, exported to gaul,
in a town that was barely roman —
and the most roman thing
in the whole empire.

the general who mourned 12 bce rome i attended agrippa's funeral — augustus weeping for his right hand, the admiral of actium and builder of rome — the empire's engineer gone, nothing working quite as well after. agrippa died —
augustus's right hand,
the admiral of actium,
the builder of the pantheon,
the general who never lost.
i attended the funeral.
augustus mourned publicly —
the eulogy, the tears —
and privately, the empire
lost its builder.
agrippa had been the competence
behind the throne:
the fleets, the roads, the aqueducts,
the quiet man who got things done.
the general who mourned —
no, the general who was mourned.
augustus wept.
rome wept.
the empire's engineer was gone,
and nothing worked quite as well after.

the pepper ships 10 bce india i sailed the monsoon route to india's pepper coast — roman gold for black gold — the trade winds carrying flavor west and draining rome's coffers east. the monsoon did the work —
roman merchants learned the winds:
sail with the summer monsoon to india,
ride the winter monsoon home —
straight across the open sea,
no more hugging the coast.
i sailed that route.
the pepper coast — malabar —
black gold growing on vines,
worth its weight in roman silver.
gold for pepper.
rome's gold drained east —
pliny would complain about it —
but the tables of the rich
demanded spice.
the pepper ships:
the monsoon express,
the trade that moved gold one way
and flavor the other.
empires run on appetite.

the altar of peace 9 bce rome i attended the dedication of the ara pacis — augustus's marble altar of peace, the imperial family marching in stone — the beautiful promise everyone believed for a moment. augustus dedicated it —
the ara pacis, the altar of peace:
marble, carved with processions,
the imperial family, the gods,
the proof that the wars were over.
i attended the dedication.
the marble gleamed.
the carvings were perfect —
augustus, agrippa, the children,
all marching in stone
toward a peaceful future.
the altar of peace:
the empire's promise,
carved in marble.
the wars were over —
the civil wars, at least.
the frontier wars would continue
forever.
but the marble said peace,
and the marble was beautiful,
and for a moment,
everyone believed it.

the road of silk 8 bce central asia i followed a bale of silk partway west — a hundred middlemen, gold-weight prices at the tiber — the thread literally connecting the empires of china and rome. the silk came west —
from chang'an, through the gansu corridor,
across the pamirs, through parthia,
a hundred middlemen,
each taking a cut —
to rome.
i followed a bale partway.
by the time it reached the tiber,
it cost its weight in gold.
senators' wives shimmered in it.
moralists condemned it —
transparent, decadent, eastern.
everyone bought it anyway.
the road of silk:
the first global luxury trade,
china's secret (for a while),
rome's obsession.
two empires, connected
by a thread —
literally.

the iron of meroe 5 bce africa i stood among meroe's day-and-night iron furnaces — the birmingham of the ancient world — kushite industry smelting while europe still hammered bronze. at meroe, in kush,
the furnaces never cooled —
iron smelted day and night,
slag heaps like hills,
the birmingham of the ancient world.
i stood among the furnaces.
the heat. the smoke.
the workers, skilled as any in rome.
kushite iron armed kingdoms,
built tools, made wealth —
an african industrial center
two thousand years ago,
while europe hammered bronze.
the iron of meroe:
the furnaces history forgot,
slag heaps still there,
the smoke long gone.
industry isn't modern.
it's ancient.

amber for the romans 4 bce europe i walked part of the amber road from the baltic — fossilized sunlight traded south to roman workshops — the north's gold warming roman fingers. from the baltic shores —
where the sea throws up
the fossilized resin, golden, glowing —
amber traveled south:
trade routes, middlemen,
to roman workshops.
i walked part of the amber road.
the traders guarded their sources —
the baltic was a mystery,
the amber just appeared,
sunlight turned to jewelry.
roman ladies wore it.
physicians prescribed it.
the workshops carved it
into rings, amulets, figurines.
amber for the romans:
the north's gold,
traded for the south's silver,
sunlight from a cold sea
warming roman fingers.

the death of herod 4 bce judea i was in jericho when herod died in agony — the builder-king's kingdom split among his sons — marble and blood in equal measure, the family in ruins. the builder-king died —
herod, seventy, diseased, in agony,
they say, rotting alive —
and his kingdom was split
among his sons:
archelaus, antipas, philip.
i was in jericho at the end.
the court was a nest of fear.
the king had killed his wives, his sons —
now death took him,
slowly, horribly.
the great builder —
the temple, the fortresses, caesarea —
died as he lived:
in pain, in paranoia,
surrounded by the ruins
of his own family.
his kingdom split three ways.
rome approved.
the builder-king's legacy:
marble and blood,
in equal measure.

the tribes beyond the rhine 3 bce germany i crossed the rhine and talked with the germanic tribes — free men unimpressed by rome — watching the eagles from the far bank, unconquered, waiting. across the river, they watched —
the germanic tribes:
farmers, warriors,
free men in a way romans weren't,
gathered in their assemblies,
choosing their chiefs.
i crossed over once — trading, talking.
they were curious about rome.
they were not impressed.
the eagles stood on the far bank.
the tribes stood on theirs.
unconquered.
they would stay that way —
teutoburg was coming,
nine years off,
three legions in the forest.
the tribes beyond the rhine
watched rome's eagles
and waited.
they could afford to.

the forum of augustus 2 bce rome i walked the opening of augustus's forum — rome's heroes marching in marble porticoes, every statue leading to the emperor — history arranged as architecture. augustus opened it —
his new forum, his monument:
the temple of mars the avenger,
and the porticoes lined with statues —
rome's heroes, marching in marble:
aeneas, romulus, the great men,
all the way down to augustus himself.
i walked the opening procession.
the statues were perfect —
history as architecture,
the past enlisted
in the present's service.
the forum of augustus:
the empire's hall of fame,
carved in stone.
every hero led to augustus.
that was the point.
history, arranged
so the last statue
is the emperor.

the tin traders 2 bce britain i visited the cornish tin workings — the secret ingredient of bronze, traded across the channel for a thousand years — quiet miners arming civilizations that never knew their names. in cornwall, they dug it —
tin, the secret ingredient of bronze:
copper from cyprus, tin from britain,
alloyed into the metal of empires.
i visited the workings.
the miners — tough, taciturn —
traded the tin across the channel,
overland, to the mediterranean.
a thousand years of bronze
depended on cornish tin.
the phoenicians came for it.
the greeks wrote about the tin islands.
rome taxed it.
the tin traders:
the quiet miners at the end of the world,
supplying the metal
that armed civilizations
who never knew their names.

the green island 2 bce ireland i sailed to ireland — hillforts, gold torcs, chieftains trading across the sea — the green island rome wrote about and never touched, keeping its own counsel. beyond britain — the green island,
hibernia, never conquered,
never quite known.
i sailed there once.
the chieftains raised their hillforts —
great rings of earth and timber —
and traded gold across the sea:
torcs, brooches, the craftsmen's work,
fine as anything in rome.
ireland watched the empires
from its western edge:
too far, too wet, too troublesome.
the romans wrote about it,
never went.
the green island:
hillforts, gold, poets —
a civilization rome never touched,
keeping its own counsel
at the edge of the map.

the ships of the north 1 bce scandinavia i watched fjord boat-builders rivet the clinker hull — the flexible ship that would one day carry vikings everywhere — the future's technology built for modest needs. in the fjords, they perfected it —
the clinker hull:
overlapping planks, riveted,
flexible, strong,
the ship that could ride the north sea.
i watched the boat-builders work.
the adzes. the rivets.
the hull taking shape —
a vessel that flexed with the waves
instead of fighting them.
the ships of the north:
one day they would carry vikings
to england, to vinland, to constantinople.
but that year, they were just fishing boats,
trading boats —
the technology of the future,
built for the present's modest needs.
the fjords kept their secret:
the best ships in the world,
waiting for their moment.

the mines of spain 1 bce spain i descended a spanish silver mine — water wheels, lamplight, dying slaves — the engineering genius and human cost that fed the empire's coins. in iberia, the romans drained them —
the silver mines, the deepest in the world:
water wheels, archimedes' screws,
galleries going down and down.
i descended one.
the dark. the noise.
the slaves — thousands —
working by lamplight, dying young.
the silver fed the empire's coins —
the denarii, the trade, the legions' pay.
spain's mountains paid for rome's peace.
the mines of spain:
engineering genius,
human cost,
the equation of empire.
the water wheels turned.
the silver flowed.
the slaves died.
rome counted the coins.

the breadbasket 1 bce north africa i walked numidia's endless wheat harvest — the breadbasket feeding rome's million mouths — empire as logistics: the grain arriving every year or the city starving. numidia's fields —
wheat, endless wheat,
the granaries of africa —
fed rome.
i walked the harvest.
the grain ships loaded at the ports,
the grain dole's supply,
the city's daily bread
grown under an african sun.
the breadbasket:
rome ate because africa reaped.
a million mouths in the capital,
fed by provinces.
the granaries never slept.
the ships never stopped.
empire is logistics:
the wheat has to arrive,
every year, or the city starves.
it arrived.

the grain fleet 1 bce egypt i sailed with the alexandrian grain fleet — a hundred wheat-heavy hulls, rome's unarmed lifeline — the empire eating because egypt reaped, every summer without fail. every summer, they sailed —
the great grain ships from alexandria,
heavy with egyptian wheat,
to ostia, to rome.
i sailed with the fleet once.
the huge hulls, the steady winds,
the cargo that mattered more
than gold.
rome ate because egypt reaped.
a bad nile — a low flood —
meant hunger in the subura,
riots, emperors nervous.
the grain fleet:
the empire's lifeline,
a hundred ships of wheat,
every summer, without fail.
the most important navy in the world
carried no weapons —
just bread.

the city in the rock 1 bce arabia i stood before petra's treasury at dawn — the facade cut from living cliff, glowing rose and gold — the desert's masterpiece, carved top-down with no mistakes allowed. the nabataeans carved it —
petra, the rose-red city:
the treasury, the great facade,
cut from the living cliff,
columns, pediments, gods —
all rock, all one piece.
i stood before the treasury at dawn.
the sun hit the facade
and the whole cliff glowed —
rose, gold, red.
a temple cut from a mountain.
the carvers worked from the top down —
one mistake, and the face was ruined.
no mistakes.
the city in the rock:
the desert's masterpiece,
the caravan kings' capital,
a facade so perfect
it looks like a dream
the cliff had.

the scrolls by the sea 1 bce judea i visited the qumran brotherhood copying scriptures in desert silence — the scrolls hidden in jars, waiting two thousand years for a shepherd boy's lost goat. by the dead sea, they waited —
the brotherhood at qumran,
strict, pure, copying the scriptures
in the desert caves.
i visited the settlement.
the scribes worked in silence.
the scrolls piled up —
every book of the law,
copies for a future
they believed was ending.
they waited for the end of days —
the war of the sons of light
against the sons of darkness.
the end didn't come.
the romans did.
but the scrolls survived —
hidden in jars, in caves,
two thousand years,
waiting for a shepherd boy
and a lost goat.

the breath that made glass 1 bce syria i watched a sidon craftsman blow the first glass bubble — thin as soap, any shape — the breath that invented the material the modern world is made of. in sidon, they discovered it —
the blowpipe:
gather the molten glass on the pipe,
blow, and the bubble grows —
thin as a soap bubble,
any shape you want.
i watched a craftsman work.
the breath. the turning.
the glass swelling like a lung.
before: cast glass, precious, rare.
after: blown glass, cheap, everywhere —
cups, bottles, windows,
the transparent revolution.
the breath that made glass:
a syrian craftsman's lungs,
two thousand years ago,
inventing the material
the modern world is made of.

athens the university 1 bce greece i walked athens' shaded schools — the empire's college town, where roman nobles' sons took notes from the conquered — power in rome, mind in athens, landlords happy. the city of pericles —
of the parthenon, the assembly, the empire —
was now a college town.
i walked its streets.
the schools were everywhere:
academy, lyceum, stoa, garden —
philosophers arguing in the shade,
roman nobles' sons
taking notes.
athens the university:
the empire's school,
where the conquerors sent their children
to learn from the conquered.
the power had moved to rome.
the mind stayed in athens.
it was a fair trade —
the romans got culture,
the athenians got students.
everyone was happy.
especially the landlords.

the villas of the bay 1 bce italy i visited a bay of naples villa — marble, fishponds, mosaic floors — rome's glittering playground where everyone pretended the republic's virtues still mattered. around the bay of naples —
baiae, puteoli, the golden shore —
the rich built their villas:
marble, mosaics, fishponds,
fishing from mosaic floors.
i visited one.
the luxury was obscene —
and beautiful.
the bay glittered.
the vesuvius loomed —
nobody worried.
the villas of the bay:
rome's playground,
where senators schemed,
poets wrote,
and everyone pretended
the republic's virtues
still mattered.
they didn't.
but the mosaics were lovely.

the concrete revolution 1 bce rome i watched roman builders mix pozzolana concrete — setting hard as stone, even underwater — the moldable material that poured the empire into shapes still standing. they mixed it —
volcanic ash from pozzuoli,
lime, water, aggregate —
and it set hard as stone.
underwater, even.
i watched the builders work.
the pantheon's dome — to come —
the harbors, the baths,
all concrete.
the concrete revolution:
rome's real secret weapon.
not the legions — the material.
cheap, strong, moldable,
it built the empire's infrastructure:
the domes, the vaults, the ports.
stone is carved.
concrete is poured.
rome poured its empire
into molds —
and the molds are still standing.

the baths 1 bce rome i sweated in rome's public baths — senators and slaves side by side in the steam — the most democratic institution in the empire, rome at its most human. they steamed across the city —
the public bathhouses:
the caldarium, the tepidarium, the frigidarium,
hot, warm, cold —
and everyone went.
i bathed with them.
senators and slaves,
side by side, sweating —
the most democratic institution in rome.
the baths:
hygiene, gossip, politics,
business done in the steam.
agrippa built the first great ones.
everyone copied him.
a civilization that bathes together —
clean, social, naked, equal
in the hot water.
the baths were rome
at its most human.

the sauce of empire 1 bce rome i visited a garum factory — fish, salt, and time fermented into rome's indispensable sauce — the flavor of empire, salty and utterly addictive from britain to syria. the factories lined the coasts —
fish, salt, time:
garum, the pungent sauce,
fermented in vats,
shipped in amphorae
across the empire.
i visited a factory.
the smell — indescribable.
the product — indispensable.
every roman table demanded it.
the sauce of empire:
the flavor of rome,
made from fish guts and salt,
worth a fortune,
tasted from britain to syria.
empires have flavors.
rome tasted like garum —
salty, strong, acquired,
and utterly addictive.

the one-wheeled cart 1 bce china i pushed a han wheelbarrow — one wheel carrying a mule's load — the quiet revolution no one writes epics about, moving the empire's harvests one wheel at a time. the farmers pushed it —
one wheel, two handles, a bed:
the wheelbarrow,
carrying what a mule would,
guided by a man.
i pushed one.
the balance — the wheel takes the weight,
the man just steers.
simple. brilliant.
the one-wheeled cart:
china's quiet revolution,
centuries before europe.
a farmer, a wheel, a load —
the physics of it perfect.
no one writes epics
about wheelbarrows.
but the harvests moved,
the bricks moved,
the empire moved —
one wheel at a time.

the lodestone spoon 1 bce china i watched a han diviner's lodestone spoon tremble south on its bronze plate — the first compass, pointing for ghosts a thousand years before it pointed for sailors. the diviners carved it —
a spoon of lodestone, magnetic stone,
balanced on a bronze plate:
the spoon's handle always pointed south.
i watched a diviner use it.
not for navigation — for feng shui,
for aligning the mystical,
the spoon trembling to the south.
the lodestone spoon:
the first compass,
pointing south for diviners
a thousand years before sailors.
the south-pointer.
the needle's ancestor.
a spoon that knew the way —
even if its makers
only asked it about ghosts.

the steel of the south 1 bce india i watched an indian smith draw water-marked wootz steel from the crucible — the metal of damascus blades — the south's gift to the swords of empires. in the south, they forged it —
wootz steel:
the crucible metal,
water-marked, rippled,
the steel swords would be named for —
damascus, they called it later.
i watched a smith work.
