the suffering of eastern christians.
god wills it — take the cross, and your sins are forgiven.
i was at the edge of that crowd,
and i felt it go through them like a current —
men weeping, men shouting, cutting crosses from their cloaks
and sewing them on.
deus vult. god wills it.
within a year, armies were marching east —
princes, knights, peasants, all of them —
and nothing in the mediterranean world
would ever be the same.
one sermon. two centuries of war.

the people's crusade 1096 ce rhineland peasant armies march east for the crusade and turn first on the rhineland's jewish communities — the crusade's first victims, murdered by christians in germany before the turks destroy the column. before the princes marched, the peasants did —
tens of thousands of them, following a preacher called peter the hermit,
barefoot, starving, certain god would part the seas for them.
i walked with that column through the rhineland,
and i watched what certainty does to the certain:
at speyer, at worms, at mainz,
they turned on the jewish communities —
god's first crusade, against the neighbors —
and the blood ran in the streets.
the chronicles call them martyrs, the jews who died
rather than convert; i call them murdered.
the people's crusade never reached jerusalem —
the turks slaughtered them in anatolia, to a man, almost.
but the rhineland remembered:
the crusade's first victims were not muslims.
they were jews, killed by christians, in germany.

antioch taken 1098 ce syria after an eight-month siege of starvation, crusaders storm antioch through a traitor's gate — then, besieged in turn, break out behind the holy lance and march on jerusalem. eight months.
eight months outside the walls of antioch —
starving, freezing, eating their horses, eating worse —
and then a traitor opened a tower gate in the night,
and the crusaders poured in like water through a crack.
i walked the streets the morning after:
the slaughter was total, the chronicles don't exaggerate this time —
turks, armenians, anyone in the way —
and the crusaders, half-mad with hunger and triumph,
looting the great city they'd dreamed of for a year.
then kerbogha's relief army arrived,
and the starving besiegers became the besieged —
until the holy lance was "found,"
and they marched out barefoot and broke the turks.
antioch taken.
jerusalem next.
god, they were sure, was marching with them.

the charter of liberties 1100 ce england henry i seizes the throne and issues the charter of liberties — promises made for politics, written down, and remembered a century later at runnymede. william rufus died in the new forest —
an arrow, a hunting accident, nobody's fault officially —
and his brother henry moved fast:
rode for winchester, seized the treasury,
got himself crowned in three days.
i was at westminster for the coronation,
and henry did the cleverest thing a usurper can do:
he promised.
the charter of liberties — read aloud, nailed up, sworn:
no more arbitrary taxes, no more seizing the church's lands,
the old laws of edward the confessor restored.
it was politics, pure politics —
buy the barons, buy the church, buy the crown.
but the promises were written down,
and written promises have a way of outliving
the men who make them.
a century later, at runnymede,
the barons would remember henry's charter —
and ask for it back, with interest.

the crusader kingdom 1100 ce jerusalem baldwin is crowned king in bethlehem — the latin kingdom of jerusalem begins, a frankish state in the levant that will build great castles and last a century. baldwin was crowned in bethlehem —
not in jerusalem (the patriarch quarreled over that),
but in the town of christ's birth,
king of a kingdom that shouldn't have existed:
the latin kingdom of jerusalem,
a frankish state in the levant,
held by a few thousand knights
surrounded by a sea of enemies.
i stood in the church of the nativity that christmas morning
and watched a french adventurer become an eastern king —
and the thing that struck me was the audacity of it:
they meant to stay.
they built castles — krak des chevaliers, the great ones —
they married, they traded, they learned arabic,
they became something neither frankish nor arab.
outremer. the land beyond the sea.
it would last a hundred years.
for a while, it shone.

acre falls to the franks 1104 ce holy land crusaders take the great port of acre — not a trophy but a lifeline, the window to the sea through which the crusader kingdom will survive for eighty years. acre was the prize —
the great port, the deep harbor,
the door through which everything came:
reinforcements, pilgrims, grain, gold.
i watched the siege from the hills:
baldwin's engines battering the walls,
the genoese fleet blockading the harbor,
the garrison holding on, month after month,
until the terms were made and the city opened its gates.
the crusaders kept their word, this time —
the inhabitants lived, the trade continued —
because acre wasn't a trophy, it was a lifeline.
without acre, no kingdom.
with it, the franks had their window to the sea,
and through that window, for the next eighty years,
would come everything outremer needed to survive.

tinchebray 1106 ce england henry i crushes his brother robert at tinchebray, reuniting england and normandy — and keeps his brother caged in cardiff castle for twenty-eight years. two brothers, one battlefield —
henry, king of england, against robert, duke of normandy,
the conqueror's sons, settling it the norman way.
i stood on the hill at tinchebray and watched
henry's dismounted knights grind robert's cavalry down —
the new warfare beating the old,
and by evening robert was a prisoner,
and normandy was henry's again.
henry kept his brother locked up for twenty-eight years —
cardiff castle, comfortable, hopeless —
until robert died, still a prisoner, at eighty.
the conqueror's lands, reunited under one son.
the other son, caged for life.
family business, norman style:
no hard feelings, just a lifetime in a tower.

the fat king 1108 ce france louis vi takes the french throne and begins taming his robber-barons castle by castle — the fat fighting king who makes the french crown mean something beyond paris. louis the fat —
they called him that because he was,
enormously, cripplingly fat by the end,
carried in a litter because he couldn't ride —
but in 1108 he was a young king with a mission:
tame the barons.
i rode with his men on one of the early campaigns,
against some robber-lord in his castle outside paris —
and louis was there in the mud with them,
a fighting king, even then too heavy for his horse.
he spent his reign grinding down the petty tyrants
of the ile-de-france, castle by castle,
making the french crown mean something
beyond the walls of paris.
the fat man built the kingdom
that philip augustus would make great.
never underestimate a king
who does his own fighting.

the painter emperor 1110 ce china huizong holds the song throne — a genius painter and calligrapher, a disaster as emperor — ruling the loveliest court on earth right up to the jurchen catastrophe. huizong should never have been emperor.
he was an artist — a genius with a brush,
birds, flowers, rocks, calligraphy like no one before or since —
and the throne was the worst thing that ever happened to him.
i visited his court at kaifeng:
the imperial painting academy, the catalogues of antiquities,
the garden he'd built with rocks shipped from a thousand miles —
while the army rotted, the treasury bled,
and the jurchen watched from the north like wolves.
he fiddled. they came.
in 1127 they'd take the capital and drag him north in a cage.
but the paintings —
the paintings are still perfect.
history's most beautiful failure,
ruling the loveliest court on earth
right up to the edge of the cliff.

the builder king 1113 ce cambodia suryavarman ii seizes the khmer throne and begins the building program that will raise angkor wat — the largest religious monument on earth, a usurper's apology in stone. suryavarman took the khmer throne by force —
killed his great-uncle for it, the inscriptions admit —
and then spent his reign building like a man
trying to apologize to the gods in stone.
i walked the causeways of angkor that decade,
past the reservoirs big enough to be called seas,
the temples rising in the jungle heat —
and the king's architects were already dreaming
the biggest one:
angkor wat.
five towers like lotus buds.
a moat like an ocean.
the largest religious monument on earth,
built for vishnu by a usurper
who wanted heaven to forget how he got the throne.
heaven, i suspect, was impressed anyway.

clairvaux 1115 ce france bernard founds clairvaux with twelve monks — the white monks of citeaux, stripped to stone and silence, whose mother house will plant three hundred daughters across europe. bernard was twenty-five —
a nobleman's son who'd talked his whole family into the monastery —
and the abbot sent him out with twelve monks
to found a new house in a valley called the valley of wormwood.
clairvaux. the valley of light, he renamed it.
i visited in the early years:
no ornament, no color, stone and silence,
the white monks of citeaux —
work, prayer, work, prayer,
the cistercian rule stripped to the bone.
and bernard preached.
kings listened. popes listened.
he would launch a crusade with a sermon
and condemn a philosopher with a letter.
it started with thirteen men in a wormwood valley.
within his lifetime, clairvaux would mother
three hundred daughter houses across europe.

the poor knights 1118 ce jerusalem nine knights vow to guard the pilgrim roads — the poor knights of christ, who will become the templars, bankers to kings, until a king burns them for their gold. nine knights.
that's how it started — nine french knights,
led by hugh of payns,
taking vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience
before the patriarch of jerusalem,
and promising to guard the pilgrim roads
against the bandits who infested them.
i met them in their first headquarters —
a wing of the royal palace, on the temple mount,
in the place they called solomon's temple —
poor men, patched cloaks, one horse between two of them, they said.
the poor knights of christ.
within a century they'd be the templars:
bankers to kings, warriors in white mantles,
the most feared and richest order in christendom —
until a french king burned their grand master
for their gold.
but it started with nine men and a vow.

the field of blood 1119 ce holy land ilghazi annihilates the army of antioch at the field of blood — the crusader states reel, and the franks learn that overconfidence in the east is suicide. roger of salerno rode out confident —
the prince of antioch, with his knights in their pride —
and ilghazi, the old turkish warlord, was waiting
with every horseman he could gather.
ager sanguinis. the field of blood.
i walked it the day after:
the antiochene army annihilated, roger dead,
the field — they say — running red to the ankles.
the crusader states reeled.
antioch itself nearly fell; only baldwin's desperate march
saved it.
the franks learned the lesson that day
and kept relearning it for a century:
in the east, overconfidence is a kind of suicide,
and the turks are always, always waiting.

the white ship 1120 ce england the white ship sinks off barfleur with henry i's heir and three hundred souls — england's succession drowns in the channel, and nineteen years of civil war begin with one drunken race. the white ship was the finest vessel in the norman fleet —
new, fast, crewed by fifty oarsmen —
and william adelin, henry i's only legitimate son,
the heir to england and normandy,
sailed on her from barfleur that november night,
drunk, racing the king's own ship.
i was on the quay. i watched her leave.
she struck a rock at the harbor mouth —
the sober say the crew was drunk, the passengers drunker —
and she went down with three hundred souls.
one man survived: a butcher from rouen,
clinging to wreckage in the cold black water.
england's succession drowned that night in the channel.
henry would never get another legitimate son.
nineteen years of civil war — the anarchy —
started with one drunken race in the dark.

the concordat of worms 1122 ce germany at worms, pope and emperor compromise on the appointment of bishops — ending fifty years of investiture war with a settlement that teaches bishops to serve two masters. fifty years of war over who appoints bishops —
the investiture contest, pope against emperor,
excommunications, antipopes, armies —
and it ended at worms with a compromise,
because that's how these things always end.
i was there for the ceremony:
the emperor renounces investiture with ring and staff,
the pope concedes the emperor's presence at elections,
everyone bows, everyone saves face.
pope and emperor split the difference on bishops.
it wasn't peace — they'd be at each other's throats again
within a generation —
but it was a settlement,
and christendom exhaled.
the great lesson of worms:
when god and caesar both claim the same bishop,
the bishop learns to serve two masters
and charge them both.

the almohad spark 1124 ce north africa ibn tumart proclaims himself mahdi in the atlas mountains — the almohad spark, a stern reform movement that will topple the almoravids and rule from spain to tunisia. in the high atlas, a berber scholar named ibn tumart
looked at the almoravid empire — rich, lax, worldly —
and pronounced it corrupt.
he called himself the mahdi, the guided one,
and preached a stern, pure, unitarian islam:
the almohads, the unitarians.
i heard him preach once, in a mountain village —
a small man with a huge certainty,
and the tribes were listening.
the almoravids laughed. then they sent armies.
then they stopped laughing.
within twenty years the almohads would take marrakesh,
topple the empire that had toppled ghana,
and rule from spain to tunisia —
the strictest, most learned, most formidable power
the medieval maghreb ever saw.
all from one man's sermon in the mountains.

the jingkang shame 1126 ce china jurchen jin sack kaifeng and drag two emperors north in chains — the jingkang shame, the fall of northern china and the flight of the song across the yangtze. the jurchen came down like winter —
the jin, horsemen from the northern forests,
and kaifeng, the greatest city on earth,
a million people, the clock towers, the restaurants,
the painted scrolls of its teeming life —
fell.
i was in the city during the siege:
the hunger, the cold, the emperor abdicating in panic,
his son abdicating after him,
and then the gates opened,
and the jin took them both —
two emperors, the whole court, the artisans, the musicians,
marched north in chains through the snow.
the jingkang shame.
the north of china, lost.
the song court fled south across the yangtze,
and china would never be whole again
in the song's lifetime.

the southern song 1127 ce china gaozong proclaims the southern song at hangzhou — the court in exile that becomes the richest, most cultured, most brilliant china there ever was, blooming on the memory of the lost north. gaozong proclaimed it at hangzhou —
the southern song, the court in exile,
half an empire, clinging to the south of the yangtze —
and then did the strangest thing:
he made it thrive.
i walked hangzhou in those early years —
the west lake, the teahouses, the markets
stacked with porcelain and silk and books —
and the refugees had brought everything with them:
the painters, the poets, the printing shops,
the whole civilization, transplanted south,
blooming in exile like a cutting taken in winter.
china split. commerce booming.
the southern song would be the richest, most cultured,
most technologically brilliant china there ever was —
all of it built on the memory of the north they'd lost.

roger crowned 1130 ce sicily roger ii is crowned king of sicily — norman, arab, and greek in one trilingual court, proof that three faiths could share a throne room under a clever king. roger ii was crowned at palermo on christmas day —
king of sicily, and his court was the strangest in europe:
norman knights, arab administrators, greek scholars,
all of them serving one king in three languages.
i attended the coronation —
the crown itself was byzantine work,
the robes embroidered with arabic lions and camels,
the ceremony half latin, half greek.
roger's sicily was the mediterranean in miniature:
muslim geographers mapping the world for a christian king,
arab poets in the palace, norman law in the courts.
it worked. for a while, gloriously, it worked —
proof that the three faiths could share one throne room,
if the man on the throne was clever enough.
roger was clever enough.
his successors, less so.

hildegard's visions 1132 ce germany hildegard of bingen begins writing her visions — abbess, composer, healer, and prophet, whose scivias makes her the most famous woman in germany, advising emperors and scolding popes. she was thirty-four when she started writing them down —
the visions she'd had since she was a child:
light, wheels within wheels, the cosmos as a living body,
god speaking through images she could barely describe.
hildegard of bingen.
i visited her at disibodenberg —
abbess, composer, healer, prophet —
and she showed me the pages:
the scivias, "know the ways,"
theology as vision, medicine as cosmology,
music she'd composed for her nuns to sing.
the church didn't know what to do with her —
a woman, unlettered in latin, instructing bishops —
so they let the pope examine her, and he approved,
and she became the most famous woman in germany:
advising emperors, scolding popes,
healing with herbs and hearing the music of the spheres.

the anarchy begins 1135 ce england henry i dies, stephen seizes the throne from matilda, and nineteen years of civil war — the anarchy — begin: castles sprouting, barons robbing, christ and his saints asleep. henry i died of a surfeit of lampreys —
that's what the chronicles say, and i believe them;
the man loved his eels —
and he'd made his barons swear to his daughter matilda,
but oaths are cheap when a crown is empty.
stephen of blois moved first: seized the treasury, got crowned,
and matilda — henry's daughter, the empress —
came back from anjou with an army and a claim.
i lived through those nineteen years —
the anarchy, they called it, and the chronicles say
christ and his saints slept through it:
castles sprouting like mushrooms, barons robbing everyone,
the coinage debased, the countryside bled white.
two cousins, one crown, nineteen years of war —
until they were both exhausted,
and made the peace that gave england the plantagenets.

eleanor's dowry 1137 ce france fifteen-year-old eleanor inherits aquitaine — the richest prize in europe — and marries the heir of france: the beginning of the most powerful woman of the middle ages. she was fifteen —
eleanor of aquitaine, duchess in her own right,
heir to the richest, most cultured land in europe:
aquitaine, poitou, the troubadours, the wine, the courts of love —
and her father died on pilgrimage,
leaving her the greatest prize in christendom.
i saw her at bordeaux that summer —
a girl, really, but with eyes that had already learned to measure men —
married within weeks to louis, the french king's heir,
aquitaine folded into france like a jewel into a crown.
she would be queen of france, then queen of england,
mother of kings, grandmother of emperors —
the most powerful woman of the middle ages —
and it all started with a fifteen-year-old orphan
and the richest dowry in europe.

ourique 1139 ce portugal afonso henriques wins at ourique and is hailed portugal's first king — legend says christ appeared in the sky; the kingdom that followed lasted eight hundred years. they say he saw christ on the cross in the sky before the battle —
afonso henriques, the young count of portugal,
outnumbered, facing the almoravid host at ourique —
and won.
i wasn't close enough to see visions,
but i saw the aftermath: the muslim army broken,
the field afonso's,
and his men lifting him on their shields
and hailing him king —
the first king of portugal.
ourique is half legend now —
five moorish kings defeated, the miracle in the sky —
but the kingdom was real enough,
and it lasted.
eight hundred years of portugal
started on a battlefield in the alentejo,
with a young count, a vision,
and men shouting him king.

the lover condemned 1140 ce france abelard's teachings are condemned at sens — the brilliant logician broken by bernard, ending the middle ages' most famous love story in silence and separate cloisters. they condemned him at sens —
peter abelard, the brightest mind in paris,
the logician who'd dared to apply reason to the mysteries of faith —
and bernard of clairvaux was his prosecutor,
the mystic against the logician,
and the mystic won.
i knew abelard in his better days —
brilliant, arrogant, the rock star of the schools,
until the affair with heloise:
the secret marriage, the uncle's revenge, the castration,
the two of them ending in separate cloisters,
writing the most famous love letters of the middle ages.
at sens, broken in body, he was broken in reputation too —
his teachings condemned, his books burned.
philosophy's most famous lover fell silent.
heloise outlived him by twenty years,
and asked to be buried in his grave.

the first qur'an in latin 1143 ce spain robert of ketton translates the qur'an into latin at toledo — the first time europe reads islam in its own tongue, beginning eight centuries of argument and occasional understanding. at toledo, in the translation workshops,
robert of ketton — an englishman in spain —
sat down with the qur'an and rendered it into latin:
the first time europe could read islam in its own tongue.
i watched him work —
word by word, the arabic giving up its meanings,
the latin stretching to hold them —
and peter the venerable, the great abbot of cluny,
had commissioned it: know the enemy, he'd said,
refute him properly.
it wasn't friendly. it wasn't fair, in places.
but it was a beginning:
for the first time, a christian scholar in paris
could open the muslim scripture and read.
eight centuries of argument, misunderstanding, and occasional understanding —
all starting with one englishman's latin,
in a toledo workshop, in 1143.

edessa falls 1144 ce holy land zengi takes edessa, the first crusader state — the shock that launches the second crusade, all because one count left his city unguarded. edessa was the first crusader state —
the county, far to the east, exposed, half-armenian —
and zengi, the atabeg of mosul, had been watching it for years,
waiting for its count to leave.
i was in the city when the siege engines came up —
the walls were strong, but the count was away,
and zengi's miners brought a tower down,
and then the slaughter.
the chronicles say the streets ran with blood;
the chronicles, this time, were right.
when the news reached europe,
the shock was electric:
the first crusader state, fallen.
the pope preached a new crusade.
kings took the cross.
all because one count left his city unguarded,
and one turkish warlord didn't miss.

bernard preaches war 1146 ce france bernard of clairvaux preaches the second crusade at vezelay — kings take the cross on the spot, a hundred thousand march east, and most of them die. vezelay, easter —
a field outside the abbey, a crowd too big for any church,
and bernard of clairvaux preaching the second crusade.
i was in that crowd, and i have never heard preaching like it:
the man was on fire, literally shaking,
holding up the pope's letter, crying out for jerusalem,
and the kings — louis of france, conrad of germany —
taking the cross on the spot,
the nobles tearing their cloaks for crosses.
they say the supply of cloth crosses ran out,
and bernard threw his own habit to the crowd
to be torn into more.
it worked too well.
a hundred thousand marched east —
and died, most of them, in anatolia and at damascus.
the greatest preacher of the age,
and his greatest sermon was a catastrophe.

damascus holds 1148 ce holy land the second crusade breaks against damascus's walls — four days of quarrel and thirst, then humiliating retreat — while a young kurdish officer named saladin watches and learns. they'd marched across anatolia dying of hunger and turkish arrows,
the two kings, louis and conrad, with their broken armies —
and at jerusalem the crusader lords talked them into attacking damascus:
rich, they said. weak, they said. easy, they said.
it wasn't.
i watched from the mount of olives country as the siege collapsed —
four days, the water cut off, the muslim relief armies closing in,
the crusader camps quarreling over who'd get which palace
before a single wall had fallen —
and then the retreat, the humiliation,
kings slinking home to europe with nothing.
the second crusade died at damascus.
the muslims learned the franks could be beaten.
and in damascus, a young kurdish officer named saladin
was watching, and learning, and waiting.

angkor wat rises 1150 ce cambodia suryavarman's builders raise angkor wat — five lotus towers, half a mile of carved galleries, the largest religious monument on earth, rising out of the jungle heat. in the jungle heat, they were raising a mountain —
angkor wat, suryavarman's temple to vishnu:
five lotus towers, a moat a mile around,
galleries of carved stone running for half a mile,
the churning of the ocean of milk,
heaven and hell and every god in between.
i walked the causeway at dawn, past the stone lions,
and the scale of it stopped my breath:
the largest religious monument on earth,
built by a king who'd murdered his way to the throne
and was building his way to forgiveness.
thousands of laborers. decades of work.
sandstone blocks fitted without mortar,
carvings so fine you could read the jewelry.
the jungle would take it back, in time.
but stone remembers longer than jungle —
and angkor wat is still there,
still rising out of the green.

eleanor remarries 1152 ce france eleanor's marriage to louis is annulled; within eight weeks she weds henry of anjou — aquitaine changes hands, and the most consequential divorce of the middle ages tilts the map of power. the marriage was annulled —
louis vii and eleanor, fifteen years,
two daughters, one disastrous crusade,
and the pope dissolved it on grounds of consanguinity
that everyone knew was an excuse.
i was in paris when the news broke:
eleanor, free, thirty years old,
the richest heiress in europe, twice over —
and within eight weeks she'd married henry of anjou,
nineteen, red-haired, terrifyingly able,
eleven years her junior.
aquitaine changed hands that summer —
from france to the angevins —
and the map of power tilted.
henry would be king of england in two years,
ruling from scotland to the pyrenees,
and eleanor would give him eight children
and forty years of trouble.
the most consequential divorce of the middle ages,
settled in eight weeks.

the treaty of winchester 1153 ce england stephen and henry make peace at winchester — nineteen years of anarchy settled with handshakes, peace through exhaustion, and the plantagenets begin. they were both exhausted —
stephen, old and grieving his son,
henry, young and unbeatable in the field —
and at winchester they made the peace:
stephen keeps the crown for life,
henry succeeds him,
the anarchy ends.
i was in the hall when they swore it —
nineteen years of civil war, settled with handshakes,
the barons weeping with relief,
the bishops blessing everything in sight.
stephen died the next year — the crown barely had time to cool —
and henry plantagenet took it without a fight.
the treaty held because nobody had anything left:
not men, not money, not the will for one more campaign.
peace through exhaustion.
it's not glorious, but it works —
and england got its greatest dynasty out of the deal.

henry plantagenet crowned 1154 ce england henry ii is crowned at twenty-one, ruling an empire from scotland to the pyrenees — the restless founder of the common law, whose greatness and impossibility arrive together. he was twenty-one —
henry plantagenet, henry fitzempress,
crowned at westminster in december,
and his empire was the marvel of europe:
england, normandy, anjou, and — through eleanor —
aquitaine:
from the scottish border to the pyrenees,
more of france than the french king held.
i watched the coronation procession —
the young king, red-haired, restless,
already arguing with his chancellor about taxes —
and nobody there doubted it:
this one would be great.
he was: the law courts, the juries,
the common law taking shape in his reign,
the angevin empire run like a business.
he was also impossible —
his wife would rebel, his sons would rebel,
becket would die for crossing him —
but that december, in the abbey,
the future looked like morning.

munich founded 1158 ce germany henry the lion founds munich on the isar — monks, markets, and a salt toll bridge — the muddy market town that will become one of europe's great cities. henry the lion wanted a toll bridge —
that's the whole story, really:
the duke of saxony and bavaria burned down
the bishop's bridge at fohring,
built his own crossing over the isar,
and founded a market town to collect the salt tolls.
monks, markets, and salt.
i walked the first streets — mud, mostly,
a few dozen houses, the smell of the tanneries —
and the duke's men were already calling it
"by the monks": munchen. munich.
eight hundred years later it would be
one of the great cities of europe —
beer halls, opera, the alps on the horizon —
all of it downstream from one duke's burned bridge
and a toll booth on the isar.

the great canoes 1160 ce pacific polynesian navigators settle the far pacific — hawaii, rapa nui — crossing thousands of miles of empty ocean by stars, swells, and memory, the greatest navigators in history. they read the ocean like a book —
the polynesian navigators, in their double-hulled canoes,
crossing thousands of miles of empty pacific
with no compass, no charts, no instruments:
just stars, swells, birds, clouds,
and memory.
i sailed with one crew from the societies to hawaii —
forty days, the canoe flexing over the swells,
the navigator lying in the bow,
feeling the waves with his body,
reading the night sky like a map he'd memorized as a boy —
and we made landfall on a green island
nobody in europe knew existed.
hawaii. rapa nui. the far islands, settled.
the greatest navigators in human history,
and they did it by feel.

the boy temujin 1162 ce mongolia on the mongolian steppe, a chief's son named temujin is born — the abandoned boy who will become genghis khan and redraw the map of the world. he was born on the steppe that year —
temujin, son of yesugei,
a chief's son, nothing special,
in a felt tent, in the wind.
i held him once — a small red-faced baby
with a blood clot in his fist, the midwives said,
an omen.
within ten years his father would be poisoned,
his family abandoned,
and the boy would be hunting rats to survive,
captured, enslaved, escaped —
and then, slowly, impossibly,
he would unite the steppe tribes
and become genghis khan,
and redraw the map of the world in blood.
but in 1162 he was just a baby
with a blood clot in his fist,
crying in a felt tent
while the steppe wind worked the ropes.

notre-dame begins 1163 ce france the first stone of notre-dame de paris is laid on the ile de la cite — the beginning of a hundred years of building, and of gothic's great cathedral statement. they laid the first stone on the ile de la cite —
notre-dame de paris, our lady of paris —
and the bishop who dreamed it, maurice de sully,
meant it to be the greatest church in france.
i was there for the foundation rites —
the choir singing, the relics processed,
the whole island crowded to watch —
and the work would take a hundred years:
the twin towers, the rose windows,
the flying buttresses holding the stone lace to the sky.
gothic was being born in those years —
the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, light instead of mass —
and notre-dame was its cathedral statement:
eight centuries of kings crowned and buried,
revolutions survived, fires endured.
it started with one stone,
on an island, in 1163.

the hanseatic spark 1167 ce northern europe lubeck's merchants band together for protection — the seed of the hanseatic league, the trading empire with no king that will one day count two hundred cities. it started with merchants looking out for each other —
lubeck's traders, banding together for protection on the roads
and in the ports:
shared warehouses, shared ships, shared muscle
against pirates and princely tolls.
i drank with a lubeck merchant that year —
a hard man with ink on his fingers —
and he told me the plan:
if the towns stand together, no lord can squeeze us alone.
the hansa. the league.
within a century it would be two hundred cities,
from london to novgorod,
a trading empire with no king,
its own laws, its own wars, its own flag —
the merchants' answer to feudalism.
it started with a handshake in lubeck,
and the idea that money, organized,
is stronger than swords.

the normans land 1169 ce ireland norman knights land in ireland at strongbow's side, hired by a deposed king — a mercenary contract on a wexford beach that begins eight centuries of trouble. they came at dermot's invitation —
the deposed king of leinster, who'd gone to england
and hired himself some normans:
strongbow, richard de clare,
with his knights in their mail and his welsh archers —
and they landed at bannow bay in may.
i watched them come ashore —
a few hundred men, professional soldiers,
against irish kings who fought the old way —
and within two years they'd taken dublin, waterford, wexford,
and henry ii was sailing over to make sure
his barons didn't get too independent.
eight centuries of trouble, the timeline says.
it started as a mercenary contract:
one irish king's revenge,
a norman earl's ambition,
and a landing on a wexford beach.

murder in the cathedral 1170 ce england four knights murder thomas becket at canterbury's altar on the king's angry words — the martyr's shrine rises as henry does barefoot penance, and kings learn to watch their words. "will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?"
henry said it in a rage — or so the story goes —
and four knights took him literally:
rode to canterbury, found becket at vespers,
and killed him on the cathedral steps,
his brains on the pavement, the monks screaming.
i was in canterbury that winter —
the whole city in shock, the shrine already gathering pilgrims,
the king doing public penance, walking barefoot to the tomb.
thomas becket, the chancellor turned archbishop,
the king's friend turned the king's conscience —
murdered for the liberties of the church,
or for his own stubbornness, depending who you asked.
henry got his penance.
becket got his sainthood.
the church got its martyr —
and kings learned to watch their angry words.

saladin takes egypt 1171 ce egypt saladin ends the fatimid caliphate with a changed friday sermon — egypt, its grain and gold, becomes the base from which he will face the crusaders. he did it with a sermon —
saladin, the kurdish vizier, nur al-din's man in cairo,
simply had the friday prayer read in the abbasid caliph's name
instead of the fatimid's —
and the fatimid caliphate, two hundred years old,
ended with a change of words.
i was in cairo that friday —
the city barely stirred.
the old caliph was a child, the regime was hollow,
and saladin — yusuf ibn ayyub —
stepped into the vacuum like a man born to it.
egypt was his now: its grain, its gold, its armies.
he would use them all —
first to take syria, then to face the crusaders —
and the ayyubid line he founded
would rule egypt and the levant
until the slave-soldiers took it from his heirs.

saladin's damascus 1174 ce syria saladin takes damascus, uniting egypt and syria — the muslim counterweight to the crusaders grows, and the vise closes around the frankish states. nur al-din died, and syria was up for grabs —
his son a child, his emirs circling —
and saladin moved faster than all of them:
marched north from egypt, took damascus
almost without a fight,
the city opening its gates to the man
who'd once served its master.
i walked damascus that autumn —
the umayyad mosque, the markets, the citadel —
and the mood was relief:
no siege, no sack, just a new master,
and a competent one.
with egypt and damascus both his,
saladin held the crusader states in a vise —
north and south, the muslim powers united
for the first time in a century.
jerusalem could see it coming.
everyone could see it coming.

myriokephalon 1176 ce anatolia the seljuks ambush manuel's army in the pass at myriokephalon — byzantium's last great eastern gamble fails, and anatolia is never recovered. manuel komnenos led his army into the anatolian highlands —
the greatest byzantine force in a generation,
siege engines, imperial guard, the works —
meaning to crush the seljuk turks for good.
i watched the column wind through the pass at myriokephalon —
miles long, strung out, vulnerable —
and the turks did what turks do:
hit the baggage, hit the rear, melt away, hit again.
by evening the army was wrecked,
the siege engines burned,
manuel himself fighting in the ranks.
he got out alive. the empire didn't, quite —
myriokephalon was byzantium's last great eastern gamble,
and it failed.
anatolia would never be recovered.
the turks would never be driven out.
one pass, one afternoon, one more turning
of the long byzantine decline.

the taira ascendant 1178 ce japan taira no kiyomori rules japan from behind the throne — the samurai age dawns in silk and ceremony, with the minamoto sharpening their swords in the east. taira no kiyomori ruled japan without the title —
the emperor reigned, the cloistered emperor schemed,
and kiyomori — the samurai who'd risen by the sword —
held the real power from his mansion at fukuhara.
i visited his court —
silk, poetry, the old heian elegance,
but with armed men at every door —
and kiyomori was already overreaching:
marrying his daughter to the emperor,
putting his grandson on the throne,
exiling his enemies, taxing everyone.
the samurai age was dawning —
government by the sword, behind a screen of ceremony —
and the minamoto, his great rivals,
were sharpening theirs in the east.
seven years of peace left.
then the genpei war,
and the taira would drown with a boy emperor
in the straits of dan-no-ura.

philip augustus crowned 1180 ce france fifteen-year-old philip ii is crowned at reims — the boy king who will take normandy, win bouvines, and make france, the plantagenets' doom freshly anointed. he was fifteen —
philip, son of louis vii,
crowned at reims while his father still lived,
a boy king with a sickly reputation
and eyes that missed nothing.
i watched the coronation —
the holy oil, the great lords, the boy standing straight —
and nobody there guessed:
this was the king who would humble kings.
philip augustus.
he would take normandy from the english,
crush the greatest coalition europe had seen at bouvines,
triple the royal domain,
and make france — france.
fifteen years old, crowned in november,
and the plantagenet empire didn't know it yet,
but its doom had just been anointed
with the sacred oil of reims.

the genpei storm gathers 1182 ce japan minamoto and taira sharpen their swords — the genpei storm gathers, ronin crowding the inns, five years of clan war brewing like weather before a typhoon. the swords were being sharpened —
in the east, minamoto no yoritomo,
in exile, building his network;
in the west, the taira, drunk on power,
kiyomori dead but his clan still ruling;
and in the middle, the boy emperor,
a pawn in armor.
i traveled the roads that year
and every inn was full of ronin —
masterless samurai, selling their swords,
waiting for the war everyone could smell coming.
the genpei war: five years,
clan against clan, samurai against samurai,
the most romanticized war in japanese history —
the battles, the duels, the loyalties,
the boy emperor drowning at dan-no-ura
with his grandmother holding him.
in 1182 it was just tension —
armies gathering in the mist,
like weather before a typhoon.

the new jerusalem 1184 ce ethiopia king lalibela begins carving eleven churches from living rock at roha — a new jerusalem for ethiopian christians, faith expressed in negative space, cut down into the mountain. king lalibela had a dream —
or a vision, the priests say —
and he set out to build a new jerusalem in the highlands of lasta:
eleven churches, carved down into living rock,
not built up, but cut down,
roofs at ground level, the whole church
excavated from the stone like sculpture.
i stood at bete giyorgis — st. george's —
a perfect cross cut forty feet into the rock,
and the workmen were still at it,
the chips flying, the chanting going on below.
when the muslims held old jerusalem,
lalibela reasoned, ethiopian christians needed their own —
so he carved one, church by church, out of the mountain.
faith, expressed in negative space:
the building is what's left
after you remove everything that isn't church.

dan-no-ura 1185 ce japan at dan-no-ura the minamoto destroy the taira fleet — and the boy emperor drowns in his grandmother's arms, ending the genpei war and beginning japan's warrior age. the straits ran red —
dan-no-ura, the naval battle that ended the genpei war:
minamoto ships against taira ships,
archers in the rigging, swords on the decks,
and the tide — the minamoto knew the tides,
the taira didn't, and that was the battle.
i watched from a hillside as the taira line broke —
and then the thing no chronicle can make untrue:
the emperor's grandmother took the boy emperor,
antoku, eight years old,
in her arms, and stepped into the sea.
the taira drowned with their emperor.
the minamoto stood alone.
eight hundred years of samurai government —
the shogunate, the whole warrior age of japan —
started with a grandmother and a child
walking into the water.

hattin 1187 ce holy land saladin destroys the crusader army at the horns of hattin — the true cross captured, the king taken — and jerusalem falls within months, ending eighty-eight years of the kingdom. the horns of hattin —
a double hill in the galilee heat,
and guy of lusignan marched his army into saladin's trap:
cut off from water, harried by horse-archers,
the wells of hattin just out of reach,
men dying of thirst in their armor.
i was with the baggage train when the line broke —
the true cross captured, the knights ridden down,
the king himself taken,
and saladin — courteous, cold —
had reynald of chatillon beheaded before his eyes
and sent the king water with his own hands.
within months jerusalem fell.
eighty-eight years of the crusader kingdom,
ended in one july afternoon of thirst and pride.
the pope died of the news, they say.
europe reached for its swords.

the third crusade 1189 ce europe richard the lionheart and philip augustus take the cross and sail for the holy land — the crusade of kings, glorious in song, that wins every battle and loses the war. they took the cross —
richard of england, the lionheart,
philip of france, the boy king grown canny,
and old barbarossa, the german emperor,
with the greatest army europe had ever sent east.
i watched them sail from marseille and genoa —
fleets of ships, the flower of chivalry,
banners, trumpets, the whole shining terrible pageant —
off to win back jerusalem.
it was the crusade of kings,
and it had everything except success:
barbarossa would drown in a river,
philip would quarrel and go home,
richard would win every battle and lose the war —
and jerusalem would stay muslim.
but the songs —
the songs of richard and saladin,
the lion and the sultan,
are sung to this day.

the emperor drowns 1190 ce holy land barbarossa drowns in the saleph river — the third crusade's greatest army dissolves, and legend sets the emperor sleeping in his mountain, beard growing through the table. the saleph river, in cilicia —
snowmelt, fast, cold —
and frederick barbarossa, seventy years old,
the greatest emperor of the age,
rode in to cool off, or to cross, the stories differ —
and the current took him.
i was with the rearguard when the news came up the column:
the emperor is dead, drowned,
and the greatest army of the third crusade
came apart like wet parchment —
most of them turning home,
a remnant marching on to acre under his son,
who died of fever on the way.
the germans said barbarossa wasn't dead, only sleeping —
in the kyffhauser mountain, beard growing through the table,
waiting for germany's hour.
he's still waiting.
the crusade went on without him,
a head shorter.

acre retaken 1191 ce holy land after a two-year double siege, richard retakes acre — the crusaders' great prize — then massacres the prisoners when the ransom stalls, a stain the plain remembers. two years.
that's how long the siege of acre lasted —
two years of the crusaders besieging the city
while saladin besieged the crusaders,
a double ring of hunger and dying,
kings arriving, queens dying of plague in the camps.
i walked those camps —
the stench, the flies, the endless building of siege towers
that the defenders burned, again and again —
until richard arrived, and the end came fast:
the garrison surrendered, the city opened,
the great port was frankish again.
richard's great prize.
then he had the prisoners massacred —
two thousand seven hundred of them, on the plain outside —
when the ransom stalled.
the chronicles argue about it still.
the plain outside acre doesn't argue.
it remembers.

the first shogun 1192 ce japan minamoto no yoritomo becomes shogun at kamakura — japan's warrior government begins, emperors reigning while shoguns rule, for seven hundred years. yoritomo took the title —
sei-i taishogun, barbarian-subduing great general —
and set up his government at kamakura,
far from the kyoto court and its silken intrigues:
a warrior government, for warriors,
run from a tent-city turned capital.
i visited kamakura in those first years —
all mud and new timber, the shogun's headquarters
buzzing with vassals, petitions, judgments —
and the emperor in kyoto still reigned,
still performed the ceremonies,
while the real power sat in the east with a sword.
it would last seven hundred years:
shoguns ruling, emperors reigning,
japan governed by the military
until the modern age pried it open.
the first shogun.
the longest military government in history.

the truce of jaffa 1192 ce holy land richard and saladin make peace at jaffa — the coast stays frankish, jerusalem stays muslim — the crusade of kings ending in a handshake between legends who never met. they never met —
richard and saladin, the lion and the sultan,
the two most famous enemies of the age —
but they negotiated like men who respected each other:
letters, envoys, gifts of horses and falcons,
richard even offering his sister's hand
to saladin's brother (it came to nothing).
i was at jaffa when the truce was sealed:
three years, the coast stays frankish,
jerusalem stays muslim,
pilgrims may visit the holy places unarmed.
richard sailed home — to shipwreck, capture, ransom —
and saladin died within the year.
the third crusade ended not with triumph
but with a handshake across the lines:
jerusalem lost, honor kept,
and two legends who never once stood face to face.

death of saladin 1193 ce syria saladin dies at damascus — his treasury holds one gold piece, his funeral is mourned by three faiths, and his empire divides among his kin before the body is cold. he died at damascus, of a fever —
fifty-five years old, worn out by war and rule —
and they opened his treasury to pay for his funeral
and found almost nothing:
one gold piece, forty pieces of silver.
saladin — who had held egypt and syria,
who had taken jerusalem, faced richard, been the terror of the franks —
died poor, because he'd given it all away.
i stood in the funeral procession through damascus —
muslims, christians, jews, all of them mourning,
even the franks across the lines honoring him —
and his empire divided among his kin
before the body was cold:
sons, brothers, nephews, carving it up.
the man was greater than the realm.
the realm knew it, and wept anyway.

cahokia at its peak 1200 ce north america cahokia holds perhaps twenty thousand souls — the greatest city north of mexico, mounds and plazas and sun-circles on the mississippi — at a peak nobody knows won't last. twenty thousand souls —
maybe more —
cahokia at its height, the greatest city north of mexico:
monk's mound at the center, the great plaza,
the woodhenge circles tracking the sun,
neighborhoods stretching to the horizon,
the mississippi below, fat with trade.
i climbed the mound at midsummer —
the chunkey games in the plazas,
the smell of cooking fires, the river traffic,
a city with no stone, no wheel, no writing,
running on earth and ceremony and corn —
bigger than london, bigger than paris would be for a century.
and then — within two hundred years —
it emptied.
nobody knows why. the mounds don't say.
i stood on monk's mound at the peak,
and the whole valley breathed below me,
and none of us knew it wouldn't last.

the fourth crusade 1202 ce europe crusaders take the cross, can't pay venice for ships, and the blind doge turns their swords toward christians — the crusade for jerusalem becomes the road to constantinople. they took the cross —
the flower of french chivalry, counts and knights —
and then they made a deal with venice:
ships for the whole army, on credit.
i was in venice when the bill came due —
the crusaders couldn't pay,
and old blind doge dandolo, ninety years old,
made them an offer:
take zara for us — a christian city, mind —
and we'll talk about the ships.
they did it. zara fell.
then the exiled byzantine prince showed up
with his promises of gold and reunion —
and the crusade turned east, toward constantinople.
a crusade to free the holy land
ended up sacking the greatest christian city on earth.
venice got its money's worth.
god, i suspect, got other plans.

the sack of the queen of cities 1204 ce constantinople crusaders storm constantinople and loot it for three days — the queen of cities stripped, byzantium shattered into pieces, the crusade destroying what it was called to save. three days.
for three days the crusaders looted constantinople —
the queen of cities, the richest city in christendom —
churches stripped, palaces emptied,
the bronze horses of the hippodrome shipped to venice,
nuns raped on the altars, the libraries burned for the parchment's... no,
they just burned.
i walked the streets on the third day —
the smoke, the drunks, the weeping greeks,
a thousand years of accumulated glory
being hauled onto venetian ships.
byzantium shattered: the empire broke into pieces —
nicaea, trebizond, epirus —
and though the greeks would take the city back in fifty years,
it never recovered.
the fourth crusade's great achievement:
it destroyed the very civilization
it had been called to save.

the slave dynasty 1206 ce india the ex-slave qutb al-din aibak founds the delhi sultanate and begins the qutb minar — property become king, the first of history's strangest aristocracy. qutb al-din aibak had been a slave —
bought, trained, risen through the ghori armies
by sheer competence —
and when his master died, the slave took the throne:
the first sultan of delhi,
founder of the slave dynasty.
i watched him lay the first courses of the qutb minar —
the victory tower, two hundred and forty feet of carved red sandstone,
rising over the new capital —
a slave's monument to his own unlikely crown.
the mamluk pattern: the slave-soldier,
bought as a boy, forged into a warrior,
rising past free men to rule.
it would work in delhi for a century,
in egypt for two and a half —
the strangest aristocracy in history:
men who'd been property, wearing crowns.

the albigensian crusade 1209 ce france innocent iii turns crusade against the cathars of southern france — "kill them all, god will know his own" — twenty years of war grinding the languedoc under the northern heel. pope innocent iii had had enough of the cathars —
the heretics of languedoc, with their two gods,
their perfecti, their rejection of the church's wealth —
so he called a crusade:
not against muslims, but against christians,
in the south of france.
i rode with the northern army to beziers —
and when the city fell, the legate was asked
how to tell heretic from faithful,
and gave the answer that stains the century:
"kill them all. god will know his own."
twenty thousand dead at beziers, they say.
twenty years of war followed —
the burning of the perfecti, the fall of montsegur —
and the south of france, its troubadours, its tolerance,
was ground under the northern heel.
a crusade against one's neighbors.
christendom, eating itself.

las navas de tolosa 1212 ce spain christian kings smash the almohads at las navas de tolosa — the reconquista's turning point, after which muslim spain's fall becomes only a matter of time. the kings came together for once —
castile, aragon, navarre, portugal,
with crusaders from france —
and met the almohad host at las navas de tolosa,
in the passes of the sierra morena.
i stood on the ridge and watched the christian charge break through —
the almohad caliph's tent, his bodyguard of chained-together africans,
the whole great army coming apart in the july heat —
and when it was over, the power of muslim spain was broken for good.
the reconquista's turning point.
after las navas, it was only a matter of time:
cordoba in twenty-four years, seville in thirty-six,
the long slow christian tide
washing down to the sea.
one battle, in a mountain pass,
and eight centuries of spanish history
turned on it.

the children's crusade 1212 ce europe thousands of children march for the holy land behind shepherd boys — most never come home; the sea doesn't part, and the innocent learn what the age does with innocence. they were children —
thousands of them, following a shepherd boy named stephen
in france, a boy named nicholas in germany —
convinced that god would part the sea for their innocence
as he'd parted it for no army.
i watched the french column pass through a village —
barefoot, singing, the little ones riding on the older ones' shoulders,
their parents weeping at the roadside, unable to stop them.
most never came home.
the french children reached marseille and waited for the sea to part;
it didn't, and merchants offered ships —
and sold them, the chronicles say, into slavery.
the germans died crossing the alps.
the children's crusade: faith at its purest,
and its most helpless —
and the sea, inconsiderate, stayed closed.

magna carta 1215 ce england at runnymede, barons force john to seal the great charter — sixty-three clauses hiding the sentences that become the foundation of liberty: no imprisonment without lawful judgment. runnymede, june —
a meadow by the thames, and king john,
cornered, hated, beaten by the french and his own barons both —
sealing the great charter.
i stood in the crowd of barons' men and watched him press his seal:
sixty-three clauses, most of them about feudal dues and fish weirs —
but buried in the latin, the sentences that would outlive them all:
no free man shall be seized or imprisoned except by lawful judgment.
due process. the rule of law.
john repudiated it within weeks — got the pope to annul it —
and died the next year, and the charter was reissued, and reissued,
and grew.
a failed peace treaty between a bad king and angry barons —
that became the foundation stone of liberty
in the english-speaking world.

the fifth crusade 1217 ce egypt crusaders take damietta, refuse the sultan's offer of jerusalem itself, march on cairo instead — and the nile rises and traps them; they surrender everything to get out alive. they'd learned the lesson, sort of —
jerusalem couldn't be taken from the sea-coast;
egypt was the key, the nile the road —
so the fifth crusade sailed for damietta,
and took it, after a grinding siege.
i was in the camp when the sultan offered them everything:
jerusalem, the true cross, the whole kingdom back —
for damietta.
and the legate said no.
pride. papal pride.
so they marched on cairo instead —
and the nile rose, as the nile does,
and trapped them in the floodplain,
and they surrendered damietta to get out alive.
the fifth crusade: offered jerusalem for free,
and chose the flood instead.
the legate's pride, paid for in drowned men
and one more empty crusade.

the mongol storm breaks 1219 ce central asia genghis khan's armies shatter the khwarezmian empire — bukhara, samarkand, merv fall, cities vanish from the map, and the mongol storm breaks over the world. the shah of khwarezm made the mistake —
seized a mongol trade caravan, executed the envoys —
and genghis khan, who'd have taken the trade deal,
took the war instead.
i rode with the mongol tumens into transoxiana —
a hundred thousand horsemen, moving like weather —
and watched bukhara fall, then samarkand:
the great silk road cities, the libraries, the observatories,
emptied.
the chronicles say the mongols killed everyone;
the chronicles exaggerate, but not enough.
cities vanished from the map —
merv, nishapur, herat —
their populations put to the sword
as policy, as terror, as arithmetic.
the khwarezmian empire: erased in two years.
the mongol storm, broken over the world —
and it had only just begun.

karakorum founded 1220 ce mongolia genghis khan founds karakorum on the steppe — walls instead of tents, a polyglot capital of artisans, merchants, and priests where the empire's roads meet. in the orkhon valley, where the rivers run,
genghis khan ordered his capital built —
karakorum, the black gravel:
not tents, but walls; not a camp, but a city.
i walked its first streets —
a strange, polyglot place from the start:
chinese artisans, muslim merchants, nestorian priests,
the khan's palace with its great silver fountain
shaped like a tree, pouring wine and mare's milk.
the mongols were nomads ruling the world,
and karakorum was their concession to permanence:
a fixed point on the steppe,
where the empire's roads met
and the world's tribute flowed in.
it would never be large.
it didn't need to be.
the empire was the city;
karakorum was just its tent-peg.

lalibela's churches stand 1221 ce ethiopia the last of lalibela's eleven rock-hewn churches is finished — forty years of cutting complete, a holy city excavated from the mountain, still standing eight centuries on. the last of the eleven was finished —
forty years of cutting, the chips flying,
the chanting going on below ground level —
and lalibela's new jerusalem stood complete:
eleven churches, carved from living rock,
joined by tunnels and courtyards,
a whole holy city excavated from a mountainside.
i walked the dark passage between bete maryam and bete golgotha —
the pilgrims' tunnel, worn smooth by centuries of knees not yet come —
and came up into the light at the next church,
blinking, like being reborn.
they say angels helped at night,
finishing what the workmen started by day.
i don't know about angels.
i know the stone is cut true,
and the churches are still standing,
eight hundred years later,
still full of priests and pilgrims and candle-smoke.

the lion king rises 1225 ce mali the exiled sundiata keita begins gathering the malinke clans — the lion king's rise, mali's founding epic, starting not with battle but with chiefs bending the knee one by one. they called him the lion king —
sundiata keita, son of a malinke chief,
crippled as a boy, mocked, exiled —
and the griots still sing how he rose:
stood up from his lameness, they say,
by sheer will, and began gathering the clans.
i heard the epic sung in a village that year —
the hunter's songs, the prophecies,
the boy who would break the sorcerer-king —
and the clans were listening.
soumaoro kante held the land then,
the sorcerer-king of sosso, cruel and feared —
and sundiata was building the alliance
that would break him at kirina.
mali's founding epic, starting here:
not with a battle, but with a gathering —
a lame boy, a prophecy,
and chiefs one by one bending the knee.

death of genghis khan 1227 ce mongolia genghis khan dies on campaign and is buried in secret — his empire splits among his sons into four khanates, the greatest land empire in history divided like an inheritance. he died on campaign —
against the tanguts, in the west,
of wounds or sickness, the accounts differ,
and the mongols hid it:
the funeral cortege killing everyone it met,
so no one would know where the khan was buried —
and no one does, to this day.
i rode in the shadow of that secret column —
the empire holding its breath —
and when the news broke, the empire split
the way he'd ordered it split:
four sons, four khanates,
the greatest land empire in history
divided like a inheritance.
jochi's line to the west, chagatai in the middle,
ogedei the great khan, tolui's sons waiting.
he'd conquered from korea to hungary.
his sons would quarrel over the pieces
for the next hundred years.

frederick's crusade 1228 ce italy the excommunicated frederick ii sails east and wins jerusalem back by treaty, not battle — crowning himself in the holy sepulchre, the crusade that worked through diplomacy. frederick ii was excommunicated —
twice, actually —
and he went on crusade anyway,
because the pope telling him not to
was reason enough.
i sailed with his fleet —
the stupor mundi, the wonder of the world,
the emperor who spoke six languages
and kept a harem and corresponded with muslim scholars —
and what he did in the holy land
no crusader had done before:
he negotiated.
with al-kamil, the sultan of egypt —
a treaty, not a battle:
jerusalem, bethlehem, nazareth,
returned to christian hands for ten years,
the muslims keeping the temple mount.
he crowned himself in the holy sepulchre —
no priest would do it, excommunicate and all —
and sailed home.
the pope was furious.
jerusalem was christian.
diplomacy: the crusade that worked.

castile and leon united 1230 ce spain ferdinand iii joins castile and leon for good — the reconquista's engine assembled, one king pointed south, and within eighteen years only granada will remain. ferdinand iii took both crowns —
castile from his mother, leon from his father,
and this time the union stuck:
one king, one realm, one direction —
south.
i was at his court in those early years —
a young king, pious, tireless,
with the reconquista's engine finally assembled:
the two great christian kingdoms,
their knights, their orders, their money,
all pointed at muslim spain.
within six years he'd take cordoba.
within eighteen, seville.
ferdinand the saint, they'd call him —
and he earned it the hard way,
campaign after campaign,
until only granada was left,
a small bright ember of al-andalus
in the far south.

the samurai law code 1232 ce japan the kamakura shogunate issues the goseibai shikimoku — fifty-one articles of warrior law, the operating system of feudal japan for seven hundred years. the shogunate needed laws —
not the court's elegant heian codes,
but law for the warrior age:
land disputes, vassal duties, what happens
when a samurai kills a samurai.
i was at kamakura when the goseibai shikimoku was proclaimed —
fifty-one articles, plain language,
the first warrior law code in japanese history —
and the shogun's judges read them aloud
to the assembled vassals.
it was practical stuff:
inheritance, debts, the duties of stewards,
punishments fitted to rank —
the operating system of feudal japan,
running for the next seven hundred years.
the sword had conquered.
now the brush organized the conquest —
and japan's warrior government got its rulebook.

kirina 1235 ce mali sundiata crushes the sorcerer-king soumaoro at kirina — the mali empire is born, the lame boy become mansa, ruler of the gold lands and the niger trade. the sorcerer-king against the lion king —
soumaoro kante of sosso, with his magic and his terror,
against sundiata keita, with his alliance of the clans —
and they met at kirina.
i watched from the hills as the malinke line held —
sundiata's hunters and horsemen,
against soumaoro's dread —
and when the sorcerer-king broke and fled,
the thing he'd built broke with him.
the mali empire was born that day —
the griots date everything from kirina —
and sundiata, the lame boy, the exile,
became mansa, king of kings,
ruler of the gold lands, the niger trade,
the greatest empire west africa had ever seen.
one battle. one morning.
the lion king's epic, fulfilled.

cordoba retaken 1236 ce spain ferdinand iii takes cordoba — the great mosque becomes a cathedral, five centuries of muslim rule ending in the city of the caliphs, the reconquista made stone. ferdinand took cordoba in june —
the city of the caliphs, the great mosque,
the libraries, the streetlights —
after five centuries of muslim rule,
and he walked into the mosque
and had it consecrated as a cathedral.
i was there that summer —
the forest of columns, the mihrab,
the christian altar being raised
in the most beautiful mosque on earth —
and the symbolism was the point:
the reconquista, made stone.
cordoba the victorious, they called it now.
the taifa kings watched from their shrinking courts
and understood:
the tide had turned for good,
and ferdinand wasn't stopping.
seville was next.
then the long wait for granada.

the mongols come west 1237 ce russia batu's horsemen burn ryazan — "none left to weep for the dead" — and the long tartar night begins for russia: two and a half centuries of the mongol yoke. batu's horsemen came out of the east —
the golden horde, the western arm of the mongol empire —
and ryazan was first:
five days of siege, then the storm,
then the chronicles' terrible sentence:
there was none left to weep for the dead.
i rode through ryazan the week after —
the smoke still rising, the streets empty,
a whole city, gone —
and the other russian princes were already quarreling
about who'd help whom, which is to say, no one.
the long tartar night was beginning for russia:
two hundred and fifty years of the yoke,
the tribute, the khans' baskaks in every town.
it started at ryazan,
in the winter of 1237,
with no one left to weep.

kiev falls 1240 ce russia the mongols storm kiev — the mother of russian cities falls, the center of rus' moves north, and the lands bow to the golden horde for two centuries. kiev — the mother of russian cities,
the golden domes, the caves monastery,
two hundred years of rus' glory —
fell in december.
i was outside the walls when the siege towers came up —
the mongol engines battering day and night,
the defenders fighting street by street,
the last of them dying in the church of the tithes
when the walls came down on their heads.
the chronicles say the mongols killed everyone;
the city never recovered its greatness —
the center of rus' moved north, to vladimir, to moscow,
and kiev became a memory of itself.
the rus' lands bowed to the golden horde:
princes traveling to sarai for the khan's patent,
tribute flowing east,
and russia's long schooling in autocracy —
learned, in part, from the khans.

the mongols turn back 1241 ce europe ogedei khan dies, and the mongol armies wheel away from hungary's edge for the kurultai — europe spared by a death five thousand miles away, the tide that never returns. they were at the gates —
the mongols, past kiev, past hungary,
their scouts probing toward vienna,
europe lying open before them like a map —
and then the news came from karakorum:
ogedei khan was dead.
and mongol law was iron:
the princes must return for the kurultai,
the election of the new khan.
i watched the tumens wheel away from hungary —
the greatest anticlimax in european history —
turning east, leaving the burning villages behind,
because a man had died five thousand miles away.
europe, spared by a death.
the chroniclers called it a miracle.
it was politics — steppe politics —
but the result was the same:
the mongol tide turned back at the edge of europe,
and never came again.

battle on the ice 1242 ce russia alexander nevsky defeats the teutonic knights on the frozen lake peipus — the eastward crusade dies on the ice, and russia gets the hero who bowed to the mongols and turned back the west. lake peipus, april —
the ice still holding, barely,
and alexander nevsky's russians met the teutonic knights:
the german crusaders, pushing east,
the drang nach osten in armor —
and the ice became the battlefield.
i watched from the shore as the russian wings closed —
the knights' wedge broken, the heavy cavalry floundering,
men and horses going through the ice in their mail —
and the livonian crusade died that afternoon
on a frozen lake.
nevsky became the hero of russia —
the prince who turned back the west,
while bowing, pragmatically, to the mongol east.
seven hundred years later they'd name an order after him,
and eisenstein would film the battle
with the ice cracking under the knights.

jerusalem lost for good 1244 ce holy land khwarezmian horsemen sack jerusalem — the crusaders never hold it again; the crusading age's one prize, gone forever in a week of blood. they came out of the wreckage of khwarezm —
the khwarezmian horsemen, refugees of the mongol storm,
hired by egypt, turned loose on the franks —
and they took jerusalem in august:
sacked it, slaughtered, desecrated,
the holy places running with blood.
i walked the streets afterward —
the worst sack the city had seen in a century,
and this time there was no recovery:
the crusaders never held jerusalem again.
frederick's treaty had given it back;
the khwarezmians took it away for good.
the seventh crusade would try — louis the saint,
with all his piety and all his army —
and fail in egypt.
jerusalem, lost.
the crusading age had one prize,
and now it was gone forever.

the friar's embassy 1245 ce mongolia friar john of plano carpini reaches karakorum — europe's first envoy to the great khan — and brings home the khan's reply (submit or be destroyed) and the west's first real account of the mongols. pope innocent sent him —
friar john of plano carpini, sixty-five years old,
with a letter for the great khan:
stop killing christians, by the way, consider baptism —
and john walked.
i met him on the road east —
through russia, through the steppe,
eating with mongols, sleeping in felt tents,
a fat old friar crossing the largest empire on earth
on foot and horseback —
and he reached karakorum,
saw the new khan enthroned,
delivered the pope's letter,
and got the khan's reply:
submit, or be destroyed.
he brought it home, with the first real account
of the mongol empire ever written in the west:
the ystoria mongalorum.
europe's first envoy to the great khan —
and the khan's answer was an ultimatum.

the slave kings 1250 ce egypt mamluk slave-soldiers seize egypt — the slave kings, bought as boys and forged into the finest cavalry on earth, who will stop the mongols and finish the crusaders. the mamluks did what slave-soldiers do —
they killed their master.
aybak, qutuz, the mamluk emirs of egypt:
the ayyubid sultan dead, his son a child,
and the slave regiments simply... took over.
i was in cairo during the coup —
quick, professional, almost bloodless by the standards —
and egypt had a new dynasty:
the slave kings, the mamluks,
bought as boys on the steppe,
forged into the finest cavalry on earth,
ruling the richest country in the mediterranean.
they would rule for two hundred and fifty years —
stop the mongols at ain jalut,
finish the crusaders at acre,
and run egypt like a military corporation.
the strangest dynasty ever:
kings who'd been property,
and never let anyone forget
they'd earned the throne with a sword.

mongke's census 1251 ce mongolia mongke khan orders the empire counted — every household from china to persia inventoried, the nomad empire's most ambitious bureaucracy, tax rolls that outlast the khans. mongke khan wanted to know what he owned —
so he ordered the empire counted:
every household, every field, every workshop,
from china to persia, from russia to korea.
i traveled with one of the census teams in persia —
the clerks with their scrolls, the local headmen sweating,
every name written down, every tax assessed —
the mongol empire, inventoried like domesday,
but on a continental scale.
it was the most ambitious bureaucracy in history:
an empire of nomads, counting farmers,
so the tribute would flow precisely,
predictably, forever.
the census made the empire legible —
and taxable —
and the tax rolls of mongke's clerks
would outlast the khans themselves,
used by every successor state
that inherited the mongol machinery.

the sorbonne's seed 1253 ce france robert de sorbon founds his college for poor theology students in paris — the seed of the sorbonne, seven centuries of french intellect from one chaplain's charity. robert de sorbon was the king's chaplain —
a commoner's son, risen by brains —
and he looked at the poor theology students of paris,
living in garrets, begging their bread,
and founded them a college:
a house, a library, stipends,
so poor scholars could study divinity
without starving.
i visited in the early years —
a modest building on the left bank,
the students in their black gowns,
disputing in the hall the way paris students always have —
and nobody guessed the name would become
the university itself:
the sorbonne.
seven centuries of french intellect,
starting with one chaplain's charity
for poor theologians.

the traveler is born 1254 ce italy marco polo is born in venice — unremarked, a merchant's son in a canal house, with the whole of asia waiting seventeen years down the road. in venice, in a merchant house by the canal,
a boy was born —
marco, son of niccolo polo,
and nobody marked the day.
i like to think i walked past that house
without knowing —
the most famous traveler in history,
being born unremarked,
while his father and uncle were away
in the east, at the khan's court,
laying the road the boy would follow.
seventeen years later he'd set out after them.
twenty-four years after that he'd come home
with stories no one believed.
seven centuries after that, we'd still be reading them.
but in 1254, in venice,
he was just a merchant's son,
crying in a canal house,
with the whole of asia waiting.

the mongols repelled 1257 ce vietnam tran dynasty armies drive the mongols out of dai viet — the first of three repelled invasions; the empire that took hungary could not take vietnam. the mongols came down through the passes —
veterans of a hundred victories,
expecting another province —
and dai viet was ready:
the tran kings, the generals, the people,
the scorched earth, the guerrilla war,
the rivers they'd known all their lives.
i watched the mongol columns struggle south —
the heat, the disease, the ambushes,
an empire of horsemen drowning in a green wet country
that wouldn't stand and fight —
and they turned back.
then they came again — twice more, in later years —
and the vietnamese beat them twice more:
the bach dang river, the stakes in the mud,
the whole fleet destroyed at low tide.
three invasions. three defeats.
the mongols conquered everything from korea to hungary —
but not dai viet.

ain jalut 1260 ce holy land the mamluks crush the mongols at ain jalut — the first pitched battle the mongols ever lost, the high-water mark of their tide, broken by slave-soldiers at the spring of goliath. the mongols had never lost a pitched battle —
not once, in fifty years —
and then they met the mamluks at ain jalut,
the spring of goliath, in galilee.
i stood on the hillside and watched qutuz work:
the mamluk feigned retreat — the mongols' own trick, turned on them —
the hidden squadrons closing like a fist —
and kitbuqa, the mongol commander, dying in the trap.
the high-water mark of the mongol tide.
after ain jalut, the myth was broken:
the mongols could be beaten,
by slave-soldiers who'd learned their trade
on the same steppe.
syria was saved. egypt was safe.
the mamluks became the shield of islam —
and the mongol empire, for the first time,
had a frontier it couldn't cross.

the city retaken 1261 ce constantinople michael palaiologos retakes constantinople through an unguarded postern — byzantium restored, diminished, beginning its long luminous two-hundred-year sunset. it was almost an accident —
michael palaiologos's general, scouting the walls,
found an unguarded postern, slipped in at night,
and constantinople — the queen of cities,
fifty-seven years in latin hands —
was greek again by morning.
i walked through the blachernae gate at dawn,
past the cheering, the weeping,
michael entering in triumph a month later,
the empire restored —
diminished, broke, a shadow with a crown,
but restored.
byzantium would last another two hundred years:
the palaiologan renaissance, the scholars, the art —
a long, brilliant sunset.
the latins were gone.
the city was greek.
and the empire that had been the center of the world
settled in for its long, luminous decline.

the first parliament 1264 ce england simon de montfort summons knights and burgesses to westminster — parliament's first breath, commoners in the council of the realm, planted in a losing war by a desperate man. simon de montfort was losing —
the barons' war against henry iii, going badly —
so he did something desperate and brilliant:
he summoned a parliament,
and invited not just the barons and bishops,
but knights from every shire
and burgesses from every town.
i was in westminster hall that january —
commoners, in parliament, for the first time —
farmers' sons and merchants' sons,
sitting with earls, advising the realm.
montfort died at evesham within the year —
hacked down, the pope's legate calling it murder —
but the idea survived him:
that the commons had a place in the council of the realm.
parliament's first breath.
it would take centuries to grow into its power —
but the seed was planted at westminster,
in a losing war, by a desperate frenchman.

dante is born 1265 ce italy dante alighieri is born in florence — the moneylender's son who will write the comedy, invent the italian language, and turn a childhood glance at beatrice into eternity. in florence, in a modest house,
a boy was born —
durante, called dante,
son of a moneylender, nobody special —
and the century turned around him:
the guelphs and ghibellines, the popes and emperors,
the whole violent flowering of the italian cities.
i like to think i passed him in the street as a boy —
nine years old, they say, when he first saw beatrice,
eight years old herself, in a red dress,
and the whole comedy turning on that glance.
exile, politics, love, hell —
all of it ahead of him.
the greatest poem of the middle ages,
the italian language itself, more or less invented —
and it started with a moneylender's son in florence,
breathing his first,
in 1265.

baybars takes antioch 1268 ce holy land the mamluk sultan baybars storms antioch and destroys it utterly — the queen of the crusader east emptied and smoking, the states bleeding out castle by castle. baybars didn't take prisoners at antioch —
the mamluk sultan, the panther, the greatest of the slave kings —
stormed the city that had held out for a hundred and seventy years
and put it to the sword:
every man killed, the women and children enslaved,
the city so ruined it never recovered.
i walked the ruins the week after —
antioch, the queen of the crusader east,
where the first crusade had starved and triumphed —
emptied, smoking, finished.
baybars wrote the prince of antioch a letter about it,
absent at the time, mocking him:
you should have been here, it said, more or less.
the crusader states were bleeding out —
castle by castle, city by city —
and the panther was just getting started.

the solomonic restoration 1270 ce ethiopia yekuno amlak overthrows the zagwe and restores ethiopia's solomonic line — claiming descent from sheba and solomon, founding seven hundred years of continuous monarchy. yekuno amlak overthrew the zagwe —
the dynasty of lalibela, the church-builders —
and claimed the throne of ethiopia
for the line of solomon:
descended, he said, from the queen of sheba
and the wise king of israel,
three thousand years of lineage,
restored.
i was at the coronation —
