the priests, the drums, the ancient liturgy in ge'ez —
and whether the bloodline was real hardly mattered:
the story was.
the solomonic line would rule ethiopia
for seven hundred years —
the oldest continuous monarchy on earth,
lasting into the age of airplanes —
all of it founded on a claim
that a queen once visited a king
and came home with a dynasty.

the polos depart 1271 ce venice marco polo sets out with his father and uncle for kublai khan's court — three venetians walking into the largest empire on earth, not to return for twenty-four years. they set out from venice that year —
niccolo and maffeo polo, the merchants,
and seventeen-year-old marco with them —
with the pope's letters and holy oil from jerusalem,
bound for the court of kublai khan.
i watched them leave —
three venetians, a handful of servants,
walking into the largest empire on earth,
and nobody in venice gave them a thought:
just merchants, off on another eastern venture.
they wouldn't be back for twenty-four years.
marco would come home with a story
so vast no one believed it —
the khan's court, the paper money, the black stones that burned —
and a book that would sit on columbus's shelf,
annotated, dreamed over,
two hundred years later.
it started with three men walking out of venice,
in 1271.

the divine wind 1274 ce japan a typhoon shatters kublai khan's invasion fleet — the first kamikaze, the divine wind, saving japan and becoming scripture: the gods protect these islands. kublai khan sent nine hundred ships —
the greatest amphibious force the world had ever seen —
to take japan:
mongol horsemen, chinese infantry, korean sailors,
an empire's army, crossing the strait.
i watched them land at hakata —
the samurai fighting the old way, duels and challenges,
against an enemy that fought like a machine —
and japan was losing.
then the typhoon came.
the divine wind — kamikaze —
smashing the fleet against the rocks,
drowning the invasion in a night of storm.
the mongols went home.
japan was saved by weather —
and the story became scripture:
the gods protect these islands,
the wind itself fights for japan.
seven centuries later, young pilots
would take the name into battle,
diving into american ships.
the wind, weaponized.

marco at the khan's court 1275 ce china marco polo reaches shangdu and enters kublai khan's service — paper money, burning black stones, post-horses — seventeen years of wonders, all written down for the book no one believes. they reached shangdu —
the polos, after four years on the road,
deserts, mountains, bandits, the whole silk road —
and kublai khan received them:
the great khan, the emperor of china,
sixty years old, gouty, magnificent.
i was in the court that season —
the porcelains, the silks, the paper money
that made marco stare,
the black stones they burned for heat,
the post-horses, the census, the canals —
an empire run like a machine,
and the khan took a liking to the young venetian:
made him an envoy, sent him across the realm,
let him see everything.
marco at the khan's court.
seventeen years of service ahead —
and every wonder written down,
for a book no one would believe
and everyone would read.

the yuan dynasty 1279 ce china kublai khan completes the conquest of song china — the last boy emperor drowned off the coast, the yuan dynasty begins, mongol khans on the dragon throne. the last song emperor was eight years old —
a child, on a ship, off the guangdong coast —
and when the yuan fleet closed in,
his minister took him in his arms
and jumped into the sea.
i heard the story from a fisherman
who watched the sails go down:
the boy emperor, the loyal minister,
the end of three hundred years of song.
kublai khan was emperor of all china now —
the yuan dynasty, the first foreign dynasty
to rule the whole country —
mongol khans on the dragon throne,
ruling the richest civilization on earth
from their new capital at dadu.
china, conquered entire.
it had never happened before.
the scholar-officials wept —
and then, mostly, went back to work.

great zimbabwe rises 1280 ce africa stone walls rise on the zimbabwe plateau — great zimbabwe, mortarless granite enclosures ruling the gold trade, eighteen thousand people in a city of stone. on the plateau, they were building in stone —
no mortar, just granite blocks,
fitted by hand, course on course,
walls thirty feet high, curving like a held breath:
great zimbabwe.
i walked the enclosures while the builders were at it —
the great enclosure, the hill complex,
the soapstone birds on their columns,
watching over the gold trade:
the interior's gold, flowing to the swahili coast,
to kilwa, to arabia, to china.
a city of stone in a land of thatch —
eighteen thousand people at its height,
ruled by kings whose names the stones don't tell.
the europeans would later refuse to believe
africans built it.
the stones don't care what europeans believe.
they're still standing.

the second divine wind 1281 ce japan a second, greater mongol armada — four thousand ships — breaks on japan's shores in a second typhoon; the kamikaze twice proven, and kublai never tries again. kublai tried again —
bigger this time: four thousand ships,
a hundred and forty thousand men,
the largest naval invasion in history
until normandy —
and japan was ready:
the wall at hakata, the samurai waiting,
the whole country mobilized.
i watched the fleets gather off the coast —
mongol, chinese, korean banners,
an armada to end the world —
and then the typhoon came again.
bigger than the first.
the divine wind, twice.
the fleet was annihilated —
ships smashed, men drowned,
the invasion destroyed in days of storm —
and kublai never tried a third time.
japan's founding miracle, confirmed:
the gods protect these islands.
twice proven.
never forgotten.

the ring of stone 1283 ce wales edward i's great castles close around wales — caernarfon, conwy, harlech, beaumaris — conquest built in stone, the most beautiful subjugation ever raised. edward built them to last —
the ring of castles around wales:
caernarfon, conwy, harlech, beaumaris,
the greatest fortresses in europe,
designed by master james of st. george,
paid for with english taxes,
garrisoned with english soldiers.
i walked the walls at conwy while the masons were finishing —
eight towers, the town walled with it,
the whole thing a machine for holding a country down —
and the welsh understood exactly what it was:
conquest, built in stone,
a ring of iron around their mountains.
seven hundred years later the castles are still there —
tourists photograph them now —
but the welsh remember what they were for.
the most beautiful subjugation
ever built.

kilwa's golden age 1285 ce east africa the kilwa sultanate mints its own gold coins — swahili traders ruling the ocean's western shore, middlemen of the monsoon, one of the finest cities ibn battuta will ever see. on an island off the african coast,
the sultans of kilwa were minting gold coins —
their own currency, their own name on the metal —
and the dhows came from everywhere:
arabia, persia, india, china,
trading cloth and porcelain for gold and ivory.
i walked the markets of kilwa kisiwani —
the great mosque, the palace on the cliff,
husuni kubwa with its hundred rooms —
and the swahili traders ran the ocean's western shore
like the venetians ran theirs:
middlemen of the monsoon,
rich on the wind's schedule.
ibn battuta would visit in fifty years
and call it one of the finest cities in the world.
he wasn't wrong.
the gold coins are still being found —
kilwa's name, in arabic script,
on metal from the interior's rivers.

the grand canal reborn 1288 ce china kublai khan rebuilds the grand canal — a thousand miles of waterway pumping southern rice to the northern capital, the yuan's great artery, empires running on logistics. kublai needed grain in the north —
his capital at dadu, a million mouths,
and the rice grew in the south —
so he rebuilt the grand canal:
a thousand miles of waterway,
cutters and locks, the greatest engineering project
of the medieval world.
i rode a grain barge down the new canal —
the locks lifting us, the towpaths,
the endless procession of barges,
rice for the capital, moving north like a river in reverse —
and the engineers told me the numbers:
tens of thousands of laborers, years of digging,
a waterway the sui had dreamed
and the yuan finally finished.
grain flows north.
empires run on logistics —
and the canal was the yuan's great artery,
pumping rice to the throne.

the expulsion 1290 ce england edward i expels the jews from england — sixteen thousand people, property seized, the first complete expulsion in europe, a shame that stands three and a half centuries. edward signed the edict in july —
the jews of england, all of them,
expelled:
their property seized, their debts canceled
(the king kept the profitable ones),
sixteen thousand people given months to leave
the only country most had ever known.
i watched them go from the ports —
london, the cinque ports,
families with what they could carry,
the sea crossing to france, to flanders —
and england became the first country in europe
to expel its jews entirely.
three and a half centuries, the shame stood —
until cromwell let them back, quietly, unproclaimed.
the edict was about money, mostly —
the king's debts, the lenders' usefulness ended —
dressed up as piety.
it always is.

acre falls 1291 ce holy land the mamluks take acre and raze it — the last crusader stronghold falls, two hundred years of crusading ending not with a treaty but with a wrecking crew. the mamluks came in may —
al-ashraf khalil, with the great siege engines,
the trebuchets, the sappers —
and acre, the last crusader stronghold,
the great port, the kingdom's window to the sea,
held for six weeks, and fell.
i was on a ship in the harbor when the walls went —
the street fighting, the towers coming down,
the templars dying in their fortress to the last man,
the refugees clawing onto the boats —
and when it was over, the mamluks razed it:
acre, leveled, so no crusader would ever hold it again.
the crusades ended there —
two hundred years, from clermont to acre —
not with a treaty, but with a wrecking crew.
the holy land was muslim again.
it would stay that way
for six hundred years.

death of kublai khan 1294 ce china kublai khan dies at dadu — the empire he built begins its slow, stately unraveling into four khanates, one in name, four in fact. he died at dadu, at seventy-eight —
kublai khan, the great khan, the emperor of china,
gouty, grieving, grown huge and melancholy
after his wife chabi's death —
and the empire he'd built began, gently, to come apart.
i stood in the mourning crowds at the capital —
mongols, chinese, persians, all of them,
for a ruler who'd been all things to all of them —
and the succession was already quarreling:
the yuan in china, the ilkhans in persia,
the golden horde in russia, chagatai in the middle —
one empire in name, four in fact.
he'd conquered china. built the canal.
sent the fleets to japan and java.
failed at both, and it hardly mattered:
the yuan would hold china for another seventy years.
the great khan was dead.
the unraveling, slow and stately, had begun.

the million dictated 1298 ce italy prisoner in genoa, marco polo dictates his travels to rustichello — the million, the book the scoffers call lies, that will sit annotated on columbus's shelf two centuries later. he was a prisoner in genoa —
marco polo, captured in a sea battle between venice and genoa,
stuck in a cell with a romance writer named rustichello —
and to pass the time, he talked.
i like to imagine that cell —
the venetian merchant, the pisan hack,
and the story pouring out:
the khan's court, the paper money,
the burning black stones, the millions of cathay —
rustichello writing it all down,
dressing it up like an arthurian romance,
calling it the million —
a million lies, the scoffers said.
it wasn't lies. it was the truth,
stranger than any romance —
and the book went everywhere:
translated, copied, read by kings and merchants —
and two hundred years later,
a genoese sailor named columbus
would carry it, annotated, across the atlantic,
looking for the khan.
end of volume iii — continued in volume iv.

the first holy year 1300 ce rome boniface viii opens the first jubilee, and pilgrims flood rome in numbers no one has ever seen, all of them hungry for forgiveness. i stood in the road-dust with a hundred thousand others,
bare feet, staffs, the whole year spilling toward one city.
boniface had thrown the doors of heaven open wide
and promised: come to rome, and your sins go with the tide.
old women who had never left their villages
walked over mountains for a pardon.
i watched them kneel on the worn stone steps,
and i tell you — they believed. they believed hard enough
to carry their whole villages on their backs.
that is a power no army ever owned.

the yuan at its height 1300 ce china under kublai's heirs the yuan rules all china — paper money, the grand canal, and cities of unmatched size — at the very crest of its power. in hangzhou i counted bridges like stars in a river,
paper money changing hands before the ink dried,
the grand canal a black shining road of barges
carrying grain to cities bigger than any in the world.
kublai is gone but his heirs hold the whole of it —
every roof, every harbor, every taxed stalk of rice.
i ate noodles in a market with a thousand stalls
and thought: this is what the peak feels like.
nobody on a peak knows they are standing on one.

dante is cast out 1302 ce florence florence exiles dante alighieri under sentence of burning, and the homeless poet begins the long road that will produce his great vision. they sentenced him to fire if he ever came back —
burned alive, by his own neighbors, over a street fight of politics.
i saw him leave through the gate at dusk,
a man with nothing but his name and his tongue.
florence thought it was throwing away a troublemaker.
florence did not know it was forging one.
give a man exile and grief enough,
and he will build you a world out of it —
hell, heaven, and everything in between.

the king summons the three estates 1302 ce france philip iv gathers clergy, nobles, and townsmen into the first estates-general — a king borrowing the people's voice to pay for his quarrels. priest, sword, and plow — philip called them all into one room,
the first time a king of france ever asked the town men to sit down with him.
he needed their money for his war with the pope,
so he dressed it up as counsel.
i watched the burghers take their benches,
awkward, new, learning the weight of the thing they'd been handed.
kings only summon people to share a table
when they are too poor to eat alone.

the golden spurs of kortrijk 1302 ce flanders flemish townsmen and farmers crush the french knighthood at kortrijk and hang the dead knights' golden spurs as trophies — the common man's day. five hundred pairs of golden spurs, hung in a church,
stripped from french knights by weavers and farmers.
i walked that field at kortrijk after the pikes did their work —
the flower of france trampled in a ditch by men with guild banners.
the knights had laughed at them that morning.
nobody laughed by evening.
a pike in a craftsman's hands
does not care about your grandfather's name.

the outrage at anagni 1303 ce italy french agents seize pope boniface viii in his palace at anagni; the humiliation breaks him, and he dies within weeks. they broke into the pope's own palace at anagni,
french roughs with a grudge and a king's orders,
and laid hands on boniface — the vicar of christ,
dragged about like a thief.
he lived three weeks after, and died of it —
of the shame, they said. of being shown
that a crown can reach into the sanctuary
and find nothing there to stop it.
i stood outside when they carried him out.
even the bells sounded smaller.

the fall of chittor 1303 ce india alauddin khalji storms chittor, and the rajput defenders choose the funeral fire over surrender — a fortress taken, a people unconquered. when the walls could not hold, the rajputs chose the fire.
i have never seen anything like that morning at chittor —
women and children walking into the flames in their wedding silks,
the men riding out in saffron to die on the swords below,
because surrender to alauddin was worse than the pyre.
the sultan got his fortress.
what he did not get were its people.
some victories are just ruins with nobody left to rule.

death of the mongol ruler 1304 ce persia ghazan khan, the mongol ruler who made islam the faith of his persian realm, dies — conqueror turned believer. ghazan is dead — the khan who traded the sky-father's worship
for the faith of the prophet, and made persia bow with him.
i rode past tabriz the week the news came,
and the bazaars went quiet in a way bazaars never do.
a mongol king on a persian throne, praying toward mecca:
that was the world turning over in one man's lifetime.
the horsemen who came to conquer stayed to belong.
that is the oldest story the steppe ever told.

stirling falls 1304 ce scotland edward i's siege engines smash stirling castle, the last scottish stronghold — and the hammer mistakes a fallen fortress for a finished war. edward brought his great engines north and aimed them at stirling
until the walls came down in pieces.
i watched the stones fall — months of hammering,
the last stronghold of the scots broken open like a nut.
the garrison walked out barefoot with ropes around their necks.
the hammer thought that was the end of it.
castles fall. countries don't, not that easy.
he'd learn. they always learn late.

giotto paints the chapel 1305 ce padua giotto fills the scrovegni chapel with frescoes that give saints real bodies, real grief, real weight — heaven learning to look human. i slipped into the scrovegni chapel while the plaster was still damp
and watched giotto's saints look back at me like neighbors.
before him, holy figures floated flat and gold and far away.
giotto gave them weight. grief with a face on it.
a mother holding her child like a real mother.
standing there among those wet blue walls,
i understood: he wasn't painting heaven.
he was teaching heaven how to look like us.

the death of wallace 1305 ce london william wallace is executed in london with full medieval cruelty — and england makes him the martyr scotland will never let die. they hanged him, cut him down living, and quartered him at smithfield —
wallace, who had beaten england's armies and asked for nothing but scotland.
i was in the crowd. i will not describe the worst of it.
here is what matters: they meant it as a warning.
they sent his head to london bridge and his limbs to four towns,
and scotland gathered every piece of him up into a story
no king's sword could ever touch again.
kill the man. crown the ghost.

a frenchman takes the papacy 1305 ce france clement v, a frenchman, becomes pope and never goes to rome — the papacy's long captivity to france begins with a smile and a handshake. clement v — a gascon, a frenchman, philip's friend —
takes the chair of peter, and rome feels the ground shift.
he never even set foot in rome as pope.
the papacy was already walking north,
out of the smoke of anagni, toward the rhone,
toward a king's protection that would cost everything.
i watched the cardinals congratulate each other.
they thought they'd chosen a pope.
they'd chosen a leash.

the bruce takes the crown 1306 ce scotland robert the bruce murders his rival in a church, then seizes scotland's crown — a kingdom's freedom founded on a sacrilege the scots accept. he killed his rival comyn inside a church — on holy ground, with a dagger —
then rode to scone and took the crown with blood still on his conscience.
i saw robert the bruce crowned that march day,
a small ceremony, a stolen throne, a kingdom half-beaten.
murder in a sanctuary. then the anointing.
scotland's freedom was born in a sacrilege,
and the scots decided they could live with that.
desperate countries forgive their kings almost anything.

the hammer of the scots dies 1307 ce england edward i dies on campaign against scotland, and the weak edward ii inherits — the whole weight of an empire shifting in a single heartbeat. edward i died on the road north, in his armor, still marching on scotland —
the hammer of the scots, worn out at last by his own wars.
his son edward ii took the crown: soft hands, favorites, no stomach for the work.
i stood among the soldiers when the news came.
relief ran through the scottish hills like a thaw.
one man's whole reign ends, and everything tilts —
that's how fragile an empire is. it fits inside one dying chest.

the ottoman turks rise 1307 ce anatolia osman i's small frontier princedom quietly swallows byzantine border forts one by one — the hairline crack nobody in constantinople noticed. out on the byzantine frontier, osman's riders were taking one border fort at a time —
small work, patient work, the kind nobody in constantinople bothered to fear.
i rode with a caravan through those hills and heard the talk:
the old empire rotting, the new ghazis rising,
village by village, tower by tower.
nobody writes songs about the year the foundation cracked.
they write them later, when the whole house comes down.
this was the crack.

henry vii elected emperor 1308 ce germany henry vii takes the imperial crown dreaming of restoring the empire's lost glory in italy — one more generation chasing the old ghost. henry of luxembourg took the imperial crown
and dreamed the old dream: rome, italy, the empire made whole again.
i watched him ride south with his knights,
a decent man carrying a hundred-year-old fantasy on his shoulders.
the german princes cheered him. the italian cities braced.
every generation elects somebody to chase a ghost.
sometimes the ghost chases back.

the papacy moves to france 1309 ce avignon clement v settles the papal court in avignon, beginning seventy years of exile — rome abandoned, heaven's machinery relocated to france. clement settled his court at avignon, by the rhone,
and the popes would not see rome for seventy years.
seventy years. a lifetime.
i walked the streets of avignon as they built the palace up —
clerks, bankers, petitioners, the whole machinery of heaven
relocating to france like a government in exile.
rome sat empty, its churches crumbling.
the fisherman's chair had moved house,
and nobody asked the fishermen.

the arsenal's assembly line 1310 ce venice venice expands its great arsenal, the shipyard that assembles war galleys on a production line — organization as a weapon. i stood at the arsenal's gates and watched war galleys come off the line
like loaves from an oven — ribs, planks, oars, rigging,
each crew at its station, the ships moving down the canal
faster than any shipwright's yard on earth had ever built.
venice had turned shipbuilding into a machine.
no prayers, no miracles — just organization.
that is the real venetian secret, and it sailed.

the roads of gold and salt 1310 ce mali across the sahara, salt trades weight for weight with gold, and mali grows rich on the desert road — an empire built on thirst. weight for weight — salt for gold, across the burning sahara.
i traveled with a salt caravan out of taghaza,
men wrapped against the white glare, camels groaning under slabs of salt
worth their weight in gold at the other end.
mali grew fat on that road. timbuktu glittered because of it.
the desert is not empty. it is a river, and it flows with wealth —
if you are hard enough to sail it.

the slaughter at halmyros 1311 ce greece catalan mercenaries lure the frankish knights of athens into a marsh at halmyros and annihilate them in a single morning — hired swords changing history. one morning at halmyros, the catalan company — hired swords, owed back pay —
stood in a marsh and butchered the flower of frankish athens.
i walked the field after. the knights had charged straight into the bog,
heavy horse, bright banners, straight into the mud,
and the catalans cut them down like wheat.
athens changed masters before noon.
mercenaries don't need a cause. they need a grievance and a dry place to stand.

the council of vienne 1311 ce france bishops gather at vienne to judge the age's scandals — the templars dissolved, the church's map of power redrawn under a watching king. bishops from everywhere gathered at vienne to judge the age's scandals —
the templars' gold, the priests' sins, the map of power redrawn
while philip of france watched from the edge of the room.
i sat in the back and listened to the latin roll on.
they condemned, they dissolved, they reorganized.
that is what councils do: they bury the old sins under new paperwork
and call it reform.
the templars were already dead. this was the funeral.

mansa musa takes the throne 1312 ce mali mansa musa takes mali's throne, inheriting a gold empire — and already dreaming of the journey that will carry his name across the world. the throne of mali passed to musa, and the man had dreams
bigger than any king before him —
not just gold, but the name of his kingdom carried to the ends of the earth.
i saw him hold court at niani, the griots singing his line,
the gold of bambuk piled like harvest.
he was already planning the journey that would make him legend.
some kings inherit a crown. he intended to inherit the world's attention.

an emperor dies in tuscany 1313 ce italy henry vii dies of fever on campaign in tuscany — and dante's dream of a united italy is buried with him. henry vii died of fever at buonconvento, on campaign in tuscany,
and with him died dante's great hope — a united italy under one emperor.
i was in siena when the body passed through.
the ghibellines wept. the guelfs breathed again.
one man's fever, and a poet's dream of a nation
goes into the ground with him.
history turns on such small things: a mosquito, a summer, a tired heart.

bannockburn 1314 ce scotland robert the bruce's spearmen shatter edward ii's great army at bannockburn — scotland wins its freedom in two days of mud and courage. two days by the bannock burn, and bruce's spearmen —
a bristling hedge of scottish pikes — broke the greatest army england ever sent north.
i was on the ridge when the english knights charged into that thicket of points
and came apart like cloth on thorns.
edward ii ran. his nobles died or were taken.
scotland won its freedom in a day of mud and shouting,
and no english king would ever take it back.
some battles end wars. this one made a nation.

the great hunger begins 1315 ce europe endless rains drown the harvests and the great famine begins — no enemy, no war, just a closed sky and bread worth more than gold. the rains came and did not stop. the grain rotted in the fields,
the seed for next year went into hungry mouths,
and bread became worth more than gold.
i walked through villages where the children had bellies like drums
and the churchyards filled faster than the gravediggers could dig.
no enemy did this. no king ordered it.
the sky just closed, and kept closed,
and europe learned what it is to be small.

the ambush at morgarten 1315 ce switzerland swiss mountaineers crush habsburg knights in the pass at morgarten with rocks and halberds — the valleys' freedom born in an avalanche. the habsburg knights rode into the pass at morgarten in their shining armor,
and the swiss were waiting above with rocks, logs, and halberds.
i heard it before i saw it — the avalanche of stone and men,
the great horses screaming in the narrow defile.
fifteen hundred nobles' pride, broken by farmers who knew their mountains.
the valleys would never kneel again.
freedom, in switzerland, was born in a rockslide.

the hunger's worst year 1316 ce europe in the famine's worst year the starving dead outnumber any army's toll — europe's quietest catastrophe, buried without trumpets. this was the blackest year — the third harvest failed,
and the starving dead outnumbered any army's toll.
i saw mothers trade their wedding rings for a loaf,
saw men eat grass, bark, things i will not name.
the chroniclers wrote it down in careful latin.
the dead did not care about the latin.
when the famine finally lifted, europe had buried
more of its children than any war had ever taken.
remember this when men boast of their battles.

a bruce crowned across the sea 1316 ce ireland edward bruce is crowned high king of ireland, carrying scotland's war across the sea — a brave, doomed gamble for irish freedom. edward bruce — robert's brother, all fire and no patience —
was crowned high king of ireland, carrying scotland's war
onto english-held land across the sea.
i watched the irish chiefs kneel to a foreign bruce,
hoping a scottish sword would cut their english chains.
it was a brave gamble. it was a doomed one.
but for a little while, the irish had a king of their own choosing,
and that is a thing no defeat can take back.

the hunger breaks 1317 ce europe after three years the rains relent and the famine breaks — europe buries its dead, counts the terrible cost, and weeps over bread. after three years the rains relented. the sun came back like a pardon.
i walked through fields where the new wheat stood green and trembling,
and people wept over bread — actual tears, over bread.
europe buried its dead and counted the cost:
villages emptied, children gone, a generation thinned.
the famine ended. the fear didn't, not for years.
every full granary after that was a small prayer of thanks.

the razor of ockham 1318 ce oxford william of ockham teaches that the simplest answer is usually right — a razor that cuts dogma too, and the church will not forgive him. a thin friar at oxford named william of ockham
taught his students to shave the world down:
when two answers explain a thing, take the simpler.
don't multiply mysteries. cut.
the church heard the blade and did not forgive him —
a razor like that cuts through dogma too.
i sat in his lectures, cold stone, hot ideas.
he gave the world a tool sharper than any sword,
and paid for it with exile.
truth is simple. saying so is dangerous.

the white battle 1319 ce england scots raiders rout a host of yorkshire priests and levies at myton — the white battle, where war shows it doesn't spare holy men. at myton the scots fell on an english host of priests and levies —
the white battle, they called it, for all the clerics in the ranks.
i saw the rout from a hillside: the northern men scattering,
their holy banners trampled in the mud of yorkshire.
war does not check your collar before it kills you.
the north paid dearly that day, in coin and in clergy,
and the border learned again what it always learns:
nobody is safe when the raiders come down.

the declaration of arbroath 1320 ce scotland scotland's lords write to the pope at arbroath: they will never submit to england, under any king — a letter wielded like a weapon. they wrote to the pope on parchment at arbroath —
the lords of scotland, in latin, plain as a punch:
we will never submit to england. not under this king. not under any king.
it is for freedom alone that we fight, they wrote,
not for glory or riches.
i watched the seals pressed into the wax, one by one.
a letter. that was their weapon — a letter to rome.
and it worked. words, aimed right, can hold off an army.

the tughlaqs take delhi 1320 ce delhi ghiyasuddin tughlaq founds a new dynasty over delhi, india's richest sultanate — another season turning in the city's long wheel of kings. ghiyasuddin tughlaq rode into delhi and founded his dynasty
over the richest sultanate in india —
a soldier's hand on a jeweled throne.
i walked the streets as the new banners went up,
the old officials bowing low, the new ones counting the treasury.
dynasties change the way seasons do in delhi:
suddenly, completely, and everyone pretends it was always going to happen.
the tughlaqs would rule hard and strange and brilliant.
this was the first stone of it.

the shepherds' crusade 1320 ce france peasant crusaders march south, then turn their crosses on jews and priests — a holy dream curdling into a mob, put down in blood. they started as shepherds with crosses, marching south for the holy land —
poor boys with a holy dream and empty bellies.
then the dream curdled. they turned on the jews in the southern towns,
then on priests who wouldn't bless their plunder.
i saw the columns pass: ragged, singing, dangerous.
a crusade without a king is just a mob with a banner.
france put them down in blood, the way france does.
the crosses went into the mud. the hatred stayed.

dante dies in exile 1321 ce ravenna dante dies in ravenna, still exiled from florence — his great vision of hell and heaven complete, the homeless poet at rest at last. he died in ravenna, far from florence, the sentence of fire still on his head —
dante, who never saw home again after that dusk at the gate.
but he had finished the work: the whole journey,
hell's circles, the mountain, the stars,
written out of exile and grief and one unshakeable woman.
i stood at his tomb. florence wanted the body back.
ravenna kept it. ravenna was right to keep it —
the city that sheltered the poet owns the poet.
exile made him. exile keeps him.

the last direct capetian 1322 ce france charles iv takes the french crown and the direct capetian line runs out — three hundred years ending not with a battle but with no more sons. charles iv took the french crown, and with him the old line ran out —
three hundred years of capetians, father to son, ending in a quiet room.
no drama. no battle. just no more sons.
i watched the courtiers do the arithmetic on their fingers:
who inherits now? whose claim? whose blood?
a dynasty doesn't always fall to the sword.
sometimes it just... stops. like a candle burned to the socket.
and in the dark after, men start reaching for knives.

the defender of peace 1324 ce padua marsilius of padua writes that the people, not the pope, should rule the city — the whole order of things questioned in clean sentences. marsilius of padua wrote it plain: the people should rule the city,
not the pope. power comes from the citizens, not from heaven's keys.
i read the defensor pacis by lamplight in a paduan lodging,
and felt the floor tilt — this was the whole order of things, questioned,
in clean sentences, by a university man.
the church called it heresy. the cities called it hope.
ideas like that don't die when you burn the book.
they just find new paper.

mansa musa's golden pilgrimage 1324 ce mecca mansa musa crosses the desert to mecca with a caravan of gold so vast it crashes the price of gold in cairo — africa's king revealed to the world. he crossed the desert to mecca with sixty thousand in his train
and gold — so much gold that the price of gold fell in cairo
and stayed fallen for years.
i was in cairo when the caravan arrived: the dust, the drums,
musa handing out gold like a man scattering seed.
the whole world learned his name that year.
a king from beyond the desert, richer than the caliphs,
on his knees in mecca like the poorest pilgrim.
gold passes. that image never did.

tenochtitlan is founded 1325 ce mexico the mexica raise tenochtitlan on an island in lake texcoco — a muddy beginning for the city that will rule an empire. on an island in lake texcoco, the mexica drove the first stakes
and raised the first thatch — tenochtitlan, the city that would rule an empire.
they were wanderers then, latecomers, told the lake was all that was left for them.
i stood on the shore and watched the causeways begin.
a muddy island. an eagle on a cactus, if you believe the story.
nobody looking at that swamp would have guessed:
this becomes the greatest city in the world that europe never imagined.

ibn battuta sets out 1325 ce morocco a young scholar leaves tangier for mecca and doesn't come home for thirty years — ibn battuta walks the whole known world and writes it down. a young scholar walked out of tangier bound for mecca,
meaning to come straight home — and didn't come home for thirty years.
i met him years later, older, thinner, full of roads:
india, china, the steppe, the swahili coast, mali.
seventy-five thousand miles on foot, horse, and dhow.
ibn battuta didn't discover the world. he just walked all of it
and wrote it down so the rest of us could follow.

the queen invades 1326 ce england isabella of france lands with an army and topples her husband edward ii — a queen deposing her king, cleanly and forever after imitated. isabella of france landed with an army and a grievance —
her husband edward ii had given his heart to favorites
and his kingdom to ruin.
i watched her march on london, and london opened its gates to her.
the king ran. they caught him. the rest was a cell and a rumor
too ugly to write down.
a queen deposing her king: it had never been done so cleanly.
she didn't just topple a throne. she showed every wife of every weak king
exactly how it was done.

bursa falls to the ottomans 1326 ce anatolia orhan takes bursa, giving the ottoman turks their first true capital — frontier raiders becoming a state with a throne-city. orhan took bursa after a long siege, and the ottomans had their first true capital —
a real city, with walls and markets and a future.
i walked its streets as the new banners went up over the gates.
this was the moment the frontier raiders became a state:
not just horsemen taking forts, but rulers with a throne-city.
bursa would be their heart for a century.
every empire starts with one city it can call home.
this was theirs.

a boy becomes king 1327 ce england edward iii is crowned at fourteen, with his mother and her lover ruling through him — a boy watching, learning, and counting the days. edward iii was crowned at fourteen — a boy king,
with his mother isabella and her lover mortimer ruling through him.
i saw the boy at westminster, straight-backed, trying to look older.
everyone in the hall knew who really held the reins.
but boys grow. and this one was watching, learning,
counting the days.
three years. that's all the regents got.
then the boy struck, and england learned what kind of king he'd be.

death of the mystic 1327 ce germany meister eckhart dies — the mystic who preached that god lives in the soul's deepest ground, in plain german the church couldn't silence. meister eckhart died — the preacher who told the crowds
that god lives in the soul's deepest ground,
closer than your own breath, past all the church's machinery.
they tried him for heresy. he died before they could finish.
i heard him preach once, in a packed church:
plain german, no latin tricks, god as near as your heartbeat.
the church buried the man. it couldn't bury the sentence.
it's still out there, working.

the valois take the crown 1328 ce france philip vi is crowned, first of the valois — a new house on the old throne, while across the channel edward iii studies his own claim. philip vi was crowned, first of the valois —
a new house, a cousin's line, because the old capetians ran out of sons.
i stood in the crowd at reims and watched the anointing.
new crown, new name, same throne.
but across the channel, edward of england was doing his own arithmetic:
his mother was a capetian princess. why not him?
a succession settled in reims. a war conceived in london.
nobody cheered louder than the future.

moscow rises under ivan the moneybag 1328 ce russia ivan kalita gathers the mongols' tribute and quietly buys moscow's rise — no battles, just money, patience, and the khan's favor. ivan kalita — ivan the moneybag — gathered the mongols' tribute
and skimmed, saved, and bought, quietly making moscow russia's center.
i drank with merchants in his moscow and heard how it worked:
collect for the khan, keep a little, lend a little, buy a village.
no battles. just money, patience, and the khan's favor.
while the other princes fought over scraps, ivan bought the table.
empires have been built with less.

cassel: the peasants are crushed 1328 ce flanders french knights slaughter the flemish rebels at cassel, ending the peasants' rising — kortrijk's triumph answered in blood. at cassel the french knights rode down the flemish rebels
and ended the peasants' rising in a morning of slaughter.
twenty-six years after kortrijk's golden spurs,
the wheel turned: the horsemen learned, the footmen bled.
i walked that field too. different field, same lesson —
the poor can win a battle, but the rich own the war,
until the day they don't.
flanders would remember both fields.
so would france.

the bruce dies 1329 ce scotland robert the bruce dies; his embalmed heart is carried toward the holy land by his knight — the king's last crusade, fought by his heart alone. robert the bruce died in his bed — the king who won scotland at bannockburn,
gone quietly after a life of war and hiding and murder and glory.
his last wish: his heart cut out, embalmed, and carried to the holy land
by his knight douglas, since his body couldn't make the crusade.
i saw the casket leave. douglas died fighting in spain with it at his neck.
the heart came home. the legend never left.
some men die. some men get carried.

velbazhd: serbia breaks bulgaria 1330 ce balkans the serbs crush the bulgarians at velbazhd and serbia becomes the balkans' great power — while across the strait, the turks take notes. at velbazhd the serbs crushed the bulgarians,
and serbia stood up as the balkans' great power.
i watched stefan dusan's host break the bulgarian line —
two christian kingdoms bleeding each other
while the turks watched from across the strait and took notes.
the balkans' tragedy in one afternoon:
the strong devouring the strong, and the real enemy waiting offshore.
serbia's noon. the shadow was already lengthening.

the young king strikes 1330 ce england edward iii arrests his mother's lover mortimer and seizes power — three years of watching ended in one night of action. at nineteen, edward iii struck — his men seized mortimer in the queen's own chambers
at nottingham, dragged him out, and took him to the block.
his mother fell to her knees begging. the boy didn't blink.
i was at court that autumn and felt the whole room recalculate:
the regency was over. the king was the king.
three years of watching, and one night of action.
that is how you take back a throne — all at once, no rehearsal.

the weavers cross the sea 1331 ce england edward iii lures flemish weavers to england, planting the looms that will clothe a nation — centuries of wealth, one immigrant shuttle at a time. edward lured the flemish weavers across the sea —
master craftsmen with their looms and their secrets,
planted in english towns to clothe a nation.
i watched them set up their frames in the cotswolds,
strange accents, deft hands, the shuttle flying.
england had the wool. now it had the weavers.
centuries of wealth started here, in workshops smelling of lanolin,
one immigrant loom at a time.

amda seyon's holy wars 1331 ce ethiopia ethiopia's christian king amda seyon campaigns south, widening his mountain empire — holy war in africa while europe fights its own. down in the highlands, amda seyon — ethiopia's christian king —
campaigned south with his armies, widening his mountain empire
against muslim sultanates and pagan tribes alike.
i traveled with a caravan through the highlands after one campaign:
burned villages, new churches, the cross planted further south.
a holy war in africa while europe fought its own —
the world is wider than the maps in rome.
his chronicles called it god's work. the burned villages had another word.

ibn khaldun is born 1332 ce tunis in tunis a boy is born who will invent the science of how civilizations rise and fall — ibn khaldun, the historians' historian. in tunis a boy was born who would invent the science
of how civilizations rise and fall —
ibn khaldun, who watched dynasties crumble in north africa and spain
and asked why. why do empires harden, soften, rot?
he'd write the answer in a book called the muqaddima,
centuries before anyone else thought to ask the question.
i held the newborn's century in my hands and didn't know it.
the historians' historian, born in an ordinary house.

kamakura falls 1333 ce japan kamakura falls and emperor go-daigo briefly retakes the throne — a bright, brief restoration, doomed when the swords disagree. the shogun's capital at kamakura fell to the emperor's forces,
and go-daigo took back the throne his family had lost a century before.
i walked the smoking streets after the siege —
the hojo regents dead by their own hands, the old order in ashes.
the emperor ruled again. for three years.
three years, and then the warriors took it all back.
restorations are like that: bright, brief, and doomed
when the swords disagree.

halidon hill 1333 ce scotland english longbows mow down the scots at halidon hill — bannockburn's lesson reversed, and the border bleeds again. at halidon hill the english longbows did their terrible new work —
scots charging uphill into a storm of arrows,
mown down in ranks before they ever reached the line.
i stood on that hill and watched chivalry die by archery:
the flower of scotland falling like cut grain,
the border bleeding again.
bannockburn was nineteen years gone.
the english had learned. the scots paid the tuition.

the mongol realm crumbles 1335 ce persia the last strong ilkhan dies and persia's mongol empire shatters — a hundred years of conquest dissolving like salt in rain. the last strong ilkhan died, and persia's mongol empire
shattered into warring pieces — amirs, claimants, little kings,
every province for itself.
i rode through tabriz that year and felt the center go out of things:
no khan, no law, just swords and negotiations.
a hundred years of mongol persia, dissolving like salt in rain.
the horsemen had conquered a civilization.
then the civilization quietly conquered them —
and outlived them.

the ashikaga take kyoto 1336 ce japan ashikaga takauji seizes kyoto, crushing the emperor's restoration and founding the shogunate that will rule japan for two centuries. ashikaga takauji seized kyoto and founded the shogunate
that would rule japan for two hundred years —
the emperor's brief restoration crushed by the very general
who had made it possible.
i watched his banners go up over the capital.
betrayal? politics? in japan they called it the way of the warrior.
two centuries of ashikaga rule started here,
in a coup against the throne they'd sworn to restore.

timur is born 1336 ce transoxiana near samarkand a lame boy is born who will make the world tremble — timur, history's most unlikely vessel, already walking toward his destiny. near samarkand a boy was born with a lame leg and a boundless hunger —
timur, who would make the world tremble from delhi to damascus.
i saw the village. nothing in it promised anything.
a crippled shepherd's son in the back country of a broken mongol realm.
but history loves an unlikely vessel.
the lameness kept him off the khan's throne —
so he built a bigger one beside it, out of skulls.

gajah mada swears his oath 1336 ce java gajah mada vows to taste no spiced food until the whole archipelago bows to majapahit — the palapa oath, an empire built on an empty stomach. gajah mada, minister of majapahit, stood before his king and swore:
no spiced food would touch his lips until the whole archipelago
bowed to majapahit — every island, every harbor.
i heard the oath repeated in the markets of java,
men shaking their heads at the madness of it.
then he did it. island by island, year by year.
they called it the palapa oath.
a man can conquer an ocean on an empty stomach,
if the hunger is for something bigger than food.

vijayanagara is founded 1336 ce india two brothers raise vijayanagara, a new hindu capital defying delhi's sultans — the city of victory rising from river boulders. two brothers, harihara and bukka, raised a new hindu capital
on the tungabhadra — vijayanagara, the city of victory —
defying the sultans of delhi who thought the south was theirs.
i stood on the rocky hills above the river
and watched the first temples rise from the boulders.
a refuge, a fortress, a statement:
the south would not bow.
it would stand for two hundred years, glittering,
until the day it fell — but that day was far off,
and the stones were just being laid.

the hundred years' war begins 1337 ce france philip vi seizes aquitaine, edward iii claims the french throne — a century of war begins, and nobody understands what they've started. philip seized aquitaine. edward claimed the french throne.
and the long war started — the one that would grind for a hundred years,
fathers to sons to grandsons, over a crown and a coastline.
i was in paris when the news came, and nobody understood
what they were beginning. nobody ever does.
they thought it would be a campaign. a season.
it was a century.
the hundred years' war: the longest argument in europe's history,
and it started with paperwork.

edward iii marches into france 1339 ce france edward iii burns his way through northern france, daring philip to fight — smoke on every horizon, and a countryside taught to hate for a century. edward burned his way through northern france —
villages, barns, mills, everything that could feed an army,
daring philip to come out and fight.
i walked behind that chevauchee and saw what "daring" costs:
smoke on every horizon, farmers hiding in the woods,
a whole countryside taught to hate the english for a hundred years.
philip wouldn't fight. he just watched his kingdom burn.
sometimes the bravest thing a king can do is nothing.
sometimes it's the cruelest.

sluys: england rules the waves 1340 ce flanders english ships destroy the french fleet at sluys — twenty thousand men and the sea itself, and england rules the channel. at sluys the english ships closed on the french fleet
and destroyed it — masts, hulls, twenty thousand men,
the sea off flanders red and wreck-strewn.
i sailed those waters a week later and the wreckage was still washing up.
england ruled the channel now. no french army would ever cross it
while edward lived.
command of the sea: it sounds like a phrase from a chronicle.
it's actually just this — the other fellow's ships, on the bottom.

petrarch crowned with laurel 1341 ce rome petrarch is crowned poet laureate on the capitol, rome's first in a thousand years — the renaissance beginning with a laurel wreath, not a painting. on the capitol at rome, they crowned francesco petrarch with laurel —
poet laureate, the first in a thousand years, since the ancients.
i was in the crowd on that april day, and the romans wept:
their city, ruined and half-empty, crowning a poet like an emperor.
it wasn't about petrarch. it was about rome remembering itself —
the old glory, the old words, reaching up out of the rubble.
the renaissance didn't start with a painting.
it started with a wreath.

sailors reach the canaries 1341 ce atlantic portuguese and genoese sailors raid the canaries — europe reaches past the map's edge for plunder and comes back with a horizon. portuguese and genoese sailors raided the canary islands —
europe's first reach into the open atlantic, past the edge of the known map.
i talked to one of those sailors in lisbon, an old man by then,
and he described the islands rising out of nowhere,
the strange people, the birds, the feeling of sailing off the world's edge
and finding more world.
they went for plunder. they came back with a horizon.
that horizon would swallow everything.

the magnificent pope 1342 ce avignon clement vi lives in avignon like a king among kings — glittering, worldly, and yet the pope who will shield the jews when the plague comes. clement vi took the papal throne and lived in avignon
like a king among kings — feasts, jewels, mistresses, the works.
the fisherman's successor, dripping with gold.
i saw his court once: it glittered harder than any royal court in europe.
and yet — when the plague came, this same pope
would protect the jews of avignon with bulls and guards
while the rest of europe burned them.
men are complicated. even popes. especially popes.

the great banks fail 1345 ce florence edward iii's unpaid debts sink the bardi and peruzzi, florence's mightiest banks — kings borrow, bankers lend, kings don't pay. edward iii never paid his debts, and the bardi and peruzzi —
florence's mightiest banks, the lenders of kings — went down.
i was in florence when the doors closed: the panic,
the merchants ruined overnight, the whole city's credit in ashes.
kings borrow. bankers lend. kings don't pay.
that is the oldest story in finance, and florence learned it
the way everyone learns it — by losing everything.
the war went on. the money didn't.

crecy: the longbow's day 1346 ce france english yeomen with longbows shred french chivalry at crecy — the age of the knight ends, though the knights take a century to notice. at crecy the english yeomen stood in the mud with their longbows
and shredded the flower of french chivalry —
charge after charge, prince after prince,
cut down by clothyard arrows loosed by common men.
i walked that field at dusk. the french dead lay in windrows,
their armor worth more than the villages they'd ridden through.
the age of the knight ended at crecy.
it just took the knights another hundred years to notice.

dusan crowned emperor 1346 ce balkans stefan dusan is crowned emperor of serbs and greeks at skopje — serbia's beautiful noon, nine years from its afternoon. at skopje they crowned stefan dusan emperor of serbs and greeks —
the balkans' great power at its noon, law codes, churches, glory.
i watched the coronation procession wind through the streets,
gold and incense, the new emperor shining.
serbia's empire. it would last nine years past his death.
that's the thing about noons: they're beautiful,
and they're always followed by afternoon.
dusan didn't know. nobody at a coronation ever knows.

cola di rienzo seizes rome 1347 ce rome the young notary cola di rienzo seizes rome and proclaims the republic reborn — one bright season of the ancient dream, then the nobles return. cola di rienzo — a young notary, all fire and old books —
seized rome and proclaimed the republic reborn: the tribune, the ancient glory,
the people ruling as in the days of the caesars.
i was there for his first speech on the capitol. the crowd went mad with hope.
for a season, rome dreamed again.
then the nobles came back, and the dream went the way of dreams.
but for one season — one bright season — the republic lived.
that's more than most dreams get.

the plague ships dock at messina 1347 ce sicily plague galleys limp into messina and the pestilence comes ashore — the black death reaches europe, and a third of the world begins to die. the galleys limped into messina harbor from the east,
their crews dying at the oars, black swellings in their groins —
and the pestilence came ashore with them.
i stood on the docks and watched them tie up.
nobody knew what was in those holds.
nobody could have stopped it if they had.
the black death had reached europe.
everything after this — every empty village, every mass grave,
every bell tolling for a third of the world — started here,
with ropes thrown to a dying ship.

boccaccio begins the decameron 1348 ce florence fleeing plague-ravaged florence, boccaccio begins his hundred tales — laughter as defiance, stories as a wall against the dark. fleeing plague-ravaged florence, boccaccio started his hundred tales —
ten young people in a country villa, telling stories of love and wit
while the city died below them.
i read the first pages as he wrote them, in a borrowed room:
laughter as defiance, stories as a wall against the dark.
the plague took his father, his stepmother, half his city.
he answered with a hundred tales.
that is the human reply to the end of the world:
tell a story. tell another. keep telling them until morning.

a university for the empire 1348 ce prague in the plague year charles iv founds prague's university, the first in central europe — planting learning while the world buries its dead. in the plague year, charles iv founded a university at prague —
the first in central europe, scholars and masters,
a whole studium rising while the world was burying its dead.
i walked the building site that autumn: masons, timber, plans,
men arguing about aristotle over the sound of hammers.
plant a university in a plague year.
that is either madness or faith, and i have never been able
to tell the two apart.
prague's university still stands. the plague passed.

ayutthaya rises 1350 ce siam king ramathibodi founds ayutthaya, the siamese capital that will shine for four centuries — gold leaf and spires rising from the floodplain. king ramathibodi founded ayutthaya on its island in the river —
the siamese capital that would shine for four centuries,
temples and palaces rising from the floodplain.
i sailed upriver to see it new: the gold leaf, the spires,
the markets already humming.
four hundred years. that is a long time for a city to shine.
most capitals are lucky to get one good century.
ayutthaya got four — and the river still remembers.

the inca leave their valley 1350 ce andes inca warriors push beyond cuzco under capac yupanqui — the long climb to empire beginning, one next valley at a time. capac yupanqui's warriors pushed beyond the valley of cuzco —
the inca leaving home, the long climb to empire beginning.
i traveled those mountain trails and saw the first conquests:
small chiefdoms bowing, roads being cut through the clouds.
nobody in cuzco called it an empire yet.
it was just the next valley. then the next.
empires are built one "next valley" at a time,
until one day the map runs out of valleys.

the statute of labourers 1351 ce england parliament tries to freeze wages after the plague — and fails, because you can't legislate the value of arms when half the workers are dead. with half the workers dead of plague, parliament tried to freeze wages by law —
no man to ask more than he got before the pestilence,
on pain of prison.
i watched the justices try to enforce it in the villages.
the laborers laughed. the harvest couldn't wait for parliament's prices.
you cannot legislate the value of a man's arms
when there aren't enough arms left to bring the wheat in.
the statute failed. the workers won.
the plague had done what no revolt ever could:
made the poor expensive.

the red turbans rise 1351 ce china starving peasants tie red cloths round their heads and rise against the mongol yuan — hunger, the oldest revolutionary, losing its patience. starving peasants tied red cloths round their heads
and rose against the mongol yuan — the red turbans,
a famine turned into an army.
i saw them march through the yellow river country:
ragged, furious, numberless, the dynasty's granaries their target.
the yuan had ruled china for eighty years.
it took starving farmers with red headbands to end it.
hunger is the oldest revolutionary,
and it never loses its temper — it just loses its patience.

a king defies the mongols 1352 ce korea king gongmin moves to break the mongols' grip on korea — a small king with a long memory standing up to the greatest empire on earth. king gongmin of goryeo moved to break the mongols' grip on his court —
purging the pro-yuan faction, reclaiming korean land,
a small king standing up to the greatest empire on earth.
i was in kaesong when the orders went out.
the courtiers were terrified. the king was not.
eighty years of mongol domination, and one man decided:
no more.
small kingdoms have long memories and short tempers.
korea was about to be korea again.

the turks cross into europe 1354 ce thrace an earthquake topples gallipoli's walls and the ottomans walk in — their first foothold in europe, handed to them by the shaking earth. an earthquake toppled the walls of gallipoli,
and the ottomans walked in — their first foothold in europe,
handed to them by the shaking earth.
i stood in the rubble of those walls and felt the hinge of history move:
one tremor, and the turks were across the strait,
and they would never leave.
constantinople was still a hundred years from falling.
but the crack that started with osman's border forts
had just crossed the water.

the black prince's burning march 1355 ce france the black prince burns a black road across southern france — war as economics, and the terrible part is that it works. edward the black prince burned a swath through southern france —
town by town, farm by farm, the great chevauchee,
leaving a black road from bordeaux to the mediterranean.
i rode through languedoc after he'd passed:
the smell of it still in the air, the mills gutted, the vines trampled.
this was war as economics — burn the tax base,
and the king of france can't pay his armies.
it worked. it always works.
that's the terrible part.

poitiers: a king captured 1356 ce france the black prince captures john ii of france at poitiers — a kingdom without its king, and england holding the head. at poitiers the black prince's outnumbered english
captured john ii of france himself — the king, taken on the field,
led away to london to wait for a ransom that would beggar his kingdom.
i saw the french army dissolve that september day:
the flower of the nobility dead or fled, the oriflamme in the mud.
france reeled. paris rioted. the dauphin hid.
a kingdom without its king is a body without its head —
and england held the head.

the golden bull 1356 ce germany charles iv's golden bull fixes how emperors are chosen — seven electors sealed in gold, and germany's rules written for centuries. charles iv issued the golden bull, fixing how emperors are chosen —
seven electors, sealed in gold, the law of the empire for centuries.
i was in nuremberg when it was proclaimed.
no more disputed elections, no more civil wars over the crown —
at least, that was the idea.
it worked, after a fashion. germany got its rules.
whether rules make an empire is another question,
one the germans would spend four hundred years answering.

zhu yuanzhang takes nanjing 1356 ce china the peasant-rebel zhu yuanzhang seizes nanjing — twelve years from beggar's bowl to emperor's seal, and the yuan already a ghost. the peasant-rebel zhu yuanzhang — beggar, monk, red turban —
seized nanjing, his stepping-stone to the throne.
i walked that city as his banners went up:
a starving boy from the famine years, now master of the great southern capital.
twelve years from beggar's bowl to emperor's seal.
the yuan was finished; it just didn't know it yet.
when the poor boy takes the capital, the dynasty is already a ghost.

the hansa finds its voice 1356 ce lubeck the baltic merchant towns meet at lubeck and swear to sail and trade together — the hansa, a league of cities with no king, only contracts. the baltic merchant towns met at lubeck and swore to sail and trade together —
the hansa finding its voice, a league of cities with no king,
only contracts and convoys.
i drank in a lubeck guildhall that winter and heard the talk:
one fleet, one law of the sea, one fist against pirates and princes.
merchants had discovered what kings always knew —
there is strength in numbers —
and they'd done it without a single crown.

the jacquerie: the peasants rise 1358 ce france french peasants rise in the jacquerie, burn castles, and are drowned in blood — the poor speak, the rich answer, and france will hear it again. the peasants rose — the jacquerie — burning castles across northern france,
killing nobles, crying for bread and an end to the war-taxes.
for weeks the countryside belonged to them.
then the nobles came back with steel, and drowned the rising in blood —
villages burned in revenge, thousands hanged.
i walked those roads after. the silence was the worst of it.
the poor had spoken. the rich had answered.
france would hear that conversation again, four hundred years on.

the treaty of bretigny 1360 ce france england and france sign the treaty of bretigny — a truce neither believes, nine years of quiet bought by exhaustion. at bretigny they signed the truce — edward keeps his conquests,
john's ransom set at a king's weight in gold, the war pausing to breathe.
i was in the fields outside chartres where they met:
two exhausted kingdoms, signing a peace neither believed.
nine years of quiet. then it started again, as everyone knew it would.
treaties don't end wars. exhaustion pauses them.
this one bought france time — and france would use it well.

english returns to parliament 1362 ce england parliament orders english, not french, spoken in debates and laws — three hundred years after hastings, the people's tongue takes power. parliament ordered english — not french — spoken in its debates and laws.
three hundred years after hastings, the conquerors' tongue
gave way to the people's.
i sat in the gallery and heard it: plain english, in the king's own parliament,
the language of plowmen arguing the law of the land.
a quiet revolution, no blood, no banners —
just words changing their master.
england would never speak french in power again.

adrianople falls to the ottomans 1362 ce thrace the ottomans take adrianople, planting their flag deep in europe — constantinople now an island in a turkish sea, down to a city and a prayer. the ottomans took adrianople — the great city of thrace,
second city of the shrinking byzantine world —
and planted their flag deep in europe.
i walked its walls after the surrender: the mosques going up,
the turkish administration settling in like it had always been there.
constantinople was now an island in a turkish sea.
the empire that had stood for a thousand years
was down to a city and a prayer.
the prayer would last ninety-one more years.

lake poyang: the great river battle 1363 ce china two rebel fleets clash on lake poyang in one of history's greatest naval battles — the ming dynasty decided on a burning lake before it had a name. on lake poyang two rebel fleets clashed —
zhu yuanzhang against chen youliang, hundreds of war-junks,
tower ships, fire ships, one of the greatest naval battles in history.
i watched from the shore for three days: the smoke,
the burning towers toppling into the water, the lake itself on fire.
zhu won. chen died.
one lake, one battle, and the ming dynasty was decided
before it had a name.

charles the wise takes the throne 1364 ce france charles v is crowned — the canny king who will win france back without great battles, outlasting where others bled. charles v was crowned — charles the wise, the canny king
who would win france back without great battles:
no more crecys, no more poitiers, just patience, money, and du guesclin.
i saw him at reims: slight, sickly, bookish —
nothing like a warrior king.
the court underestimated him. everyone did.
then, castle by castle, tax by tax, year by year,
he took his kingdom back.
the wise don't need to win battles. they need to outlast them.

a king of cyprus sacks alexandria 1365 ce egypt peter i of cyprus storms alexandria in a last flash of crusading fire — magnificent, pointless, and already history by the time the sails go home. peter i of cyprus stormed alexandria —
a last flash of crusading fire, knights bursting through the gates
of the great muslim port, looting for days.
i walked the sacked streets after: the warehouses emptied,
the harbor full of christian sails, the mamluks regrouping inland.
it was magnificent. it was pointless.
they couldn't hold it. they sailed home with the plunder
and the dream died on the docks.
the crusades ended not with a trumpet but with a raid —
brave, brilliant, and already history.

the bastard invades 1366 ce castile henry of trastamara invades castile to tear the crown from his half-brother — brother against brother, and the throne changing hands like dice. henry of trastamara — the bastard — invaded castile
to tear the crown from his half-brother pedro the cruel,
with french knights at his back and a grudge in his heart.
i rode with the columns through the passes:
brother against brother, the whole kingdom choosing sides.
pedro fled. henry took the throne.
then pedro came back with the black prince, and henry fled.
then henry came back again.
crowns in castile changed hands like dice that decade.

the ming dynasty is born 1368 ce china zhu yuanzhang drives out the mongols and proclaims the ming — the beggar boy on the dragon throne, china for the chinese again. zhu yuanzhang drove the last mongols out and proclaimed the ming —
china for the chinese again, after eighty years of the yuan.
the hongwu emperor. the beggar boy on the dragon throne.
i was in nanjing for the proclamation: the drums,
the new calendar, the whole empire turning its face home.
a peasant's son had taken the greatest throne on earth.
if that doesn't prove the world can turn over,
nothing does.

du guesclin's slow reconquest 1369 ce france bertrand du guesclin takes france back castle by castle, avoiding open battle — ten years of slow, quiet winning while glory looks elsewhere. bertrand du guesclin took france back castle by castle —
no great battles, no glory charges, just sieges, ambushes, patience,
avoiding open battle the way a wise man avoids a drunk.
i followed his campaigns through the west:
one fortress starved, one garrison bought, one town opened its gates.
the english called him a coward. the french called him constable.
ten years of slow work, and aquitaine was french again.
glory is loud. winning is quiet.

timur takes samarkand 1370 ce transoxiana timur seizes samarkand and proclaims himself ruler — the lame boy beginning the long conquest the world will learn in ruins. timur seized samarkand and proclaimed himself ruler —
the lame boy from the back country, now master of transoxiana,
beginning the long conquest that would stack skulls from delhi to damascus.
i saw him enter the city: not tall, not handsome,
but with eyes that made strong men look away.
he couldn't claim the khan's title — the lameness, the blood —
so he ruled as amir, and made the title irrelevant.
the world was about to learn his name.
it would learn it in ruins.

the house of stuart begins 1371 ce scotland robert ii takes the throne, first stuart king of scots — a small spring in the hills, no hint of the ocean of history waiting downstream. robert ii took the throne — the first stuart king of scots,
the bruce's grandson, a steward's son made monarch.
i was at scone for the crowning, a quiet affair after bruce's thunder.
nobody guessed what that name would become:
three hundred years of stuarts, two kingdoms, a civil war,
a beheaded king, an exiled line.
dynasties start like rivers start — a small spring in the hills,
no hint of the ocean waiting downstream.

la rochelle: france takes back the sea 1372 ce atlantic a french-castilian fleet smashes the english at la rochelle — thirty years of english sea-rule ending in an afternoon of smoke. off la rochelle a french-castilian fleet smashed the english —
burning ships, captured nobles, the sea itself changing hands.
i watched the smoke from the cliffs: england's rule of the waves,
won at sluys thirty years before, ending in an afternoon.
the channel wasn't english anymore.
the war had tilted — slowly, the way du guesclin liked it —
and france was coming back, one wave at a time.

julian's visions 1373 ce england near death in norwich, julian receives the visions she'll call her showings — the first known book in english by a woman, gentleness out of a cell. an englishwoman named julian lay near death in norwich,
and in her sickness received the visions she would call her showings —
sixteen revelations of christ's love, written down by an anchoress
walled into a cell for the rest of her life.
i never met her. nobody much did — that was the point of the cell.
but her book survived: the first book in english
we know was written by a woman.
"all shall be well, and all shall be well."
out of a plague-age cell, the gentlest sentence in english.

petrarch dies 1374 ce italy petrarch dies at arqua with his head resting on a book — the laureate who tried to drag rome back from the dead with nothing but words. the great poet died at arqua with his head resting on a book —
petrarch, asleep over his pages, as if he'd just paused mid-sentence.
i visited the little house after: the quiet, the hills,
the manuscripts stacked like a life's work — because they were.
he'd crowned himself with laurel on the capitol thirty years before
and spent a lifetime trying to drag rome back from the dead
with nothing but words.
heads on books. there's no better way for a poet to go.

the atlas paints a golden king 1375 ce majorca abraham cresques draws mansa musa on his golden throne in the catalan atlas — europe learning africa's king by name, in gold on vellum. on majorca, abraham cresques the mapmaker drew mansa musa
on his golden throne, gold crown, gold scepter, a nugget in his hand —
and europe learned africa's king by name.
i saw the catalan atlas new: the vellum glowing,
musa seated at the edge of the known world, richer than any christian king.
fifty years after the pilgrimage, the gold still shone on the map.
that is what a legend looks like when it's drawn:
a black king on a gold throne, at the center of his own world.

the good parliament 1376 ce england the commons rise against royal corruption in the good parliament — impeachment forged as a tool, a ghost that will live long after. the commons rose against royal corruption in the parliament men call good —
impeaching the king's ministers, demanding accounts,
the first time the people's house bit the hand that fed it.
i sat in the gallery and watched commoners question lords,
and the lords squirm.
it didn't last — the court struck back within months —
but the precedent was set, the tool was forged.
impeachment. accountability. words england would use again.
the good parliament died young. its ghost lived on.

tenochtitlan chooses its first king 1376 ce mexico the mexica elect acamapichtli, first king of tenochtitlan — wanderers no more, a city choosing a crown to give itself weight. the mexica elected acamapichtli, first king of tenochtitlan —
a city fifty years old, choosing a monarch to give it weight among nations.
i watched the ceremony on the island: the feathers, the drums,
the new king taking up the reed-mat throne.
they'd been wanderers. now they had a king.
nobody on that island knew what was coming —
the empire, the temples, the sacrifices, the fall.
they just knew: a city with a king is a city that matters.

the pope comes home 1377 ce rome gregory xi brings the papacy home from avignon after seventy years — rome's bells ringing, the old city breathing again, if only for a season. gregory xi brought the papacy back from avignon to rome
after seventy years away — seventy years of exile, ended.
i was in rome when he arrived: the bells, the crowds,
the ruined churches, the tiber shining.
the romans wept. the french cardinals sulked.
he'd die within the year, and the church would split in two —
but for that one homecoming, heaven's address was rome again,
and the old city could breathe.

the boy king richard ii 1377 ce england richard ii is crowned at ten, a beautiful boy with a dangerous pride — a child on the throne, and an invitation to every schemer in england. richard ii was crowned at ten — a beautiful boy with a dangerous pride,
grandson of edward iii, king before he could grow a beard.
i saw him at westminster, small in the great abbey,
the crown too big for his head.
everyone smiled. everyone schemed.
a child on the throne is an invitation —
to uncles, to counselors, to anyone with ambition and patience.
richard would grow up believing he was sacred.
that belief would kill him.

the great schism: two popes 1378 ce christendom rival popes in rome and avignon excommunicate each other, splitting christendom — the fisherman's chair sawed in half for forty years. two popes now — one in rome, one in avignon —
excommunicating each other, each with his cardinals,
each with his kings, christendom split down the middle.
i traveled through france and italy that year and heard both sides curse the other:
antipope, usurper, schismatic, heretic.
the fisherman's chair, sawed in half.
it would last forty years — forty years of two (then three) popes,
and every christian in europe forced to choose.
the church survived it. barely. and never the same.

the ciompi: wool workers seize florence 1378 ce florence florence's wool carders seize the city and rule for six wild weeks — the world turned over, then turned back, but never forgotten. florence's wool carders — the ciompi, the lowest of the low —
seized the city and ruled it for six wild weeks:
their own guilds, their own government, the poor in power.
i was in the piazza della signoria when they took the palace.
six weeks of the world turned over.
then the great guilds took it back, and the ciompi
went back to carding wool — those who survived.
but florence had seen its poorest rule it,
and no city ever forgets a thing like that.

kulikovo: the yoke cracks 1380 ce russia dmitry donskoy's russians break the golden horde at kulikovo — the mongol yoke cracking after 140 years, the spell broken forever. on kulikovo field, dmitry donskoy's russians broke the golden horde's army —
the first great russian victory over the mongols,
the yoke cracking after a hundred and forty years.
i walked that field at dawn before the battle: the mist,
the prayers, the knowledge that everything was at stake.
they won. the horde would come back — it always came back —
but never the same. the spell was broken.
russia had stood up. it would not kneel again.

the saint who scolded popes 1380 ce italy catherine of siena dies — the dyer's daughter who scolded popes to their faces and moved them with plain, fierce letters. catherine of siena died — the mystic, the unlearned daughter of a dyer,
who told popes to their faces what god demanded:
go back to rome, end the schism, reform the church.
and they listened. gregory went home because of her letters.
i read those letters: plain, fierce, tender —
a young woman scolding the vicar of christ like a wayward son.
saints are supposed to be gentle.
catherine was gentle the way a sword is gentle —
when it's on your side.

wat tyler's revolt 1381 ce england kentish peasants march on london behind wat tyler, burn palaces, and demand an end to serfdom — the revolt fails, but the point stands. the kentish peasants marched on london behind wat tyler —
burning palaces, killing tax collectors, demanding an end to serfdom,
the young king richard meeting them at mile end and promising everything.
i was in london when they took the tower.
for days the poor owned the greatest city in england.
then tyler was cut down at smithfield, the promises were broken,
and the hangings began.
but serfdom died anyway — slowly, quietly, of the plague's economics.
the revolt failed. the point stood.

wycliffe's english bible 1382 ce england wycliffe's followers put the scriptures into plain english for common readers — the hardest contraband ever smuggled, and still winning. john wycliffe's followers put the scriptures into plain english —
the whole bible, for common readers, no priest required.
i held one of those handwritten copies: heavy, precious,
the word of god in the tongue of the marketplace.
the church called it heresy. the lollards carried it anyway,
village to village, hidden in carts and cloaks.
ideas are the hardest contraband.
a hundred years later, men would still be dying for this book —
and the book would still be winning.

jadwiga crowned king 1384 ce poland young jadwiga is crowned king of poland at ten — a child carrying two nations' future, and the union of poland and lithuania to come. young jadwiga was crowned king of poland — king, not queen,
the title masculine because the throne was —
a girl of ten, crowned to hold a kingdom together.
i saw the procession in krakow: the child, the crown, the weight of it.
her marriage would soon join poland and lithuania,
the greatest union in eastern europe.
a ten-year-old girl, carrying two nations' future in her small hands.
