askia the great 1493 ce west africa askia muhammad seizes songhai and builds an empire of scholars and gold, with timbuktu's universities at its heart. askia muhammad seized songhai —
not by birth but by merit, a general taking the throne,
and built an empire of scholars and gold:
timbuktu's universities, djenne's mosques,
the law of islam from the niger to the sahara.
i studied in timbuktu under his reign —
the libraries, the astronomers, the jurists,
manuscripts by the thousand in private houses.
while europe stumbled toward the renaissance,
this african empire was already a kingdom of books.
askia made the pilgrimage to mecca, a king among kings.
the gold of the sudan flowed north. the learning flowed everywhere.

the last great inca 1493 ce peru huayna capac takes the throne at the inca empire's height — its greatest extent, with the clock already ticking. huayna capac took the throne at the empire's height —
the last great inca, though no one knew it then.
i traveled his realm: four quarters, ten million people,
roads running like veins through the andes,
storehouses full, the sun god honored from quito to chile.
he pushed the frontier north, into the forests,
where the empire finally met its limit —
and its doom, though it came as a fever,
not an army: the plagues from the east,
running ahead of the spaniards.
the greatest empire in the americas,
at its peak, with the clock already ticking.

the line in the ocean 1493 ce rome the pope draws a line splitting the undiscovered world between spain and portugal — continents divided like a pie. the pope drew a line in the ocean —
inter caetera, alexander vi's bull,
splitting the undiscovered world between spain and portugal:
everything west of the line for spain, east for portugal.
i was in rome when it was proclaimed.
two kingdoms, one pope, and the whole planet
divided like a pie — without asking a single person
who actually lived on any of it.
the arrogance of it still stuns me:
a line drawn on water, carving up continents
the ink hadn't even dried on.
portugal protested. the line moved. the theft continued.

the treaty line moves 1494 ce atlantic tordesillas shifts the dividing line west — brazil falls to portugal by a pen stroke on a map. june seventh, at tordesillas —
spain and portugal moved the pope's line west,
370 leagues west of the cape verde islands,
and neither of them knew what they'd done:
the bulge of south america — brazil —
fell on portugal's side.
i was there when they signed. two diplomats,
a map, a line shifted on paper —
and half a continent changed owners
before any european had seen it.
the treaty held for centuries. the line on the map
became a line in the language, the law, the blood.
brazil speaks portuguese because of a pen stroke in 1494.

the pocket book inventor 1494 ce italy aldus manutius sets up his venetian press — inventing the pocket book, the italic, and the modern reader. aldus manutius set up his press in venice —
and changed what a book could be:
small, clean, in italic type, cheap enough
to fit in a saddlebag and a student's purse.
i bought one of his pocket virgils, fresh off the press —
the classics, portable, for the first time in history.
he invented the paperback, the italic, the semicolon —
the furniture of reading we still use.
venice was drowning in printers, but aldus
wasn't printing books. he was printing readers.
the renaissance, pocket-sized, for anyone with a coin.

the new found land 1497 ce atlantic john cabot claims north america for england — eighteen men, a small ship, and waters thick with cod. john cabot sailed from bristol — a venetian
sailing for england, looking for asia —
and found the coast of north america instead:
newfoundland, the "new found land,"
its waters so thick with cod, they said,
you could scoop them up in baskets.
i was aboard the matthew. eighteen men,
fifty days at sea, and a continent.
england's claim on the new world began here —
with a genoese captain, an english flag,
and fish enough to feed a kingdom.
the cod would build empires. the claim would build more.

the cape doubled 1497 ce africa vasco da gama rounds the cape of good hope in november — the voyage to india is truly underway. vasco da gama rounded the cape in november —
i was on the sao gabriel, watching the southern stars
wheel over seas no european ship had ever crossed:
the long run up the african coast, the monsoon leap
to india, guided by an arab pilot's knowledge.
dias had found the way around. da gama
was sailing it — all the way, to the spice itself.
the indian ocean opened before us like a treasure chest.
nine years after dias, the dream was real:
europe was about to reach the riches of the east by sea.

the sea road found 1498 ce india da gama reaches calicut in may — the sea road to india is found, and the old spice roads tremble. may, and we made calicut — i stood on the deck
and watched india rise out of the heat haze:
the pepper warehouses, the arab dhows, the crowds,
the spice that had traveled ten thousand miles by land
now reachable by sea.
da gama's men had sailed thirty thousand miles.
the cargo they brought home would pay for the voyage
sixty times over.
the old roads trembled — the caravans, the middlemen,
the whole ancient machinery of the spice trade —
because the sea road was open now, and the sea
doesn't charge tolls to sultans.

the friar's fire 1498 ce italy savonarola burns at florence — the bonfire of the vanities ends with the friar's own fire. may twenty-third — they burned savonarola in florence,
the friar who had burned the vanities:
paintings, books, mirrors, dice, wigs —
piled in the piazza della signoria and set alight.
i watched the bonfire of the vanities burn.
then i watched them burn him — hanged first,
then the flames, his followers with him.
he had ruled florence like a prophet, denounced the pope,
called down god's wrath on the corrupt —
and the wrath came down on him instead.
the ashes went in the arno, like joan's in the seine.
florence went back to its bankers and its painters.
the fire was over. the smoke lingered.

the new coast 1500 ce brazil portuguese ships land on brazil's coast and claim the vast green land for their king, while the native people watch from the trees. i stood on the beach when the caravels came,
thirteen white sails out of the blue —
the tupi watched from the palm shade,
and the portuguese knelt and named it new.
cabral raised a cross where the river meets the sea,
claimed a whole green world with a wooden sign;
the land was ancient, but on their maps
that morning, brazil was born mine.
i heard the surf, i smelled the salt and wood,
and knew: this green shore would not stay green —
ships would come and come and never stop,
till the forest's giants went unseen.

the india road 1500 ce portugal cabral's fleet reaches india, locking in portugal's long sea lane around africa to the spice trade. cabral lost ships to storm and wreck,
but thirteen limped to calicut's shore —
thirteen guns, a treaty, pepper bought,
and the long road open evermore.
around the cape, past the cape's cold storms,
a ribbon of ocean held in hand:
portugal's highway to the indies' gold,
drawn across water, not on land.
i watched them load the holds with spice,
black pepper worth its weight in gold —
the road was theirs, the sea was theirs,
and the old world bought what the new world sold.

the scholar's city 1500 ce west africa under askia the great, timbuktu's book markets and libraries make songhai the pride of west africa. in timbuktu the market sells books like grain —
manuscripts stacked in the morning sun,
astronomy, law, the prophet's words,
copied by hand, every one.
under askia the great the scribes keep time,
the mosques are full, the lamps burn late;
a book is worth a horse, they say,
and learning is the city's freight.
i walked those streets of mud and gold,
heard scholars argue in the shade —
while europe's presses were just learning,
here the word of god was bought and weighed.

the red crown 1501 ce persia young shah ismail seizes tabriz and founds safavid persia, a shi'ite empire born on the sword. a boy of fourteen with a red-capped army,
ismail rides into tabriz at dawn —
he takes the crown, he takes the city,
and the old sunni order is gone.
"shi'a!" his soldiers cry, their turbans red,
a faith made steel, an empire born;
persia will pray to the prophet's kin
and stand against the turk's cold scorn.
i saw the boy-king's eyes — half saint, half sword —
and the poets singing at his feet.
an empire raised on sacred fire;
persia, reborn, stands at his heat.

the sleeping giant 1501 ce italy michelangelo begins carving the seventeen-foot david in florence — a boy carved from marble, staring down a giant. a mountain of marble stood in florence,
abandoned, flawed, nineteen feet high —
two carvers had walked away from it.
then a young man, michelangelo, looked it in the eye.
he saw inside the stone a giant sleeping,
a boy with a sling, about to fight —
seventeen feet of david, every muscle taut,
staring down goliath in the florentine light.
i watched the chips fall for three long years,
the hammer ringing like a bell —
out of the stone a shepherd stepped,
and all of florence knew him well.

letters that run 1501 ce venice aldus manutius prints the first pocket books in slanted italic type, made to be carried in saddlebags. in venice, aldus set a new kind of type —
slanted letters, leaning fast,
small pages a traveler could pocket,
books built to ride, not just to last.
italic — the hurry of a handwritten hand,
pressed into lead, printed by the score;
virgil and horace in saddlebags,
classics riding out the door.
i held one — light as a folded map —
and felt the world get small and near:
learning, once chained to desks and stone,
now ran beside the cavalier.

the last voyage 1502 ce atlantic columbus sails his fourth and final voyage, ending stranded for a year in jamaica, a broken admiral in the world he found. four leaky ships, one broken dream —
columbus sailed his last road west,
searching for straits that weren't there,
his luck, his gold, his fame unblest.
worms ate the hulls off panama's coast,
the sea turned cruel, the men turned thin —
he ran aground in jamaica's bay
and waited a year for rescue to begin.
i saw him there: gray, sick, undone,
writing letters that begged the crown —
the admiral of the ocean sea,
shipwrecked in a world he'd found.

the lady with the smile 1503 ce italy leonardo begins painting lisa del giocondo — the portrait the world will call the mona lisa, and her unknowable smile. leonardo took up his brush in florence
to paint a merchant's quiet wife —
lisa del giocondo, hands folded,
ordinary as ordinary life.
but layer by layer, the smile came,
half here, half gone, like morning mist —
no one could say what she was thinking,
and nobody has, since she was kissed by paint.
i stood behind him in the studio,
watched thirty years of glances grow —
the most famous face in all the world,
and nobody truly knows.

a queen's death 1504 ce spain isabella of castile dies, leaving her unstable daughter juana heir to the spanish crown. isabella died in medina del campo,
the iron queen who paid for ships and war —
she left her crown to juana, her daughter,
whose mind was slipping from the shore.
they called the daughter juana the mad,
locked away her living years —
the queen who launched a thousand sails
ended in her daughter's tears.
i stood outside the dying chamber,
heard the prayers, the bells' slow chime —
an age went out with that old woman,
and spain marched on without her time.

the first viceroy 1505 ce india francisco de almeida sails as portugal's first viceroy of the indies, to rule the pepper trade by cannon. almeida sailed from lisbon with twenty ships
and a title never held before —
viceroy of the indies, lord of pepper,
ruling trade by cannon's roar.
no more quiet bargaining in the ports,
no more bribes along the shore —
portugal would tax the indian ocean
with gunpowder behind every door.
i watched the fleet drop anchor at cochin,
the soldiers landing rank on rank —
an empire not of land but water,
and pepper was the bank.

the grand stone 1506 ce vatican pope julius ii lays the first stone of a new st. peter's basilica, meant to dwarf old rome. julius stood where the old church crumbled,
the warrior pope with a builder's dream —
he laid the first stone of a new st. peter's,
bigger than rome had ever seen.
domes that would swallow the pantheon,
a church to dwarf the ancient town —
they'd sell indulgences to pay for it,
and that sale would shake his crown.
i heard the trowel tap the cornerstone,
felt the ambition in the air —
a pope building heaven out of marble,
while thunder gathered everywhere.

the christian king 1506 ce kongo afonso i takes the kongo throne and writes to the pope as a catholic king in africa, even as the slave trade grows around him. afonso took the kongo throne as a christian,
baptized, crowned, a catholic king —
he wrote to the pope in latin letters,
asking priests and teachers to bring.
in africa, a cross on the royal standard,
a church beside the king's own door —
while europe fought its wars of faith,
the kongo knelt and asked for more.
i read his letters in the archives,
dignified, shrewd, and sad —
a king who loved the christian word
but watched his nobles turn to trade — in men.

the name america 1507 ce germany a small german press prints the first map to call the new world "america," after amerigo vespucci's letters. in a small german town, a printer's press
stamped out a map the world had never seen —
a new continent drawn on paper,
and under it, a brand-new name: america.
not columbus, who had sailed it first,
but amerigo vespucci, who wrote it well —
the letters of a florentine traveler
outweighed the admiral's bell.
i held that map, the ink still fresh,
and laughed at how the world is made —
not by who finds it, but by who names it,
and the name that never fades.

the ceiling of heaven 1508 ce vatican michelangelo climbs the sistine scaffold and begins painting genesis overhead, on his back, high above the chapel floor. michelangelo climbed the scaffold stairs,
cursing the pope with every breath —
he was a carver, not a painter,
but julius would not take no for death.
sixty-eight feet above the floor,
on his back, with paint in his eyes,
he began the story of the world —
god reaching down through painted skies.
i lay beside him on the planks one night,
watched the lamplight on wet paint —
a man making heaven out of plaster,
half angel, half complaint.

the golden boy king 1509 ce england seventeen-year-old henry viii takes the english throne — handsome, athletic, and hungry for glory. seventeen, six feet of golden muscle,
henry took the english throne —
handsome, athletic, laughing loud,
a renaissance prince fully grown.
he jousted, hunted, wrote love songs,
the ladies sighed, the court applauded —
europe's brightest, boldest boy-king,
by every herald lauded.
i saw him ride through london's streets,
the crowds throwing flowers at his feet —
no one guessed the fat old tyrant
hiding in that golden heat.

the battle of diu 1509 ce india portugal smashes a mamluk fleet off diu and seizes mastery of the indian ocean in a single day of cannon fire. off diu the mamluk fleet lay waiting,
egyptian ships with turkish guns —
almeida's son was dead, and vengeance
sailed with the rising sun.
the portuguese carracks closed like wolves,
their broadsides spoke in iron thunder —
by dusk the mamluk fleet was broken,
the indian ocean torn asunder.
i smelled the powder on the water,
heard the timbers crack and groan —
one battle, and the sea changed masters:
the ocean was portugal's own.

the school of athens 1510 ce italy raphael paints philosophers debating in the vatican — plato and aristotle at the center of the school of athens. raphael painted thinkers on a vatican wall —
plato pointing up to the sky,
aristotle pressing his hand earthward down,
the whole debate of "what" and "why."
euclid bends over his compass,
diogenes sprawls on the stair —
two thousand years of arguing minds
gathered in painted air.
i stood in that room of frescoed stone,
and felt the old questions start —
every age has asked them since:
the mind, the world, the heart.

the city of spices 1510 ce goa afonso de albuquerque storms goa and makes it portugal's capital of the indian ocean. albuquerque stormed the walls of goa,
twice he took it, blood and fire —
and made it portugal's eastern capital,
the seat of the spice empire.
from goa the fleets would sail each year,
to malacca, hormuz, and beyond —
a city of churches on an asian shore,
built on cannon, bound by bond.
i walked its streets of stone and palm,
heard portuguese bells ring out —
an empire's capital in the tropics,
where the monsoons turned about.

the key of the east 1511 ce malacca albuquerque seizes malacca, the great strait port where all of asia's trade funnels through. malacca sat where the straits run narrow,
where china's junks and india's met —
the key of the east, the traders called it,
the richest lock the ocean set.
albuquerque broke it with nineteen ships,
his cannon spoke from dawn to night —
the sultan fled into the jungle,
and portugal held the strait's tight might.
i saw the warehouses burst with spice,
cloves and nutmeg, silk and gold —
who holds malacca holds the east:
a saying the sailors told.

the ceiling finished 1512 ce vatican michelangelo uncovers the sistine ceiling — nine scenes from creation to noah, painted in four years on his back. four years on his back, and then —
the scaffolds came down, the candles lit,
and rome looked up and gasped aloud
at what the angry carver had writ.
nine scenes from creation to the flood,
god's finger reaching for man's hand —
the whole of genesis overhead,
in color no one could withstand.
i was there when they uncovered it,
heard the silence, then the roar —
a ceiling that made painters weep
and kings feel small once more.

the grim son 1512 ce ottoman empire selim i seizes the ottoman throne — cold, ruthless, and called "the grim," clearing rivals without mercy. selim took the throne from his old father,
forced him down, then poisoned the cup —
eight brothers' sons were strangled after,
so no rival could rise up.
cold, ruthless, reading persian verse
between the orders for the knife —
they called him yavuz, the grim, the stern,
a sultan who dealt in life.
i watched him pray at dawn in istanbul,
his face a mask of stone —
the empire's sword had found its hand,
and mercy was unknown.

the prince's mirror 1513 ce italy machiavelli writes the prince in exile — cold counsel on how rulers keep power. in exile on his little farm,
machiavelli wrote by candlelight —
a handbook for the men who rule,
cold counsel in the night.
be feared, not loved, if you must choose,
keep promises when they pay —
the prince held up a mirror to power
and showed its ruthless face that day.
i read it in manuscript, page by page,
and felt the chill run through —
five hundred years of rulers since
have found its counsel true.

the south sea 1513 ce panama balboa wades into the pacific and claims the whole ocean for spain. balboa crossed the jungle's green hell,
ninety men through mud and thorn —
and from a mountain top he saw it:
an ocean no european had sworn.
he waded in, waist-deep in the surf,
sword in hand, the banner high —
claimed the whole pacific for spain,
the sea, the coast, the sky.
i stood beside him on that peak,
saw the blue stretch without end —
a man naming an ocean his,
and the ocean his to lend.

the field of chaldiran 1514 ce ottoman empire selim crushes shah ismail at chaldiran — ottoman guns beat safavid holy swords, and gunpowder wins the day. at chaldiran the two empires met —
ismail's holy warriors, sword and faith,
against selim's cannon and muskets,
cold iron against the wraith.
the safavid horsemen charged like lions,
straight into the ottoman guns —
by noon the field was red with martyrs,
and persia's pride was undone.
i walked that field when the smoke cleared,
saw the red caps scattered wide —
the age of the holy sword was ending;
the age of gunpowder had arrived.

the protector's voice 1514 ce hispaniola bartolome de las casas gives up his own slaves and begins a lifelong fight for the native peoples of the americas. las casas was a priest with slaves of his own,
a settler priest in the indies' sun —
till one sunday the words of the gospel
struck him like a loaded gun.
he freed his indians, gave up his lands,
and began a fight of fifty years —
for the souls the spaniards were crushing,
he'd spend his voice, his ink, his tears.
i heard him preach in santo domingo,
his voice shaking the church's stone —
the first white voice in the new world
to say: leave these people alone.

the boy king of france 1515 ce france twenty-year-old francis i is crowned at reims — europe's most dazzling prince. at twenty, francis was crowned at reims,
the handsomest prince in christendom —
tall, laughing, a patron of artists,
a king the poets would succumb.
he'd build chateaux along the loire,
bring leonardo to his court to die —
europe's most dazzling sovereign,
under a renaissance sky.
i saw him ride beneath the banners,
the crown just set upon his hair —
a golden age in a golden king,
and glory in the air.

the rhinoceros 1515 ce germany durer carves his famous rhinoceros in wood — a beast he never saw, built from a sketch and a letter. durer never saw the rhinoceros —
a sketch, a letter, that's all he had,
a beast unloaded at lisbon's docks,
a gift that drove a king half mad.
he carved it into wood with armor plates,
a second horn upon its nose —
wrong in the details, true in wonder,
the most famous beast art knows.
i watched him cut each careful line,
inventing what he'd never seen —
for two hundred years, all europe's rhinos
looked like durer's dream.

the lion's last roar 1516 ce ottoman empire selim defeats the mamluks at marj dabiq; syria falls to the ottomans and the old sultan dies on the field. at marj dabiq the mamluk lion roared —
the old sultan rode out in state,
his mamluk knights in shining armor,
to meet the ottoman fate.
selim's guns spoke first, as at chaldiran,
and the old lion fell in the dust —
syria opened its gates to the turk,
an empire turned to rust.
i saw the sultan's body on the field,
his royal tent in ottoman hands —
the mamluk age was breathing out,
and istanbul ruled the lands.

an island of reason 1516 ce england thomas more publishes utopia, dreaming of a perfect commonwealth on an imaginary island. thomas more dreamed an island —
utopia, the nowhere place,
where no one owns and no one hungers,
and reason rules the human race.
he wrote it in latin, half in jest,
a lawyer's game, a scholar's art —
but underneath the clever jokes,
a longing in his heart.
i read it by a winter fire,
and felt its pull, its sting —
a perfect world, imagined once,
that no one built, but many sing.

the spark at wittenberg 1517 ce germany martin luther posts 95 theses against indulgences at wittenberg and sets europe alight. an unknown monk with a hammer and nails —
luther pinned his theses to the door,
ninety-five complaints against indulgences,
and the church would be whole no more.
the printing press caught the spark
and carried it on wings of lead —
in weeks, all germany was reading,
and the old world's order fled.
i stood in the crowd at wittenberg,
heard the paper flutter in the wind —
one monk, one door, one autumn day,
and europe's fate rescinded.

the fall of the mamluks 1517 ce egypt selim rides into cairo; the mamluk sultans are finished, and mecca answers to istanbul. selim rode into cairo through the bab al-nasr,
the mamluk sultans' line was done —
tumanbay hanged at the city gate,
and the long mamluk sun had run.
mecca and medina bowed to istanbul,
the holy cities' keys changed hands —
an empire of slave-soldiers, two hundred years,
now dust in the desert sands.
i watched the ottoman banners rise
over the nile's slow green —
cairo, the city of a thousand minarets,
had a new master, cold and keen.

the licenses of chains 1518 ce atlantic spain licenses the first mass shipments of enslaved africans to the americas — the slave trade's machinery begins. spain signed the licenses in seville —
paper permits for human freight,
thousands of africans in chains,
sold by the crown, sealed by the state.
the sugar fields were hungry for hands,
the mines were hungry too —
so merchants bought and sold in bulk,
and called it legal, called it true.
i saw the first ships load at sao tome,
heard the iron, smelled the fear —
the licenses of chains began that year,
and the horror ran for centuries here.

cortes gets his orders 1518 ce cuba hernan cortes receives command of the expedition to mexico's mainland. in cuba, velazquez signed the paper —
cortes would lead the ships to shore,
to trade with the mainland, to explore,
to bring back gold and more.
eleven ships, five hundred men,
a lawyer's son with a hungry eye —
cortes kissed the governor's hand
and planned, already, to defy.
i saw him muster on the beach,
the banners flying in the heat —
a small force with a giant hunger,
and mexico at his feet.

the round-the-world gamble 1519 ce spain magellan sails from seville with five ships to find the westward way to the spice islands. magellan sailed from seville with five ships,
two hundred and seventy men —
to find the westward road to spice,
and bring them home again.
the king of spain had paid the price,
portugal had closed the eastern door —
so west they'd sail, through straits unknown,
to seas no keel had cut before.
i watched them clear the guadalquivir,
the sails like wings against the sky —
a gamble on the whole round world,
and most of them would die.

the stranger on the shore 1519 ce mexico cortes lands at veracruz and marches inland toward tenochtitlan with native allies at his side. cortes landed at veracruz in april,
burned his ships — no way back —
and marched inland with native allies,
the tlaxcalans at his back.
four hundred spaniards, thousands of friends,
guns and horses, smallpox to come —
toward tenochtitlan, the lake-bound city,
greater than seville, beating like a drum.
i walked that road beside the column,
saw the volcanoes crowned with snow —
a stranger stepping toward an empire,
and neither knowing how it'd go.

the night of sorrows 1520 ce mexico the mexica rise against the spaniards; cortes's men flee tenochtitlan in a night of slaughter. they came for the gold in the dead of night,
the causeways narrow, the lake black deep —
the mexica rose with a roar of drums,
and the spaniards ran, and the spaniards wept.
la noche triste — the night of sorrows —
men drowned in armor, weighed with gold,
horses screaming in the darkness,
a retreat the bards have told.
i heard the war cries from the rooftops,
saw the causeway slick with rain —
cortes wept under the ahuehuete tree,
and swore he'd come again.

the bull in the fire 1520 ce germany luther publicly burns the pope's bull of excommunication at wittenberg's gates — the break with rome is final. the pope's bull came to wittenberg,
excommunicating the monk by name —
luther built a bonfire at the city gates
and threw the parchment in the flame.
the students cheered, the priests went pale,
the books of canon law burned too —
a point of no return, in fire,
the old church breaking in two.
i stood in the smoke of that december fire,
felt the heat upon my face —
a monk burning the pope's own words:
the reformation's loudest grace.

the field of cloth of gold 1520 ce france henry viii and francis i feast in tents of gold outside calais — then return to scheming against each other. two kings met in a field of gold —
henry and francis, young and proud,
their tents were cloth of gold and silk,
their retinues a shining crowd.
they wrestled, feasted, jousted, drank,
swore friendship with a royal kiss —
then went straight home to scheme and plot,
for gold can't buy what kings dismiss.
i wandered through that gilded camp,
saw the wine flow like a stream —
the most expensive party ever thrown,
and nothing but a dream.

the magnificent 1520 ce ottoman empire twenty-five-year-old suleiman takes the ottoman throne for a reign of nearly half a century. at twenty-five, suleiman took the throne,
the tenth sultan of the ottoman line —
they'd call him the magnificent,
and kanuni, the lawgiver, in time.
forty-six years he'd hold the sword,
belgrade, rhodes, and hungary's plain —
the empire's peak in a single reign,
its glory and its pain.
i saw him ride through istanbul's gates,
young, grave, with a poet's eyes —
a ruler who would write the laws
and watch his empire rise.

the stand at worms 1521 ce germany hauled before the emperor at worms, luther refuses to recant: "here i stand." they hauled the monk before the emperor,
the diet of worms, the empire's might —
"recant," they said. he asked a day.
he came back in the morning light.
"here i stand, i can do no other" —
the words rang through the hall —
a single conscience against an empire,
and the empire seemed so small.
i was there in the crowded chamber,
heard the silence after he spoke —
one man refusing to bend his soul:
the sound of the old world broke.

the fall of tenochtitlan 1521 ce mexico after a brutal siege the mexica capital falls; an empire passes into spanish hands. seventy-five days the siege held on,
the lake city starving, street by street —
smallpox in the houses, hunger in the squares,
the brigantines controlling the fleet.
cuauhtemoc fought till the canoes were gone,
till the last warriors fell in the mud —
on august thirteenth, the city fell,
and the lake ran red with blood.
i walked the ruins of the great temples,
saw the stones the spaniards tore —
an empire's heart cut from its body,
and mexico would bleed for more.

the last harbor 1521 ce philippines magellan dies in a skirmish on mactan; his expedition sails on without him. on mactan's beach, magellan fell —
a poisoned arrow, a native spear,
trying to play the conquistador
in a war that wasn't his, out here.
he'd crossed an ocean no man had crossed,
named the pacific its calm name —
and died in a skirmish on a island shore,
a footnote to his fame.
i saw him fall in the shallow surf,
his men retreating to the boats —
the captain never saw the finish
of the voyage his courage floats.

belgrade falls 1521 ce balkans suleiman takes belgrade, the white fortress guarding the road to hungary. belgrade stood white above the danube,
the fortress guarding hungary's door —
suleiman brought his guns against it,
and the white walls held no more.
seven hundred cannon battered the towers,
the mines blew the bastions wide —
in august, the garrison surrendered,
and the road to hungary lay open wide.
i watched the ottoman banners rise
over the fortress on the hill —
the first step of the magnificent's march,
and europe felt the chill.

the first circle 1522 ce world the victoria staggers into seville — the first ship to sail around the entire earth. eighteen men on a rotting hulk —
the victoria staggered into seville,
three years gone, around the world,
eighteen left of the brave and still.
they'd lost four ships, they'd lost their captain,
they'd starved and scurvied, crossed the vast —
but they'd sailed clean around the earth,
the first to do it, first and last.
i stood upon the guadalquivir,
saw the ragged sailors kneel —
they'd proved the world was round and wide,
and brought the proof in spice and steel.

rhodes falls 1522 ce mediterranean suleiman takes rhodes from the knights hospitaller after a six-month siege, and lets them sail away with honor. six months the knights of rhodes held out,
behind their walls against the turk —
suleiman's mines and cannon pounded,
and still the knights would work.
by christmas, the walls were breached,
the grand master sued for grace —
suleiman let them sail away with honor,
knights without a place.
i watched them board their galleys,
the cross still flying from the mast —
rhodes was ottoman by new year's,
and the knights' long stand had passed.

the liberator king 1523 ce sweden gustav vasa drives out the danes and is crowned king of a free sweden. gustav vasa came down from the mountains,
where he'd hidden from the danish crown —
the stockholm bloodbath fresh in memory,
he'd take the tyrant's power down.
the peasants rose, the castles fell,
and in strangnas they crowned him king —
a free sweden, a vasa line,
and the bells began to ring.
i marched with the dalecarlian men,
saw the danes retreat in snow —
a nation born in winter's cold,
and a king the swedes would know.

the peasants rise 1524 ce germany fired by the reformation, german peasants take up arms against their lords. fired by luther's words of freedom,
the peasants took up flail and scythe —
"if all are priests, why are we serfs?"
they rose with a righteous cry.
the twelve articles, their charter,
demanded what the gospel gave —
an end to serfdom, tithes, and labor,
the rights of the free, not the slave.
i walked with them through swabian fields,
heard them sing the psalms of war —
the reformation's children rising,
knocking on the castle door.

the hammer of pavia 1525 ce italy imperial troops crush france at pavia and drag king francis i off as a prisoner. at pavia the imperial troops closed in,
the french knights charged in shining pride —
but spanish muskets spoke from the woods,
and king francis's horse was shot, and he was tied.
the flower of french chivalry fell
in a single february day —
a king taken prisoner by his foes,
and italy's fate gave way.
i saw them drag the king away,
his armor dented, crown askew —
pavia's hammer broke the french,
and the habsburgs' power grew.

the peasants broken 1525 ce germany the peasants' war is drowned in blood; luther turns on the rebels he once inspired. at frankenhausen the princes' armies came,
with cannon against the peasants' bands —
muntzer prayed for a miracle,
but iron answered prayer with hands.
a hundred thousand peasants died that year,
drowned in blood across the land —
and luther, who had lit the fire,
turned and blessed the princes' hand.
i walked the fields after the battle,
saw the crows above the slain —
the reformation's promise broken,
and the poor in chains again.

the tiger's descent 1526 ce india babur's small army smashes the delhi sultanate at panipat — the mughal empire is born. babur came down from kabul's hills,
twelve thousand men, both tough and lean —
against ibrahim lodi's hundred thousand,
and elephants, a war machine.
at panipat, babur chained his carts,
his muskets spoke in ordered fire —
the delhi sultanate broke and ran,
and the tiger took his empire.
i watched the mughal banners rise
over the field of the slain —
a new empire born in india,
and it would long remain.

the field of mohacs 1526 ce hungary suleiman destroys hungary's army in two hours at mohacs; a kingdom dies in an afternoon. two hours. that's all it took —
suleiman's guns against the magyar pride,
king louis rode into the marsh
and never came out alive.
hungary's army died in an afternoon,
its nobles in the mud and rain —
a kingdom's heart cut out at mohacs,
and never beat again.
i stood upon that drowned field,
saw the crown floating in the mire —
two hours of cannon and cavalry,
and a nation lost to fire.

the princes' peace 1526 ce germany the diet of speyer lets each german prince choose his land's faith — for now, the wars pause. at speyer the princes made their peace —
each ruler chooses his land's faith,
lutheran here, catholic there,
a truce the empire wraith.
it wouldn't hold — the wars would come —
but for a moment, the swords stayed sheathed,
and germany breathed a little easier,
the storm for now bequeathed.
i sat in the diet's crowded hall,
heard the compromise read out —
peace bought with a prince's conscience:
that's what it's all about.

the sack of rome 1527 ce italy mutinous imperial soldiers loot rome for days; the renaissance's proudest city is stripped bare. mutinous, unpaid, the imperial troops
broke through rome's walls in may —
lutheran landsknechts, spanish tercios,
and the city became their prey.
for days they looted, burned, and killed,
churches stripped, nuns defiled —
the renaissance's proudest city,
by its own emperor's men defiled.
i fled through streets of smoke and screams,
saw the vatican's treasures torn —
rome, the eternal, humbled low,
and a pope in the castel sant'angelo forlorn.

the king's great matter 1527 ce england henry viii asks the pope to annul his marriage to catherine of aragon — the king's great matter begins. henry wanted a son, not a wife —
catherine had borne him only a girl,
and anne boleyn had caught his eye,
set his middle age in a whirl.
he asked the pope to annul the marriage,
called it the king's great matter —
but the pope was the emperor's prisoner,
and the answer came back: never.
i watched the court hold its breath,
saw wolsey fall from grace —
a king's desire against a pope:
the schism's starting place.

the narvaez ruin 1528 ce florida panfilo de narvaez's expedition collapses in florida; only four men will walk out alive. narvaez landed in florida with four hundred men,
seeking gold where none was found —
the ships sailed off, the men marched in,
and the swamps swallowed them down.
hunger, storms, and native arrows,
barges wrecked upon the shore —
of all that proud expedition,
only four men walked out alive, no more.
i saw them build their desperate boats,
saw the gulf take them one by one —
a ruin written in the sand,
under the florida sun.

the ladies' peace 1529 ce europe two royal women sign the treaty of cambrai — peace made by women while kings made war. two royal women met at cambrai —
louise of savoy, margaret of austria,
and signed a peace their men couldn't make,
ending the wars with a woman's quill.
the ladies' peace, they called it,
france and the empire at rest —
while kings made war with cannon,
queens made peace the best.
i watched them sign in the abbey,
two widows, wise and gray —
the men had fought for seven years;
the women ended it in a day.

the gates of vienna 1529 ce ottoman empire suleiman's army reaches vienna, but winter and high walls turn it back — the ottoman high-water mark. suleiman marched to vienna's gates,
a hundred thousand strong —
but the rains came, the walls held,
and the siege dragged on too long.
winter whispered in the tents,
the janissaries grumbled low —
the sultan turned his army home,
and vienna did not bow.
i stood upon the city walls,
watched the turkish campfires fade —
the high-water mark of the ottoman tide,
where europe's fate was made.

the name "protestant" 1529 ce germany princes who defy the emperor at speyer earn the name protestants — the ones who protest. at speyer the emperor demanded
that the lutherans all recant —
six princes and fourteen cities
stood and filed their protestant.
"we protest," they said, "we cannot yield" —
and the name stuck like a brand —
protestant: the ones who stood
against the emperor's command.
i heard them read the protestation,
felt the hall go still and cold —
a name born in defiance,
that the centuries would hold.

the confession 1530 ce germany melanchthon reads the augsburg confession; lutheranism gains its founding charter. melanchthon read it at augsburg,
the confession, article by article —
lutheran faith in twenty-eight points,
calm, learned, not a particle.
the emperor listened, unmoved,
but the words were now on record —
a church with a charter of its own,
its faith by ink secured.
i sat among the crowded princes,
heard the gentle scholar's tone —
not luther's thunder, but reason's voice,
claiming the faith as its own.

the virgin of guadalupe 1531 ce mexico an indian convert reports a vision of mary on tepeyac hill; a new shrine rises and millions will come. on tepeyac hill, juan diego saw her —
a lady in the morning light,
speaking nahuatl, gentle, brown-skinned,
mary in an indian's sight.
the bishop doubted till the roses bloomed
in december, out of season —
and on the tilma, her image burned,
a miracle beyond reason.
i climbed that hill at dawn myself,
saw the shrine the indians raised —
a faith that spoke their mother tongue,
and a mother to be praised.

the holy office 1531 ce portugal king john iii brings the inquisition to portugal to hunt heresy and secret jews. king john brought the inquisition home —
the holy office, black and grim,
to hunt the heretics and secret jews,
the conversos hiding him.
the autos-da-fe in lisbon's square,
the dungeons under the palace stone —
portugal's faith would now be policed,
and fear would rule alone.
i watched them lead the accused away,
heard the whispered prayers at night —
a kingdom turning on its own,
in the name of holy light.

the reformer falls 1531 ce switzerland ulrich zwingli dies sword in hand at kappel — the first reformer killed in war. zwingli died at kappel with a sword in hand,
the reformer turned soldier-priest —
catholic pikes against zurich's men,
and the battle was a feast.
they found his body on the field,
quartered it, burned the parts —
the first reformer killed in war,
a sword through switzerland's hearts.
i saw him march out with the zurich troops,
bible in one hand, halberd in the other —
a pastor who would die in battle,
like a father, like a brother.

the trap at cajamarca 1532 ce peru pizarro ambushes the inca atahualpa at cajamarca; a room filled with gold is set as the ransom. pizarro waited in cajamarca's square,
one hundred sixty-eight men in all —
against atahualpa's thousands camped outside,
the inca, greatest of all.
the friar read the requerimiento,
the inca threw the bible down —
the cannon fired, the horsemen charged,
and the square became a killing ground.
i hid behind the stone walls,
heard the screams, the trumpet's call —
an empire's lord taken in an hour,
by treachery in a plaza small.

the boleyn wedding 1533 ce england henry secretly marries anne boleyn and breaks toward schism with rome. henry married anne in secret,
in a chapel, before the dawn —
a pregnant bride, a desperate king,
and the break with rome was on.
cranmer would bless what rome condemned,
the pope's authority denied —
england's church would answer now
to the king, and none beside.
i stood outside that quiet chapel,
heard the whispered vows within —
a wedding that would split a kingdom
and drown a queen in sin.

the ransom paid in blood 1533 ce peru atahualpa is strangled despite the ransom of gold; the inca empire's heart is cut out. the room was filled — gold to the ceiling,
the ransom paid, the promise made —
atahualpa bought his freedom
with the inca's golden trade.
but pizarro feared to let him go,
so the garrote closed at night —
strangled in the cajamarca square,
an emperor's stolen light.
i saw the gold piled in the chamber,
heard the inca's final prayer —
the ransom paid, the promise broken,
and the andes left in despair.

a princess named elizabeth 1533 ce england anne boleyn bears a daughter — the future elizabeth i, unwanted by her father, destined for greatness. anne bore a daughter in september,
at greenwich palace, small and red —
not the son that henry wanted,
but a princess in his stead.
they named her elizabeth, for his mother,
and the king turned away in gloom —
he could not know the girl in the cradle
would fill england's greatest room.
i saw her first in the nurse's arms,
a tudor with her father's eyes —
the unwanted daughter of a doomed queen,
destined for the crown's high prize.

the child on the throne 1533 ce russia three-year-old ivan inherits muscovy while the boyars feast on the regency — the terrible is being made. three years old, and grand prince of muscovy —
ivan sat the throne as the boyars schemed,
his mother dead, the regents feasting,
while the child watched, and dreamed.
they'd brawl before him in the palace,
throw his tutors from the stair —
a boy learning that power is cruelty,
breathing the kremlin's air.
i saw him small upon the throne,
his eyes too old, too wise —
the terrible was being made
before the world's eyes.

the supreme head 1534 ce england parliament declares henry viii supreme head of the church of england — the break with rome is law. parliament spoke, and it was law —
henry, supreme head of the church,
no more appeals to rome's high throne,
no more the papal perch.
the monasteries would follow soon,
their gold to fill the crown —
england's faith by act of state,
the old religion broken down.
i sat in the parliament that day,
heard the statutes read aloud —
a kingdom's soul by legislation,
and the king above the cloud.

the river of canada 1534 ce canada jacques cartier sails up the st. lawrence and claims the land for france. cartier sailed up the st. lawrence,
past the cliffs where quebec would stand —
he claimed the river and the forests
for the king of france's hand.
the iroquois watched from the shoreline,
the french planted their cross —
"canada," the natives called the village,
and the name would bear the loss.
i rode those waters in his wake,
saw the wilderness run wide —
a river that would carry empires,
and the dreams that sailed its tide.

the society of jesus 1534 ce paris ignatius of loyola and six companions vow themselves to the pope in paris — the jesuits are born. seven men in a montmartre chapel —
ignatius, the soldier turned saint,
and six companions, young and burning,
vowed by candlelight's faint.
poverty, chastity, obedience,
and a special vow to the pope —
the jesuits were born that morning,
the church's last best hope.
i knelt with them in the crypt below,
heard the latin vows ascend —
an army of scholars and missionaries,
on whom rome would depend.

the tailor king of munster 1534 ce germany anabaptists seize munster and crown a tailor king; the siege ends in cages and torture. the anabaptists seized munster town,
and crowned a tailor, jan van leiden, king —
polygamy, communism, apocalypse,
a new jerusalem to bring.
the bishop's army ringed the walls,
starved them out through winter's cold —
the tailor king in an iron cage,
his story grimly told.
i walked the streets of that besieged town,
saw the faithful starve and pray —
a kingdom of heaven on earth,
that ended in dismay.

the silent chancellor 1535 ce england thomas more is beheaded for refusing henry's supremacy; conscience dies with him on tower hill. thomas more climbed the scaffold stairs,
the silent chancellor, the wit —
he'd refused the king's supremacy,
and would not bend a bit.
"i die the king's good servant,"
he said, "but god's first" —
the axe fell on tower hill,
and england felt the worst.
i stood among the watching crowd,
heard his final jest —
a conscience that would not be bought,
laid finally to rest.

the queen loses her head 1536 ce england anne boleyn is executed in the tower; henry weds jane seymour days later. anne boleyn knelt on the tower green,
a french swordsman, not the axe —
she'd given henry a daughter, not a son,
and paid the final tax.
eleven days later, henry wed jane seymour,
the court moved on, the bells rang out —
a queen's head in a velvet bag,
and nobody dared to doubt.
i watched her climb the scaffold,
heard her pray in french —
three years a queen, a thousand years a story,
ended on a bench.

the institutes 1536 ce switzerland john calvin publishes his institutes of the christian religion in basel — a theology of iron logic. calvin published his institutes in basel,
a french lawyer's systematic mind —
god's sovereignty, man's depravity,
predestination, tightly lined.
the book would travel further than its author,
to geneva, scotland, and the new world's shore —
a theology of iron logic,
that would shape the world and more.
i read it fresh off the basel press,
felt its cold and brilliant art —
a god who'd chosen before time,
and the terror in the heart.

the walking men return 1536 ce mexico cabeza de vaca and three companions stumble into mexico after eight lost years crossing the continent. eight years lost in the wilderness —
cabeza de vaca and three more,
naked, starving, enslaved, escaped,
walked out of the desert's door.
from florida to mexico they wandered,
healers, beggars, ghosts of men —
the first europeans to cross the continent,
and live to tell it then.
i met them at the spanish outpost,
saw their beards, their hollow eyes —
men who'd walked through hell itself
and come back with the prize.

the translator's fire 1536 ce flanders william tyndale is strangled and burned for putting the bible into english. tyndale gave the english their bible —
"let the plowboy know the word" —
for that, they strangled him at vilvoorde,
then burned him, as absurd.
his last prayer: "lord, open the king's eyes" —
and the king's eyes would open wide,
for henry's own great bible
was tyndale's work inside.
i stood outside the stake that day,
heard the flames take the pyre —
a man who died for english words,
consumed by holy fire.

the prince at last 1537 ce england jane seymour bears henry a son, edward — then dies twelve days later of childbed fever. jane seymour bore the son at last —
edward, the prince, the heir —
the court rejoiced, the bonfires burned,
thanksgiving filled the air.
twelve days later, jane was dead,
childbed fever took the queen —
henry wept for the only wife
who'd given him what he'd seen.
i heard the bells of celebration,
then the bells of mourning toll —
a prince born, a mother lost,
and a king with half a soul.

the venus of urbino 1538 ce italy titian paints the reclining venus that teaches europe a new way to look at a body. titian painted her reclining —
venus, naked, on a couch,
looking straight out at the viewer,
no goddess on a cloud.
a woman, real, unashamed,
a dog asleep at her feet —
europe had never seen a body
rendered half so sweet.
i stood before the canvas,
felt the centuries stare back —
a new way of looking at a woman,
that the old masters lacked.

the golden cities 1540 ce north america coronado marches north for the seven cities of cibola while de soto hunts gold through florida — both find no gold, but map a continent. coronado marched north for cibola,
the seven cities paved with gold —
de soto hacked through florida's swamps,
both chasing what they were told.
they found no gold, just desert and plains,
the grand canyon, the mississippi's flow —
two expeditions, empty-handed,
but the maps would ever grow.
i rode with coronado's column,
saw the pueblos in the sun —
the golden cities were a story,
but the journey had begun.

the pope's soldiers 1540 ce vatican paul iii formally approves the society of jesus — the jesuits become rome's shock troops. paul iii signed the bull at last —
the society of jesus approved,
ten men to start, then thousands,
a spiritual army moved.
they'd teach in universities,
sail to asia, brave the rack —
the pope's own shock troops,
and there'd be no turning back.
i watched ignatius kneel for the blessing,
saw the tears upon his face —
a soldier's order for the church,
armed with learning and grace.

the conqueror's end 1541 ce peru almagro's partisans murder francisco pizarro in his lima palace — the conqueror conquered. almagro's partisans broke down the door,
in pizarro's palace at noon —
the conqueror of peru, seventy old,
fell to the assassin's tune.
he drew his sword, he fought them off,
killed two before he fell —
throat cut on his own dining floor,
the mighty brought to hell.
i heard the shouts in lima's square,
saw the body on the floor —
the man who'd toppled an empire,
toppled by his own war.

the end of the world, painted 1541 ce vatican michelangelo unveils the last judgment — christ hurling the damned down, twenty-five years after the ceiling. twenty-five years after the ceiling,
michelangelo climbed again —
the last judgment on the altar wall,
christ in wrath among men.
the damned hurled down to charon's boat,
the saved ascending to the light —
a sixty-six-year-old's vision
of the world's final night.
i stood beneath that terrible wall,
felt the painted thunder roll —
the end of the world in fresco,
and the judgment of each soul.

the new laws 1542 ce spain charles v issues the new laws to protect the indians — las casas's victory on paper, resisted in the colonies. charles signed the new laws in barcelona —
las casas's victory on paper,
the indians freed from encomienda,
the settlers' rage and vapor.
the colonists rose in fury,
a viceroy murdered in peru —
the laws were softened, bent, and broken,
as paper victories do.
i read the laws in seville's archive,
saw the emperor's hopeful hand —
good intentions on parchment,
drowned in the new world's sand.

the queen of a week 1542 ce scotland mary queen of scots is born as her father dies; a six-day-old inherits a crown. mary was born as her father died —
six days old, and queen of scots,
a baby in a cradle, crowned,
while the regents cast their lots.
james v had turned his face to the wall,
hearing it was a girl, not a boy —
"the crown came with a lass," he sighed,
"and it'll go with a lass," no joy.
i saw the infant in linlithgow,
the crown too big for her head —
a queen of six days, in swaddling clothes,
with a kingdom to be led.

the missionary lands 1542 ce india francis xavier reaches goa and begins the jesuit mission along asia's coasts. xavier landed at goa in may,
the jesuit with a burning heart —
he'd sail from port to port along the coasts,
the gospel to impart.
fishermen, pearl divers, the poor —
he learned their tongues, he shared their bread —
from india to the moluccas,
the seed of faith was spread.
i watched him preach on goa's shore,
saw the crowds gather round —
a saint with salt upon his robe,
and the mission's trumpet sound.

the upper sea 1542 ce california cabrillo sails up the california coast — the first european to see it. cabrillo sailed up the california coast,
past the channel islands' shore —
the first european eyes to see it,
the fog, the cliffs, the roar.
he claimed it all for spain's king,
san diego bay his mark —
then sailed on north into the mist,
and vanished in the dark.
i stood upon those headlands,
watched his ships fade in the haze —
a coastline no map had drawn,
at the edge of the world's maze.

the earth moves 1543 ce poland copernicus publishes his sun-centered cosmos — and dies as the book comes off the press. copernicus lay dying in frombork,
as the book came off the press —
de revolutionibus, the earth in motion,
the sun at the center, no less.
he'd held it back for thirty years,
fearing the church's frown —
he died as the pages reached his hands,
and the old cosmos tumbled down.
i held that first edition,
felt the weight of what it said —
the earth was just a planet,
and the heavens weren't overhead.

the body opened 1543 ce italy vesalius publishes the first true atlas of the human body, drawn from the dissecting table. vesalius stole bodies from the gibbet,
opened them on the table wide —
and drew what he saw, bone and muscle,
the human frame inside.
de humani corporis fabrica —
seven books of the body's art —
galen's errors corrected at last,
by the anatomist's true heart.
i stood beside the dissecting table,
saw the candlelight on skin —
the first true map of the human body,
drawn from deep within.

the guns arrive 1543 ce japan portuguese merchants land on tanegashima with the first muskets japan has ever seen. a chinese junk blew off course,
and landed on tanegashima's sand —
two portuguese with matchlock guns,
the first firearms in the land.
the daimyo watched them fire,
saw the smoke, heard the roar —
within a decade, japan's smiths
were making guns by the score.
i stood upon that southern beach,
saw the future in the smoke —
a weapon that would end the samurai age,
with a single trigger's stroke.

the bitter gift 1544 ce spain maya nobles present jars of frothing cacao to prince philip — europe tastes chocolate for the first time. maya nobles brought their jars to spain,
frothing cacao, bitter, dark —
a drink of kings in the new world,
now a curiosity's spark.
prince philip tasted, and frowned —
bitter! but the court was keen,
they'd add sugar, add vanilla,
and chocolate would be queen.
i watched them pour the frothing cups,
saw the spaniards' puzzled face —
a bitter gift from the maya,
that would conquer every place.

the silver mountain 1545 ce bolivia the cerro rico at potosi is found — a mountain of silver that will flood the world's coinage. a shepherd found it on cerro rico —
silver veins running through the hill,
a mountain of the shining metal,
that the world could never fill.
potosi rose in the thin cold air,
the highest city on the earth —
and the silver flowed to spain's king,
beyond all counting's worth.
i climbed that red and barren hill,
felt the altitude's thin breath —
a mountain that would buy an empire
and pay for it in death.

the council opens 1545 ce italy the council of trent convenes to answer the reformation — the counter-reformation begins. the bishops gathered at trent in december,
to answer luther's rebel cry —
the council that would last eighteen years,
and the old faith fortify.
doctrine defined, abuses trimmed,
seminaries, catechism, art —
the counter-reformation's engine,
with the jesuits at its heart.
i sat in the cathedral's shadow,
heard the debates run long —
a church refusing to surrender,
and growing hard and strong.

the reformer's death 1546 ce germany martin luther dies in eisleben, the town of his birth, worn out at sixty-two. luther died in eisleben town,
where he was born, sixty-two —
worn out by controversy, gout, and grief,
his work still to pursue.
"i am a worm," he'd sometimes say,
but the world he'd cracked in two —
the monk who'd challenged pope and empire
was mortal, through and through.
i stood beside his deathbed,
heard his final whispered prayer —
the reformation's thunder quiet,
in the february air.

the woman who would not bend 1546 ce england anne askew is burned for heresy — the only woman tortured in the tower, unbroken to the end. anne askew was racked in the tower —
the only woman tortured there —
they stretched her on the rack till her joints gave way,
but she would not recant or swear.
carried to smithfield in a chair,
too broken now to stand —
she burned for her protestant faith,
unbroken to the end, by god's hand.
i watched them light the faggots,
heard her pray above the flame —
a woman who would not bend,
and history knows her name.

the king of france dies 1547 ce france francis i dies; his sickly son henry ii takes the french crown and france slides toward religious war. francis died at rambouillet,
the dazzling king grown old and ill —
thirty-two years upon the throne,
the renaissance's brightest will.
his son henry, sickly, took the crown,
a lesser light, a darker day —
france would slide to religious war,
and the golden age decay.
i stood among the mourners,
saw the coffin draped in black —
an era ended with that king,
and would not be coming back.

the boy king 1547 ce england nine-year-old edward vi inherits england; his uncles rule in his name and push the reformation. nine years old, and king of england —
edward rode through london's cheer,
a protestant prince, a scholar's hope,
his uncles ruling near.
somerset first, then northumberland,
the boy king learned his creed —
the prayer book and the articles,
a reformation at speed.
i saw him small upon the throne,
a child with a man's mind —
england's brief protestant dawn,
before the dark behind.

the first tsar 1547 ce russia sixteen-year-old ivan iv is crowned "tsar of all rus" — ivan the terrible begins. sixteen, and crowned in the kremlin —
ivan took the title tsar,
"caesar of all rus," the first,
a star both bright and far.
the boyars bowed, the church anointed,
the bells rang through the snow —
russia had an emperor now,
and the world would come to know.
i watched the crown placed on his head,
saw the ambition in his eyes —
the terrible had begun his reign,
under the northern skies.

the emperor's victory 1547 ce germany charles v crushes the protestant princes at muhlberg — the reformation's darkest hour. at muhlberg, charles crushed the princes —
the schmalkaldic league in rout,
john frederick taken in the woods,
the protestants put out.
the emperor stood at his triumph's peak,
the reformation's darkest hour —
luther dead, the princes broken,
and charles held all the power.
i saw the prisoners led away,
heard the te deum sung —
but the victory wouldn't hold,
and the songs were barely sung.

the last conquistador 1548 ce peru pedro de la gasca defeats gonzalo pizarro; the age of the conquistadors ends in peru. gonzalo pizarro raised rebellion,
against the king's new laws —
de la gasca came with royal pardon,
and the rebels' cause gave pause.
at jaquijahuana, the troops deserted,
gonzalo left alone to stand —
beheaded in the cuzco square,
the last conquistador's hand.
i watched him kneel before the block,
the proudest of them all —
the age of the conquistadors
ended with his fall.

the prayer book 1549 ce england cranmer's book of common prayer gives england worship in its own tongue. cranmer gave england its own words —
the book of common prayer,
english worship for english folk,
morning and evening prayer.
no more latin only the priests could speak,
the liturgy in the people's tongue —
a book that would outlive its maker,
and be for centuries sung.
i held the first edition,
felt the language sing —
the most beautiful english ever prayed,
for peasant and for king.

the cross lands 1549 ce japan francis xavier reaches kagoshima — the first christian missionary in japan. xavier landed at kagoshima,
the first priest in japan's land —
he'd learn the tongue, he'd brave the cold,
the gospel in his hand.
the daimyo listened, some believed,
kyoto's monks debated long —
a seed planted in foreign soil,
a strange and fragile song.
i watched him step upon the beach,
saw the samurai stare —
the cross had landed in japan,
and nothing would be fair.

the great debate 1550 ce spain at valladolid, las casas and sepulveda argue whether the indians have souls and rights — the first great human-rights debate. at valladolid, the scholars met —
las casas against sepulveda,
"do the indians have souls?" they asked,
"are they men, or beasts instead?"
las casas argued for their humanity,
sepulveda for natural slaves —
the first great debate on human rights,
above the new world's graves.
i sat in that valladolid hall,
heard the arguments unfold —
the conscience of an empire,
weighed in words of old.

the lives of the artists 1550 ce italy vasari publishes his lives — the first art history, turning painters into legends. vasari wrote the lives in florence —
the first art history ever made,
giotto to michelangelo,
the masters and their trade.
he turned painters into legends,
gave the renaissance its tale —
without his book, we'd hardly know
the men behind the veil.
i read it fresh from the torrentino press,
felt the gossip and the glory —
the first time artists had a history,
and it was quite a story.

the new world's first university 1551 ce mexico the royal university of mexico opens — the new world's first university, older than harvard by eighty years. the royal university opened in mexico city —
the new world's first, by royal decree,
theology, law, and medicine,
for the colony's degree.
older than harvard by eighty years,
a spanish lamp in the west —
learning crossing the ocean,
to give the new world its best.
i walked its first courtyards,
heard the latin disputations —
a university in the americas,
among the new nations.

kazan falls 1552 ce russia ivan the terrible storms kazan; the tatar khanate falls and russia turns east. ivan stormed the walls of kazan,
the tatar khanate's pride —
mines blew the breaches open,
and the russians poured inside.
the khan was taken, the city sacked,
the volga opened to the east —
russia turned its face to asia,
and the conquests never ceased.
i watched the kremlin's banners rise
over kazan's fallen wall —
the first step of the russian empire,
and it would take it all.

the saint on the shore 1552 ce china francis xavier dies on shangchuan island, within sight of the china he never entered. xavier died on shangchuan island,
within sight of china's shore —
fever took him in a hut,
the middle kingdom nevermore.
he'd dreamed of converting the emperor,
of baptizing the whole land —
but died alone, a saint unmet,
with china close at hand.
i stood upon that lonely beach,
saw the mainland through the haze —
the saint who'd crossed half the world,
ended his days.

the nine days' queen 1553 ce england lady jane grey reigns nine days before mary tudor seizes the throne. lady jane grey was sixteen,
crowned by northumberland's plot —
nine days a queen, then mary came,
and jane's brief reign was not.
the tower took her, the axe would follow,
a pawn in others' game —
the nine days' queen, the innocent,
history remembers her name.
i saw her small upon the throne,
a scholar, not a queen —
nine days of borrowed majesty,
the shortest ever seen.

the catholic restoration 1553 ce england mary i takes the throne and drags england back to rome; the burnings follow and she becomes "bloody mary." mary took the throne in triumph,
the catholic queen at last —
she'd drag england back to rome,
and burn the protestant past.
the burnings followed — latimer, ridley,
cranmer too, at last —
"bloody mary," they'd call her,
for the fires she cast.
i watched the crowds cheer her entry,
saw the hope in catholic eyes —
a restoration built on ashes,
and the smoke would never rise.

the spanish marriage 1554 ce england mary marries philip of spain; england is yoked to the spanish crown. mary married philip of spain,
at winchester, in july —
england yoked to the spanish crown,
under a foreign sky.
the people feared a spanish king,
the protestants feared worse —
a marriage made for politics,
that felt like half a curse.
i stood among the wedding guests,
saw the spanish banners fly —
an english queen, a spanish prince,
and the future asking why.

the jesuit village 1554 ce brazil jesuit priests found sao paulo in the brazilian wilderness — a mission that will become a megacity. two jesuits in the wilderness —
anchieta and nobrega by name,
founded sao paulo de piratininga,
a mission, not for fame.
a village of converts and priests,
in the brazilian wild —
that would grow to twenty million,
from a mission meek and mild.
i stood upon that plateau,
saw the huts, the chapel small —
the seed of south america's giant,
the greatest of them all.

the peace of augsburg 1555 ce germany each german prince chooses his land's faith — cuius regio, eius religio; the wars pause for sixty years. at augsburg, the princes made their peace —
cuius regio, eius religio,
each ruler chooses his land's faith,
lutheran or catholic, high or low.
the wars would pause for sixty years,
a truce, not a true accord —
but germany could breathe again,
and lay aside the sword.
i heard the recess read aloud,
felt the tension ease —
peace bought with a prince's soul:
the price of such release.

the oxford martyrs 1555 ce england bishops latimer and ridley burn at oxford; latimer's candle "shall never be put out." latimer and ridley burned at oxford,
in the ditch outside the wall —
latimer's last words to his friend:
"we shall light a candle that shall never be put out."
the flames took them in october,
the crowd watched, some wept —
a candle lit in oxford
that england ever kept.
i stood among the onlookers,
heard the fire's roar —
two bishops burning for their faith,
and the light forevermore.

the two sultans' peace 1555 ce ottoman empire suleiman and persia sign the peace of amasya — the first ottoman-safavid treaty. suleiman and tahmasp made their peace —
at amasya, the treaty signed,
the first between the turk and persian,
a border defined.
mesopotamia to the sultan,
the caucasus divided fair —
two empires, two faiths, one frontier,
and a pause in the warfare.
i watched the envoys exchange the seals,
saw the relief on every face —
the first ottoman-safavid peace,
and a moment's grace.

the boy on the throne 1556 ce india thirteen-year-old akbar inherits the mughal throne; a regent holds it for him while he grows. thirteen, and emperor of hindustan —
akbar took the mughal throne,
a boy with a regent at his side,
bairam khan, the power known.
his father humayun was dead,
the empire hung by a thread —
but the boy would grow to greatness,
as the histories have said.
i saw him crowned at kalanaur,
a brick for a throne, they say —
the greatest mughal of them all,
beginning his long day.

the second panipat 1556 ce india akbar's regent bairam khan crushes hemu at panipat; the boy keeps his crown. hemu marched on delhi with his elephants,
the hindu king, the victor's pride —
bairam khan met him at panipat,
and turned the turning tide.
an arrow took hemu in the eye,
his army broke and fled —
akbar's regent held the throne,
and the boy's crown was wed.
i watched the elephants panic,
saw the field turn red —
the second battle of panipat,
and the mughal line held.

the emperor abdicates 1556 ce europe charles v gives up his thrones and retires to a monastery; his empire splits between spain and austria. charles gave up his thrones at brussels,
in tears, before the court —
the empire that the sun never set on,
now too heavy to support.
he retired to yuste's monastery,
to pray, and fish, and die —
his empire split between his son and brother,
spain and austria, low and high.
i watched him lean upon his staff,
saw the gout-racked emperor bow —
the mightiest monarch of the age,
a monk at last, somehow.

the king's bankruptcy 1557 ce spain philip ii's spain goes bankrupt — even silver mountains cannot pay for endless war. philip's spain went bankrupt —
even potosi's silver couldn't pay,
for endless wars in france and flanders,
the debts piled day by day.
the genoese bankers held the notes,
the crown suspended payment due —
the richest empire on earth,
and the coffers empty too.
i saw the ledgers in seville,
the red ink running deep —
silver mountains couldn't fill
the debts that war would keep.

the virgin queen 1558 ce england elizabeth i takes the throne — twenty-five, brilliant, protestant england's hope. elizabeth took the throne at twenty-five,
at hatfield, in november's chill —
brilliant, learned, protestant,
with an iron will.
"i have the heart of a king,"
she'd say, "though a woman's frame" —
and england would have its golden age,
under the virgin's name.
i saw her ride to london,
the crowds in wild delight —
the unwanted daughter of anne boleyn,
now england's guiding light.

calais retaken 1558 ce france france seizes calais; england's last foothold on the continent is gone. the french took calais in january,
england's last foothold on the shore —
two hundred years the english held it,
and would hold it nevermore.
mary wept to lose it,
"calais will be found in my heart" —
an island nation, cut adrift,
from the continent apart.
i watched the french banners rise
over the harbor's gray —
the end of england's continental dream,
on a winter's day.

the monk emperor's end 1558 ce spain charles v dies in his monastery cell at yuste — the monk emperor's end. charles died in his cell at yuste,
the monk emperor, alone —
gout, malaria, and melancholy,
on a simple wooden throne.
they'd buried him as a monk,
then moved him, grand, to the escorial —
the mightiest ruler of his age,
ended monastical.
i stood outside his narrow cell,
heard the monks chant low —
an emperor who gave it all away,
and died with nothing to show.

the joust that killed a king 1559 ce france henry ii dies of a splintered lance in a tournament; france slides toward religious war. henry jousted at the tournament,
to celebrate the peace —
montgomery's lance splintered,
and the king's life would cease.
a splinter through the visor,
into the eye, the brain —
ten days of agony,
then france would feel the pain.
i watched them carry him away,
the golden king brought low —
a splintered lance in a summer joust,
and the wars of religion would grow.

the trumpet of the kirk 1559 ce scotland john knox returns to scotland and preaches the kirk into revolution. knox came home to scotland,
the trumpet of the kirk —
his sermons shook the nation,
and set the catholics to work.
"the first blast of the trumpet,"
against the female rule —
but scotland heard the gospel,
in his thunder, not so cruel.
i heard him preach at perth,
saw the crowds stand still —
a voice that toppled altars,
by the power of its will.

the kirk is born 1560 ce scotland scotland's parliament adopts the protestant confession; the old faith is outlawed and the kirk is born. the scottish parliament met,
and voted the old faith out —
the protestant confession adopted,
the mass no more, no doubt.
the kirk was born in law that day,
presbyterian, stern, and free —
a nation choosing its own conscience,
for all the world to see.
i sat in the parliament hall,
heard the vote ring out —
scotland's soul by legislation,
beyond a shadow of doubt.

the bay retaken 1560 ce brazil portugal drives the french from guanabara bay, ending france's antarctic dream in brazil. the french had built their antarctic dream,
on guanabara's lovely bay —
villegagnon's colony, france antarctique,
but portugal had its say.
mem de sa sailed with his fleet,
and drove the french away —
the bay was portugal's once more,
and rio's future day.
i watched the ships exchange their fire,
saw the french flag come down —
a bay that would hold a marvelous city,
now a portuguese town.

the widowed tsar 1560 ce russia ivan buries his beloved wife anastasia; the gentle years of his reign end and the terror begins. anastasia died in august,
the tsar's beloved wife —
ivan buried her in the kremlin,
and the darkness took his life.
the gentle years were over,
the boyars would feel his wrath —
the terrible turned terrible,
on a darker path.
i watched him at the funeral,
saw the grief turn to rage —
the widowed tsar, alone,
would fill a bloody page.

the massacre at vassy 1562 ce france catholic troops slaughter huguenots at prayer at vassy; france's wars of religion begin. the duke of guise's men rode in,
on huguenots at prayer —
at vassy, in a barn, they killed,
and france was laid bare.
fifty dead, a hundred wounded,
worship turned to war —
the wars of religion had begun,
and would rage for decades more.
i heard the shots in that small town,
saw the prayer books in the mud —
a massacre at a country barn,
that drowned a land in blood.

the first slave run 1562 ce atlantic john hawkins sails the first english slaving voyage to the spanish caribbean — england joins the trade in souls. john hawkins sailed from plymouth,
with three ships and a plan —
to steal africans from the guinea coast,
and sell them, man by man.
the spanish bought them in the caribbean,
the profit was immense —
the first english slaving voyage,
a commerce of offense.
i watched them load the human cargo,
heard the chains, the cries —
england had joined the trade in souls,
under the seagull skies.

the council closes 1563 ce italy the council of trent ends, having redrawn catholic doctrine for four centuries. eighteen years, and then it closed —
the council of trent was done,
doctrine defined for centuries,
the counter-reformation won.
the mass in latin, the saints restored,
the seminaries decreed —
a church rebuilt, refortified,
for the battles it would lead.
i heard the final session,
saw the bishops sign —
four hundred years of catholic faith,
defined in black and white.

the great hand is stilled 1564 ce italy michelangelo dies in rome at eighty-eight; the renaissance's great hand is stilled. michelangelo died in rome,
eighty-eight years old —
the great hand stilled at last,
the master growing cold.
david, the ceiling, the judgment,
the dome not yet complete —
the renaissance's greatest artist,
admitted his defeat.
i stood beside his deathbed,
in his house near the forum's stone —
a giant who had carved the ages,
now lying still, alone.

the swan of avon is born 1564 ce england william shakespeare is born in stratford-upon-avon — the glover's son who will remake the world's stage. in stratford, in a timber house,
a boy was born in april —
william shakespeare, the glover's son,
who'd make the world his chapel.
no one marked the day,
no bells, no great acclaim —
just a baby in a market town,
with an ordinary name.
i stood outside that house,
heard the infant cry —
the swan of avon, newly born,
under the warwickshire sky.

the tsar walks away 1564 ce russia ivan abandons moscow in a staged abdication, then returns with absolute power and the oprichnina. ivan left moscow in december,
a staged abdication, a test —
he'd return with absolute power,
the oprichnina, his behest.
the boyars begged him to return,
he named his price: no limit —
absolute power, life and death,
and they'd submit.
i watched the sledges leave the kremlin,
saw the city hold its breath —
a tsar who walked away to rule,
by terror and by death.

the road home 1565 ce pacific urdaneta finds the return sailing route from asia to mexico — the manila galleon run is born. urdaneta found the way back —
north to japan's cold stream,
then east across the pacific,
to mexico, a dream.
the manila galleons would sail it,
for two hundred fifty years —
silver west, and silk east,
through storms and hopes and fears.
i sailed that first return voyage,
felt the kuroshio's pull —
the road home across the ocean,
that made the spanish full.

the great siege 1565 ce malta suleiman's fleet besieges malta; the knights hold, and the ottoman tide turns. suleiman sent his fleet to malta,
thirty thousand men or more —
the knights of st. john held the forts,
on that rocky shore.
four months of siege, of mines and assaults,
the turks bled on the walls —
then the relief came from sicily,
and the ottoman tide falls.
i stood upon the ramparts,
saw the turkish dead —
the great siege broken,
and the legend spread.

the oldest city 1565 ce florida spain founds st. augustine — the oldest lasting european city in north america. menendez founded st. augustine,
on florida's sandy shore —
the oldest lasting european city,
in north america, evermore.
he'd massacred the french at matanzas,
then built his town of wood —
a spanish flag on the atlantic,
where the palmettos stood.
i walked its first muddy streets,
saw the fort rise slow —
a city that would never die,
four centuries ago.

the breaking of the images 1566 ce netherlands calvinist mobs smash church statues across the low countries — the beeldenstorm, the breaking of the images. the calvinists rose in the low countries,
and smashed the church's art —
statues, altars, paintings,
torn apart.
the beeldenstorm, the image-breaking,
swept from town to town —
a fury against the idols,
that brought the churches down.
i watched them in antwerp's cathedral,
saw the saints fall from their niche —
a reformation of the hammer,
that left the churches rich in pitch.

the magnificent falls 1566 ce ottoman empire suleiman dies campaigning in hungary; the ottoman peak passes with him. suleiman died in his tent,
campaigning in hungary's plain —
seventy-one, the magnificent,
would never march again.
they hid his death from the army,
till the fortress fell —
then carried him home to istanbul,
where the great mosques tell.
i stood outside his campaign tent,
heard the silence in the camp —
the ottoman peak had passed,
like a snuffed-out lamp.

the queen in chains 1567 ce scotland mary queen of scots is forced to abdicate; her infant son james vi is crowned. mary was forced to abdicate,
at lochleven's lonely isle —
her infant son was crowned james vi,
and she was left awhile.
she'd escape, she'd flee to england,
and elizabeth would hold her fast —
nineteen years a prisoner,
till the axe fell at last.
i saw her sign the abdication,
saw the tears upon her face —
a queen in chains, a crown in cradle,
and scotland's dark disgrace.

the beggars' war 1568 ce netherlands william of orange raises the revolt; the dutch fight for freedom begins and will last eighty years. william of orange raised the revolt,
the beggars' war began —
against the spanish tercios,
