the dutch would make their stand.
they'd fight for eighty years,
for freedom and for trade —
a nation born in the marshes,
that the sea had made.
i marched with william's rebels,
saw the dikes, the floods —
the dutch fight for freedom,
written in their blood.

the prince's death 1568 ce spain philip's heir don carlos dies a prisoner in madrid; the succession darkens and rumors haunt the court. don carlos died in madrid,
a prisoner in his father's keep —
mad, deformed, and dangerous,
his secrets buried deep.
philip's heir, the troubled prince,
locked away from light —
did his father have him murdered?
the question haunts the night.
i walked the palace corridors,
heard the whispers low —
a prince who died a prisoner,
and no one truly knows.

the mountain revolt 1568 ce spain the moriscos of granada rise against forced conversion; spain answers with fire and don john crushes them. the moriscos rose in the alpujarras,
against forced conversion's chain —
they'd been muslims, made christians,
now they'd fight again.
spain answered with fire and sword,
don john of austria's might —
two years of mountain warfare,
in the cold and in the night.
i climbed those mountain villages,
saw the smoke rise high —
a revolt of the converted,
that was doomed to die.

the world remapped 1569 ce flanders mercator publishes his world map with the projection that will guide sailors for centuries. mercator published his world map,
with the projection sailors know —
the loxodrome as a straight line,
wherever the winds blow.
it stretched the poles, it warped the lands,
but the compass course ran true —
for centuries, every chart at sea
would follow mercator's clue.
i saw that first great atlas,
felt the world grow wide —
a map that guided sailors,
on every ocean's tide.

the island falls 1570 ce cyprus ottoman troops take nicosia; venice's cyprus begins to crumble in blood. the ottomans took nicosia,
after a brutal siege —
twenty thousand dead in the streets,
no quarter, no reprieve.
famagusta held a little longer,
then bragadin was flayed —
venice's cyprus crumbling,
and the price was paid.
i walked nicosia's broken walls,
saw the aftermath of war —
an island falling to the turk,
and the sea's red shore.

the tomb of the father 1570 ce india humayun's tomb rises in delhi — the first great mughal garden-tomb, model for the taj. humayun's tomb rose in delhi,
the first great mughal garden-tomb —
red sandstone and white marble,
a paradise from gloom.
his widow built it for his memory,
a garden for the dead —
the model for the taj to come,
in beauty widespread.
i walked its charbagh gardens,
saw the dome against the sky —
the first of the mughal wonders,
where emperors lie.

the cross against the crescent 1571 ce mediterranean at lepanto the holy league smashes the ottoman fleet — the sea's greatest galley battle. at lepanto the fleets collided —
two hundred galleys on each side,
the holy league against the turk,
on the turning tide.
don john led the christian left,
the turks broke by noon —
thirty thousand dead at sea,
under the autumn moon.
i stood upon the spanish deck,
heard the cannon's roar —
the sea's greatest galley battle,
and the ottoman no more.

the pearl of the orient 1571 ce philippines legazpi founds manila, the far anchor of spain's pacific empire. legazpi founded manila,
on the bay's fair shore —
the far anchor of spain's pacific,
the pearl of the orient's door.
the galleons would come each year,
from acapulco's strand —
silver for silk, the trade of empires,
across the ocean's hand.
i walked manila's first streets,
saw the walls rise high —
a spanish city in the tropics,
under the asian sky.

the wedding of blood 1572 ce france on st. bartholomew's day, catholics massacre thousands of huguenots in paris — the wedding of blood. they came to paris for a wedding —
margaret and henry of navarre,
a catholic bride, a huguenot groom,
to end the religious war.
but on st. bartholomew's day,
the bells rang for the kill —
thousands of huguenots slaughtered,
in paris, on the hill.
i fled through streets of blood,
saw the seine run red —
a wedding turned to massacre,
and the marriage of the dead.

the horde broken 1572 ce russia at molodi, russia crushes the crimean tatars' last great raid toward moscow. the crimean tatars rode for moscow,
forty thousand strong —
but at molodi, the russians waited,
and the battle wasn't long.
the gulyay-gorod, the mobile fortress,
broke the tatar charge —
the last great raid toward moscow,
ended, small and large.
i watched the tatar horsemen fall,
saw the steppe turn red —
the horde was broken at molodi,
and the raiders fled.

the last shogun falls 1573 ce japan oda nobunaga drives out the ashikaga shogun; japan's warring age tilts toward union. nobunaga drove the shogun out,
the last ashikaga, yoshiaki —
japan's warring age was tilting,
toward union, toward the key.
the shogunate was over,
the daimyo fought alone —
but nobunaga's guns and ambition
would claim the chrysanthemum throne.
i watched the shogun flee kyoto,
saw nobunaga's banners fly —
an age of warlords ending,
under the japanese sky.

the draft of the mines 1574 ce bolivia viceroy toledo chains the andes to potosi with the mita labor draft; silver flows, villages empty. toledo chained the andes to potosi,
the mita draft, the forced labor —
villages emptied of their men,
for the silver's favor.
they'd work the mines in the freezing cold,
mercury poisoning their breath —
the silver flowed to spain's king,
and the andes paid in death.
i saw the conscripts march away,
heard the women weep —
a mountain eating a people,
while the empire slept.

the guns win 1575 ce japan at nagashino, nobunaga's musket lines shred the takeda cavalry — the gun beats the sword. at nagashino, the takeda charged —
the finest cavalry in japan,
against nobunaga's palisades,
and the muskets of his clan.
three thousand guns in rotating ranks,
fired volley after volley —
the horsemen fell like autumn leaves,
in the summer's folly.
i stood behind the wooden stakes,
heard the muskets' roar —
the gun had beaten the sword,
forevermore.

the house of worship 1575 ce india at fatehpur sikri, akbar opens the ibadat khana — a hall where every faith is invited to argue before the emperor himself. i stood in the courtyard at fatehpur sikri
when the doors swung open and the arguing began.
akbar had built a hall for every god on earth
and told the priests: come in, and speak your truth.
i watched a muslim scholar pace the marble floor,
a brahmin unroll his scrolls, a jesuit cross himself,
a jain monk covering his mouth so no small life
would die on his breath — all of them shouting at once.
the emperor sat above it all, listening,
as if the clamor of all faiths at once
might add up to something single and quiet —
one house big enough for every kind of prayer.

the house of debate 1575 ce mughal india night after night at the ibadat khana, scholars of four faiths argue before akbar — and the traveler listens to the world argue with itself. i came back the second night, and the third —
the debates ran hotter than the desert outside.
the mullah called the jesuit a liar;
the jesuit called the mullah blind.
the hindu pandit smiled at both of them
and said the truth was older than their books.
akbar leaned forward on his cushion, hungry,
drinking it all in like water in a drought.
he wanted one faith for all his people,
but what he got was better — the honest noise
of minds that would not bend.
i left before dawn, my ears still ringing,
glad to have heard the world argue with itself
and live to tell it.

the spanish fury 1576 ce antwerp unpaid spanish troops sack antwerp for three days, burning its city hall — and turning the whole netherlands against spain for good. i was in antwerp when the pay ran out.
the spanish tercios had not been paid in months,
and hunger is a better general than any king.
they came through the gates like a breaking dam —
three days of fire, three days of the sword.
i hid in a cellar and heard the city hall burn,
heard the richest city in the netherlands
screaming in five languages.
when it was over, a thousand lay dead in the streets,
and every burgher in the low countries
knew exactly who the enemy was.
spain had paid its soldiers in blood and ash —
and the dutch would remember the price forever.

the star castle 1576 ce denmark on a danish island, tycho brahe raises uraniborg — the grandest observatory of the age — and maps the heavens by naked eye alone. i sailed to the island of hven to see it —
uraniborg, tycho brahe's castle of the stars,
red brick and gardens and brass instruments
bigger than a man, polished like church bells.
no telescope yet — only the naked eye,
but an eye trained like a swordsman's arm.
tycho measured every star to the minute of arc,
twenty years of nights, his nose half gold
from a duel, his moose drunk in the stairwell.
i stood beside him on the terrace at midnight
while he called out numbers to his scribe,
and understood: this strange proud man
was building the ladder the next age would climb.

drake sails into the unknown 1577 ce plymouth francis drake slips out of plymouth with five small ships, bound to circle the globe through seas spain claims as its own. i watched them slip out of plymouth at dawn —
five little ships, a hundred and sixty men,
francis drake at the prow with the queen's secret blessing
and a hold full of hunger.
the spanish owned those seas; every chart said so.
drake meant to steal through them anyway,
around the bottom of the world and up the far side,
taking what he could and burning what he couldn't.
i stood on the dock till the sails were specks.
some men sail for god, some for gold —
drake sailed for the sheer joy of the taking.
the pacific had never seen his like,
and it was about to.

the great comet 1577 ce the skies a great comet blazes over europe for months; tycho brahe's measurements prove it flies far beyond the moon — and the old heavens crack. it hung there for months — a sword of light
across the winter sky, and all of europe
held its breath and read it as an omen.
kings would fall, the preachers said. plague. war.
only tycho did the arithmetic.
night after night he measured its place
against the fixed stars, and the numbers told him
what no one dared to say aloud:
it flew beyond the moon, out in the deep —
where the old books said nothing could change.
i watched him write it down, hand shaking,
not with fear but with the thrill of it.
the heavens were not perfect and unchanging.
the sky had cracked, and through the crack
we could all see further than before.

the battle of three kings 1578 ce morocco at alcacer quibir, portugal's young king and two rival sultans all die in one battle — and portugal's throne falls vacant. three kings rode out that morning at alcacer quibir.
by sunset all three were dead.
young sebastian of portugal, twenty-four,
dreaming of crusades in shining armor —
drowned in a moroccan river, his body never found.
the old sultan died in his litter, watching.
the rival sultan died of his sickness in the rout.
i walked the field the next day among the flies,
twenty thousand portuguese dead or taken,
and a kingdom with no king, no heir, no hope.
portugal's throne stood empty in lisbon,
and across the border old philip of spain
was already counting the crowns.
one hot afternoon in morocco,
and an empire changed hands.

the union of utrecht 1579 ce netherlands seven northern provinces swear the union of utrecht against spain — the first stone of the dutch republic, signed with a pen in winter. in a cold hall at utrecht, seven provinces
put their names to a piece of paper
and swore to stand together against spain —
calvinist holland, catholic stragglers, all of them,
bound by nothing but a shared refusal.
i watched the delegates argue over every clause,
suspicious as cats, stubborn as mules —
and sign anyway.
no king gave them leave. no pope blessed it.
seven small provinces looked at the greatest empire
on earth and said: we will be one thing now.
it was the first stone of a republic
nobody had planned and nobody could stop.
i have seen empires founded with trumpets;
this one was founded with a pen,
in winter, by tired men who would not kneel.

one crown for two kingdoms 1580 ce iberia philip ii marches into portugal and takes its throne — the two greatest seafaring empires now wear a single crown. philip did not even have to fight for it.
he marched into portugal with his tercios,
the nobles opened the gates, the cortes bowed,
and the two greatest seafaring empires on earth
wore one crown.
i stood in lisbon as the spanish banners rose
over the harbor where the caravels had sailed
for india, for brazil, for the spice islands.
from the tagus to manila, from bahia to macao,
one king's writ now ran across half the world.
the portuguese wept in the taverns that night —
not for sebastian, long dead in morocco,
but for themselves, become a province
of somebody else's empire.
i drank with them, and understood:
this was the high-water mark of spain,
and high water always turns.

the dutch say no more 1581 ce netherlands the dutch formally depose philip ii — the first modern republic is declared, and a king is unmade by paperwork. they did it with a document — the act of abjuration —
read aloud in the hague on a summer day:
philip ii, king of spain, was hereby deposed,
his sovereignty renounced, his name struck out.
i was in the crowd outside, and i heard the cheer
that went up from the burghers and the sailors —
a sound like a dam breaking.
no more king. no more distant throne in madrid
telling them what god to pray to.
it was the first time in the modern age
that a people had fired their king by paperwork.
the ink was barely dry and the war went on,
but something had changed in the air of europe:
a king could be unmade by the people he ruled.
i wrote the date down carefully.
i knew i would need it later.

across the stone belt 1581 ce russia the cossack yermak leads a few hundred men over the urals into siberia — and opens a continent-sized land for russia. yermak took five hundred cossacks over the urals —
the stone belt, the russians called those mountains —
into a land no tsar had ever ruled.
i traveled with the supply train part of the way,
through forest that went on past imagining,
rivers wide as seas, winter already breathing
down our necks in september.
they fought the khan's men with muskets and nerve,
took his capital at kashlyk, and kept going.
five hundred men against a continent —
and the continent gave way.
siberia opened like a door nobody had pushed.
the furs, the rivers, the endless taiga:
russia doubled, tripled, became a giant
while europe was looking the other way.
i stood on a ridge and looked east
and could not see the end of what they'd won.

the single whip 1581 ce ming china zhang juzheng folds every ming tax into a single silver payment — steadying china's economy for a generation on foreign silver. zhang juzheng did it with a brushstroke —
folded every tax in the empire into one:
a single payment, in silver, no more grain levies,
no more labor service, no more local extortion
dressed up as a dozen different dues.
i watched the clerks in a county yamen
redo their ledgers, grumbling at the new simplicity.
the peasants understood it at once:
one whip instead of many.
pay the silver, and the year is yours.
for a generation the ming breathed easier —
granaries filled, the coin ran clean,
the great machine of china hummed.
one man's reform, one metal, one rule.
i have seen empires saved by less,
and lost by more.
but silver has a price, and the mines were far away —
across an ocean the ming barely knew existed.

ten days vanish 1582 ce rome pope gregory xiii cuts ten days from the calendar to fix its drift — catholic europe goes to sleep on october 4 and wakes on october 15. pope gregory signed the bull, and ten days vanished.
october 4th went to sleep a thursday;
october 15th woke up a friday.
the calendar had drifted eleven minutes a year
since julius caesar's time, and easter was sliding
toward summer — so the pope simply cut the knot.
i was in rome that week, and the confusion
was delicious: rents due on days that never happened,
saints' feasts leaping forward, protestants
refusing the whole thing as popish trickery.
england kept the old calendar for 170 years
out of sheer spite.
but the stars don't care about spite.
the new calendar fit the heavens,
and one by one the nations came around.
i keep two dates for that autumn in my journal —
the day that was, and the day that wasn't.

fire at honno-ji 1582 ce japan betrayed at kyoto's honno-ji temple, oda nobunaga takes his own life as the flames close in — and hideyoshi seizes his chance. i was in kyoto the night honno-ji burned.
oda nobunaga, the great unifier, the demon king,
lay sleeping in the temple with a handful of guards
when his own general akechi turned his banners
and ringed the walls with fire.
no escape. no last charge. nobunaga knew it —
he went inside, shut the doors, and did
what a samurai does when the game is lost:
the blade, the poem, the flames closing in.
i stood in the street and watched the roof fall in,
and all of japan held its breath.
who would take the sword now?
far away, hideyoshi — the monkey, the peasant's son —
heard the news on campaign, made peace in a day,
and force-marched his army back to avenge his lord.
the fire at honno-ji lit more than a temple.
it lit the fuse on everything that came next.

the mystic dies 1582 ce spain teresa of avila — reformer of her order, author of the soul's interior castle — dies at alba de tormes. she died at alba de tormes, worn out at sixty-seven —
teresa of avila, the nun who had reformed her order
one convent at a time, riding mule-back across spain
while the inquisition watched her sideways.
i had read her book, the interior castle —
seven mansions of the soul, each one brighter,
god waiting in the innermost room.
she wrote of prayer the way other people write of love:
direct, bodily, unashamed.
they say her last words were about going home.
the church would make her a saint and a doctor,
the first woman to hold the title —
but i remember her best as the prioress
who laughed at her own failures
and told her nuns that god walks among the pots and pans.

england's first claim 1583 ce newfoundland humphrey gilbert plants the english flag at st. john's, claiming newfoundland — england's first overseas territory — with turf and twig. humphrey gilbert waded ashore at st. john's
with a charter from the queen and a twig in his hand —
the old ceremony, turf and twig,
taking possession for england in the sight of god
and thirty foreign fishermen who didn't care.
i stood on that rocky harbor and watched him
read the proclamation to the gulls and the cod boats.
newfoundland: england's first piece of the new world,
claimed with words and a stick.
he never saw it grow. on the way home
his little ship went down in a storm off the azores,
and the last anyone saw of him he was sitting
on the deck reading a book, calling out
that they were as near to heaven by sea as by land.
the claim outlived the claimant.
they usually do.

the silent falls 1584 ce netherlands william of orange, father of the dutch revolt, is assassinated on his own staircase in delft — but the cause survives him. i was in delft the day it happened —
in the prinsenhof, on the staircase,
where balthasar gerard waited with a pistol
bought with spanish money.
william of orange — the silent, the father
of the whole revolt — came down for his dinner
and took three balls in the chest.
his last words, they say: god have mercy
on my soul, and on this poor people.
i heard the shot from the courtyard
and ran up to find him bleeding on the stairs,
his wife screaming, the assassin caught
trying to climb the wall.
spain had put a price on his head for years;
at last somebody collected.
the dutch wept in the streets that night —
but they did not surrender.
you cannot kill a cause with a pistol.
philip would learn that, slowly, at great cost.

the stone palace finished 1584 ce spain after twenty-one years of building, philip ii's vast escorial — palace, monastery, and tomb of kings — is completed. twenty-one years. i watched it rise, stone by stone,
out of the guadarrama granite —
the escorial: palace, monastery, basilica,
tomb of kings, all in one gray grid,
built to the measure of philip's god and philip's gloom.
i walked its corridors the week it was finished:
a hundred miles of passageways, they said,
courtyards cold as a chessboard,
the king's own rooms small and plain as a monk's cell,
looking out at the high altar.
philip built it to hold spain's soul still —
one faith, one king, one geometry.
it is magnificent, and it is a mausoleum
that happens to have a throne in it.
i stood in the pantheon of kings, under the dome,
and felt the weight of an empire
trying to pray itself into permanence.

the colony lands 1585 ce roanoke english settlers wade ashore on roanoke island — england's first colony in the americas takes root in hope and bad planning. i came ashore with them at roanoke —
a hundred and eight souls wading through the surf,
soldiers and planters and gentlemen adventurers,
planting england's flag in the sand of the new world.
the island was beautiful: live oaks, wild grapes,
the sound sweet in the air.
the algonquians watched from the treeline,
wondering what these pale hungry people wanted.
we built the fort, we planted the crops,
we quarreled magnificently among ourselves.
raleigh's money, grenville's temper, lane's suspicion —
a colony founded on hope and bad planning.
i helped raise the first palisade
and wondered, driving the stakes,
how many of us would see england again.
the gulls cried over the sound.
the forest kept its own counsel.

the scheldt closed 1585 ce antwerp parma retakes antwerp after a brutal siege — and its merchants flee north, carrying their wealth and craft to amsterdam. parma took antwerp the slow way — a bridge of boats
across the scheldt, a siege of fourteen months,
hunger doing what cannon could not.
when the city yielded, the terms were merciful
and the meaning was not.
i was there when the merchants made their choice:
stay under spanish catholic rule,
or pack the ledgers and run north.
they ran — thousands of them, the richest,
the cleverest, the most protestant of antwerp —
up the coast to amsterdam, to middelburg, to london,
carrying their capital, their contacts, their craft.
spain won the city and lost the economy.
i watched the barges leave, low in the water
with strongboxes, and thought:
this is how the future moves —
not with armies, but with account books,
floating north on the tide.

the babington plot 1586 ce england mary queen of scots is caught backing the babington plot to kill elizabeth — her ciphered letters, all read by walsingham, seal her fate. it was the letters that killed her —
letters smuggled in beer barrels, written in cipher,
answered in cipher, every word read by walsingham's men
before mary ever saw them.
anthony babington, young and catholic and foolish,
laid out the whole bright plan: kill elizabeth,
raise the north, put mary on the throne
with spanish swords behind her.
and mary — nineteen years a prisoner,
a queen in a cage — wrote back her approval,
in her own hand, in cipher.
i read the deciphered copies years later,
and my blood ran cold at the neatness of it:
walsingham had built the trap, baited it,
and let her walk in with her eyes open.
the warrant was only a matter of time now.
a queen had signed her own death
in invisible ink, and the ink had become visible.

a queen loses her head 1587 ce england after nineteen years a prisoner, mary queen of scots is beheaded at fotheringhay — in crimson, the color of martyrdom. fotheringhay, on a february morning, in the great hall —
they had built the scaffold draped in black,
and mary came down the stairs in a gown of crimson,
the color of catholic martyrdom, her head held high.
i was not in the hall — few were —
but i heard it from those who stood close enough
to see: the first blow missed its mark,
the second severed, the executioner held up the head
and the auburn hair came away in his hand —
a wig, and beneath it gray, close-cropped,
the hair of a woman of forty-four
who had been a prisoner half her life.
her little dog had hidden in her skirts
and would not leave the body.
elizabeth signed the warrant and then raged at it,
as queens do when the thing is done
and cannot be undone.
two queens, one island, one axe.
it could never have ended otherwise.

singeing the king's beard 1587 ce cadiz drake storms into cadiz harbor in daylight and burns the ships spain was gathering for invasion — singeing the king's beard. drake did it in broad daylight — sailed straight
into cadiz harbor with twenty-odd ships
and burned everything that floated.
i watched from the cliffs as the smoke went up:
twenty-four spanish ships, ten thousand tons
of invasion stores, barrels and biscuit and cordage
meant for the armada gathering down the coast.
drake's men rowed in among the anchored hulls
with fire and laughter, and rowed out again
before the forts could find the range.
he called it singeing the king of spain's beard —
and the beard took a year to grow back.
philip's great invasion, meant for that summer,
waited for the next.
one raid, one harbor, one afternoon:
sometimes history turns on a match.

the galleon taken 1587 ce the pacific thomas cavendish captures the spanish treasure galleon santa ana off california — the richest prize of the age. off the california coast, in november fog,
cavendish's little desire ran down the santa ana —
a 700-ton manila galleon, fat with the wealth of asia:
silks, spices, musk, and gold, the richest prize
any englishman had ever taken.
i sailed with cavendish's crew that season,
and i saw the spanish captain strike his colors
without a fight he couldn't win.
they stripped her for six days — sails, rigging,
treasure — then set her adrift with the crew
and burned what they couldn't carry.
the share-out made every man aboard rich for life.
back in plymouth they rang the bells.
spain's pacific, the closed sea, the private lake —
was open water now, and every sea-dog in england
knew the galleons bled gold.

the armada broken 1588 ce english channel storms and english fireships scatter philip ii's great armada — spain's dream of invading england drowns in the channel. a hundred and thirty ships came up the channel
in a crescent a mile wide — the greatest fleet
the world had seen, carrying the pope's blessing
and thirty thousand men to conquer england.
i watched from the cliffs of cornwall as they passed,
tall castles of oak moving like a floating city.
and then the english came — smaller, faster,
their guns firing four shots to spain's one —
and at gravelines the crescent broke.
but it was the wind that finished it.
the fireships at calais scattered them in panic;
the gales off scotland and ireland did the rest.
wrecks from the giant's causeway to the hebrides,
men drowning in armor, the sea giving back nothing.
philip heard the news in the escorial
and said, i sent them against men, not winds.
half the fleet never came home.
england's island story begins here —
in a storm, with a prayer answered sideways.

the young shah 1589 ce persia sixteen-year-old abbas takes persia's throne amid enemies on every side — and begins the long climb to greatness. sixteen years old, and they put the crown on him —
abbas, grandson of the great tahmasp,
inheriting a persia eaten by uzbeks in the east,
ottomans in the west, and his own qizilbash chiefs
carving the kingdom like a roast.
i was in qazvin when he took the throne,
a boy with old eyes, watching everything.
he had learned the lesson of his father's weakness:
trust no chief, build your own musketeers,
take back the land inch by inch.
he would do it. in the years to come
this boy would retake tabriz and baghdad,
move the capital to isfahan, make persia
shine again — abbas the great, they would call him.
but that winter he was only sixteen,
standing very straight under a very heavy crown,
and i could see him deciding, already,
to be greater than everyone expected.

the counter-armada fails 1589 ce lisbon drake and norris sail to strike back at spain off lisbon — but disease and bad luck break their fleet, and england's revenge fails. england tried to return the favor — drake and norris
with a fleet as big as the armada's, sailing for lisbon
to smash spain while it was down and put a pretender
on the portuguese throne.
i watched them leave plymouth in a fair wind,
the whole country drunk on the armada year.
it went wrong from the start: no siege guns,
no money, the portuguese who were supposed to rise
staying prudently indoors, disease eating the crews
like fire eats paper.
they burned some shipping at corunna, failed at lisbon,
limped home with half their men dead of sickness.
drake's luck had run out; the queen never forgave him.
i stood on the dock as the survivors staggered ashore,
and learned what every gambler learns:
the same sea that makes you can unmake you,
and glory spends fast.

hunger behind the walls 1590 ce paris henry iv's siege starves paris into submission — thirty thousand dead of hunger before politics opens the gates. henry laid his siege and waited. paris was catholic,
paris hated him, paris would starve first —
and nearly did.
i slipped through the lines that summer with a grain convoy
that never arrived, and saw what hunger looks like
in a great city: dogs gone, then cats, then rats,
then the leather of harnesses boiled for soup.
thirty thousand died, they said, before the end.
the spanish held the walls; the parisians held their pride;
the children held nothing, being dead.
in the end it was politics, not bread, that opened the gates —
henry would come to terms, convert, be crowned.
but i have never forgotten the silence of those streets,
the great city eating itself while the king waited outside,
patient as winter.

the dome is raised 1590 ce rome giacomo della porta crowns st. peter's with its great dome, completing michelangelo's design — the mother of all domes since. giacomo della porta raised it — the great dome
over st. peter's, michelangelo's design made real:
a hundred and thirty-six meters of stone and faith,
the biggest dome in christendom, floating
over the tomb of the fisherman.
i climbed the scaffolding in the last months,
up past the ribs of it, the workers singing
as they hauled the final stones into place.
from the lantern at the top, all rome lay below —
the tiber, the seven hills, the ruins of the caesars —
and the dome seemed to hold the whole city
in the palm of its hand.
michelangelo had died twenty-six years before,
never seeing it finished. but his geometry stood there
in the roman sky, perfect as mathematics,
and every dome built since — in london, in washington —
is a child of this one.
i touched the stone. it was warm from the sun.

croatoan 1590 ce roanoke john white returns to roanoke to find every settler vanished — one word carved on a post: croatoan. america's first mystery. john white came back after three years —
three years of war and weather keeping him in england —
and found the colony gone.
not burned. not massacred, by the look of it.
the houses taken down careful, the fort dismantled,
the boats gone. a hundred and sixteen people —
men, women, children, his own granddaughter
virginia, the first english child born in america —
vanished into the trees.
one word, carved on a palisade post: croatoan.
the name of the friendly island nearby.
no cross, the distress sign they'd agreed —
so they had gone willingly, or at least alive.
i walked that empty settlement with white,
calling names into the silence.
the word on the post is still there in my mind,
cut deep and plain: croatoan.
america's first mystery, and nobody
has ever solved it.

tondibi 1591 ce west africa moroccan musketeers crush the mighty songhai empire at tondibi in a single afternoon — west africa's golden age ends in gunpowder smoke. one afternoon. that is all it took —
one afternoon at tondibi to end an empire.
the songhai came down to the niger plain
in their tens of thousands, horsemen in mail,
the greatest army west africa had ever raised.
the moroccans had four thousand men —
and muskets, and cannon, and a spanish renegade
who knew his business.
i stood on a rise and watched the future arrive
in smoke: the volleys rolling like thunder,
the cavalry breaking like waves on rock,
the askia's host dissolving into the dust
it had raised.
by evening the songhai empire — timbuktu,
gao, djenne, the scholars and the gold —
was a moroccan province.
the scholars were chained and marched to marrakesh.
the libraries were looted.
west africa's golden age ended in a single afternoon,
and the desert wind covered the tracks.

the invasion begins 1592 ce korea hideyoshi's armies storm ashore at busan — japan's great invasion of korea begins at dawn. they came across the strait at dawn —
hideyoshi's armies, a hundred and sixty thousand strong,
landing at busan with arquebuses and banners,
the largest overseas invasion japan had ever launched.
i was in the south when the news came running:
the japanese took busan in a day, dongnae in a day,
the korean armies melting before the gunfire.
hideyoshi's dream was enormous — korea first,
then china, then, he said, india.
the peasant's son who had become the taiko
meant to rule the world.
the court at seoul fled north. the king fled north.
everything fled north — except the sea,
where a one-eyed admiral was waiting
with ships like turtles.
but that is another story.
this one begins with the landing:
dawn, busan, and the sound of a hundred thousand feet
marching into somebody else's country.

turtle ships at hansan 1592 ce korea admiral yi sun-sin smashes the japanese fleet at hansan with his armored turtle ships — cutting the invaders' lifeline in a single day. yi sun-sin built them like a dream of war —
turtle ships, armored in iron plates,
a dragon's head at the prow breathing smoke,
oars and cannon and a roof no arrow could pierce.
at hansan the japanese came in strength,
seventy-three warships confident and proud.
yi met them with his turtles and his cranes —
the crane-wing formation, he'd drilled it for years —
and closed the wings around them like a trap.
i watched from a headland as the sea caught fire:
japanese hulls splitting under cannon fire,
men leaping into water that boiled with wreckage,
the invaders' lifeline cut in a single day.
hideyoshi's armies in the north never got their rice,
never got their reinforcements.
one admiral, one strait, one perfect battle —
and the greatest invasion of the age
began to starve.

paris is well worth a mass 1593 ce france henry iv converts to catholicism — "paris is well worth a mass" — and the city opens its gates, ending thirty years of religious war. he said it with a soldier's grin — or so they say:
paris is well worth a mass.
henry of navarre, the protestant king,
rode into saint-denis and knelt before the altar
and became catholic, just like that.
i was in paris when the gates opened.
the city that had starved rather than take him
as a heretic took him as a convert —
cheering in the streets, bells ringing,
the white plume of navarre riding through
triumphant at last.
was it faith or politics? the priests debated it
for centuries. henry's answer was france itself:
thirty years of religious war ending
not with a battle but with a baptism.
he gave them peace, and peace was worth
whatever the mass had cost him.
i watched him ride past, and he looked —
for the first time in his life —
like a man who could finally rest.

the first tulips 1593 ce holland botanist carolus clusius plants the first tulips at leiden — neighbors steal the bulbs, and a flower begins its conquest of holland. carolus clusius planted them at leiden —
a few bulbs from turkey, strange striped flowers
nobody in holland had ever seen.
he was a botanist; he only wanted to study them.
i walked his garden that spring and saw them:
tulips, red and yellow, standing like small flames
in the dutch rain.
clusius refused to sell a single bulb.
so the neighbors stole them in the night —
over the wall, out of the beds, into every garden
in the low countries.
that theft was the seed of everything:
the mania, the fortunes, the crash to come.
a flower conquered holland the way no army could —
one stolen bulb at a time.
i kept one clusius gave me freely,
pressed it in my journal, and wrote beside it:
here begins the strangest bubble in history.

a poet murdered 1593 ce england christopher marlowe — tamburlaine, faustus — is stabbed dead in a deptford tavern at twenty-nine, over a reckoning no one can explain. deptford, in a tavern room, over the reckoning —
christopher marlowe, twenty-nine years old,
the brightest bad boy of the london stage,
took a dagger above the eye and died on the spot.
tamburlaine. faustus. the jew of malta.
he had written the mighty line and made kings talk
like thunder, and now he was dead in a tavern
over who paid for dinner — or over spying,
or atheism, or a quarrel about nothing.
nobody knows. the inquest was quick
and the witnesses were liars.
i had seen faustus at the rose, the devil
coming for his due, the crowd gasping.
shakespeare was still finding his voice;
marlowe had already found his, and lost it
in a deptford afternoon.
cut is the branch that might have grown full straight —
his own line, from faustus, and truer
than he ever meant it to be.

tintoretto dies 1594 ce venice jacopo tintoretto — il furioso, the furious painter of light and storm — dies in venice after a lifetime covering its walls. they called him il furioso — the furious one —
and he painted like a storm: fifty men on a scaffold,
canvases the size of walls, light breaking
like surf over the whole of venice.
i saw him once in his workshop near the church
of the madonna dell'orto, an old man
still climbing the ladders himself,
still furious, still covering venice wall by wall —
the paradiso in the doge's palace,
the biggest painting in the world,
a heaven crowded with five hundred souls.
he died in may, worn out at seventy-five,
and they buried him under his own last judgment.
venice kept his light on its walls;
the fury went with him into the ground.
i stood before the paradiso afterward
and felt small, the way you feel small
before weather.

the search for el dorado 1595 ce south america walter raleigh sails up the orinoco hunting el dorado, the golden city — and finds only jungle, fever, and a story england wanted to believe. raleigh sailed up the orinoco with his dreams
packed alongside the powder —
el dorado, the golden city, the king
dusted with gold from head to foot,
waiting somewhere in the green.
i went upriver with his men part of the way:
the heat, the mosquitoes, the water the color of tea,
the jungle closing over the wake behind us.
we found gold dust in the river sand,
parrots, caimans, fever —
and no city. never any city.
raleigh wrote it up golden anyway —
the discovery of guiana, all promise and maps —
and england believed him, because england wanted to.
i kept my journal honest: the jungle keeps
what it keeps. the gold was in the story,
and the story was enough to launch a hundred ships
toward a city that never existed.

drake's last harbor 1596 ce panama francis drake dies of fever off portobelo and is buried at sea in a lead coffin — the sea that made him takes him back. he died of the bloody flux off portobelo —
francis drake, the dragon of the spanish main,
fifty-five years old, raging at a war
that had stopped going his way.
i was aboard when it happened. the expedition
had failed at panama, failed at san juan;
the men were dying of fever faster than of shot.
drake took to his hammock and never rose,
and we buried him at sea in a lead coffin,
two miles off the harbor he'd meant to take.
the spanish fired a salute, they say —
even his enemies honored him.
the queen's pirate, the circumnavigator,
the singe-beard of cadiz:
the sea that made him took him back,
as the sea does with its own.
i watched the coffin sink, and the water closed
without a ripple, as if he'd never been.

cadiz burned again 1596 ce spain essex and howard storm cadiz and burn the spanish fleet in its harbor — spain scuttles its own treasure ships rather than yield them. this time it was essex — young, golden, reckless —
with howard and the fleet, storming cadiz
the way drake had nine years before,
only bigger, and this time they took the town itself.
i watched the galleons burn in the harbor,
the smoke visible for twenty miles,
the spanish scuttling their own treasure ships
to keep them out of english hands —
millions in silver going to the bottom
rather than into essex's coffers.
all europe watched, all europe applauded,
and nothing much changed.
philip built more ships. essex came home a hero
and quarreled with the queen within the year.
i walked the blackened waterfront afterward
and thought about how war eats money:
spain burned its own wealth to deny it to england,
and both empires were poorer for the fire.

the great herbal 1596 ce ming china after twenty-seven years of work, li shizhen's compendium of materia medica is published — nearly two thousand medicines, honestly cataloged. twenty-seven years. li shizhen spent twenty-seven years
on it — traveling, tasting, testing,
correcting the old errors one root at a time.
the compendium of materia medica:
fifty-two volumes, nearly two thousand medicines,
eight thousand prescriptions, every herb drawn
and described, the wrong names struck out,
the dangerous doses marked in red.
i met him once, near the end — an old man
with stained fingers and a walking stick,
still checking a specimen against his notes.
he had done for medicine what the great historians
did for the past: made it honest.
they published it after his death; he never saw it bound.
but every doctor in china for the next three centuries
reached for li shizhen first.
twenty-seven years, one book, two thousand cures —
i have never seen patience built so large.

the second invasion 1597 ce korea hideyoshi launches a second invasion of korea — a hundred and forty thousand men sent by a dying man who won't admit the first one failed. hideyoshi would not let it go.
the first invasion had bled out on korean mountains
and drowned in korean straits —
so he sent them back: a hundred and forty thousand men,
the second wave, vowing to finish it this time.
i was in the south when the sails appeared again,
and the korean villagers looked at the horizon
with the flat stare of people who have seen
the end of the world twice.
the ming were coming too, in greater force;
the war was bigger now, and crueler,
both sides exhausted and neither yielding.
hideyoshi was dying in osaka and wouldn't admit it,
sending orders to an army he would never see again.
the invasion's master was already a ghost;
his soldiers just didn't know it yet.
i watched the troop ships land and thought:
this is what pride looks like
when it outlives the man who owned it.

thirteen against one hundred thirty-three 1597 ce korea at myeongnyang, the disgraced admiral yi returns with 13 ships against 133 — and wins without losing one, the current fighting beside him. they had taken his command, tortured him, disgraced him —
and then, when the japanese fleet came again,
the court begged yi sun-sin to come back.
he had thirteen ships. the japanese had a hundred
and thirty-three.
he chose the strait at myeongnyang —
narrow, with a current that ran like a millrace,
reversing with the tide.
he knew those waters the way you know your own hands.
the japanese, confident in their numbers,
sailed in — and the current took them.
i watched from the cliffs as thirteen ships
fought a hundred and thirty-three to a standstill:
the whirlpools doing half the killing,
yi's cannon doing the rest.
thirty-one japanese ships sunk or broken,
not one korean lost.
thirteen against a hundred and thirty-three —
and the thirteen won.
i have walked a thousand battlefields,
and i have never seen anything like it,
before or since.

the humble potato 1597 ce england john gerard's herball describes the potato for english readers — a humble root that will one day feed millions, and starve them too. john gerard wrote it down in his herball —
the potato, a lumpy root from the andes,
described for english readers for the first time:
how to plant it, how it flowers,
that the tuber eats well enough.
nobody was impressed. the gentry thought it
pig food, fit for the irish maybe.
gerard himself got the details half wrong,
confusing it with other roots.
i held one in my hand in gerard's garden —
a brown, knobbled, unlovely thing —
and thought of the andes terraces where it had fed
empires, and of the irish fields where it would feed
millions, and of the famine it would one day bring
when millions depended on a single root.
the mightiest revolutions come disguised
as vegetables. this one sat in gerard's book,
quiet as a stone, waiting two hundred years
to change the world.

the edict of nantes 1598 ce france henry iv's edict of nantes grants french protestants the right to worship — ending thirty years of religious war with a signature. thirty years of war. thirty years of neighbors
cutting neighbors' throats over the mass —
and henry ended it with a signature at nantes.
the edict: protestants could worship freely,
hold their towns, keep their schools,
serve in the king's offices.
not equality — the catholics kept the crown's favor —
but peace. real, breathing peace.
i was in a village in the south when the news came,
and i watched a huguenot farmer and his catholic neighbor
shake hands over a fence for the first time
in a generation, both of them crying.
it would last eighty-seven years — a lifetime,
in those days. then a king's grandson would tear it up.
but for eighty-seven years, france proved
that people who pray differently
can live on the same street.
i wrote that down, and underlined it twice.

the taiko dies 1598 ce japan hideyoshi dies at osaka castle, leaving a child heir and feuding regents — his generals quietly begin pulling the armies home from korea. he died in osaka castle in the autumn —
hideyoshi, the taiko, the peasant's son
who had climbed to the top of japan
and reached for korea, for china, for the world.
i was in the castle town when the word spread,
quiet as snowfall: the great man was gone,
leaving a five-year-old heir and a council of regents
who hated each other.
his last order, they say, was to bring the armies home
from korea — the dream abandoned at the end,
as dreams are.
the generals obeyed, quietly, gratefully,
already measuring each other for the war to come.
hideyoshi had unified japan by force of will;
his will died with him.
what followed — sekigahara, the tokugawa peace —
was built on the foundation he laid
and the grave he dug.
i watched the funeral procession wind through osaka,
and all japan held its breath, waiting
to see who would pick up the sword.

a painter is born 1599 ce spain diego velazquez is born in seville — the boy who will paint kings as they truly are, and light as it truly falls. in seville, in june, a boy was born —
diego velazquez, son of a notary,
baptized in the church of san pedro
with no one suspecting anything at all.
i like to imagine the midwife handing him
to his mother, neither of them knowing
that those infant eyes would one day
paint kings as they truly were —
philip iv's habsburg jaw, the dwarfs and jesters
of the court rendered with more dignity
than the grandees, the light of las meninas
falling across four centuries.
he was only a baby, crying in the seville heat.
but i have learned to pay attention
to quiet births in ordinary towns.
the future was swaddled in that cradle,
holding a brush it could not yet lift.

the philosopher burned 1600 ce rome giordano bruno — who taught of infinite worlds around infinite suns — is burned at the stake in rome's campo de' fiori. they burned him in the campo de' fiori —
giordano bruno, the nolan, who had taught
that the stars are suns, and around them circle
infinite worlds, with infinite living things.
eight years in the inquisition's prisons.
they offered him recantation; he offered them
the universe instead.
on the last morning they gagged him —
afraid, even then, of what he might say
to the crowd.
i stood at the edge of the square and watched
the flames take him, and the smoke rise
over the flower market.
he had said the universe has no center
and no edge; rome answered with a stake
in the center of a square.
two hundred years later they would put up
his statue on that spot, hooded, defiant,
facing the vatican.
i go back sometimes, in my mind,
and stand in both squares at once —
the fire, and the statue.

nieuwpoort 1600 ce netherlands maurice of nassau's dutch army beats the feared spanish tercios on the dunes at nieuwpoort — proving the new way of war works. maurice of nassau fought it on the dunes at nieuwpoort —
the tide coming in, the spanish tercios
drawn up in their bristling squares,
the dutch outnumbered and far from home.
i watched from the dunes as maurice did
what his father never could: he beat them
in the open field, infantry against infantry,
his drilled battalions wheeling like clockwork
against the finest foot soldiers in europe.
it changed nothing on the map — the siege
he'd come to relieve went on regardless —
but it changed everything in the mind.
the spanish tercio could be beaten.
the dutch could beat it.
maurice's new way of war — drill, volley,
discipline — had passed its examination.
the tide came in over the battlefield that evening
and washed it clean.
the lesson stayed.

sekigahara 1600 ce japan tokugawa ieyasu crushes his rivals in the mist at sekigahara — one october day that decides the next two and a half centuries of japan. the mist lay on the field at sekigahara
when a hundred and sixty thousand men
decided who would rule japan.
i stood on the ridge with the morning fog
in my throat and watched tokugawa ieyasu's
eastern army grind against the western lords —
six hours of musket smoke and screaming horses,
the outcome balanced on a knife's edge
until kobayakawa's betrayal broke the west.
by noon it was a rout. by evening the heads
were being counted in kyoto.
ieyasu, patient ieyasu, who had waited
decades for this morning, walked the field
and claimed the sword of japan.
one battle, one misty october day —
and the next two hundred and fifty years
were decided.
the tokugawa peace began here,
in the fog, with the crows already circling.

the company chartered 1600 ce london elizabeth i charters the east india company — two hundred merchants, a few ships, and a piece of parchment that will one day rule an empire. elizabeth signed the charter on the last day
of the year — a piece of parchment giving
two hundred london merchants the right
to trade with the east, and to make war
and peace in her name, fifteen thousand miles away.
i was in the city when the news went round
the coffeehouses: the east india company,
a joint stock of seventy thousand pounds,
a few ships, a great deal of nerve.
none of them imagined what they'd chartered.
a trading company that would one day
rule a subcontinent, field armies larger
than most kingdoms, and answer to no one
but its shareholders.
it began with pepper and a signature.
it ended with an empire.
i keep a copy of that charter in my mind
as a warning: the mightiest things
start as paperwork.

essex loses his head 1601 ce london the earl of essex, elizabeth's fallen favorite, is beheaded on tower green after his foolish rebellion — charm without judgment. he came home from ireland in disgrace,
the golden boy with the tarnished sword,
and did the stupidest thing a courtier can do:
he marched on the queen with three hundred men,
expecting london to rise for him.
london stayed home. the gates shut.
essex surrendered in his own house,
was tried, and lost his head on tower green
on a cold february morning.
i watched him die — he'd been elizabeth's favorite,
her beautiful young earl, and she signed the warrant
with a hand that shook, then wept, then raged.
he had everything: looks, courage, charm.
what he lacked was judgment,
and in the end that was the one thing
that mattered.
the axe fell. the crowd sighed.
another bright thing the court had eaten.

kinsale 1601 ce ireland england crushes the irish and their spanish allies at kinsale — breaking gaelic ireland's last great hope in a winter morning. the irish came down from the north with spanish gold
and spanish musketeers, and at kinsale
the english met them in the winter mud —
and broke them.
i rode with the supply wagons and saw it end:
hugh o'neill's great confederacy, the last hope
of gaelic ireland, shattered in a morning's fighting.
the spanish surrendered their fort.
the irish melted back into the hills,
and the old world went with them.
what followed was the plantation —
english settlers on confiscated land,
the gaelic order dismantled piece by piece,
the language driven into the west.
kinsale was the hinge: before it, an ireland
that might have stayed irish; after it,
centuries of a different story.
i stood on the headland afterward, looking north,
and felt a whole culture exhale for the last time.

the voc is born 1602 ce amsterdam the dutch east india company is founded — the first public stock offering, a company with its own fleets, forts, and armies. the dutch did it better than the english —
folded all their little trading companies into one:
the voc, the dutch east india company,
with a charter that made it a state unto itself.
i was in amsterdam when the shares went on sale —
the first stock ever offered to the public,
any burgher with money could buy in.
six and a half million guilders raised,
and with it the right to build forts,
mint coins, sign treaties, and wage war.
a company with its own armies.
a company that answered to shareholders,
not to any king.
it would grow to be the richest corporation
in human history — forty thousand employees,
a hundred and fifty ships, a private empire
from the cape to japan.
i bought no shares. i only watched,
and wrote in my journal: the future
has just been invented, and it is owned
in pieces, by strangers.

the queen is dead 1603 ce england elizabeth i dies childless after forty-five years — and james vi of scotland rides south to become james i of england, cheered by strangers. she died at richmond in march, childless,
forty-five years on the throne —
elizabeth, gloriana, the virgin queen,
and with her the tudor line ran out like a spent candle.
i was in london when the riders went north
to fetch james of scotland — james vi and i,
a grown man with a scots accent and strange ideas,
riding south to take a kingdom he'd never seen.
the crowds lined the road, cheering a stranger.
no war, no rival claimant with an army —
just a proclamation, read aloud,
and england had a new king by dinnertime.
forty-five years of elizabeth: the armada,
the playwrights, the sea-dogs, the golden age.
and then, quietly, in a palace bedroom,
it ended — and a scotsman inherited it all.
i stood in the cheering crowd and felt the age turn,
like a great ship coming about.

the shogunate 1603 ce japan tokugawa ieyasu takes the title of shogun — opening two and a half centuries of tokugawa peace, built on control. ieyasu took the title in kyoto — sei-i tai shogun,
barbarian-subduing great general —
and with that old word he built something new:
two and a half centuries of peace.
not the peace of treaties. the peace of control:
the daimyo leashed by hostage and rotation,
the samurai turned from warriors to clerks,
the christians watched, the ports narrowed,
the whole archipelago held still
by one man's system.
i walked the new edo that year —
a castle town rising out of the marshes,
already dreaming of becoming the greatest city
on earth.
the age of civil war was over.
the age of the closed country was beginning.
and ieyasu, old and patient, sat at the center
like a spider who had finished his web
and could rest at last.

peace with spain 1604 ce london the treaty of london ends nineteen years of anglo-spanish war — the privateers come home to an england that has moved on. nineteen years of war ended with a treaty
signed in london — the treaty of london,
spain and england shaking hands at last.
i was there for the celebrations: the spanish envoy
feasted at whitehall, the bonfires lit,
the privateers paid off and sent home
to become merchants, or pirates without licenses,
or legends in taverns.
drake was dead. philip was dead.
elizabeth was dead.
the men who had made the war were gone,
and their successors counted the cost
and chose peace.
the sea-dogs came home to find england changed —
james on the throne, the war over,
no more spanish galleons to take.
some adapted. some drank.
i drank with a few of them, and listened
to the stories get better with every telling,
the way stories do when the war is over.

the gunpowder plot 1605 ce london guy fawkes is caught in the cellars under parliament with thirty-six barrels of gunpowder — and england gets its bonfire night forever. guy fawkes was caught in the cellar under parliament
at midnight, with thirty-six barrels of gunpowder —
enough to lift king, lords, and commons
into the november sky in one thunderclap.
i walked past the parliament stairs that week
and felt the city holding its breath.
the plot was catholic desperation made concrete:
kill james, kill the government, raise the country
in a rising that existed mostly in the plotters' heads.
they tortured fawkes on the rack; he gave them
the names. they hunted the rest down —
catesby shot at holbeche, the others taken,
all of them executed in the customary horror.
and england got its bonfire night:
every november 5th since, the bonfires burn
and the children chant, remember, remember.
i remember. i was there when the barrels
were carried out into the daylight,
still sweating saltpeter.

don quixote rides out 1605 ce spain cervantes publishes the first part of don quixote — the gaunt knight and his round squire ride out of cheap paper into world literature. cervantes published it in madrid — the first part,
cheap paper, quick sale —
and the gaunt knight and his round squire
rode out of its pages and into the world.
i bought a copy from a stall near the puerta del sol
and read it laughing on the road to toledo:
don quixote, who read too many romances
and mistook windmills for giants, inns for castles,
a peasant girl for a princess —
and sancho, who knew better and followed anyway.
spain laughed at the mad knight.
then spain — then the world — realized
the joke was on all of us:
who has not tilted at his own windmills,
who has not needed his own sancho?
cervantes, maimed at lepanto, poor all his life,
wrote the first modern novel without knowing it.
i finished it at an inn, closed the book,
and looked at the windmills on the horizon
with new respect.

palmares founded 1605 ce brazil escaped enslaved africans found palmares in brazil's forests — a hidden free kingdom that will defy the slavers for nearly a century. they ran — from the sugar mills, from the whip,
from the slave ships' holds —
and in the forests of pernambuco they built palmares:
a hidden kingdom of the free.
i never reached it myself; few outsiders ever did.
but i heard the stories in the port towns:
a confederation of villages, thousands strong,
africans of a dozen nations forging one people,
growing food, making laws, choosing their king —
a free black nation in the heart of slave brazil.
the portuguese sent expeditions; palmares
swallowed them in the green.
it would stand for nearly a hundred years —
a century of freedom carved out of the wilderness,
while the mills ground on around it.
every slave ship that unloaded in brazil
carried people who had heard the name.
palmares meant: run far enough, build high enough,
and you can be free.
i write this down so the name is not lost:
palmares. the free kingdom in the forest.

jamestown 1607 ce virginia three english ships land on the james river — the first lasting english colony in america takes root in a swamp, on hunger and hope. three ships — the susan constant, the godspeed,
the discovery — a hundred and four men and boys,
landing on the james river in may,
naming everything for a king
who would never see it.
i came ashore with the second supply:
a fort of logs, a church of sails,
gentlemen digging for gold that wasn't there
while the corn ran out and the marsh fever rose.
the starving time was coming — but not yet.
that first summer, it was all hope
and hammering.
powhatan's people watched from the woods,
bringing corn, wondering at these helpless strangers
who couldn't feed themselves.
john smith — braggart, hero, survivor —
kept them alive by bluff and trade.
the first lasting english colony in america:
born in a swamp, built on hunger,
saved by the people it would one day displace.
i helped raise the palisade and thought:
this fragile thing will outlast empires.

quebec founded 1608 ce canada samuel de champlain builds a trading post where the st. lawrence narrows — the seed of french canada, bought with furs and frostbite. champlain chose the narrows — where the st. lawrence
pinches between the cliffs, kebec in the algonquin tongue —
and built his trading post of logs and hope.
i traveled upriver with him that summer:
the great river rolling north, the forests
unbroken to the horizon, the winter
already waiting in the wings like an executioner.
twenty-eight men stayed. twenty froze or starved.
eight lived to see spring.
but the post held. the furs came downriver —
beaver, the soft gold of the north —
and the canoes of a dozen nations
found their way to champlain's door.
new france began here: not with conquest
but with trade, with alliances, with a handful of men
in a wooden fort at the narrowing of a river.
i stood on the cliff that winter and looked down
at the frozen st. lawrence, and understood:
this was the seed of a different america.

the spyglass 1608 ce holland hans lippershey patents the spyglass — a tube of lenses, a fairground toy that will soon be turned on the heavens. hans lippershey, spectacle-maker of middelburg,
filed the patent — a tube with a lens at each end,
making far things near, three times closer.
i looked through one at the fair that autumn:
the church tower across the market
suddenly at arm's length, the weathercock's feathers
countable. the crowd gasped and laughed.
a toy, they said. a curiosity for sailors
and soldiers.
within a year, men in padua and prague
would turn it upward — and the toy
would become the telescope, and the telescope
would unmake the universe.
but that autumn in middelburg it was only
a tube of lenses and a spectacle-maker's patent,
and i was one of the first to hold the future
up to my eye and squint through it.
three times closer. soon, infinitely further.

galileo looks up 1609 ce italy galileo turns his telescope to the night sky — and finds mountains on the moon, moons around jupiter, a universe remade in one night. he heard about the dutch toy and built a better one —
twenty times closer — and on a winter night
in padua, galileo galilei turned it upward.
i was there. i looked through it after him.
the moon: not a perfect crystal sphere
but a world — mountains, valleys, shadows,
a place, scarred and real as the earth.
jupiter: four moons circling it like a tiny solar system.
the milky way: not a cloud but a river of stars,
thousands where the eye saw dozens.
we stood on that rooftop till dawn, taking turns,
speechless.
in one night, the universe had changed shape.
the heavens were not perfect and unchanging —
they were rough, and moving, and full.
galileo wrote it up in weeks — the starry messenger —
and all europe looked up at once.
i have seen many revolutions begin.
this one began with a tube of lenses
and a man who refused to look away.

kepler's laws 1609 ce prague johannes kepler publishes his first two laws of planetary motion — the planets move in ellipses, proven on eight un-fudged minutes of arc. kepler published them in prague — the first two laws,
won from tycho's mountain of numbers
by years of grinding calculation:
the planets move in ellipses, the sun at one focus;
they sweep equal areas in equal times.
i visited him that winter: a small man
in a cold room, half-blind, surrounded by papers,
who had tried seventy shapes for the orbit of mars
before the ellipse fit — off by eight minutes of arc,
and he would not let those eight minutes go.
eight minutes. that honesty remade astronomy.
the perfect circles of two thousand years
broke on eight minutes of arc.
he wept when it came right, he told me —
not with joy but with exhaustion,
like a man who has carried a stone uphill
for a decade and finally set it down.
the planets move in ellipses.
the universe has a new geometry,
and it was found by refusing to fudge
eight minutes.

the moriscos expelled 1609 ce spain spain expels the moriscos — three hundred thousand baptized christians of muslim descent — cutting out its own craftsmen to purify its blood. they had been christians for a century —
baptized, or their grandparents had been —
but spain never believed the conversion,
and now philip's son was done pretending.
i watched them go from the port at valencia:
families with bundles, craftsmen, farmers,
the best silk-workers and irrigators in spain,
marched to the ships and ferried to north africa —
three hundred thousand souls, more or less,
in the greatest expulsion europe had seen.
the villages emptied. the silk looms fell silent.
the huertas went back to scrub.
spain cut out a third of its own skill
to purify its blood, and called it victory.
i stood on the quay as the last boats pulled away,
and a morisco woman pressed a sprig of rosemary
into my hand — for remembrance, she said.
i have kept it pressed in my journal ever since.
spain's loss. africa's gain.
the rosemary still smells faintly, after all these years.

yanga's free town 1609 ce mexico gaspar yanga — african rebel, thirty years free in the veracruz highlands — founds the free town of san lorenzo after forcing spain to treat with him. gaspar yanga had been free for thirty years —
a prince of the bran people, stolen from africa,
escaped into the veracruz highlands,
raiding the spanish roads with his band of runaways
until the viceroy sent an army to finish him.
the army failed. yanga's people knew the mountains;
the spanish knew the roads.
so they negotiated — the first treaty of its kind:
yanga's town would be free, self-governing,
and in return the raids would stop.
i visited san lorenzo de los negros years later:
a free black town in the hills of new spain,
its people farming, its church bell ringing,
yanga an old man now, walking with a stick,
a king without a crown.
thirty years a rebel, then a founder.
the spanish called it peace; yanga's people
called it what it was: victory.
i bowed to the old man, and he laughed
and offered me chocolate.

the king is stabbed 1610 ce paris henry iv is knifed in his carriage in paris — the king who ended the religious wars dies, and a nine-year-old inherits the throne. the carriage stopped in the rue de la ferronnerie —
traffic, a narrow street — and ravaillac stepped up
with his knife and struck twice, into the king's chest.
henry iv — the white plume, the mass of paris,
the man who had ended the wars —
died in his carriage on a may afternoon,
and his nine-year-old son became louis xiii
with marie de' medici holding the reins.
i was two streets away and heard the screaming.
paris went mad with grief and fury;
they tore the assassin apart in the place de greve,
which changed nothing.
fourteen years of peace henry had given france —
fourteen years, and it died with him in a carriage.
the regency began in blood and suspicion,
and france would not know another like him
for a long time.
i stood in the crowd at the funeral procession
and wept with strangers.
we all knew what we had lost.

the icy bay 1610 ce hudson bay henry hudson sails into the vast frozen bay that will bear his name — and the next summer his mutinous crew sets him adrift to vanish. hudson sailed into it in august — the vast bay,
ice already forming at the edges,
a sea where the maps said a continent should be.
i was not aboard the discovery that voyage —
no one i knew was, except by reputation —
but i met the survivors later, in london,
and heard the story from men who'd lived it:
the winter frozen in, the food gone,
the crew turning on their captain.
in june they set hudson adrift in an open boat
with his son and seven loyal men —
and sailed home without them.
no one ever saw them again.
the bay kept his name. the mutineers kept their lives,
mostly. the passage to asia stayed unfound.
i think of that little boat sometimes,
drifting on that enormous gray water,
the greatest discoverer of his age
abandoned by his own men to the ice.

the king james bible 1611 ce england king james's scholars publish their great english bible — fifty-four men, seven years, and the book that will shape the language for centuries. fifty-four scholars, six companies, seven years —
and out of it came the book:
the king james bible, in english a common man could read,
printed in london and carried to the ends of the earth.
i bought one of the first printings —
the he bible, they called it, for a misprint in ruth —
and read it through that winter.
the language! salt of the earth. a still small voice.
the valley of the shadow of death.
tyndale's bones and coverdale's phrases,
polished by committees into thunder.
it shaped the english tongue more than shakespeare —
or as much, which is saying everything.
for three centuries, when an english speaker
reached for the grand phrase, this was the well.
i keep mine still, the pages soft with reading.
whatever you believe, it is the most beautiful
book ever made by committee —
which tells you something about committees,
and something about god.

the empress rises 1611 ce mughal india jahangir marries nur jahan — the brilliant widow who will all but rule the mughal empire beside him, her name struck on the coinage. jahangir married her in the spring — nur jahan,
the widow of a persian noble, thirty-four years old,
brilliant, educated, and beautiful in the way
that makes emperors forget their caution.
i saw her at court in agra within the year:
she sat behind the screen, but everyone knew
whose hand was on the empire.
coins were struck in her name — beside the emperor's,
unheard of. orders went out with her seal.
she designed gardens, patronized painters,
shot tigers from an elephant's back.
jahangir drank and dreamed; nur jahan ruled.
for fifteen years the mughal empire
was steered by a woman the histories
almost forgot to mention.
i watched her once, giving audience,
and thought: here is power that needs no throne,
no army, no proclamation —
only a mind, and the ear of a king.

artemisia testifies 1612 ce rome artemisia gentileschi testifies against her attacker under thumbscrews in a roman court — and goes on to paint heroines who fight back. she was nineteen, and they put her on trial —
not her attacker, her.
the roman court made artemisia gentileschi
submit to thumbscrews to prove she told the truth
about being raped by her father's colleague.
i sat in that courtroom. i heard her testimony —
clear, unflinching, furious —
and i watched the judges squirm
as the thumbscrews proved what her word should have.
her attacker got a sentence he never served.
she got the truth, on record.
and then she painted.
judith beheading holofernes — blood, effort, two women
doing the work with their own hands.
susanna, lucretia, heroines who fight back,
painted by a woman who knew what fighting cost.
rome tried to break her into silence.
instead it made an artist who would outpaint
every man in that courtroom.
i bought no painting that year;
i only remembered her face,
set like stone, telling the truth.

england's first indian foothold 1612 ce surat after english ships beat the portuguese off surat, the east india company plants its first trading post on indian soil — a shed that will grow an empire. the english ships beat the portuguese off surat —
captain best's little squadron, outgunned,
outmaneuvered the great carracks in the swally roads —
and the mughal governor took notice.
i was in surat when the firman came:
the east india company could build a factory —
a trading post, a warehouse with a flag —
on indian soil. england's first foothold
in the land that would one day be its empire.
it was a shed. a shed with bales of broadcloth
and a clerk with a ledger.
the portuguese laughed. the dutch shrugged.
nobody saw it for what it was:
the thin end of a wedge three centuries long.
i stood on the beach at the swally
and watched the bales come ashore,
and wrote in my journal: small beginnings.
the mightiest oak in history
was just planted as an acorn,
in the sand, at surat.

the romanovs chosen 1613 ce russia after the time of troubles, the assembly elects sixteen-year-old michael romanov tsar — founding a dynasty that will rule for three centuries. the time of troubles had eaten russia alive —
famine, pretenders, polish armies in the kremlin,
three false dmitrys and a murdered boy —
and the assembly at moscow was desperate
for anyone, someone, a name to rally round.
they chose michael romanov. sixteen years old,
hiding in a monastery with his mother,
related to the old dynasty by marriage
and to nobody's faction strongly enough to object.
i was in moscow when the embassy found him.
his mother wept and refused; they begged;
at last the boy accepted, terrified,
and they led him to the capital through crowds
that had forgotten what hope felt like.
three hundred years that dynasty would rule —
from this frightened boy in a monastery
to the last tsar in a cellar at ekaterinburg.
i watched the coronation procession
and thought: every empire begins
with somebody who didn't want the job.

the globe burns 1613 ce london a stage cannon sets the globe theatre's thatch alight — shakespeare's playhouse burns to the ground in an hour, and is rebuilt within the year. it was the cannon in henry viii — a stage cannon,
fired for the king's entrance —
that set the thatch alight.
in less than an hour, shakespeare's globe
was a ring of fire on the bankside.
i was across the river and saw the smoke go up:
the playhouse where hamlet had first spoken,
where lear had raged, where the groundlings
had stood in the rain for a penny —
burning to the waterline while the actors
carried out the costumes and the scripts.
nobody died — one man's breeches caught fire,
and they put him out with a bottle of ale.
the company rebuilt within the year,
finer than before, on the same ground.
but something ended that afternoon:
shakespeare had retired to stratford;
the great age was guttering.
the globe burned, and was rebuilt —
and the plays, thank god, survived the fire.

pocahontas marries 1614 ce virginia pocahontas marries john rolfe at jamestown — a political marriage sealing a fragile peace that will die with her at twenty-one. she was nineteen, or thereabouts — matoaka,
daughter of powhatan, baptized rebecca —
and she married john rolfe, the tobacco planter,
in the little church at jamestown.
i was there. the colony turned out in its best —
which wasn't much — and powhatan's people came too,
uneasy, watching.
it was a political marriage, everyone knew,
sealing the peace between the english fort
and the great chief's domain.
for eight years it held. pocahontas sailed to england,
was presented at court, stared at like a wonder —
and died at gravesend at twenty-one,
of a stranger's disease, on the way home.
rolfe went back to his tobacco. the peace died with her,
slowly, then all at once.
i remember her best not as the legend
but as the girl in the jamestown church,
saying her vows in a language not her own,
trying — genuinely trying — to bridge two worlds
that would not be bridged.

logarithms 1614 ce scotland john napier publishes his tables of logarithms — a shortcut through heavy arithmetic that astronomers and sailors will use for centuries. john napier of merchiston published the tables —
logarithms, he called them, the arithmetic of exponents —
and every astronomer and navigator in europe
breathed easier.
i met him once at his tower near edinburgh:
a strange, brilliant laird who dabbled in alchemy
and theology and hated the long multiplications
that ate his days.
so he found a shortcut: turn multiplication
into addition, division into subtraction,
by the magic of exponents tabulated once and for all.
kepler used them within the decade.
sailors used them for a century.
the slide rule, the computer's ancestor,
was born from napier's tables.
he died three years later, worn out at sixty-seven.
but his bones — napier's bones, the numbering rods —
and his logarithms outlived him by centuries.
i keep a set of his tables still:
proof that the greatest gifts are sometimes
just a shorter road through the arithmetic.

osaka falls 1615 ce japan tokugawa troops storm osaka castle and wipe out the toyotomi — ending the last challenge to tokugawa rule in fire and smoke. the tokugawa came in the summer with everything —
two hundred thousand men around osaka castle,
the toyotomi's last stronghold,
the child hideyori inside with his mother.
i watched from the hills as the great fortress fell:
the outer works stormed, the moats filled,
the keep set ablaze in the final assault.
hideyori and his mother died in the flames —
suicide, the chronicles say, like nobunaga before him.
the toyotomi line ended in that fire.
no more rivals. no more western lords
dreaming of the old days.
ieyasu's peace was now unchallenged,
bought with the last great siege of the age.
i walked through the ruins afterward —
blackened timbers, the smell of smoke and rain —
and thought of hideyoshi, the peasant's son,
whose whole mighty house had lasted
seventeen years past his death.
ambition builds fast. time unbuilds faster.

chocolate comes to paris 1615 ce france anne of austria marries louis xiii, bringing her spanish taste for drinking chocolate to the french court — and paris never drinks the same again. anne of austria married louis xiii —
a spanish infanta for a french king —
and in her baggage, among the jewels and the linen,
came chocolate.
i tasted it at court that winter: the dark drink
of the spanish, bitter and spiced,
served in porcelain cups to ladies
who had never imagined such a thing.
the french were suspicious at first —
a foreign brew, a papist drink —
but the queen drank it every morning,
and fashion follows queens.
within a generation, paris had its chocolatiers,
its salons thick with the smell of cacao.
a whole civilization of the cup —
the gossip, the intrigue, the slow afternoons —
began with a princess's luggage.
empires are moved by stranger things than armies.
sometimes by a taste, carried across the pyrenees
in a dowry chest, changing what a nation drinks
at breakfast for three hundred years.

three playwrights die 1616 ce england, spain, china shakespeare, cervantes, and china's tang xianzu all die within months of each other — three masters, three worlds, one turning year. within months of each other, three masters died —
shakespeare at stratford, fifty-two, of a fever;
cervantes at madrid, sixty-eight, worn out and poor;
tang xianzu in china, author of the peony pavilion,
the greatest playwright of the ming.
i had seen shakespeare's company play at the globe.
i had read cervantes laughing on the road to toledo.
tang i knew only by reputation — his peony pavilion,
fifty-five scenes of love and ghosts,
still performed in china four centuries on.
three men, three languages, three worlds —
none knowing the others existed —
all writing the human heart at the same moment
in history, all dying in the same turning year.
the coincidence haunts me.
as if the age had hired three voices
