to sing its story, and then, the song complete,
dismissed them together.
1616: the year the world's stages went dark,
in england, in spain, and in china —
all at once.

the plaza mayor rises 1617 ce madrid work begins on madrid's great plaza mayor — the grand square where the city will gather, celebrate, and judge for centuries. they began it under philip iii — the plaza mayor,
madrid's great square: three stories of brick and slate,
a hundred and fourteen balconies looking inward,
a stage for the whole city.
i watched the foundations go down that year,
the old market square leveled and rebuilt
to the new geometry — processions, bullfights,
autos-da-fe, royal weddings, all to play out
under those identical windows for centuries.
a plaza mayor is spain's answer to the agora:
the city gathering to see itself.
madrid was still half village then,
but the square dreamed bigger —
it dreamed the capital into being around it.
four hundred years later the cafes still fill it,
the tourists still photograph the balconies.
i sat there once, centuries on in my mind,
drinking coffee where the scaffolding had stood,
and marveled at how a square can outlive
every king who ever waved from its windows.

out the window 1618 ce prague protestant nobles hurl two catholic officials from a prague castle window — they survive the fall, and the thirty years' war begins. they threw them out the window — the two catholic regents
and their secretary, hurled from the high windows
of prague castle by protestant nobles
who'd had enough of the emperor's decrees.
seventy feet down. they lived —
landed in a dung heap, the catholics said
by angels, the protestants said by manure.
the defenestration of prague, the history books call it,
with a straight face.
i was in the castle yard that morning
and saw them pick themselves up, bruised and furious,
and run for their lives.
nobody laughed then. but the act was a declaration:
bohemia would not be ruled from vienna
in matters of faith.
within months, armies were marching.
the thirty years' war — the most terrible war
europe had ever seen — began
with three men flying out of a window
and landing, improbably, alive.

raleigh's head falls 1618 ce london walter raleigh is beheaded at whitehall for his failed guiana voyage — fifteen years after his first death sentence, a king's diplomacy kills him. fifteen years he'd lived under the sentence —
in the tower, writing his history of the world,
growing old in a cell —
and then james let him out for one last voyage
to find the gold of guiana.
it failed. the spanish complained.
james needed spanish friendship more than raleigh's life,
so the old sentence was dusted off
and the axe was sharpened.
i stood in the crowd at whitehall that october morning.
raleigh was sixty-six, gray, calm —
he tested the axe's edge with his thumb
and joked about his long journey.
his last words were for the headsman:
strike, man, strike.
they struck. the golden age's brightest adventurer —
courtier, colonist, poet, pirate —
died for a fifteen-year-old sentence
and a king's diplomacy.
i kept the pamphlet of his speech.
the crowd went home quiet.
even his enemies felt the shame of it.

sarhu 1619 ce manchuria the manchu leader nurhaci annihilates four ming armies at sarhu — and the ming dynasty's doom begins in the manchurian snow. nurhaci laid the trap in the manchurian forests —
four ming armies, a hundred thousand men,
marching in separate columns through the snow,
and the manchus falling on each in turn.
i traveled with a ming supply column that spring
and saw the disaster unfold: at sarhu the first army
was annihilated, then the second, then the third —
the manchu cavalry moving like wolves
through the pines, the ming guns useless
in the close trees.
forty thousand dead. the ming never recovered.
nurhaci, the jurchen chief the chinese had dismissed
as a barbarian, had broken the greatest army in asia
in a week of forest fighting.
the dynasty's doom began here, in the snow,
among the pines of the northeast.
i stood on the battlefield afterward —
the crows, the abandoned cannon, the silence —
and understood: china would fall
not to numbers, but to patience and the trees.

batavia founded 1619 ce java jan pieterszoon coen seizes jayakarta and founds batavia — the dutch east india company's asian capital, raised on a burned town's ashes. coen took jayakarta with cannon and fire —
burned it, leveled it, and raised batavia
on its ashes: the voc's asian capital,
a dutch city under a tropical sun,
canals and warehouses and a castle.
i walked its streets in the first years:
the company men in their black coats sweating,
the javanese, chinese, and malay laborers
building the walls that would hold them all,
the nutmeg and cloves flowing through the harbor
like a spice-scented tide.
jan pieterszoon coen — brilliant, ruthless —
ran it like a fortress and a counting-house at once.
batavia would rule the archipelago for two centuries,
the hinge of the dutch empire in asia.
it began with a burned town and a new name.
empires often do.
i stood on the castle wall at sunset,
smelling cloves on the wind,
and watched the ships come in from every point
of the compass, all of them flying
the company's flag.

the music of the spheres 1619 ce prague kepler publishes his third law of planetary motion — the harmony of the spheres, the solar system singing in mathematics. kepler found it at last — the third law,
the harmony he'd been hunting for twenty years:
the square of a planet's year is proportional
to the cube of its distance from the sun.
he called it the music of the spheres —
each planet singing its note as it circled,
the whole solar system a chord
in the mind of god.
he even wrote out the melodies,
note by note, planet by planet.
i visited him the year it was published:
older now, poorer, his eyes failing,
but triumphant — holding the harmony of the world
in his hands like a newborn.
pythagoras had dreamed it two thousand years before;
kepler had proved it with tycho's numbers.
the universe, he said, is not silent.
it sings in mathematics.
i walked home under the prague stars that night
and listened, or tried to —
and for a moment, i swear,
i heard it too.

the white lion 1619 ce virginia a dutch ship lands the first enslaved africans at point comfort — twenty souls traded for food, the quiet beginning of america's wound. the dutch ship came into point comfort in august —
the white lion, a privateer —
and traded twenty-odd africans for food.
i was in jamestown that month and saw them led ashore:
men and women stolen from angola,
survivors of a portuguese slave ship
the dutch had robbed at sea.
they were sold — or indentured, the records blur —
into a colony desperate for labor.
nobody marked the day. no bell rang.
it was a transaction, entered in a ledger,
twenty souls for victuals.
but that ledger entry was the seed
of everything: two and a half centuries of bondage,
millions in chains, a wound america
has never fully closed.
i wish i could say i knew, watching them land,
what it would become.
i didn't. none of us did.
that is the horror of it —
how quietly the worst things begin.

the mayflower sails 1620 ce the atlantic a hundred pilgrims cross the atlantic in a leaky ship — half will die the first winter, but the compact they sign will outlive them all. a hundred souls in a leaky ship —
the mayflower, out of plymouth in september,
bound for virginia, blown to new england,
carrying separatists who'd fled to holland
and back, seeking a place to pray their own way.
i stood on the plymouth dock and watched them go:
families, children, old men, the whole venture
staked on faith and a bad map.
half of them would die that first winter —
hunger, cold, sickness, the new world's indifference.
but they signed the compact first —
government by consent, in a ship's cabin,
before they ever saw the shore.
and they endured, somehow, the dying and the burying,
till spring.
i have crossed that ocean a hundred times since,
in comfort no pilgrim dreamed.
but i never forget the leaky ship,
the hundred souls, the september sailing —
how much of america began
with people who had nowhere else to go.

the white mountain 1620 ce prague catholic armies crush the bohemian rebels at white mountain in two hours — and bohemia's protestant hopes die for three centuries. two hours. the battle lasted two hours —
catholic armies under tilly against the bohemian rebels
on the white mountain outside prague,
and by noon it was over.
i watched from the city walls as the protestant cause
in bohemia died in a morning:
the winter king's army broken, frederick fleeing,
the rebel lords captured — twenty-seven of them
executed in the old town square the next summer,
their heads on spikes.
what followed was the recatholicizing —
the jesuits, the confiscations, the exiles,
bohemia's protestant nobility erased,
the czech language driven underground for centuries.
the thirty years' war had its first great decision,
and it went to vienna and rome.
two hours on a hill outside prague,
and a nation's fate for three hundred years.
i walked the field at dusk —
the crows already at work —
and felt the weight of how fast
history can close a door.

the new organon 1620 ce england francis bacon publishes his call for a new science built on experiment, not ancient authority — the workshop replaces the cathedral. francis bacon published it — the new organon,
the new instrument —
and told the world to stop arguing from aristotle
and start looking at things.
experiment, he said. induction.
torture nature for her secrets —
his phrase, not mine, and a rough one —
but the meaning was clear: knowledge comes
from doing, not from quoting.
i read it in london that winter, by candlelight,
and felt the ground shift under philosophy.
the old learning had been a cathedral;
bacon proposed a workshop.
he was lord chancellor, corrupt and brilliant,
and he would fall from power within the year —
but the book outlived the man.
every laboratory since, every experiment,
every peer-reviewed paper, descends
from bacon's insistence:
don't tell me what the ancients said.
show me.

the first thanksgiving 1621 ce plymouth the surviving pilgrims share a harvest feast with their wampanoag neighbors — three days of food and laughter after a year of burials. the harvest came in — barely, but it came —
and the survivors feasted: fifty-one pilgrims left
of the hundred who'd sailed, and ninety wampanoag,
their neighbors, who'd taught them to plant corn
and where to fish.
i sat at the edge of that three-day feast —
venison, wildfowl, corn, the woods providing —
and watched massasoit's people and the english
eat together, suspicious and grateful by turns.
no one called it thanksgiving. it was just dinner —
dinner after a year of burials.
squanto was there, the interpreter,
the man who'd made it all possible.
within a generation his people's world
would be unrecognizable.
but that autumn, for three days,
there was food, and company, and peace.
i remember the laughter more than the food.
hungry people laughing —
that is the sound of survival,
and i have never heard it so clearly
as at plymouth, in 1621.

moliere is born 1622 ce paris jean-baptiste poquelin is born in paris — the boy who will become moliere and teach france to laugh at itself. in paris, in january, a boy was born —
jean-baptiste poquelin, son of an upholsterer
to the king, baptized at saint-eustache,
with no one suspecting anything at all.
he would become moliere — the actor, the manager,
the playwright who taught france to laugh at itself:
the miser, the hypocrite, the learned ladies,
the bourgeois gentleman, all of them
held up to the mirror and found ridiculous.
i like to think of the upholsterer's son
playing in his father's workshop,
among the tapestries and the offcuts,
learning the textures of the world
he would later stitch into comedy.
louis xiv would laugh at his plays
and protect him from the devout.
the stage would be his church,
laughter his sacrament.
a boy born in january, in paris —
and france would never be so honest again
as when he was mocking it.

the jamestown massacre 1622 ce virginia opechancanough's warriors strike the scattered settlements at dawn — a third of the colony dead in a single morning, trust dead for a century. they came at dawn on a march morning —
opechancanough's warriors, moving among the settlements
as visitors, as trading partners,
borrowing the colonists' own tools —
and then the killing began.
i was upriver when the news came running:
a third of the colony dead in a single morning —
three hundred and forty-seven men, women, children,
the outlying farms wiped out, jamestown itself
saved only by a warning from a friendly indian boy.
the english called it a massacre.
the powhatans called it war —
a strike to push the strangers back into the sea
before they swallowed the land whole.
it failed. the english stayed, and the retaliation
was ten years of burning villages and poisoned wells.
i walked through the burned settlements afterward
and saw what fear does to people:
the colony that had lived beside its neighbors
now lived behind its walls, forever.
one morning in march, and trust —
the fragile, necessary trust —
was dead for a century.

the sultan strangled 1622 ce constantinople the janissaries murder the young sultan osman ii — the first ottoman sultan killed by his own soldiers — for trying to reform them. they dragged him from the palace —
osman ii, eighteen years old, the young sultan
who'd tried to reform the janissaries
and learned what janissaries do to reformers.
i was in constantinople that may
and heard the city holding its breath:
the soldiers mutinied, seized the boy-sultan,
and strangled him with a bowstring
in the seven towers — the first ottoman sultan
killed by his own troops.
they put his uncle on the throne instead —
mustafa, mad mustafa, who'd spent half his life
in the cage.
the empire shuddered, and went on.
reform in the ottoman house was now a capital crime,
proven on a sultan's neck.
it would be a century before anyone tried again.
i stood outside the seven towers afterward
and looked up at the stones,
and thought about how empires eat their young
when the young try to change them.

the first folio 1623 ce london shakespeare's friends publish his collected plays in the first folio — rescuing eighteen of them, half his work, from oblivion. shakespeare's friends did it — heminges and condell,
two actors who'd known him —
gathered his plays and printed them in one great folio:
thirty-six plays, nine hundred pages,
half of them never printed before.
i bought a copy from the shop at the blackfriars gate
and turned the pages with shaking hands:
macbeth — saved. the tempest — saved.
julius caesar, twelfth night, antony and cleopatra —
eighteen plays that would have vanished
like breath off a mirror, rescued by friendship.
without that book, we would have half a shakespeare —
no storm on the heath, no "tomorrow and tomorrow,"
no prospero drowning his book.
two actors, a printer, and a debt of love:
that is all that stood between the greatest writer
in english and oblivion.
i keep my folio wrapped in cloth.
it is the most valuable thing i own,
and the cheapest miracle i know.

the amboyna massacre 1623 ce amboyna the dutch torture and execute english merchants on amboyna for a plot that never existed — poisoning anglo-dutch friendship for a generation. the dutch accused them of conspiracy —
ten english merchants on amboyna,
a few japanese mercenaries, a portuguese overseer —
tortured with water and fire till they confessed
to a plot that never existed.
i heard the account from a survivor's letter,
smuggled out of the banda sea:
the trial a farce, the evidence the confessions,
the executions methodical — beheaded,
one by one, on the beach at amboyna.
england howled. the pamphlets flew.
"amboyna" became the english word for dutch treachery,
poisoning every negotiation for a generation —
cromwell would still be citing it thirty years later.
ten merchants dead on a spice island beach,
and two nations' friendship dead with them.
the spice trade ran on nutmeg and blood,
and i have never been able to smell cloves since
without thinking of amboyna.

queen nzinga 1624 ce west africa nzinga takes the throne of ndongo and begins her forty-year defiance of portuguese slavers — sitting on her servant's back rather than sit lower than a governor. she took the throne of ndongo —
nzinga, sister of the dead king,
in a world where women did not rule
and portuguese slavers did as they pleased.
i never met her, but i heard the stories
from traders on the kwanza:
how she received the portuguese governor
with no chair offered, and sat on her servant's back
rather than sit lower than him —
how she fought, negotiated, converted,
un-converted, moved her capital, built alliances,
and defied the slavers for forty years.
forty years. she died at eighty-one,
still queen, still undefeated,
having kept her people free
while kingdoms around her fell.
the portuguese called her savage.
history calls her what she was:
one of the great sovereigns of the age,
who looked the slave trade in the face
and said: not here. not my people.
not while i breathe.

salvador taken 1624 ce brazil a dutch fleet seizes salvador, brazil's capital — the shock proves no empire's possessions are safe, and holland's brazilian dream begins. the dutch came with twenty-six ships —
the west india company, holland's other great company —
and took salvador, brazil's capital,
before the portuguese knew what hit them.
i was in the reconcavo that year and watched
the sugar world turn upside down:
dutch admirals in the governor's palace,
the planters fleeing inland, the mills idle,
the whole captaincy holding its breath.
it didn't last — the portuguese took it back
within the year, and the dutch would have to try again
to build their brazilian empire.
but the shock never faded:
the greatest sugar colony on earth
had been seized in a morning,
and everyone in the atlantic world understood —
no empire's possessions were safe anymore.
the dutch learned. they'd be back.
and when they came back, they'd stay —
and recife would bloom, briefly,
as holland's tropical capital.

charles takes the throne 1625 ce england charles i becomes king of england — handsome, devout, and convinced kings rule by divine right; his quarrels with parliament begin at once. james died in march, and charles took the throne —
twenty-four, handsome, devout, convinced
that kings ruled by god's own right
and parliaments were an inconvenience.
i watched the coronation at westminster:
the young king pale under the crown,
the crowd cheering out of habit,
the old counselors exchanging looks
that said what no one would say aloud —
this one will not bend.
within months he was quarreling with parliament
over money, over religion, over everything.
he married a catholic french princess.
he dismissed the parliament that displeased him.
the pattern was set in the first year,
and it never changed.
eleven years of personal rule were coming,
then civil war, then the scaffold.
but that spring day at westminster,
with the crown on his head and the choir singing,
charles i looked like the future.
the future had other plans.

the island bargain 1626 ce manhattan dutch traders buy manhattan from the lenape for goods worth sixty guilders — a misunderstanding wrapped in a trade, on an island no one could imagine. peter minuit — or whoever held the company's purse —
traded with the lenape for manhattan:
goods worth sixty guilders, the legend says —
beads and cloth and kettles —
for an island that would become the center of the world.
i walked that island before the dutch built much:
forest, streams, the great harbor glittering,
the lenape fishing where wall street would stand.
the "purchase" was a misunderstanding wrapped in a trade —
the lenape didn't sell land the way europeans meant it;
they thought they were sharing use-rights.
new amsterdam rose: a fort, a windmill,
a wall across the island's neck —
wall street, named for a wall against the english
and the natives both.
sixty guilders. the most famous real-estate deal
in history, and neither side understood it.
i stood on the shore at the tip of the island,
looking out at the harbor,
and tried to imagine what would stand here.
i failed. everyone fails.
that is the point of manhattan.

st. peter's consecrated 1626 ce rome after 120 years of building, the new st. peter's basilica is consecrated — the grandest church in christendom, an ocean of marble and song. a hundred and twenty years. bramante, raphael,
michelangelo, maderno — four architects,
nineteen popes — and on a november morning
urban viii consecrated the new st. peter's,
the grandest church in christendom.
i stood in the crowd in the piazza —
a hundred thousand souls, they said —
as the procession wound through the nave,
seven hundred feet of marble and light,
bernini's baldacchino rising over the altar
like a bronze prayer.
above it all, the dome — michelangelo's dome —
floating against the roman sky.
below it, the tomb of the fisherman,
two thousand years deep.
they had torn down the old basilica of constantine
to build this. some called it sacrilege.
standing in that ocean of stone and song,
i could only call it what it was:
the largest room ever built for god,
and for the men who spoke in his name.

la rochelle besieged 1627 ce france richelieu's armies ring the protestant stronghold of la rochelle and starve it for fourteen months — the huguenots keep their faith but lose their walls. richelieu ringed it — the protestant stronghold,
la rochelle, the city the huguenots called their rome —
with an army on land and a mole across the harbor,
starving it the slow way.
i slipped through the lines that winter
with a relief boat that never got through:
inside the walls, the hunger —
the mayor's own family on rations,
the dead buried in the night,
fifteen thousand souls shrinking to five.
the english fleet came, sailed about,
and left. no one else came.
after fourteen months the city yielded —
the survivors staggering out, ghosts in rags —
and richelieu rode in, merciful and absolute.
the huguenots kept their faith but lost their walls,
their armies, their state within the state.
france would have one king, one law —
and, soon enough, one religion.
i walked the empty streets afterward,
past the houses with no one left to live in them,
and heard only the gulls.

the petition of right 1628 ce england parliament forces charles i to sign the petition of right — no taxes without consent, no arbitrary prison; paper that will outlast the king. parliament cornered him — charles, who believed
god had made him king —
and made him sign the petition of right:
no taxes without parliament's consent,
no imprisonment without cause,
no quartering soldiers on civilians,
no martial law in peacetime.
i was in westminster hall when the news came out:
the commons had done it — put the ancient liberties
in writing, and made the king agree.
coke, the old lion of the law, had drafted it;
the king had tried to dodge it;
in the end he signed.
he didn't mean it. within the year
he'd be ruling without parliament,
and the petition would be a scrap of paper
for eleven years.
but paper outlasts kings.
the words were written down, and written words
have a way of coming back.
in 1689 they'd be back, in the bill of rights.
i kept a copy, and underlined the first line twice:
the rights and liberties of the subject.
someone, someday, would collect.

the blood circulates 1628 ce england william harvey publishes his proof that the heart pumps blood around the body in an endless circuit — fourteen centuries of galen overturned. william harvey published it — de motu cordis,
on the motion of the heart —
and proved what no one had dared to prove:
the blood goes round.
not ebb and flow, as galen taught for fourteen centuries —
but a circuit: the heart a pump, the arteries carrying out,
the veins carrying back, the same blood
returning again and again.
i watched him demonstrate it in london:
the ligature on the arm, the veins swelling below,
the valves in the veins like tiny gates
allowing flow one way only.
simple. obvious — once shown.
fourteen hundred years of medicine,
overturned by observation and arithmetic:
the heart beats a hundred thousand times a day,
moving more blood than the body could make —
so it must go round.
harvey was the king's physician.
the king would lose his head in twenty years;
harvey's discovery never lost its head at all.
it circulates still — in every chest,
including yours.

the edict of restitution 1629 ce germany the catholic emperor orders protestants to return all seized church lands — a victor's overreach that guarantees ten more years of war. the emperor overplayed his hand —
ferdinand, flushed with catholic victories,
issued the edict of restitution:
every church land seized by protestants
since 1552 must be given back.
i was in augsburg when it was proclaimed,
and i watched the protestant princes go white.
it meant the bishoprics, the abbeys,
two archbishoprics, a hundred monasteries —
a map redrawn by decree, a century of settlements
torn up at a stroke.
it was meant to finish the war.
instead it guaranteed ten more years of it —
the protestants would fight to the death now,
having nothing left to lose,
and france, watching the habsburgs grow too strong,
decided to enter the war itself.
victory disease: the oldest sickness of empires.
ferdinand had won so much he couldn't stop winning,
and the edict turned his triumph
into everyone's desperation.
i wrote in my journal that night:
this edict will kill more men
than any battle of the war.

the city on a hill 1630 ce massachusetts john winthrop's puritan fleet lands in massachusetts bay — "a city upon a hill," a godly commonwealth the whole world will watch and argue over. winthrop preached it aboard the arbella —
the sermon, "a model of christian charity" —
before they ever saw the shore:
we shall be as a city upon a hill,
the eyes of all people upon us.
i sailed with that fleet — eleven ships,
a thousand puritans, the great migration —
and watched them land at massachusetts bay,
building boston out of wilderness
with prayer and axes.
a city on a hill: a godly commonwealth,
visible to the world, judged by its righteousness.
they meant it as a warning to themselves —
fail, and the world will see you fail.
they built it — the town, the church, the college —
and the world did watch, for centuries,
arguing ever since about what it saw.
i stood on that hill the first winter,
the wind off the bay like a knife,
and thought: they have set themselves a task
no people can complete, and they will try forever.

the lion lands 1630 ce germany gustavus adolphus of sweden lands in germany with his modern army — the lion of the north comes ashore praying, and the thirty years' war turns. he came ashore at usedom in july —
gustavus adolphus of sweden, the lion of the north,
with thirteen thousand men and the most modern army
in europe: light guns, volley fire,
cavalry that charged with the sword, not the carbine.
i watched the landing from the dunes:
the swedish king kneeling in the sand
to pray, the troops filing ashore in perfect order,
the banners snapping in the baltic wind.
germany's protestants, bled white by twelve years of war,
looked north and saw — hope, with artillery.
the catholics laughed. another northern king
come to be buried in germany, like christian of denmark
before him.
they stopped laughing at breitenfeld.
but that july day on the beach at usedom,
it was only a landing — a king on his knees in the sand,
an army in good order, and a war
about to change its nature forever.

magdeburg burns 1631 ce germany catholic troops sack magdeburg and massacre twenty thousand — the thirty years' war's most infamous atrocity, a city wedded to fire. tilly's men broke in in may — the great protestant city,
magdeburg, twenty-five thousand souls —
and what followed was the war's blackest day.
i arrived two days after, with a relief column
that had nothing to relieve:
the city burned to the ground, street by street,
the cathedral standing alone in the ashes
like a bone in a burned field.
twenty thousand dead — by fire, by sword,
by drowning in the elbe trying to flee.
the catholics called it magdeburg's sacrifice.
the protestants called it the magdeburg wedding —
wedded to fire.
all europe shuddered; the pamphlets flew;
gustavus adolphus swore vengeance
and marched south with fury in his ranks.
i walked through the ruins — the heat still rising
from the rubble, the smell of it in my clothes for weeks —
and understood what total war looks like
before the phrase existed.
magdeburg: the word itself became a warning.

breitenfeld 1631 ce germany gustavus adolphus smashes tilly's undefeated catholic army at breitenfeld — volley fire and mobile guns prove the new way of war in an afternoon. september, on the plain at breitenfeld —
gustavus adolphus drew up his swedes
against tilly's catholic veterans,
the finest army in europe, undefeated for a decade.
i watched from a village rooftop as the new way of war
proved itself: the swedish brigades,
thin and flexible, pouring volley fire
while their light guns galloped forward;
the cavalry charging home with cold steel;
tilly's great tercio squares, slow and deep,
shot to pieces before they could close.
by evening the catholic army was destroyed —
seven thousand dead, the rest fled or captured,
tilly himself wounded.
the lion of the north had done in a day
what twelve years of war had not.
protestant germany rose. the road to munich
lay open. the war had a new master.
i climbed down from that rooftop
with my ears ringing, having watched
the art of war change forever
in a single afternoon.

the anatomy lesson 1632 ce amsterdam twenty-five-year-old rembrandt paints dr. tulp's anatomy lesson — and amsterdam learns his name overnight. he was twenty-five — rembrandt van rijn,
fresh from leiden —
and the surgeons' guild commissioned the group portrait:
dr. tulp demonstrating the anatomy of the arm
on a dead criminal, his colleagues crowded round.
i saw it unveiled in amsterdam:
not a stiff row of faces but a moment —
the doctor lifting the tendons with his forceps,
the surgeons leaning in, one peering over his spectacles,
the corpse pale in the center of all that curiosity.
it made his name overnight.
the light on the dead man's flesh,
the living eyes all fixed on the mystery of the body —
a twenty-five-year-old had painted
the whole enlightenment in embryo:
look closely, together, and learn.
i stood before it a long time.
the surgeons look out at us, the viewers,
as if to say: come closer.
this is how knowledge is made —
by hand, by eye, by gathering round the dead
to understand the living.

lutzen 1632 ce germany gustavus adolphus dies victorious in the fog at lutzen — the lion of the north falls at thirty-seven, and protestant europe mourns. the fog lay thick on the field at lutzen —
so thick the armies blundered into each other —
and in that white blindness the lion fell.
gustavus adolphus led a cavalry charge himself,
as he always did, got separated in the fog,
and was shot — pistol, then sword-cuts,
stripped by looters, found at dusk
face down in the mud.
i walked that field the next day:
the swedes had won — wallenstein's army broken,
driven off — but their king lay dead,
and protestant europe's heart broke with him.
they carried his body home through germany,
the towns turning out in silence.
the lion of the north, thirty-seven years old,
victorious and dead in the fog.
the war went on without him for sixteen more years —
as if it had forgotten what it was for.
i think of him often: the king who prayed on the beach
at usedom, and died in the fog at lutzen,
and changed war forever in between.

the child queen 1632 ce sweden six-year-old christina becomes queen of sweden — the clever girl who will astonish europe, argue with descartes, and abdicate for rome. she was six years old — christina,
daughter of the lion, heir of sweden —
and they put the crown on her small head
in a kingdom at war.
i saw her at court years later, a teenager:
brilliant, restless, speaking six languages,
riding like a cavalryman, dressing like one too,
arguing theology with the bishops
and philosophy with descartes —
whom she summoned to stockholm
and accidentally killed with the cold
and the 5 a.m. lessons.
she would abdicate at twenty-eight,
convert to catholicism, and ride to rome
to become its most scandalous celebrity —
minerva of the north, they called her.
but in 1632 she was six, fatherless,
queen of a great power by the arithmetic of birth.
i watched the little girl at the coronation feast,
solemn among the generals,
and wondered what it costs a child
to inherit a lion's throne.

the taj begun 1632 ce agra shah jahan commissions a marble tomb for his beloved mumtaz, dead in childbirth — the taj mahal begins as stakes and trenches on the yamuna. mumtaz died in childbirth — her fourteenth child —
and shah jahan, the emperor, was broken.
so he built her a tomb: not a tomb, a poem in marble,
on the banks of the yamuna at agra.
i watched the foundations go down that year:
the call going out across the empire —
twenty thousand workers, a thousand elephants,
marble from makrana, jasper from the punjab,
turquoise from tibet, carnelian from arabia.
it would take twenty years. the dome would float
like a moonrise; the minarets would stand
like prayers; the whole thing would change color
with the hours — pink at dawn, white at noon,
gold at dusk.
all for love. all for grief.
the most beautiful building on earth,
built because a man could not bear
that the woman he loved should disappear.
i stood on the riverbank that first year,
looking at stakes and trenches,
and could not imagine what would rise there.
no one could. that is what makes it a wonder.

yakutsk founded 1632 ce siberia russian cossacks found yakutsk on the lena river — a log fort in the permafrost from which an empire will reach the pacific. the cossacks built it on the lena —
yakutsk, a wooden fort in the permafrost,
two thousand miles east of moscow,
the fur frontier's new capital.
i traveled with a fur convoy that decade:
the endless taiga, the rivers like roads,
the sable traps, the yasak tribute
collected from the yakuts in pelts.
a single black sable could buy a village;
the lena basin was a treasury
walking around on four legs.
yakutsk held — through fifty-below winters,
through scurvy and mutiny —
and from it the russians pushed on:
to the sea of okhotsk, to kamchatka,
to the very edge of asia.
a log fort on a frozen river,
and from it an empire reached the pacific.
i stood on the lena's bank in winter,
the ice groaning like a living thing,
and watched the sledges come in
laden with the soft gold of siberia.

galileo on trial 1633 ce rome the inquisition forces the old astronomer to kneel and deny that the earth moves — but the earth, indifferent to the verdict, keeps moving. they made the old man kneel —
galileo, seventy years old, sick, half-blind —
in the inquisition's hall, and read him the sentence:
he must abjure, curse, and detest
the lie that the earth moves.
i was in rome that june. the city buzzed with it:
the great astronomer, the starry messenger,
brought low by the holy office.
he knelt. he recited the formula.
they say he muttered under his breath —
eppur si muove, and yet it moves —
but i doubt it. i think he just wanted to go home.
they gave him house arrest for life.
he went back to arcetri, blind, and wrote
his greatest book anyway — the two new sciences —
smuggled out and printed in holland.
the church had its obedience.
galileo had the truth.
i know which one lasted.
three centuries later they'd admit it.
the earth, indifferent to the verdict,
kept moving all along.

nordlingen 1634 ce germany the catholic armies crush the swedes at nordlingen — and france, watching the habsburgs win everything, decides to enter the war itself. the catholic armies did it properly at nordlingen —
the spanish tercios marching up from italy,
joining the imperialists, catching the swedes
and their german allies in the open —
and crushed them.
i saw the swedish army break that september day:
twelve thousand dead or captured,
the guns lost, the protestant cause in germany
shattered at a stroke.
two years after lutzen, the lion's work
lay in ruins on a bavarian field.
the consequences ran straight to paris:
france, watching the habsburgs win everything,
decided it could no longer pay others to fight —
richelieu would send french armies into germany,
and the war of religion would become
a war of crowns.
nordlingen: the battle that made the war french.
i walked the field afterward, among the captured guns,
and thought about how defeat, like victory,
has children no one expects.

the french academy 1635 ce paris richelieu founds the academie francaise — forty immortals to guard the french language, a dictionary as a state project. richelieu founded it — the academie francaise,
forty immortals to guard the french language:
to fix it, purify it, make it the clearest tongue
in europe, fit for kings and philosophers.
i was in paris when the letters patent were read:
a salon of writers made official,
a dictionary as a state project,
the language itself declared a matter of national interest.
it worked, after its fashion.
french became the language of diplomacy,
of courts, of the enlightenment —
the whole continent learned to speak
in the academy's polished sentences.
forty immortals, meeting under the dome,
voting on words.
i find it charming and slightly mad —
as if language were a garden
that could be kept free of weeds by decree.
but the french proved me half wrong:
their garden grew the most admired flowers in europe,
even if a few wild ones got in anyway.

the closed country 1635 ce japan a new seclusion edict forbids japanese to travel abroad — the island nation turns its face inward for two hundred years. the edict came down like a lid —
no japanese ship to leave for foreign ports,
no japanese abroad to return on pain of death,
the great ocean-going junks broken up,
the ports narrowed to a crack.
i was in nagasaki when it was proclaimed:
the merchants reading it in silence,
the shipwrights putting down their tools,
an island nation turning its face inward
like a flower closing at dusk.
it wasn't complete — not yet.
the dutch would keep their little island at deshima,
the chinese their quarter, the koreans their embassies.
but the age of the red-seal ships was over,
the japanese diaspora cut off at the root.
two hundred years of seclusion began here —
two hundred years of peace, of art, of cities,
of a culture ripening in a sealed jar.
i stood on the nagasaki waterfront
and watched the last foreign-bound junk
unload its cargo for good,
and wondered what japan would become,
alone with itself.

harvard founded 1636 ce massachusetts the puritans found a college in the wilderness to train their ministers — harvard begins as a bequest, a library, and a clearing in the woods. the puritans voted it in the wilderness —
a college, in a clearing, to train their ministers:
named for john harvard, the young charlestown minister
who died at thirty and left his library
and half his estate to the school.
i visited it in the early years:
a single building, a handful of students,
the forest pressing close on every side,
the curriculum all latin and greek and god.
it was an act of faith as much as learning —
a bet that this raw settlement
would need scholars as well as farmers,
that the city on the hill required a school.
the bet paid off beyond all imagining.
that clearing in the wilderness became harvard —
the college, the university, the yard
where the american mind would be made.
i sat in on a disputation that first winter —
boys in black gowns arguing in latin
while the snow came down outside —
and thought: this is how civilizations plant themselves:
a library, a bequest, a clearing in the woods.

the qing proclaimed 1636 ce manchuria hong taiji declares his people's new dynastic name — the great qing — and claims the mandate of heaven eight years before it will be true. hong taiji proclaimed it — the new dynastic name:
the great qing, the pure —
and with the name, the claim:
the mandate of heaven itself,
no longer the ming's to hold.
i was at the ceremony at mukden:
the banners, the shamans, the assembled chiefs
of manchu, mongol, and chinese bannermen,
all kneeling to a name that meant
we are not rebels anymore — we are the dynasty.
it was audacious. the qing held only the northeast;
the ming still ruled china proper, two hundred million souls.
but names have power. the great qing —
a promise, a threat, a future
spoken aloud before it existed.
eight years later the ming would fall,
and the name would be true.
i stood among the kneeling chiefs that day
and heard the future being named,
and wrote it down exactly as proclaimed:
the great qing has begun.

the tulip crash 1637 ce holland tulip prices collapse overnight in a haarlem tavern — the first great market bubble bursts, and holland laughs, moralizes, and moves on. it ended in a tavern in haarlem, in february —
an auction, no buyers, the prices falling
like a stone down a well.
overnight, the tulip mania was over.
i was in amsterdam that week and saw the wreckage:
bulbs that had sold for the price of a canal house
now worthless as onions;
fortunes made of paper promises
evaporating by morning;
the pamphleteers already turning it into a joke,
a moral, a warning.
a single viceroy bulb for 2,500 florins —
a craftsman's lifetime wages for a flower.
then nothing. then laughter, and lawsuits,
and the courts refusing to enforce the contracts.
the dutch survived it — shrugged, moralized,
went back to work.
but the story stuck: the first great market bubble,
the template for every one since.
i kept a semper augustus bulb,
the striped kind that started it all,
and planted it in my garden.
it blooms every spring, oblivious —
which is more than can be said for the speculators.

i think, therefore i am 1637 ce holland rene descartes publishes his discourse on method — rebuilding philosophy from a single certain thought: i think, therefore i am. descartes published it in leiden — the discourse on method,
in french, not latin, so anyone could read it —
and rebuilt philosophy from a single stone.
i met him in holland in those years:
a soldier turned thinker, living quietly,
dissecting, calculating, doubting everything
until only one thing could not be doubted —
that he was doubting.
cogito, ergo sum. i think, therefore i am.
from that one certain point he rebuilt the world:
god, the soul, the material universe
as a machine of moving parts.
it was the charter of the modern mind —
reason as the foundation, method as the path,
everything else up for questioning.
the church banned it. europe devoured it.
i walked with him once along a canal,
and he talked of animals as clockwork
and the heart as a furnace.
a strange, cold, brilliant man —
who taught the world to think
by first teaching it to doubt.

shimabara rises 1637 ce japan catholic peasants rise at shimabara behind a boy messiah — and the shogunate answers with an army, sealing japan's closing. they rose in the winter — catholic peasants
of shimabara and amakusa, ground down by taxes,
led by a sixteen-year-old boy they called
their messiah, amakusa shiro —
and seized the old castle at hara.
i traveled through kyushu that year
and heard the stories: forty thousand rebels,
banners with crosses and saints,
holding the ruined fortress against the shogun's armies
for three months of siege.
the shogunate answered with everything —
a hundred thousand troops, dutch cannon
firing from offshore, and when the castle fell,
no quarter: every defender killed,
the boy messiah beheaded, his head displayed at nagasaki.
after shimabara came the final closing —
the portuguese expelled, the last crack sealed.
japan's christians went underground for two centuries,
the hidden faithful.
i stood before the ruins of hara castle afterward,
the crosses still painted on the broken walls,
and grieved for peasants who asked only
to pray and to eat — and were granted neither.

the covenant 1638 ce scotland scots sign the national covenant in greyfriars kirkyard — some in blood — swearing to defend their presbyterian church against the king. they signed it in greyfriars kirkyard, in edinburgh —
the national covenant, on a february day —
thousands of scots pressing forward to put their names
to the parchment, some signing in their own blood.
i was there, in the cold churchyard:
ministers, nobles, burgesses, common folk —
all swearing to defend the presbyterian kirk
against charles's bishops and his prayer book,
which they called popery in disguise.
it was a revolution by subscription.
the covenanters raised an army, took the castles,
and humbled the king in the bishops' wars —
forcing him to call the parliament
that would destroy him.
scotland's covenant with god became england's crisis.
i watched them sign — rank after rank,
the parchment filling with names —
and thought: this is what a nation looks like
when it decides, together, to say no.

the sultan retakes baghdad 1638 ce baghdad murad iv storms baghdad back from persia after a forty-day siege — restoring ottoman power in the east at a terrible price. murad iv came himself — the young sultan,
twenty-six, terrible in his energy —
with the whole ottoman host, and laid siege to baghdad,
the pearl the persians had held for fifteen years.
i traveled with the camp followers that autumn:
the great siege works, the mines, the assaults,
forty days of it, the city starving,
until the walls broke and the ottomans poured in.
what followed was a slaughter — the garrison,
and thousands of the city's people with them.
murad, they said, watched from his tent
and did not stop it.
conquerors make examples; baghdad was the example.
but the empire's eastern door was shut again —
mesopotamia ottoman, the persian tide turned back.
murad would die in two years, burned out at twenty-seven,
but baghdad stayed ottoman for centuries.
i entered the city after the sack —
the smoke, the silence, the tigris running brown —
and thought about the price of doors:
some are bought with gold, and some with this.

peace of zuhab 1639 ce persia the ottomans and safavids sign the treaty of zuhab — drawing a border that, near enough, still stands today. they drew the line at zuhab —
the ottomans and the safavids, exhausted by a century
of war over mesopotamia and the caucasus,
signed the treaty and fixed the border.
i was with a caravan crossing that country the next year,
and the guards at the passes were already bored —
a good sign. baghdad to the sultan,
yerevan to the shah, the mountains between them
belonging to whoever lived there.
it was the first real border in the region's history —
not a frontier of raids but a line on a map,
and it held.
it holds still, near enough: the line drawn at zuhab
is the ancestor of the borders there today.
four hundred years of diplomats have redrawn
the map of the middle east a hundred times,
but that one line — drawn by two tired empires
in 1639 — never moved.
i crossed it on foot, unchallenged,
and thought: peace is just a line
that everyone agrees to pretend is real —
until it becomes real.

the portuguese expelled 1639 ce japan japan expels the portuguese and closes its doors to nearly all europeans — a century of contact ends in a single season. the edict gave them weeks —
the portuguese, a century in japan,
the black ship, the silver trade, the missionaries —
all of it over, ships seized, priests hunted,
the whole connection cut.
i was in nagasaki for the last sailing:
the great carrack loading in silence,
the merchants' faces gray,
the japanese officials watching from the shore
with the new closed-country edicts
fresh in their hands.
shimabara had decided it. the shogunate
would risk no more christian rebellion,
no more foreign priests, no more divided loyalties.
only the dutch would remain —
protestants, traders, no missionaries —
on their little fan-shaped island at deshima,
a keyhole through which japan would watch the world.
a hundred years of contact ended in a season.
i stood on the waterfront as the last sails
dropped below the horizon,
and japan closed its doors behind them
with a sound like a temple bell.

the braganza restoration 1640 ce portugal portuguese nobles rise and crown the duke of braganza — ending sixty years of spanish rule in a single december morning. sixty years they'd waited — since philip marched in,
since the spanish crown swallowed portugal whole —
and on a december morning the nobles struck:
the spanish vicereine arrested in her palace,
the duke of braganza proclaimed john iv
in the terreiro do paco.
i was in lisbon that week, and the joy
was like a held breath released:
bells ringing, the spanish garrison surrendering,
a nation remembering it was a nation.
it would take twenty-eight years of war
to make spain accept it — twenty-eight years
of border fighting, of english alliance,
of brazil's sugar paying for portugal's freedom.
but the moment was pure: december 1st, 1640,
a small conspiracy in a palace,
and sixty years of foreign rule ended
before lunch.
i drank with the conspirators that night —
tired, exultant men who had bet their lives
on a duke — and the wine tasted
like independence.

the long parliament 1640 ce england charles i summons the parliament that will sit for twenty years — and destroy him; england's parliament stops being the king's instrument. charles needed money for the scottish war —
the covenanters had humiliated him —
so he called parliament, the first in eleven years,
and got more than he bargained for.
i sat in the gallery that november:
pym, hampden, the whole opposition,
elected and furious, and they went to work —
strafford attainted and executed,
laud imprisoned, the star chamber abolished,
ship money declared illegal,
a law that parliament could not be dissolved
without its own consent.
it would sit for twenty years — the long parliament —
through civil war, through the king's execution,
through cromwell's rule, till cromwell himself
drove it out with soldiers.
but that first session was the hinge:
the moment england's parliament stopped being
the king's instrument and became his master.
i watched charles watch it happen,
pale on his throne, and i knew —
as he must have known —
that he had summoned his own destruction.

sugar and chains 1640 ce barbados barbados planters switch to sugar — and the island's hunger for enslaved labor begins to reshape the atlantic in chains. the planters made the switch — from tobacco
and cotton to sugar, the white gold —
and barbados was never the same.
i walked those fields in the years after:
the cane standing ten feet tall,
the mills grinding day and night,
the boiling houses reeking of molasses,
and the labor — the endless, killing labor —
done by enslaved africans, imported by the thousand,
worked to death and replaced.
sugar made barbados the richest spot in the english world —
and the cruelest.
the island's hunger for enslaved labor
reshaped the whole atlantic: the slave ships,
the triangular trade, the fortunes of bristol and liverpool,
all feeding the mills' appetite.
a sweet tooth, and an ocean of chains.
i stood in a boiling house, the heat like a furnace,
the enslaved men feeding the rollers,
and tasted sugar afterward with ashes in my mouth.
the traveler counts coins, the era note says.
i counted these coins, and they were black and bitter.

the irish rebellion 1641 ce ireland irish catholics rise against english settlers in ulster — and the bloodshed poisons english politics past saving. it began in ulster in october —
the irish catholics rising against the english settlers,
seizing the plantations, and the bloodshed
ran beyond anyone's control.
i traveled through ulster that winter
and saw what civil war looks like up close:
settlers murdered in their beds,
irish hanged without trial,
both sides' pamphleteers multiplying the dead
by ten to feed the fury in london.
the stories — true, false, uncheckable —
poisoned english politics past saving:
parliament would trust no army to a king
who might use it against them,
having heard what "popish" armies did in ireland.
the rebellion became the excuse
for everything that followed.
eight years of war in ireland followed —
and then cromwell.
i left ulster in the spring,
the smoke still on the horizon,
and understood: some fires are lit
to warm a cause, and burn the house down instead.

edgehill 1642 ce england king and parliament meet in battle at edgehill — an indecisive sunday slaughter that means the english civil war will go on. they met on a sunday in october —
king and parliament, on the field at edgehill,
the first great battle of the english civil war.
i watched from the ridge as the armies formed:
the king's cavaliers in their shining armor,
parliament's men raw and earnest,
both sides praying to the same god
for opposite victories.
prince rupert's cavalry swept all before it —
then chased the baggage and left the field,
as cavaliers do.
the king's infantry held; parliament's held;
by dusk both armies stood bleeding
where they'd started, neither beaten,
neither victorious.
an indecisive battle — and therefore the worst kind,
because it meant the war would go on.
i walked the field at evening, among the wounded,
and heard men on both sides calling for water
in the same english voices.
one nation, one god, one field —
and no way back to peace.

the night watch 1642 ce amsterdam rembrandt unveils his great company portrait — the night watch, all motion and torchlight, amsterdam itself marching out of the dark. rembrandt unveiled it — the great company portrait,
captain cocq's militia marching out:
fifteen feet wide, all motion and torchlight,
a girl with a chicken at her hip,
a standard-bearer unfurling the colors,
a dog barking at the drummer's sticks.
i stood before it in the kloveniersdoelen
with the militiamen themselves, arguing:
not a stiff row of faces but a moment caught —
the company pouring out of the shadows,
muskets and pikes and banners,
rembrandt's light falling like a blessing
on the chaos.
they'd paid a hundred guilders each
to be in it, and some complained
their faces were half hidden.
rembrandt didn't care. he'd painted
not a portrait but an event —
amsterdam itself, marching.
it hung in the town hall, then the rijksmuseum,
growing darker and more famous with the years.
i go back to it in my mind whenever i need
to remember what genius looks like:
a militia company, stepping out of the dark,
into the light, forever.

tasman's voyage 1642 ce the pacific abel tasman sights tasmania and new zealand — the first european eyes on those shores, finding the future and being blamed for it. abel tasman sailed for the voc —
south from batavia, into the empty ocean,
looking for the great southern continent
the maps insisted was there.
i was not aboard — but i traced his track later,
port by port:
first van diemen's land, tasmania,
claimed for holland in a storm;
then the west coast of new zealand —
where the maori met his boats with war canoes
and tasman, wisely or not, sailed on.
the first european eyes on those shores.
he missed australia's east coast entirely,
sailed around it without knowing,
and came home to be scolded for finding nothing profitable.
nothing profitable! only tasmania,
only new zealand — two lands that would outlast
every spice cargo the voc ever carried.
i laughed when i read his instructions afterward:
find the continent, find the gold.
he found the future instead,
and was blamed for it.

the old man dies, the boy is born 1642 ce italy and england galileo dies blind at arcetri in january; that christmas, isaac newton is born in lincolnshire — the baton passed in the dark. galileo died in january at arcetri —
blind, under house arrest, seventy-seven —
the old man who had seen the moons of jupiter
closing his eyes at last.
that christmas, in a farmhouse in lincolnshire,
a premature baby was born —
so small they said he could fit in a quart pot —
isaac newton, fatherless, unpromising,
unlikely to live the week.
i stood at both ends of that year, in my fashion:
at the villa where the inquisition's prisoner
was buried quietly, and at the manor
where the widow held her tiny son
and prayed he'd survive.
the old astronomy died with galileo.
the new physics was born with newton —
in the same turning of the year,
as if the universe had arranged the handoff.
one man forced to kneel for saying the earth moves;
another, born as he died, who would prove
exactly how it moves, and why.
1642: the baton passed in the dark.

rocroi 1643 ce france the twenty-one-year-old duke of enghien shatters spain's famed infantry at rocroi — ending a century of spanish battlefield supremacy in a day. the duke of enghien was twenty-one —
the future great conde —
and at rocroi he did what no one had done in a century:
he broke the spanish infantry.
i watched from the french lines as the tercios
stood in their great squares, pikes bristling,
the finest foot soldiers in europe —
and conde's cavalry charged them, broke,
rallied, charged again, while his guns
pounded the squares to ruin.
by evening the spanish army was destroyed —
eight thousand dead, the tercios' legend dead with them.
a century of spanish battlefield supremacy,
from pavia to this field, ended in a day.
spain would remain a great power,
but never again the terror of the battlefield.
france had a new hero, twenty-one years old,
and europe had a new lesson:
no supremacy lasts forever —
not even one that lasted a hundred years.

the sun king, aged four 1643 ce france four-year-old louis xiv inherits the french throne — the child in the lace collar who will rule for seventy-two years. louis xiii died in may, and his son —
four years old, a child in a lace collar —
became louis xiv, with his mother anne as regent
and mazarin holding the real reins.
i saw the boy king carried into notre-dame
for the coronation rites: small, solemn,
utterly unaware that he would rule france
for seventy-two years — the longest reign
in european history.
the fronde was coming — the nobles' revolt,
the humiliations that would teach him
never to trust paris, never to share power —
and then the sun king: versailles,
the arts, the wars, the glory and the ruin.
but in 1643 he was four, and the crown
was bigger than his head.
i watched the procession pass,
the child waving because he'd been told to,
and thought: here is the future of france,
in short trousers, not yet able to read
the history he is about to make.

the ming falls 1644 ce beijing rebels take beijing, the last ming emperor hangs himself on coal hill — and the manchu qing ride through the opened gates. the rebels took beijing in april —
li zicheng's armies through the gates,
the ministers fleeing or hanging themselves —
and the last ming emperor, chongzhen,
climbed coal hill behind the palace
and hanged himself from a tree,
leaving a note blaming his officials.
i was in the city in those terrible days:
the looting, the fires, the great dynasty
ending not with a battle but with a rope
on a hill.
and then — the greater shock —
the ming general at the wall opened the gates
to the manchus, to help against the rebels,
and the qing rode through:
eight banners, the shaved heads and queues,
into the capital of china.
two hundred and seventy-six years of ming —
ended in a month.
i stood on coal hill afterward,
looking down at the palace roofs,
and watched the manchu banners go up
over the forbidden city.
the mandate had passed.
heaven had chosen new tenants.

areopagitica 1644 ce england john milton publishes his thundering defense of a free press — parliament ignores it, and the centuries adopt it. milton wrote it in a fury — areopagitica,
his speech for the liberty of unlicensed printing —
aimed at parliament, his own side,
which had replaced the king's censors with its own.
i read it hot off the press in london:
"give me the liberty to know, to utter,
and to argue freely according to conscience,
above all liberties" —
and the great metaphor, books as living things:
who kills a man kills a reasonable creature,
but he who destroys a good book
kills reason itself.
parliament ignored it. the licensing continued.
milton lost the argument and won the centuries —
every defense of a free press since
is a footnote to areopagitica.
i keep my copy beside my bible.
it is the angriest, most beautiful thing
ever written about the right to be wrong in print —
by a blind man, twenty years before his blindness,
who saw further than all of them.

naseby 1645 ce england cromwell's new model army destroys the king's forces at naseby — the decisive battle; the future belongs to the disciplined, not the dashing. cromwell's new model army did it at naseby —
the decisive battle, the king's army destroyed
in a summer afternoon in northamptonshire.
i watched from a hillside as it unfolded:
the royalist cavalry charging as always,
rupert sweeping the field —
and then cromwell's ironsides, disciplined,
godly, holding their formation,
rolling up the king's infantry like a carpet.
by evening charles had lost his guns,
his baggage, his infantry —
and his private letters, captured in the baggage train,
published to prove his double-dealing to the world.
the war wasn't over, but it was decided.
the new model army — paid, drilled, promoted by merit —
had beaten the cavaliers at their own game.
i walked the field at dusk, past the abandoned guns,
and thought: the future belongs to the disciplined,
not the dashing.
england had just proved it.

milton's poems 1645 ce england john milton publishes his first book of poems at thirty-six — l'allegro, il penseroso, lycidas: the promise of the epic to come. he published them himself — poems of mr. john milton,
his first book, at thirty-six —
and announced, quietly, a great voice.
i bought a copy from the printer's shop:
l'allegro and il penseroso, the twin moods —
the cheerful man, the thoughtful man —
lycidas, the elegy for a drowned friend,
the nativity ode, written at twenty-one,
comus, the masque.
the learning in it was staggering —
latin, greek, italian, hebrew behind every line —
but the music was what caught me:
a young man writing as if the english language
were an instrument he'd been born holding.
no one knew paradise lost was coming —
twenty years off, blindness, the epic.
but the promise was all here, in this slim volume:
the voice, the ambition, the nerve.
i read lycidas aloud that winter,
to an empty room, and the room
didn't feel empty afterward.

the king surrenders 1646 ce england charles i surrenders to the scots — who keep him nine months, then sell him to parliament for £400,000: a king priced and delivered. he gave himself up to the scots —
charles, beaten at naseby, his cause lost,
riding into the scottish camp at newark
in disguise, hoping to play his enemies
against each other.
i heard the story from a scottish officer afterward:
the king arrived expecting to negotiate as a king,
and found he was a prisoner with good manners.
the scots kept him for nine months,
then sold him to parliament for £400,000 —
the back pay of their army, the king
thrown in like a bonus.
it was the coldest transaction of the war:
a king, priced and delivered.
charles kept scheming — secret treaties,
promises to everyone, loyalty to none —
and every scheme made his position worse.
he thought he was playing chess.
he was the chess piece.
i watched the handover from a distance —
soldiers, ledgers, a king changing hands —
and thought: this is what happens
when majesty becomes merchandise.

the levellers' agreement 1647 ce england radical soldiers demand the agreement of the people — votes for all men, a written constitution; cromwell crushes it, but the words survive. the soldiers wrote it — the agreement of the people,
drawn up in the army's debates at putney:
votes for all men, not just property-holders;
a written constitution; parliament elected fairly;
no one above the law, not even the king.
i sat in on the putney debates, in the church:
rainsborough, the leveller, answering ireton,
cromwell's son-in-law, with the words
that still ring —
the poorest he that is in england hath a life to live
as the greatest he.
it was democracy, raw and plain,
proposed by soldiers in 1647 —
a century and a half before the french revolution,
two centuries before it happened in england.
cromwell crushed it. the grandees won.
the agreement was never adopted.
but the words survived — rainsborough's words —
and every democratic movement since
has spoken in their echo.
i copied them into my journal that night,
in the church, by candlelight,
and i have never underlined anything so hard.

westphalia 1648 ce germany the peace of westphalia ends the thirty years' war — eight million dead, and the birth of the modern state system from the ashes. they signed it in two towns — munster and osnabruck —
after five years of talking, while the war
went on around them:
the peace of westphalia, ending the thirty years' war.
i traveled between the two congresses that year:
the greatest diplomatic gathering europe had seen —
a hundred delegations, every prince and power,
arguing over every village and bishopric
while the ink dried on the map of the modern world.
eight million dead. germany halved in places.
the treaties redrew the map: france gained,
sweden gained, the dutch and swiss recognized as independent,
each prince sovereign in his own land —
cuius regio, eius religio, and an end to the wars of faith.
it was the birth of the state system —
sovereign states, borders, diplomacy —
the world we still live in.
i watched the signings, town after town,
and thought of magdeburg, of lutzen, of the white mountain —
eight million ghosts, looking on
as the diplomats divided up the peace.

khmelnytsky rises 1648 ce ukraine bohdan khmelnytsky's cossacks rise against polish rule — the steppe catches fire, and ukraine's fateful turn toward moscow begins. bohdan khmelnytsky raised the cossacks —
against the polish lords who'd taxed and scorned them,
against the jesuits, against the whole polish order
in ukraine — and the steppe caught fire.
i rode with a merchant caravan through ukraine that year
and saw the rising spread like a grass fire:
the cossack host, the tatar allies,
the polish armies broken at zhovti vody,
at korsun — the commonwealth's finest
destroyed in weeks.
what followed was the deluge's first wave —
and a horror for ukraine's jews,
caught between the armies, massacred by the thousands
in the worst pogroms europe had seen.
khmelnytsky would turn to moscow for protection —
the pereyaslav agreement —
and ukraine would pass from polish hands
to russian, the fateful step.
i stood on the steppe that autumn,
watching the smoke of burned manors on the horizon,
and felt the ground shifting under eastern europe —
a new power rising in the east,
on cossack horses.

around the frozen cape 1648 ce siberia semyon dezhnev sails around the eastern tip of asia — proving it is not joined to america, in a feat europe forgets for a century. semyon dezhnev did it — sailed from the kolyma
around the eastern tip of asia,
through the strait that would be named for bering
eighty years later, proving asia was not joined
to america.
i met old fur men in yakutsk who'd heard the tale:
seven ships leaving, four lost,
dezhnev's own vessel wrecked south of the strait,
the survivors walking the arctic coast,
most dying, a handful reaching the anadyr —
and the report filed away in yakutsk,
forgotten for nearly a century.
europe never heard of it.
bering got the strait, the glory, the name —
for discovering what dezhnev had already found.
it galls me still. the man sailed wooden koches
through arctic ice, around the top of the world,
and his own government lost the paperwork.
i raise a glass, when i'm in those parts,
to semyon dezhnev —
the discoverer history forgot,
because history misfiled him.

the king loses his head 1649 ce london charles i is beheaded outside whitehall — a king tried by his subjects and executed; england becomes a republic, and the world changes its mind about kings. january 30th, outside whitehall —
on a scaffold hung with black,
charles i, king of england,
laid his head on the block.
i was in the crowd, close enough to see:
he wore an extra shirt, so the cold
wouldn't make him shiver and seem afraid.
he forgave the executioner.
one blow — the masked headsman held up the head,
and the crowd groaned, a sound, they said,
like nothing heard before.
a king, tried by his subjects,
found guilty, and executed —
in the name of the people, by an act of parliament.
no one in europe had done such a thing.
the other kings heard the news in horror;
the poets heard it in awe.
england became a republic that afternoon —
the commonwealth, cromwell rising.
i walked home through the silent streets,
the extra shirt, the single blow,
the groan of the crowd ringing in my ears.
the world had changed its mind about kings,
and there was no changing it back.

dunbar 1650 ce scotland cromwell crushes the scottish army at dunbar — outnumbered, sick, and trapped, then victorious by a dawn attack in the rain. cromwell did it at dunbar — outnumbered,
sick, trapped between the scots army
and the sea, his men starving —
and then the scots came down from the hill,
and cromwell struck.
september 3rd, in the rain and the dark:
the new model army smashed the covenanters
in a morning — three thousand dead,
ten thousand taken, the scottish cause broken
at a stroke.
i walked that battlefield afterward:
the rain washing the blood into the soil,
the prisoners herded south, many dying on the march.
cromwell called it a crowning mercy —
his phrase, and a chilling one.
scotland would fight on — worcester next year,
the boy charles ii crowned at scone —
but dunbar decided it.
the republic's northern border was secured
by the most unlikely victory of the war:
a sick army, a desperate general,
and a dawn attack in the rain.

the tenth muse 1650 ce massachusetts anne bradstreet, mother of eight on the massachusetts frontier, publishes her poems — the first book of verse from the new world. she was a mother of eight, in the wilderness —
anne bradstreet, sailing to massachusetts
with winthrop's fleet, burying children,
keeping house on the frontier —
and writing poems in the stolen hours.
i visited her at andover in the later years:
a quiet woman, plain-dressed, who showed me
her verses with an apology —
not seeking publication, only the truth of her heart:
her children, her husband, her god,
her house burned down — "farewell, my pelf" —
her faith tested and holding.
her brother-in-law carried the manuscript to london
and published it without her full consent:
the tenth muse lately sprung up in america —
the first book of verse from the new world,
by a woman, from the wilderness.
eight children, a frontier, a book of poems.
i think of her when men talk of what women couldn't do.
she did it all — the living and the writing —
and the muse she sprung was her own.

the regent dies 1650 ce beijing dorgon, the manchu prince-regent who put the qing boy-emperor on china's throne, dies on a hunting trip — and power shifts behind the palace walls. dorgon died on a hunting trip — the manchu prince-regent,
the man who'd led the qing through the gates of beijing,
put the boy-emperor shunzhi on the throne,
and ruled china in his name for six years.
i was in beijing when the news came back from the hunt:
a sudden death, out in the field,
and the court holding its breath —
because dorgon's power had been absolute,
and absolute power leaves a vacuum
shaped exactly like a man.
what followed was the settling:
the young emperor's faction moving against dorgon's,
the regent's titles stripped posthumously,
his allies purged, the balance of the court
shifting behind the palace walls
like pieces on a board no outsider could see.
the qing boy-emperor was twelve.
the men around him were deciding
what kind of dynasty this would be.
i watched the funeral rites from a distance —
the banners, the drums, the ritual grief —
and thought: every new dynasty is a gamble,
and the dice are still rolling.

cromwell's shadow 1650 ce ireland the sieges of drogheda and wexford in 1650, where cromwell's campaign turned a war into a wound ireland carried for centuries. i walked behind that army into drogheda's walls,
heard the new model drums where the shannon calls.
they took the town by storm, and the storm took all —
old men, young men, stacked along the hall.
the siege-fire writes in smoke what books won't say:
that "god's englishman" could kill and kneel and pray.
sixty years gone, and the fields still remember —
the bitter roots dug up each irish november.

the cook writes it down 1651 ce france francois pierre de la varenne's le cuisinier francois made french cooking a written art, changing how the world eats. la varenne took his quill where the kitchen sweats,
and wrote what every master cook forgets:
butter made honest, sauces made light,
the broth that turns a meal to appetite.
i ate at tables where his recipes were read —
the printed page became the daily bread.
before him, cooking died with every cook;
after him, france opened a book.

the navigation acts 1651 ce england parliament's trade monopoly law that choked dutch shipping and helped ignite three anglo-dutch wars. only english keels may carry english goods —
so read the parliament's new rules.
i watched the dutch captains shake their heads
and saw the first shots smoke above their beds.
a paper law, a line of ink —
enough to make two navies sink.
trade is war with sails instead of swords,
and every barrel pays the lords.

the first coffeehouse 1652 ce england london's first coffeehouse opened the age of the "penny universities," where news, science, and revolution were argued over coffee. pasqua rosee boiled his bitter brew
in a shed off cornhill, and london queued.
a penny bought a cup and all the news —
the merchant's loss, the sailor's views,
plots in the corner, pamphlets on the wall.
i sat and listened through it all:
the century thinking out loud at last,
the future brewed from the burnt past.

the first dutch war 1652 ce north sea england and the dutch republic fought the first of three naval wars over trade routes and naval pride. i stood on deck when the broadsides began,
english oak against the dutchman's plan.
they fought for flags dipped and trade denied —
for who may sail where the herring glide.
the smoke lay thick from kent to the texel sands;
two merchant peoples killing with hired hands.
three wars would bloom from this first seed —
the sea itself the field of greed.

the taj completed 1653 ce india the taj mahal was completed at agra — a grieving emperor's monument that became the world's most famous building. twenty years, twenty thousand hands,
a love-song raised in marble on the sands.
i walked the garden as the last stone set —
the inlay flowers not finished yet.
shah jahan came at dusk to stand and stare
at mumtaz sleeping in the moonlit air.
grief had learned the mason's trade;
the most beautiful thing grief ever made.

the lord protector 1653 ce england oliver cromwell dissolved parliament and ruled as lord protector — a republic with a king in everything but name. he walked into the house with musketeers
and ended twenty years of hopes and fears.
"no crown," he said — but took the sword,
the palace, and the thankless lord.
i watched him rule by army's might,
a king who'd murdered kings outright.
the protector's chair was cold and bare;
no son could sit for long in there.

the queen abdicates 1654 ce sweden queen christina of sweden gave up her throne, converted to catholicism, and became europe's most famous exile. she laid the crown on the uppsala floor,
walked out the palace, shut the door.
christina — scholar, queen, and flame —
rode south to rome to change her name.
i watched her cross the alps that fall,
a sovereign answering a different call.
she traded scepters for the mass,
and europe's gossip let her pass.

jamaica taken 1655 ce caribbean england seized jamaica from spain, turning it into the sugar-and-slavery powerhouse of the british caribbean. the english fleet came soft at dawn,
and spanish jamaica was soon gone.
i walked the cane-fields years from then,
saw sugar worked by shackled men.
an island taken for the crown's coffer
became the engine that made planters richer —
and every hogshead shipped to sea
was sweetened with somebody's misery.

the clock that keeps time 1656 ce netherlands christiaan huygens patented the pendulum clock — the first timekeeper accurate enough for science and navigation. huygens hung a weight on a swinging line
and taught the hours to keep true time.
i watched the pendulum's patient sweep
while old clocks stumbled in their sleep.
for sailors lost on empty seas,
true minutes meant the longitudes' keys.
a tick, a tock — the world grew small;
the seconds marched, and conquered all.

the provincial letters 1656 ce france blaise pascal's witty provincial letters mocked jesuit casuistry and made theology the talk of paris. pascal took up his pen to fight,
and made the jesuits squirm all night.
i read each letter hot off the press —
wit turned to theological finesse.
all paris laughed at holy fraud,
and monks were mocked in print abroad.
a genius with a joker's art
stuck reason's dagger in the heart.

the great fire of meireki 1657 ce japan fire destroyed most of edo (tokyo), killing tens of thousands; the shogunate rebuilt it grander and better planned. the wind took edo in a single night,
a hundred thousand souls in flight.
i ran with them through streets of flame
where wooden houses fed the game.
the shogun's city burned to bone —
then rose in stone, in streets of stone,
wider, straighter, built to last,
a phoenix risen from the ash-cast.

the protector dies 1658 ce england cromwell's death and his son richard's collapse ended england's republican experiment within months. fever took him on a stormy night,
and london lost its iron might.
his son, poor richard, held the reins
for months, then dropped them in the lanes.
i watched the army eat its own —
the republic melted like a stone
left out in summer's heat to bake.
the crown was coming back to take.

the throne of blood 1658 ce india aurangzeb imprisoned shah jahan and seized the mughal throne in a fratricidal war of succession. brother killed brother for the peacock throne,
and aurangzeb stood last alone.
he locked his father in agra's tower
to watch the taj through bars of power.
i walked the fort where old shah jahan
wept at the marble of his plan.
an empire built on a father's chain —
the mughal crown was bought with pain.

the pyrenees peace 1659 ce europe the treaty of the pyrenees ended the franco-spanish war and made france europe's dominant power. on an island in the river's flow,
two kings made peace and let war go.
louis took the spanish bride,
and france stood tallest, far and wide.
i watched the wedding train depart —
a marriage sealing europe's heart.
twenty years of war laid down;
the sun was rising on his crown.

the king comes home 1660 ce england charles ii's return ended the republic — theatres reopened, christmas returned, and the monarchy was restored. the crowds at dover cheered him through,
the bells rang out the old made new.
charles came home from exile's shore
to open what the saints shut door:
the theatres lit, the maypoles high,
christmas carols split the sky.
i drank that may with all the rest —
the restoration at its best.

the painter of the court dies 1660 ce spain diego velazquez died in madrid, leaving las meninas — a painting that still puzzles and delights every viewer. velazquez laid his brushes down
in the quiet palace of the crown.
las meninas kept his stare —
the painter in the mirror there,
the king and queen a ghostly pair,
the dog asleep without a care.
