i stood before it, and it stood —
arguing still, as great art should.

the sun takes the reins 1661 ce france louis xiv seized personal rule after mazarin's death, beginning the long reign of the sun king. mazarin was dead, the boy was grown —
louis said, "i rule alone."
no minister, no guiding hand,
just the sun king and the land.
i watched the courtiers learn to bow
to the young god they serve now.
seventy years of "i am the state" —
france shone bright, and burned, and ate.

paper money 1661 ce sweden stockholm's bank issued europe's first banknotes — money became a printed promise rather than metal. in stockholm town a banker found
that paper could be passed around.
no heavy coins to drag and clink —
just printed promise, signed in ink.
i held one in my wondering hand:
wealth you couldn't understand,
a kingdom's word on a paper scrap.
the future folded in the map.

the royal society 1662 ce england charles ii chartered the royal society, and experimental science became a public, shared enterprise. the king gave charter, seal, and hall
to men who'd test and measure all.
i watched them weigh the air and rain,
pump out the vacuum, count the vein.
wigs and frock coats, but minds set free —
"take nobody's word" their decree.
the world's first club of curious men
made knowledge public with the pen.

pascal's last wager 1662 ce france blaise pascal died at thirty-nine, leaving the pensees — fragments where reason argues for faith. thirty-nine years, and the light went out —
the geometer, the saint, the doubt.
he left his pensees, scattered leaves,
where reason argues and believes:
bet on god, the wager cries,
for infinite stakes and finite dies.
i read him in the candle's gleam —
a mind awake inside a dream.

the sugar code 1663 ce caribbean barbados's slave code declared enslaved africans property for life — the legal blueprint for plantation slavery across the americas. in barbados they wrote it plain:
a black man's bondage would remain —
for life, and for his children's lives,
property, not men with wives.
i read the code with a sickened eye,
the law that taught the world the lie:
that some are born to be unfree,
and sugar sweetens slavery.

new amsterdam falls 1664 ce north america england seized new amsterdam bloodlessly and renamed it new york — a small port with an enormous future. four english frigates in the bay,
and stuyvesant gave the town away.
no shot was fired, no blood was shed —
new amsterdam was simply dead.
they named it for the duke of york,
a village soon to be new york.
i walked its wall street, small and new,
not dreaming what the town would do.

the plague year 1665 ce england bubonic plague ravaged london in 1665, emptying the city and killing tens of thousands. the red cross marked the stricken door,
the dead-cart rumbled more and more.
the rich fled west, the poor stayed home
to watch the churchyards fill with loam.
"bring out your dead!" the night-bell tolled —
i walked those streets, and i was told
to keep my distance, hold my breath,
and count the arithmetic of death.

news in print 1665 ce england the london gazette's first issue began england's oldest continuously printed newspaper. the gazette rolled off the press that fall,
two pages answering the town's call:
the court's decrees, the fleet's return,
the plague's own numbers, stern and stern.
i bought a copy for a coin or two —
the first of millions coming through.
three hundred years and running still,
the news goes on, for good or ill.

the world under glass 1665 ce england robert hooke's micrographia revealed the microscopic world in stunning detail — the microscope's first bestseller. hooke put a flea beneath his lens
and drew it armored, huge, immense.
i turned the pages, lost in wonder —
a world of small, split wide asunder.
the cork's small rooms he named the cell;
the microscope had news to tell.
a bestseller born of tiny things —
the small world suddenly had wings.

the great fire 1666 ce england the great fire of london destroyed most of the medieval city in four days; it was rebuilt in brick and stone. a baker's oven in pudding lane
set half of london to the flame.
four days the fire ate street and spire,
a city dying in the pyre.
i stood on southwark's bank and saw
st. paul's collapse in smoke and awe.
then london rose in brick and stone —
a cleaner city from the bone.

the academy of sciences 1666 ce france colbert founded the paris academy of sciences, giving french scholars royal salaries and laboratories. colbert gathered scholars in the king's own name,
gave them salaries, labs, and fame.
i watched them chart the moons above,
weigh the metals kings most love.
french science wore a royal coat —
the sun king's money kept afloat
the minds that mapped the age of reason.
knowledge had become the season.

the builder in his tower 1666 ce india shah jahan died imprisoned in agra fort, gazing across the river at the taj mahal he could never visit. old shah jahan, in agra's keep,
watched the taj through bars of sleep.
his son had locked the builder-king
to gaze upon his marble thing —
the tomb across the river's bend,
his love, his loss, his bitter end.
i stood beside him, and he sighed:
"let me die looking." and he died.

paradise lost 1667 ce england blind john milton published paradise lost — his epic of satan, adam, and the fall, dictated from memory. blind, he dictated — line by line —
satan's defiance, eve's decline.
"better to reign in hell," the cry
that made the fallen angel fly.
i heard him speak the verses slow,
his daughters writing what he'd know:
the fall, the garden, and the flame —
and justified god's ways the same.

the raid on the medway 1667 ce netherlands dutch warships sailed up the thames, burned english ships, and towed away the flagship — the republic's boldest naval triumph. up the thames the dutchmen came,
and put the english fleet to shame.
they broke the chain, they burned the ships,
they towed the royal charles by the hips.
i watched from rochester's shore that day —
the boldest raid war ever saw at play.
de ruyter's guns sang through the mist:
the republic's triumph, none could resist.

bombay changes hands 1668 ce india the east india company took bombay — a swampy portuguese dowry port destined to become a megacity. a dowry port, a swampy shore —
portugal's gift, and england's door.
the company took the seven isles,
the mud, the monsoon, and the miles.
i stood on docks that barely stood,
and dreamed of what the merchants could:
a megacity of towers and trade
on the muddy ground the treaty made.

the laureate 1668 ce england john dryden became poet laureate, bringing his sharp satirical tongue to the restoration stage. dryden took the laurel and the wine,
and made the restoration stage shine.
his tongue was sharp, his couplets true —
he flayed the fools and praised the few.
i sat in drury lane to hear
the wits applaud, the gallants cheer.
the sharpest tongue the age would find
wore the crown of england's rhyming mind.

rembrandt's last light 1669 ce netherlands rembrandt died poor in amsterdam, painting self-portraits to the very end — darker, truer, and freer than ever. he died poor in amsterdam that fall,
painting himself against the wall.
the late portraits — darker, freer, true —
a face that age had battered through.
i stood where he stood, brush in hand,
a bankrupt master of the land.
the market left him; the light stayed on.
the man was gone; the gaze lived on.

crete falls 1669 ce mediterranean after a twenty-one-year siege, candia fell to the ottomans and venice's eastern empire ended. twenty-one years the siege held on,
then candia's walls were finally gone.
the ottomans took the cretan shore;
venice's eastern empire was no more.
i walked the breached and broken gate,
the price of pride, the cost of fate.
an empire measured in the sea
drowned in the waves it used to be.

the bay company 1670 ce north america the hudson's bay company was chartered, and beaver pelts began flowing from frozen forests to london hats. a charter signed, a frozen bay —
the beaver trade was underway.
from hudson's ice to london's hat,
the pelts flowed in, and that was that.
i paddled north with the first brigade,
through forests where the bargains made
built an empire on a rodent's fur —
the coldest commerce ever were.

the secret treaty 1670 ce england charles ii secretly promised louis xiv he would convert to catholicism — in exchange for french gold. at dover, in the candle's glow,
charles signed what none must know:
turn catholic for louis's gold,
a secret bought, a kingdom sold.
i read the parchment years gone by —
a king who'd wear another sky
for frenchmen's coins. the realm was priced;
the crown itself was sacrificed.

morgan's sack of panama 1671 ce panama the buccaneer henry morgan sacked and burned panama city, hauling away its silver — piracy at its grandest and cruelest. henry morgan crossed the isthmus line,
burned panama, and took the mine.
the silver flowed in mule-train rows;
the city died where the jungle grows.
i saw the smoke above the bay —
piracy's grandest, cruelest day.
a knight's reward for theft and flame:
the crown called murder by his name.

the disaster year 1672 ce netherlands invaded on all sides, the dutch flooded their own land to survive — while a hague mob murdered the de witt brothers. france, england, bishops — all at once —
invaded in the year's first months.
the hague mob dragged the de witts down
and murdered them in the market town.
i saw the water-gates let through
the floods that saved the dutch — it's true:
they drowned their land to keep it free.
despair became the victory.

coffee comes to paris 1672 ce france paris got its first coffeehouse, and soon the whole city was arguing philosophy over tiny cups. an armenian set his pots to steam,
and paris woke as from a dream.
the tiny cups, the bitter brew,
the talk that all the night ran through.
i sat with wits and watched the tide —
the whole city caffeinated wide.
from london's lead to paris' art,
coffee had conquered every heart.

moliere's last bow 1673 ce france moliere collapsed on stage during the imaginary invalid and died hours later — comedy's greatest actor exiting mid-performance. he played the dying man that night —
and dying was the part done right.
on stage, mid-cough, the master fell;
the invalid rang his final bell.
i was there when the curtain came —
comedy's king went out in flame.
they buried him at the edge of ground;
the laugh he left still shakes the town.

the maratha crowned 1674 ce india shivaji was crowned chhatrapati at raigad, founding the maratha kingdom that would humble the mighty mughals. at raigad fort, beneath the sun,
shivaji's coronation was done.
chhatrapati — the umbrella's shade —
a hindu kingdom newly made.
i watched the drums, the sacred fire,
the mountain kingdoms lift him higher.
the mughal giant felt the sting:
a free man's crown, a people's king.

the star observatory 1675 ce england greenwich observatory was founded to map the heavens and solve the puzzle of longitude at sea. on greenwich hill they raised the dome,
and made the turning sky their home.
to find the longitude at sea,
they mapped the stars for you and me.
i climbed the hill on a frosty night
and watched them chase the charted light.
england's eye upon the sphere —
the heavens measured, far and near.

king philip's war 1675 ce north america the wampanoag sachem metacom led a desperate uprising that burned new england and destroyed a tenth of its towns. metacom rose, the wampanoag chief,
and new england drowned in grief.
a tenth of towns went up in flame;
the frontier would not be the same.
i walked the ashes, heard the cry
of two worlds learning how to die.
the desperate war, the broken land —
the blood was on the white man's hand.

the martyr on the scaffold 1675 ce india guru tegh bahadur was beheaded in delhi for defending the right to worship — a martyrdom the sikhs never forgot. in delhi's square they raised the block
for tegh bahadur — hear the clock.
he died defending others' right
to worship in their own true light.
i stood among the silent crowd
and heard no voice, though hearts were loud.
the sikhs remember to this day:
the martyr showed the steel the way.

vermeer's quiet rooms 1675 ce netherlands vermeer died young and poor in delft, leaving luminous interiors — milkmaids and map-rooms full of northern light. he died young, poor, in delft that year,
leaving milkmaids, maps, light clear.
a window's glow, a pearl's soft gleam —
the quiet rooms of a painter's dream.
i stepped inside his painted air
and found the northern light still there.
the world forgot him for a while;
the light remembered, with a smile.

bacon's rebellion 1676 ce north america bacon's rebels — poor whites and enslaved blacks fighting together — burned jamestown before the planters crushed and divided them. bacon's mob burned jamestown down —
poor whites and blacks against the crown.
one time they fought side by side,
then the planters split them wide.
i watched the torches light the town,
the governor's men hunt rebels down.
the lesson that the rich men learned:
divide the poor, or get burned.

light has a speed 1676 ce france ole rømer timed jupiter's moons and proved light travels at a finite speed — fast, but not instantaneous. rømer watched io's faithful dance
around great jupiter's expanse,
and timed the moons with patient art —
light took time to play its part.
not instant, no — but swift and true,
it crossed the void to me and you.
i felt the universe expand:
a speed limit on god's own hand.

the ethics 1677 ce netherlands spinoza's ethics, published after his death, argued god and nature are one — scandalizing every pulpit in europe. spinoza's book came after death —
god and nature, one same breath.
no pulpit thunder could abide
the heresy he preached inside.
i read it in a quiet room
and felt the old certainties' doom.
the scandal shook the church's towers:
the universe is ours — and ours.

the red priest is born 1678 ce italy antonio vivaldi was born in venice — the sickly boy who would make violins sing like weather. a sickly boy in venice born,
with red hair like the autumn corn —
antonio, priest and violin,
who'd make the strings begin to spin.
i heard his first small concert play
and knew the weather'd come that way:
storms and seasons in his bow,
the red priest tuning even now.

the popish plot 1678 ce england titus oates invented a catholic conspiracy, and panicked london hanged innocent men before the lie collapsed. titus oates spun his lying thread —
a catholic plot, the king half-dead.
panicked london strung men high
for a conspiracy — a lie.
i watched the innocent ascend
the gallows for a fiction's end.
fear will hang a man as true
as any guilt the courts e'er knew.

the pilgrim's road 1678 ce england imprisoned tinker john bunyan published the pilgrim's progress — the allegory every english cottage would own. a tinker sat in bedford jail
and dreamed the road, and told the tale:
christian's burden, vanity fair,
the slough where pilgrims lose their prayer.
i walked that road in my mind's eye —
the book that taught the poor to fly.
every cottage came to own
the journey every soul has known.

habeas corpus 1679 ce england parliament's habeas corpus act forbade imprisonment without charge — a leash on arbitrary power, written into law. no more the dungeon's silent door,
no more the jailer keeping score.
produce the body — show the charge —
or set the prisoner at large.
i read the act with a lifted heart:
the law had learned its noblest art —
to leash the jailer, bind the king,
and let the accused their answer bring.

the steam pot 1679 ce france denis papin built his steam digester — a rattling pressure cooker carrying the future of engines. papin sealed his iron pot
and let the pressure build and hot.
the digester rattled, hissed, and sang —
the future in its clanging rang.
i watched the steam lift lid and bone,
and knew the age of iron had grown.
a pressure cooker, small and loud,
would one day move the merchant crowd.

the jizya returns 1679 ce india aurangzeb reimposed the jizya tax on non-muslims, and the mughal empire's old tolerance began to crack. aurangzeb brought back the tax —
non-muslims paid, the old cracks
widened in the empire's wall.
tolerance began its fall.
i watched the hindus count their coin,
the empire's seams begin to join
in anger. what akbar's wisdom won,
his great-grandson came to undone.

the pueblo revolt 1680 ce north america pope led the pueblo peoples in revolt, driving the spanish from santa fe for twelve years. pope raised the pueblos as one hand
and drove the spanish from the land.
twelve years santa fe stood free —
the desert's own democracy.
i walked the mesa, heard the drums,
the oldest freedom story comes:
a people rising, staff in hand,
to take back water, sky, and land.

bernini's farewell 1680 ce italy gian lorenzo bernini died in rome — the sculptor who made marble breathe and stone fly. bernini laid his chisel down
in the eternal, marble town.
he made the stone fly, made it weep —
colonnades that seem to sweep
the faithful in. i touched the stair
he carved, and felt him standing there.
the sculptor who made marble breathe
left rome a city none can leave.

the holy experiment 1681 ce north america william penn founded pennsylvania as a colony promising religious freedom to all comers. william penn took his woodland grant
and built the colony they'd haunt —
quakers, germans, all who'd pray
in their own unfettered way.
i walked the streets of brotherly love
before the name fit like a glove.
religious freedom, bought with trees —
penn's holy experiment in the breeze.

the king's canal 1681 ce france the canal du midi opened, joining the atlantic to the mediterranean across southern france. they cut a water-road of stone
from sea to sea, through france alone.
the canal du midi ran its course —
no sail, no wind, just level force.
i rode a barge from end to end
and watched the southern vineyards bend.
two oceans joined by human hands:
the boldest ditch in all the lands.

louisiana claimed 1682 ce north america la salle reached the mississippi's mouth and claimed the entire vast basin for louis xiv. la salle paddled to the river's mouth
and claimed it all for louis — south
to the gulf, and north to snow,
the whole vast basin's ebb and flow.
i heard him name it louisiane
beneath a hot louisiana sun.
a continent claimed with a planted flag —
an empire bought in a leather bag.

the siege of vienna 1683 ce austria the ottomans besieged vienna until polish lancers broke them at the kahlenberg — and europe exhaled. the ottoman tents ringed vienna round,
their drums the city's only sound.
then sobieski's lancers broke the hill —
the kahlenberg ran red, and still
the gates held. europe breathed at last;
the crescent's high tide had passed.
i stood upon the broken wall
and watched an empire start to fall.

the croissant legend 1683 ce austria legend says viennese bakers invented the crescent roll to mock the defeated ottoman crescent — victory you can eat. they say the bakers shaped the dough
into the crescent's overthrow —
a crescent roll to mock the foe,
and eat the victory, row by row.
i bit one in a viennese cafe,
flaky and golden, light as day.
if legends lie, the taste is true:
breakfast remembers waterloo.

taiwan falls 1683 ce china qing admiral shi lang conquered taiwan, completing kangxi's china from the steppe to the sea. shi lang sailed with the qing fleet west
and put taiwan's ming hold to the test.
the island fell; kangxi's domain
ran from the steppe to the southern rain.
i watched the junks return in pride —
an empire's reach grown ocean-wide.
china's map was whole again,
from desert dune to tropic rain.

the theorist of harmony 1683 ce france jean-philippe rameau was born in dijon — the organist who would write the rulebook of western harmony. in dijon town a babe was born
who'd write the rules the chords are sworn:
rameau, the organist of law,
who found the harmony's own flaw
and fixed it. chords have roots, he said —
and music raised its learned head.
i heard his treatise change the game:
the rulebook bore a frenchman's name.

watteau is born 1684 ce france antoine watteau was born — the painter of fetes galantes, elegant parties that never quite happened. a child of valenciennes that year —
watteau, who'd paint the parties dear:
fetes galantes in the evening air,
lovers who were never there.
i wandered through his painted park
and felt the daylight lose its spark.
beautiful, fleeting, slightly sad —
the happiest paintings ever had.

the revocation 1685 ce france louis xiv revoked the edict of nantes, and hundreds of thousands of huguenots fled — carrying their skills abroad. louis tore the edict down that fall;
the huguenots fled, one and all.
by hundred thousands they took flight —
silk, watchmaking, banking's light —
to london, berlin, amsterdam's shore,
enriching every foreign door.
i watched them go with packs and tears:
france bled its best for twenty years.

two geniuses born 1685 ce germany bach and handel were born weeks apart in germany — one for the church organ, one for the world's stage. weeks apart, in german towns,
two babies wore no royal crowns —
bach for the organ's sacred air,
handel for the world's affair.
i held the century in my hand
and heard the future fill the land:
two lives, one year, the music's height —
twin stars igniting in one night.

scarlatti is born 1685 ce italy domenico scarlatti was born in naples — the keyboard acrobat who would write 555 sonatas. in naples town the keys were blessed —
domenico scarlatti, manifest
with 555 sonatas in him,
an acrobat on every whim.
i heard his fingers fly and leap,
the keyboard waking from its sleep.
no hand before had dared so much:
the future lived in his light touch.

the catholic king 1685 ce england james ii took the throne; monmouth's rebellion was crushed at sedgemoor, and the bloody assizes hanged the rest. james took the throne, the catholic heir;
monmouth rose, and met despair
at sedgemoor field. the assizes ran —
judge jeffreys hanged the common man.
i watched the bloody assizes' toll:
the gallows claimed both heart and soul.
a king who'd rule by rome's command
soon lost the scepter of the land.

the thermometer's father 1686 ce germany daniel fahrenheit was born in danzig — the man who would put numbers on hot and cold. in danzig born, a merchant's son —
fahrenheit, when all was done,
would put numbers on hot and cold,
and make the weather's story told.
i held his glass with mercury's gleam
and watched the silver column dream.
before him, heat was guess and feel;
he made the temperature real.

the conductor's cane 1687 ce france lully struck his own foot with his conducting staff; the wound festered, and france's musical dictator died of gangrene. lully beat time with a heavy staff,
and struck his foot — no time to laugh.
the wound went bad, the gangrene spread;
france's musical dictator dead.
i stood beside the maestro's bed
and heard the court's last whisper said:
the man who ruled the sun king's song
was gone — the silence twice as long.

the glorious revolution 1688 ce england william of orange landed, james ii fled, and parliament remade the monarchy — the glorious revolution. william landed at torbay's shore;
james dropped the seal and fled for more.
no battle fought, the crown made new —
parliament took its measure true.
i watched the king slip through the night,
the thames receiving seal and flight.
bloodless, almost — history's sleight:
the people won without a fight.

oroonoko 1688 ce england aphra behn, england's first professional woman writer, published the antislavery tale oroonoko. aphra behn — spy, playwright, pen —
wrote of oroonoko, noblest men
enslaved, betrayed, in suriname's heat.
england's first professional woman's feat.
i read her tale with a burning shame —
she named the slave trade's sin by name.
before the abolition's cry,
one woman's pen asked england why.

the coffeehouse of ships 1688 ce england edward lloyd's coffeehouse became the sailors' and insurers' haunt — the seed of lloyd's of london. at edward lloyd's the sailors came
to drink, to talk, to play the game:
insure the hulls, insure the crew,
and lloyd's of london slowly grew.
i sat among the captains' din —
the coffee strong, the wagers in.
a coffeehouse of ships and charts
became the market of all hearts.

the poet is born 1688 ce england alexander pope was born in london — the sickly boy who would sharpen english verse to a razor's edge. a sickly catholic boy that year,
in london born — pope, small, severe.
he'd sharpen english verse to edge,
each couplet honed, each rhyme a wedge.
i watched him grow, the twisted frame,
the mighty mind, the burning flame.
the smallest poet of the age
would set the standard for the page.

the grandmother's counsel 1688 ce china the empress dowager xiaozhuang died — the steady grandmother's hand behind kangxi's throne. xiaozhuang died, the steady hand
behind the throne of all the land.
kangxi's grandmother, wise and true,
had guided what the young must do.
i stood before her quiet tomb
and felt the passing of the room:
the counsel gone, the emperor grown —
china's fate was his alone.

the bill of rights 1689 ce england parliament's bill of rights barred catholic kings and standing armies — the contract that made monarchs answerable. parliament wrote it, line by line:
no catholic king, no standing line
of soldiers at the monarch's call —
the contract binding one and all.
i watched them sign with steady hands
the law that leashed the crown's commands.
monarchs answerable, subjects free —
the paper roots of liberty.

locke's two treatises 1689 ce england john locke's two treatises argued governments exist only by the people's consent — the pamphlet that would arm two revolutions. locke wrote: governments exist
by consent — resist, resist!
the people's will, the social trust —
kings rule by leave, or turn to dust.
i carried copies through the town,
each page a stone to bring kings down.
the pamphlet that would arm the free
in boston and in paris' sea.

nerchinsk 1689 ce china china and russia signed the treaty of nerchinsk, drawing a siberian border with jesuits translating between empires. on siberia's frozen ground,
two empires drew their border's bound.
jesuits translated, word by word,
the treaty that the steppes had heard.
i watched them sign in the cold air —
china and russia, then and there.
the first great treaty, east to west,
put empires' quarrels to the test.

peter takes power 1689 ce russia peter the great seized the throne from his sister sophia and began dragging russia toward the sea. young peter seized the throne from kin —
his sister's regency wore thin.
he'd drag old russia to the sea,
to ships, to guns, to being free
of moscow's ancient, bearded ways.
i watched him through those early days:
a giant with an axe in hand,
remaking an entire land.

the narrow road 1689 ce japan basho set out on his long walk to japan's deep north; the travel diary became japan's most beloved journey. basho shouldered his walking pack
and set out north — no looking back.
the narrow road to the deep north's cold
became the journey ever told.
i walked beside him, step by step,
through mountain passes where snows wept.
japan's most beloved travel diary:
a poet's road, extraordinary.

locke's essay 1690 ce england locke's essay argued the mind is a blank slate — experience writes everything on it. the mind's a blank slate, locke declared —
experience writes, and none is spared.
no innate truths, no royal mind —
we're made by what we see and find.
i read the essay through the night
and felt the old dogmas lose their light.
if all are blank at birth, then all
may rise — or none may ever fall.

the boyne 1690 ce ireland william iii smashed james ii at the boyne — a battle irish protestants would commemorate for three centuries. william's army crossed the boyne that day;
james's cause was swept away.
the protestants would march for years
about this field of hopes and fears.
i stood upon the river's bank
and watched the orange banners flank.
three centuries of marching feet —
one battle neither side'd repeat.

calcutta founded 1690 ce india job charnock planted the east india company's flag on the hooghly mudflats — a trading post that became an empire's capital. job charnock planted on the mud
the flag that'd rule with iron and blood.
the hooghly's banks, a trading post —
an empire's capital, at most.
i walked the marsh where huts were few
and saw what merchants' dreams could do:
a city rising from the slime
to rule a subcontinent in time.

salem's trials 1692 ce north america hysteria gripped salem village; twenty were executed for witchcraft before the colony came to its senses. the girls accused, the judges burned
with holy fear; the town unturned
its reason. twenty met their end
on gallows hill — no true friend.
i watched the trials, sick at heart,
as neighbor tore neighbor apart.
hysteria's fever, cruel and grim —
salem's shame still haunts the dim.

port royal sinks 1692 ce caribbean an earthquake dropped jamaica's pirate haven of port royal into the sea — half the city drowned in minutes. the earth shook and the sea rushed in;
half of port royal drowned in sin —
or so the preachers said that day.
the pirate haven sank away.
i watched the water take the street,
the taverns where the rogues would meet.
in minutes, gone — the wickedest town
the caribbean sea would drown.

william and mary 1693 ce north america a royal charter founded the college of william and mary in virginia — the south's first seat of learning. a royal charter, signed and sealed —
virginia's scholars took the field.
the college rose, the south's first seat,
where learning and the planters meet.
i walked the yard in later years
and heard the founding hopes and fears.
the second college in the land
was built by a king's own hand.

the bank 1694 ce england the bank of england was founded to fund a war with france — and it has never stopped funding things since. to fund a war with france's king,
they built a bank — a curious thing.
the bank of england took its stand
and lent the crown a helping hand.
i watched the gold flow in and out,
the paper promises about.
three centuries and running strong —
the bank that funded right and wrong.

voltaire is born 1694 ce france francois-marie arouet was born in paris — voltaire, the sharpest pen the enlightenment would ever hold. francois-marie arouet — the name
the world would shorten into flame:
voltaire, the sharpest pen of all,
who'd make the mighty fear and fall.
i heard his first cry in the night
and knew the dark would fear the light.
the enlightenment's own sword and shield
was born — and tyrants learned to yield.

basho's last verse 1694 ce japan matsuo basho died on the road in osaka, leaving haiku that fit the whole world into seventeen syllables. he died upon the road in fall,
in osaka — the last call.
seventeen syllables, the whole world wide:
sick on a journey, dreams still ride.
i knelt beside the master's bed
and heard the final words he said.
the haiku master, traveling still —
the road goes on, beyond the hill.

purcell's farewell 1695 ce england henry purcell died at thirty-six; england buried its greatest composer in westminster abbey. thirty-six years, and the music stopped —
purcell's bright candle simply dropped.
they buried him in the abbey's shade,
england's greatest ever made.
i heard his anthems fill the air
one final time, beyond compare.
dido's lament still breaks the heart —
the master played his final part.

sor juana's silence 1695 ce mexico sor juana ines de la cruz, the nun-scholar of new spain, died — her library sold off, her voice stilled by the church. the nun of new spain, the scholar's light —
sor juana's pen was burning bright
till the church demanded her library sold,
her voice stilled, her wisdom cold.
i stood before her empty cell
and heard the silence ring its bell.
the greatest mind the colony knew
was hushed — but not before she grew.

tiepolo is born 1696 ce italy giovanni battista tiepolo was born in venice — the last great painter of ceilings full of sky. in venice born, the ceiling's king —
tiepolo, who'd make the heavens sing.
the last great painter of the sky,
whose clouds would lift the viewers high.
i watched him as a boy at play,
not knowing what his brush would say:
whole cathedrals full of air,
the baroque's final, bright affair.

canaletto is born 1696 ce italy canaletto was born in venice; his crisp canal scenes would hang in every english country house. another venice child that year —
canaletto, crystal-clear.
his canals would hang in english halls,
the grand tour's prize on country walls.
i walked beside the painted tide
and saw the city open wide:
every brick, each ripple's gleam —
venice preserved inside a dream.

hogarth is born 1696 ce england william hogarth was born in london — the engraver who would roast the city's gin, greed, and rakes. in london born, the engraver's son —
hogarth, who'd roast them one by one:
the gin, the greed, the rakes, the lot,
each print a sermon, sharp and hot.
i watched him sketch the city's sin
with a grin both out and in.
the moralist with the satirist's art —
he drew the city, heart to heart.

tales of mother goose 1697 ce france charles perrault published his fairy tales — cinderella, sleeping beauty, puss in boots — and childhood got its classics. perrault wrote them, one by one —
cinderella's shoe, the sleeping one,
puss in boots with his clever purr:
childhood's classics, told for her.
i read them to the children near
and watched their eyes grow wide with fear
and wonder. fairy tales took flight —
the nursery gained its own delight.

the grand embassy 1697 ce russia peter the great toured europe in disguise, working as a ship's carpenter to learn how navies are built. peter traveled in disguise that year,
a carpenter's apprentice, far from fear.
he learned to build the ships of war
in holland's yards, on england's shore.
i watched the giant plane the wood,
the tsar who'd make his country good.
a king who'd work with his own hands
to lift the future of his lands.

ryswick 1697 ce europe the treaty of ryswick ended nine years of war; louis xiv kept strasbourg and swallowed the slight. nine years of war came to its end
at ryswick, where the powers penned
the peace. louis kept strasbourg's towers
and swallowed all the lesser hours.
i watched the diplomats depart —
a continent with a lighter heart.
the war was done, the treaties signed;
the next one waited, close behind.

the miner's friend 1698 ce england thomas savery patented a steam pump to drain mines — the first engine sold to do work with fire and water. savery's pump, with fire and steam,
drained the mines — the miners' dream.
the first engine sold to work the deep,
where water made the tunnels weep.
i watched the piston rise and fall,
the iron heart that'd change it all.
fire and water, harnessed tight —
the steam age dawning in the night.

the khalsa 1699 ce india guru gobind singh founded the khalsa at anandpur — baptized sikhs in steel bracelets and uncut hair, sworn to justice. at anandpur, the guru called —
gobind singh, with justice walled
in steel: the khalsa, baptized true,
bracelets bright and hair uncut through.
i watched them take the sacred vow,
the sword and spirit joined somehow.
sworn to protect the weak and right —
the lion's brotherhood of light.

karlowitz 1699 ce balkans the treaty of karlowitz rolled back the ottomans; hungary returned to christendom after a century and a half. the treaty signed at karlowitz town
rolled the ottoman tide back down.
hungary returned to christian hands
after a century and a half's demands.
i watched the borders redrawn in ink —
an empire's fortunes start to sink.
the crescent's reach began to wane;
the cross reclaimed its old domain.

the childless king dies 1700 ce spain charles ii of spain died heirless, and every crown in europe reached for his empire. charles the second breathed his last,
no heir to hold the empire fast.
every crown in europe's hall
reached out to catch the spanish fall.
i stood beside the empty throne
and heard the continent's low moan.
a kingless empire, vast and wide —
the vultures circled, open-eyed.

narva 1700 ce baltic charles xii of sweden routed peter's army at narva in a blizzard — the boy-king's most dazzling victory. in a blizzard's blinding, swirling white,
charles of sweden won the fight.
peter's army broke and fled —
the boy-king's glory widely spread.
i watched the snow turn red with war,
the dazzling victory, the gore.
narva's name would ring for years —
the triumph bought with soldiers' tears.

a kingdom in prussia 1701 ce germany the elector of brandenburg crowned himself king in prussia — a small title with enormous ambitions. at konigsberg, the elector took
the crown — a small title, by the book,
but with enormous hunger's fire.
prussia's king, the new desire.
i watched the coronation's gleam —
a minor prince's major dream.
that little crown would grow and grow
till europe learned what prussians know.

the golden stool 1701 ce west africa osei tutu united the asante beneath the golden stool, and a gold-rich kingdom rose in the forest. osei tutu raised the golden stool —
the asante's sacred, binding rule.
the forest kingdom, rich in gold,
united under one strong hold.
i watched the stool descend from sky
(in legend's telling, none know why).
a nation forged in gold's bright gleam —
the stool's the soul, or so they dream.

the pirate hanged 1701 ce england captain kidd was hanged at wapping for piracy — the treasure-hunter turned into a cautionary tale. captain kidd swung at wapping's dock —
the treasure-hunter met the clock.
from privateer to pirate's fate,
the gallows sealed the sailor's date.
i watched him dance the hempen jig
while london's crowds stood watching big.
a cautionary tale in rope:
the sea gives gold, but takes all hope.

yale founded 1701 ce north america connecticut ministers founded a college at new haven to keep the ministry orthodox — it became yale. connecticut ministers, stern and true,
founded a college, small but new —
to keep the ministry orthodox
in new haven's sturdy box.
i walked the green in later days
and saw it grow in worldly ways.
yale was born of pious fear;
the ivy'd tower'd soon appear.

the act of settlement 1701 ce england parliament settled the crown on protestant heirs — the law that still chooses britain's monarchs. parliament settled, firm and plain:
the crown to protestant heirs remain.
the law that still, through centuries,
chooses britain's royalties.
i read the act with a thoughtful eye —
a dynasty's future, by and by,
decided not by sword or birth
alone, but law's enduring worth.

sowing in straight lines 1701 ce england jethro tull invented the seed drill, sowing in neat rows instead of scattering — farming's quiet revolution. jethro tull built his seed drill true —
in neat rows, not scattered through.
no more the broadcast, wild and wide;
the seeds in ordered lines abide.
i watched the furrows, straight and deep,
where future harvests learned to sleep.
farming's quiet revolution:
order's seed, and earth's solution.

queen anne 1702 ce england anne took the throne — the last stuart, gouty, grieving seventeen lost children, and stubborn as an oak. anne took the throne, the last stuart line —
gouty, grieving, by design
stubborn as oak, with seventeen lost,
she paid the motherhood's high cost.
i watched her court, the favors swirled,
the last queen of the stuart world.
she'd see the union, war, and art —
and carry england in her heart.

news every morning 1702 ce england the daily courant became england's first daily newspaper — news every morning, forever after. the daily courant hit the street —
news every morning, fresh and fleet.
no more the weekly's patient wait;
the daily paper sealed our fate.
i bought the first, the ink still wet,
and placed a very certain bet:
the world would never be the same —
the morning news became the game.

the spanish succession war 1702 ce europe france and the grand alliance went to war over spain's empty throne — a world war before the world knew the phrase. france and the grand alliance clashed
for spain's empty throne — war smashed
across the continent and sea,
a world war before the phrase would be.
i marched with armies, watched them fall,
the first true global brawl of all.
empires bled for a vacant chair —
the cost was more than kings could bear.

st. petersburg 1703 ce russia peter founded his new capital on a baltic swamp — a window to the west built on bones. peter raised his city on the swamp —
a window west, a northern camp.
the bones of workers paved the way;
the neva's marshes saw the day.
i walked the streets not yet complete,
the mud still clinging to my feet.
a capital from nothing made —
the tsar's ambitious, bold parade.

the great storm 1703 ce england the worst storm in british history sank fleets and flattened towns; daniel defoe rode out to interview the survivors. the worst storm in the island's lore —
it sank the fleets and shook the shore.
towns flattened, ships gone down,
defoe rode out from town to town
to interview the ones who lived.
i felt the wind, the terror sieved
through every heart. the tempest's roar
was like no storm they'd seen before.

the forty-seven 1703 ce japan forty-seven ronin avenged their murdered lord, then accepted death — loyalty's most famous arithmetic. forty-seven ronin, sworn and true,
avenged their lord — the deed they drew
through winter's snow to the final breath,
then accepted honorable death.
i watched them in the falling snow,
their loyalty's unyielding glow.
the most famous arithmetic of all:
forty-seven answered honor's call.

blenheim 1704 ce germany marlborough and eugene smashed the french at blenheim, saving vienna and shattering louis xiv's aura of invincibility. marlborough and eugene joined that day
and swept the french command away.
vienna saved, the myth undone —
louis's invincibility was gone.
i stood upon the bloodied field
where france was forced at last to yield.
blenheim's name rang through the land:
the tide had turned by england's hand.

a tale of a tub 1704 ce england jonathan swift's savage satire on religious excess appeared — anonymous, brilliant, and never forgiven. swift's savage satire, sharp and sly,
on religious excess — oh my!
anonymous, brilliant, never forgiven,
it cut the church like a knife from heaven.
i read it laughing, wincing too —
the truth it told was far from new.
the dean would wield his bitter art
till satire broke the reader's heart.

the insect painter 1705 ce suriname maria sibylla merian published her great book on suriname's insects — a woman artist-scientist alone in the tropics. maria merian sailed alone
to suriname's tropic zone —
an artist-scientist, brave and free,
to paint the insects' mystery.
i watched her in the jungle's heat,
her brushwork delicate and sweet.
a woman's eye, a scholar's hand:
she mapped the small world's wonderland.

the comet's return 1705 ce england edmond halley predicted the great comet of 1682 would return in 1758 — staking his name on the sky's schedule. halley staked his name that year:
the comet would return — no fear —
in 1758, on schedule's grace,
the sky would keep its measured pace.
i watched him calculate the arc,
the numbers glowing in the dark.
he'd be long dead, but still he'd win —
the heavens keep their discipline.

ramillies 1706 ce belgium marlborough routed the french at ramillies, and the spanish netherlands fell like dominoes. marlborough routed france that spring;
the spanish netherlands took wing
and fell like dominoes in line.
the allied cause began to shine.
i watched the cavalry's grand sweep,
the french in full and fast retreat.
ramillies' field, the victory's song —
the war would not be very long.

the union 1707 ce britain england and scotland united into great britain — one parliament, one flag, and endless argument. england and scotland joined as one —
great britain's flag, the work begun.
one parliament, one common crown,
and endless argument renown.
i watched them sign with ink and quill,
two nations bending to one will.
the union's birth, both proud and sore —
a marriage argued evermore.

aurangzeb's long twilight 1707 ce india aurangzeb died at eighty-eight in the deccan, his empire at its largest — and already cracking apart. eighty-eight years, the emperor died
in the deccan, far and wide.
his empire at its largest spread —
and cracking even as he bled.
i stood beside the simple grave —
no marble tomb for one so brave
in war, so harsh in peace's art:
the empire broke with his heart.

the galleon that sank 1708 ce caribbean the san jose exploded off cartagena, carrying a king's ransom in silver down to the seabed. the san jose went down in flame
off cartagena — none to blame
but war. a king's ransom deep
in silver found its ocean sleep.
i watched her sink beneath the wave,
the treasure in its watery grave.
three hundred years, the divers dream
of silver in the gulf stream.

poltava 1709 ce russia peter crushed charles xii at poltava; sweden's empire ended, and russia's began. peter crushed the swedish king that day;
charles's empire slipped away.
at poltava's field, the north was won —
russia's empire had begun.
i watched the boy-king's star descend,
the russian giant on the mend.
sweden's glory, bright and brief —
the north wind brought a new belief.

the great frost 1709 ce europe the coldest winter in living memory froze rivers, split trees, and starved a continent. the coldest winter ever known —
rivers froze to solid stone.
trees split with a cannon's crack;
the starving poor looked vainly back.
i walked the ice where ships had been
and saw the famine's gaunt and grin.
a continent in winter's hold —
the great frost, bitter, deep, and cold.

malplaquet 1709 ce france the bloodiest battle of the age: the allies won the field at malplaquet and lost their stomach for the war. the bloodiest battle of the age —
the allies won the field, the rage
of war had spent their stomach's fire.
they'd won the day, but lost desire.
i walked the field where thousands lay,
the price of glory, come what may.
a victory that felt like loss:
war's triumph nailed upon its cross.

white gold 1710 ce germany meissen cracked the secret of hard porcelain — europe could finally make its own china. at meissen, they cracked the secret true —
hard porcelain, white as morning dew.
europe could make its own fine china,
no more the eastern trade's arena.
i held the cup, so thin and light,
the "white gold" gleaming in the light.
a chemist's dream, a king's delight —
the porcelain age was burning bright.

st. paul's crowned 1710 ce england wren's st paul's cathedral was finished, its dome rising where the great fire's ashes fell. wren's great dome rose to the sky
where the fire's ashes used to lie.
st. paul's was finished, stone by stone —
london's phoenix, not alone.
i climbed the whispering gallery's height
and looked on london in the light.
the city risen from the flame
would never be the same again.

handel lands 1710 ce england george frideric handel arrived in london, and would give england its anthems, oratorios, and water music. george frideric handel came to town —
london's music wore his crown.
anthems, oratorios, water's song —
the city's heart would sing along.
i heard his first notes fill the hall
and knew the greatest of them all
had come to make the thames resound:
handel's england, newly found.

the south sea company 1711 ce england the south sea company was chartered to trade with spanish america — and mostly to gamble on it. chartered to trade with spanish gold,
the south sea company's story told
of gambling more than honest trade —
a bubble in the making, made.
i watched the shares begin to climb,
the frenzy building over time.
the promise shone, the prospect gleamed —
but it was never what it seemed.

the spectator 1711 ce england addison and steele launched the spectator, teaching london how to be witty and polite over coffee. addison and steele took up the pen
to teach the town's good women and men
to be witty, polite, and refined —
over coffee, well-designed.
i read each issue, fresh and bright,
the essays sparkling in the light.
london learned to laugh and think —
the spectator's charm, in ink.

the atmospheric engine 1712 ce england thomas newcomen's steam engine started pumping at a staffordshire mine — the industrial revolution's first breath. newcomen's engine pumped that year
in staffordshire — the miners' cheer.
steam and iron, fire and air:
the industrial revolution's first breath there.
i stood beside the clanking frame
and felt the world would not be same.
the engine breathed, the piston drove —
the age of steam began to move.

utrecht 1713 ce europe the treaty of utrecht ended the great war; britain took gibraltar, nova scotia, and the slave-trade contract. the treaty signed, the great war done —
britain had won, and france had none
of its old glory. gibraltar's rock,
nova scotia, and the slave-trade stock.
i watched the diplomats agree —
the map of empires, plain to see.
peace at last, but at what cost?
the human ledger, tempest-tossed.

corelli's silence 1713 ce italy arcangelo corelli died in rome — the violinist whose concertos taught europe how strings should sing. corelli died in rome that year —
the violinist, ever dear,
whose concertos taught the strings to sing
with an almost sacred, holy ring.
i heard his christmas concerto play
one final time on that sad day.
the master of the violin's art
had played his way into the heart.

the longitude prize 1714 ce england parliament offered £20,000 to whoever could find longitude at sea — the richest puzzle in navigation. twenty thousand pounds the prize —
for him who'd chart the sailor's skies
and find the longitude at sea.
the richest puzzle there could be.
i watched the dreamers take their aim,
each hoping for the lasting fame.
the sea would keep its secret well
till harrison broke the ocean's spell.

the first german king 1714 ce england george i of hanover took the throne, speaking little english and trusting his ministers — parliament's quiet gain. george of hanover took the throne,
speaking little english, all alone
among his ministers' english ways.
parliament gained in those quiet days.
i watched him at the court's first ball,
the german king, so strange to all.
the crown grew distant, power near —
the ministers' ascendancy was here.

the sun sets 1715 ce france louis xiv died after seventy-two years on the throne; france was glorious, exhausted, and bankrupt. seventy-two years upon the throne —
louis the great, now left alone.
france was glorious, spent, and broke;
the sun king's final, fading smoke.
i watched them carry him away,
the grandest monarch of the day.
the palace shone, the coffers bare —
an empire's end hung in the air.

the treasure fleet wreck 1715 ce caribbean a hurricane scattered spain's treasure fleet off florida; divers and pirates raced each other for the silver. a hurricane scattered spain's fleet wide
off florida's stormy, sandy tide.
divers and pirates raced the wave
for silver in its watery grave.
i watched them dive in the churning sea,
each hoping rich as kings to be.
the ocean keeps what storms have tossed —
the treasure fleet forever lost.

the fifteen 1715 ce scotland jacobites rose for the exiled stuarts; the rebellion fizzled, but the songs last forever. the jacobites rose for the exiled line —
the fifteen's cause, the stuart sign.
the rebellion fizzled, cold and brief,
but left the songs of love and grief.
i heard the pipes on the highland air
and felt the doomed and brave despair.
the songs would last when swords were still:
the stuart dream on every hill.

law's bank 1716 ce france john law founded his bank in paris, and paper money's grandest experiment began. john law founded his bank that year —
paper money's grand frontier.
the grandest experiment of all:
would paper rise, or would it fall?
i watched the notes fly hand to hand,
the mississippi's promised land.
the dream was bright, the scheme was vast —
but paper bubbles never last.

water music 1717 ce england handel's water music drifted down the thames behind the king's barge — the river became a concert hall. handel's music drifted down the thames,
behind the king's bright royal gems.
the river became a concert hall —
the barges answered music's call.
i floated in a boat nearby
and heard the horns go sailing by.
the water music, light and free —
london's night of jubilee.

the grand lodge 1717 ce england four london lodges united as the first grand lodge — freemasonry stepped into the open. four london lodges joined as one —
the grand lodge's work begun.
freemasonry stepped in the light,
with aprons, secrets, and rite.
i watched them in their quiet hall,
the brethren answering the call.
a brotherhood of stone and square —
the craft's new age was in the air.

blackbeard falls 1718 ce north america lieutenant maynard cornered blackbeard at ocracoke; the pirate died with five shots and twenty sword-cuts in him. maynard cornered him at ocracoke's shore —
blackbeard fought with twenty cuts or more,
five shots within his mighty frame,
before he fell to the lieutenant's aim.
i watched the pirate's final stand,
the cutlass falling from his hand.
the terror of the atlantic main
would never sail the seas again.

new orleans founded 1718 ce north america bienville founded new orleans on a mississippi crescent — a french port in a swamp of mosquitoes. bienville planted on the crescent's bend
a french port where the rivers wend.
new orleans rose from swamp and mire,
a city built on bold desire.
i walked the muddy, nascent street
where french and spanish fates would meet.
the crescent city's humble start —
a swamp with music in its heart.

robinson crusoe 1719 ce england daniel defoe published the castaway's tale — the novel england will never stop reading. defoe published the castaway's tale —
crusoe's shipwreck, friday's hail.
the novel england never'd cease
to read: of solitude and peace.
i read it in a single night,
the island's lonely, long delight.
the first true novel, some would say —
a castaway who found his way.

the bubble bursts 1720 ce england the south sea bubble popped; fortunes vanished in a week, and the whole mad game was outlawed. the south sea bubble popped that fall;
fortunes vanished, one and all.
in a single week, the mad game done —
the whole wild gamble overrun.
i watched the brokers tear their hair,
the ruined lords in blank despair.
the lesson writ in ink and pain:
what rises fast will fall again.

the women pirates 1720 ce caribbean anne bonny and mary read stood trial in jamaica — pirates who fought as fiercely as any man, and said so in court. anne bonny and mary read stood trial —
pirates both, with fearless style.
they fought as fiercely as any man,
and said so boldly, as they can.
i watched them in the courtroom's glare,
defiant, proud, beyond compare.
the women pirates' tale was told —
braver than the brave and bold.

nystad 1721 ce baltic the treaty of nystad ended the great northern war; russia was an empire now, and sweden a memory of one. the treaty signed at nystad's shore —
the great northern war no more.
russia an empire, proud and free;
sweden a memory of what'd be.
i watched the borders redrawn anew,
the baltic's power shifting true.
an age had ended, one begun —
the northern star had found its sun.

the last pirate king 1722 ce west africa bartholomew roberts, the most successful pirate of the age, died in battle off africa — the golden age of piracy died with him. bartholomew roberts met his end
off africa — no more to fend
the navy's guns. the golden age
of piracy closed its final page.
i watched him fall in battle's heat,
the most successful, most complete
of pirate kings. his flag came down —
the jolly roger lost its crown.

the giant dies 1725 ce russia peter the great died at fifty-two, leaving russia an empire, a navy, and a city raised from a swamp. peter the great breathed his last —
fifty-two years, the die was cast.
an empire, a navy, a city grand
raised from the swamp by his own hand.
i stood beside the giant's bier
and felt the loss, both far and near.
russia wept for the tsar who'd made
her great — the price his people paid.
end of volume iv — continued in volume v.

the cantor's thousand songs 1725 ce leipzig, germany bach in leipzig, writing a new cantata nearly every week — music his own congregation barely noticed, though the traveler did. i was there in the thomaskirche loft,
a nobody with ink on his cuffs,
watching a tired man with failing eyes
hand out new music like it was nothing —
a fresh cantata, every single week,
as regular as bread, as wild as prayer.
the choir boys grumbled at the hard parts,
the congregation half-asleep in the pews,
and none of them knew. i knew.
he was writing for god and for nobody,
a thousand songs poured out like rain
on a town too small to hold them,
and the whole of heaven leaning in to listen.

the academy of the north 1725 ce st. petersburg, russia peter the great's academy of sciences opens in st. petersburg, and russia starts studying the world in earnest. peter's dead, but his school stands tall —
stone walls raised on the frozen neva's shore.
he sent for scholars from every land,
told them: teach my russia to understand.
no more groping blind through priest and czar —
measure the stars, and name them where they are.
i walked those halls the winter they began,
and watched a sleeping giant turn, and plan.

gulliver's wild voyage 1726 ce london, england jonathan swift publishes gulliver's travels, and london laughs at tiny emperors and giant fools without seeing itself in the mirror. swift sold them a traveler's tale,
of little kings and giants hale —
and london roared at every page,
not seeing its own face in the rage.
i sat in the coffeehouse and heard them cheer
the lilliput court's affairs so dear,
each minister a strutting ape,
each war a quarrel over which end to break an egg's shape.
they laughed at gulliver's mad crew,
and never guessed the joke was you.

the young printer comes home 1726 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania twenty-year-old benjamin franklin returns from london to philadelphia, broke but burning to make his mark. he stepped off the boat with empty pockets
and a head full of london's noise —
twenty years old, ink under his nails,
hungry the way only the young are hungry.
i watched him walk the philadelphia streets,
already measuring every shop and sign,
already planning. the colonies didn't know
what had just sailed home to them:
a printer's devil with a thunderstorm inside.

the man who weighed the stars, laid to rest 1727 ce london, england isaac newton is buried in westminster abbey like a king, and the age of reason mourns the man who gave it its laws. they buried him like a king in westminster,
this quiet man who weighed the sun and stars
and found the numbers wouldn't lie.
i stood among the mourners in the abbey
and thought of all he'd set in motion —
the apple, the moon, the tides obeying
one law written across the sky.
the age of reason lowered its father down
into english earth, and wept,
because we all knew: there would not be another.

the housewife's book 1728 ce london, england eliza smith publishes the compleat housewife, a book of recipes and remedies for every working kitchen in england. while the philosophers argued god,
eliza smith wrote down the dinner.
stew it slow. skim the fat.
mend the wound with this poultice.
i held her book in a working kitchen
and smelled the truth of it:
empires rise on the backs of women
who know which herb heals the fever.

the sailor who found the strait 1728 ce kamchatka, russia vitus bering sails the icy strait between asia and america and puts it on the map. i sailed with bering into the fog,
a dane in russian service, stubborn as ice.
the strait was there — nobody knew for sure —
a cold gray seam between two worlds.
we threaded it in the endless arctic light,
waves slapping, men half-frozen at the rails,
and put it on the map: asia here,
america there, the water between.
empires would fight over that line someday.
we just found it, and shivered, and turned home.

the printer's gazette 1729 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania franklin buys a struggling philadelphia newspaper and turns it into the colonies' sharpest voice. he bought a failing paper for a song
and sharpened it like a butcher's knife.
franklin's gazette cut at governors,
mocked the pious, praised the plain —
the colonies' boldest voice,
set in type by the boldest printer alive.
i read it fresh off the press,
ink still wet, and thought: this town
will never be quiet again.

the terrible joke that told the truth 1729 ce dublin, ireland swift's modest proposal suggests starving irish families sell their children as food — a savage joke that shames england's real cruelty. eat your children, swift said.
he said it with a straight face,
in perfect logic, in perfect prose —
the irish are starving, so let the rich
dine on the poor's own sons.
i watched dublin read it and go pale,
because the joke was not a joke:
england was already devouring them,
just slower, and with better manners.
the cruelest sentence ever written,
and every word of it true.

the potter who made the world beautiful 1730 ce staffordshire, england josiah wedgwood is born in staffordshire, the boy who will turn common clay into art and build a fortune on it. in the potteries' smoke a boy was born
who'd make the whole world set a finer table.
josiah wedgwood — clay on his hands,
experiments in his kiln, a fortune in his head.
queens would drink from his blue-and-white,
and common folk would eat off beauty too.
i held one of his plates years later
and thought: this is what a life's for —
taking common earth and firing it into grace.

the library that opened its doors 1731 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania franklin and his friends pool their private books to found america's first lending library. they had no money for books, so they pooled them —
fifty men, each bringing what he owned,
shelving their private shelves together
so anyone could read them all.
franklin's junto, a library born of friendship.
i borrowed a volume there myself,
smelling of pipe smoke and binding glue,
and understood: this is how a new country learns —
not from kings, but from neighbors sharing pages.

the boy born on the farm 1732 ce virginia, british america george washington is born on a virginia plantation, the first son of a modest planter — nobody dreaming what he will become. on a virginia plantation, in a plain farmhouse,
a boy was born to a middling planter —
no gold spoon, no great name,
just red-brown hair and a tall man's frame.
i held no crystal to see his future;
nobody at his christening dreamed
that this squalling infant, george by name,
would one day turn down a crown
and walk away from power like it was nothing.

poor richard's almanac 1732 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania franklin begins publishing poor richard's almanac, a yearly book of weather, jokes, and proverbs for plain country folk. early to bed and early to rise
makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.
god helps them that help themselves.
fish and visitors stink in three days.
franklin dressed as poor richard sold the farmers
weather, wit, and proverbs by the thousand —
plain wisdom in plain words,
the kind you pin above the hearth.
i read those pages and laughed out loud:
the colonies' first philosopher wore a joke for a mask.

the shuttle that flew 1733 ce lancashire, england john kay's flying shuttle doubles the weaver's speed — the machines begin to quicken, and nothing will slow them down. john kay's shuttle flew across the loom,
faster than any hand could throw it —
and the weavers cursed his name
because the machines had begun to quicken.
i watched the threads fly double-time
and felt the ground tilt under england:
this was the first breath of the factory age,
and no king's army could stop what a shuttle started.

the fire on st. john 1733 ce st. john, danish west indies enslaved africans seize the island of st. john and hold it for months before the planters crush them. they rose in the cane fields of st. john —
enslaved africans with machetes and torches —
and took the island, held it for months,
free men on stolen ground.
i saw the smoke from a passing ship,
black columns against the caribbean blue.
the planters came back with soldiers and hanged them all,
but for one bright season the enslaved were masters,
and the fire they lit would not go out —
it would burn again, and again, until the chains broke.

the preacher in the wilderness 1734 ce massachusetts, british america jonathan edwards' thundering sermons set new england ablaze with the great awakening. jonathan edwards thundered from the pulpit
and new england caught fire.
sinners in the hands of an angry god —
his voice rolled over the frontier towns
like a storm off the mountains.
i sat in the back of a packed meetinghouse
and watched farmers weep and children tremble,
the great awakening shaking every pew.
love him or fear him, you couldn't sleep through him —
he made heaven and hell feel one breath away.

the man who named every living thing 1735 ce uppsala, sweden carl linnaeus publishes systema naturae, giving every plant and animal its two latin names. linnaeus looked at the chaos of creation
and gave it order: two names for everything.
homo sapiens. rosa canina. felis catus.
latin labels, neat as a ledger,
so a botanist in uppsala and one in batavia
could speak of the same flower.
i walked his garden among the pressed specimens
and marveled: one man, naming the living world,
leaf by leaf, beast by beast, as if taking attendance
for the whole of god's green earth.

the young emperor takes the throne 1735 ce beijing, china the qianlong emperor takes the throne in beijing, beginning sixty years of china's greatest wealth and power. a young man ascended the dragon throne
and china entered its golden age —
sixty years of wealth and power,
granaries full, borders quiet, poets paid.
qianlong, they called him: the emperor
who would out-reign them all.
i walked the beijing markets in those early years,
silk and tea and porcelain piled high,
and thought the middle kingdom might stand forever.
forever, as always, turned out to be shorter than it looked.

the fire company 1736 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania franklin founds the union fire company — neighbors banding together with buckets against the flames. when the fire bell rang, they came running —
not soldiers, not the king's men,
just neighbors with buckets and ladders.
franklin's union fire company:
the first to the flames gets the glory,
and everybody's house is everybody's business.
i stood in the bucket line one winter night,
passing water hand to hand through the smoke,
and learned what america would be built on —
not crowns, but neighbors who show up.

the clock that found the way 1736 ce london, england john harrison's sea clock survives its ocean trial, promising sailors their true position at sea at last. sailors died lost at sea for want of one thing:
knowing the time, far from land.
john harrison built a clock that could —
brass and springs that kept true time
through storm and rolling wave.
i watched it survive its ocean trial,
ticking steady while the ship pitched and groaned,
and thought of all the drowned men
who'd never needed to die.
the sea had a clock now. the sea had mercy.

the opera house falls silent 1737 ce london, england bankrupt and broken in health, handel abandons italian opera and turns toward the oratorio. bankrupt. broken in health. the italian opera —
his grand, expensive dream — collapsed around him.
handel gave it up and turned his face
toward the oratorio, toward scripture set to music.
i was there the night the opera house went dark,
the singers dismissed, the costumes sold —
and i wanted to tell him: the best is coming.
messiah is coming. the hallelujah is coming.
sometimes ruin is just the door to glory.

the heart strangely warmed 1738 ce london, england john wesley's conversion at aldersgate chapel launches the methodist movement. at a quarter to nine on a may evening,
in a chapel on aldersgate street,
john wesley felt his heart strangely warmed —
and methodism was born.
not in a cathedral, not by decree,
but in one man's chest, on an ordinary night.
i stood outside and heard the singing start,
plain voices raised in plain words,
and watched a movement walk out into the streets
that would circle the globe on horseback and prayer.

the salons where ideas caught fire 1738 ce paris, france in candlelit paris drawing rooms, brilliant hostesses set philosophers arguing and all paris listening. by candlelight, in drawing rooms of silk,
the cleverest women in paris held court —
and philosophers came to argue at their feet.
voltaire sparred, diderot dreamed aloud,
while the hostess poured the wine and steered the wit.
i sat in the corner, invisible, delighted:
here was the enlightenment at play,
ideas catching fire between the courses,
all paris listening through the keyhole of a salon door.

the drums at stono 1739 ce south carolina, british america enslaved men rise at stono, south carolina, marching for freedom in spanish florida before they are cut down. they rose at stono on a september sunday,
twenty men with stolen guns,
drumming as they marched for spanish florida —
for freedom, for a life of their own.
the militia cut them down within the day,
heads on stakes along the road.
i heard the drums before i saw the smoke.
it lasted hours. it cost everything.
but every enslaved soul in carolina heard those drums,
and freedom had a sound now — it had a beat.

the hospital for lost children 1739 ce london, england captain coram wins his royal charter for a hospital to shelter london's abandoned babies. captain coram had seen them on the streets —
babies left in doorways, in gutters, in the snow —
and he would not look away.
seventeen years he begged and argued,
until the king signed the charter at last.
i stood in the courtyard on opening day
and watched the first abandoned infants
carried in from the cold.
london had a thousand cruelties;
this was the day it built one mercy.

the flute-playing king 1740 ce berlin, prussia frederick the great takes the prussian throne — a flute-playing warrior who will forge prussia into a great power. he took the throne with a flute in his hand
and a philosopher's library in his head —
then marched his armies out and never stopped.
frederick the great: warrior by day,
musician by night, writing verses between battles.
i heard him play once, in a lamplit room at potsdam,
delicate as lace — and the next morning
watched him drill his grenadiers like a machine.
prussia would be forged in that strange fire:
art and iron, the flute and the cannon, one man.

the young queen who would not bow 1740 ce vienna, austria twenty-three-year-old maria theresa inherits the austrian empire, and every neighbor reaches for a piece of it — but she will not bow. twenty-three years old, a woman, alone —
and every neighbor in europe reached for her empire
like wolves at a lamb.
maria theresa would not bow.
she rode out, she bargained, she fought,
she held the habsburg lands together by sheer will.
i saw her in vienna that first hard year,
young and grieving and absolutely unbreakable,
and understood: some thrones are held
not by armies, but by refusing to fall.

the voyage that cost the captain his life 1741 ce alaska, russian america bering sights alaska, then dies of scurvy on the barren island that will bear his name. he found alaska through the fog and mist —
new land, new coast, the prize of his life —
and died of scurvy on the way home,
on a barren island that would bear his name.
i was aboard when bering breathed his last,
the captain who'd mapped the strait
buried in russian soil at the edge of the world.
the sea gives, and the sea takes;
he gave his life for a coastline on a chart,
and the island keeps his name forever.

the seed drill's quiet revolution 1741 ce berkshire, england jethro tull dies, leaving the seed drill that taught farmers to sow in straight, thrifty rows. no battles, no trumpets — just straight rows.
jethro tull died in berkshire, little-mourned,
leaving behind a machine that sowed seed
in neat, thrifty lines instead of scattered handfuls.
i walked a drilled field at harvest time
and saw the difference: order where waste had been,
more wheat from the same earth.
the quietest revolution ever made —
a farmer's gadget that would help feed the world.

the hallelujah that shook the hall 1742 ce dublin, ireland handel's messiah premieres in dublin, and legend says the king himself stood for the great hallelujah chorus. they say the king stood for the hallelujah —
whether legend or truth, i was there in dublin
when those first great chords rolled out,
and the whole hall rose like a wave.
handel, bankrupt five years before,
had written heaven into music in three weeks.
i wept with the strangers beside me.
some music entertains; this music
reached down and lifted every soul in the room
straight up through the roof.

the thermometer's new tongue 1742 ce uppsala, sweden anders celsius proposes his hundred-degree scale, and heat learns to speak in numbers. zero for freezing. one hundred for boiling.
anders celsius gave heat a language —
a hundred degrees from ice to steam,
so a doctor in uppsala and a sailor in batavia
could speak of fever in the same numbers.
i watched him demonstrate it in his laboratory,
the mercury climbing the glass like a promise:
the world was becoming measurable,
and mystery was learning to count.

the red-haired boy of monticello 1743 ce virginia, british america thomas jefferson is born in virginia — the awkward boy who will write the words of a revolution. an awkward red-haired boy was born in virginia,
all elbows and questions, never quite fitting in —
the kind of child who reads when others play
and argues with the teacher just to see.
thomas jefferson. i saw him as a boy
taking apart a broken lock to learn its secret,
and i thought: this one will take apart bigger things.
kingdoms, for instance. the whole order of the world.
he'd write the words of a revolution
in handwriting nobody could quite read.

the last king to lead his men 1743 ce bavaria, germany george ii charges at dettingen — the last british monarch to lead his troops into battle. at dettingen, old george the second
drew his sword and rode into the cannon smoke —
the last british king to lead his troops in battle.
his horse bolted; he fought on foot,
waving his men forward like a common officer.
i watched from the ridge as the old man charged,
and felt the age turn: never again
would a king risk his skin beside his soldiers.
after that day, monarchs commanded from maps —
and something brave went out of kingship.

the girl who grew blue gold 1744 ce south carolina, british america twenty-two-year-old eliza lucas perfects indigo in south carolina, dyeing her colony's fortune blue. she was twenty-two, running her father's plantations
while he stayed in england, a girl with ledgers and nerve.
eliza lucas tried indigo seed after seed —
failure, failure, then blue.
blue gold: the dye that colored the colony's fortune,
flooded the markets, built the great houses.
i walked her indigo fields at harvest,
the air sharp with the vats, the workers' hands stained blue,
and marveled at this young woman
who'd grown an empire's wealth from a seed packet.

the prince who came home 1745 ce scotland, britain bonnie prince charlie lands in scotland, and the highlands rise for the stuarts one last time. bonnie prince charlie landed in the mist,
a young stuart with a claim and a smile,
and the highlands rose for him —
tartan and claymore, the old songs sung again.
i marched a little way with that gay army,
all hope and bagpipes, bound for london
they would never reach.
it was the last rising of the clans,
a bonfire of loyalty in the northern rain —
beautiful, doomed, and gone within the year.

the seamstress who ruled the court 1745 ce versailles, france jeanne poisson becomes madame de pompadour — the king's mistress and the maker of french taste. jeanne poisson, a banker's daughter —
clever, charming, impossibly polished —
caught the king's eye and never let it go.
madame de pompadour: the uncrowned queen of versailles,
maker of french taste, patron of the arts,
the power behind the gilded throne.
i watched her hold court in silks and diamonds,
every artist in france bowing for her favor,
and thought: here is power in its strangest dress —
a seamstress's daughter ruling the grandest court on earth.

the last battle on british soil 1746 ce scotland, britain at culloden the jacobite dream dies in the rain, and the highland clans are broken forever. rain. mud. the highland charge broken on british cannon.
at culloden the jacobite dream died in an hour,
and the clans were broken forever —
the tartan banned, the pipes silenced, the chiefs scattered.
i walked the field afterward among the dead,
young men in plaids lying in the scottish rain,
and felt a whole way of life go quiet.
bonnie prince charlie fled to the hills;
scotland would never rise again.

a college rises in the pines 1746 ce new jersey, british america the college of new jersey is founded in the wilderness — the school that will become princeton. in the new jersey wilderness, among the pines,
a few ministers raised a college —
the college of new jersey, humble as a barn,
teaching latin and scripture to farm boys.
i sat in on a lesson there that first winter,
breath fogging in the unheated room,
and never dreamed this rough school
would become princeton, proud and ivied —
but seeds don't look like trees, do they?

the cook who wrote it down 1747 ce london, england hannah glasse's art of cookery teaches england's kitchens to roast, bake, and feast. hannah glasse never ran a grand kitchen —
she just wrote down what every good cook knew,
plain and clear: roast it thus, bake it so.
her art of cookery taught england to feast,
from the squire's table to the tradesman's board.
i cooked from her book in a london kitchen,
flour on my sleeves, following her plain directions,
and the dinner came out perfect.
empires need philosophers; kitchens need hannah glasse.

the book that taught kings to fear 1748 ce paris, france montesquieu's spirit of the laws argues that liberty lives only where power is divided. montesquieu wrote that liberty lives only
where power is divided — king against parliament,
judge against minister, each watching the other.
the spirit of the laws: a quiet book,
no barricades, no blood — just an idea
that would frighten every throne in europe.
i read it in a paris bookshop,
and watched a young lawyer copy passages by hand,
his eyes bright. ideas are slow gunpowder;
this one would blow up the century.

the peace that pleased no one 1748 ce aachen, germany the treaty of aix-la-chapelle ends a war and satisfies nobody — planting the seeds of the next one. they signed the peace at aix-la-chapelle
and nobody went home happy —
the diplomats bowed, the maps were redrawn,
and every king began planning the next war before the ink dried.
i walked the treaty halls afterward,
all marble and muttering,
and felt the whole thing for what it was:
a pause, not a peace. a held breath.
the seeds of the next war were planted that day,
watered with everyone's disappointment.

the rake's wild ride 1749 ce london, england henry fielding's tom jones makes the novel the people's art — funny, bawdy, and full of life. tom jones came roaring off the press —
bawdy, funny, bursting with life —
and the novel became the people's art.
fielding wrote of rakes and rogues and good hearts
in trouble, and all england devoured it.
i read it in a coffeehouse, laughing out loud,
milk-sellers and lords alike bent over their copies.
no more heroes on pedestals;
