this was life as it was lived — messy, merry, human.

the thinker in the tower 1749 ce paris, france diderot is locked in vincennes for his daring writings, and all paris takes his side. they locked diderot in vincennes
for daring to think in print —
and all paris took his side.
the prison made him famous;
the bars made his ideas louder.
i visited the tower town and heard the talk:
cab drivers quoting him, ladies defending him,
the whole city buzzing like a kicked hive.
lock up a thinker and you advertise him —
france learned that lesson in a stone cell.

the farewell of the cantor 1750 ce leipzig, germany bach dies in leipzig, blind and half-forgotten; his music will sleep for eighty years before the world wakes to it. he died blind, half-forgotten,
the great bach of leipzig —
the town buried him and moved on,
and his music slept for eighty years.
eighty years of silence for the thousand songs.
i stood at his plain grave and wanted to shout
at the whole forgetful century:
you buried the greatest of us in an unmarked plot!
but time would wake the world to him —
mendelssohn would find the scores, and the sleeping giant would rise.

the unknown who scolded civilization 1750 ce dijon, france an unknown rousseau wins a prize for asking whether progress has corrupted mankind. an unknown entered the essay contest at dijon
and asked the rude question:
has progress corrupted mankind?
rousseau — nobody had heard the name —
won the prize and scolded civilization to its face.
i read his essay in a crowded salon
and watched the fine folk squirm:
their silks, their sciences, their polished manners —
all of it, he said, had made men worse, not better.
the age of reason had just been insulted by its own son.

the book that held all knowledge 1751 ce paris, france diderot's encyclopedie begins to appear volume by volume, blessing and scandalizing france. volume by volume, it began to appear —
diderot's encyclopedie, all human knowledge
between covers, blessed by some, burned in effigy by others.
priests denounced it; philosophers wept with joy.
i held the first volume, heavy as a brick,
and turned its pages: arts, sciences, trades —
the whole world explained, in alphabetical order.
france would try to stop it and fail;
you can't unprint an idea whose time has come.

the bell that would ring for freedom 1751 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania a great bell is hung in philadelphia's state house tower, not yet knowing the name it will one day earn. they hung a great bell in the state house tower —
bronze and hopeful, ordered from london —
not yet knowing the name it would one day earn.
i stood beneath it the day it was raised,
its first dull testing note rolling over philadelphia,
and felt nothing special. just a bell.
but bells outlive the hands that hang them,
and this one was waiting for its moment —
twenty-five years off, in a hot july,
when it would ring a new nation into being.

the kite in the thunderstorm 1752 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania franklin flies his kite in a thunderstorm and proves lightning is electricity — taming the sky's fire. he flew a kite into a thunderstorm —
silk, string, and a brass key —
and when the lightning came down the line
and the key sparked in his hand,
franklin laughed: the sky's fire was electricity,
tameable, knowable, his.
i watched from a safe distance, soaked to the skin,
as the most famous kite in history
proved the heavens ran on the same stuff
as a rubbed amber rod.
after that day, men would bottle lightning.

the year that lost eleven days 1752 ce london, england britain adopts the new calendar, and sleepers wake to find eleven days simply gone. britain adopted the new calendar that year,
and sleepers woke to find eleven days simply gone —
september the 2nd followed by september the 14th,
as if time itself had skipped.
riots, they say — give us back our eleven days!
i walked the london streets in the confusion,
landlords and tenants arguing over rent,
saints' days vanished, birthdays displaced.
the strangest theft in history:
the government stole eleven days, and nobody could get them back.

the museum for everyone 1752 ce london, england the british museum is founded, opening its treasures to any curious visitor, free of charge. the british museum opened its doors —
not to lords, not to scholars only,
but to any curious visitor, free of charge.
mummies, manuscripts, marble gods:
the world's treasures for the price of showing up.
i wandered those first galleries
among clerks and seamstresses staring wide-eyed
at things they'd only dreamed of.
knowledge had left the private library;
it belonged to everyone now.

the young officer in the wilderness 1753 ce ohio country, british america twenty-one-year-old washington carries a warning through the winter snows to the french forts. twenty-one years old, in the dead of winter,
washington carried a warning through the snows
to the french forts on the ohio —
a boy officer on a man's errand, half-frozen, undaunted.
i tracked with him through that white wilderness,
rivers half-ice, forests endless,
and watched him deliver his message like a veteran.
the french read it and smiled politely.
nobody smiled for long: that winter errand
was the first step toward a world war.

the first shot of a world war 1754 ce ohio country, british america washington's men fire on french soldiers at jumonville glen — the first shot of a world war. at jumonville glen, in the morning mist,
washington's men fired on french soldiers —
a skirmish in a pennsylvania forest,
and the empires took notice.
i heard that first ragged volley
and felt the earth tilt: this was no border quarrel.
within two years the whole world would be at war —
europe, america, india, the seas between —
all from one shot fired by a young virginian
who couldn't have been more surprised than the french.

a king's college in new york 1754 ce new york, british america a college chartered by the king opens in new york — the seed of what will become columbia. a college chartered by the king opened its doors
in new york — king's college, loyal and anglican,
teaching the sons of merchants their latin.
i attended a lecture in its first term,
eight students in a borrowed room,
and thought it a small enough beginning.
small beginnings: this little loyal school
would become columbia, and outlive the king
whose name it bore by two centuries and counting.

the day the earth shook the faith 1755 ce lisbon, portugal an earthquake swallows lisbon on all saints' day, and philosophers ask how a good god allows it. on all saints' day the earth rose up and swallowed lisbon —
churches full of worshippers crushed in their prayers,
the sea rushing in to finish what the quake began.
tens of thousands dead in a morning.
i walked the ruins as the fires burned,
and heard the question on every lip:
how does a good god allow this?
voltaire would ask it in print;
the priests had no good answer.
faith itself cracked that day, along with the cathedral walls.

the book of words 1755 ce london, england samuel johnson's dictionary fixes the english language between two covers — nine years in the making. nine years, alone, in a garret —
samuel johnson fixed the english language
between two covers: the dictionary.
forty thousand words, defined with wit and growling common sense.
oats: a grain, which in england is generally given to horses,
but in scotland supports the people.
i watched him finish the last page,
this shambling giant of a man,
and hand the language its mirror.
every word we speak still walks through his book.

the child who heard music in everything 1756 ce salzburg, austria wolfgang amadeus mozart is born in salzburg, and music will never be the same again. in salzburg a child was born
who heard music in everything —
wolfgang amadeus mozart, and the world
would never sound the same again.
at five he was composing; at six, performing for emperors.
i heard him play as a boy, tiny hands flying,
and the room went silent the way rooms do
before a miracle.
he had thirty-five years. he filled them
with more beauty than ten lifetimes.

the war that swallowed the world 1756 ce europe the seven years' war erupts — the first war fought on nearly every continent and ocean. it started in europe and swallowed the world —
the seven years' war, fought on nearly every continent,
on every ocean: america, india, africa, the seas.
prussia against austria, britain against france,
and a million dead before it ended.
i walked battlefields from quebec to bengal,
the same war wearing different uniforms,
and understood: this was the first world war,
a rehearsal for the century of slaughter to come.

the battle that bought an empire 1757 ce bengal, india clive wins at plassey, and a mere trading company begins to swallow a subcontinent. at plassey, robert clive's small army
broke the nawab's great host —
by bribery as much as battle —
and a mere trading company began to swallow a subcontinent.
i stood on that field in the bengal heat
and watched the east india company
become something no company had ever been:
a ruler of millions, with ledgers for laws.
an empire bought at a battle,
paid for in other men's blood.

the knife that missed the king 1757 ce paris, france damiens scratches louis xv with a penknife and is torn apart for it, to voltaire's horror. damiens scratched louis xv with a penknife —
a scratch, no more — and for that
they tore him apart in the public square,
horses and hot irons, to voltaire's horror.
i turned away from the scaffold;
some things a traveler should not watch.
but paris watched, and remembered,
and thirty years later the crowd
would take its revenge on kings
with a neater machine.

the comet that kept its appointment 1758 ce the heavens halley's comet returns on schedule — proof that the heavens run like clockwork. halley was dead, but his comet kept the appointment —
it came blazing back on schedule,
right when the dead man said it would.
proof, written across the sky in fire,
that the heavens run like clockwork.
i stood in a field with the astronomers that winter night,
watching it climb, and felt the ground shift under reason:
if a man could predict a comet's return,
what else in the universe might be knowable?

the fortress that fell 1758 ce nova scotia, british america the british take louisbourg, breaking french sea power in the atlantic. louisbourg: france's great atlantic fortress,
stone walls and cannon against the sea —
and the british took it, siege by grinding siege.
i watched the walls crumble under the bombardment,
the french flag come down in the smoke.
with louisbourg fell french sea power in the atlantic;
the road to quebec lay open,
and an empire's fate turned on a fortress
at the edge of a cold northern sea.

the battle on the plains 1759 ce quebec, new france wolfe and montcalm both die before quebec, and canada passes to britain. on the plains of abraham, in fifteen minutes,
two generals died and an empire changed hands.
wolfe, shot through, lived just long enough
to hear the french were running;
montcalm, dying in quebec, whispered his relief
that he would not live to see the surrender.
i walked that field at dusk, the dead of two nations
lying in the same grass,
and canada passed to britain while the sun went down.

the laugh that mocked the world 1759 ce geneva, switzerland voltaire's candide skewers priests, philosophers, and optimists in one merry tale. voltaire wrote candide in three days —
a merry tale that skewered priests, philosophers,
and optimists in one laughing stroke.
this is the best of all possible worlds, said pangloss,
as the disasters piled up around him.
i read it in geneva and laughed until i wept,
then wept a little at the truth of it:
the world is not the best of anything,
but a garden we must tend ourselves.

the fire of tacky 1760 ce jamaica, british west indies tacky leads enslaved rebels in jamaica's great uprising; the planters drown it in blood. tacky led them up from the plantations —
hundreds of enslaved africans, torches in hand —
and jamaica burned in its greatest uprising.
for weeks they fought through the cane fields,
free men taking back their lives with fire.
the planters drowned it in blood in the end,
as planters always did.
i saw the smoke from kingston harbor,
black against the green hills,
and knew: every chain forged
is a rebellion waiting for its day.

the young king takes the crown 1760 ce london, england george iii ascends at twenty-two, determined to rule as well as reign. george iii ascended at twenty-two,
a serious young man, determined to rule as well as reign —
no more letting ministers run the kingdom
while the king looked the other way.
i watched the coronation crowds in london,
all hope and bunting, and thought:
here is a decent man with a heavy crown,
and ahead of him the loss of america
and a long slow slide into madness.
the crown is a weight no head was built to bear.

the slaughter at panipat 1761 ce india ahmad shah durrani crushes the marathas at panipat in one of history's bloodiest days. at panipat the armies met like oceans —
ahmad shah durrani against the marathas —
and the field drank blood all day,
one of the bloodiest days in history.
a hundred thousand dead, the maratha power broken,
the road to british india left wide open.
i walked that field when the vultures had finished,
and the silence was the loudest thing i'd ever heard.
empires are built on days like this,
and nobody who sees one ever forgets the smell.

the day the world watched the sun 1761 ce the heavens astronomers across the globe time venus crossing the sun to measure the size of the heavens. astronomers scattered across the globe —
from siberia to the cape of good hope —
all timed venus crossing the face of the sun,
to measure the size of the heavens themselves.
i stood with one expedition in the cold dawn,
watching the little black dot crawl across the fire,
and felt the whole human race
doing science together for the first time:
one question, one sky, a hundred telescopes.

the german princess who became russia 1762 ce st. petersburg, russia catherine seizes the throne from her feeble husband and begins her long, brilliant reign. a german princess seized the throne from her feeble husband —
no blood on her own hands, just a coup in the night —
and became catherine the great of russia.
she would reign for thirty-four years,
write laws, build schools, collect art,
and make russia a power europe had to reckon with.
i saw her in the winter palace that first year,
brilliant and utterly in command,
and thought: the feeble husband never had a chance.

the book that said man is born free 1762 ce paris, france rousseau's social contract declares that rightful rule rests on nothing but the people's will. man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains —
rousseau wrote it, and the social contract
declared that rightful rule rests on nothing
but the people's will.
no divine right. no ancient custom.
just the agreement of the governed.
i read it in paris and watched young men
copy the dangerous sentences by hand.
within thirty years those words
would be painted on banners and barricades,
and kings would learn to fear a book.

the peace that redrew the map 1763 ce paris, france the treaty of paris ends the world war; france loses an empire and britain gains one. the treaty of paris ended the world war:
france lost an empire, britain gained one —
canada, india, the seas, all changing hands
in a gilded paris room.
i watched the diplomats sign away continents
like merchants settling accounts,
and thought of the soldiers dead in a dozen lands
for lines drawn with a quill.
the map was new. the resentments were old.
france would not forget; america would not stay grateful.

the chief who said no 1763 ce great lakes, british america pontiac's warriors rise against the british forts, and the frontier burns from detroit to the ohio. pontiac said no.
when the british took the french forts and treated
the tribes like conquered subjects,
the ottawa chief raised the nations —
and the frontier burned from detroit to the ohio.
i traveled that burning country in the summer of the rising,
forts besieged, supply lines cut,
and saw what the british would learn slowly:
this land had owners, and they were not done fighting.
the rising failed. the warning stood.

the jenny that spun eight threads 1764 ce lancashire, england hargreaves' spinning jenny lets one worker spin eight threads at once. one worker, eight threads at once —
hargreaves' spinning jenny multiplied hands like magic.
the spinners smashed the machines, of course;
they always do, at first.
i watched a jenny work in a lancashire cottage,
wheels turning, thread flying,
and did the arithmetic of the future:
eight threads, then sixteen, then eighty —
the factory age arriving one multiplied hand at a time.

the book against the torturer 1764 ce milan, austria beccaria's on crimes and punishments denounces torture and the death penalty. a young milanese wrote against the rack and the noose —
beccaria's on crimes and punishments,
denouncing torture and the death penalty
in calm, reasonable, devastating prose.
punishment should fit the crime, he said,
and never be cruel.
i read it in a milan bookshop and watched
the judges' faces as the idea spread:
within a generation, nations would rewrite their laws,
and the torturer's trade would begin its long decline.

the tax on paper 1765 ce london, england the stamp act taxes every colonial paper and document, and america learns to say no together. parliament taxed every piece of paper —
newspapers, contracts, playing cards, diplomas —
the stamp act, reaching into every colonial pocket.
and america learned to say no together:
boycotts, riots, effigies hanging from liberty trees.
i was in boston when the news arrived,
and watched thirteen quarreling colonies
find one voice for the first time.
a tax on paper taught them
they were one people. the irony was perfect.

the first restaurant opens its doors 1765 ce paris, france boulanger hangs his sign in paris, and the pleasure of dining out is born. boulanger hung his sign in paris —
restoratives, soups to restore the weary traveler —
and the pleasure of dining out was born.
before him: taverns and inns, eat what you're given.
after him: a menu, a choice, a table of your own.
i ate there in the first year, a simple broth,
and never guessed this modest shop
would become the restaurant, the bistro, the cafe —
half of civilization conducted over a paid-for meal.

the invisible fire 1766 ce london, england henry cavendish bottles hydrogen, the lightest stuff in the world, and names it inflammable air. henry cavendish bottled the lightest stuff in the world —
hydrogen, which he called inflammable air —
a gas so light it rose through everything,
invisible, and it burned.
i watched him fill a bladder with it in his laboratory
and hold a flame to the mouth: whoomph.
the age was learning that air was not one thing
but many, each with its secrets.
within twenty years men would fly in it;
within two hundred, they'd split it for the sun's own fire.

the tax repealed, the claim kept 1766 ce london, england parliament repeals the stamp act but declares it may bind america in all cases whatsoever. parliament repealed the stamp act —
the colonists cheered, the bells rang —
but in the same breath declared it could bind america
in all cases whatsoever.
repeal with one hand, a claim of absolute power with the other.
i read the declaratory act in a london coffeehouse
and shook my head: they had learned nothing.
you cannot tell free men you own them
and expect gratitude for lifting one tax.
the next fight was already loading.

the empress who wrote the law 1767 ce st. petersburg, russia catherine's nakaz instructs her lawmakers in enlightenment, and all europe reads it. catherine wrote the nakaz — her instruction —
to guide her lawmakers in enlightenment:
equality before the law, proportionate punishment,
torture abolished, serfs treated as human.
all europe read it and applauded.
i held a copy in st. petersburg, beautifully printed,
and admired the words — while outside the palace
the serfs remained serfs, and the knout remained the knout.
the age of enlightened despots in one document:
magnificent principles, and the power to ignore them.

the taxes on tea and glass 1767 ce london, england the townshend acts tax colonial imports, and boycotts spread from boston to charleston. tea, glass, paper, paint —
the townshend acts taxed colonial imports one by one,
and the boycotts spread from boston to charleston.
homespun instead of british cloth;
no tea in the pot but the smuggled kind.
i walked through boston's empty warehouses that winter
and saw the merchants' ledgers bleeding red.
britain was taxing a people
who had already decided they were not subjects.
the harbor would answer soon enough.

the ship that sailed for the stars 1768 ce plymouth, england cook's endeavour departs to watch venus cross the sun, then to hunt the great southern continent. the endeavour sailed from plymouth
to watch venus cross the sun —
a scientific errand, officially —
then to hunt the great southern continent,
unofficially, and claim what it found.
cook: the finest navigator of the age,
with banks the botanist beside him.
i stood on the plymouth hoe as the sails shrank,
and felt the old thrill: a ship bound past the edge of the map,
carrying science, empire, and doom in one hull.

the first circus 1768 ce london, england philip astley opens his riding ring in london, and the modern circus is born. philip astley opened his riding ring in london —
horses, riders, tumblers, clowns —
and the modern circus was born.
no kings, no priests, no philosophy:
just wonder, for the price of a ticket.
i sat in the sawdust seats that first season,
cheering with the crowd as the riders stood
on galloping horses' backs,
and thought: humanity needs this —
a place where the impossible is the whole point.

the separate condenser 1769 ce glasgow, scotland james watt patents his improved steam engine, and the world begins to run on steam. james watt stared at a wheezing steam engine
and saw the waste in it — the cylinder
heated and cooled, heated and cooled —
and invented the separate condenser.
a small change. a world change.
i watched him test it in a glasgow workshop,
the engine breathing easy at last,
and understood: the world was about to run on steam,
and this quiet scotsman had just handed it the key.

the mill that never slept 1769 ce lancashire, england arkwright's water frame spins thread by waterpower, and the factory age dawns. arkwright's water frame spun thread by waterpower —
day and night, never tiring, never sleeping —
and the factory age dawned on a lancashire riverbank.
i stood in the roar of that first mill,
the frames clattering, the water thundering,
children tending machines taller than themselves.
the cottage was finished; the factory had begun.
no one there that day could imagine
what those mills would make — and unmake.

the snow, the shots, the five dead 1770 ce boston, massachusetts british soldiers fire on a boston mob; five lie dead, and the colonies have their martyrs. snow on king street. a jeering crowd.
british soldiers, nervous, outnumbered —
then the shots, and five men down in the snow.
crispus attucks first: a free black man,
the first to die for american liberty.
i was there in the cold, and heard the volley,
and saw boston turn those five dead
into martyrs overnight.
the colonies had their blood now;
there is no going back after blood.

the storm-child of bonn 1770 ce bonn, germany ludwig van beethoven is born in bonn — the boy who will make music roar like thunder. in bonn a boy was born to a drunkard father
and a hard childhood — ludwig van beethoven,
who would make music roar like thunder.
deaf by middle age, he heard it all inside:
symphonies no ear but his would ever truly hear.
i watched him as a boy, pounding the keys
through his father's beatings,
and thought: suffering is forging something here —
a storm with a human face, and music as its lightning.

the scottish book of everything 1771 ce edinburgh, scotland the first encyclopaedia britannica is completed — three stout volumes of useful knowledge. three stout volumes, printed in edinburgh —
the first encyclopaedia britannica,
all useful knowledge, a to somewhere past b.
(it would take a century to finish the alphabet.)
i bought a set from a bookseller on the high street,
heavy as bricks, smelling of fresh ink,
and lugged them home like treasure.
the scots had decided knowledge should be orderly,
portable, and sold by subscription.

the slave who sued for freedom 1772 ce london, england lord mansfield's somerset ruling frees an enslaved man and shakes the whole slave trade. james somerset was enslaved in virginia,
brought to england, and ran —
and when his master seized him for jamaica,
he sued for his freedom in an english court.
lord mansfield ruled: slavery had no basis in english law.
one man walked out of that courtroom free,
and the whole slave trade shuddered.
i was in the gallery when the judgment came down,
and watched the planters' faces go white:
their empire of chains had just met the law.

the country carved like a cake 1772 ce poland russia, prussia, and austria carve up poland among themselves in the first partition. russia, prussia, and austria sat down together
and carved up poland like a cake —
a slice for each, no permission asked,
the first partition of a living nation.
i was in warsaw when the news came,
and watched a country learn it had been divided
by its neighbors' dinner conversation.
poland would be carved twice more,
then vanish from the map entirely —
the century's lesson in what happens
when your neighbors are hungry and you are not strong.

the tea in the harbor 1773 ce boston, massachusetts disguised as mohawks, bostonians heave british tea into the harbor. disguised as mohawks, with hatchets and nerve,
the bostonians boarded the tea ships at night
and heaved three hundred chests into the harbor.
the tea steeped; the harbor turned brown;
britain turned purple with rage.
i watched from the wharf as the chests splashed,
the crowd cheering each one,
and knew: this was no protest anymore.
this was a people daring an empire to do its worst.

the enslaved poet of boston 1773 ce london, england phillis wheatley's poems are published in london — genius in chains that shames her masters. her poems were published in london —
phillis wheatley, enslaved in boston,
writing verses in the style of the ancients
that shamed her masters with their brilliance.
genius in chains. i read her book
and thought of the lie it killed:
that the enslaved had no minds worth freeing.
every line she wrote was an argument
no auction block could answer.

the library of ten thousand books 1773 ce beijing, china qianlong commands the siku quanshu, gathering all chinese learning into one vast library. qianlong commanded it: gather all chinese learning
into one vast library — the siku quanshu,
tens of thousands of volumes, copied by hand,
the greatest book project on earth.
but the emperor's scholars also burned
what the emperor disliked: thousands of books
declared dangerous, gone forever.
i walked the copying halls in beijing,
brushes scratching in unison,
and saw the double edge of it:
the greatest library ever built,
and the greatest book-burning beside it.

the congress that dared to meet 1774 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania delegates from twelve colonies gather in philadelphia to answer britain with a single voice. twelve colonies sent their delegates to philadelphia —
farmers, lawyers, merchants, firebrands —
to answer britain with a single voice.
they had quarreled for a century; now they agreed on one thing:
no.
i sat in the gallery of carpenters' hall
and watched america invent itself in a room,
one speech at a time.
the congress dared to meet; the meeting
dared to become a nation.

the sorrows of the young romantic 1774 ce weimar, germany goethe's werther makes heartbreak fashionable, and young men weep across europe. goethe wrote of young werther's hopeless love,
and europe wept itself sick over him —
young men dressed like werther, talked like werther,
and some, god help them, died like werther.
i read it in weimar and watched the fever spread:
heartbreak had become fashionable,
feeling had become the highest truth.
the romantics were coming, and reason
was about to get a run for its money
from a generation that preferred to swoon.

the shot heard round the world 1775 ce massachusetts, british america at lexington and concord, farmers fire on redcoats, and the war for independence begins. at lexington, at dawn, the redcoats faced the farmers —
someone fired; nobody knows who —
and at concord the farmers fired back,
and the war for independence began.
i heard that shot on the village green,
a crack in the cold morning air,
and felt it travel: across the ocean,
across the century, around the world.
emerson would call it the shot heard round the world,
and he was right — we're still hearing it.

the cossack who crowned himself 1775 ce russia pugachev's great peasant rebellion is crushed, and catherine's age of mercy comes to an end. pugachev the cossack crowned himself emperor —
a pretender with a peasant army —
and half of russia rose: serfs, miners, tribesmen,
burning manor houses from the volga to the urals.
catherine crushed him in the end, of course;
they brought him to moscow in a cage.
i watched the rebellion burn itself out
and saw the empress's age of mercy end with it:
after pugachev, there would be no more gentle reforms,
only the knout, held tighter.

fifty-six names on parchment 1776 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania in a sweltering hall, fifty-six men sign a declaration that all men are created equal. in a sweltering philadelphia hall,
fifty-six men signed their names to treason —
a declaration that all men are created equal,
written by the red-haired virginian,
signed at the risk of every neck in the room.
i watched them step up one by one,
quills scratching, sweat on their brows.
they were signing their death warrants
if the war went wrong — and they knew it.
the boldest signatures in history,
written in the hottest summer of the century.

the book that set the market free 1776 ce london, england adam smith's wealth of nations argues that free hands bake more bread than commanded ones. adam smith argued that free hands
bake more bread than commanded ones —
the wealth of nations, the market's bible:
let men trade, let prices speak,
and the invisible hand will do the rest.
i read it in london the year it appeared
and watched merchants nod along,
already living what smith described.
empires had tried to command prosperity
for a thousand years; smith said: stop commanding.
the world has been arguing with him ever since.

the captain's last voyage 1776 ce plymouth, england cook sails on his third voyage, seeking the northwest passage, never to return. cook sailed on his third voyage,
seeking the northwest passage through the arctic ice —
the great navigator, at the height of his powers,
sailing toward the voyage that would kill him.
i watched the resolution leave plymouth sound,
flags flying, and felt the old foreboding:
the pacific had given him glory twice;
the third time, it would take payment.
he never came home. the sea keeps
its greatest sailors in the end.

the turning of the tide 1777 ce new york, british america burgoyne surrenders at saratoga, and france decides america might win after all. burgoyne surrendered at saratoga —
an entire british army, laying down its arms
in the new york wilderness —
and france decided america might win after all.
i walked that surrender field in october,
redcoats stacking their muskets,
americans trying not to grin too wide.
the war's tide turned that day:
with french ships and french gold coming,
the rebellion became a revolution
the world had to take seriously.

the winter that forged an army 1777 ce pennsylvania, usa at valley forge the continental army starves, freezes, and learns to be soldiers. at valley forge they starved and froze —
no shoes, no coats, no pay, no food —
and learned to be soldiers anyway.
washington held them together by will alone;
von steuben drilled them into an army
in the snow.
i walked that frozen camp in february,
men's feet wrapped in rags, breath white in the air,
and watched a rabble become a force.
nations are not born in declarations;
they are born in winters like this.

the two old lions fall 1778 ce paris, france voltaire and rousseau die within weeks of each other; the enlightenment buries its prophets. within weeks of each other they died —
voltaire, the laughing philosopher, and rousseau,
the scold of civilization, both old lions of the enlightenment.
paris buried its prophets in the same season
it was learning to live without them.
i attended both funerals, and felt the age turn:
the men who'd taught france to think
were gone, and their students were restless.
eleven years later the students
would put the lessons into practice — with a guillotine.

the islands in the middle of the sea 1778 ce hawaii, pacific cook names them the sandwich islands — paradise found at the very heart of the ocean. cook found them at the very heart of the ocean —
green volcanic islands, a paradise
no european had ever seen —
and named them for an english earl: the sandwich islands.
i went ashore with the landing party,
breadfruit and waterfalls, surfers riding the waves,
a people living in abundance.
hawaii. the middle of the sea.
the sailors thought they'd found eden;
eden, as always, would not survive being found.

the captain who did not come home 1779 ce hawaii, pacific in a quarrel over a stolen boat, hawaiians kill cook on the beach at kealakekua. it started over a stolen boat —
a quarrel on the beach at kealakekua,
and ended with captain cook dead in the surf,
the greatest navigator of the age
killed by the people of his paradise.
i was offshore when the news reached the ships,
and watched the crew's disbelief turn to grief.
he had mapped half the pacific;
the pacific kept him.
they buried what the hawaiians returned
at sea, with full honors, in the bay he'd named.

the bridge made of iron 1779 ce shropshire, england the world's first iron bridge rises over the severn — an arch of fire-forged metal. over the severn in shropshire they raised it —
the world's first iron bridge,
an arch of fire-forged metal spanning the river,
built like a giant's meccano, no bolts, just fit.
i walked across it the week it opened,
my boots ringing on iron,
and felt the future under my feet:
stone had ruled for five thousand years;
now iron would carry the world.

the general who sold his name 1780 ce new york, usa benedict arnold's treason is unmasked, and his name becomes the word for traitor. benedict arnold: the bravest officer in the american army,
the hero of saratoga — and he sold it all
for british gold and a general's commission.
the plot failed; his name didn't survive it.
i was in the american camp when the treason broke,
and watched men's faces as they understood:
their hero had been bargaining with the enemy.
arnold escaped. his name became the word for traitor,
in every language that has one.

the siege that ended the war 1781 ce virginia, usa washington and the french trap cornwallis at yorktown, and britain's american war is lost. washington and the french trapped cornwallis at yorktown —
land and sea both closed, the noose tightening
week by week, trench by trench —
until the british marched out and laid down their arms.
i watched the surrender from the american lines,
the band playing (they say) the world turned upside down.
six years of war ended in a virginia field,
and britain's american war was lost.
a new nation had been sieged into existence.

the ship that threw men overboard 1781 ce the atlantic the zong's crew drowns 142 enslaved africans for the insurance money, and england is sickened. the zong was running low on water,
so the crew threw 142 enslaved africans overboard —
drowned them, one by one, for the insurance money.
murder, filed as a cargo claim.
i read the court records in london afterward,
the owners suing the insurers for their lost "goods,"
and felt sick: this was the slave trade
with its mask off, doing arithmetic with lives.
england was sickened too — and the abolitionists
finally had the horror story they needed.

the musician who found a new world 1781 ce bath, england organist william herschel spots uranus — the first new planet in recorded history. william herschel was an organist in bath
who built telescopes in his spare time —
and one march night he spotted uranus,
the first new planet in recorded history.
a musician found a world.
i looked through his great telescope afterward,
at the pale green disk swimming in the eyepiece,
and thought: the sky just got bigger.
for all of human history there were six planets;
now there were seven, because a church musician looked up.

the engine that learned to turn 1782 ce birmingham, england watt patents the rotary steam engine, giving factories a wheel that never tires. watt did it again: the rotary steam engine —
not just pumping up and down anymore,
but turning a wheel, round and round,
a wheel that never tired.
i watched it drive a mill in birmingham,
belts and shafts spinning off that one iron heart,
and saw the whole industrial future in it:
factories, locomotives, ships —
everything that turns, turning because
a scotsman taught steam to go in circles.

the battle that saved jamaica 1782 ce the caribbean rodney smashes the french fleet at the saintes, and britain keeps its sugar islands. rodney smashed the french fleet at the saintes —
broke their line, took their flagship —
and britain kept its sugar islands.
i watched the battle from a frigate's deck,
cannon smoke hiding the sea,
and understood the arithmetic of empire:
jamaica's sugar was worth more than armies,
and this victory kept the sweet trade british.
france's american revenge ended in caribbean water;
the planters slept safe, and the enslaved did not.

the marathas rise again 1782 ce india mahadji scindia forces the british to the peace table at salbai, and maratha power rises again. mahadji scindia forced the british to the peace table at salbai —
the marathas, broken at panipat twenty years before,
rising again to humble the east india company.
i was in the maratha camp during the negotiations,
and watched british envoys learn respect:
india was not yet theirs, not by a long road.
the treaty held for twenty years of peace —
a pause in the long swallowing,
a reminder that the subcontinent had teeth.

the peace that made a nation 1783 ce paris, france the treaty of paris recognizes american independence; a new nation steps onto the stage. in paris they signed it: american independence,
recognized by the king of england himself —
a new nation stepping onto the world's stage,
all thirteen colonies of it, raw and hopeful.
i walked the paris streets that autumn
among celebrating americans,
and thought of the farmers at lexington,
the frozen men at valley forge:
their gamble had paid. the parchment said so.
the experiment was about to begin for real.

the general who laid down his sword 1783 ce annapolis, maryland washington resigns his commission — a victorious general surrendering power of his own will. he could have been king. everyone knew it —
the army would have followed him anywhere.
instead washington walked into congress at annapolis
and resigned his commission,
a victorious general surrendering power of his own will.
i was in the chamber when he laid down his sword,
and heard the silence: kings in europe
were calling it the greatest act of the age.
cincinnatus, come again —
the man who won everything and took nothing.

the brothers who taught fire to fly 1783 ce annonay, france the montgolfiers' hot-air balloon rises over france, and mankind leaves the ground. two paper-makers' sons in annonay
filled a great silk bag with hot air —
and it rose. the montgolfiers' balloon
climbed over france, and mankind left the ground.
i watched that first ascent, the crowd gasping
as the impossible floated upward,
and felt the oldest dream come true:
since icarus, we'd wanted the sky.
now we had it — in a bag, with fire,
for as long as the hot air lasted.

the barber who mocked the count 1784 ce paris, france beaumarchais' marriage of figaro laughs at aristocrats, and revolution laughs with it. beaumarchais wrote a comedy about a barber
who outwits his aristocratic master —
figaro, laughing at counts and privilege —
and all paris laughed with the revolution in its throat.
the king tried to ban it; paris demanded it.
i sat in the theater on opening night,
the audience roaring at every insult to rank,
and thought: this is how it starts —
not with cannon, but with laughter,
the sound of authority losing its dignity.

the oath before the battle 1784 ce paris, france david paints three brothers swearing to die for rome, and the coming revolution finds its favorite picture. david painted three brothers, arms outstretched,
swearing to die for rome —
the oath of the horatii, all straight lines and sacrifice —
and the coming revolution found its favorite picture.
i stood before it in the paris salon,
the crowd thick around the canvas,
and watched young radicals drink it in:
this was how they wanted to see themselves —
stern, united, ready to die for the republic.
art had handed the revolution its mirror.

the loom that wove itself 1785 ce england cartwright's power loom weaves by steam, and the handloom weavers' doom is sealed. cartwright's power loom wove by steam —
no hands on the shuttle, no feet on the treadle —
cloth pouring out like water from a tap.
the handloom weavers' doom was sealed that year,
though it would take them decades to understand it.
i watched the loom work in a mill at dawn,
the pattern emerging with no weaver in sight,
and felt the old world of the craftsman
give way to the new world of the machine.

the necklace that ruined a queen 1785 ce paris, france the diamond necklace scandal blackens marie antoinette's name beyond repair. a diamond necklace, worth a fortune —
a cardinal fooled, a queen impersonated,
a scandal that blackened marie antoinette's name
beyond repair, though she was innocent of it.
i followed the trial in paris, the pamphlets flying,
and watched the people's love turn to venom:
the austrian woman, the spendthrift, the cheat.
a necklace did what no enemy could —
it made the queen hateful before the revolution
ever laid a hand on her.

the farmers who shut the courts 1786 ce massachusetts, usa debt-crushed farmers follow daniel shays against the courts, frightening the nation into a stronger union. debt-crushed farmers followed daniel shays
against the massachusetts courts —
shut them down, seized the arsenals,
demanded the foreclosures stop.
the rebellion failed, but it frightened the nation
into building a stronger union:
the articles were too weak, everyone saw it now.
i walked with the shays men one cold march,
honest farmers turned rebels by debt,
and understood: america would need a real government,
or it would tear itself apart farm by farm.

the summer that wrote the rules 1787 ce philadelphia, pennsylvania behind closed doors, the constitutional convention writes america's frame of government. behind closed doors, through a sweltering summer,
they wrote the rules: the constitutional convention,
washington presiding, franklin dozing and waking
to say the wise thing at the wise moment.
i slipped into the gallery once, unnoticed,
and watched them argue the republic into being —
compromise by compromise, clause by clause.
no trumpets, no crowds: just men in a hot room,
writing the frame the whole experiment would hang on.

the committee that said no more 1787 ce london, england twelve men, quakers and anglicans together, found the society to abolish the slave trade. twelve men in a london printing shop —
quakers and anglicans together —
founded the society to abolish the slave trade.
twelve. against the richest trade on earth.
i sat in on their meetings, all minutes and resolve,
and watched them plan the long campaign:
pamphlets, petitions, the diagram of a slave ship
that would sicken a nation.
they said: no more. and twenty years later,
the trade was dead by law.

the prison ships land 1788 ce sydney cove, australia the first fleet lands its convicts at botany bay, and european australia begins. the first fleet landed its convicts at botany bay —
thieves and poachers, irish rebels and pickpockets —
and european australia began in chains.
i watched them stumble ashore at sydney cove,
gaunt from the eight-month voyage,
a prison camp that would become a nation.
the aboriginal people watched from the treeline,
and their long sorrow began that day —
two histories colliding on one beach,
one of them written in leg-irons.

the captain who never came home 1788 ce the pacific la perouse's expedition vanishes in the pacific, and france waits decades for word. la perouse sailed into the pacific
with two fine ships and france's hopes —
and vanished. no word, no wreckage,
nothing for decades.
i was in paris when the years of waiting began,
the maps with his route drawn hopefully,
the rumors from every south sea trader.
france's cook, swallowed by the same ocean
that had taken the english one.
some voyages end in harbors; his ended in mystery.

the fortress that fell in a day 1789 ce paris, france the bastille falls to the paris mob on july 14th, and the old order trembles. on july 14th the paris mob stormed the bastille —
the old fortress, the king's prison —
and tore it down stone by stone.
seven prisoners inside; a revolution outside.
i was in the streets that day, the air electric,
the crowd roaring as the gates gave way,
and felt the old order tremble to its foundations.
kings across europe heard the news
and went pale: if paris could do this,
what was safe?

the rights of man, written down 1789 ce paris, france the declaration of the rights of man proclaims liberty, equality, and fraternity. liberty. equality. fraternity.
the declaration of the rights of man
put it in writing: men are born free and equal,
sovereignty lives in the nation, not the king.
i read the broadsheet in a paris cafe,
the words still wet from the press,
and watched ordinary people read them aloud to each other,
slowly, like a prayer.
it was the most photocopied idea in history —
every revolution since has cribbed from it.

the first president takes the oath 1789 ce new york, usa washington is sworn in on a balcony, and the great republican experiment begins. on a balcony in new york, before a cheering crowd,
washington took the oath — the first president,
the great republican experiment beginning for real.
i stood in wall street that april morning,
and watched the general become something new:
not a king, not a dictator, a president —
a word the world would have to learn.
he was nervous. the crowd was joyful.
nobody knew if it would work. it worked.

the money that built a nation 1790 ce united states hamilton's financial plan founds the bank, the mint, and america's credit. hamilton's plan: a national bank, a mint,
the government's debts honored, america's credit founded —
money as the mortar of the new nation.
jefferson hated it; washington signed it.
i watched the bank's charter debated in congress,
the future of the republic argued in dollars and cents,
and understood: revolutions are won with muskets,
but nations are built with ledgers.
hamilton gave america its money,
and its money gave it a future.

the book that defended the old order 1790 ce london, england edmund burke's reflections warns that revolution devours its children. edmund burke looked at the french revolution
and warned: this will devour its children.
his reflections defended the old order —
tradition, church, crown — against the wreckers,
in prose like organ music.
i read it in london as the paris news grew darker,
and watched conservatives find their bible.
he was right about the terror, wrong about everything else —
but what a voice. the revolution's enemies
would quote burke for two hundred years.

the ten promises 1791 ce united states the bill of rights is ratified — ten amendments guarding the citizen from the state. ten amendments, ratified one by one —
the bill of rights: promises the new government
made to its citizens, in writing, forever.
speech. religion. arms. trial by jury.
no quartering soldiers, no seizing papers.
i read them posted in a philadelphia tavern,
and watched farmers nod over their ale:
these were the things they'd fought for,
spelled out plain, so no future congress could forget.

the night the cane fields burned 1791 ce saint-domingue, caribbean enslaved africans rise in haiti, and the greatest slave revolt in history begins. in the august night the cane fields burned —
enslaved africans rising across saint-domingue,
the greatest slave revolt in history,
led by men who would become legends: toussaint, dessalines.
i saw the fires from a ship offshore,
the whole northern plain alight,
and knew the plantation world was finished.
it would take twelve years of war,
but haiti would be born from those flames —
the first free black republic on earth.

the requiem left unfinished 1791 ce vienna, austria mozart dies at thirty-five, his last mass half-written, and vienna weeps. he died at thirty-five, in a pauper's winter —
mozart, the child who heard music in everything —
his requiem half-written on the desk,
the last notes dictated from his deathbed.
vienna wept. i stood in the rain
outside st. stephen's as the small coffin passed,
and thought of all the music still inside him,
unwritten, unheard, gone.
thirty-five years, and he filled them
with more beauty than ten lifetimes.

the woman who demanded everything 1792 ce london, england mary wollstonecraft's vindication claims reason and rights for women as well as men. mary wollstonecraft wrote it plain:
if reason and rights belong to men,
they belong to women too —
a vindication of the rights of woman,
demanding everything, apologizing for nothing.
i read it in london and watched men scoff
and women read it in secret, by candlelight.
the revolution had declared all men equal;
wollstonecraft asked the rude question:
what about the other half of humanity?
two centuries of feminism start here.

one and indivisible 1792 ce paris, france the monarchy falls and france declares itself a republic, one and indivisible. the monarchy fell, and france declared itself
a republic — one and indivisible —
no more king, no more divine right,
just the nation, sovereign and alone.
i was in paris for the proclamation,
the crowds singing in the rain,
and felt the ground shift under europe:
a great power had beheaded monarchy itself.
the kings of europe heard it as a threat —
and it was. the wars would come soon enough.

the guillotine falls on a king 1793 ce paris, france louis xvi is guillotined in the place de la revolution as the crowd watches in silence. on a january morning in the place de la revolution,
louis xvi climbed the scaffold —
the drums rolled, the blade fell,
and a king's head dropped into the basket
as the crowd watched in silence.
i was there, in the cold, among the thousands,
and felt history snap like a bone:
no one had done this to a king in a thousand years.
the age of divine right ended
with one falling blade.

the emperor who said no 1793 ce beijing, china qianlong dismisses britain's macartney embassy; china needs nothing from the west. britain sent lord macartney to beijing
with gifts and trade proposals —
and qianlong dismissed him:
china needs nothing from the west.
our celestial empire has everything; your trinkets amuse us.
i watched the embassy sail home empty-handed,
and thought of the pride in that refusal —
and the price. within fifty years
british guns would teach china
what saying no had cost.

the woman who wrote women's rights 1793 ce paris, france olympe de gouges, author of the rights of woman, is guillotined by the revolution she served. she wrote the declaration of the rights of woman —
olympe de gouges, playwright and firebrand —
demanding the revolution keep its promises to women.
the revolution answered with the guillotine.
i watched her climb the scaffold in november,
unbroken to the end,
and felt the revolution's shame:
it had killed the woman who believed in it most.
her rights of woman would wait two centuries;
her courage needed no waiting.

the young gunner of toulon 1793 ce toulon, france twenty-four-year-old napoleon retakes toulon with his artillery, and france notices him. he was twenty-four, an artillery officer from corsica,
and at toulon he did what the older generals couldn't:
placed his guns right, pounded the british out,
retook the port for the republic.
napoleon bonaparte. france noticed him that winter.
i watched him sighting cannon in the mud,
all intensity and mathematics,
and thought: this one is different.
the revolution had found its sword —
and the sword would soon hold the revolution.

the terror eats its own 1794 ce paris, france robespierre is guillotined, and the terror ends with its architect's head in the basket. robespierre sent them all to the blade —
danton, desmoulins, thousands of nobodies —
until the terror turned and ate its architect too.
they guillotined him in july, the incorruptible,
and the terror ended with his head in the basket.
i watched from the crowd as the cart rolled past,
and felt paris exhale: it was over.
the revolution had devoured its children,
exactly as burke warned —
and france was sick of blood at last.

the chemist on the scaffold 1794 ce paris, france lavoisier, father of modern chemistry, is executed; france loses its finest mind. lavoisier — the father of modern chemistry,
the man who named oxygen and weighed the air —
climbed the scaffold because he'd been a tax farmer,
and the revolution needed heads more than it needed science.
the judge's famous words: the republic has no need of savants.
i stood in the crowd that may morning
and watched france execute its finest mind.
it took a moment, the blade;
it took a century to replace him.

the machine that multiplied slavery 1794 ce georgia, usa eli whitney's cotton gin makes cotton king and chains millions more to the fields. eli whitney built a simple machine —
the cotton gin, teeth and wire —
that cleaned cotton fifty times faster than fingers.
it was supposed to make slavery uneconomical.
it did the opposite: cotton became king,
and millions more were chained to the fields
to feed the hungry gins.
i watched one work in georgia, the lint flying,
and felt the cruelest irony of the age:
a labor-saving machine that multiplied slavery.

the five men who ruled 1795 ce paris, france the directory takes power — five directors steering a tired, bloody republic. after the terror, five directors took power —
the directory, steering a tired, bloody republic
through bankruptcy and war and conspiracy.
five men, quarreling in the luxembourg palace,
while france waited for someone stronger.
i watched them parade in their ridiculous uniforms,
all velvet and feathers, no authority,
and thought: this cannot last.
it didn't. a young general was waiting in the wings,
and his name was bonaparte.

the milkmaid's gift 1796 ce berkeley, england a country doctor scratches cowpox into a boy's arm, and smallpox begins its long defeat. a country doctor noticed the milkmaids —
the ones who'd had cowpox never caught smallpox —
and scratched cowpox into a boy's arm:
the first vaccination, and smallpox began its long defeat.
edward jenner. i was in berkeley that may,
and watched him test the boy against the real disease.
it worked. the boy lived.
from a milkmaid's clear skin to the saving of billions —
the greatest medical gift ever given,
wrapped in a country doctor's hunch.

the boy general's lightning march 1796 ce italy twenty-six-year-old napoleon outruns and outfights austria's armies across italy. twenty-six years old, commanding in italy,
napoleon outran and outfought austria's armies —
lightning marches, impossible victories,
soldiers who'd follow him into hell.
i rode with that army through the italian spring,
dust and glory, town after town falling,
and watched a legend being born in real time.
the boy general moved faster than news could travel;
europe woke up to find a new master of war
had arrived, and he was barely shaving.

the mutiny of the fleets 1797 ce the english channel britain's sailors mutiny for better pay and bread, and the mighty navy must listen. britain's sailors mutinied — the whole channel fleet,
then the north sea fleet — for better pay and bread,
rotten food and brutal officers no more.
the mighty navy, anchor of the empire,
had to listen to its own men.
i was at spithead when the red flags flew,
delegates rowing between the ships,
discipline holding even in revolt.
they won their demands. the admiralty learned:
even wooden walls are built of men,
and men must eat.

the general who sailed for the pyramids 1798 ce egypt napoleon lands in egypt with soldiers and scholars, wins at the pyramids, and strands his army. napoleon sailed for egypt with soldiers and scholars —
an army and a university in one fleet —
won at the pyramids, then watched nelson
burn his ships at the nile and strand him there.
i marched with that army through the desert heat,
past the sphinx, into cairo,
and watched the scholars sketch temples
while the soldiers looted them.
glory and folly, side by side:
the expedition failed as conquest
and triumphed as the birth of egyptology.

the rising of '98 1798 ce ireland wolfe tone's united irishmen rise against british rule and are crushed; ireland's hope goes underground. wolfe tone's united irishmen rose —
catholic and protestant together, for an irish republic —
and were crushed: vinegar hill, the pitchcappings,
the hangings afterward.
ireland's hope went underground that year.
i walked the roads of wexford after the battles,
the dead still unburied in the ditches,
and felt a nation's heart break —
then harden. the rising failed;
the cause went into the soil like seed,
to rise again, and again, and again.

the coup of the eighteenth brumaire 1799 ce paris, france napoleon overthrows the directory at bayonet point, and the revolution ends in one man's hands. on the 18th of brumaire, napoleon walked into the directory's palace
with soldiers at his back and overthrew it —
the revolution ending, at bayonet point,
in one man's hands.
i was in paris that november day,
the confusion, the shouting, the troops in the streets,
and watched ten years of republic
dissolve into a general's ambition.
liberty, equality, fraternity —
and now, one consul, soon one emperor.
the revolution was over. the legend was beginning.

the death of the general 1799 ce virginia, usa washington dies at mount vernon, and a young nation mourns the father it cannot replace. he died at mount vernon in december —
washington, the father of the country,
gone in two days from a throat infection,
bled by his doctors, as was the custom.
a young nation mourned the father it could not replace.
i stood among the mourners in the cold virginia air,
and felt the loss like a missing foundation stone:
who would hold it together now?
nobody, quite. america would have to hold itself.

the city in the swamp 1800 ce washington, usa the government moves into a half-built capital on the potomac — all mud and marble dreams. the government moved into a half-built capital
on the potomac — all mud and marble dreams,
a few grand buildings rising from a swamp,
streets that were still forest paths.
i walked pennsylvania avenue that first winter,
sinking to my ankles, the capitol dome unfinished,
and laughed: this was to be the seat of empire?
but cities grow into their ambitions.
the swamp would drain, the marble would multiply,
and the muddy dream would become washington.

the pile that made lightning obey 1800 ce como, italy alessandro volta stacks metal discs and makes the first battery, bottling electricity at last. alessandro volta stacked metal discs —
silver, zinc, brine-soaked cloth, silver, zinc —
and made the first battery: steady, bottled electricity,
lightning made to obey.
i watched him demonstrate it in como,
the wire sparking, the frog legs twitching,
and felt the age of electricity begin:
no more waiting for storms like franklin's kite.
power on demand, in a pile of discs.
the world would run on this idea —
every battery since is volta's pile, refined.

the president's house 1800 ce washington, usa john adams becomes the first president to live in the unfinished white house in 1800, blessing a half-built house that would grow into a nation's home. i stood on mud where pennsylvania avenue
was more of a promise than a street —
a half-built house of pale virginia stone,
with stairways going nowhere, plaster wet.
adams came in by coach that november,
the first man to sleep beneath that roof,
and wrote a blessing in a letter home
that every president has read since — proof
that even half a house can hold a nation,
if someone's willing to move in and stay.

gabriel's doomed rising 1800 ce virginia in 1800, enslaved blacksmith gabriel prosser's planned march on richmond collapses after betrayal and a storm; he is hanged, but the dream of freedom doesn't die with him. i watched him plan it by the blacksmith's fire,
a freeman's mind inside a slave's skin —
gabriel, hammering freedom into iron,
gathering ten thousand with a whispered grin.
a traitor sold him for a few spare coins,
then heaven itself turned traitor too —
a storm drowned roads the night they meant to march,
and richmond's gallows did what storms don't do.

marengo's narrow escape 1800 ce italy at marengo in 1800, general desaix's last-minute evening charge snatches napoleon victory from certain defeat, costing desaix his life. at two o'clock the french were beaten —
the austrians were writing their dispatches home,
napoleon staring at disaster,
when desaix rode in through the dust alone.
one charge, one cannonade at evening,
and a lost battle turned completely round —
desaix died in the moment of it,
his name carved in the turning of the ground.

two kingdoms become one 1800 ce britain the act of union of 1800 joins ireland to great britain under one parliament, a paper unity that ireland never accepted and that fueled a century of resistance. i walked through london as they rang the bells
for a union signed with bribed and bought votes —
ireland folded into great britain,
one parliament, one flag, two heavy coats.
it was sold as peace. it wore like chains.
the irish never signed it in their hearts,
and every rising for a century after
was this day's paper coming back in parts.

counting the kingdom 1801 ce britain britain's first census in 1801 counts over ten million people, the first time a nation counted its living population rather than its armies. ten million, two hundred eighty-three thousand, souls —
i watched the counters go from door to door,
chalk in hand, a new century's new habit:
a kingdom wanting, finally, to know its score.
not how many spears. not how many ships.
how many mouths, how many hands, how many beds —
the first time a state counted its people
instead of counting only its war dead.

nelson turns his blind eye 1801 ce denmark at copenhagen in 1801, admiral nelson raises his telescope to his blind eye to ignore the recall signal, then destroys the danish fleet. i was on the elephant when the signal ran
for nelson to pull back and end the fight —
he lifted his glass to his blind eye,
smiled, and said, "i really do not see the sight."
so on we sailed into the harbor's guns,
and the danish line came all undone.
sometimes the bravest order ever given
is the one the captain doesn't run.

the black general's constitution 1801 ce haiti toussaint louverture, the formerly enslaved black general who freed saint-domingue, writes haiti's 1801 constitution and names himself governor for life, openly defying napoleon. he wrote it in his own hand, the man born a slave,
a constitution for a free black land —
toussaint, who beat the british and the spanish,
daring napoleon to raise a hand.
governor for life, he signed himself,
and sent the paper sailing to paris town:
here is a colony that calls itself a people —
come and try to sit it down.

the truce of amiens 1802 ce france the treaty of amiens in 1802 gives war-weary europe one brief year of peace between britain and napoleonic france before the fighting resumes. for one whole year the guns went quiet —
amiens, and europe drew a breath,
shook hands across the channel water,
and almost remembered life from death.
i sat in cafes where french and english
drank each other's health like it would last —
then the year ran out, the drums came back,
and the quiet folded into the past.

one emperor, one vietnam 1802 ce vietnam nguyen anh defeats his last rivals in 1802, takes the name gia long, and unites vietnam under a single imperial throne. thirty years of war, and then one man —
nguyen anh, patient as the tide,
outlasted every rival house and army,
and took the dragon throne with none beside.
he called himself gia long, the first emperor
of a vietnam whole from north to south —
i watched the banners change in hue that summer,
and heard one name in every mouth.

the trap at cap-francais 1802 ce haiti napoleon betrays toussaint louverture with false peace talks in 1802, ships him to die in a french mountain prison — but haiti's revolution fights on without him. they called it talks. it was a cage.
they asked him to parley, shook his hand,
then chained him in the night and sailed him
to a stone cell in a freezing land.
toussaint died in joux, in the jura cold,
april air too thin for a caribbean man —
but the army he'd built kept fighting on,
and finished what the prisoner began.

america doubles overnight 1803 ce north america napoleon's 1803 sale of the louisiana territory doubles the size of the united states overnight for fifteen million dollars — the greatest land bargain in history. three cents an acre. eight hundred twenty-eight thousand
square miles for fifteen million in gold —
napoleon needed money for his wars,
and jefferson couldn't refuse it, i'm told.
i watched the map get redrawn in a morning:
a nation doubled by a signature's scratch —
the biggest land deal in the human story,
and nobody alive could match it.

into the unknown west 1803 ce north america lewis and clark's corps of discovery sets out in 1803 to map the louisiana purchase from the missouri to the pacific, opening the american west. i poled beside them up the missouri,
lewis with his compass, clark with his map,
into a country no white man had charted —
bear and buffalo, river and gap.
sacagawea carried her baby the whole way,
and the mountains didn't kill them after all —
two years out, two years back again,
and a continent's curtain starts to fall.

emmet's last speech 1803 ce ireland robert emmet's 1803 dublin rising collapses in a day, but his speech from the dock before his execution makes him ireland's immortal rebel. the rising failed before the sun went down —
a riot, not a revolution, lost by noon.
but then they gave him the dock to speak from,
and ireland has been listening since that afternoon.
"let my epitaph be written when my country
takes her place among the nations of the earth" —
twenty-five years old, and he outlived them all,
because words can outlive any birth.

assaye breaks the marathas 1803 ce india arthur wellesley's vastly outnumbered british army crushes the marathas at assaye in 1803, tightening britain's grip on india and making his reputation. seven thousand against forty thousand —
wellesley looked at the odds and grinned,
led his line straight at the maratha guns
and broke the finest army india could send.
i walked the field when the smoke had cleared;
he'd call it the bloodiest day he knew,
the battle that made his name in india —
assaye, where the few ran down the true.

the world's first black republic 1804 ce haiti on january 1, 1804, jean-jacques dessalines declares haiti independent — the first nation in history founded by a successful slave revolt. on new year's day, in gonaives,
dessalines stood up and read it plain:
haiti — free, forever, independent,
never a colony of france again.
the first nation ever born of a slave revolt,
built by hands that broke their own chains —
i heard the drums that afternoon,
and they never sounded like drums again.

the scholar's holy war 1804 ce west africa in 1804 the islamic scholar usman dan fodio launches his jihad in hausaland, founding the sokoto caliphate that will rule millions across west africa. he was a teacher, not a warlord —
usman dan fodio, with books for swords,
calling the hausa kings corrupt,
calling the people back to the lord.
the scholars rose, the students marched,
kingdom after kingdom bent the knee —
and out of sermons came an empire,
the sokoto caliphate, ruling millions, free.

the black george rises 1804 ce serbia in 1804 karađorđe leads the serbs in revolt against ottoman rule, the first spark of the balkan national independence movements. they called him karađorđe — black george —
a pig-dealer with a warrior's heart,
and when the serbs had taken all they could take,
he was the spark that set the fire to start.
against the ottomans, against the odds,
the first balkan rising of the modern age —
i saw the standard raised at orasac,
and heard the first page of a turning page.

law for an empire 1804 ce france napoleon's civil code of 1804 unifies french law under one book — and outlives every battle he ever fought, still shaping legal systems worldwide. every battle he ever fought is dust —
waterloo's a field trip now, they say.
but the book he signed in 1804,
the code civil, is still law today.
one law for rich man, poor man, city, farm —
no more feudal maze, no lordly whim.
i watched the clerks copy it out by hand,
and empires fade, but laws outlast him.

the albanian who made modern egypt 1805 ce egypt muhammad ali seizes power in egypt in 1805 and begins forging a modern state — schools, factories, and a european-style army. he came as an ottoman soldier, albanian-born,
and stayed to take the whole machine apart —
muhammad ali, who looked at crumbling egypt
and decided to rebuild it with a modern heart.
schools, factories, an army trained like europe's,
the nile made to serve a new design —
i walked cairo's streets and felt the shift:
an old land learning a new kind of time.

trafalgar's thunder 1805 ce atlantic at trafalgar in 1805 nelson destroys the combined french and spanish fleets, securing british naval supremacy — and dies of a sniper's wound in the hour of victory. twenty-seven ships against thirty-three,
and nelson split them like a wedge through pine —
"england expects that every man will do his duty,"
and every man did, down the line.
a french sharpshooter found him on the deck
at the very hour the victory was won —
he died hearing that the day was his,
and britain ruled the waves from that day on.

the sun of austerlitz 1805 ce moravia napoleon crushes the austrian and russian armies at austerlitz in december 1805 — his most tactically perfect victory, fought in a single winter day. december second, and the sun came up
through the mist exactly as he planned —
napoleon, who had drawn the russians and austrians
onto the ground he'd chosen, like a hand.
seventy-three thousand against ninety thousand,
and by evening it was done —
the most perfect battle he ever fought,
his masterpiece beneath the winter sun.

mungo park's last river 1806 ce west africa explorer mungo park drowns in the niger rapids in 1806 on his second expedition, and africa's interior keeps its secrets a while longer. he'd come back to the niger a second time,
the scotsman with the mapmaker's dream,
determined to follow the great river
down to wherever rivers meet the sea.
the rapids took him at bussa falls —
his boat went over, and the river kept the rest.
i stood on that bank and watched the water run,
and africa kept its secret best.

an empire a thousand years old ends 1806 ce germany in 1806 napoleon dissolves the thousand-year-old holy roman empire, and francis ii becomes simply emperor of austria — germany's map is redrawn forever. a thousand years. let that sit a moment —
an empire older than most nations' names,
and napoleon ended it with a signature,
the holy roman empire, gone in flames.
francis ii laid down the ancient crown
and called himself plain emperor of austria —
i watched a millennium fold up quietly,
and germany begin to be itself, at last.

jena shatters an army 1806 ce prussia at jena-auerstedt in 1806 napoleon's army destroys the famed prussian military machine in a single day, and french troops march into berlin. the prussians marched in frederick's glory,
powdered wigs and eighteen-century pride —
and napoleon's corps hit them at jena
like a hammer, and the whole machine died.
one day. one battle, and an army
that europe feared for fifty years was gone —
french eagles flying over berlin
before the month was out. move on. move on.

the trade in humans outlawed 1807 ce britain after twenty years of william wilberforce's campaigning, parliament abolishes the slave trade across the british empire in 1807. twenty years wilberforce stood up
in a parliament that laughed and looked away —
twenty years of "not yet" and "next time,"
until the year the "ayes" outshouted "nay."
the ships were outlawed, not the chains —
slavery itself would take another fight.
but i watched the vote that night in london,
and for the first time, the dark cracked light.

two emperors on a raft 1807 ce russia napoleon and tsar alexander i meet on a raft at tilsit in 1807 and divide europe's future between them. a raft on the niemen river, midstream,
where neither bank could claim the ground —
napoleon and the tsar met on the water
and carved up europe while the oars made sound.
alexander, young and charmed and cornered,
agreed to everything the frenchman drew —
i watched from the bank as two men on a raft
decided what the continent would do.

the steamboat that beat the river 1807 ce new york robert fulton's steamboat clermont powers up the hudson in 1807, proving steam can beat wind and current — the age of steam travel begins. they called it "fulton's folly" on the dock —
a boat with wheels, a chimney, and a dream.
then the clermont churned up the hudson,
thirty-two hours against wind and stream.
i rode her deck and felt it in my bones:
the river hadn't changed, but we had —
sail and oar were done, steam was king,
and the world would never travel sad.

davy's electric fire 1807 ce england in 1807 humphry davy uses electric current to isolate potassium from potash, opening the age of electrochemistry and a flood of new elements. he wired a battery to a lump of potash
and watched it melt and bubble, strange and bright —
then out of the froth came shining metal,
potassium, born of electric light.
humphry davy, showman of the royal institution,
pulling new elements out of the air —
i stood in that lecture hall and understood:
chemistry would never be the same out there.

the slave ships stop — legally 1808 ce america the united states bans the importation of enslaved africans in 1808 — but slavery itself continues and grows within the country. the law said: no more ships, no more cargo,
no more middle passage, by decree —
america banned the import of the enslaved
in 1808, and called the ocean free.
but the auctions went on in every southern town,
and the cotton kept the coffles on the road —
i watched a law close the sea door
while slavery built a bigger house to hold.

the rum rebellion 1808 ce australia in 1808 sydney's military officers arrest governor bligh in australia's only military coup — the rum rebellion, fought over the rum trade. australia's only coup, and it was over rum —
governor bligh, of bounty fame, tried to break
the officers' monopoly on spirits,
and the new south wales corps wouldn't take.
they marched him out at bayonet point,
arrested their own governor in his home —
i watched sydney's strangest morning:
a rebellion fought for rum, in a colony built of stone.

madrid rises with knives 1808 ce spain on may 2, 1808, the people of madrid rise against french occupation with knives and stones, igniting the brutal peninsular war. i was in madrid on the second of may
when the people came out with kitchen knives and stones
against murat's cavalry and cannon —
a city deciding it would rather break its bones
than kneel. the french shot them in the streets,
and goya would paint it later, dark and red —
but that morning belonged to butchers and tailors,
and the long peninsular war was born of the dead.

fate knocks at the door 1808 ce vienna in december 1808 beethoven premieres his fifth and sixth symphonies in a single freezing four-hour concert in vienna. four hours, one freezing december night,
a concert so long the audience nearly froze —
beethoven, already going deaf,
premiered two symphonies at once, heaven knows.
the fifth: fate knocking at the door,
four notes that everyone on earth would learn —
and the sixth: a walk through summer fields,
the pastoral, green as anything could turn.

two giants born on one day 1809 ce england on february 12, 1809, abraham lincoln is born in a kentucky log cabin and charles darwin in an english manor — two lives that would each change the world. february twelfth, eighteen-oh-nine:
a dirt-floor cabin in kentucky, cold and bare —
a baby named abraham lincoln.
a manor house in shrewsbury, warm with care —
a baby named charles darwin.
two boys who'd each, in his own way,
free the world from an old idea's chain —
one would free the slaves, the other
would free the mind from how life came.

wagram's bloody field 1809 ce austria napoleon defeats austria at wagram in 1809 in one of the bloodiest battles yet fought, then seals the peace by marrying into the habsburg family. i walked wagram's field when the guns went quiet —
one hundred fifty thousand men a side,
the danube running red between them,
and napoleon, who would not be denied.
he beat the austrians at a butcher's price,
then married a habsburg princess for his pains —
a wedding to seal a victory,
and blood enough to water the plains.

the first theory of evolution 1809 ce france in 1809 jean-baptiste lamarck publishes the first theory of evolution — wrong in its mechanism, but daring in its central idea that life changes over generations. lamarck said it first, and got it wrong —
that giraffes stretched their necks by reaching high,
that what you use grows strong, what you don't
withers away, and passes to your child thereby.
the mechanism failed. the idea didn't.
living things change over generations — true —
and i sat in his lecture hall in paris
watching the first man dare to say it through.

the may revolution 1810 ce argentina in may 1810 buenos aires throws off spanish rule in the may revolution, launching south america's wars of liberation. may twenty-fifth, and buenos aires
filled the square before the cabildo hall —
no more spanish viceroy, the people said,
we'll govern ourselves, one and all.
it started with a council, not a battle,
a polite revolution, papers signed —
but i watched that crowd and knew the truth:
south america's liberation had begun in kind.

the french marshal who became a king 1810 ce sweden in 1810 sweden elects napoleon's marshal bernadotte as crown prince; he founds the bernadotte dynasty that still reigns in sweden today. sweden needed an heir, and chose —
of all the men on earth — a frenchman,
bernadotte, one of napoleon's marshals,
a soldier of the revolution's span.
he took the name charles john, learned swedish,
ruled wisely, and founded a royal line —
his descendants sit on sweden's throne today.
i watched a marshal become a king by design.
