the cry of dolores 1810 ce mexico on september 16, 1810, father miguel hidalgo rings his church bell at dolores and cries out for mexican independence, igniting the war against spain. before the dawn, in little dolores town,
father miguel hidalgo climbed the tower
and rang the church bell hard and long,
crying freedom in the dark hour.
"death to bad government! long live the virgin!"
the indians and mestizos took up the call —
i stood among them in the square that morning
when mexico's war of independence lit them all.

the machine-breakers 1811 ce england in 1811 starving english weavers begin smashing the factory machines they blame for their misery, giving the world the word "luddite." they came at night with hammers and with hunger,
the weavers of the midlands, gaunt and grim —
the frames were eating their children's bread,
so they smashed the frames, limb from limb.
they signed their letters "ned ludd," a ghost,
and the name stuck to them ever since —
luddites, the first to ask the question
we're still asking: who does the machine convince?

the quiet republic 1811 ce paraguay in 1811 paraguay quietly breaks from spain and becomes south america's first lasting independent republic. no great battle, no famous cry —
paraguay just slipped the spanish leash,
quietly, in the night, and woke up free,
south america's first lasting republic of peace.
while the continent burned with war around it,
this small land chose the steady hand —
i crossed its border in that year
and found the calmest newborn in the land.

tippecanoe's dawn battle 1811 ce indiana william henry harrison's troops defeat tecumseh's confederacy at tippecanoe in 1811, breaking organized native resistance in the old northwest. they hit at dawn, tecumseh's warriors,
while harrison's camp was still half-asleep —
but the soldiers held, and by the sunrise
the prophet's town was ash in a heap.
it broke the confederacy tecumseh built,
the dream of one great native stand —
i walked that field at tippecanoe
where the old northwest changed hands.

the second war with britain 1812 ce america the united states declares war on britain in 1812 over impressment and trade, beginning three years of fighting on land and sea. they called it the second war of independence —
impressment, trade, the frontier's flame —
and congress voted, close and bitter,
to fight the british once again.
i watched them burn and bleed for three years,
from detroit's shame to new orleans' pride —
a war nobody won and everybody claimed,
and a young nation that proved it could survive.

the road to moscow 1812 ce russia in june 1812 napoleon invades russia with a grand army of six hundred thousand men — the greatest invasion europe had ever seen. six hundred thousand men — the largest army
europe had ever seen in one array —
poles, frenchmen, germans, italians,
marching east in the summer's sway.
napoleon at their head, invincible,
certain the tsar would sue for peace —
i watched that river of men cross the niemen,
and felt the old world start to crease.

moscow burns, the army freezes 1812 ce russia napoleon captures a burning, empty moscow in 1812, then retreats through the russian winter that destroys his grand army. he took moscow and found it empty —
then the fires started, street by street,
and the tsar would not come to the table,
so the grand army turned in retreat.
then came the russian winter, the general
no army has ever beaten yet —
snow, hunger, cossacks at the flanks,
and half a million men the snows forget.

fairy tales for a dark time 1812 ce germany in 1812 the brothers grimm publish their first collection of folk tales, preserving cinderella, snow white, and the world's great fairy tales. while armies marched and empires fell,
two brothers in kassel bent to write —
jacob and wilhelm grimm, collecting stories
old women told by firelight.
cinderella, snow white, hansel and gretel —
they saved them all from being lost —
i sat in that cold year of war
and watched them pay the storyteller's cost.

mr. darcy walks in 1813 ce england jane austen publishes pride and prejudice in 1813, and elizabeth bennet becomes one of literature's most beloved heroines. she wrote it at a little wooden desk,
anonymous — "by a lady," nothing more —
and elizabeth bennet walked off the page
and into every english heart's front door.
i read it in the year it came,
pride and prejudice, sharp and bright and true —
jane austen, who never left her village,
saw the whole world clearer than most ever do.

perry's flagship victory 1813 ce great lakes oliver hazard perry destroys the british fleet on lake erie in 1813, the first time a full british squadron ever surrendered to americans. "we have met the enemy and they are ours" —
perry wrote it after lake erie's fray,
having rowed through cannon fire to a new flagship
when his own was shot away.
i watched the british colors come down
on every ship of barclay's line that day —
the first time an entire british squadron
ever struck to an american array.

the battle of the nations 1813 ce germany at leipzig in 1813 half a million men fight the battle of the nations, and napoleon's empire in germany collapses. half a million men on one field —
leipzig, four days of smoke and roar,
russians, prussians, austrians, swedes
against the french, and then no more.
napoleon's empire in germany broke there,
his allies melting in the fray —
i stood on the heights and watched the tide
of twenty years of conquest drain away.

napoleon gives up the throne 1814 ce france defeated on all sides in 1814, napoleon abdicates at fontainebleau and sails into exile on the island of elba. they came for him from every side,
and paris opened up its gates —
so at fontainebleau he signed the paper,
and gave up what the world calls great.
i watched him try to take his own life first —
the poison failed, as if even death said no —
then he sailed for elba, a tiny island kingdom,
an emperor with nowhere left to go.

a constitution in the snow 1814 ce norway norway writes one of the world's freest constitutions at eidsvoll in 1814, though the great powers then force it into union with sweden. at eidsvoll, in a manor house in spring,
one hundred twelve norwegians wrote it down —
one of the freest constitutions on the earth,
a people's law, no king to wear the crown.
then the great powers gave them to sweden,
and the freedom tasted half like loss —
but the paper held, and holds to this day,
a constitution written at freedom's cost.

the capital in flames 1814 ce washington in august 1814 british troops march into washington and burn the white house and the capitol — the only foreign capture of america's capital. i watched them come up bladensburg road,
the british redcoats, steady as a drum —
the americans ran, the city emptied,
and the torchmen did what torchmen come to do.
the white house burned. the capitol burned.
dolly madison saved the portrait of george —
and in the smoke of washington that night,
a young republic learned what war will forge.

the dance of the peacemakers 1814 ce vienna europe's rulers gather at the congress of vienna in 1814 to redraw the map after napoleon, waltzing while they trade nations. they waltzed while they redrew the map —
kings and ministers, a glittering crowd,
dancing till dawn in vienna's ballrooms,
then carving up the continent, calm and proud.
"the congress dances, but it does not move" —
i watched them trade whole peoples like wine —
and the peace they built would hold for decades,
bought with borders drawn in ballroom time.

the battle after the peace 1815 ce louisiana two weeks after the war of 1812's peace treaty is signed, andrew jackson's riflemen crush the british at new orleans — a battle fought after the war was over. the treaty was signed on christmas eve
in ghent — the war was done, they'd say.
but nobody told the ships at sea,
and jackson didn't get the news till january.
so the british came at new orleans,
and his riflemen cut them down in rows —
two thousand casualties to thirteen,
a battle fought after the peace nobody knows.

the mountain that darkened the world 1815 ce indonesia mount tambora erupts in april 1815 in the largest volcanic explosion in recorded history, and its ash will chill the entire planet. april tenth — the sky tore open
over sumbawa, and tambora blew —
the loudest explosion in recorded history,
heard a thousand miles, the whole sky askew.
three plumes of ash, a column miles high,
villages buried where the mountain stood —
i watched the sea boil and the sun go strange,
and the world would pay for it in cold and flood.

waterloo ends it 1815 ce belgium on june 18, 1815, wellington and blucher crush napoleon at waterloo, ending twenty years of napoleonic war. one rainy sunday in june, the mud held —
napoleon's guns bogged down till noon,
wellington held the ridge at mont-saint-jean,
and blucher's prussians came that afternoon.
the old guard broke. the guard that never broke.
i watched the emperor's carriage roll away —
twenty years of war ended in a field in belgium,
and europe exhaled at the end of day.

eighteen hundred and froze to death 1816 ce the world tambora's ash veils the sun in 1816, the year without a summer — crops fail worldwide and famine stalks the globe. they called it eighteen-hundred-and-froze-to-death —
snow in july in new england's fields,
frost in august, crops black in the ground,
and famine walking where the harvest yields.
tambora's ash had veiled the sun,
and the whole earth shivered through the year —
i traveled through that starving summer
and felt the planet's cold draw near.

a monster dreamed by a lake 1816 ce switzerland trapped indoors by the cold summer of 1816, eighteen-year-old mary shelley dreams up frankenstein during a ghost-story contest at lake geneva. the summer never came that year —
rain and cold kept them indoors by the lake,
lord byron, percy shelley, and eighteen-year-old mary,
telling ghost stories for storytelling's sake.
"each of us will write a ghost story," byron said —
and mary dreamed a monster into life that night,
a creature stitched from dead men's parts,
and woke to write it by the candlelight.

the south declares itself free 1816 ce argentina in july 1816 the congress at tucuman declares the united provinces of south america independent of spain. in tucuman, in a congress hall,
the delegates of the south stood one by one
and signed their names to independence —
the united provinces, free of spain, begun.
no king across the ocean anymore,
no viceroy's seal on what they do —
i watched them sign it in july,
and south america signed it too.

digging the ditch to the west 1817 ce new york ground breaks on the erie canal in 1817 — a 363-mile hand-dug waterway that will tie the american frontier to the sea. they called it clinton's ditch, a fool's canal —
three hundred sixty-three miles through the wild,
dug by hand, by irishmen and mules,
a water road for a young and hungry child.
i walked the towpath as they dug,
through forest, swamp, and limestone deep —
and when it opened, the west poured east,
and the east poured west, in one long sweep.

bolivar's river fortress 1817 ce south america in 1817 simon bolivar establishes angostura on the orinoco as his revolutionary capital and rallies the south american liberation. he'd lost venezuela twice and come back —
bolivar, who would not stay beat,
made angostura his capital on the orinoco,
a river fortress none could cheat.
from there he planned the march across the andes,
the wildest campaign of them all —
i sat with him by the river's edge
and watched the liberator stand tall.

the first seminole war 1817 ce florida in 1817 andrew jackson invades spanish florida pursuing seminoles, seizing forts and breaking spain's hold on the peninsula. jackson crossed the line with an army,
chasing seminoles into spanish ground —
florida belonged to spain on paper,
but spain's grip was nowhere to be found.
he took the forts, he hanged the traders,
and madrid could only watch and frown —
i rode that border in the heat
and watched an empire's claim burn down.

frankenstein walks 1818 ce england mary shelley's frankenstein is published in 1818, giving the world the modern monster — and inventing science fiction. anonymous — no name upon the title —
a novel by an eighteen-year-old girl,
about a student and his creature,
and the world it set in a whirl.
victor frankenstein, the modern prometheus,
who made a man and ran from what he'd done —
i read it in that first edition year
and knew a new kind of story had begun.

maipu wins a nation 1818 ce chile jose de san martin's crushing victory at maipu in april 1818 ends spanish rule in chile for good. san martin had crossed the andes in the snow,
an army where no army ought to go —
and at maipu, on the fifth of april,
he broke the spanish power's final flow.
six thousand royalists, dead or captured,
chile free forever from that day —
i stood upon that plain at evening
and watched an empire walk away.

shaka forges the zulu 1818 ce southern africa shaka's disciplined regiments triumph at gqokli hill in 1818, and the zulu kingdom rises over southern africa. at gqokli hill his regiments stood,
disciplined as any in the world —
the short stabbing spear, the buffalo horns,
and a kingdom like a storm unfurled.
shaka took scattered clans and made an army,
made an army and made a nation —
i watched his warriors drill in the dust
and felt the earth change its vibration.

the prairie state joins 1818 ce illinois illinois becomes the twenty-first american state in 1818, and settlers pour onto the tall-grass prairie. the twenty-first star on the flag —
illinois, the tall-grass prairie sea,
joined the union in december's cold,
and the settlers came, and came, and came to be.
i walked that grass when it was taller
than a man on horseback, waving gold —
and watched the plows turn under heaven
to make the breadbasket of the world.

raffles plants a flag 1819 ce singapore stamford raffles founds singapore as a free-trade british port in 1819 — the seed of a future great city. a swampy island at the tip of malaya,
tigers in the jungle, pirates in the strait —
stamford raffles saw a free-trade port
where others saw a worthless piece of fate.
he raised the union jack in january,
signed a treaty with the local lord —
i stood on that muddy shore and watched
the founding of what trade would make adored.

peterloo's bloody field 1819 ce manchester in august 1819 cavalry charges a peaceful crowd demanding voting reform at st. peter's field, manchester — eleven die in the peterloo massacre. sixty thousand came in peace that day,
with banners, children, sunday-best attire,
to hear a man speak about the vote —
and the magistrates sent in the cavalry's fire.
eleven dead. six hundred hurt.
sabres against unarmed men in a field —
i was at st. peter's when they charged,
and "peterloo" is what that day would yield.

the old gods fall 1819 ce hawaii in 1819 young king kamehameha ii breaks the sacred kapu taboos, and hawaii's ancient religion collapses within a season. the young king broke the kapu —
ate with women, which no man may do,
and the priests waited for the gods to strike —
but no lightning came, no thunder through.
in one season, centuries of taboo
crumbled like a temple in the rain —
i watched hawaii's ancient religion
fall without a battle, without pain.

the white continent sighted 1820 ce antarctica in 1820 sealers and explorers glimpse antarctica's icy coast — the last continent discovered by humanity. sealers chasing fur, explorers chasing fame,
pushed south through the screaming fifties' foam —
and there it rose: a wall of white,
the last continent, the last unknown home.
no flag had ever flown above that ice,
no human foot had touched that shore —
i stood on a pitching deck and saw it:
the earth's final locked door.

the missouri bargain 1820 ce america the missouri compromise of 1820 draws a line across the west — slavery permitted below it, banned above — postponing america's reckoning. they drew a line across the west —
thirty-six thirty, latitude's cold line:
slavery below it, freedom above,
a bargain signed in congress, by design.
it held the union together for a while,
a compromise of maps and human fate —
i watched them draw it, and i knew:
you can't split freedom with a line and call it straight.

the venus of milo unearthed 1820 ce greece in 1820 a farmer on the greek island of melos digs up the armless marble venus, now one of the louvre's great treasures. a farmer digging on the isle of melos
struck marble with his spade that spring —
a goddess, armless, two thousand years old,
and the world stopped to look at the thing.
they carried her to paris, to the louvre,
where she stands to this very day —
i was there when they brushed the dirt away,
and beauty came back from so far away.

a nurse is born 1820 ce florence florence nightingale is born in florence in 1820 — the girl who will one day carry a lamp through the wards of war and found modern nursing. she was born in florence, hence the name —
florence nightingale, a rich man's girl,
who heard a different calling in the night
and answered it, and changed the world.
no lamp yet. no war yet. just a baby.
but i held the thread of what would come —
the girl who'd carry light through dying wards
and make nursing what it would become.

the greeks rise 1821 ce greece in 1821 the greeks revolt against four centuries of ottoman rule, beginning a war of independence that captures europe's imagination. four hundred years beneath the turk —
and then, in the peloponnese that spring,
the priests blessed banners, the klephts came down,
and the greeks rose up to be greeks again.
it was brutal, both sides, no quarter —
but byron would die for it, and europe's heart
beat with the land of marathon and homer.
i watched a nation tear itself apart — to start.

the emperor dies alone 1821 ce st. helena napoleon dies on st. helena in may 1821, alone on his atlantic rock, dictating the legend of himself to the very end. a rock in the atlantic, a damp house,
a man who'd ruled from madrid to moscow's gate —
napoleon, fifty-one, dying of the stomach,
dictating his legend, spinning his fate.
"tete d'armee" — head of the army, he whispered,
and was gone by the evening of may the fifth —
i stood outside longwood that night,
and the century's loudest voice went quiet.

the cry becomes a country 1821 ce mexico after eleven years of war, mexico wins independence in 1821 and iturbide enters mexico city in triumph. eleven years since hidalgo rang the bell —
eleven years of war, of loss, of flame —
and then iturbide rode into mexico city,
and a nation had a flag and a name.
the viceroy's palace changed its master,
the cry of dolores found its end —
i watched the trumpets in the plaza
and a colony become a country, my friend.

liberia's first shore 1822 ce west africa in 1822 freed american slaves land on the west african coast to found the colony that will become liberia. they came home to a land they'd never seen —
freed american slaves, crossing the sea,
landing on the african coast to build
a colony of the free, for the free.
it was hard. the fever took its toll.
but they raised a flag on that foreign shore —
i watched the first boats land that year,
and a new nation's story found its door.

vesey's secret plot 1822 ce charleston denmark vesey's planned 1822 slave uprising in charleston is betrayed; he is hanged, and the south tightens its slave codes in fear. he'd bought his own freedom with lottery luck —
denmark vesey, carpenter, literate, free —
and planned a rising for the enslaved of charleston,
a city turned to liberty.
betrayed. tried in secret. hanged with thirty-four.
the south, terrified, tightened every chain —
i walked charleston's streets that summer
and felt the fear curdle into law's hard rain.

the cry of ipiranga 1822 ce brazil on september 7, 1822, prince dom pedro shouts "independence or death!" by the ipiranga river, and brazil breaks from portugal. by a little river, on september seventh,
prince dom pedro lifted up his sword
and shouted what brazil had waited to hear:
"independence or death!" — his word.
no war like the spanish colonies' —
a prince's cry, a bloodless break —
i stood on the ipiranga's bank that day
and watched a continent's giant wake.

the stone speaks again 1822 ce egypt in 1822 jean-francois champollion deciphers the rosetta stone's hieroglyphs, and ancient egypt begins to speak again after fourteen silent centuries. for fourteen centuries the hieroglyphs were silent —
pretty pictures, nobody could read.
then champollion, young and brilliant,
found the key in a cartouche's royal seed.
ptolemy. cleopatra. the names rang out,
and three thousand years began to talk —
i watched him crack the rosetta stone,
and ancient egypt learned to walk.

the emperor falls 1823 ce mexico agustin de iturbide's short-lived mexican empire collapses in 1823, and mexico becomes a republic. iturbide crowned himself in 1822,
emperor of mexico, with pomp and plume —
but emperors need more than a crown,
and his fell in less than a year's room.
the army turned, the congress fled,
and mexico became a republic instead —
i watched the crown come off that fast,
and learned how quickly glory's fled.

hands off the americas 1823 ce america in 1823 president monroe warns europe to stay out of the americas — the monroe doctrine, backed by british sea power. president monroe stood up in december
and told the crowned heads of europe plain:
the western hemisphere is closed to colonizing —
don't come back here again.
he had no army to enforce it,
no navy worth the name at sea —
but britain's fleet stood behind the words,
and the doctrine held for a century.

britain's first burmese war 1824 ce burma in 1824 britain invades burma, beginning the long carving-up of southeast asia by colonial powers. the company's troops sailed up the irrawaddy,
british and indian, red coat and brown —
burma's golden kingdom, proud and ancient,
watched the foreigners take town by town.
it was the first cut of a long carving,
southeast asia divided by the pen —
i marched with that column in the jungle heat
and saw an old world yielding to new men.

the ode to joy 1824 ce vienna totally deaf, beethoven conducts the 1824 premiere of his ninth symphony and its ode to joy — music's great hymn to brotherhood. stone deaf. he couldn't hear a note.
but beethoven stood before the choir that night
and conducted his ninth into the world —
the ode to joy, humanity's delight.
"alle menschen werden bruder" — all men brothers —
sung by voices he could only see —
i stood in that hall in vienna,
and watched a deaf man set joy free.

ayacucho ends an empire 1824 ce peru at ayacucho in december 1824 sucre destroys the last spanish army in south america — three centuries of rule, finished. high in the andes, on december ninth,
sucre's rebels met the last spanish host —
and when the smoke cleared from ayacucho,
three hundred years of empire was a ghost.
the viceroy himself was taken prisoner,
the last royal army in the americas done —
i watched the sun set on that battlefield
and on spain's american empire, gone.

the prince who defied an empire 1825 ce java in 1825 prince diponegoro launches the java war against dutch rule — five years of guerrilla warfare, the costliest colonial war of its age. prince diponegoro, javanese royalty,
watched the dutch carve up his father's land —
and raised the banner of holy war,
a kris in every loyal hand.
five years of guerrilla fire in the jungle,
the costliest colonial war they'd known —
i rode those mountain trails beside them
and watched a prince fight for his own.

a continent names a country 1825 ce bolivia in 1825 upper peru declares independence and names itself bolivia after simon bolivar — a nation named for a living liberator. upper peru was free at last,
and needed a name for what it'd become —
so they named it for the liberator,
bolivar — bolivia — and the deed was done.
a country named for a living man,
the only one on earth, they say —
i was in chuquisaca when they voted,
and a continent tipped its hat that day.

the iron horse goes public 1825 ce england in september 1825 stephenson's locomotion no. 1 hauls the first public railway train on the stockton and darlington line — the railway age begins. september twenty-seventh, county durham —
stephenson's locomotion no. 1 took the strain,
hauling wagons and six hundred passengers
down the stockton and darlington line.
twelve miles an hour, and the crowd went wild —
i rode that first public railway train,
and felt the future shake the ground:
the iron horse had left the lane.

the decembrists' doomed dawn 1825 ce russia in december 1825 young russian officers rise for a constitution in st. petersburg; the decembrist revolt is crushed and its leaders hanged or exiled. they were young officers, back from paris,
with constitutions in their heads and hope —
and on a freezing december morning
they stood in senate square and couldn't cope.
the tsar's guns spoke. five were hanged,
a hundred more marched off to siberia's snow —
i watched that dawn in petersburg
and saw russia's first revolution go.

missolonghi's last stand 1826 ce greece starving missolonghi falls to the turks in 1826, and its doomed midnight breakout becomes greece's sacred national legend. starving, out of powder, out of hope,
the people of missolonghi made their run —
a midnight breakout through the turkish lines,
and most of them died before the sun.
byron had died there two years before,
and now the town became his song —
i walked those walls where they fell,
and greece's legend grew that long.

two founders die on the fourth 1826 ce america on july 4, 1826 — fifty years to the day after independence — john adams and thomas jefferson die within hours of each other. fifty years to the day — july the fourth —
and within hours of each other, both were gone:
adams in massachusetts, jefferson in virginia,
the second and third presidents, at dawn.
adams's last words: "thomas jefferson survives" —
but jefferson had died hours before —
i stood between two houses that morning
and watched a founding generation close its door.

the first photograph 1826 ce france in 1826 niepce fixes the first permanent photograph — a blurry rooftop view exposed for eight hours — and the age of captured light begins. all day the light fell on the rooftops,
all day the pewter plate drank it in —
niepce, in his workshop at le gras,
let the sun do what no hand had been.
eight hours for one blurry image,
a rooftop view, all shadows and haze —
i watched the first permanent photograph
develop out of the morning's rays.

ohm's quiet law 1827 ce germany in 1827 georg ohm publishes his law of electric current — v=ir — the quiet foundation of the entire electrical age. no thunder. no spectacle. just a teacher
in cologne with a wire and a galvanic cell,
measuring current, patient as prayer,
until the numbers began to tell.
voltage equals current times resistance —
the law that runs the wired world —
i watched georg ohm write it down,
and the electric age quietly unfurled.

the musket wars rage 1827 ce new zealand in the 1820s hongi hika's musket-armed warriors sweep new zealand's north island in the bloodiest of the musket wars. hongi hika sailed to england, met the king,
came home with muskets by the score —
and turned them on his maori rivals
in the bloodiest tribal wars ever saw.
pa fell to volleys where mere spears had ruled,
the north island bled for a decade's span —
i watched the old warfare die that year,
and a new and terrible arithmetic began.

navarino's guns free greece 1827 ce greece in october 1827 the allied british, french, and russian fleets annihilate the ottoman navy at navarino, sealing greek independence. october twentieth, in navarino bay —
the british, french, and russians came as one,
and in four hours of point-blank cannonade
the ottoman fleet was burned and done.
it was meant to be a show of force,
a "demonstration" that got out of hand —
but i watched those ships go down in flames,
and greece's freedom washed up on the sand.

webster's american words 1828 ce america noah webster publishes his american dictionary in 1828, giving american english its own spelling and swagger. seventy thousand words, and every one
spelled the american way, not the king's —
noah webster, twenty years at his desk,
giving a young nation its own wings.
color, not colour. center, not centre.
a dictionary as a declaration —
i held that first edition in my hands:
american english, a sovereign nation.

the lion is slain 1828 ce southern africa shaka is murdered by his half-brothers in 1828, but the zulu kingdom he built marches on. his half-brothers came in the night —
dingane and mhlangana, with an assassin's art —
and shaka, the lion of the zulu,
fell with an assegai in his heart.
but the kingdom didn't fall with him;
the regiments stood, the nation held —
i watched the funeral fires that week
and the empire its founder's hands had spelled.

old hickory takes the white house 1828 ce america andrew jackson wins the presidency in 1828, bringing the frontier and the common man to power in america. the frontiersman beat the aristocrat —
jackson, the duelist, the general, the man
of the people, stormed the white house,
and the common folk came with the clan.
they trashed the place on inauguration day,
drank the punch and stood on the chairs —
i watched democracy get rowdy that march,
and the frontier take the nation's affairs.

catholics get the vote 1829 ce britain the catholic emancipation act of 1829 lets catholics sit in parliament, ending three centuries of political exclusion in britain. three hundred years of penal laws,
of catholics barred from parliament's door —
and daniel o'connell, the liberator,
forced the issue to the floor.
catholic emancipation, 1829 —
they could sit in parliament at last —
i watched the vote that cracked the wall
of three centuries of exclusion past.

the rocket wins the race 1829 ce england stephenson's rocket wins the 1829 rainhill trials at thirty miles an hour — the locomotive has definitively arrived. five locomotives lined up at rainhill
to prove which iron horse was best —
and stephenson's rocket left them all behind,
thirty miles an hour, the ultimate test.
i stood beside the track that october
and felt the wind of it go by —
the locomotive had arrived for good,
and the world would never travel by and by.

dots that let the blind read 1829 ce france in 1829 blind fifteen-year-old louis braille publishes his raised-dot alphabet, opening books to blind readers forever. he was fifteen, blind since he was three,
louis braille, a student in paris town —
and he took a soldier's night-writing code
and turned its dots upside down.
six dots. sixty-three combinations.
every letter, every word, every song —
i ran my fingers where his went,
and the sightless world read, lifelong.

three glorious days 1830 ce france paris rises in the july revolution of 1830 — three glorious days that topple charles x and crown the "citizen king" louis-philippe. three days in july, and paris rose —
barricades in every street and square,
charles x fled with his ordinances,
and the tricolor flew in the air.
they crowned louis-philippe, the "citizen king,"
with an umbrella instead of a crown —
i walked those barricades at dawn
and watched another bourbon tumble down.

the iron road between cities 1830 ce england the liverpool and manchester railway opens in 1830 — the world's first true intercity passenger railway. not a coal line this time — a passenger road,
liverpool to manchester, thirty-one miles —
the first true intercity railway,
and the crowds came out in smiles.
huskisson died beneath the wheels that day,
the first railway casualty of fame —
but i rode in those first carriages,
and travel was never again the same.

a new nation is born 1830 ce belgium brussels revolts against dutch rule in 1830, and belgium declares itself an independent kingdom. it started at the opera, they say —
auber's "la muette," a patriotic song,
and brussels rose against the dutch
and the revolt ran swift and long.
by year's end belgium was a kingdom,
independent, neutral, free —
i watched them raise the new flag
over a nation born from an opera's plea.

the hunchback of paris 1831 ce france victor hugo publishes notre-dame de paris in 1831, and his hunchbacked bell-ringer saves both a novel and a cathedral. victor hugo looked at notre-dame,
crumbling, slated for the wrecking crew —
and wrote a novel to save a cathedral,
with a bell-ringer the world fell for too.
quasimodo. esmeralda. frollo.
paris in 1482, alive and loud —
i read it in the year it came,
and the cathedral was saved by the crowd.

nat turner's rebellion 1831 ce virginia nat turner leads enslaved rebels through southampton county, virginia, in 1831; the revolt is crushed and the south's slave codes harden. he saw signs in the sun and the sky —
nat turner, preacher, led them out at night,
through southampton county, farm to farm,
a rebellion of the wronged, by lantern light.
fifty-seven whites dead. then the militia came.
turner hid for weeks, then swung —
and the south's fear hardened into law:
tighter chains for every slave, old and young.

faraday's spinning miracle 1831 ce england in 1831 michael faraday discovers electromagnetic induction — the principle behind every generator and motor of the electric age. a bookbinder's boy with no university,
michael faraday, in the royal institution's gloom,
moved a magnet through a coil of wire
and made a needle jump across the room.
electromagnetic induction — the spark
that would light the whole electric age:
motors, generators, power stations,
all born in that quiet man's cage.

the beagle sails 1831 ce england on december 27, 1831, young charles darwin boards hms beagle for the five-year voyage that will seed on the origin of species. december twenty-seventh, plymouth sound —
a little brig, a seasick young man,
charles darwin, twenty-two, the ship's naturalist,
off on a voyage with no certain plan.
five years around the world he'd go,
collecting finches, fossils, coral, bone —
i watched the beagle clear the harbor,
carrying the seed of the origin, unknown.

the vote gets wider 1832 ce britain the great reform act of 1832 sweeps away rotten boroughs and extends the vote to the middle class — the first great widening of british democracy. the rotten boroughs fell at last —
old sarum, with its seven voters, gone —
and the middle class got the franchise,
the great reform act's new dawn.
not the workers. not the women. not yet.
but the door had cracked, and through it shone
the first real widening of the vote —
i watched the old corruption come undone.

black hawk's last war 1832 ce illinois sauk chief black hawk's doomed 1832 resistance ends in slaughter on the mississippi, opening the prairie to white settlement. he came back across the mississippi
with a thousand hungry, hopeful souls —
black hawk, to plant corn in his old village,
and found the settlers had taken the shoals.
they chased him north, they cut him down
at bad axe, where the river ran red —
i watched the last resistance of the prairie
end with the sauk's bravest dead.

the lion of the desert rises 1832 ce algeria in 1832 abd al-qadir begins his fifteen-year holy war against the french conquest of algeria. the french had taken algiers in a summer —
but the interior was another land,
and abd al-qadir, scholar and horseman,
raised the tribes with a holy hand.
fifteen years he'd fight them, raid and vanish,
a desert ghost they couldn't catch —
i rode those atlas trails beside him
and watched an empire meet its match.

the chains fall across an empire 1833 ce britain in 1833 parliament abolishes slavery throughout the british empire — eight hundred thousand enslaved people walk free. eight hundred thousand people —
imagine it: a nation set free in a day —
parliament abolished slavery itself,
and the chains fell where the union jack held sway.
the planters got their compensation;
the freed got their freedom, nothing more —
but i walked the caribbean that august
and heard the singing from shore to shore.

children leave the mills — a little 1833 ce britain britain's 1833 factory act limits child labor in textile mills — the first crack in the dark satanic system. nine years old to work the night shift?
not anymore — not quite, not yet —
the factory act said: no child under nine,
and the older ones got hours, and sunset.
inspectors — four of them, for all england —
to walk the mills and check the law —
i stood outside a manchester mill that year
and watched the smallest workers walk out the door.

the penny press is born 1833 ce america the new york sun sells for a penny in 1833, and news becomes something ordinary working people can afford. six cents was the price of knowing —
until benjamin day had a cheaper plan:
the new york sun, for just a penny,
news for the ordinary working man.
he sold it on the street, he hawked the headlines,
police courts, gossip, wonders, crime —
i bought one off a newsboy's arm
and watched the news become the people's time.

pushkin's wasted dandy 1833 ce russia alexander pushkin publishes eugene onegin in 1833, the novel in verse that made russian literature. he wrote it in stanzas, a novel in verse —
eugene onegin, bored and bright and vain,
tatiana's letter, lensky's duel,
russian life in joy and pain.
pushkin, the father of it all,
gave russia her own tongue to sing —
i read it in the year it came,
and felt a literature take wing.

one market, many princes 1834 ce germany prussia's zollverein customs union of 1834 binds most german states into a single market — the economic foundation of a united germany. thirty-nine states, thirty-nine tariffs,
every border a tollbooth's hand —
until prussia's zollverein swept them away
and made one market of the german land.
the princes kept their crowns and courts,
but trade flowed free from rhine to oder —
i crossed those borders as they fell,
and felt germany gathering toward order.

the workhouse age 1834 ce britain britain's 1834 poor law herds the destitute into workhouses — relief deliberately made harsher than the lowest wage. the new poor law had a simple creed:
relief must be worse than the lowest wage —
so they built the workhouses, grim and gray,
and herded the destitute inside the cage.
families split. oakum picked. gruel served.
help with a hard and shaming edge —
i stood outside st. pancras workhouse
and watched the poor cross over the ledge.

parliament burns down 1834 ce london fire guts the houses of parliament in october 1834, and london watches its medieval legislature burn — only westminster hall survives. it started with the tally sticks —
old wooden tax records, burned in a furnace,
and the furnace overheated, and the flames
took the whole medieval palace in a trance.
london watched its legislature burn,
westminster hall alone survived the night —
i stood across the thames and watched
democracy's old house go up in light.

the great trek begins 1835 ce south africa in 1835 boer families begin the great trek north out of british-ruled cape colony, seeking their own promised land. they loaded the wagons and rolled north —
boer families, out from under british rule,
seeking their own promised land
beyond the orange river's pool.
ten thousand souls in ox-drawn laagers,
into the unknown, with bible and gun —
i rode beside those creaking wheels
and watched a wandering nation run.

tocqueville reads a nation 1835 ce america alexis de tocqueville publishes democracy in america in 1835 — the frenchman's clear-eyed portrait of the young republic. a young french aristocrat came to look —
alexis de tocqueville, twenty-six years old —
and saw america clearer than americans,
in a book both admiring and cold.
the tyranny of the majority, he warned,
and the restless hunger to be free —
i traveled with him down the mississippi
and watched him read a nation like the sea.

come and take it 1835 ce texas texans refuse to surrender a cannon at gonzales in october 1835, and the texas revolution begins. the mexicans came for the little cannon
at gonzales — come and take it, the texans said,
flying a flag with a cannon and a star,
and the first shot of the revolution sped.
santa anna answered with an army,
and texas answered with a war —
i stood on that field in october
where a republic was keeping score.

halley's comet returns 1835 ce the sky halley's comet blazes across the sky in 1835, and mark twain is born beneath it — he would die with its return in 1910. it came on schedule, as halley said it would —
a blazing sword across the autumn sky,
and in florida, missouri, a baby cried:
samuel clemens, born beneath it, high.
"i came in with halley's comet," he'd joke,
"and i expect to go out with it too" —
and he did, seventy-five years later.
i watched it blaze, and watched him too.

remember the alamo 1836 ce texas santa anna's army storms the alamo in march 1836; every defender dies, and texas gains its immortal battle cry. thirteen days they held the mission —
a hundred eighty-odd against four thousand men —
travis drew his line in the sand,
and nobody stepped back over it again.
santa anna's troops came over the walls
at dawn on march the sixth, and every defender died —
but "remember the alamo" became the cry
that carried texas through the countryside.

san jacinto's eighteen minutes 1836 ce texas sam houston routs santa anna at san jacinto in april 1836 in eighteen minutes — and texas is free. eighteen minutes. that's all it took.
houston's men came screaming from the trees —
"remember the alamo! remember goliad!" —
and santa anna's army fell to its knees.
the dictator himself was captured napping,
texas free before the sun went low —
i ran with that charge that afternoon,
the shortest battle history knows.

pickwick makes them laugh 1836 ce england dickens publishes the pickwick papers in 1836, and all england laughs with mr. pickwick — a literary star is born. a young nobody, twenty-four years old,
writing monthly numbers for a laugh —
charles dickens, and mr. pickwick,
sam weller, and the whole mad staff.
all england waited for the next installment,
laughed till they cried at pickwick's crew —
i stood in the crowd at the print shop door,
and watched a genius break through.

the girl who became queen 1837 ce britain eighteen-year-old victoria takes the british throne in 1837, beginning the sixty-three-year victorian age. eighteen years old, and woken in the night —
"the king is dead," they told the girl —
and victoria, small and sheltered,
inherited the greatest crown in the world.
she'd reign for sixty-three years,
give her name to an age, an empire, a time —
i watched her first council that morning,
a girl becoming a queen in her prime.

the panic that broke the banks 1837 ce america the panic of 1837 collapses america's banks and brings breadlines — the young nation's first great depression. the banks just stopped — doors locked, windows dark —
and the breadlines formed in every town —
the panic of 1837, america's first
great depression, dragging the nation down.
five years of hunger, of worthless paper,
of men who'd been rich begging for bread —
i walked wall street in that hard year
and watched a young republic learn to dread.

dots and dashes 1837 ce america samuel morse builds a working electric telegraph in 1837 — messages racing along a wire in dots and dashes. a painter with an obsession —
samuel morse, who'd lost his wife to time and tide,
built a machine that talked in dots and dashes,
messages racing where no horse could ride.
what hath god wrought — he'd ask it later —
but first he had to make it go:
a wire, a key, a code of clicks,
and distance dying, row by row.

rebellion in the snow 1837 ce canada patriots rise in upper and lower canada in 1837 for responsible government; both rebellions are crushed, but reform follows. they rose in the cold of december —
papineau's patriotes in lower canada's snow,
mackenzie's farmers in upper canada's fields,
for responsible government, they'd go.
both were crushed. the leaders fled or hanged.
but london listened, in the end —
i walked those snowy battlefields
where a nation's freedom found a friend.

the people's charter 1838 ce britain working men publish the people's charter in 1838 demanding the vote — chartism, the first mass workers' movement, is born. six points on a single page —
a vote for every man, the ballot secret, pay for mps —
the people's charter, published in may,
and the working men took to the streets.
chartism — the first mass workers' movement,
a million signatures, and then some more —
i marched with them to parliament's door
and watched the people's charter roar.

oliver asks for more 1838 ce england dickens publishes oliver twist in 1838, and little oliver's "please, sir, i want some more" shames a nation into seeing its poor. "please, sir, i want some more" —
a workhouse boy, holding out his bowl,
and all england felt the shame of it,
dickens's oliver, body and soul.
the parish beadles, fagin's den,
the artful dodger picking pockets in the street —
i read it as the numbers came,
and a nation couldn't look away from the beat.

the trail where they cried 1838 ce america in 1838 federal troops force the cherokee west at bayonet point; thousands die on the trail of tears. they marched them at bayonet point —
the cherokee, sixteen thousand strong,
a thousand miles to oklahoma,
through winter's cold and summer's long.
four thousand died along the way —
of hunger, cold, and broken heart —
i walked that trail of tears with them,
and watched a nation's cruelest art.

blood river 1838 ce south africa outnumbered voortrekkers defeat the zulu at blood river in december 1838, and a nation-shaping afrikaner myth is born. four hundred sixty-four voortrekkers
in a laager of wagons, guns in hand —
against ten thousand zulu warriors
on the banks where the river ran red with the land.
they called it blood river after,
and made a covenant that day —
i stood upon that bloody bank
and watched a nation-shaping myth hold sway.

the world learns to pose 1839 ce france daguerre announces the daguerreotype in 1839 — sharp, silvery photographs that anyone could sit for. daguerre stood before the academy
with a silvered plate, sharp as sight —
hold still for thirty minutes, please,
and the camera will steal your light.
no more blurry eight-hour rooftops —
portraits, clear as morning air —
i sat for one that very year,
and watched the world learn how to stare.

the opium goes up in smoke 1839 ce china in 1839 commissioner lin zexu seizes and destroys foreign opium at canton, and britain answers with warships — the opium war begins. commissioner lin zexu meant business —
twenty thousand chests of british opium,
seized at canton and burned and drowned,
to save his people from the poison's gloom.
britain answered with warships, not words —
the first opium war had begun —
i watched the smoke rise off the pearl river
and an old empire come undone.

reform from the throne 1839 ce ottoman empire in 1839 the young ottoman sultan proclaims the tanzimat reforms, promising equality and modern law to all his subjects. a sixteen-year-old sultan on the throne,
abdulmejid, with reformers at his side —
proclaimed the tanzimat: equality,
modern law, for all, both far and wide.
muslim, christian, jew — one law, he promised,
an empire remade from the top —
i heard it read in the rose garden
and watched an old world try to stop.

the treaty of waitangi 1840 ce new zealand maori chiefs and the british crown sign the treaty of waitangi in february 1840, founding new zealand — and arguing over its meaning ever since. on a lawn at waitangi, in february,
maori chiefs made their marks one by one —
a treaty with the british crown,
and new zealand's founding day begun.
two versions, two languages, two meanings —
and the argument's been running ever since —
i stood on that lawn that morning
and watched a nation born, and tense.

the penny black 1840 ce britain the world's first adhesive postage stamp, the penny black, goes on sale in may 1840 — a penny to send a letter anywhere in britain. a penny to send a letter anywhere —
rowland hill's mad idea, they said —
but on may the first the penny black went on sale,
with the young queen's head in black and red.
the mail exploded. everyone wrote.
distance shrank to a penny's worth —
i posted one of the very first,
and watched the letter conquer earth.

two canadas, one parliament 1840 ce canada britain merges upper and lower canada into a single province in 1840 after the rebellions — one parliament for two peoples. after the rebellions, london's answer:
merge them — upper, lower, one province, one crown —
one parliament for both canadas,
and the french fact tamped further down.
it didn't work the way they planned —
the french held firm, the union strained —
i sat in that first united house
and watched two solitudes remain.

the moon, photographed 1840 ce new york in 1840 john draper takes the first photograph of the moon — twenty minutes of exposure, and the heavens become capturable. john draper aimed his camera at the sky —
a daguerreotype plate, twenty minutes of light —
and caught the moon, cratered and silver,
the first photograph of the night.
astronomy would never be the same;
the heavens could be captured, kept, and shown —
i stood beside him on that rooftop
and watched the moon become our own.

the rock becomes a colony 1841 ce china britain seizes hong kong island in 1841 during the opium war — a barren rock that will become one of the world's great harbors. a barren rock at the pearl river's mouth —
hong kong, "fragrant harbor," nothing there —
but britain seized it in the opium war,
and planted a colony in the air.
nobody guessed what it would become,
a harbor of millions, a merchant's dream —
i stood on that bare rock that year
and watched an empire's farthest scheme.

the frozen sea named ross 1841 ce antarctica in 1841 james clark ross sails into the great antarctic sea that bears his name, reaching nearer the south magnetic pole than anyone before. james clark ross sailed further south
than any ship had ever gone before —
into the great icy sea, past the volcanoes,
to the edge of the ice shelf's shore.
he named it for himself, as explorers do,
and found the magnetic pole's near place —
i stood on that deck in the polar light
and watched him map the bottom of the world with grace.

poe invents the detective 1841 ce america edgar allan poe publishes "the murders in the rue morgue" in 1841 — the first detective story ever written. a locked room in the rue morgue,
a brutal murder, no way in or out —
and c. auguste dupin, with logic cold,
figured what it was all about.
edgar allan poe invented him —
the first detective ever put to page —
i read it in graham's magazine that year,
and watched a whole genre take the stage.

livingstone enters africa 1841 ce africa in 1841 young missionary david livingstone lands in africa, beginning thirty years of exploration across the continent. he was twenty-eight, a scottish doctor,
a missionary with a mapmaker's soul —
david livingstone landed in africa
and made the continent his goal.
thirty years he'd walk it, river by river,
chasing the nile's source to the end —
i watched him step ashore that year,
and africa gained its strangest friend.

the retreat from kabul 1842 ce afghanistan in january 1842 britain's army retreats from kabul through the afghan snows; of sixteen thousand, one survivor rides into jalalabad. sixteen thousand souls marched out of kabul —
soldiers, wives, and children, in the snow —
and the passes closed behind them
with jezails on every height below.
one man rode into jalalabad —
dr. brydon, on a dying horse, alone —
i watched him come through the gates,
the sole survivor, to tell what the snows had known.

children out of the mines 1842 ce britain britain's 1842 mines act bans women and young children from working underground in the coal mines. they sent them down at five years old —
girls and boys, hauling coal in the dark,
crawling where no grown man could go,
little ghosts with a candle's spark.
the mines act said: no more —
no women, no children, underground —
i stood at a pithead in yorkshire
and watched the smallest miners come unbound.

the unequal treaty 1842 ce china the 1842 treaty of nanking ends the opium war, cedes hong kong, and forces china open — the first of the "unequal treaties." the war was lost before it started —
british guns against chinese walls of old —
so at nanking they signed the paper:
hong kong ceded, five ports sold.
the first of the "unequal treaties,"
extraterritorial, open, bound —
i watched the seals go on that page,
and china learn what defeat had found.

britain takes sindh 1843 ce india charles napier conquers sindh in 1843 and sends home the famous one-word dispatch "peccavi" — latin for "i have sinned" (i have sindh). charles napier took sindh with a swagger
and sent home the dispatch of the age —
one latin word: "peccavi" —
i have sinned. a pun for history's page.
(i have sindh — get it? he got it.)
the ameers fell, the indus ran british —
i marched with that column in the heat
and watched an empire's joke turn vicious.

the great migration west 1843 ce america in 1843 a thousand settlers roll out for oregon in the largest wagon train yet — the great migration west. a thousand settlers, a hundred wagons,
rolling out for oregon's green shore —
the great migration, the largest train yet,
and the trail got longer than before.
six months of dust and river crossings,
of graves dug shallow by the way —
i walked beside those wagons westward
and watched america move that day.

a christmas carol 1843 ce england dickens publishes a christmas carol in 1843, and scrooge's redemption warms a million hearths — inventing the modern christmas spirit. he wrote it in six weeks, fevered, fast —
dickens, with the poor of london on his mind —
and scrooge walked out of the counting-house
and left his miserly self behind.
the ghosts, the goose, tiny tim's crutch —
a million hearths have warmed to it since —
i read it by a fire that christmas,
and watched a story make the cold relent.

what hath god wrought 1844 ce america on may 24, 1844, morse taps "what hath god wrought" over the first american telegraph line, washington to baltimore. may twenty-fourth, washington to baltimore —
morse tapped the key, and vail received:
"what hath god wrought" — the bible's words,
the first message the wire ever breathed.
forty miles in an instant. think of it.
news that once took days now took a breath —
i stood at both ends of that wire
and watched distance suffer a kind of death.

a club for young workers 1844 ce england in 1844 draper's clerk george williams founds the ymca in london for the city's lonely young working men. george williams was a draper's clerk,
twenty-two, in london's lonely sprawl —
and he saw the young men drowning there,
in gin and gambling, with no one to call.
so he started a club — prayer, reading, friendship —
the young men's christian association —
i sat in that first meeting room
and watched a quiet kind of salvation.

across the burning outback 1844 ce australia in 1844 ludwig leichhardt leads an expedition across australia's harsh interior to the northern sea, crossing the continent's burning heart. leichhardt led them into the interior —
an expedition no white man had survived before,
across the burning heart of australia
to the northern sea's far shore.
they ate their horses. they drank mud.
but they made it — port essington, at last —
i walked that track of thirst and fire
and watched the outback's secret passed.

the rules of baseball 1845 ce new york in 1845 alexander cartwright writes down the first rules of baseball for his knickerbocker club — ninety feet, nine men, three strikes. alexander cartwright wrote them down —
ninety feet between the bases, nine men a side,
three strikes, three outs, foul lines marked —
and the knickerbockers took them with pride.
no more town ball, no more chaos —
a game with rules, a diamond true —
i stood on that elysian field
and watched america's game come through.

the blight begins 1845 ce ireland potato blight blackens ireland's fields in 1845, beginning the great famine — a million dead, a million fled. it came as a blackness on the leaves —
the potato blight, in a wet september —
and by winter the fields were rot,
and ireland would always remember.
a million dead. a million fled.
the great famine, the hunger's reign —
i walked those blackened fields that fall
and watched a nation drown in rain.

war on the sutlej 1845 ce india in 1845 the british clash with the sikh khalsa along the sutlej river in the first anglo-sikh war — four hard-fought winter battles. the khalsa was the finest native army
asia had ever put in the field —
sikh artillery, sikh discipline,
and the british barely made them yield.
along the sutlej's banks they fought it,
four battles in a winter's span —
i stood in the smoke at ferozeshah
and watched two empires' fates ran.

texas joins the union 1845 ce texas the united states annexes the republic of texas in 1845, and mexico reaches for its guns. nine years a republic, lone and proud —
but the debts were deep and mexico still claimed —
so texas voted to join the union,
and the twenty-eighth star was named.
mexico called it theft and reached for guns;
the border would bleed for what they'd done —
i watched the flag go up at austin
and a republic's solo run was done.

war between neighbors 1846 ce mexico american and mexican troops clash on the rio grande in 1846, beginning the mexican-american war. it started on the rio grande —
a skirmish in disputed land, they said —
and polk had his war with mexico,
"american blood on american soil" shed.
two years of it, from palo alto
to the halls of montezuma's fall —
i marched that road with taylor's men
and watched a neighbor's empire crawl.

the smithsonian is born 1846 ce washington james smithson's bequest founds the smithsonian institution in 1846 — "the increase and diffusion of knowledge," the nation's attic. james smithson never set foot in america —
an english scientist, rich and strange —
but he left his fortune to a nation he'd never seen,
"for the increase and diffusion of knowledge" — the range.
congress argued for eight years what to do,
then built it: the smithsonian, the nation's attic —
i watched the cornerstone go down
and a country's memory get systematic.

the stitch that sewed the world 1846 ce america elias howe patents the sewing machine in 1846, making ready-made clothes possible and stitching the modern garment world. elias howe had a dream of cannibals —
spears with holes in their tips, can you believe? —
and woke with the lockstitch in his head,
the sewing machine the world would need.
he patented it in september,
and the needle learned to fly —
i watched that first machine stitch straight,
and ready-made clothes wave tailor's prices goodbye.

the pain killer 1846 ce boston in october 1846 a boston dentist demonstrates ether anesthesia in surgery — and the agony of the operating table begins to end. october sixteenth, mass general —
a dentist named morton, a flask of ether,
a patient breathing deep, then nothing —
no scream when the surgeon's knife went neither.
"gentlemen, this is no humbug" —
warren said it, and the room went still —
i stood in that operating theater
and watched surgery lose its agony's will.

zion in the desert 1847 ce utah in july 1847 brigham young's mormon pioneers reach the salt lake valley — "this is the place" — and build zion in the desert. a thousand miles of prairie, mountain, desert —
the mormon pioneers, driven from nauvoo,
followed brigham young to the salt lake valley,
and he looked out and said: "this is the place. this'll do."
they planted crops in the desert's edge,
made the wasteland bloom with will —
i stood beside him on that overlook,
and watched a people bend the land to will.

liberia raises its flag 1847 ce west africa liberia declares itself an independent republic in 1847 — africa's first, founded by freed american slaves. twenty-five years after the first boats landed,
the colony declared itself a state —
liberia, independent republic,
africa's first, opening the gate.
joseph jenkins roberts, the first president,
a freedman's son, raised the flag that day —
i stood on that shore in july
and watched a free black nation have its say.

sleep without pain 1847 ce scotland in 1847 james simpson discovers chloroform anesthesia, and childbirth loses its terror. james simpson tried it on himself first —
chloroform, in his edinburgh dining room —
then gave it to a woman in childbirth,
and took away the delivery room's gloom.
the churches called it against god's will —
"in sorrow thou shalt bring forth," they cried —
but the mothers voted with their relief,
and painless sleep spread far and wide.

gold at sutter's mill 1848 ce california in january 1848 james marshall spots gold flakes in sutter's millrace in california — and the gold rush begins. james marshall saw it in the millrace —
a flake that didn't look like river stone —
he bit it, and it bent, not broke:
gold, in john sutter's mill, alone.
he tried to keep it quiet. he couldn't.
the word ran faster than any horse —
i was there that january morning
when the world changed its course.

a continent redrawn 1848 ce mexico the 1848 treaty of guadalupe hidalgo ends the mexican-american war; mexico cedes half its land to the united states. the war was over; the treaty waited
at guadalupe hidalgo, signed in february —
mexico ceded half its territory:
california, texas, the whole southwestern query.
fifteen million dollars for half a nation,
the map of north america redrawn —
i watched the seals go on that paper,
and a continent wake to a new dawn.

a manifesto for the workers 1848 ce london marx and engels publish the communist manifesto in london in 1848 — "workers of the world, unite!" two germans in a london print shop —
marx, thirty, engels, twenty-seven, young —
wrote the pamphlet that would shake the world:
"workers of the world, unite!" — well-sung.
"a spectre is haunting europe," it began —
the communist manifesto, twenty-three pages thin —
i held a first edition in my hands,
and felt the century's argument begin.

february days in paris 1848 ce paris barricades rise in paris in february 1848, king louis-philippe flees, and the second republic is born. the banquets were banned, so paris built
barricades instead — february's cold days —
and louis-philippe, the citizen king,
fled to england in a cab, in a haze.
the second republic was proclaimed at the hotel de ville,
lamartine reading to the crowd —
i stood among them in the rain
and heard a nation thinking out loud.

metternich flees in disguise 1848 ce vienna revolution drives prince metternich from vienna in march 1848, and the old conservative order of europe trembles. the students marched on the thirteenth of march,
and the old order trembled in its shoes —
prince metternich, the system's architect,
fled vienna in disguise, with the evening news.
thirty-three years he'd held europe together
with congresses, spies, and fear —
i watched his carriage slip away at dusk,
and the old empires' trembling year.

the rights of women 1848 ce new york three hundred gather at seneca falls in july 1848 and demand the vote for women — the birth of the organized women's rights movement. three hundred people in a wesleyan chapel —
seneca falls, in july's heat —
elizabeth cady stanton read the declaration:
all men and women are created equal, complete.
they demanded the vote. the men laughed.
frederick douglass stood and spoke them through —
i sat in that chapel as they signed,
and the women's movement found its voice, true.

the first woman doctor 1849 ce america elizabeth blackwell graduates first in her class in 1849 — america's first woman medical doctor. they let her in as a joke, they said —
geneva medical college, a dare —
but elizabeth blackwell finished first in her class,
and walked out with the degree to spare.
america's first woman m.d.,
in a profession that said she didn't belong —
i watched her take that diploma,
and the door cracked open, hard and long.

the punjab falls 1849 ce india britain crushes the sikhs in 1849 and annexes the punjab — the last free kingdom of india is gone, and the koh-i-noor goes to london. the khalsa fought like lions at chillianwala —
the bloodiest day the british knew in india —
but at gujrat the guns decided,
and the punjab fell, and the sikh star
went out. the koh-i-noor went to london.
the last free kingdom of india was gone —
i walked that field when the smoke had cleared,
and an old world's final dawn.

the revolution is crushed 1849 ce hungary russian troops help austria crush hungary's 1848–49 revolution; its leaders die on the gallows at arad. kossuth's hungary had fought for a year —
a nation risen, a constitution, a war —
but the tsar sent two hundred thousand russians
to help austria settle the score.
vilagos. the surrender. the gallows at arad.
thirteen generals hanged in october's gloom —
i stood in budapest that autumn
and watched a revolution meet its doom.

the forty-niners 1849 ce california eighty thousand gold-hungry argonauts flood california in 1849 — the greatest gold rush the world had ever seen. eighty thousand in a single year —
by ship around the horn, by wagon, by foot —
the argonauts, the forty-niners,
chasing gold with pick and pan and soot.
san francisco went from village to madhouse,
prices madder than the gold —
i panned beside them in the sierra streams,
and watched the greatest rush the world would hold.

the bargain that delayed war 1850 ce america the compromise of 1850 admits california as a free state but tightens the hunt for runaway slaves — delaying the civil war by a decade. henry clay's last great compromise —
california free, the territories choose,
a tougher fugitive slave law for the south,
and everybody got something to lose.
it held the union together for ten years,
a bargain built on borrowed time —
i watched the senate vote it through,
and heard the clock begin to chime.

the heavenly king rises 1850 ce china in 1850 hong xiuquan proclaims his heavenly kingdom, lighting the fuse of the taiping rebellion — the bloodiest civil war in human history. hong xiuquan had failed the exams four times —
then dreamed he was god's chinese son,
jesus's younger brother, come to cleanse
the demons — and the qing would come undone.
he proclaimed the heavenly kingdom,
taiping — great peace — in guangxi's hills —
i heard that proclamation read aloud,
and the fuse of the bloodiest war lit its fills.

the scarlet letter 1850 ce america i was in boston when hawthorne's novel of sin and shame became america's first great book. i stood in the boston bookshop the week it came out,
and watched a clerk slide it across the counter like contraband.
a woman's shame, stitched in red on grey cloth —
hawthorne had done what no american had dared:
written a book the old world had to take seriously.
the letter burned. the colony watched. the reader knew
the minister's secret before the last page said it.
i bought two copies. one for the shelf,
one to remember the day our literature grew teeth.

california joins the union 1850 ce america i was in gold-rush san francisco when california became the 31st state and tipped the nation's balance. thirty-first star, sewn on in a hurry —
they hadn't even finished counting the gold dust
before the statehood papers were signed.
i walked the san francisco mud streets that fall,
tents going up faster than the rain could knock them down,
and heard the news read out in a saloon
to a cheer that shook the bottles off the shelves.
free soil, by a hair. the south felt the scale tip
and started sharpening its knives that same night.

the fugitive slave act 1850 ce america i saw the fugitive slave act read aloud in boston, and watched the north turn cold against the south. i watched them read it in a boston meeting hall,
and the room went so quiet you could hear the rain.
now every man in the north was a slave-catcher by law,
every runaway a crime walking upright.
i saw a mother carried back to georgia in chains
while the crowd that couldn't stop it wept openly in the street.
they meant it to save the union.
instead they taught the north what the south really was —
and the road to war got shorter by ten years.

the taiping rise 1851 ce china i heard hong xiuquan preach in southern china before his holy army rose and twenty million died. he failed the exams four times, hong xiuquan —
then dreamed he was the younger brother of jesus christ.
i heard him preach in the south, and the poor believed him,
because he told them the manchus were devils
and heaven was coming down to earth.
they rose by the hundreds of thousands.
nanjing would fall to them. twenty million would die —
more than any war the world had ever seen.
i walked through villages afterward where no dog barked,
no child cried, nothing moved but the wind.

singer's sewing machine 1851 ce america i watched singer's machine sew a shirt in an hour and saw factory speed come into the home. an hour. a whole shirt in an hour.
i stood in singer's new york workshop and watched the needle fly,
stitch after stitch, never tiring, never pricking its finger.
the women who'd sewn by candlelight for pennies
looked at it the way you'd look at a ghost.
some wept. some laughed. one old seamstress
put her hand on the humming machine and said,
"there goes my living, and there goes my backache."
both were true. the factory had come home.

moby-dick 1851 ce america i bought a remaindered copy of moby-dick the year it flopped and read it on the ocean crossing home. call me ishmael — i read it the year it failed.
three thousand copies printed, and the world yawned.
i found melville's great white whale of a book
gathering dust in a london shop for a shilling,
and i bought it and read it straight through on the crossing home.
the sea in it was bigger than the sea outside.
ahab's madness, the pequod's doomed crew,
a whole philosophy harpooned onto one white back.
nobody wanted it then. i wanted it enough for all of them.

the channel cable 1851 ce europe i watched the first channel telegraph cable pay out from the deck and link london and paris in minutes. a wire under the sea, dover to calais —
i watched them pay it out from the deck, fathom by fathom,
copper sinking into the cold green dark.
then london spoke, and paris answered in minutes,
not days. the water between the two old enemies
had been crossed by something thinner than a finger.
i stood on the cliff and thought: the world just got smaller,
and there is no going back to the wide, slow world.
messages now fly. armies will follow.

uncle tom's cabin 1852 ce america i watched stowe's novel sweep the nation, 300,000 copies in a year, and felt the country split open. three hundred thousand copies in a year —
i never saw anything like it.
women weeping on trains, men arguing in taverns,
the whole country reading the same story at once.
stowe took the slave's suffering and set it down
in plain words on a million kitchen tables,
and the north finally saw what it had been looking away from.
years later lincoln would meet her and say,
"so you're the little lady who started this great war."
he wasn't joking. neither was she.

napoleon iii takes the crown 1852 ce france i watched louis-napoleon crown himself in paris and remembered how his uncle's dream had ended. i was in paris when louis-napoleon put the crown on his own head —
his uncle's trick, second time around.
the crowds cheered. the boulevards were widened,
the railways multiplied, the empire glittered.
but i remembered the first napoleon, and the graves from moscow to waterloo,
and i thought: france has hired the same dream twice.
it would end the same way — in a german field,
with the emperor a prisoner and the dream in ruins.
empires of boulevards are still empires.

india's first railway 1853 ce india i rode india's first train from bombay to thane with crowds who had never seen a locomotive. twenty-one miles, bombay to thane —
i rode it with a crowd that had never seen a train.
the engine breathed fire and the people cheered,
children running alongside until the smoke beat them.
an iron road across india. the british built it
to move their troops and their cotton faster,
but the rails didn't care who laid them.
i looked at the faces pressed to the windows
and thought: this road will carry more than freight.
one day it will carry a nation.

the black ships 1853 ce japan i stood on the tokyo bay shore when perry's black warships forced closed japan to open. four black hulls in tokyo bay, smoke on the water —
i was on the shore when perry's ships dropped anchor.
two hundred years of closed doors, and now
american guns politely asking to come in.
the japanese officials came out in their fine robes,
all ceremony and thin smiles, while the cannon
sat silent in their ports like a held breath.
i watched a fisherman stare at the steam frigates
and whisper to his son, "the world has changed."
he was right. nothing in japan would be small again.

the crimean war begins 1853 ce crimea i watched the allied fleets sail for the crimea over a quarrel about church keys in jerusalem. they called it a war over holy places in jerusalem —
monks arguing about keys to a church door.
i watched the british and french fleets sail east,
bands playing, flags flying, everyone sure of a short war.
the ottoman empire was dying, russia wanted the pieces,
and europe wanted russia stopped.
so they sailed to the crimea, to a peninsula most of them
couldn't find on a map, and the dying began —
of cold, of cholera, of generals' stupidity —
long before the first great battle was fought.

the treaty of kanagawa 1854 ce japan i was at kanagawa when japan's seclusion ended with a treaty signed beneath american guns. they signed it under the guns — i was there at kanagawa,
the american warships riding at anchor in plain sight.
coal for the steamers, water, a harbor open to trade.
the shogun's men signed with all the old courtesy,
bows and seals and formal phrases,
while perry's marines stood at parade rest behind him.
two hundred years of seclusion ended with a signature
no one in that room truly wanted to give.
i thought of the fisherman's son. his world had changed indeed.

the killer pump 1854 ce england i walked soho's streets with john snow as he mapped cholera deaths to a single pump handle. soho was dying, and john snow drew a map.
i walked those streets with him — broad street, the pump,
each cholera death marked as a black dot,
clustering around the handle like iron to a magnet.
he didn't have a microscope powerful enough,
didn't know the germ, only the pattern.
"take the handle off," he told the parish board.
they did. the dying stopped.
i watched him stare at his dotted map afterward —
a whole new science born from dots on paper.

the charge of the light brigade 1854 ce crimea i watched the light brigade ride into the wrong valley at balaclava — magnificent and meaningless. "someone had blundered" — tennyson wrote it later,
but i saw it happen at balaclava.
six hundred horsemen, sabres out, riding straight
down the wrong valley into the mouths of the russian guns.
the orders were confused. the courage was not.
i watched them ride through the fire and back,
a third of them gone, the valley full of riderless horses.
half a league, half a league — it was magnificent
and it was meaningless, and i never forgot the difference.

nightingale at scutari 1854 ce crimea i was in the scutari hospital when nightingale arrived with her nurses and her lamp. she came with thirty-eight nurses and a lamp,
and found men dying on bare floors in their own filth.
i was in the scutari hospital that winter —
the stench, the rats, the wounds gone green.
florence nightingale walked the wards all night,
writing down everything, counting everything,
scrubbing the place into something like a hospital.
more men were dying of disease than of russian bullets,
and she knew it, and she proved it with numbers.
the lady with the lamp. the soldiers kissed her shadow.

the fall of sevastopol 1855 ce crimea i watched the allies march into ruined sevastopol after the eleven-month siege broke russia's fortress. eleven months of siege, and then the great fortress fell.
i stood on the heights and watched the allies march in —
french, british, turks — through streets of rubble
where the russian guns had finally gone silent.
the harbor was full of sunken ships, scuttled by their own crews.
sevastopol had bled russia white to hold it.
now it was a ruin, and the war was a ruin,
and everyone on both sides was counting a cost
no church-key quarrel could ever have been worth.

leaves of grass 1855 ce america i met whitman in brooklyn the summer he self-published the twelve poems that invented the american voice. he set the type himself. he printed it himself.
twelve wild poems, no publisher willing —
i met whitman in brooklyn that summer, big bearded man,
handing out his own book like a street preacher.
"i celebrate myself, and sing myself" —
nobody in america had ever written like that,
loose and vast and shameless as the continent.
the critics called it filth. emerson called it genius.
i read it on the ferry and felt the language
stretch like a man waking up from a long sleep.

bessemer's steel 1855 ce england i watched bessemer's converter turn cheap iron to cheap steel with a blast of air — and thought of bridges and guns. a blast of air through molten iron —
that's all it was. i watched bessemer do it
in his sheffield works, the converter tipping,
the white-hot metal roaring as the air burned the carbon out.
cheap iron in, cheap steel out, in minutes
instead of days. the foreman laughed out loud.
i thought of every bridge unbuilt, every rail unlaid,
every tower still a dream for want of steel —
and then i thought of the guns. steel makes both.
the steel age began that day, for better and worse.

the treaty of paris 1856 ce europe i watched the russians leave the paris peace talks, defeated — and turn inward toward freeing the serfs. they signed the peace in paris, and the black sea
was declared neutral — no warships, no fortresses.
i watched the russian delegation leave the hall
with the walk of men who'd been bled and knew it.
the war had cost them everything and gained them nothing.
now russia turned inward, brooding over reform,
over serfs, over the question the defeat had forced:
why did we lose? the answer would free twenty-three million souls.
peace treaties end wars. this one started a reckoning.

the arrow war 1856 ce china i was in canton when britain and france attacked china again over a seized ship and forced more trade. a seized ship called the arrow, a torn flag —
excuse enough. i was in canton when the british guns opened up,
and then the french joined in, and the second opium war began.
they wanted more ports, more trade, more opium sold legally.
china wanted to be left alone. china lost.
i walked through the burned suburbs afterward,
past the bodies of men who'd died for a flag on a smuggler's boat,
and i understood: this was never about the arrow.
it was about an empire that had decided china was a shop to be broken into.

madame bovary 1856 ce france i read madame bovary in paris the winter it scandalized france and remade the novel. flaubert spent five years on one bored housewife —
i read it in paris the winter it scandalized everyone.
emma bovary, dreaming of romance in a provincial town,
ruining herself for love affairs that weren't love.
the government prosecuted him for obscenity.
acquitted — and the novel was changed forever,
because flaubert had shown you could write a masterpiece
about an ordinary woman's ordinary discontent,
every sentence polished like a stone.
