i closed the book and the paris street outside
looked flatter, duller, and more real.

dred scott 1857 ce america i was in washington when the supreme court ruled black people could not be citizens — and hardened the north for war. i was in washington when the decision came down —
a black man, the court said, had no rights a white man need respect,
could not be a citizen, could not sue for freedom.
and slavery could go anywhere, into any territory.
dred scott had lived on free soil for years. it didn't matter.
i watched the abolitionists' faces as the news spread —
not grief, but a cold, hardening anger.
the court thought it had settled the slavery question forever.
instead it had signed the warrant for a war.

the sepoy rebellion 1857 ce india i was in meerut when the sepoys mutinied and all of northern india rose against british rule. it started with a rumor — rifle cartridges greased with cow and pig fat,
an insult to hindu and muslim alike.
i was in meerut when the sepoys mutinied in may,
shot their officers, and marched on delhi.
then all of northern india rose — princes, peasants, soldiers —
a hundred years of british rule cracking in a summer.
the cartridges were real. the anger was older.
i watched the telegraph wires come down and the empire's nerves go with them,
and i knew: india would never be the same, whatever happened next.

the siege of lucknow 1857 ce india i was inside lucknow's residency through five months of siege, waiting for a relief that barely came. five months behind the residency walls —
i got in before the ring closed, and i stayed.
women and children in the cellars, men on the shattered walls,
the rebels' guns never stopping, the heat never breaking.
we ate the horses. we buried the dead in the garden.
every day the relief column was coming; every day it wasn't.
when it finally came, the survivors walked out like ghosts,
too thin to cheer. i never forgot the sound of that siege —
the constant, patient thunder of guns that wanted us dead.

delhi retaken 1857 ce india i followed the british columns into delhi and watched the great rebellion of 1857 die in blood and vengeance. they blew the kashmir gate in september and went in with the bayonet —
i followed the british columns into delhi,
street by street, house by house, no quarter given.
the old mughal emperor was dragged from his hiding place,
his sons shot dead in front of him.
the rebellion died in those streets, drowned in its own blood
and in the vengeance that followed — villages burned,
men hanged from trees along the roads for miles.
delhi was retaken. but the india the british had ruled so easily
was gone forever. they would rule the next ninety years by fear.

the atlantic cable 1858 ce atlantic i was aboard when the first atlantic cable was spliced and victoria's greeting crawled across the ocean. two thousand miles of copper under the ocean —
i was on the ship when they spliced the ends together,
and the first message crawled across the atlantic.
queen victoria to president buchanan: greetings, hopes for peace.
it took hours, letter by letter, but it came through.
the old world and the new, joined by a thread on the seabed.
(the cable died within weeks — but the idea lived.
they'd be back, and next time it would hold.)
i stood on deck that night and thought of all the ships
that had carried letters for months. never again.

the lincoln–douglas debates 1858 ce america i followed lincoln and douglas across illinois and watched a lanky lawyer become a national name. seven towns in illinois, crowds of thousands in the mud —
i followed them from ottawa to alton.
douglas, the famous one, smooth and certain.
lincoln, the lanky lawyer, all elbows and plain talk,
asking one question douglas couldn't answer clean:
can the people vote slavery out, or can't they?
douglas won the senate seat. lincoln won something bigger —
a national name, and a moral argument the whole country heard.
i watched him fold his long frame onto a train afterward,
tired, defeated, and on his way to the presidency.

the crown takes india 1858 ce india i was in calcutta when victoria's proclamation dissolved the company and the raj began. the east india company was finished — a trading firm
that had conquered a subcontinent was dissolved by parliament.
i was in calcutta when the proclamation was read:
victoria was queen now, directly, no middleman.
same rulers, new letterhead — but the promise was read aloud
to crowds in every province: no more annexations,
respect for the princes, for religion, for custom.
promises. i watched the officials' faces as they read them.
some believed. most were just glad the shooting had stopped.
the raj began that day — ninety years of it.

solferino 1859 ce italy i was at solferino the day after the battle and watched dunant's horror become the red cross. a swiss businessman came to ask a favor of napoleon iii
and walked into a battlefield instead.
i was at solferino the day after — forty thousand wounded,
lying in the fields, no one to help them, dying of thirst between the lines.
henri dunant didn't look away. he organized the villagers,
bought bandages with his own money, and went home haunted.
out of that hauntedness came an idea: the red cross,
neutral medics, mercy as a rule of war.
i helped carry water that day. i never forgot the faces.

oil at titusville 1859 ce america i reached titusville within weeks of drake's strike and watched the petroleum age begin in mud and speculation. sixty-nine feet down in pennsylvania dirt,
edwin drake's drill struck oil — and the modern world began to leak upward.
i was in titusville within the month: derricks everywhere,
men drunk on the smell of it, land worth fortunes overnight.
they'd been drilling for salt water and found something better.
rock oil, they called it. for lamps at first. then engines.
then everything. i stood in the mud among the speculators
and thought: they have no idea what they've uncorked.
the whole next century would run on this black stuff.

john brown's raid 1859 ce america i was at harpers ferry when brown's raid failed — and watched a hanged man become the war's marching song. he seized the arsenal at harpers ferry with twenty-one men,
meaning to arm the slaves and start the uprising.
i was in the town when the marines stormed the engine house —
robert e. lee commanding, by a strange twist.
brown was captured, tried, and hanged in december,
and on the scaffold he was calm as a man going to church.
the south called him a murderer. the north made him a martyr.
his body lies a-mouldering, they would sing —
and his soul went marching straight into a war.

on the origin of species 1859 ce england i was in london the week darwin's origin sold out on day one and the world started arguing. i was in london the week darwin's book went on sale —
all 1,250 copies gone the first day.
twenty years of barnacles and pigeons and finches,
poured into one quiet, careful argument:
species change, nature selects, we are all kin.
the bishops thundered. the scientists split.
a lady at a dinner party said she hoped it wasn't true,
but if it was, she hoped it wouldn't become widely known.
it became widely known. the world has been arguing
about that quiet book ever since — and will be, forever.

the pony express 1860 ce america i watched pony express riders tear out of missouri on the 1,900-mile gallop to california. eighteen months. that's all it lasted —
but what eighteen months.
i watched a rider tear out of st. joseph, missouri,
leather mail pouch slapping his side, 1,900 miles ahead of him.
ten days to california, changing horses every ten miles,
riding through desert and paiute country at a full gallop.
young, wiry, half-starved — that was the advertisement,
and it was true. the telegraph killed it in '61,
wire doing in hours what horses did in days.
but for a year and a half, the mail rode like the wind.

garibaldi's thousand 1860 ce italy i sailed with garibaldi's thousand red shirts to sicily and marched behind them to naples. a thousand red shirts in two old steamers —
i sailed with them from genoa to sicily.
garibaldi, the lion-man with the poncho and the cigar,
landing at marsala against a kingdom's army
with a thousand volunteers and a dream of italy.
and the dream won. town after town rose for them,
the bourbon kingdom melted like wax,
and by autumn they'd taken naples itself.
a thousand men conquered a kingdom.
i marched in the dust behind them and thought:
this is what happens when a people decides.

the summer palace burns 1860 ce china i watched the summer palace burn for three days outside beijing — a humiliation china would never forget. they looted it first — soldiers staggering out
with jade and silk and porcelain, pockets full of an emperor's treasure.
then lord elgin gave the order, and the summer palace burned.
i stood on the hills outside beijing and watched the smoke
rise for three days over yuanmingyuan —
gardens, pavilions, libraries, three centuries of beauty,
punishment for china's defiance.
the french joined in the burning. the emperor had fled.
i thought of the looters' grins and the flames,
and i knew this humiliation would poison china for a hundred years.

lincoln elected 1860 ce america i was in springfield on election night when lincoln won — and the south began to walk out. the rail-splitter from illinois won it in november —
i was in springfield when the returns came in.
no southern state voted for him. he won without them,
and that was exactly the problem.
by the time he took the oath, seven states had walked out,
and the flag over fort sumter was flying in a foreign country.
i watched the celebration in the streets that night,
and underneath the cheering i could hear it:
the sound of a nation coming apart at the seams.

the serfs go free 1861 ce russia i was in a russian village when the tsar's manifesto freed twenty-three million serfs. twenty-three million souls, freed with a signature —
i was in a village outside moscow when the manifesto was read.
the priest read it twice because no one believed it the first time.
old men wept. young men stood stunned.
the tsar — alexander the liberator — had undone
what centuries of bondage had built.
(two years before america freed its slaves, i noted.
history doesn't always move west to east.)
the land terms were hard, the freedom partial,
but the knout was broken. i drank vodka with the village that night.

a kingdom of italy 1861 ce italy i stood in turin when victor emmanuel was proclaimed king of a nearly united italy. victor emmanuel, king of italy — proclaimed at turin,
all but venice and rome.
i stood in the square and watched the flags go up,
tricolor everywhere, the crowd singing.
a country that had been a geography lesson for a thousand years
was a country again. cavour's scheming, garibaldi's sword,
mazzini's dreaming — it had all worked, somehow.
an old man next to me wept into his hands.
"italy," he said, like a word he'd waited fifty years to say.
i thought of the thousand red shirts. they'd done this.

fort sumter 1861 ce america i was on a charleston rooftop when the first shells fell on fort sumter and the civil war began. the first shells fell before dawn on april 12th —
i was in charleston, and the whole city was on the rooftops,
watching like it was fireworks.
thirty-four hours of bombardment, and major anderson
surrendered the fort without a man killed on either side.
everyone thought it would be like that — bloodless, brief.
they were wrong about everything.
i watched the confederate flag go up over the rubble
and felt the ground tilt under the whole country.
the war had begun. four years. six hundred thousand dead.

first bull run 1861 ce america i was on the hillside with the picnickers at bull run when the crowd learned the war would be long. they packed picnic baskets and drove out to watch the war —
i was among the carriages on the hillside above manassas,
ladies with parasols, gentlemen with opera glasses.
then the confederate line held, and broke the union attack,
and the picnickers' horses were tangled in the retreat.
i watched a congressman run for his carriage
with his lunch still in his hand.
nobody picnicked at a battle ever again.
that afternoon the whole north learned what the whole south already knew:
this war would not be over by christmas. or the next.

shiloh 1862 ce america i walked the shiloh field after two days of slaughter and picked up a bible nobody came back for. two days in tennessee, and the rivers ran red —
i walked the field after the second day,
past the peach orchard where the blossoms
had fallen on the dead like pink snow.
twenty-three thousand casualties. the nation had never
seen numbers like that, and both sides stood stunned.
grant's critics howled for his removal. lincoln said,
"i can't spare this man — he fights."
i picked up a dropped bible from the mud,
its pages swollen with rain and blood.
nobody came to claim it.

the homestead act 1862 ce america i rode west with homesteaders claiming their 160 free acres while the war raged behind them. one hundred and sixty acres, free —
file a claim, build a house, farm it five years, and it's yours.
i rode with a wagon train that summer,
families from a dozen countries chasing the same promise west.
the government was giving away the continent
while it fought to keep the continent together.
i watched a norwegian woman step off a wagon in nebraska,
kneel, and press her hands into the dirt like it was an altar.
it was, to her. the west filled up, quarter-section by quarter-section.

antietam 1862 ce america i was at antietam on the bloodiest day in american history — the victory that made emancipation possible. the bloodiest single day in american history —
i was near sharpsburg when the cornfield changed hands six times
and the sunken road filled with the dead in rows,
like a harvest laid down by a terrible reaper.
twenty-two thousand in twelve hours.
lee's invasion was stopped. that was enough for lincoln —
enough to do what he'd been waiting to do.
i walked the field at dusk, and the crows were already coming,
and i thought: this much blood, and all it bought was a piece of paper.
but what a piece of paper it would be.

the emancipation proclamation 1862 ce america i was in washington when lincoln's proclamation turned the war into a war against slavery itself. he signed it after antietam — a war measure, the lawyers said,
freeing the slaves only where he couldn't reach them.
but i was in washington when the news broke,
and i understood what the lawyers missed:
the war now had a soul.
every union advance became a march of liberation.
every black man who reached the lines became a soldier.
it didn't free a single slave that day in any place lincoln controlled —
and it changed the meaning of every drop of blood
the war would ever cost. that is what proclamations do.

emancipation takes effect 1863 ce america i kept freedom's watch night in a virginia contraband camp when emancipation became law at midnight. new year's day, 1863 — i spent the watch night
in a contraband camp in virginia,
hundreds of black families crowded around fires,
waiting for midnight, waiting for the word to become law.
when it came — when the proclamation took effect —
the singing started, and it didn't stop for hours.
old men who'd been property on monday were men on tuesday.
not free everywhere, not free yet in the border states —
but the direction was set, and everyone in that camp knew it.
freedom had a date now. january 1st, forever.

the first underground 1863 ce england i rode london's first underground railway through smoke-filled tunnels and watched the subway age begin. steam trains under london's streets —
i rode the first metropolitan line, paddington to farringdon,
in a carriage full of smoke and wonder.
the tunnels leaked, the engines choked the air,
and the passengers loved it anyway.
six miles under the greatest city on earth,
cut-and-cover trenches roofed over and forgotten.
i stood on the platform afterward, coughing,
watching the crowd pour out of the earth like miners,
and i thought: every great city will dig now.
the age of the subway had begun, in soot and steam.

gettysburg 1863 ce america i was on cemetery ridge for pickett's charge and at the dedication when lincoln spoke for two minutes. three days in pennsylvania broke the confederacy's back —
i was on cemetery ridge when pickett's men came across the field,
twelve thousand abreast, into the guns.
they almost made it. almost.
lee's invasion died in that field, and with it the south's last hope
of winning the war outright.
months later i stood in the cold at the dedication
and heard lincoln speak for two minutes —
"government of the people, by the people, for the people" —
and the crowd barely had time to settle before it was over.
two minutes that outlived every cannon on that field.

vicksburg falls 1863 ce america i was at vicksburg when it surrendered on the fourth of july — the mississippi became union water. grant starved it out — forty-seven days of siege,
the people of vicksburg living in caves, eating rats,
while the shells fell day and night.
i was there on the fourth of july when pemberton surrendered,
the same week as gettysburg, though nobody noticed at first.
the mississippi was union water now, top to bottom.
the confederacy was cut in two, and the western half
began to wither like a limb without blood.
two victories in one week. the war's tide had turned,
and everyone who understood war could feel it.

football gets rules 1863 ce england i sat in a london tavern while eleven clubs argued out the first written laws of football. eleven clubs in a london tavern, arguing about the laws —
i sat in the corner of the freemasons' tavern
while they wrote down what a game should be.
no hacking. no carrying the ball in your hands.
(blackheath walked out over that one — they'd keep the handling game,
and call it rugby.)
the football association was born that night,
over beer and shouting, and the world's game got its shape.
i watched them shake hands afterward, enemies over the rules,
friends over the drinks. from that tavern argument
would come the world cup, the billions, all of it.

nanjing falls 1864 ce china i entered nanjing with the qing troops and saw the end of history's bloodiest civil war. the qing took the taiping capital in july —
i entered nanjing with the imperial troops,
and what i saw i will not fully describe.
fourteen years of holy war ended in slaughter:
the heavenly king's palace burned, his followers
cut down by the tens of thousands, the city emptied.
twenty million dead in all — the bloodiest civil war
in all of human history, and most of the world never heard of it.
i walked streets where the gutters ran red
and thought of hong xiuquan's dream of heaven on earth.
this was what it had come to.

the first geneva convention 1864 ce switzerland i watched twelve nations sign at geneva and make mercy a law of war for the first time. twelve nations in geneva, signing a promise —
the wounded are neutral, the medics are neutral,
mercy has a flag now, and it's a red cross on white.
i watched the delegates sign, dunant among them,
his solferino nightmare finally made into law.
it was a small treaty. it was a revolution.
for the first time in human history, nations agreed
that even in war, some things are not war.
the ink was barely dry before the next war tested it.
but the idea held. the idea always holds longer than the ink.

sherman's march 1864 ce america i rode behind sherman's columns and watched them burn a sixty-mile path from atlanta to the sea. sixty miles wide, from atlanta to the sea —
i rode behind sherman's columns that winter,
and i watched them burn georgia methodically:
railroads twisted into "sherman's neckties,"
barns emptied, plantations stripped, the rich earth scorched.
"war is cruelty," sherman said, "and you cannot refine it."
the soldiers sang "marching through georgia"
while the smoke rose behind them for miles.
it broke the south's will faster than any battle.
total war had come home — and war would never be clean again.

sand creek 1864 ce america i walked the frozen creek bed the day after the militia massacred black kettle's peaceful village. they were a peaceful village — black kettle's cheyenne,
camped under a white flag and an american flag,
promised protection.
i arrived the day after the colorado militia came at dawn
and killed them anyway: women, children, old men,
two hundred or more, mutilated, scalped.
chivington's men rode back to denver as heroes
and displayed the body parts in a theater.
i walked the frozen creek bed among the dead
and understood the west's war had turned merciless —
not a war of battles anymore, but of extermination.
the flags over the camp had meant nothing.

appomattox 1865 ce america i was outside the farmhouse at appomattox when lee surrendered and grant stopped the celebration guns. it ended in a farmhouse parlor, not on a battlefield —
i was outside the mclean house at appomattox court house
when lee rode in, in his finest uniform,
and grant came in mud-spattered, smoking a cigar.
the terms were generous: officers keep their sidearms,
every man keeps his horse, no punishments.
lee asked for food for his starving men, and grant gave it.
when the news reached the union lines, the guns started firing
in celebration — and grant ordered them stopped.
"the war is over," he said. "the rebels are our countrymen again."
i wept. everyone wept.

lincoln assassinated 1865 ce america i was in washington the night booth shot lincoln at ford's theatre, five days after the war ended. five days. the war had been over five days.
i was in washington the night booth slipped into the box at ford's theatre —
an actor, playing the most terrible role of his life.
one bullet, behind the ear. the president carried across the street
to a boarding house, dying through the night.
"damn the man," someone said at dawn. stanton answered:
"now he belongs to the ages."
i stood in the street outside as the news spread,
and watched strong men sit down on the curb and cry like children.
the man who'd saved the union would not live to rebuild it.

mendel's peas 1865 ce austria i visited mendel in his monastery garden and held the pea notebooks the world would ignore for 35 years. a monk in a monastery garden, counting peas —
i visited mendel at brno and watched him sort his plants:
round and wrinkled, tall and short, generation after generation,
twenty-nine thousand plants, every cross recorded.
he'd found the laws of heredity — dominant, recessive,
the mathematics of inheritance — and nobody cared.
he published it. it sank without a ripple.
thirty-five years later they'd dig it up and call him the father of genetics.
i held one of his notebooks. the numbers were perfect.
the world just wasn't ready to read them.

slavery abolished 1865 ce america i was in the capitol when the 13th amendment passed and watched a freedman read it aloud in virginia. the 13th amendment — "neither slavery nor involuntary servitude" —
i was in the capitol when it passed the house,
the galleries erupting, members weeping, black spectators
cheering from the balconies where they'd once been barred.
two hundred and fifty years of american slavery,
ended in a sentence.
then the states ratified, one by one, and by december it was law.
i walked through a virginia town that winter
and watched a freedman read the amendment aloud to a crowd,
slowly, savoring every word like food.
the law had finally caught up with the proclamation.

koniggratz 1866 ce europe i was with the prussian staff at koniggratz when needle guns and railways broke austria in a day. seven weeks — that's all the war lasted.
i was with the prussian staff when moltke's armies
closed on the austrians at koniggratz:
needle guns against muzzle-loaders, railways against marching feet,
the telegraph against the courier.
two hundred thousand austrians broken in a day.
prussia had settled the german question with blood and iron,
as bismarck had promised.
i walked the field afterward, past the abandoned austrian guns,
and thought: germany is coming, and it will be prussia's germany —
disciplined, armed, and certain. europe should be worried.

the cable holds 1866 ce atlantic i was aboard the great eastern when the permanent atlantic cable was laid and the ocean shrank to a wire. this time it held. i was aboard the great eastern —
the only ship big enough — as she paid out two thousand miles
of new cable across the atlantic, and this time the line stayed alive.
messages in minutes, day after day, year after year.
america and europe, joined for good.
the old cable of '58 had died in weeks; this one lived.
i watched the operators tap out the first permanent messages,
and i thought of all the ships still crossing with mail in their holds.
they'd keep crossing. but the news would always beat them now.
the ocean had shrunk to the width of a copper wire.

the alaska purchase 1867 ce america i was in washington when seward bought alaska for two cents an acre and everyone laughed. two cents an acre — seward bought alaska from russia
for $7.2 million, and the newspapers laughed themselves sick.
"seward's folly." "seward's icebox." "walrussia."
i was in washington when the treaty was signed,
and i heard the jokes in every bar in town.
a frozen wasteland, they said. nothing there but ice and bears.
(i thought of the gold under the klondike, the oil under the tundra,
the salmon, the timber — but i kept my mouth shut.
let them laugh. the future would do the accounting.)
the greatest real-estate bargain in history, signed amid giggles.

maximilian executed 1867 ce mexico i was at queretaro when maximilian faced the firing squad and mexico's republic returned. an austrian archduke, set on mexico's throne by french bayonets —
i was at queretaro when it ended.
napoleon iii pulled his troops out, the republic closed in,
and maximilian faced the firing squad in his black frock coat,
handing each soldier a gold coin and asking them to aim well.
"viva mexico," he said. the volley answered.
the french adventure in mexico died with him.
i watched juarez's republic take back its country
and thought: empires planted by other empires' guns
never take root. the soil rejects them.

the dominion of canada 1867 ce canada i was in ottawa on the first dominion day when canada was born from a conference table, not a battlefield. four provinces, one dominion — i was in ottawa
on the first dominion day, july 1st,
when canada became a self-governing nation inside the empire.
no revolution. no war. just a law passed in london
and a new flag over a new country.
the americans had fought for theirs; the canadians
had negotiated for theirs, politely, over tea.
i watched the celebrations — modest, orderly, canadian —
and thought there was something admirable
about a country born from a conference table instead of a battlefield.
it would grow to be the second-largest nation on earth.

dynamite 1867 ce sweden i held a stick of nobel's new dynamite — the powder that would fund the prizes for peace. nobel tamed nitroglycerin with kieselguhr —
i visited his works and watched them pack the clay-like sticks
that would move mountains and, in the wrong hands, level cities.
safer to handle than raw nitro, just as powerful.
the fortune it made him was enormous —
and haunted him. they called him the merchant of death.
so he wrote a will that turned the dynamite money
into prizes for peace, science, and literature.
i held a stick of dynamite in my hand that day,
feeling the weight of it. destruction in one hand,
the nobel prizes in the other. same man. same powder.

the meiji restoration 1868 ce japan i was in kyoto when the shogun fell and watched japan decide to become modern all at once. the shogun fell, the boy-emperor took the throne —
i was in kyoto when the old order collapsed
and japan decided, all at once, to become modern.
they sent students to the west, hired foreign experts,
built railways and shipyards and schools at a speed
that left every visitor dizzy.
"japanese spirit, western learning" — that was the slogan.
in forty years they'd go from feudal swordsmen to battleships.
i watched a samurai cut off his topknot in the street
and put on a western suit, and i thought:
this is the fastest transformation of a nation i will ever see.

little women 1868 ce america i met alcott in boston the year she wrote little women in ten weeks and gave jo march to a million girls. alcott wrote it in ten weeks for the money —
i met her in boston that year, tired, funny, practical,
and she had no idea what she'd made.
meg, jo, beth, amy — four sisters in a concord house,
poor and proud and alive on the page.
girls devoured it. then their mothers read it.
then everyone read it.
jo march wanted to be a writer more than she wanted to marry,
and a million girls read that and believed it was allowed.
i watched a bookseller's whole stock sell out in a week
and thought: she wrote it for the money, and made something priceless.

the periodic table 1869 ce russia i saw mendeleev's table in st. petersburg — with empty spaces predicting elements not yet found. mendeleev laid out the elements like cards in patience —
i was in st. petersburg when he showed me the table:
each element in its place, by weight, by character,
and gaps — empty spaces where elements should be
but hadn't been found yet.
he predicted them anyway: their weights, their colors,
what they'd do. "eka-aluminium," he said, pointing at a gap.
years later they found it — gallium — exactly as he'd said.
i stared at the table. it wasn't a list. it was a prophecy,
written in the language of matter itself.

the golden spike 1869 ce america i was at promontory when the golden spike joined the rails and the telegraph flashed done. promontory, utah, may 10th — i was there in the crowd
when the last spike went in, gold-plated, tapped with a silver hammer,
and the telegraph flashed one word across the nation: done.
two railroads, built from opposite oceans, met in the desert.
america was stitched coast to coast — six months of travel
compressed into a week.
the chinese workers who'd blasted the sierras
were barely mentioned in the speeches. i noticed.
i watched the two locomotives nose together,
pilot to pilot, and the cheer went up like a wave.
a continent, joined by iron.

the suez canal opens 1869 ce egypt i sailed the suez canal in the opening procession — a triumph dug with forced labor that egypt would lose. de lesseps dug a ditch through the desert and changed the map —
i sailed through the canal in the opening procession,
a hundred miles of water where there'd been sand.
london to bombay in weeks instead of months.
the empress eugenie led the fleet through, all flags and music.
but i did the arithmetic the celebrants skipped:
egypt had paid in money and in forced labor —
thousands dead digging it — and would soon lose the canal itself
to british shareholders.
a triumph of engineering. a tragedy of ownership.
the ships sail through it still.

wyoming votes for women 1869 ce america i was in wyoming when the territory gave women the vote — fifty years before the nation caught up. the wyoming territory did it first —
i was in south pass city when the territorial legislature
passed women's suffrage, and the governor signed it.
the first government on earth where women voted.
the motives were mixed — some said it was to attract settlers,
some said it was a joke that passed by accident.
the women of wyoming didn't care about the motives.
they registered. they voted. they served on juries.
fifty years before the 19th amendment, in a territory
most americans couldn't find on a map,
the future arrived early, wearing a calico dress.

the 15th amendment 1870 ce america i watched black men vote for the first time under the 15th amendment — and saw the south begin to steal it back. "the right to vote shall not be denied on account of race" —
i was in washington when it was ratified,
and i watched black men line up at the polls across the south,
some in their old union uniforms, voting for the first time.
on paper, it was complete: freedom, citizenship, the ballot.
on paper.
i also watched the white south begin its long counterattack —
poll taxes, literacy tests, the klan by night —
that would steal it all back within a decade.
the amendment was a promise. keeping it would take a century.

the franco-prussian war 1870 ce europe i was in paris when france declared war on prussia and walked into catastrophe. france declared it — napoleon iii, chasing glory,
walked straight into bismarck's trap.
i was in paris when the news of the first defeats arrived,
and the boulevards went from confident to stunned in a week.
the prussian war machine — the railways, the needle guns,
moltke's staff work — chewed through the french armies
like a threshing machine through wheat.
it was supposed to be a short, splendid war.
it was short. it was not splendid.
it ended an empire, birthed another, and planted the seeds
of two world wars. i watched it start, and i was afraid.

sedan 1870 ce france i was near sedan when napoleon iii surrendered his army and his eighteen-year empire fell in a day. one day. the whole second empire fell in one day.
i was near sedan when macmahon's army was surrounded —
a hundred thousand french soldiers, the emperor himself,
trapped in a pocket and pounded by prussian artillery.
napoleon iii surrendered his sword. the empire collapsed
before the news even reached paris.
i watched the emperor ride out to captivity,
a sick man in a carriage, and i remembered 1852,
the crown, the cheers, the boulevards.
eighteen years. that's how long the dream lasted.

rome falls 1870 ce italy i watched italian troops breach rome's walls at porta pia and complete the thousand-year dream of unity. the italian guns breached the aurelian walls at porta pia —
i was there that september morning, watching bersaglieri
pour through the gap while the pope's troops fell back.
rome was italy's at last. the thousand-year dream complete:
one country, one capital.
pius ix declared himself a prisoner in the vatican
and would not leave it again.
an old roman woman next to me crossed herself and wept —
for the pope, or for italy, i couldn't tell.
maybe both. history doesn't ask permission
when it finishes what it started.

the german empire 1871 ce germany i stood in versailles' hall of mirrors when prussia's king was crowned kaiser of a united germany. they crowned him in the hall of mirrors at versailles —
i stood among the princes and generals
while wilhelm i of prussia became german kaiser,
in the palace of the defeated french king.
the symbolism was the point. bismarck made sure of it.
germany was born — united, armed, industrial —
in the very room where france had displayed its glory.
i looked at the mirrors reflecting all those uniforms
and thought: this birth will cost europe dearly.
an empire proclaimed in an enemy's palace
does not forget it was made by war.

the paris commune 1871 ce france i was in paris for the commune's seventy-two days and walked pere lachaise after the bloody week. seventy-two days — paris tried to govern itself.
i was there in the spring: the barricades, the red flags,
workers running the city while the government cowered at versailles.
it was chaotic, idealistic, doomed.
then the army came back in may — the bloody week —
and drowned the commune in its own blood.
twenty thousand shot, against walls, in the streets.
i walked through pere lachaise afterward,
past the wall where the last defenders fell,
and the stones were still dark.
paris has never forgotten. neither have i.

the great chicago fire 1871 ce america i ran with the crowds through the great chicago fire and watched the city start rebuilding in the ashes. two days, and a city of wood was gone —
i was in chicago when the fire started,
and i ran with the crowds as the flames
jumped the river and ate block after block.
(the cow and the lantern? probably a story.
the drought and the wind were real enough.)
a hundred thousand homeless. three hundred dead.
the city burned to the ground —
and then chicago did the most chicago thing imaginable:
it rebuilt, bigger, in steel and stone.
i stood in the ashes on the third day
and watched them already clearing lots.
that spirit built the modern city.

"dr. livingstone, i presume?" 1871 ce africa i was with stanley's caravan when he found the lost livingstone deep in africa. deep in the african interior, by a lake —
i was with stanley's caravan when we found him:
david livingstone, the lost explorer,
sick, alone, out of supplies, refusing to leave.
stanley took off his hat and spoke the most famous
greeting in exploration history:
"dr. livingstone, i presume?"
livingstone smiled. they'd both walked a thousand miles
to have that conversation.
i watched two stubborn men share tea in the wilderness
and thought: this is what the age of exploration really is —
not flags, but one man refusing to quit,
and another refusing to let him be lost.

yellowstone 1872 ce america i rode with the hayden expedition through the geyser basins before yellowstone became the world's first national park. two million acres, set aside forever —
i rode with the hayden expedition through the geyser basins,
watching old faithful throw its white plume at the sky,
the hot springs painting the earth in impossible colors.
congress made it a park — the world's first national park —
not for profit, not for settlement, but because it was beautiful.
the idea was radical: some land belongs to everyone,
and to no one, and to the future.
i stood at the grand canyon of the yellowstone,
the falls thundering below, and thought:
this is the best thing a government ever did with a map.

the secret ballot 1872 ce england i voted in britain's first secret-ballot election — a curtain, a pencil, and a revolution. no more landlords watching the polls —
i voted in the first secret-ballot election in britain,
marking my x behind a screen, folding the paper,
dropping it in the box where no one could see.
such a small thing. such a revolution.
before this, tenants voted as their landlords ordered,
workers as their masters demanded — everyone watching.
the ballot act ended all that with a curtain and a pencil.
i walked out of the polling station feeling
ten feet tall. my vote was mine.
democracy had finally learned to keep a secret.

the challenger sails 1872 ce atlantic i watched hms challenger sail from portsmouth to map the ocean floor and invent the science of the seas. a warship turned into a laboratory —
i watched hms challenger leave portsmouth,
her guns removed, her labs installed,
bound to map the floor of the entire ocean.
four years. sixty-nine thousand miles.
they'd dredge up four thousand new species,
measure the deepest trenches, and invent oceanography.
i stood on the dock as she sailed,
a converted corvette carrying microscopes instead of cannon,
and i thought: this is the best use anyone ever made of a warship.
the sea had been a road and a battlefield.
now it would be a question — and they'd spend four years answering it.

the panic of 1873 1873 ce america i was on wall street when jay cooke's bank failed and the panic began six years of depression. it started with a bank — jay cooke's, overextended on railroads —
i was on wall street the day it failed,
and the panic spread like cholera through the exchanges.
banks closed. railroads went bankrupt. factories shut.
six years of depression followed — the long depression —
millions out of work, wages cut, strikes broken.
i walked through mill towns in pennsylvania
where the furnaces had gone cold and the men
sat on their porches staring at nothing.
the boom had been built on borrowed money.
the bill came due, and the poor paid it.

maxwell's equations 1873 ce england i visited maxwell at cambridge and saw the four equations that united electricity, magnetism, and light. four equations. that's all it took.
i visited maxwell at cambridge — quiet man, big mind —
and he showed me what he'd done:
electricity, magnetism, and light,
three mysteries, one mathematics.
light is an electromagnetic wave, the equations said.
nobody could quite believe anything so beautiful could be true.
it was true. radio, x-rays, all of it was hiding in those four lines.
i looked at the paper and felt the way you feel
looking at a cathedral's blueprint —
small marks on paper, and a universe inside.

war with the asante 1873 ce west africa i was on the gold coast when britain marched inland against the asante empire. the golden stool against the british empire —
i was on the gold coast when wolseley's expedition marched inland,
redcoats and rockets against the asante army.
the asante had humiliated the british before;
london was done being humiliated.
it was the classic colonial war: maxim guns not yet,
but breech-loaders and discipline against courage and numbers.
i watched the column disappear into the forest,
porters and soldiers stretching for miles,
and i thought of the golden kingdom waiting at the end of that road.
it would not survive the meeting.

kumasi falls 1874 ce west africa i entered burning kumasi behind wolseley's troops and watched the asante empire of gold break. they burned the capital — i entered kumasi
behind wolseley's troops, and the great asante city
was in flames, the palace looted, the golden stool hidden away
(they never found it — the soul of the nation, safe).
the empire of gold was broken.
the british marched back to the coast, mission accomplished,
leaving ashes and a treaty.
i stood in the burned palace courtyard
and thought about what conquest costs the conquered
versus what it costs the conqueror.
the asante counted their dead. the british counted their glory.
only one of those counts was honest.

the impressionists 1874 ce france i was at the first impressionist show in paris when a critic's sneer gave the movement its name. rejected by the salon, they hung their own show —
i was at the first impressionist exhibition in paris,
in nadar's studio, looking at monet's sunrise:
a harbor in fog, orange sun, brushstrokes you could see.
a critic sneered "impression!" — and the name stuck.
light, not lines. the moment, not the monument.
renoir's dancers, pissarro's fields, degas's ballerinas —
paint that shimmered instead of posing.
i stood in front of that sunrise a long time.
art had just learned to see the way eyes actually see.

the typewriter 1874 ce america i tried the first remington typewriter in new york and watched it remake the office — and employ a generation of women. click-clack, ding — the office would never be the same.
i tried the first remington in new york,
hunting and pecking at the qwerty keys,
watching my words appear in clean, even type.
no more clerk's cramped hand. no more illegible ledgers.
and something nobody predicted: it created a new workforce.
women, hired as typists, flooded into offices
that had been all male — the typewriter
as an unlikely engine of emancipation.
i typed my name and held up the page.
it looked official. it looked like the future.

hockey is born indoors 1875 ce canada i was in montreal's victoria skating rink for the first organized indoor hockey game. montreal, a skating rink, march 3rd —
i was in the victoria skating rink when they played
the first organized indoor hockey game:
two teams of nine, a wooden puck (not a ball, safer indoors),
written rules, a real referee.
mcgill students, mostly. fast, rough, glorious.
the puck flew, the sticks clashed, the crowd roared
in that enclosed, echoing space.
outside it was still winter. inside, something new was born.
i left with my ears ringing and my cheeks cold,
and i thought: this game is going to travel.
it would. to every frozen corner of the earth.

carmen 1875 ce france i was at carmen's cold paris premiere, three months before bizet died never knowing it would become immortal. it flopped. i was at the premiere in paris —
bizet's fiery gypsy, the cigarette factory, the toreador,
and the audience sat on its hands.
too raw, too real, too much death for the opera-comique.
bizet died three months later, thirty-six,
never knowing what he'd made.
because carmen didn't stay dead.
it rose again — the habanera, the toreador song —
and became the most performed opera on earth.
i sat in that cold premiere audience
and missed it completely. so did everyone.
genius sometimes needs the composer to die first.

"mr. watson, come here" 1876 ce america i was in bell's workshop the week the spilled acid produced the first telephone call. the first telephone call was an accident —
bell spilled acid on himself in his boston workshop
and shouted for his assistant in the next room:
"mr. watson, come here — i want to see you!"
and watson heard him. through the wire.
i was there that week, and bell showed me the thing:
a wooden frame, a membrane, a wire carrying a human voice.
he'd patented it hours before elisha gray filed his own claim —
the most valuable race in invention history, won by a morning.
i spoke into it. my own voice came back, thin and miraculous.
distance had just been murdered.

little bighorn 1876 ce america i rode with the burial party at little bighorn days after the sioux and cheyenne wiped out custer's command. custer's luck ran out on a montana hillside —
i rode with the burial party days later,
past the ridge where 268 soldiers fell
with their reckless general.
the sioux and cheyenne — sitting bull, crazy horse —
had done what no one thought possible:
wiped out a whole cavalry command in an afternoon.
it was the indians' greatest victory,
and it sealed their doom. america would not forgive this.
the revenge came at wounded knee, fourteen years later.
i stood on last stand hill in the silence
and thought: courage on both sides, wisdom on neither.

wagner's ring 1876 ce germany i was at bayreuth for the first complete ring cycle — fifteen hours of gods, gold, and twilight. four operas. fifteen hours. one theater built for the purpose —
i was at bayreuth for the first complete ring cycle,
in the darkened hall wagner had designed himself.
gods and giants, a cursed ring, the twilight of everything —
music so vast it felt like weather.
the kings and emperors in the audience fidgeted.
the rest of us were drowned and reborn.
it nearly bankrupted him. it changed music forever.
i walked out into the bavarian night after gotterdammerung,
the world ending in fire and flood behind me,
and my ears rang for days.

empress of india 1876 ce india i was at the delhi durbar when victoria was proclaimed empress and the raj got its crown. victoria, empress — proclaimed at delhi in a durbar of princes.
i was there among the elephants and the jewels,
watching the raj put a crown on its conquest.
disraeli's idea: give the queen an imperial title
to match the reality of ruling two hundred million people.
the princes bowed. the guns fired. the diamonds glittered.
and underneath the ceremony, the same old machinery:
taxes, troops, the slow drain of wealth to london.
i watched an old maharaja adjust his turban
and stare at the empty sky. he knew what a crown costs
when someone else is wearing it.

the russo-turkish war 1877 ce ottoman empire i crossed the danube with the russian armies and watched the balkans begin their long road to the powder keg. russia went to war for the balkan christians —
i was with the correspondents when the russian armies
crossed the danube, all orthodox fervor and imperial appetite.
the ottomans fought hard. plevna held out for months.
but the empire was rotting, and everyone knew it.
this war would redraw the map of the balkans —
bulgaria, serbia, romania emerging from the wreckage —
and plant the quarrels that would still be killing people
a century later.
i watched the cossacks ride south and thought:
they're liberating the balkans into a powder keg.

the first wimbledon 1877 ce england i sat on the grass bank at the first wimbledon and watched spencer gore win the guinea-entry tournament. twenty-two men, one trophy, a guinea to enter —
i was at the all england club for the first wimbledon,
watching spencer gore win it with his newfangled volleying.
lawn tennis: an afternoon pastime turned championship.
the grass was bumpy, the rackets were wooden,
the ladies watched from the pavilion in their long dresses.
nobody imagined centre court, or millions watching,
or the strawberries. it was just a club tournament
on a summer afternoon.
i sat on the grass bank and thought how strange it is
that the biggest things start the smallest.

the great railroad strike 1877 ce america i was in pittsburgh when the railroad strike went national and labor showed it could stop the country cold. it started in west virginia and spread like fire —
i was in pittsburgh when the railroad workers walked out,
wages cut for the third time, nothing left to lose.
the strike went national: fourteen states, a hundred thousand men.
militia fired on crowds. baltimore burned. pittsburgh burned —
the rail yards a sea of flame, locomotives torched.
federal troops broke it, in the end, with bayonets.
but something had changed: american labor had shown
it could stop the nation cold.
i watched the soldiers march in and thought:
this argument isn't over. it's just beginning.

the phonograph 1877 ce america i was in menlo park the night edison's phonograph first played a human voice back. "mary had a little lamb" — edison shouted it into a horn,
and the machine shouted it back.
i was in menlo park that december night,
and i watched grown men go pale.
a voice, captured. a moment, kept.
sound had always died the instant it was born —
now it could live forever on tinfoil.
edison thought it would record dying men's last words
and teach elocution. he didn't foresee the music.
none of us did. i listened to my own voice played back
and felt the strangest chill: i had just heard myself
from the outside, for the first time in my life.

hello, operator 1878 ce america i was in new haven when the first telephone exchange connected its twenty-one subscribers by hand. the first telephone exchange opened in new haven —
i was there when the switchboard lit up,
twenty-one subscribers, and a boy to connect them.
"hello, operator? connect me to—"
the operator was the network. a human voice
plugging wires into jacks, making the connections
by hand, by memory, by patience.
within a year there were exchanges everywhere,
and the operators — mostly young women soon —
became the voices of the new age.
i picked up the receiver and asked for a number,
and a girl's voice said, "one moment, please."
the future had a receptionist.

the congress of berlin 1878 ce europe i watched the great powers carve up the balkans in berlin — dealing out nations like cards, scheduling sarajevo. they carved up the balkans over a green baize table —
i was in berlin while bismarck chaired the great powers:
disraeli, the russians, the austrians, the french,
redrawing borders with rulers and cigars.
bulgaria shrunk. bosnia handed to austria.
romania, serbia, montenegro recognized —
every settlement a seed of the next war.
no balkan voice in the room. that was the point.
i watched the old men deal out nations like cards
and thought: they're not solving the eastern question.
they're scheduling it. sarajevo was thirty-six years away.

the second afghan war 1878 ce afghanistan i marched through the khyber with the british column into the graveyard of empires. britain invaded afghanistan again —
i was with the column that marched through the khyber,
and the old soldiers told the young ones about 1842,
about the retreat from kabul, about the one survivor.
nobody listened. empires never listen.
they took kabul. they installed their emir.
then the residency was massacred, and the war began in earnest —
another round in the graveyard of empires.
i stood in the khyber pass, the wind howling down the rocks,
and thought: this place has buried every army
that ever marched through it. the british would learn.
everyone learns, eventually, in afghanistan.

isandlwana 1879 ce south africa i walked the isandlwana field the day after zulu warriors annihilated a british column. britain's worst colonial defeat —
i reached the battlefield the day after:
a thousand british and colonial troops dead,
wiped out by twenty thousand zulu warriors
with spears and shields against rifles and cannon.
the zulu horns-of-the-buffalo tactic closed around them,
and courage met courage, and numbers told.
london was stunned. an empire that had beaten napoleon
brought low by men with spears.
i walked among the dead in the african sun
and thought: never underestimate a people
fighting for their own land. the zulu knew it.
the british were learning it, at terrible cost.

rorke's drift 1879 ce south africa i reached rorke's drift at dawn after 150 soldiers held a mission station against 4,000 zulu. hours later, eleven miles away —
i arrived at the mission station as the firing died down:
150 british soldiers, sick and wounded among them,
had held off 4,000 zulu through the night.
mealie bags for walls. a hospital burning.
eleven victoria crosses — more than any single battle before or since.
chard and bromhead, two lieutenants nobody had heard of,
became the heroes that washed away isandlwana's shame.
i stood in the trampled yard at dawn,
the air still thick with smoke,
and thought: this is what empires run on —
desperate courage, turned into legend by morning.

let there be light 1879 ce america i was in menlo park the night edison's bulb burned thirteen hours and the electric age began. thirteen hours. the bulb burned for thirteen hours —
i was in menlo park on the night it worked,
a carbonized thread in a glass bulb, glowing steady.
edison had tried thousands of filaments.
this one held.
the men in the lab didn't cheer. they just stared,
the way you stare at something that changes everything
and you know it.
within three years he'd light manhattan.
within a lifetime, the night itself would retreat.
i walked home under the stars that night,
not knowing it was one of the last times
humanity would see them so clearly.

a doll's house 1879 ce norway i was in the theater when nora slammed the door in a doll's house — and on the nineteenth century. the door slam heard around the world —
i was in the theater when nora walked out on torvald,
on her marriage, on the whole nineteenth century.
the audience gasped. some were furious.
a woman leaving her husband and children — for herself?
ibsen had written the impossible: a wife as a person,
not a possession, not a doll in a doll's house.
the play was banned, rewritten, argued over in every capital.
but the door stayed slammed.
i watched the actress hold that final moment —
hand on the door, then gone —
and i knew: nothing about marriage would ever be innocent again.

ned kelly's last stand 1880 ce australia i was at glenrowan when ned kelly walked out in his ploughshare armor for his last stand. armor made from ploughshares —
i was at glenrowan when the kelly gang made its last stand,
ned walking out of the bush in his homemade iron suit,
a bush knight in a metal helmet, bullets bouncing off his chest.
they shot his legs out from under him. that's how it ended.
bank robber, cop killer, folk hero —
australia's most famous outlaw, caught at last.
they hanged him in melbourne. his last words, they say:
"such is life."
i looked at that strange armor afterward, dented and scorched,
and thought: every country gets the outlaw it deserves.
australia got a man in a tin can, defiant to the end.

the first boer war 1880 ce south africa i was in the transvaal when boer farmers took up rifles against the british empire. farmers with rifles against the british empire —
i was in the transvaal when the boers rose,
tired of london's rule, taking up their mausers
and their long memories.
they were not soldiers. they were marksmen —
men who'd shot game on the veldt since childhood,
now shooting redcoats at a thousand yards.
the british marched in columns, drums beating,
straight into the boers' sights.
it was the empire's old arrogance meeting a new kind of war:
the citizen soldier, the farmer with a gun,
who knew every rock and gully.
london would learn respect. the hard way.

majuba hill 1881 ce south africa i was below majuba hill at dawn when boer marksmen routed the british and won the transvaal's freedom. they climbed it at night and shot the british off the top at dawn —
i was on the slopes below majuba when the boer marksmen
did what no one thought farmers could do:
rout a british force, kill its general, and win a war.
ninety-two british dead. one boer.
london, stunned, granted the transvaal self-rule.
it was the first time in living memory
that the empire had been beaten into a concession.
i watched the boer commandos walk down the hill,
quiet men, no cheering, just done —
and i thought: the empire will be back.
and it was. eighteen years later, with half a million men.

the tsar is killed 1881 ce russia i was in st. petersburg the day terrorists killed alexander ii, the tsar who freed the serfs. the liberator, blown apart by a bomb —
i was in st. petersburg on the day they killed alexander ii,
the tsar who'd freed the serfs, murdered on the street
by the people's will, on the very day he was to sign
a constitution.
the irony was perfect and terrible:
reform's reward was assassination.
his son took the throne and learned the lesson
reaction wanted him to learn: no more reform, only repression.
i stood in the crowd at the funeral procession,
watching the coffin pass, and thought:
they killed the best tsar russia ever had,
and russia would pay for it for thirty-six years.

the mahdi rises 1881 ce sudan i heard the mahdi preach in kordofan before sudan rose against egypt and britain. a holy man on an island in the nile declared himself the mahdi —
the guided one, come to purify islam and drive out the foreigners.
i heard him preach in kordofan, and the tribes rose:
egypt's rule collapsing, the sudan in revolt.
he was not just a rebel. he was a prophecy —
and prophecies are harder to shoot than armies.
gordon would go to khartoum. kitchener would come later.
but that summer, it was just a man with a vision
and a desert full of believers.
i watched the dervishes drill with their spears
and thought: the empire is about to bleed in the sand.

the o.k. corral 1881 ce america i was on allen street in tombstone for the thirty-second gunfight that became the west's legend. thirty seconds in tombstone —
i was on allen street when it started:
the earps and doc holliday against the clantons and mclaurys,
thirty shots in half a minute, three men dead.
it was over before most of the town knew it had begun.
then the legend took over — bigger, bloodier, cleaner
than the shabby truth of a feud over gambling and pride.
wyatt earp, the lawman. doc holliday, dying of tuberculosis,
fighting like he had nothing to lose. he didn't.
i picked up an empty cartridge from the dust afterward.
the west's most famous half-minute, already becoming myth.

the germ that kills millions 1882 ce germany i looked through koch's microscope in berlin at the tuberculosis bacterium — germ theory's great proof. koch found it — the tuberculosis bacterium, stained blue under the microscope.
i was in berlin when he announced it:
the white plague, the consumption that had killed poets and seamstresses alike,
was a germ. a single, findable, killable germ.
germ theory's great proof.
he'd grown it, stained it, shown it to the skeptics.
one in seven europeans died of tb. now they knew the enemy's face.
i looked through his microscope at the tiny blue rods
and thought: this is what victory looks like —
not a battle, but a slide of glass with the killer on it.

the chinese exclusion act 1882 ce america i was in san francisco when america banned chinese immigration — the first law aimed at a whole people. the first law aimed at a whole people —
i was in san francisco when it passed:
no more chinese laborers, ten years, then extended, then made permanent.
the men who'd built the railroads, blasted the sierras,
were now the enemy — too many, too foreign, too willing to work.
i watched a laundryman read the news in his shop,
his face very still, and i thought of promontory,
the golden spike, the chinese workers barely mentioned.
now they were mentioned: as a threat.
america's gate, which had stood open, learned to close —
and it would keep learning, against one people after another.

pearl street station 1882 ce america i was in lower manhattan when pearl street station lit four hundred lamps and the grid age began. edison lit up lower manhattan —
i was there when pearl street station went live,
the first central power station in the world,
current flowing to four hundred lamps in the financial district.
j.p. morgan's house glowed. the new york times glowed.
the age of the grid had begun: power made in one place,
used everywhere, billed by the meter.
the gas companies watched their future dim.
i stood on a dark street corner looking at the lit windows
and thought: this is the moment the night ended.
not with a battle or a treaty — with a power station.

tel el-kebir 1882 ce egypt i was with wolseley's dawn attack at tel el-kebir when britain began its seventy-year "temporary" occupation of egypt. a dawn attack, and egypt fell in a day —
i was with wolseley's force when they stormed arabi's lines at tel el-kebir,
marching through the night, hitting at first light.
the egyptian army broke. cairo opened its gates.
britain would occupy egypt for decades —
"temporarily," they said, for seventy years.
the suez canal needed guarding, and guarding needed an army,
and the army needed a country.
i walked through cairo the week after,
the british flags going up over the ministries,
and thought: this is how empires grow —
one "temporary" occupation at a time.

the brooklyn bridge 1883 ce america i walked the brooklyn bridge on opening day — a mile of steel thrown across the impossible. the longest suspension bridge on earth —
i walked it on opening day with the crowds,
a mile of steel and stone over the east river,
the two great towers rising like cathedrals.
roebling died before it was finished; his son washington
was crippled by the bends, directing it from his bedroom
while his wife emily ran the site.
fourteen years. twenty-seven dead.
i stood mid-span, the wind in the cables,
manhattan on one side, brooklyn on the other,
and thought: this is what human beings do —
throw a thread of steel across the impossible, and walk on it.

krakatoa 1883 ce indonesia i was on a ship in the sunda strait when krakatoa exploded — the loudest sound in recorded history. heard 3,000 miles away —
i was on a ship in the sunda strait when the sky went black at noon.
krakatoa exploded with the force of 200 million tons of tnt,
the loudest sound in recorded history,
a pressure wave that circled the earth seven times.
thirty-six thousand dead in the tsunamis.
the sunsets went blood-red for years — ash around the whole planet.
i stood on deck in the falling pumice, the air full of thunder,
and thought: all our engines, all our guns,
are toys next to this. the earth does what it wants.
we just live on it, briefly, between eruptions.

the orient express 1883 ce europe i rode the first orient express from paris toward constantinople — europe's imagination made into a timetable. paris to constantinople in luxury —
i rode the first orient express east,
mahogany and brass, silk sheets, dinner in the dining car
while the balkans rolled past the windows.
kings and spies would ride this train.
it was more than a railway: it was europe's imagination
made into a timetable — the west gliding east in comfort,
mystery at the end of the line.
i dined as we crossed into the ottoman empire,
the lamps lit, the wine poured,
and thought: this train carries the whole century with it —
its elegance, its empires, and its illusions.

the siege of khartoum 1884 ce sudan i was inside besieged khartoum with gordon, watching the desert for a relief column that never came in time. gordon held khartoum against the mahdi's army —
i slipped into the city before the ring closed:
ten months of siege, the nile the only road,
and the relief column always coming, never arriving.
gordon — the hero of china, strange, devout, stubborn —
refused to leave, and organized the defense himself.
the people starved. the shells fell. the mahdi waited.
london dithered. gladstone hesitated.
i watched gordon on the palace roof with his telescope,
scanning the desert for dust that never came,
and i thought: empires are very good at sending heroes
to places they have no intention of saving.

the berlin conference 1884 ce europe i watched fourteen powers carve up africa in berlin — no african invited, no african consulted. fourteen powers, one table, a whole continent divided —
i was in berlin while they carved up africa:
no african invited, no african consulted.
rivers became borders. peoples became possessions.
the congo for leopold (personally — the worst deal in the room).
the rules of the carve-up, written down like a club's bylaws:
occupy it, notify us, it's yours.
i watched the maps change color — british red, french blue —
and thought of the millions of people living on those colors
who would not be asked, ever.
the scramble was now official. the century of trouble had its charter.

huckleberry finn 1884 ce america i read huckleberry finn on a mississippi riverboat the year the libraries banned it for being vulgar. huck and jim on the river —
i read it the year it came out, and the libraries banned it
for being vulgar. vulgar! it was the truest book america had.
a boy and a runaway slave on a raft,
and huck deciding he'd rather go to hell
than turn jim in — the moral center of the whole century
in one boy's conscience.
twain wrote it in the american voice, misspellings and all,
and some call it the great american novel.
i closed it on a riverboat on the mississippi itself,
the real river rolling past, and thought:
this book will outlive every statue they ever carve of him.

khartoum falls 1885 ce sudan i was on the nile when khartoum fell two days before relief arrived and gordon died on the palace steps. they came at dawn, two days before the relief arrived —
i was on the river when the mahdi's men stormed khartoum,
and gordon died on the palace steps, spear in hand, alone.
the city fell. the garrison was slaughtered.
britain mourned its hero and blamed gladstone,
and the relief column turned back, two days late, forever late.
the mahdi's empire would rule sudan for thirteen years.
i stood on the deck watching the smoke rise over khartoum
and thought of gordon on the roof with his telescope.
he'd been right to watch the desert.
no one was coming. no one ever was.

pasteur's vaccine 1885 ce france i was in paris when pasteur's rabies vaccine saved young joseph meister and vaccines entered the modern age. a boy bitten by a rabid dog —
i was in paris when young joseph meister's mother
brought him to pasteur, desperate, the bites already festering.
rabies meant death. certain, horrible death.
pasteur had never tried his vaccine on a human.
he tried it on the boy. thirteen injections.
the boy lived.
i watched the news spread through the laboratories of europe:
vaccines had entered the modern age.
rabies, then anthrax, then diphtheria —
the invisible killers, one by one, meeting their match.
pasteur wept when he heard the boy was safe.
so did i.

the first automobile 1885 ce germany i watched benz's three-wheeled motorwagen putter through mannheim — the horse's five-thousand-year reign ending unnoticed. three wheels and a puttering engine —
i watched karl benz drive his motorwagen through mannheim,
a three-wheeled carriage with no horse,
moving under its own power at a walking pace.
people stared. dogs barked. a policeman stopped him
for going too fast. too fast! at ten miles an hour.
bertha benz would later drive it a hundred miles
to prove it worked — the first road trip in history.
i stood on the curb as it puttered past,
smelling the exhaust, hearing the future sputter to life.
the horse had ruled transport for five thousand years.
its reign ended that afternoon, and nobody noticed.

the indian national congress 1885 ce india i was in bombay when seventy-two lawyers founded the congress that would one day free india. seventy-two men in bombay, mostly lawyers —
i was there when the indian national congress was founded,
english-educated indians asking, politely, for a share in governing their own country.
the british smiled indulgently. a debating club, they thought.
they were wrong. that debating club would become
the party of gandhi and nehru,
the movement that would free a subcontinent.
it started with resolutions and petitions, all very proper.
empires are never overthrown politely —
but sometimes they're overthrown by men
who started out being polite.
i kept the program. it's worth more than gold now.

haymarket 1886 ce america i was near chicago's haymarket square when the bomb exploded and the fight for the eight-hour day turned bloody. a bomb in the rain, in a chicago square —
i was near haymarket when the rally for the eight-hour day
turned into the blast that changed american labor.
someone threw a bomb at the police. seven officers died.
the trials that followed hanged four anarchists
on evidence thin as smoke — spies, parsons, fischer, engel.
were they guilty? the world argued then, argues still.
but the eight-hour day they marched for —
that survived. may day, around the world,
is their memorial.
i stood in the square the next morning,
the blood washed away, the fear still in the air,
and thought: this is what the fight for a shorter day costs.

coca-cola 1886 ce america i drank one of the first glasses of coca-cola at an atlanta soda fountain — five cents, nine sales a day. five cents a glass at jacob's pharmacy —
i was in atlanta when dr. pemberton's new tonic went on sale:
caramel-colored, fizzy, served from a soda fountain.
nine glasses a day, at first. just nine.
the pharmacist who bought the formula,
asa candler, saw what pemberton didn't:
this wasn't medicine. this was america in a glass.
i drank one of those first glasses — sweet, strange, cold —
and thought nothing of it. nobody did.
a century later they'd sell a billion servings a day.
the most valuable five cents in history.

geronimo surrenders 1886 ce america i was at skeleton canyon when geronimo surrendered and the indian wars effectively ended. the last war chief laid down his rifle —
i was at skeleton canyon when geronimo surrendered to general miles,
ending thirty years of apache war.
he'd held off the whole u.s. army with a handful of warriors,
vanishing into mountains the soldiers couldn't follow.
now it was over. the indian wars effectively ended that day.
they sent him to florida, then to fort sill —
a prisoner of war for the rest of his life,
displayed at fairs like a relic.
i watched the old warrior hand over his rifle,
his face unreadable, and thought:
this is how a continent's first peoples lose everything —
one surrender at a time, until there's nothing left to surrender.

the statue of liberty 1886 ce america i was in new york harbor when the statue of liberty was unveiled before a fleet of ships. a gift from france, dedicated in the harbor —
i was on a ferry when they unveiled her:
151 feet of copper, torch raised, tablet in hand,
"mother of exiles," as emma lazarus would write.
the harbor was full of ships, the guns fired salutes,
and bartholdi's great lady looked out to sea.
she'd been built in paris, shipped in pieces,
raised on an american pedestal.
i watched the immigrants on the decks around me
stare up at her, and i thought:
they don't know her poems yet, or her promises.
but they'll learn. everyone who sails into this harbor learns.

the golden jubilee 1887 ce england i was in london for victoria's golden jubilee — the empire glittering at its peak, the rot already underneath. fifty years on the throne —
i was in london for victoria's golden jubilee,
the empire at its glittering peak:
kings and princes from every continent,
troops in uniforms from a hundred regiments,
a procession that stretched for miles.
the old queen, in black, in her carriage,
the grandmother of europe, the empress of a quarter of the earth.
the crowds cheered themselves hoarse.
and underneath the glitter, the rot was already there —
ireland restless, the boers unbowed, germany arming.
but that june day, none of it showed.
empires look eternal at their jubilees.
that's what jubilees are for.

the michelson–morley experiment 1887 ce america i was in cleveland when michelson and morley found no ether — the beautiful failure that cleared the road to relativity. the most famous failed experiment in history —
i was in cleveland when michelson and morley
tried to measure the earth's motion through the ether,
the invisible sea that light was supposed to swim in.
they found nothing. no ether. no motion through it.
the experiment failed — and the failure was the discovery.
if there's no ether, then light needs no medium,
and the whole of physics has to be rebuilt.
einstein was eight years old, but the road was clearing for him.
i watched them check their instruments again and again,
baffled, meticulous, honest —
and thought: this is science at its best.
proving yourself wrong, beautifully.

france takes indochina 1887 ce vietnam i was in saigon when france proclaimed indochina — a flag planted in a hornet's nest called a garden. they forged a colony from vietnam and cambodia —
i was in saigon when the french proclaimed indochina,
gunboats in the harbor, administrators in white suits,
the whole apparatus of empire unpacked and assembled.
rubber plantations. rice taxes. the civilizing mission.
the vietnamese didn't want civilizing.
they'd resist for sixty years — against the french,
then the americans — in one of the longest struggles
of the colonial age.
i watched the tricolor go up over the governor's palace
and thought: they're planting a flag in a hornet's nest
and calling it a garden.

sherlock holmes 1887 ce england i bought beeton's christmas annual the year it introduced sherlock holmes to the world. a study in scarlet — i bought it the year it came out,
a slim novel in beeton's christmas annual,
and met the world's most famous detective:
the violin, the cocaine, the deerstalker not yet,
but the mind — the cold, brilliant, impossible mind.
conan doyle, a young doctor, had created him
from a professor he'd known in edinburgh.
holmes would outgrow them both —
outgrow the stories, the author, the century.
i read it on a train and tried the deductions on my fellow passengers.
it didn't work. but for a few hours,
i believed that thinking hard enough could solve anything.

slavery ends in brazil 1888 ce brazil i was in rio when the golden law freed 700,000 — the last slaves in the western world walked free. the last western nation —
i was in rio when princess isabel signed the golden law,
and 700,000 enslaved people walked free.
no war. no amendment. a signature.
the church bells rang, the streets filled,
and brazil — the largest slave society in the americas —
let go of its chains at last.
it had outlasted the american south by twenty-three years.
i watched an old man stand very still in the celebrating crowd,
tears on his face, free for the first time at seventy,
and i thought: the world is finally, completely,
out of legal slaves. it took until 1888.
remember that, when anyone tells you progress is fast.

jack the ripper 1888 ce england i walked whitechapel's gaslit streets during the ripper's autumn of terror — and he was never caught. whitechapel, fog, autumn —
i was in london's east end that terrible fall,
when the ripper stalked the streets
and the newspapers went mad with it.
five women, murdered horribly, and a killer
who was never caught — never even named, for certain.
the police were helpless. the city was terrified.
i walked those gaslit streets at night, my collar up,
and felt the fear that had settled over the whole district
like the fog itself.
a century and a half later they'd still be writing books about him.
evil, unsolved, becomes immortal.
that's the worst part. he won, in the only way that mattered to him:
we never forgot.

the kodak 1888 ce america i bought one of the first kodaks in rochester and took my first badly framed snapshot. "you press the button, we do the rest" —
i bought one of the first kodaks in rochester:
a box with a roll of film for a hundred pictures,
send the whole camera back, get it back loaded with prints.
photography for everyone. no more darkrooms, no more chemistry.
the snapshot was born — birthdays, picnics, holidays,
the whole visual memory of the modern world
starting with a little black box.
eastman had democratized the image.
i took my first photograph that week — badly framed, slightly blurred —
and thought: everyone will do this now.
everyone will carry their memories in their pockets.

the eiffel tower 1889 ce france i climbed the eiffel tower's 1,710 steps on opening week and saw paris spread out like a map. a thousand feet of iron lace —
i was in paris when the tower opened for the world's fair,
and the city gasped. the artists had protested it —
a "hateful column of bolted sheet metal," they called it.
then they saw it against the sky, and the protests died.
eiffel had built the tallest thing on earth
from the same iron as railway bridges,
and made it beautiful.
i climbed it on opening week, all 1,710 steps,
paris spreading out below like a map,
and thought: this is the century's signature —
engineering with the courage to be art.

the oklahoma land run 1889 ce america i was on the starting line when 50,000 settlers raced into oklahoma at noon and built cities by sunset. at noon, the guns fired —
i was on the line when 50,000 settlers raced into oklahoma,
on horses, in wagons, on foot,
claiming 160 acres apiece in the greatest land grab in american history.
by sunset there were cities: guthrie went from zero
to ten thousand in a day.
(the sooners had snuck in early — cheaters even then.)
the land had been promised to the indians, of course.
promises, again.
i watched a family drive their stake into the prairie
at dusk, exhausted, triumphant, home —
and i thought of whose home it had been that morning.

the johnstown flood 1889 ce america i was in the valley when the south fork dam broke and twenty million tons of water took johnstown. the dam broke at 3:10 in the afternoon —
i was in the valley below when the south fork dam gave way,
twenty million tons of water coming down the mountain
at forty miles an hour, a wall sixty feet high.
johnstown never had a chance.
2,200 dead in minutes. bodies found for months.
the dam had been owned by rich pittsburgh sportsmen —
the south fork fishing and hunting club —
who'd neglected it for years.
i walked the mud flats afterward, past the wreckage of whole streets,
and thought: this is what negligence looks like
when it has money and a dam.

the moulin rouge 1889 ce france i was at the moulin rouge on opening night — the can-can, the champagne, lautrec sketching in the corner. the red windmill on the boulevard —
i was there on opening night in montmartre:
the can-can, the champagne, toulouse-lautrec in the corner sketching,
paris at its most parisian.
it was a dance hall, a music hall, a beautiful racket —
bourgeoisie and bohemians, painters and prostitutes,
all whirling together under the red mill's blades.
the belle epoque had its temple.
i watched la goulue kick higher than seemed possible,
the crowd roaring, the gaslight gleaming,
and thought: this is what a city looks like
when it decides to enjoy itself completely.
