the sherman antitrust act 1890 ce america i was in washington when the sherman act outlawed monopolies — a paper tiger that would grow teeth. the first shot fired at the trusts —
i was in washington when it passed:
every contract "in restraint of trade" illegal,
monopolies outlawed, the government armed against the giants.
standard oil. the railroads. carnegie.
for years it was barely used — a paper tiger.
but the idea was planted: bigness itself could be a crime.
it would take twenty years and a roosevelt to give it teeth,
but the teeth came.
i watched the senators vote, most of them friends of the trusts,
passing a law they'd spend decades trying to ignore —
and i thought: even a paper tiger casts a shadow.

van gogh dies 1890 ce france i stood in the auvers wheat field after van gogh died broke and unknown — genius recognized one funeral too late. he walked into a wheat field at auvers and shot himself —
i was in paris when the news came, and nobody much noticed.
vincent van gogh, thirty-seven, broke, unknown,
one painting sold in his lifetime (to his brother, essentially).
the wheat fields, the sunflowers, the starry night —
all of it unsold, unseen, stacked in theo's apartment.
fame came later. so much later.
now a single canvas sells for what kingdoms cost.
i stood in that wheat field afterward, the crows rising,
and thought: the world is very good at recognizing genius,
exactly one funeral too late.

wounded knee 1890 ce america i walked the frozen field at wounded knee the day after the massacre ended the indian wars. snow, and blood on the snow —
i arrived at wounded knee the day after the 7th cavalry
opened fire on big foot's lakota:
300 dead, mostly women and children,
cut down by hotchkiss guns in the frozen creek bed.
it started with a scuffle over a rifle.
it ended the indian wars.
i walked the field where the bodies lay frozen in the positions
they'd died in, photographers already at work,
and i thought of little bighorn, fourteen years before.
the revenge was complete. the continent was taken.
bury my heart, indeed.

the trans-siberian 1891 ce russia i was at vladivostok when russia began the 5,700-mile trans-siberian across the wilderness. 5,700 miles of railway across siberia —
i was at vladivostok when the tsarevich turned the first sod,
and russia began the longest railway on earth.
through taiga and permafrost, across rivers wider than seas,
built by exiles and soldiers and peasants,
thousands dying in the cold and the mud.
it would take twenty-five years.
when it was done, moscow to the pacific in days —
an empire stitched together with steel,
asia bound to europe by a single track.
i stood at the edge of the wilderness where the rails would go
and thought: this is what empires dream —
a road so long it changes the size of the world.

basketball 1891 ce america i watched naismith's first basketball game in springfield — peach baskets, a soccer ball, thirteen rules. peach baskets nailed to the gym wall —
i was in springfield, massachusetts, when james naismith,
a gym teacher with a restless winter class,
invented a game: thirteen rules, a soccer ball,
two baskets, no running with the ball.
the first game ended 1–0. someone had to climb a ladder
to get the ball out.
it was supposed to keep boys busy in winter.
it became a world religion.
i watched those first players — mustached young men
in wool uniforms — and thought:
they have no idea. none of them has any idea
what they've started.

ellis island opens 1892 ce america i was at ellis island on opening day when fifteen-year-old annie moore became the first immigrant processed. the gateway for twelve million —
i was there on opening day, january 1st,
when annie moore from ireland, fifteen years old,
became the first immigrant processed.
they'd come through the great hall by the thousands:
the inspections, the chalk marks, the tears,
the names shortened at the desks.
for most, it took hours. for some, it took a lifetime
to get past that island.
i watched a family from sicily stare at the manhattan skyline
through the windows, holding everything they owned,
and i thought: this is the door america walks through.
twelve million stories, starting here.

the homestead strike 1892 ce america i was on the monongahela when steelworkers battled pinkertons at homestead — labor's bloodiest fight. steelworkers against pinkertons on the monongahela —
i was at homestead when it exploded:
carnegie's mill, frick's wage cuts, the union locked out,
three hundred pinkerton detectives floating down the river on barges.
the workers met them at the shore with rifles.
twelve dead. the barges surrendered.
then the state militia came — eight thousand troops —
and broke the strike, and broke the union.
labor's bloodiest fight, and labor lost.
i stood on the riverbank afterward, the barges burned,
and thought: carnegie will build libraries with this money.
the men who bled for it will get the libraries. not the wages.

the nutcracker 1892 ce russia i was at the nutcracker's shrugging st. petersburg premiere — the flop that became christmas itself. a christmas ballet that flopped —
i was in st. petersburg for the premiere:
tchaikovsky's nutcracker, all sugarplums and snowflakes,
and the critics shrugged. too childish, they said.
tchaikovsky died the next year, never knowing.
but the ballet wouldn't stay down.
it rose again — in america, after the war —
and became the christmas ritual of the western world,
danced by every company, loved by every child.
i sat in that cold premiere audience,
watching the snow scene, and i missed it too.
some masterpieces need fifty years and an ocean crossing.

the queen is overthrown 1893 ce hawaii i was in honolulu when american planters overthrew queen liliuokalani — a kingdom stolen for sugar. american planters toppled a queen —
i was in honolulu when liliuokalani was forced to abdicate:
marines from the uss boston ashore "to protect american lives,"
a committee of safety that was neither,
a kingdom stolen for sugar.
the queen yielded to avoid bloodshed —
"i yield to the superior force of the united states,"
she wrote, and the republic of planters took over.
cleveland refused to annex it. mckinley would do it later.
i watched the hawaiian flag come down over the palace
and thought: this is what empire looks like up close —
not a battle, but a business meeting with guns outside.

the chicago world's fair 1893 ce america i rode the first ferris wheel at chicago's white city fair — 27 million visitors glimpsing the future lit up at night. the white city —
i walked the fairgrounds that summer with 27 million visitors:
electric lights everywhere, the first ferris wheel turning against the sky,
buildings white as marble dreams on the shore of lake michigan.
chicago, risen from the fire, showing the world what it had become.
adams called it the first expression of american thought as a unity.
the rest of us just stared.
it gave america the ferris wheel, cracker jack, the zipper —
and a vision of the future, all lit up at night.
i rode the wheel to the top at sunset,
the whole white city glowing below,
and thought: this is what the century wanted to be.

women win the vote 1893 ce new zealand i watched women queue to vote in new zealand — the first nation on earth where women voted nationally. the first nation on earth —
i was in new zealand when the petitions — 32,000 signatures,
presented by kate sheppard's suffragists —
finally moved parliament, and the governor signed.
women voted in the national election that year.
first in the world. not wyoming the territory now —
a whole nation.
the arguments against it had been endless: the family would collapse,
politics would corrupt them, the empire would fall.
none of it happened. they just voted.
i watched women queue at the polls in christchurch,
calm and orderly, and thought:
the sky didn't fall. it never does.
it just gets a little bigger.

the pullman strike 1894 ce america i was in chicago when the pullman strike stopped the nation's railroads and gave america labor day. the railroads stopped, coast to coast —
i was in chicago when debs's railway union walked out:
pullman had cut wages but not rents in his company town,
and the workers finally broke.
the strike spread nationwide. federal troops came in.
thirty dead. debs in prison — where he'd read marx
and come out a socialist.
but something else was born in the wreckage:
to calm the fury, congress made labor day a national holiday.
i watched the soldiers clear the tracks at kensington,
bayonets fixed, and thought:
they broke the strike, and the workers got a holiday.
that's the american bargain, in one sentence.

the sino-japanese war 1894 ce asia i followed the sino-japanese war and watched meiji japan dismantle qing china in eight months. asia's power shifted in eight months —
i was with the correspondents when japan's modern army and navy,
built in twenty-five years of meiji reform,
dismantled qing china's forces on land and sea.
yalu river. port arthur. weihaiwei.
the student had beaten the master —
or rather, the modernizer had beaten the empire
that refused to modernize.
the world took notice: japan was a power now,
and china was the sick man of asia.
i watched japanese troops march into port arthur
in their western uniforms, and thought:
the next fifty years of asia were decided here,
in these eight months.

the dreyfus affair 1894 ce france i watched dreyfus degraded in a paris courtyard — the forged treason case that split france in two. a jewish officer, forged evidence, a torn republic —
i was in paris when they convicted alfred dreyfus of treason:
degraded in the courtyard, his sword broken,
"judas" in the crowd's roar, shipped to devil's island.
the evidence was forged. everyone in power knew, eventually.
france split in two: dreyfusards and anti-dreyfusards,
zola's "j'accuse" shaking the nation like an earthquake.
it took twelve years to clear him.
i watched the degradation ceremony in the rain
and thought: this is what happens when an army
decides its honor matters more than the truth.
it always ends the same way: with the truth winning, late.

shimonoseki 1895 ce asia i was at shimonoseki when china ceded taiwan and japan arrived as a great power. china ceded taiwan, paid indemnities, recognized korea's independence —
i was in shimonoseki when li hongzhang signed:
the treaty that announced japan as a great power.
an assassin's bullet had grazed li's cheek during the talks;
japan, embarrassed, reduced the indemnity.
such are the manners of empire.
china paid in silver and territory for the lesson
of the war: modernize or be carved.
it would try — too late, too slowly.
i watched the chinese delegation leave the hall,
old men in a new world, and thought:
this treaty signed the next half-century of asia —
japan rising, china humiliated, everyone watching.

wireless 1895 ce italy i stood in marconi's father's garden when his wireless signals clicked across it — and made the cable obsolete. a twenty-year-old sent signals across his father's estate —
i was in bologna when young marconi showed me:
a spark, a wire, a receiver that clicked across the garden,
no cable between them.
wireless. messages through the air itself.
he'd take it to england, to the world —
ships at sea, news across oceans, all without wires.
the ether the physicists had just abolished
became the medium of the new age anyway.
i stood in that garden, listening to the clicks,
and thought of the atlantic cable, the copper on the seabed.
this boy had just made it obsolete.
the air itself would carry the world's words now.

x-rays 1895 ce germany i held rontgen's photographic plate of his wife's skeletal hand — the x-ray that made the invisible visible. rontgen photographed his wife's hand —
i was in wurzburg when he showed me the image:
bones, and a ring, floating in ghostly flesh.
he'd found rays that passed through skin
but not bone — x-rays, he called them, x for unknown.
within weeks, surgeons were using them.
within months, the whole world knew.
anna rontgen looked at her own skeleton
and said, "i have seen my death."
she'd seen the future, really —
every hospital, every broken bone, every hidden thing
made visible by invisible light.
i held the photographic plate up to the lamp
and saw my own century coming.

the movies are born 1895 ce france i was in the grand cafe basement when the lumieres screened the first paying films — a train arriving, workers leaving. thirty-three francs in the till —
i was in the grand cafe in paris on december 28th,
when the lumiere brothers charged admission
to watch moving pictures:
workers leaving a factory, a train arriving at a station —
the audience ducking as the locomotive came at them.
fifty seconds of film, and the world changed.
cinema was born that night, in a basement,
for one franc a seat.
the lumieres thought it was a novelty with no future.
"the cinema is an invention without a future," louis said.
i sat in that dark room, watching the train arrive,
and i knew better. we all did, by the second reel.

adwa 1896 ce ethiopia i was with menelik's army at adwa when ethiopia destroyed the italian invasion — africa's greatest anti-colonial victory. africa's greatest victory over the colonizers —
i was with menelik's army at adwa:
100,000 ethiopians — with rifles, with artillery, with a plan —
destroying the italian invasion force in a day.
seven thousand italians dead. the rest in flight.
europe was stunned. an african army
had beaten a european one in open battle.
ethiopia stayed free — the one african nation
never colonized, a beacon for every independence movement
that would follow.
i walked the battlefield afterward,
past the captured italian guns,
and thought: remember this day.
the colonized just proved they could win.

the modern olympics 1896 ce greece i sat in athens' marble stadium for the first modern olympics — 241 athletes, fourteen nations. athens, the panathenaic stadium, white marble —
i was there for the first modern games:
241 athletes, fourteen nations,
coubertin's dream of peace through sport made real.
spiridon louis won the marathon — a greek,
in greece, and the stadium went mad with joy.
it was small, amateur, glorious.
no one imagined what it would become —
the billions, the boycotts, the whole world watching.
i sat in that marble stadium, the sun on the stone,
and thought: the ancient games are back.
humanity had remembered how to play together.

plessy v. ferguson 1896 ce america i was in washington when the court blessed "separate but equal" — and jim crow got its law for sixty years. "separate but equal" —
i was in washington when the court blessed jim crow:
homer plessy, one-eighth black, arrested for sitting
in the white car in louisiana,
and the justices ruled the constitution allowed it.
justice harlan dissented alone:
"our constitution is color-blind."
he was right, and it didn't matter.
for sixty years, "separate but equal" was the law —
separate always, equal never.
i watched plessy leave the courtroom, a quiet man
who'd tried to break a system with a train ticket,
and thought: the 15th amendment promised the vote.
this decision promised the cage.

klondike gold 1896 ce canada i watched the stampeders sail north for the klondike — the last great gold rush on earth. gold in a yukon creek —
i was in seattle when the ships came down from the north,
men staggering off with sacks of it,
and the stampede began: 100,000 strong,
chasing the last great gold rush on earth.
they climbed the chilkoot pass with a ton of supplies each,
the mounties' rule — no one enters without a year's food —
the line of climbers like ants up the ice stairs.
most found nothing. the merchants found fortunes.
freezing, starving, scurvy — the klondike ate men alive.
but the ones who made it came back changed,
with gold dust in their pockets and stories for life.
i watched them sail north, young and hungry,
and thought: the frontier's last act.
after this, there's nowhere left to rush to.

the birth of jazz 1897 ce america i was in a new orleans dance hall when brass bands and ragtime fused into jazz. in new orleans, something new was in the air —
i was in the back of a dance hall in storyville,
listening to brass bands and ragtime piano
fuse into something nobody had a name for yet.
buddy bolden's cornet, loud enough to be heard across town —
they say he was the first to play it, the first jazzman.
african rhythms, european horns, blues feeling,
all melting in the new orleans heat.
it wasn't written down. it couldn't be.
you had to be there, sweating in the crowd,
feeling the music invent itself under your feet.
i danced — badly — and thought:
this is america's real classical music being born,
in a dance hall, on a saturday night.

dracula 1897 ce england i read dracula at 2 a.m. the year it came out — and checked the locks on my doors. the count never dies —
i read stoker's novel the year it came out,
all letters and diaries and newspaper clippings,
a vampire sailing into whitby in a ship full of dead men.
it was a sensation. then it was a legend.
then it was everything: plays, films, a hundred years
of capes and fangs and transylvanian nights.
stoker never visited transylvania.
he didn't need to — he built it from books and nightmares,
and it was more real than the real place.
i finished it at 2 a.m., candles low,
and checked the locks on my doors.
some books you read. this one reads you.

the diamond jubilee 1897 ce england i watched the diamond jubilee procession — the largest empire in history saluting its queen, at the edge of decline. sixty years —
i was in london again, ten years after the golden jubilee,
and this one was bigger: the largest empire in history
saluting its queen, troops from every continent
marching past the old lady in her carriage.
kipling wrote "recessional" for the occasion —
"lest we forget" — a warning inside the celebration.
he saw what the crowds didn't: the empire's peak
was also the view from the edge.
i watched the colonial troops march — sikhs, gurkhas,
west indians, canadians — the whole world in uniform,
and thought: this is the photograph of the empire
at its greatest extent. keep it.
nothing this big stays this big.

the electron 1897 ce england i was in thomson's cambridge lab when the electron proved the "uncuttable" atom had parts. the atom has parts —
i was in cambridge when j.j. thomson announced it:
cathode rays were particles, tiny, negatively charged,
two thousand times lighter than hydrogen.
the electron. the first subatomic particle.
the atom — uncuttable, indivisible, by definition —
had been cut.
everything followed: the nucleus, the quantum,
the whole strange architecture of matter.
i looked at his cathode-ray tube, glowing green in the dark lab,
and thought: the smallest thing anyone had ever found,
and it broke the biggest idea in science.
the universe just got deeper.

the maine explodes 1898 ce cuba i was on the havana waterfront when the maine exploded — 266 dead, and war fever ignited by headlines. havana harbor, 9:40 p.m. —
i was on the waterfront when the battleship maine blew up:
two explosions, the ship sinking in minutes,
266 american sailors dead.
nobody knew why. (a coal bunker fire, most likely —
not a spanish mine. but nobody wanted to hear that.)
"remember the maine!" — the cry went up,
hearst's papers fanning the flames,
and war fever swept the country like a fever indeed.
i watched the wreck settle in the harbor mud,
the mast still above water like a accusing finger,
and thought: this is how empires start wars now —
with a headline, not a reason.

the spanish-american war 1898 ce america i was in manila bay when dewey fired — ten weeks that turned the american republic into an empire. ten weeks, and america became an empire —
i was in manila bay when dewey's squadron
destroyed the spanish fleet before breakfast:
"you may fire when you are ready, gridley."
cuba. puerto rico. guam. the philippines —
spain's empire, transferred to washington in a summer.
the country that had been born fighting an empire
now owned colonies.
(the filipinos, who'd fought spain for freedom,
found they'd traded one master for another —
and fought america for three more years.)
i watched the flag go up over manila
and thought: the republic just became something else.
it would spend the next century deciding what.

omdurman 1898 ce sudan i was at omdurman when machine guns mowed down 10,000 dervishes in a morning — courage against the maxim. the machine guns did it in a morning —
i was with kitchener's force at omdurman:
25,000 british and egyptian troops,
maxims and artillery against 50,000 dervishes
charging with spears and swords and faith.
it wasn't a battle. it was an execution.
10,000 mahdists dead in hours. forty-eight british.
churchill was there, in the cavalry charge —
the last great cavalry charge, and the first
industrial-age massacre, on the same field.
i walked among the dervish dead afterward,
brave men mowed down in windrows,
and thought: courage means nothing against the maxim.
the age of the noble charge was over.
the age of the machine had begun.

radium 1898 ce france i visited the curies' shed laboratory and watched radium glow blue — the fire at the heart of matter. marie and pierre curie, in a paris shed —
i visited their laboratory: no ventilation, no protection,
tons of pitchblende boiled down to a pinch of glowing salt.
radium. it glowed blue in the dark.
it was millions of times more radioactive than uranium —
a word they'd just invented: radioactivity.
the strange power would heal cancers and kill its discoverers.
marie carried test tubes of it in her pockets.
i held a vial — shielded, barely — and watched it glow,
and thought: this light comes from inside matter itself,
from atoms breaking apart.
they'd found the fire at the heart of things.
it would light the world. it would burn it.

the hague conference 1899 ce netherlands i was at the hague when twenty-six nations held the first world peace conference and tried to leash war. twenty-six nations, called by the tsar —
i was at the hague for the first world peace conference:
they banned poison gas, dum-dum bullets, balloon bombing,
and created a court of arbitration.
it was idealistic. it was inadequate.
(the next century would break every rule they wrote.)
but it was the first time the nations of the world
sat down together to say: war should have limits.
the idea mattered, even when the rules didn't hold.
i watched the delegates — uniforms and frock coats,
all the old world in one room —
and thought: they're trying to leash the future.
the future was already straining at the leash.

the boer war 1899 ce south africa i was in south africa when the boer war began — the empire's hardest fight, eighteen years after majuba. the empire's hardest fight yet —
i was in south africa when it started:
the boer republics against the full might of britain,
and the boers won the first rounds — besieging ladysmith,
mafeking, kimberley, picking off columns with their mausers.
london sent half a million men in the end —
the largest army britain had ever fielded —
and still the commandos fought on for three years,
until the farms were burned and the families put in camps.
i watched the first british columns march out, confident,
and thought of majuba, eighteen years before.
the empire had come back, as i'd known it would.
this time it brought everything it had.

the paris olympics 1900 ce france i watched charlotte cooper win tennis in paris — the first female olympic champion in the games' chaotic second act. five months long, and half a sideshow —
i was in paris for the second modern games:
stretched across the world's fair, chaotic, sprawling,
some athletes never knowing they'd been in the olympics.
but the women competed — for the first time.
tennis, golf, croquet: twenty-two women,
breaking the ancient barrier quietly, without ceremony.
the games were a mess. the precedent was everything.
i watched charlotte cooper win the tennis,
the first female olympic champion in history,
and thought: athens had the marble and the glory.
paris had the future — and she was holding a racket.

the boxer rebellion 1900 ce china i was in besieged beijing during the boxer rebellion — fifty-five days that broke the qing dynasty. "the foreigners must go" —
i was in beijing when the boxers besieged the legations:
fifty-five days, the diplomats and missionaries
behind barricades, the "society of righteous and harmonious fists"
sure their rituals made them bulletproof.
they weren't. eight armies marched on beijing —
british, french, german, russian, japanese, american —
and crushed the uprising, and looted the city for good measure.
the qing dynasty never recovered.
i walked through the breached gates with the relief force,
past the bodies of boxers who'd believed the bullets couldn't touch them,
and thought: china would remember this humiliation,
nurse it, and one day answer it.

the galveston hurricane 1900 ce america i was in galveston when the hurricane drowned 8,000 — america's deadliest natural disaster. the sea came over the island —
i was in galveston when the great hurricane struck:
no warning system, no seawall, a city flat as a table
in the path of a storm no one understood.
the water rose fifteen feet. houses floated off their foundations.
8,000 dead — america's deadliest natural disaster,
then and now.
i walked the wreckage afterward, past the bodies stacked like cordwood,
the whole city a splintered ruin,
and thought: we build our proudest cities on sand,
and the sea keeps the accounts.
galveston never regained its glory. houston did.
the storm redrew the map of texas with water.

the quantum 1900 ce germany i was in berlin when planck proposed energy comes in packets — the reluctant heresy that began the quantum age. energy comes in packets —
i was in berlin when max planck, desperate to solve
the black-body radiation problem, proposed it:
energy isn't continuous. it comes in quanta —
little packets, little jumps, nothing in between.
he thought it was a mathematical trick.
it wasn't. it was the crack in the foundation
of all of classical physics.
einstein would widen it. bohr, heisenberg, schrodinger
would build a new universe through it.
the twentieth century's strangest, truest science
started with one reluctant equation.
i watched the old physicist present his heresy
to a polite, uncomprehending audience,
and thought: they have no idea what he just did.
none of us did. the quantum age had begun.

the fair of the century 1900 ce paris paris's 1900 exposition shows off the wonders of a new century — moving sidewalks, talking films, the eiffel tower — while the traveler already knows the dark years ahead. i walked the fairgrounds of 1900 and watched the future arrive on rails,
moving sidewalks carrying ladies in long skirts,
fifty million visitors under a paris sky.
the eiffel tower, that iron skeleton they'd called an eyesore,
stood tall and let the crowds forgive her.
talking films flickered in dark pavilions,
and for a summer the world believed
everything that came next would be this bright.
i smiled at them. i had seen what came next.

the boxers rise 1900 ce beijing, china anti-foreign rebels besiege beijing's legation quarter until an eight-nation army breaks through, then loots the city — the traveler's loyalty is torn between both sides of the barricade. i stood in the legation quarter when the siege began,
summer heat, barricades of furniture and sandbags,
eight nations' soldiers behind one thin line.
the boxers believed their rituals stopped bullets;
the bullets did not believe in rituals.
for fifty-five days the foreigners held,
then the armies marched in and looted beijing street by street.
i watched an old city pay for an empire's pride
and wondered which of us had been the invaders.

dreams get a map 1900 ce vienna, austria freud publishes the interpretation of dreams in vienna, mapping the unconscious mind — the traveler, who has lived a hundred lifetimes, agrees the hidden country is real. in vienna i read the book that said our nights mean something,
a doctor with a couch and a cigar,
telling the century that a locked room in every head
held the self we hide from ourselves.
he mapped the dream the way explorers map a coast:
here be dragons, here the buried city.
i have walked a hundred centuries of sleep,
and i tell you he was right —
there is a country under the skull no waking eye can see.

the sea takes galveston 1900 ce texas, usa the 1900 galveston hurricane drowns the richest port in texas, killing thousands in america's deadliest storm — the traveler helps with the burial parties. i was on the island when the water rose,
the richest port in texas, and the wind took it apart board by board.
the storm surge came like a moving wall,
and houses folded the way paper folds in a child's fist.
six to eight thousand dead — they never knew the true count,
they buried the bodies at sea and the sea gave them back.
america's deadliest storm, and no satellites warned them,
only a sky going black at noon.
i helped stack the dead. i do not forget their names were never all known.

women take the field 1900 ce paris, france women compete in the olympics for the first time in paris — tennis, golf, sailing — and the traveler sees a door open that will never close again. paris, 1900, and for the first time women run the race,
tennis, golf, sailing — a crack in a very old wall.
i watched the crowd watch them, unsure whether to cheer or look away,
and some cheered, tentatively, like people testing a new word.
the men kept the marathons for themselves a while longer,
but the door had opened, and doors do not close by themselves.
i have seen a thousand walls fall; this one began
with a tennis racket and a sail on the seine.

the airship ascends 1900 ce germany zeppelin's rigid airship floats over lake constance in 1900 — the traveler watches the crowd watch the sky grow a hull. over lake constance the great silver fish rose,
count zeppelin's rigid dream, floating on nothing but nerve.
i watched the crowd below, their hats in their hands,
as the sky grew a hull and a keel for the first time.
it wobbled, it swayed, it flew eighteen minutes —
long enough to change the meaning of up.
i have ridden storms across a thousand worlds,
and still i held my breath with them.

under the city of light 1900 ce paris, france paris opens its underground railway in 1900, and the traveler rides the first trains through the city's new second self beneath the boulevards. they bored tunnels under paris and called it the metro,
and the city learned to travel beneath itself.
i rode the first cars, the air electric and new,
commuters descending into a lit underworld every morning.
above, the boulevards kept their cafes and their sun;
below, another paris hummed in iron and tile.
every great city hides a second city under its feet —
paris was just the first to admit it.

the victorian age ends 1900 ce england queen victoria dies after a 63-year reign, and an empire mourns its grandmother — the traveler knows most of the royal mourners at her funeral will be gone within two decades. she died in january on the isle of wight,
sixty-three years on the throne, the grandmother of europe.
i watched the empire wear black for a woman
who had seen steam replace sail and telegraph replace horse.
the century she'd named was already over;
the new one stood in the doorway, uninvited.
kings and emperors took her funeral train as a family portrait —
most of them would be gone within twenty years.
i wept with the crowds. i knew what was coming for them.

the prize begins 1900 ce stockholm, sweden the first nobel prizes honor rontgen, red cross founder dunant, and a poet — funded by dynamite money, the traveler calls it nobel's strange atonement. in stockholm they handed out the first prizes
bought with dynamite money — nobel's strange atonement.
rontgen for the invisible rays,
dunant for the red cross, for mercy on battlefields,
a poet for his verses.
i watched them bow and accept,
and thought of all the brilliant minds the century would waste
while this prize went on shining, year after year,
like a candle kept lit for the better angels.

a signal crosses the ocean 1901 ce cornwall to newfoundland marconi receives three faint dots across the atlantic — the first transatlantic wireless signal, and the traveler feels the horizon dissolve. three dots, faint as heartbeats, across the atlantic,
marconi heard them and the world got smaller that day.
no cable, no wire, no poles — just the air itself carrying a message,
the letter s, tapped in cornwall, caught in newfoundland.
the scientists said the signal should have flown straight off the earth;
the sky itself bent it back down.
i stood in the cold by the receiving station
and felt the horizon dissolve.

oil erupts in texas 1901 ce texas, usa the spindletop gusher blows in texas, launching the petroleum century — the traveler stands in the spray and smells the future burning. the ground blew open at spindletop,
a hundred and fifty feet of black gold roaring skyward.
i stood in the spray of it, deafened,
while men danced in the mud and the drillers wept.
the petroleum century began in that gusher —
cars, planes, wars, plastics, the whole smoky kingdom.
nobody in that field thought past the money.
i smelled the future burning and it smelled like oil.

a nation of states 1901 ce australia six australian colonies unite peacefully as a commonwealth on new year's day 1901 — the traveler notes most nations are born screaming; this one was born talking. six colonies, one continent, and on new year's day
they stitched themselves into a commonwealth.
no war, no blood — just signatures and speeches in sydney,
a nation born by agreement, the civilized miracle.
i watched the flags go up over the harbor
and thought how rarely it happens this way:
most nations are born screaming.
australia was born talking.

blue becomes a period 1901 ce paris, france a grieving young picasso paints the world in blue — beggars, blind men, mothers — and the traveler watches heartbreak become a whole period of art. a young spaniard in paris, grieving his dead friend,
picked up blue and would not put it down.
beggers, blind men, mothers with empty arms —
he painted sorrow until sorrow had a color.
i stood in his studio among the canvases,
wet paint the blue of dusk after rain,
and watched a boy turn heartbreak into a whole period of art.
grief, he taught the century, is a kind of seeing.

an assassin in buffalo 1901 ce new york, usa mckinley is assassinated in buffalo and theodore roosevelt storms into the white house — the century's first changing of the guard by bullet, not ballot. in buffalo a man with a wrapped hand
shot president mckinley at the pan-american exposition.
i was in the crowd when the shots cracked,
and watched a nation learn the word anarchist.
mckinley lingered eight days and died;
theodore roosevelt came down from the mountains
and stormed the white house like a cavalry charge.
the twentieth century's first changing of the guard —
by bullet, not by ballot.

the mountain explodes 1901 ce martinique mount pelee buries saint-pierre in minutes in 1902, killing nearly everyone except a prisoner in a stone cell and a shoemaker — the traveler watches from a ship in the harbor. saint-pierre had a mountain and an election,
so nobody evacuated when pelee began to smoke.
i was on a ship in the harbor when the sky fell —
a black cloud of burning gas rolling down the slope
faster than any running thing could run.
thirty thousand people, gone in minutes,
the whole city except two men: a prisoner in a stone cell
and a shoemaker who outran the cloud.
the mountain did not negotiate. it never does.

peace in the veld 1902 ce south africa the boer war ends with britain victorious — the traveler remembers the scorched farms, the camps where children died, and the black africans who fought and got nothing. the boer war ended in the veld with a treaty,
britain took the transvaal and the orange free state.
i had watched farmers on horseback hold the empire for three years,
and watched the empire answer with camps where children died of fever.
peace came, but it was a soldier's peace,
bought with scorched farms and the bones of the innocent.
the boers lost their republics;
the black africans, who had fought for both sides,
got nothing at all.

cool air on demand 1902 ce new york, usa willis carrier invents modern air conditioning for a brooklyn printing plant — the traveler shivers in the first cooled room, not knowing half the modern world will run on it. a brooklyn printing plant had a humidity problem,
so willis carrier taught the air to behave.
cool, dry, on demand — nobody at the time guessed
it would redraw the map of where humans could live.
the south, the desert cities, the tropics' offices —
half the modern world runs on his machine.
i stood in that first cooled room and shivered,
not knowing the shiver would go global.

the bear gets a name 1902 ce usa roosevelt spares a bear cub on a mississippi hunt, a cartoon follows, and the teddy bear is born — the traveler calls it an empire of mercy in miniature. roosevelt went hunting in mississippi
and refused to shoot a bear cub tied to a tree.
a cartoonist drew it, a shopkeeper stuffed it,
and the teddy bear was born — named for theodore.
i have seen empires rise on smaller mercies.
a president spares one small life,
and a million children clutch the soft echo of it
in the dark, when the house is quiet.

the rose bowl begins 1902 ce california, usa michigan crushes stanford in the first rose bowl — the traveler sits in the pasadena stands while a century-long new year's ritual is invented by accident. michigan crushed stanford forty-nine to nothing
in the first rose bowl, under the california sun.
i sat in the stands in pasadena
while a new american ritual was being invented:
parades of flowers in the morning, football in the afternoon,
every new year's day for a century to come.
nobody there knew they were starting a tradition.
they thought they were just watching a game.

sixty riders, one road 1903 ce france sixty riders set off from paris in the first tour de france — the traveler follows the dust and punctures through villages seeing bicycle racing for the first time. sixty riders set off from paris on bicycles,
two thousand four hundred kilometers of french road,
dust, punctures, and cheating in the dark.
maurice garin won the first tour de france,
and i rode alongside them in my mind if not on wheels,
through villages that turned out to stare
at men doing something no one had ever done:
racing the whole of france on two thin tires.

twelve seconds at kitty hawk 1903 ce north carolina, usa the wright brothers' flyer lifts off the dunes at kitty hawk for twelve seconds — the traveler calls it the moment humanity became a flying species. twelve seconds. one hundred twenty feet.
two bicycle mechanics from ohio, a dune, a headwind,
and a machine that left the ground under its own power.
i stood on the sand at kitty hawk and held my breath
while the flyer trembled into the air —
the moment the human race became a flying species.
they did it three more times that day.
by the fourth flight they had flown nearly a minute.
i have crossed galaxies, and i still honor those twelve seconds.

the car for everyone 1903 ce michigan, usa henry ford founds the ford motor company in detroit — the traveler walks the early factory floor and senses the horse's four thousand years coming to an end. henry ford founded his motor company in detroit,
and the automobile was still a rich man's toy —
for now.
i walked the early factory floor, smelled the oil and ambition,
and watched a stubborn man with a stubborn idea:
the car not for the few but for the multitude.
he would build it on a moving line and sell it cheap,
and the world would pave itself to make room.
the horse had four thousand years. its time was up.

a canal is born 1903 ce panama panama breaks from colombia with american backing and the canal zone follows — the traveler notes empires dig, and small countries hold the shovel. panama broke from colombia with american warships offshore,
and within weeks the canal zone was washington's.
i stood on the isthmus where the french had already buried twenty thousand men,
and watched the americans arrive with mosquito nets and steam shovels.
a canal is a wound through a continent that heals into a road —
but the wound was panama's, and the road was america's.
empires dig. the small countries hold the shovel.

the fall classic begins 1903 ce usa boston beats pittsburgh in the first world series — the traveler sits in the wooden stands while october invents its own holiday. boston beat pittsburgh, five games to three,
in the first world series ever played.
i sat in the wooden stands, scorecard on my knee,
while october invented its own holiday.
no one called it the fall classic yet —
it was just the best team in the american league
against the best in the national, winner take all.
a century of octobers started there,
in the smell of peanuts and cigar smoke.

movies learn to tell stories 1903 ce usa the great train robbery gives film a plot, a chase, and a gunshot fired at the camera — the traveler watches storytelling learn a new language in twelve minutes. before this, films were just things that moved —
a train arriving, workers leaving a factory.
then the great train robbery gave the movies a plot:
a robbery, a chase, a posse, and a bandit firing his gun at the camera.
i sat in the dark while the audience ducked,
and watched storytelling learn a new language in twelve minutes.
every film you have ever loved
is a grandchild of that train robbery.

the east strikes first 1904 ce manchuria japan's surprise attack on port arthur opens the russo-japanese war — the traveler watches the world learn that the european empires are not invincible. japan's torpedo boats slipped into port arthur at night,
and an asian power struck a european empire first.
i watched the russian fleet burn in its own harbor
while the world rubbed its eyes — this wasn't supposed to happen.
the twentieth century's first great shock:
the white empires were not invincible.
in tokyo they celebrated; in st. petersburg they could not believe it.
i believed it. i had seen the future wearing a different face.

the desert war 1904 ce german south west africa germany crushes the herero uprising, driving tens of thousands into the desert to die — the traveler walks among the bones and calls it the century's first genocide, rehearsed in the sand. the herero rose, and germany answered with extermination,
driving tens of thousands into the waterless desert to die.
i walked that desert after the soldiers left,
past the bones and the abandoned wells, the silence like a held breath.
the century's first genocide, and the world looked away —
it was africa, it was colonies, it didn't count.
it counted. i counted the bones.
everything the century would do to the jews, to the armenians,
was rehearsed here first, in the sand.

old enemies shake hands 1904 ce london and paris britain and france settle their colonial quarrels in the entente cordiale — the traveler watches old enemies shake hands and knows they are making sides, not peace. britain and france sat down and settled their quarrels,
egypt for you, morocco for me — the entente cordiale.
i watched the diplomats shake hands in london and paris,
eight centuries of war filed away in a drawer.
they thought they were making peace.
they were making sides.
within ten years those handshakes would be trenches,
and the colonial bargains would be paid for in french and british blood.

the city goes underground 1904 ce new york, usa new york opens its first subway line from city hall to harlem — the traveler rides opening day and feels a city deciding to never stop growing. new york opened its first subway line,
city hall to harlem, nine miles of tunnel.
i rode with the crowds on opening day,
the car packed, the air electric, the city vibrating through the floor.
above, the horse cars and the elevated trains kept their noise;
below, the future moved at forty miles an hour.
a city that goes underground is a city that has decided
to never stop growing, up or down.

the games come to america 1904 ce missouri, usa the 1904 st. louis olympics dissolve into dust and chaos — a strychnine-dosed marathon, a cheater in a car — but the traveler sees the real games survive underneath. the olympics came to st. louis and nearly drowned in dust,
a marathon run through choking heat, one runner dosed with strychnine,
another hitched a ride in a car and almost stole it.
i watched the chaos from the sidelines, half laughing, half horrified —
the ancient games, reborn as an american county fair.
but through the mess something real survived:
men running themselves empty for no prize but the running.

blood on the snow 1905 ce st. petersburg, russia troops fire on peaceful workers marching to the tsar on bloody sunday — the traveler walks among the singing crowd and watches the snow turn red. they marched to the tsar with icons and a petition,
workers and their families, singing hymns in the snow.
i walked among them, peaceful, unafraid —
then the rifles spoke, and the snow turned red.
bloody sunday: the day russia's people learned
their little father would shoot them for asking.
the 1905 revolution rose from that blood,
barricades, strikes, a mutiny on the potemkin.
it failed. but the snow remembered, and so did i.

the patent clerk rewrites physics 1905 ce bern, switzerland einstein's miracle year in bern — relativity, photons, e=mc2 — and the traveler stands outside the patent office window knowing the atom will remember that equation. in a bern patent office a clerk did his real work in the margins,
and in one year rewrote the universe:
light comes in packets, time bends with speed,
and mass is frozen energy — e=mc2, the shortest poem ever written.
i stood outside his window on an ordinary swiss street
while inside, quietly, the cosmos changed shape.
no parade, no prize that year, just a young man
seeing further than anyone alive.
the atom would remember that equation. so would hiroshima.

the fleet that vanished 1905 ce korea strait japan annihilates the russian baltic fleet at tsushima after its 18,000-mile voyage — the traveler watches an empire's fleet sink in the mist. the russian baltic fleet sailed halfway around the world,
eighteen thousand miles, to meet japan in the korea strait.
i watched from the mist as togo crossed their t,
and in two days the russian fleet ceased to exist.
the first modern naval annihilation —
an asian navy destroying a european one, completely.
the sailors who survived were fished from the water
by the same sea that had carried them so far.
empires float, the traveler learns. and empires sink.

peace in new hampshire 1905 ce new hampshire, usa roosevelt brokers peace between russia and japan at portsmouth, new hampshire, winning the nobel — the traveler calls peace unglamorous work: rooms, papers, patience. roosevelt brought the russians and japanese to portsmouth,
and talked them into peace when both were bled dry.
i sat in the new hampshire summer heat
while the diplomats haggled over sakhalin and indemnities,
and watched a president earn a nobel prize
for stopping a war nobody else could stop.
peace is unglamorous work — rooms, papers, patience.
he did it anyway.

norway goes its own way 1905 ce norway norway peacefully leaves its union with sweden by referendum — the traveler calls it the rarest divorce in the history of nations and wishes the century would learn from it. norway left sweden the way adults end things:
talking, voting, no shots fired.
i watched the referendum — nearly unanimous —
and the two kings parting without a war,
the rarest divorce in the history of nations.
they even borrowed a danish prince for the new throne
and got on with being neighbors.
if only, i thought, watching the century arm itself,
they all did it this way.

five cents a dream 1905 ce pittsburgh, usa the first nickelodeon opens in pittsburgh — five cents buys a dark room and an hour of elsewhere, and the traveler calls it the cheapest escape ever sold. a nickel bought you a dark room and an hour of elsewhere —
the first nickelodeon opened, and the movies became the people's theater.
i sat among factory hands and shop girls,
watching flickering streets and chases for five cents,
and understood what the century had just invented:
the cheapest escape ever sold.
the rich had their opera boxes; the rest had this.
it was enough. it was always enough.

a town in the desert 1905 ce nevada, usa las vegas is founded as a railroad water stop in the nevada desert — the traveler stands on the dusty lot and laughs at how beginnings never look like what they become. they founded las vegas as a railroad water stop,
a dot in the nevada desert, nothing to see.
i stood on that dusty lot in 1905
and tried to imagine the neon, the fountains, the all-night chapels —
i could not. nobody could.
the future is a poor guesser; it put a water tank in the desert
and got the brightest city on earth.
i have learned to laugh at beginnings.
they never look like what they become.

the earth moves at dawn 1906 ce california, usa the 1906 earthquake and three days of fire level san francisco — the traveler runs through rolling streets and watches rich and poor sleep side by side in the parks. at 5:12 in the morning the earth moved,
and san francisco broke like a plate dropped on stone.
i ran through streets that rolled like water,
then watched three days of fire finish what the quake began.
the city burned block by block, and the rich and poor
slept side by side in the parks, in tents, in the rain.
they rebuilt it — of course they rebuilt it —
but for a week the whole city was equal,
and the ground had the last word.

the jungle exposed 1906 ce usa sinclair's novel about chicago's meatpackers shocks america into food-safety law — the traveler honors the writer who looked where nobody wanted to look. sinclair went into chicago's meatpacking plants
and came out with a novel that made america gag.
i walked those killing floors with him in my mind —
the rats, the filth, the men ground down like the cattle.
he wrote to save the worker; america read it and saved its stomach.
food-safety law was born from that book,
which is to say: from a writer who looked where nobody wanted to look.
look where it hurts. write what you see.

the moroccan crisis 1906 ce morocco europe's powers quarrel over morocco and germany walks out isolated — the traveler sits in the conference rooms and watches the empires learn they'd rather fight than back down. europe's powers quarreled over morocco at algeciras,
and germany walked out isolated, humiliated, alone.
i sat in the conference rooms, all polished wood and sharp smiles,
while the map of africa was traded like a hand of cards.
nobody in that room wanted war — yet.
but every crisis taught the same lesson:
the empires would rather fight than back down,
and the list of things to fight over kept growing.

women vote first 1906 ce finland finland gives women the vote and the right to stand for office, first in europe — the traveler watches them walk to the polls in the snow and calls it courage. finland did it first in europe — women at the ballot box,
full suffrage, and the right to stand for office too.
i watched finnish women walk to the polls in 1906,
calm as people doing what should have been done long ago.
nineteen women were elected to parliament the next year.
the world called it radical; the finns called it tuesday.
i have seen revolutions with less courage in them
than a woman walking to vote in the snow.

music on the air 1906 ce massachusetts, usa fessenden broadcasts voice and violin on christmas eve 1906, the first radio program — played for lonely ships' operators, the traveler says the airwaves began with a gift. on christmas eve, fessenden took the microphone
and sent voice and violin out over the atlantic —
o holy night, played live, to ships at sea.
i imagine the wireless operators at their keys,
expecting dots and dashes, hearing music instead.
the first radio program, and nobody had planned it;
a man just wanted the lonely men on the ships
to hear something beautiful on christmas.
the airwaves began with a gift.

innocent at last 1906 ce france dreyfus is cleared and restored after twelve years — the traveler watched france tear itself in two over him and stood in the courtroom when the verdict came. twelve years after the lie, dreyfus was cleared,
restored to the army, given back his name.
i had watched france tear itself in two over him —
the army, the church, the mob on one side;
zola and the truth-tellers on the other.
justice took twelve years and cost a country its illusions.
but it came. it came.
i stood in the courtroom when the verdict was read
and thought: this is what truth looks like when it refuses to die.

picasso breaks the face 1907 ce paris, france picasso paints five fractured women and modern art begins — the traveler stands before the canvas and sees a painting about seeing itself. five women, fractured, staring from the canvas —
les demoiselles d'avignon broke the human face like a mirror.
i stood before it in picasso's studio, my breath caught,
because the painting wasn't showing women; it was showing seeing itself.
african masks, cezanne's geometry, fury, genius —
modern art began in that wreckage of perspective.
friends told him it was madness. he kept the canvas rolled for years.
the future unrolled it.

the fleet sails white 1907 ce usa roosevelt sends sixteen white battleships on a 43,000-mile world cruise — the traveler calls it a parade and a threat in the same hull. roosevelt sent sixteen battleships around the world,
painted white, the great white fleet, to show the flag.
i watched them steam out of hampton roads,
forty-three thousand miles, fourteen months, twenty ports.
every nation that saw them understood the message:
america had arrived, and it had guns.
it was a parade and a threat in the same hull.
the century would learn to read that combination fluently.

the first plastic 1907 ce new york, usa bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, is invented — the traveler holds a glossy piece and already sees it ending in every ocean on earth. bakelite — the first fully synthetic plastic,
born in a yonkers laboratory from phenol and formaldehyde.
i held one of the first dark, glossy pieces,
hard as amber, cheap as dirt, shaped like anything.
the plastic age began in that beaker,
and would end — will end — in every ocean on earth.
nobody in that lab in 1907 imagined the great pacific garbage patch.
i did the imagining for them, and wished i hadn't.

the panic 1907 ce usa the 1907 bank panic nearly topples wall street until j.p. morgan locks the bankers in his library — the traveler thinks a civilization needing one rich man to save it is already in trouble. the banks started falling, and wall street shook,
and one man — j.p. morgan — personally stopped the panic.
i watched him summon the bankers to his library,
lock the door, and refuse to let them out until they'd pledged the money.
one man's will held the whole system up for a weekend.
it worked. but i stood in that marble library
and thought: a civilization that needs one rich man
to save it from itself is already in trouble.

the first helicopter hop 1907 ce france paul cornu lifts a twin-rotor machine off the ground in france — a few shaky seconds, and the traveler calls it the helicopter's birthday. paul cornu strapped himself into a twin-rotor machine
and lifted off the ground — briefly, barely, but it flew.
a few feet up, a few seconds, wobbling like a newborn foal.
i watched the crowd hold its breath for those seconds,
because everyone there understood: the helicopter had just been born.
it would take decades to grow up.
but birthdays are birthdays, even shaky ones.

the car for the multitude 1908 ce michigan, usa the model t rolls out and the automobile stops being a rich man's toy — the traveler rides one of the first down a dirt road and feels the century accelerate. the model t rolled out of detroit, black and plain,
and the automobile stopped being a rich man's toy.
i watched farmers hitch their futures to it,
doctors reaching patients, families reaching towns.
fifteen million would be built; the world would pave itself.
ford paid his workers five dollars a day so they could buy one —
the machine that made the machine's buyers.
i rode in one of the first, bouncing down a dirt road,
and felt the century accelerate under me.

fire from the sky 1908 ce siberia, russia something explodes over tunguska, flattening 2,000 square kilometers of siberian forest with no crater — the traveler walks the blasted taiga and admits some mysteries stay mysteries. something exploded over tunguska —
two thousand square kilometers of forest flattened,
trees laid down in a perfect radial pattern, no crater, no answer.
i walked that blasted taiga years later,
the strange regrowth, the scorched silence.
comet? asteroid? the sky keeps its counsel.
the evenki herders who saw it spoke of the fire god's anger.
i have crossed between stars, and even i cannot tell you
exactly what fell that morning. some mysteries stay mysteries.

the marathon's famous finish 1908 ce england dorando pietri collapses at the 1908 olympic marathon finish and is disqualified — the traveler was in the stands, and the measured distance becomes the marathon forever. dorando pietri staggered into the london stadium first,
then collapsed, rose, collapsed again —
officials half-carried him across the line, and he was disqualified.
i was in the stands for that famous finish,
the crowd roaring for a man who had nothing left.
they gave the gold to the american who finished second,
but the world remembered the italian who fell.
and the distance — 26 miles, 385 yards, measured that day for the queen's view —
became the marathon forever: 26.2.

the sultan loses power 1908 ce ottoman empire the young turks force the sultan to restore the ottoman constitution — the traveler parades with the hopeful crowds, knowing the dream will curdle but believing for an afternoon. the young turks forced the sultan to restore the constitution,
and the absolute rule of the ottomans cracked.
i stood in constantinople as the news spread,
parades in the streets, hope like a new season.
they dreamed of a modern, constitutional empire —
liberty, equality, fraternity, ottoman-style.
the dream would curdle within years into war and deportation.
but on that day, the crowd believed,
and i let myself believe with them, for an afternoon.

the champion who broke the line 1908 ce sydney, australia jack johnson beats tommy burns in sydney to become the first black heavyweight champion — the traveler watches him smile through fourteen rounds and calls it one of the bravest things he's seen. jack johnson beat tommy burns in sydney
and became the first black heavyweight champion of the world.
i watched him toy with burns for fourteen rounds,
smiling, talking, untouchable — and the white world raged.
they spent years hunting for a "great white hope" to take his crown.
he held it until 1915, grinning all the way.
a black man, the strongest man on earth, in 1908 —
i have seen few braver things than that smile in that ring.

thirty-seven minutes over water 1909 ce france to england bleriot flies the english channel in 37 minutes — the traveler watches from the dover cliffs as the moat that stopped napoleon is crossed by a frenchman in a monoplane. thirty-seven minutes over the channel,
bleriot in his monoplane, engine coughing, wind rising —
and britain was no longer an island.
i stood on the dover cliffs and watched him come,
a speck growing into a man in a machine,
landing hard in a meadow, the crowd going mad.
the moat that had stopped napoleon and the armada
was crossed by a frenchman in half an hour.
islands are a state of mind. he proved it.

the pole is claimed 1909 ce arctic peary claims the north pole in 1909, a claim disputed ever since — the traveler knows the arctic's lying distances and honors the hunger to stand where nothing stands. peary planted the american flag at the north pole —
or said he did. the claim is disputed to this day.
i know the arctic, its white silence, its lying distances,
and i know how badly men wanted to be first.
cook said he was there first; peary said cook lied;
history is still arguing in the snow.
what i know is this: men dragged sledges across the top of the world
for the honor of standing where nothing stands.
that hunger is real, whatever the coordinates say.

the long fight organizes 1909 ce new york, usa du bois and allies found the naacp in 1909 — the traveler sits in the early meetings and calls it an unromantic machine of minutes and dues that bent the arc of a nation. w.e.b. du bois and his allies founded the naacp,
and the long fight got an address and a letterhead.
i sat in those early meetings, black and white together,
planning lawsuits and boycotts in an age of lynchings.
it would take sixty years of that grinding work
to crack the laws of jim crow.
organizations are unromantic things — minutes, dues, committees.
this one bent the arc of a nation.

shopping becomes theater 1909 ce london, england selfridge's opens on oxford street and invents the modern department store — the traveler walks the marble aisles and calls it consumerism's cathedral. selfridge's opened on oxford street,
and shopping became theater — "the customer is always right."
i walked those marble aisles on opening week,
perfume, light, displays like stage sets.
harry selfridge had worked for marshall field in chicago
and brought american showmanship to london shopping.
the department store: a palace where anyone could enter
and everyone was treated like someone.
consumerism's cathedral, and i watched them build it.

the comet returns 1910 ce worldwide halley's comet returns in 1910 and crowds buy comet pills against its tail — the traveler watches from a field as earth passes through harmlessly. halley's comet returned, and the world panicked politely —
the tail would pass through earth's orbit, and astronomers said it held cyanogen.
comet pills sold by the thousand; people sealed their windows.
i stood in a field and watched it come,
that smudged torch in the sky, beautiful and utterly harmless.
the earth passed through the tail and nobody felt a thing.
seventy-six years it takes to circle the sun —
i have watched it come and go more times than i can count.

korea is swallowed 1910 ce korea japan formally annexes korea in 1910 — the traveler walks the streets of seoul and notes that swallowed nations are never digested; korea remembered its name. japan formally annexed korea, and a kingdom disappeared into an empire.
i walked the streets of seoul as the proclamations went up,
the quiet fury of a people told they no longer existed.
the independence fight went underground —
into exile, into secret societies, into the long patience of the occupied.
thirty-five years korea would wait.
i have watched nations swallowed before; they are never digested.
korea remembered its name the whole time.

viva la revolucion 1910 ce mexico madero calls for revolt against diaz's 34-year rule — the traveler rides with the early rebels, knowing the revolution will eat its children for a decade. madero called for revolt, and diaz's thirty-four-year rule began to crumble.
i rode with the early rebels in the north,
farmers and cowboys against the rurales, hope against the machine guns.
the mexican revolution would eat its own children for a decade —
zapata, villa, madero himself, all dead by treachery or battle.
but it began with a call, a plan, a date: november 20.
revolutions start with paperwork and end in blood.
i was there for the paperwork.

the union is born 1910 ce south africa four colonies unite as the union of south africa under white rule — the traveler watches the black majority written out of the nation at its christening. four colonies united as the union of south africa —
under white rule, by white votes, for white futures.
i stood at the ceremonies, the flags, the speeches,
and watched the black majority written out of the nation
as if they were not there, as if the land were empty.
it was the legal birth of apartheid's machinery,
decades before the word.
the union was born; justice was not invited to the christening.

the lady with the lamp 1910 ce england florence nightingale dies at 90 — the traveler remembers her lamp in the crimea and says every nurse who ever walked a night ward carries it still. florence nightingale died in 1910, ninety years old,
and nursing is a profession because of her.
i had seen her in the crimea, lamp in hand among the dying,
and seen her come home to spend fifty years
building the schools and statistics that made care a science.
she was fierce, difficult, brilliant — no plaster saint.
the lamp was real. so was the will behind it.
i stood at her funeral and thought of every nurse
who ever walked a night ward. they all carry her lamp.

the qing fall 1911 ce china revolution topples the qing dynasty, ending 2,000 years of emperors — the traveler watches men shear off their queues in the streets and steps over history. two thousand years of emperors ended in 1911,
the qing fell to revolution, and china became a republic.
i watched the queue-cutting in the streets —
men shearing off the braids that had marked submission for centuries,
laughing, weeping, free.
sun yat-sen's dream, bought with uprisings and exiles.
what followed was warlords and chaos, not the promised republic —
but the emperors were gone, and they were never coming back.
the braid lay in the street. i stepped over history.

first to the bottom of the world 1911 ce antarctica amundsen reaches the south pole by dogsled, beating scott — the traveler honors both the norwegian's planning and the englishman's frozen dignity. amundsen's dogsled team reached the south pole,
beating scott by a month — planning beating heroism.
i know that white desert, the cold that kills in minutes,
and i honor both men: the norwegian who prepared for everything
and the englishman who froze with his friends, writing to the end.
scott's party died on the way back, eleven miles from supply.
amundsen left a tent and a letter for his rival.
the pole doesn't care who was first. but we do.

the fire that changed work 1911 ce new york, usa 146 garment workers die in the triangle shirtwaist fire — locked doors, a collapsed fire escape — and the traveler says every workplace safety rule was written in that smoke. one hundred forty-six garment workers died in the triangle fire —
locked doors, a single fire escape that collapsed, girls jumping.
i stood on greene street and watched them fall,
young women, mostly immigrants, some still teenagers.
the city wept, then the city acted:
labor law was born in those ashes, fire codes, the forty-hour week.
every workplace safety rule you know
was written in the smoke of that saturday afternoon.

the smile disappears 1911 ce paris, france the mona lisa is stolen from the louvre and crowds gather to stare at the empty hooks — the traveler notes the theft made her the most recognized face on earth. the mona lisa was stolen from the louvre,
and paris lost its mind — the most famous missing woman in the world.
i watched the crowds gather where the empty hooks were,
staring at a blank wall, loving her more in absence.
a handyman had carried her out under his coat, meaning to return her to italy.
she came back two years later, world-famous —
the theft made her the most recognized face on earth.
sometimes, i thought, you have to lose a thing to see it.

twice crowned 1911 ce sweden marie curie wins her second nobel, the first person honored in two sciences — the traveler remembers her stirring pitchblende in a paris shed, working toward the radiation that would kill her. marie curie won her second nobel —
the first person honored in two different sciences.
i had watched her stir boiling pitchblende in a shed in paris,
hands burned, back aching, chasing the invisible.
physics, then chemistry: radium and polonium,
the elements she pulled from the dark with her own hands.
the radiation that made her famous would kill her.
she knew. she worked anyway.

the unsinkable sinks 1912 ce north atlantic the titanic strikes an iceberg and sinks on her maiden voyage — the traveler stands on the carpathia's deck at dawn and calls it the century's lesson in hubris. the titanic struck the iceberg at 11:40 at night,
and the unsinkable ship went down in two hours forty minutes.
i was not aboard, but i stood on the carpathia's deck at dawn
when the lifeboats came alongside, and heard the silence.
fifteen hundred dead in the freezing dark —
the band playing, the millionaires and the steerage alike.
the century's great lesson in hubris, taught in one night:
the sea does not read press releases.

the balkans boil over 1912 ce balkans the balkan states drive the ottomans out of europe, then turn on each other — the traveler walks the mountain battlefields knowing sarajevo is two years away. the balkan states drove the ottomans almost entirely out of europe,
serbia, greece, bulgaria, montenegro — the small nations' war.
i walked those mountain battlefields, ancient hatreds in modern uniforms,
and watched the victors turn on each other within months.
the balkans were the powder keg of europe, everyone said —
and they were right, though no one knew how right.
two years later a serb student in sarajevo
would light the fuse that burned the world.

the skull that lied 1912 ce england the piltdown skull is unveiled as the missing link, fooling science for forty years — the traveler calls wanting to believe the oldest laboratory error. the piltdown skull was unveiled as the missing link,
and science believed the lie for forty years.
i stood in the museum and looked at that doctored bone —
a human cranium married to an ape's jaw, stained to look ancient.
someone had built it as a joke or a fraud, and the experts
saw what they wanted to see: an english ancestor with a big brain.
it took chemistry, not wisdom, to expose it.
wanting to believe is the oldest laboratory error.

the girl scouts begin 1912 ce georgia, usa juliette gordon low founds the girl scouts in savannah — the traveler watches the first meetings and says millions of women's courage traces back to a troop and a campfire. juliette gordon low founded the girl scouts in savannah,
twelve girls, a promise, and a deaf woman with a mission.
i watched those first meetings — knots, first aid, campfires —
girls learning they could do anything the boys did, outdoors.
she poured her fortune into it and her health too.
a century later, millions of women trace their courage
to a troop, a badge, a campfire in the woods.
it started with one woman who believed girls deserved the wild.

the greatest athlete 1912 ce sweden jim thorpe wins the pentathlon and decathlon, then is stripped of his medals for playing semi-pro baseball — the traveler notes justice runs on its own slow schedule; they came back thirty years after his death. jim thorpe won the pentathlon and the decathlon at stockholm —
the king of sweden called him the greatest athlete in the world.
i watched him run, jump, throw, dominate every event,
a sac and fox indian who had survived the boarding schools.
then they stripped his medals for playing semi-pro baseball,
for a few dollars, years before.
the medals came back in 1983, thirty years after he died.
justice, like the olympics, runs on its own slow schedule.

modern art invades america 1913 ce new york, usa the armory show brings modern art to new york and america argues about it for months — the traveler loves a scandal that turns out to be a birth. the armory show brought duchamp and matisse to new york,
and america argued about art in the newspapers for months.
i walked the crowded galleries, hearing the outrage —
"nude descending a staircase" mocked as "an explosion in a shingle factory."
but the young artists stood before those canvases and felt the future.
modernism landed in america in that armory,
and american art was never provincial again.
i love a good scandal that turns out to be a birth.

the atom gets an address 1913 ce denmark niels bohr models the atom with electrons in orbits — the traveler calls it the first true map of the smallest country there is. niels bohr gave the atom an address —
electrons in orbits, jumping between them, the quantum atom.
i sat in copenhagen while he worked it out,
a young dane making the invisible orderly.
rutherford had found the nucleus; bohr gave it architecture.
the model was wrong in the details and right in the soul —
the first true map of the smallest country there is.
every atom in your body obeys the rules he found.

the night music rioted 1913 ce paris, france the rite of spring premieres in paris and the audience nearly riots — the traveler was in the theater and says the future usually enters through a slammed door. stravinsky's rite of spring premiered in paris,
and the audience nearly rioted — shouting, fistfights, the police.
i was in that theater, the music pounding like a pagan heart,
dancers stomping out a sacrifice to spring.
the old paris of pretty ballets was not ready.
but art doesn't ask permission; it just arrives, loud.
within years the riot became the repertoire.
that's how the future usually enters — through a slammed door.

the line that never stops 1913 ce michigan, usa ford's moving assembly line cuts car build time from hours to minutes — the traveler walks beside the first endless belt and sees the human being become a station on the line. ford's moving assembly line cut a car's build time from hours to minutes,
the line that never stops, the men who became its hands.
i walked beside that first endless belt in highland park,
watching chassis glide past while men did one motion, all day.
it made the car cheap and the worker a cog —
both true at once, which is the trouble with progress.
the century learned to build everything this way:
faster, cheaper, and the human being as a station on the line.

india's first film 1913 ce india india's first feature film premieres in bombay — a silent myth of king harishchandra, and the traveler watches an audience see its own epics move for the first time. india's first feature film premiered in bombay —
a myth on screen, in silence: the story of king harishchandra.
i sat in that dark hall while gods and kings flickered,
and watched an audience see its own epics move for the first time.
dadasaheb phalke had built it all from nothing —
camera, studio, actors, the whole dream, indian-made.
bollywood's first ancestor was a silent myth.
every song-and-dance spectacular since is its grandchild.

steel that won't rust 1913 ce england stainless steel is invented in sheffield — the traveler holds a bright first knife and notes invention aims at one thing and hits the future sideways. in sheffield they invented stainless steel,
and cutlery would never rust again.
i held one of the first bright knives,
clean, shining, immune to time and tea.
harry brearley was trying to stop gun barrels eroding;
he got the modern kitchen instead.
that's how invention works — you aim at one thing
and hit the future sideways.

the shot that lit the world 1914 ce sarajevo, bosnia a teenager's pistol kills archduke franz ferdinand in sarajevo — the traveler was on the street and says sixteen million died because a driver took a wrong turn. a nineteen-year-old with a pistol in sarajevo,
two shots — an archduke and his wife, dead in an open car.
i was on that street, franz josef street, and heard the cracks,
and felt the world tilt on its axis.
gavrilo princip wanted bosnia free; he got the great war instead.
one teenager's bullets, and the alliance dominoes fell —
sixteen million dead because a driver took a wrong turn.
history doesn't always need a reason. sometimes it just needs a corner.

the ultimatum 1914 ce vienna, austria austria-hungary declares war on serbia and the alliance dominoes fall — the traveler watches vienna cheer for a war that will last a month, they said. austria-hungary sent serbia an ultimatum designed to be refused,
then declared war — and the alliance dominoes started to fall.
i sat in the cafes of vienna as the mobilization posters went up,
young men cheering in the streets, flowers on the rifles.
they called it a fresh and merry war. it would last a month, they said.
russia mobilized, germany mobilized, france mobilized —
the timetables took over, and no one could stop the trains.
i watched the cheering and wanted to scream.

through neutral belgium 1914 ce belgium germany marches through neutral belgium and britain declares war — the traveler stands on the roads as refugees stream past and louvain burns. germany marched through neutral belgium,
and britain declared war within days — the scrap of paper.
i stood on the roads as the gray columns came,
refugees streaming the other way, carrying everything.
louvain burned; civilians were shot as franc-tireurs.
belgium, the little country that said no,
paid for its neutrality in blood and ruins.
the schlieffen plan needed belgium's roads.
belgium needed only to be left alone.

the trap in the east 1914 ce east prussia germany encircles and destroys a russian army at tannenberg — the traveler walks the battlefield of lakes and forests where an empire began its long bleeding. at tannenberg the germans encircled a russian army
and destroyed it — three hundred thousand casualties in days.
i walked that battlefield of lakes and forests,
where samsonov's men starved in the woods and their general shot himself.
hindenburg became a legend; russia began its long bleeding.
the east would devour armies for four years,
but tannenberg was the first great trap —
and the russians walked in with their bands playing.

the taxis to the front 1914 ce france paris taxicabs ferry troops to the marne and the german advance is stopped — the traveler rides with the cabbies in the most parisian army ever assembled. paris taxicabs ferried troops to the marne —
six hundred taxis, headlights blazing through the night.
i rode with them, those brave cabbies,
racing to plug the gap while the germans bore down on paris.
the marne held. the german advance was stopped.
france was saved, this time, by taximeters and courage.
the "miracle of the marne" — really just men refusing to lose,
delivered by the most parisian army ever assembled.

the race to the sea ends 1914 ce belgium the race to the sea ends and the trenches stretch from switzerland to the sea — the traveler walks the first winter line and calls it a four-hundred-mile wound. the last open flank closed, and the trenches began —
from switzerland to the sea, four hundred miles of mud and wire.
i walked that first winter line, the digging still fresh,
men learning to live like moles under the guns.
the war of movement died in those ditches;
the war of attrition was born, and would eat a generation.
they called it the western front. it was really a wound
four hundred miles long that would not close for four years.

two oceans joined 1914 ce panama the panama canal opens, joining two oceans — the traveler stands on a first ship through the locks, noting europe dug trenches while america dug a canal. the panama canal opened in 1914 —
two oceans joined, the horn rounded no more.
i stood on the first ships through the locks,
the jungle cut open, the waters lifted stair by stair.
ten years of digging, five thousand dead workers,
and the world got smaller by eight thousand miles.
while europe dug trenches, america dug a canal.
both were wounds in the earth. only one was meant to heal trade.
