japan joins the war 1914 ce china japan besieges germany's port at tsingtao and takes its pacific islands — the traveler watches britain's efficient ally and sees it collecting debts the future will pay. japan besieged germany's chinese port at tsingtao,
and took germany's pacific islands for good measure.
i watched the japanese fleet arrive off the shantung coast,
britain's ally in the east, efficient and ambitious.
they fought well — and they kept what they took.
the war gave japan a taste for empire,
and the twenty-one demands on china followed within months.
every ally, i thought, is collecting debts the future will pay.

defeat off chile 1914 ce chile a german squadron sinks two british cruisers off chile, avenged weeks later at the falklands — the traveler learns again that no navy rules forever. off coronel, chile, a german squadron sank two british cruisers —
britain's first naval defeat in a century.
i heard the news travel like a cold wind through london,
the empire's invincibility dented in one afternoon.
admiral von spee's victory lasted five weeks —
at the falklands the british avenged coronel completely.
the sea gives, the sea takes back.
i watched both battles' shadows from the shore
and learned again: no navy rules forever.

the night the guns stopped 1914 ce western front british and german soldiers climb out of their trenches on christmas 1914, trading gifts and playing football — the traveler walks that strange peace the generals furiously forbade ever after. on christmas eve the guns stopped,
and men climbed out of the trenches — british and german —
trading gifts, burying the dead together, playing football in no-man's-land.
i walked that strange peace, the frost glittering,
enemies singing each other's carols across the wire.
the generals were furious; the men were human.
it never happened again — the war machine learned to forbid it.
but for one night, the soldiers voted with their feet,
and peace won, briefly, unofficially.

the little fellow arrives 1914 ce usa chaplin's tramp shuffles onto the screen in 1914 — the traveler watches the world fall in love with a little fellow who owned nothing, and calls comedy courage in a funny hat. charlie chaplin's tramp shuffled onto the screen in 1914 —
baggy pants, cane, bowler hat, the century's most beloved clown.
i sat in the dark and watched the world fall in love
with a little fellow who owned nothing and feared nothing.
through the war years to come, through the depression,
that tramp would make millions laugh who had nothing to laugh about.
comedy is courage in a funny hat.
chaplin knew. the tramp knew.

stop and go 1914 ce ohio, usa cleveland installs the first electric traffic light — the traveler stands on the corner and calls civilization traffic management, scaled up. cleveland installed the first electric traffic light —
red and green, stop and go, at euclid and 105th.
i stood on that corner and watched the future arrive:
the automobile age would need rules, and here was the first.
a policeman in a booth worked the switch by hand.
soon the lights would time themselves, and the cities would pulse
in red-green rhythms, obedient as a heartbeat.
civilization is just traffic management, scaled up.

a pope for wartime 1914 ce vatican city benedict xv is elected and spends wwi begging for peace, calling it "useless slaughter" — the traveler honors the voice that said stop when every other said onward. benedict xv was elected in 1914
and spent the whole war begging for peace.
i heard his pleas go out — to the palaces, to the trenches —
"useless slaughter," he called it, and he was right.
both sides claimed god; he claimed neither, only mercy.
the powers ignored him, as powers do.
but in the prisoner camps his relief work fed the starving,
and history remembers the voice that said stop
when every other voice said onward.

the shore of anzac 1915 ce turkey anzac troops storm the cliffs at gallipoli in a campaign of courage and waste — the traveler was on the beaches and says two nations were baptized in those waters. at dawn the anzacs stormed the cliffs at gallipoli —
australians and new zealanders, into turkish fire.
i was on those beaches, the water red at the shoreline,
young men climbing where no army could climb.
the campaign was a legend of courage and waste —
eight months, a hundred thousand dead, evacuation in the night.
but australia and new zealand were born there,
not in parliaments but in the blood and the mateship.
nations are baptized in strange waters.

the deportations begin 1915 ce ottoman empire the ottoman roundup of armenian leaders begins a genocide that will kill 1.5 million — the traveler walks the deportation roads and holds the hands of the dying. in april 1915 the ottoman authorities rounded up armenian leaders —
and a million and a half armenians would die.
i walked the deportation roads, the desert columns,
women and children driven without water, without mercy.
the century's great unacknowledged crime —
denied still, a hundred years on, by the heirs of the killers.
i held the hands of the dying and could do nothing.
remember this when the world says "never again"
and means it only until the next time.

the ship that sank a neutral 1915 ce atlantic a u-boat sinks the lusitania with 1,198 dead — the traveler saw her sail from new york and says some sinkings steer history; this one steered america toward war. a u-boat sank the lusitania off ireland —
1,198 dead, and america edged toward war.
i had seen her sail from new york, the great greyhound,
and i read the german warnings in the newspapers beside her sailing notice.
she carried munitions; she carried civilians; the torpedo did not distinguish.
the dead included 128 americans, and the outrage crossed the ocean.
ships sink. but some sinkings steer history.
this one steered america toward the trenches.

the gas comes 1915 ce belgium germany releases chlorine gas at ypres — the traveler watches the green-yellow cloud roll in and calls gas the coward's masterpiece: it kills the air itself. at ypres the germans opened the cylinders,
and chlorine gas rolled over the trenches — poison entered modern war.
i watched the green-yellow cloud come, silent, low,
and men drowning on dry land, clawing at their masks.
the french colonial troops broke; the canadians held, urinating on handkerchiefs.
war had found a new cruelty, and both sides would use it.
i have seen many weapons. gas is the coward's masterpiece —
it kills the air itself.

gravity becomes geometry 1915 ce berlin, germany einstein completes general relativity in wartime berlin — gravity as the curve of space itself, and the traveler calls it the century's most beautiful idea born in its ugliest years. in wartime berlin, einstein finished general relativity:
gravity is not a force — it is the curve of space itself.
i sat in his study while the equations settled,
the universe bending around every mass like a trampoline.
matter tells space how to curve; space tells matter how to move.
he was forty-six, at war with no one, at peace with the cosmos.
the most beautiful idea of the century,
born in the ugliest years of the century.

the blockbuster is born 1915 ce usa birth of a nation invents the feature film and glorifies the klan — the traveler sits stunned by the craft and sickened by the lie: the blockbuster was born compromised. griffith's birth of a nation invented the feature film —
three hours, battle scenes, close-ups, the whole grammar of cinema.
i sat in the theater, stunned by the craft,
and sickened by the lie: it glorified the ku klux klan.
president wilson screened it at the white house.
the naacp protested; the klan used it as a recruiting film.
art and poison in the same reel —
the blockbuster was born, and it was born compromised.

terror from the sky 1915 ce england zeppelins bomb london in 1915 — the traveler stands in the dark streets and says the front line moved to the nursery; the sky was never safe again. zeppelins bombed london, and war came to civilians from the air.
i stood in the dark streets during the raids,
searchlights sweeping, the great silver shapes humming overhead.
the bombs fell on houses, on shops, on sleeping children —
the front line had moved to the nursery.
people called them zepp raids and carried on.
but something had changed forever: the sky was no longer safe.
every bombing campaign since began in that humming dark.

the nurse who wouldn't lie 1915 ce belgium edith cavell is shot for helping allied soldiers escape — the traveler stands outside the brussels prison at dawn and says the germans made a martyr and paid in enlistments. edith cavell was shot at dawn for helping allied soldiers escape —
two hundred of them, hidden, fed, guided to holland.
i stood outside the prison in brussels that october morning,
and heard the rifles at 7 a.m.
she would not lie to save herself; "patriotism is not enough," she said.
her courage shamed an empire and recruited armies —
the germans made a martyr and paid for it in enlistments.
one nurse, one firing squad, and the moral math of war, exposed.

italy switches sides 1915 ce italy italy abandons the triple alliance and joins britain and france — the traveler watches the army march into the isonzo meat grinder and learns alliances are interests in friendship's uniform. italy abandoned its old allies and joined britain and france —
the triple alliance became a double, and the alps became a front.
i watched the italian army march into the mountains,
into the isonzo meat grinder, twelve battles for a few miles.
they came for territory promised in a secret treaty —
trentino, trieste, the national dream.
alliances, i learned in that war, are just interests
wearing the uniform of friendship.

women against the war 1915 ce the hague, netherlands over a thousand women meet at the hague in 1915 to demand an end to the war — the traveler sits in the only peace conference of the year and says the idea outlived the generals. over a thousand women met at the hague to demand an end to the war —
jane addams, aletta jacobs, women the warring states called traitors.
i sat in that hall, the only peace conference of 1915,
while the men at the front kept killing by the hundred thousand.
they sent delegations to every capital; every capital declined.
but they founded the women's international league,
and the idea survived the war: women, organized, against war.
the generals laughed. the idea outlived the generals.

the mill at verdun 1916 ce france the battle of verdun grinds for 300 days with 700,000 casualties — the traveler walks the ossuary hills and picks up soil that is half iron, half bone. verdun: germany's plan to bleed france white,
three hundred days, seven hundred thousand casualties.
i walked that battlefield — the forts, the ossuary, the hills of bones —
and the words on the memorials: ils ne passeront pas. they shall not pass.
petain's noria rotated men through the mill like grain.
france held. france bled. france never forgot.
i picked up a handful of that soil; it was half iron, half bone.
some ground is sacred. some ground is just scarred.
verdun is both.

the bloodiest day 1916 ce france on july 1, 1916, britain loses 60,000 men in a day at the somme — the traveler was in the chalk and wire and says the poppies grow there still, red as the ledgers. on july 1, 1916, the british lost sixty thousand men in a single day —
twenty thousand dead before lunch, walking into machine guns.
i was there at the somme, in the chalk and the wire,
and watched the flower of england mown down in rows.
the somme ground on for five months, a million casualties,
for six miles of mud.
lions led by donkeys, they said later.
i say: boys led by old men who had learned nothing.
the poppies grow there still, red as the ledgers.

a rising in easter week 1916 ce dublin, ireland irish rebels seize dublin's gpo in easter 1916; the british execute the leaders and turn ireland — the traveler says the firing squads did what the rebels couldn't: they persuaded. in easter week the rebels seized dublin's post office —
pearse read the proclamation, and for six days they held.
i walked o'connell street as the shells came in,
the gpo burning, the dream going up in smoke.
the british executed the leaders — sixteen men —
and ireland, which had mocked the rising, turned in fury.
they meant to crush it; they christened it.
within six years ireland would be free.
the firing squads did what the rebels couldn't: they persuaded.

the clash of dreadnoughts 1916 ce north sea britain and germany's dreadnought fleets clash at jutland — both claim victory, but the traveler notes britain kept the sea, which was the point. at jutland the great fleets met — 250 ships, the clash of dreadnoughts.
i watched from the gray north sea mist as the big guns spoke,
british battlecruisers blowing up, german ships slipping home in the dark.
both claimed victory; britain kept the sea, which was the point.
fourteen british ships lost, eleven german — the numbers lied a little.
the german fleet never came out in force again.
the war at sea was decided by the battle both sides survived.

russia's last great blow 1916 ce eastern front brusilov's 1916 offensive shatters austria — russia's greatest victory and its last, and the traveler rides with troops whose triumph breaks the army that won it. brusilov shattered the austrian army in 1916 —
russia's greatest victory of the war, and its last.
i rode with those troops through the broken lines,
a million and a half austrians lost, the front torn open.
it was brilliance — and it broke the russian army doing it.
the casualties, the desertions, the rot underneath:
victory cost russia the strength to go on.
within a year the tsar would fall, within two the empire.
the last great blow, struck by a dying giant.

the iron monsters 1916 ce france british tanks crawl into battle at flers in 1916 — clumsy, slow, terrifying, and the traveler calls it the future of war arriving badly, which is how it usually arrives. at flers the british tanks crawled into battle —
clumsy, slow, breaking down, terrifying.
i watched those iron monsters lurch across no-man's-land,
bullets rattling off them like rain on a roof.
the infantry followed, amazed, through the wire the tanks had crushed.
it was the future of war arriving badly —
which is how the future usually arrives.
the horse cavalry watched, and did not know it was obsolete yet.

lines drawn in secret 1916 ce middle east britain and france secretly carve up the ottoman middle east in the sykes-picot agreement — the traveler has walked every border they drew and says the region is still paying the bill. in 1916 britain and france secretly carved up the ottoman middle east —
sykes-picot, lines on a map in a london room.
i was not in that room, but i have walked every border they drew,
and watched a century bleed from those pencil strokes.
the arabs were promised independence; they got mandates.
kurdistan was split four ways; palestine was promised twice.
the men with the pencils went home to dinner.
the middle east is still paying the bill.

lawrence and the desert war 1916 ce arabia lawrence of arabia helps arab riders take aqaba from the landward side — the traveler rides with the camel columns, knowing the independence promises are already being traded away in london. sherif hussein proclaimed the arab revolt,
and a young englishman named lawrence helped arab riders take aqaba —
from the landward side, where no one was watching.
i rode with those camel columns, the desert burning white,
blowing up the hejaz railway, vanishing into the sand.
guerrilla war, romantic and real at once.
but the promises lawrence carried — arab independence —
were already being traded away in london.
he knew. the desert knew. the betrayal came later, on paper.

the mad monk dies 1916 ce russia russian nobles murder rasputin in 1916 — poison, bullets, the neva — and the traveler notes killing the symptom never cures the disease; the dynasty had months left. they murdered rasputin in a petrograd palace —
poison, bullets, the river neva, and still he fought.
i heard the story from the city the next morning,
half horror, half grim satisfaction.
the mad monk who held the tsarina's trust
was dead, and the romanov court was rotting from within.
it changed nothing. the dynasty had months left.
killing the symptom never cures the disease —
russia was about to prove it on a grand scale.

nonsense as protest 1916 ce zurich, switzerland artists invent dada in a zurich cabaret in 1916 — anti-war nonsense as protest, and the traveler says you can't argue with nonsense, you can only feel it. in a zurich cabaret, artists invented dada —
art as anti-war nonsense, sound poems, collage, glorious refusal.
i sat in the cabaret voltaire while hugo ball chanted in a cardboard costume,
and the war raged a few hundred miles away.
if the world has gone mad, they said, we'll be madder, on purpose.
it was protest by absurdity — and it worked,
because you can't argue with nonsense, you can only feel it.
from that little room came surrealism, punk, everything that refuses.

birth control's first door 1916 ce new york, usa margaret sanger opens america's first birth-control clinic and is jailed within days — the traveler stands in the line of women outside and calls the right to decide the first freedom. margaret sanger opened america's first birth-control clinic in brooklyn —
and was jailed within days.
i stood in the line of women outside that door,
poor women, tired women, women who had buried children.
the law called her obscene; the women called her a lifeline.
she went to jail, and went on, and went on —
planned parenthood grew from that raided clinic.
the right to decide is the first freedom. she knew it first.

the tsar falls 1917 ce petrograd, russia bread riots topple the tsar in february 1917 — the traveler is in petrograd as three centuries of romanovs dissolve like sugar in tea, arriving before the revolutionaries do. bread riots toppled the tsar in a week —
three centuries of romanovs, ended by hungry women in the streets.
i was in petrograd for those february days,
the soldiers refusing to fire, the red flags over the barracks.
nicholas abdicated in a railway car, quietly, almost politely.
the empire that had seemed eternal dissolved like sugar in tea.
nobody planned it. nobody controlled it.
revolutions are like that: they arrive before the revolutionaries do.

america comes in 1917 ce usa america declares war on germany in april 1917 after the zimmermann telegram and u-boat sinkings — the traveler hears wilson's speech and watches the giant step in. the zimmermann telegram, the unrestricted u-boats —
america declared war on germany in april 1917.
i was in washington when wilson asked congress,
"the world must be made safe for democracy."
the doughboys came, two million strong,
and the exhausted allies got their second wind.
it took a german offer to mexico and torpedoes in the atlantic
to pull the giant in. but once in, the giant stayed —
and the twentieth century became america's century.

mud and blood 1917 ce belgium passchendaele gains five miles for half a million casualties — men drowning in mud, and the traveler calls it the standard by which all waste is measured. at passchendaele men drowned in mud —
the offensive gained five miles for half a million casualties.
i walked that battlefield, if you can call liquid earth a field,
tanks sunk to their turrets, men swallowed by shell holes.
the rain fell, the guns churned the ground to soup,
and haig kept ordering attacks into it.
five miles. half a million.
i have seen waste in every century. passchendaele is the standard.

the winter palace falls 1917 ce petrograd, russia the bolsheviks storm the winter palace in october 1917 — the traveler is in petrograd that night and believes with the workers, for a night, before history does the disbelieving. the bolsheviks stormed the winter palace in october —
a shot from the cruiser aurora, and lenin took power.
i was in petrograd that night, the city tense and dark,
the provisional government melting away like frost.
"all power to the soviets" — the promise of bread, peace, land.
what followed was civil war, terror, famine —
but on that night, the workers believed.
i believed with them, for a night. history would do the disbelieving.

a homeland promised 1917 ce palestine the balfour declaration promises a jewish national home in palestine in 67 words — the traveler calls it history's longest iou, still being collected a century on. one letter, sixty-seven words — the balfour declaration —
britain promised a jewish national home in palestine.
i read it in the newspapers, that november,
and thought of the jews i had known across the centuries,
stateless, persecuted, dreaming of zion.
one letter, a century of consequence:
two peoples, one land, a promise made by an empire
that owned neither the land nor the right to give it.
history's longest iou, still being collected.

disaster at caporetto 1917 ce italy austro-german troops rout the italians at caporetto — the traveler walks the retreat roads as an army dissolves, and notes hemingway was nearby in an ambulance. austro-german troops routed the italians at caporetto —
three hundred thousand prisoners, the front collapsing.
i walked the retreat roads, the chaos, the abandoned guns,
an army dissolving into a mob in the mountain passes.
hemingway was an ambulance driver nearby; he'd write it into a farewell to arms.
italy nearly fell out of the war that autumn.
but the piave held, and the nation held its breath,
and learned what defeat tastes like at the doorstep.

the spy who danced 1917 ce france mata hari faces the firing squad at vincennes, refusing the blindfold — the traveler watches and says guilty or scapegoat, the legend outlived the trial. mata hari faced the french firing squad at dawn —
dancer, courtesan, accused spy.
i stood in the crowd of witnesses at vincennes,
and watched her refuse the blindfold, blowing a kiss to the riflemen.
guilty or scapegoat? france needed a traitor that year,
and she was convenient, exotic, doomed.
the legend outlived the trial — the spy who danced.
the truth, whatever it was, died with her at sunrise.

jazz gets waxed 1917 ce usa the first jazz record is cut in 1917 — the traveler is in the studio and notes the irony that five white men recorded first, but the music belonged to everyone. the original dixieland jass band cut the first jazz record —
and the jazz age got its soundtrack.
i was in the studio, the horns blaring into the big horn,
that wild new orleans polyphony captured in wax.
irony: the first jazz record was made by five white men,
while the black innovators waited their turn at the microphone.
but the music was bigger than the irony —
it belonged to everyone who ever needed to swing.

the prizes begin 1917 ce usa the first pulitzer prizes honor reporting, novels, and poetry — the traveler reads the first winners and says prizes tell a country what it thinks writing is for. the first pulitzers honored reporting, novels, and poetry —
joseph pulitzer's will, rewarding the american word.
i read those first winners, the earnest beginnings,
not knowing the prize would become the profession's conscience.
a century of woodwards and bernsteins, of to kill a mockingbird echoes,
all descended from that first list.
prizes don't make writers. but they tell a country
what it thinks writing is for.

the voices of the army 1917 ce france american women operate army switchboards at the front in wwi — the hello girls under fire, called civilians for sixty years, finally recognized in 1977. american women operated army switchboards at the front —
the hello girls, under fire, connecting the calls that ran the war.
i watched them work in the chaos of the offensives,
calm voices in the static, in french and english.
they wore uniforms, took the oath, served at the front —
and the army called them civilians for sixty years.
recognition came in 1977, for the few still living.
the voices of the army, finally heard.

finland breaks free 1917 ce finland finland declares independence from revolutionary russia in december 1917 — the traveler celebrates in helsinki and calls small nations the toughest things on earth. finland declared independence from revolutionary russia —
december 6, 1917, a nation born in the empire's collapse.
i was in helsinki for the celebrations, quiet and determined,
a people who had kept their language and laws under the tsars
now keeping their country.
what followed was civil war — reds and whites, brother against brother.
but the independence held, through war and stalin both.
small nations, i have learned, are the toughest things on earth.

russia quits the war 1918 ce russia the bolsheviks sign away a third of russia's land at brest-litovsk to buy peace — the traveler watches the humiliated delegation and notes desperate bargains rarely age well. the bolsheviks signed brest-litovsk, giving germany
a third of russia's land to buy peace.
i watched the russian delegation at that table,
humiliated, with no cards left to play.
peace at any price — and the price was ukraine, poland, the baltics.
it bought the bolsheviks time to survive the civil war.
but the germans took the grain and the land
and lost the war anyway, eight months later.
desperate bargains rarely age well.

the invisible killer 1918 ce worldwide the 1918 flu circles the globe from army camps, killing more than the war — the traveler walks the wards in philadelphia, bombay, and cape town and refuses to forget. a flu born in army camps circled the globe —
and killed more than the war did.
i walked the wards in philadelphia, in bombay, in cape town,
the bodies stacked, the gravediggers working day and night.
fifty million dead, maybe more — the young and strong hit hardest.
it came in waves, and the world, busy with war,
barely recorded the greatest plague since the black death.
the invisible killer. i remember every wave.
the world chose to forget. i did not.

the last gamble 1918 ce france germany's 1918 spring offensive breaks through, then outruns its supplies and stalls — the traveler watches ludendorff's last gamble fail in the french countryside. germany's stormtroopers broke through in the spring of 1918 —
the kaiser's battle, the last gamble, and it almost worked.
i watched them advance, infiltration tactics, speed —
then outrun their supplies and stall, exhausted, in the french countryside.
ludendorff had bet everything on one throw.
the allies, with american weight arriving daily,
bent, did not break, and then pushed back.
the gamble failed. the empire had months left.

the tide turns 1918 ce france foch counterattacks at the marne and the allies begin the hundred days — the traveler is there for the turning and says the tide turns slowly, then all at once. foch counterattacked at the marne in july 1918,
and the allies began the hundred days.
i was there for the turning — tanks, planes, americans,
the german line bending, then breaking, then running.
the war's momentum reversed in those summer weeks,
and never reversed back.
four years of stalemate ended in a hundred days of movement.
the tide turns slowly, then all at once.

america's biggest battle 1918 ce france a million americans attack through the argonne — the largest battle in us history, and the traveler walks the shattered woods where the yanks grew up fast. a million americans attacked through the argonne —
the largest battle in us history, forty-seven days.
i walked those woods, the shattered trees, the fog,
doughboys learning war the hard way against a desperate enemy.
twenty-six thousand dead, the lost battalion surrounded and saved.
it broke the german army's back in the west.
america's biggest battle, and most americans have never heard of it —
the argonne, where the yanks grew up fast.

the cellar at yekaterinburg 1918 ce yekaterinburg, russia the bolsheviks shoot the tsar, his family, and their servants in a yekaterinburg cellar — the traveler stands outside in the july night and records what he cannot forgive. in a cellar in yekaterinburg the bolsheviks shot them all —
the tsar, his wife, his five children, their servants, the dog.
i stood outside that house in the july night
and heard what the walls could not contain.
three hundred years of romanovs ended in a basement,
bullets and bayonets, the bodies burned and hidden.
whatever the tsar's sins — and they were many —
the children had committed none.
i do not forgive that night. i only record it.

the guns fall silent 1918 ce france at 11 a.m. on 11/11 the guns stop — the traveler stands in the trenches as the strangest sound of all arrives: silence, and the birds singing. at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month,
the guns stopped. the war was over.
i stood in the trenches as the silence came —
men weeping, men laughing, men afraid to stand up.
four years, sixteen million dead, empires fallen.
the silence was the strangest sound of all.
they signed the armistice in a railway car at compiegne.
i walked out into no-man's-land that morning
and the birds were singing. the birds had waited.

allenby's masterstroke 1918 ce palestine allenby smashes the ottomans at megiddo — the traveler rides with the last great cavalry charge in history, which charged into the twentieth century and never charged out. at megiddo, allenby smashed the ottomans —
cavalry, planes, deception, the whole modern art of battle.
i rode with the desert mounted corps through the broken lines,
the last great cavalry victory in history.
the ottoman army in palestine ceased to exist in days.
damascus fell; the road to aleppo lay open.
empires end the way they lived — suddenly, in the dust.
the cavalry charged into the twentieth century
and never charged out again.

the hellfighters' valor 1918 ce france the black 369th infantry fights 191 days straight and earns france's croix de guerre — the traveler watches them fight for a country that lynched their brothers at home. the black 369th infantry fought 191 days straight —
longer than any other american unit — and france gave them the croix de guerre.
i watched the hellfighters in the trenches, the jazz band playing between battles,
men fighting for a country that lynched their brothers at home.
they called themselves the men of bronze; the french called them heroes.
america gave them a parade — then gave them jim crow.
valor is valor. the debt is still unpaid.

votes for some women 1918 ce england women over thirty win the vote in britain in 1918 — the traveler remembers the marches and hunger strikes and calls it a crack, not a door, but cracks spread. women over thirty won the vote in britain —
the suffragettes' long fight cracked the door.
i had watched them march, hunger-strike, be force-fed,
emily davison under the king's horse at the derby.
the war had proved women could do everything —
drive ambulances, run factories, bury the dead.
so parliament gave the vote — to some of them, the older ones.
a crack, not a door. but cracks spread.

a new nation 1918 ce prague czechoslovakia is proclaimed in prague with masaryk as president — the traveler stands in wenceslas square as the new flag goes up and sings with the crowd. czechoslovakia was proclaimed in prague —
masaryk, the philosopher-president, at its head.
i stood in wenceslas square as the new flag went up,
czechs and slovaks cheering a country that had never existed.
it was wilson's self-determination made real —
a democracy in the heart of europe, between germany and russia.
it would last twenty years before the wolves came.
but on that october day, the square sang,
and i sang with it.

the peace that punishes 1919 ce france versailles blames germany and bills her for the war — the traveler sits in the hall of mirrors and says peace is not the absence of war but the presence of justice; versailles had none. versailles blamed germany and billed her for the war —
article 231, the war guilt, reparations beyond paying.
i sat in the hall of mirrors as the germans signed,
the same room where the german empire had been proclaimed.
keynes walked out and called it a carthaginian peace.
he was right. the humiliation festered for twenty years
and gave the world hitler.
peace, i have learned, is not the absence of war.
it is the presence of justice. versailles had none.

blood at jallianwala bagh 1919 ce india dyer's troops fire on unarmed indians at jallianwala bagh — the traveler hears ten minutes of rifles in amritsar and says the road to independence began in that walled garden. general dyer's troops fired on unarmed indians at jallianwala bagh —
1,650 rounds into a walled garden, 379 dead by the official count.
i was in amritsar that april, and heard the rifles for ten minutes,
the crowd with nowhere to run, the narrow exits blocked.
dyer was unrepentant; britain was divided; india was changed forever.
gandhi called it the moment india turned —
from petitioning the empire to leaving it.
blood on the ground in punjab, and the road to independence began there.

china's youth awaken 1919 ce beijing, china students flood beijing on may fourth 1919 against the versailles betrayal — the traveler marches with them and says this awakening shook a quarter of humanity. students flooded beijing against the versailles betrayal —
shantung given to japan, and china erupted on may fourth.
i marched with those students, young, furious, brilliant,
burning for a china that would stand up.
modern chinese nationalism was born that day —
in the streets, in the journals, in the refusal.
the old culture was questioned, the new ideas rushed in.
i have seen many awakenings. this one shook a quarter of humanity.

first across the atlantic 1919 ce atlantic alcock and brown fly the atlantic nonstop in sixteen harrowing hours — the traveler tracks their open-cockpit vimy and honors the first crossing before lindbergh made it famous. alcock and brown flew the atlantic nonstop —
sixteen harrowing hours in an open cockpit, fog, ice, near-death.
i tracked their vickers vimy from newfoundland,
those two men in leather and courage, half-frozen, wholly determined.
they crashed — landed — in an irish bog, and had done it:
the first to cross the ocean by air.
lindbergh would make it famous eight years later.
these two made it first, in a converted bomber, in the fog.

the school that redesigned the world 1919 ce weimar, germany gropius founds the bauhaus at weimar — the traveler walks the workshops and says the chairs you sit in and the type on this page were designed in that school. gropius founded the bauhaus at weimar —
art, craft, and industry become one.
i walked those workshops, the looms and the metal shops,
where painters learned welding and architects learned weaving.
form follows function; the modern world was designed in that school —
the chairs you sit in, the buildings you work in, the type on this page.
the nazis closed it in 1933. too late.
the bauhaus had already redesigned the planet.

the red summer 1919 ce usa race riots burn across america in the red summer of 1919 — black veterans home from france face lynchings, and the traveler walks the burning streets of chicago. race riots burned across america in the red summer —
black veterans came home from france to lynchings.
i walked the streets of chicago during those july days,
thirty-eight dead, the city divided by the color line.
they had fought for democracy abroad and been denied it at home —
and this time, they fought back.
the "new negro" was born in that summer's fire.
america's original sin, still bleeding, still unpaid.

starlight bends 1919 ce west africa eddington photographs bent starlight during the 1919 eclipse, proving einstein right — the traveler stands on principe island and calls it science's most beautiful moment. eddington photographed the eclipse off west africa,
and the stars bent around the sun — einstein was right.
i stood on principe island in the tropical heat,
watching the moon eat the sun while the cameras clicked.
general relativity, proven by starlight:
gravity curves space, and the universe obeyed the equations.
the news made einstein world-famous overnight.
a theory confirmed by an eclipse —
science's most beautiful moment, and i was there to see the plates.

the league is born 1919 ce geneva, switzerland the league of nations is founded in geneva — the traveler watches wilson's dream become an institution and says dreams don't die when institutions do. the league of nations was founded —
humanity's first try at collective peace.
i watched the delegates gather in geneva,
wilson's dream made into an institution, sort of.
no army, no teeth, america never joined —
the league would fail at its great tests.
but the idea survived the failure:
nations, talking, in one room, against war.
the united nations is its grandchild.
dreams don't die when institutions do.

the dry years begin 1919 ce usa prohibition takes effect in america — the traveler watches the last legal bars close and the speakeasies fill, calling it thirteen years proving you cannot legislate thirst. prohibition took effect, and america went dry —
the eighteenth amendment, the noble experiment.
i watched the last legal bars close, the toasts, the tears,
and the speakeasies fill up within weeks.
the law made drinking a crime and criminals into millionaires —
capone's chicago was born in that amendment.
thirteen years of hypocrisy, poisoned moonshine, blind tigers.
the century's great lesson: you cannot legislate thirst.

the weimar republic 1919 ce germany germany's republic is proclaimed at weimar, born in defeat and street fighting — the traveler gives it fourteen brilliant years before the fire. germany's republic was proclaimed at weimar —
democracy between the trenches, born in defeat.
i was in berlin for the street fighting that winter,
spartacists and freikorps, rosa luxemburg murdered in the canal.
the republic survived — barely — and gave germany
its freest years: bauhaus, brecht, cabaret, einstein.
but it was born with a knife at its throat,
and the enemies of democracy never accepted it.
fourteen years. then the fire.

american women win the vote 1920 ce usa tennessee's ratification wins american women the vote nationwide — the traveler stands outside the statehouse for the 35-49 vote switched by one young legislator's mother's letter. tennessee ratified, and american women won the ballot nationwide —
the nineteenth amendment, seventy-two years in the making.
i stood outside the tennessee statehouse for that final vote,
one young legislator, harry burn, switching on his mother's letter: "vote for suffrage."
thirty-five to forty-nine. done.
susan anthony had died fourteen years earlier; she missed it by that much.
the long march — seneca falls to nashville —
ended in a single "aye" on a hot august day.

radio goes commercial 1920 ce pittsburgh, usa kdka broadcasts election returns from pittsburgh in 1920 — the traveler listens on a crystal set and calls it the twentieth century's nervous system switching on. kdka broadcast the election returns from pittsburgh —
harding beats cox — and commercial radio was born.
i listened on a crystal set, the crackling voice from nowhere,
and understood: the nation would never be lonely again.
within years, millions of homes had the box,
the fireside replaced by the loudspeaker.
news, music, drama, ball games — all through the air.
the twentieth century's nervous system, switched on in pittsburgh.

the saint takes charge 1920 ce india gandhi launches noncooperation in 1920 — the traveler walks with the crowds and calls nonviolence the century's most radical idea, wearing the simplest clothes. gandhi launched noncooperation in 1920 —
and india learned the power of refusing.
i walked with the crowds, the spinning wheels, the boycotted cloth,
a saint in a loincloth taking charge of a revolution.
no guns, no bombs — just refusal, on a continental scale.
the british empire had faced armies; it had never faced this.
nonviolence as strategy, morality as weapon —
the century's most radical idea, wearing the simplest clothes.

the miracle on the vistula 1920 ce poland poland smashes the red army at warsaw in 1920 — the traveler stands on the vistula as history pivots, and says miracles are preparation meeting desperation. poland smashed the red army at warsaw —
the miracle on the vistula, the eighteenth decisive battle of the world.
i stood on the riverbanks as pilsudski's counterattack broke through,
the soviets routed, lenin's dream of european revolution stopped cold.
had warsaw fallen, the red army marched on berlin —
history pivoted on those august days.
poland saved europe and got little thanks.
miracles, i have learned, are just preparation meeting desperation.

the babe goes bronx 1920 ce new york, usa the red sox sell babe ruth to the yankees — the traveler is in boston for the disbelief and calls it the worst trade in sports history, regretted for 86 years. the red sox sold babe ruth to the yankees for $125,000 —
and the curse of the bambino began.
i was in boston when the news broke, the disbelief, the rage.
ruth would hit 54 homers that first yankee season
and become the most famous athlete on earth.
boston would not win another series for 86 years.
selling the babe: the worst trade in sports history,
made for cash, regretted for a century.

ireland fights on 1920 ce ireland the ira's guerrilla war grinds britain toward a treaty — the traveler walks the cork countryside and says ireland's freedom was bought in laneways, not battlefields. the ira's guerrilla war ground britain toward a treaty —
flying columns, ambushes, the black and tans' reprisals.
i walked the cork countryside those years,
the war in the shadows, neighbors informing, houses burning.
it was brutal on both sides — war usually is —
but the guerrillas bled the empire into negotiating.
by 1921 britain would talk.
ireland's freedom was bought in laneways and farmhouses,
not on battlefields.

the queen of crime debuts 1920 ce england agatha christie's first novel introduces hercule poirot — the traveler reads it fresh off the press, not knowing the quiet woman from torquay becomes history's best-selling novelist. the mysterious affair at styles introduced hercule poirot —
agatha christie's first, the little belgian with the mustaches.
i read it fresh off the press, not knowing
the quiet woman from torquay would become the best-selling novelist in history.
poirot, miss marple, two billion books —
the golden age of the detective story began in that country house.
everyone has a motive; the little grey cells sort them out.
comfort reading for a violent century.

dry by law 1920 ce usa the volstead act takes hold and bootleggers become millionaires overnight — the traveler watches the rum-runners and says the law meant well; the law always means well. the volstead act took hold, and bootleggers became millionaires overnight —
prohibition with teeth, and the teeth bit the wrong people.
i watched the rum-runners on the great lakes, the stills in the hills,
an entire criminal economy blooming under the law's nose.
the government poisoned industrial alcohol; people died drinking it.
the law meant well. the law always means well.
thirteen years of organized crime's golden age,
funded by america's thirst.

the league meets 1920 ce geneva, switzerland the league of nations holds its first assembly in geneva — 41 nations, and the traveler calls it the first time humanity tried to govern its own violence. the league of nations held its first assembly —
forty-one nations, one hope, in geneva.
i sat in the gallery as the delegates filed in,
the war's survivors trying to build the machine that would prevent the next one.
speeches in french and english, committees, covenants.
it was earnest, and it was inadequate —
but it was the first time humanity had tried to govern its violence.
the hope was real, even if the power wasn't.

sweet blood, bitter search 1921 ce toronto, canada banting and best isolate insulin in toronto — the traveler visits the cramped lab and calls the rescue of dying diabetic children one of the few miracles he's seen. banting and best isolated insulin in toronto —
and diabetes stopped being a death sentence.
i visited that cramped laboratory, the dogs, the desperate work,
a young surgeon and a medical student chasing a pancreatic extract.
children wasted to skeletons were dying in the wards.
within a year, the dying were living.
medicine's greatest rescue — from certain death to a daily shot.
i have seen few miracles. this was one.

black wall street burns 1921 ce oklahoma, usa a white mob destroys tulsa's greenwood district — black wall street burned, hundreds dead, buried in silence for 70 years, and the traveler says the silence was the second crime. a white mob destroyed tulsa's greenwood district —
black wall street, burned to the ground, hundreds dead.
i walked those streets after the fires,
the prosperous black businesses, the homes, all ash.
airplanes dropped firebombs; the national guard interned the survivors.
it was a massacre, and america buried it for seventy years —
no memorial, no reckoning, just silence.
the silence was the second crime.
i remember greenwood. i say its name.

the treaty 1921 ce ireland the anglo-irish treaty creates the free state and partitions ireland — the traveler is in dublin for the anguished debates and says freedom came, but came divided. the anglo-irish treaty created the free state —
and split ireland in two, and split the republicans in two.
i was in dublin for the debates, the anguish,
collins signing his own death warrant, as he said.
the oath to the crown, the partition of the north —
half a loaf, or a betrayal? ireland would fight a civil war over the answer.
freedom came, but it came divided.
the treaty ended one war and started another.

thirteen men in shanghai 1921 ce shanghai, china thirteen men found the chinese communist party in a shanghai schoolhouse — the traveler walks past the modest brick house and says history's biggest parties start in the smallest rooms. thirteen men founded the chinese communist party
in a shanghai schoolhouse, in secret, in july.
i walked past that building — a modest brick house in the french concession —
not knowing it would birth the force that rules a quarter of humanity.
mao was there, a young librarian's assistant.
they were nobodies, hunted, broke.
history's biggest parties start in the smallest rooms.
i have learned to pay attention to nobodies in schoolhouses.

the prize catches up 1921 ce sweden einstein wins the nobel for the photoelectric effect, not relativity — the traveler smiles at the committee's caution and notes he gave the money to his ex-wife as promised. einstein won the nobel in 1921 —
for the photoelectric effect, not relativity.
i smiled at the committee's caution:
the universe's greatest theory was still "unproven" to them,
so they honored the safe paper instead.
he used the prize money for his divorce settlement —
mileva got the fortune, as promised.
the prize caught up with the man, sort of.
genius doesn't need permission. but the money helped.

baseball on the air 1921 ce usa the world series is broadcast on radio for the first time in 1921 — the traveler listens in a barbershop and says the imagination is the best screen. the world series was broadcast on radio for the first time —
the giants beat the yankees, and america listened.
i sat by a crystal set with a crowd in a barbershop,
the announcer painting pictures with words: "the pitch, the swing—"
no one had ever experienced a game they couldn't see.
it worked. the imagination is the best screen.
within years, baseball and radio were married —
the summer game, in every kitchen, forever.

the battleship holiday 1921 ce usa the great powers agree to limit battleships at washington — the traveler watches admirals surrender dreadnoughts on paper and says the idea survived even when the treaties died. the great powers agreed to limit battleships at washington —
arms control's first try, the battleship holiday.
i watched the admirals surrender their dreadnoughts on paper,
ratios and tonnages, 5-5-3, the arithmetic of peace.
it worked, for a while — the building race paused.
then the cheaters cheated, and the treaties died.
but the idea survived: enemies, talking about weapons,
agreeing to build fewer of them.
the first try is never the last word.

the trial of sacco and vanzetti 1921 ce massachusetts, usa sacco and vanzetti are convicted on shaky evidence in 1921 — the traveler sits in the dedham courtroom and says justice is supposed to be blind; this time it just closed its eyes. two italian anarchists were convicted on shaky evidence —
and the world protested for six years.
i sat in that dedham courtroom, the prejudice thick as fog:
they were guilty of being italian, being radical, being different.
the evidence was thin; the verdict was pre-written.
paris marched, london marched, buenos aires marched.
the state would kill them anyway, in 1927.
justice is supposed to be blind. this time it just closed its eyes.

the boy king's tomb 1922 ce egypt carter peers into tutankhamun's intact tomb — "wonderful things" — and the traveler stands in the 3,000-year-old air as the world goes mad for egypt. carter peered through the hole in tutankhamun's tomb —
"wonderful things," he said. gold, intact, everywhere.
i stood in that antechamber, the air of three thousand years,
the boy king's treasure glittering in lamplight.
the world went mad for egypt — tut-mania, everywhere.
carter had dug for years on faith; carnarvon funded the dream.
one intact tomb, and the ancient world felt close enough to touch.
some doors, once opened, never close again.

mussolini takes rome 1922 ce italy mussolini's blackshirts march on rome and the king hands him power — the traveler watches the theater and says power rarely needs as much force as it pretends. mussolini's blackshirts marched on rome,
and the king handed him power without a shot fired.
i watched the columns enter the capital, the bluff, the theater —
thirty thousand men, and the government folded.
il duce: the first fascist, the model for the worse one to come.
italy got trains that ran on time and a press that couldn't speak.
the march was mostly myth — the deal was cut beforehand.
power rarely needs as much force as it pretends.

the soviet union is born 1922 ce russia the ussr is proclaimed in 1922 — the traveler is in moscow for the red banners and calls it history's largest laboratory, results still being argued. the ussr was proclaimed — the world's first communist state,
fifteen republics under the hammer and sickle.

stalingrad: the furnace where the wehrmacht burned.

the dambusters: precision, courage, and the price.

the firestorm 1943 ce germany hamburg burns in a firestorm in 1943 — 40,000 dead in a week, and the traveler walks the melted streets asking the question argued ever since: war or murder? hamburg burned in a firestorm in 1943 —

operation gomorrah: the raf by night, the americans by day.
the old city died; the question lived:
was it war, or was it murder?
the bombing's morality, argued ever since.
hamburg: the firestorm's lesson, in ash.

italy quits 1943 ce italy italy surrenders in 1943 — mussolini falls and germany occupies its former ally; the traveler is in rome and says the soft underbelly turned out to be hard. italy surrendered in 1943 —
mussolini fell, and germany occupied its former ally.

the king dismissing il duce, the armistice, the chaos.
the germans disarmed their allies overnight —
italy became a battlefield, north and south.
mussolini was rescued, then propped up as a puppet.
italy quit. the war didn't.
the soft underbelly turned out to be hard.

the alliance at its peak — and its most fragile.
overlord agreed: the invasion, the date, the place.
stalin got his front; the west got its promises.
tehran: the high-water mark of the alliance.
within years they'd be enemies.
but for those days, in persia, they were winning together.

the hungry province 1943 ce india famine grips bengal in 1943 — millions starve while grain ships sail past, and the traveler walks the calcutta streets; the war's forgotten famine, the empire's shame. famine gripped bengal in 1943 —
millions starved while grain ships sailed past.
i walked the calcutta streets, the skeletons,
the rice denied, the boats requisitioned for the war.
churchill's policies, the japanese in burma, the hoarders —
three million dead, the empire's shame.
the hungry province: the war's forgotten famine.
bengal starved while the empire ate.
i will not forget. bengal doesn't.

the five-sided fortress 1943 ce virginia, usa the pentagon opens in 1943 — the traveler walks its rings and says it was supposed to be temporary; the building outlasted the war it was built for. the pentagon opened in 1943 —
the world's largest office building, built for war.
i walked its rings, the miles of corridor,
sixteen months to build, the war's headquarters.
it was supposed to be temporary — the war's end would empty it.
it never emptied. the war never quite ended.
the five-sided fortress: the military-industrial sublime.
the building outlasted the war it was built for.

the zoot suit riots 1943 ce california, usa sailors attack mexican-american youths in the 1943 zoot suit riots — the traveler walks the la streets; america fought racism abroad and practiced it at home. sailors attacked mexican-american youths in los angeles in 1943 —
wartime racism on the home front.
i walked those streets, the beatings,
the zoot suits stripped off, the police watching.
the pachucos were the targets — their style, their pride.
the navy blamed the victims; the press cheered the sailors.
america fought racism abroad and practiced it at home.
the zoot suit riots: the home front's shame.
the suits were fabulous. the beatings were not.

the monastery falls 1944 ce italy allied bombs flatten monte cassino's abbey in 1944 — the traveler stands in the ruins; the monastery was rebuilt stone by stone, but the dead can't be. allied bombs flattened monte cassino's abbey in 1944 —
and the gustav line finally broke.
i stood in the ruins, the ancient monastery,
founded by st. benedict, destroyed by mistake — no germans were inside.
the bombing was pointless; the battle was not.
four assaults, the poles taking the hill at last.
the monastery fell; the line broke.
the abbey was rebuilt, stone by stone.
some things can be rebuilt. the dead can't.

the longest day 1944 ce france 150,000 men storm normandy's beaches on d-day 1944 — the traveler is on omaha beach; the largest amphibious invasion ever, and the beginning of the end. 150,000 men stormed normandy's beaches on june 6, 1944 —
the liberation of europe began.
i was on omaha beach, the slaughter,
the higgins boats, the cliffs, the boys who didn't make it.
utah, omaha, gold, juno, sword — the names of the dawn.
it was the largest amphibious invasion ever —
and it worked.
the longest day: the beginning of the end.
i walked that sand. i remember every wave.

paris is free 1944 ce france paris is liberated in august 1944 — the traveler is on the streets for de gaulle's march down the champs-elysees; the city of light, lit again. leclerc's tanks rolled into paris in august 1944 —
and de gaulle marched down the champs-elysees.
i was on those streets, the joy,
the ffi rising, the germans leaving, the bells.
four years of occupation ended in a week of celebration.
de gaulle's march: the republic reclaimed.
paris was free — wounded, hungry, but free.
the city of light, lit again.
i wept with the crowds. everyone wept.

the city rises 1944 ce poland warsaw rises against the nazis in 1944 — 63 days, and the red army watches from across the river; the traveler calls it the bravest, most betrayed uprising of the war. warsaw rose against the nazis in 1944 —
and the red army watched from across the river.
i was in the city for the 63 days, the barricades,
the home army's heroism, the hope for liberation.
stalin halted — and let the nazis crush the rising.
it was deliberate: the future poland, decapitated.
200,000 dead; the city systematically destroyed.
the city rises: the bravest, most betrayed uprising of the war.
warsaw rose. the world watched. stalin waited.

the annex is betrayed 1944 ce netherlands the gestapo raids the secret annex in august 1944 — the traveler stands on the prinsengracht; anne dies in bergen-belsen, but the diary outlives the reich. the gestapo raided the secret annex in august 1944 —
anne was sent to bergen-belsen.
i stood on the prinsengracht, the trucks,
the eight people dragged out — the diary left behind.
someone betrayed them — we still don't know who.
anne died in the camp, weeks before liberation.
her father survived, and published her words.
the annex: betrayed, but not silenced.
the diary outlived the reich.

money's new order 1944 ce new hampshire, usa bretton woods creates the dollar-based money order in 1944 — the traveler sits in the new hampshire hotel as keynes and white design the peace's economy. bretton woods created the dollar-based money order in 1944 —
the imf and world bank were born.
i sat in that new hampshire hotel, the delegates,
keynes and white designing the peace's economy.
fixed exchange rates, the dollar as gold —
the system that would run the world for thirty years.
money's new order: the economists' peace.
it worked — until it didn't, in 1971.
but the institutions endured.

the last great sea battle 1944 ce philippines the us navy smashes japan at leyte gulf in 1944 — history's largest naval battle, the kamikazes' debut, and the end of the imperial japanese navy. the us navy smashed japan at leyte gulf in 1944 —
history's largest naval battle.
i watched from the waves, the four engagements,
the kamikazes' debut, the last battleship duel.
the japanese navy ceased to exist as a force.
macarthur returned — "i shall return," fulfilled.
leyte gulf: the end of the imperial japanese navy.
the largest sea battle ever, and the last of its kind.

the gi bill 1944 ce usa the gi bill promises veterans college and homes in 1944 — the traveler watches the campuses overflow; the american middle class, legislated into existence. the gi bill promised veterans college and homes in 1944 —
the american middle class was born.
i watched the vets enroll, the campuses overflowing,
the mortgages, the suburbs, the boom.
it was the most generous veterans' law ever —
and it built modern america.
black vets were cheated of its benefits — the fine print of racism.
but the bill's promise was real: serve, and the country serves you.
the middle class: legislated into existence.

the gates open 1945 ce poland soviet troops enter auschwitz in january 1945 — the traveler walks through the gates; the world had known, now it saw: murder industrialized, done by people to people. soviet troops entered auschwitz in january 1945 —
and the world saw the holocaust's machinery.
i walked those gates, the snow,
the survivors, the warehouses of hair and shoes.
the gas chambers, the crematoria — the industrialization of murder.
the world had known; now it saw.
the gates open: the proof, in brick and ash.
i will not describe it further. the facts are enough.
remember: it was done by people, to people.

yalta 1945 ce crimea the big three carve up postwar europe at yalta in 1945 — the traveler is in the livadia palace; the peace that became the cold war's first draft. the big three carved up postwar europe at yalta in 1945 —
the cold war's first draft.
i was in the livadia palace, the aging leaders,
roosevelt dying, churchill wary, stalin smiling.
poland's fate was sealed; the un was planned.
the agreements were vague; the spheres were real.
yalta: the peace that became the cold war.
the big three divided the world — and the world stayed divided.

the firestorm over dresden 1945 ce germany dresden burns in february 1945 — the traveler walks the ash and offers no verdict, only the questions that outlived the answers. dresden burned in february 1945 —
and the bombing's morality will be argued forever.
i walked the city after, the ash,
the altstadt destroyed, the refugees, the dead.
was it necessary? was it revenge? was it a message to stalin?
the questions outlived the answers.
the firestorm: the war's most controversial bombing.
dresden rebuilt; the argument didn't.
i have no verdict. i have the ash.

the flag on suribachi 1945 ce pacific marines raise the flag on mount suribachi in 1945 — the traveler is on iwo jima's black sand; 7,000 dead for eight square miles, and the photo that almost justified it. marines raised the flag on mount suribachi in 1945 —
the pacific war's iconic image.
i was on iwo jima, the black sand,
the 36 days of hell, the tunnels, the dead.
rosenthal's photo: the second flag, the famous one.
it became the statue, the symbol, the memory.
iwo jima: 7,000 marines dead for eight square miles.
the flag: the image that justified the cost — almost.

the typhoon of steel 1945 ce japan okinawa falls after 82 days in 1945 — the bloodiest pacific battle, and the traveler says it made hiroshima thinkable; the preview was horror. okinawa fell after 82 days in 1945 —
the bloodiest pacific battle, a preview of invasion.
i walked that island, the caves,
the kamikazes, the civilians caught between.
200,000 dead — the typhoon of steel.
it convinced america: invading japan would be hell.
the bomb became the alternative.
okinawa: the battle that made hiroshima thinkable.
the preview was horror. the main event was worse.

and truman inherited the war and the bomb.
i was in america for the news, the shock,
the man who'd led for twelve years, gone in an afternoon.
the nation mourned; the world wondered.
truman: the haberdasher, the decision-maker.
he learned about the bomb that day.
the presidency passed — and the atomic age with it.

the bunker 1945 ce germany hitler dies in his berlin bunker in april 1945 — the traveler is above ground in the shelling; the thousand-year reich lasted twelve, and he feels no triumph, only silence. hitler died in his bunker in april 1945 —
berlin fell, the reich was rubble.
i was above that bunker, the shelling,
the wedding, the cyanide, the gasoline.
the thousand-year reich lasted twelve years.
berlin: the rubble, the rape, the ruin.
the bunker: the end of the nightmare, in a hole.
i felt no triumph. only the silence after.
the dead were still dead. the living had to rebuild.

victory in europe 1945 ce europe ve day in may 1945 — the traveler celebrates in london, paris, and moscow; the joy was real, and so was the rubble. ve day: europe celebrated in may 1945 —
the war in the west was over.
i was in london, in paris, in moscow —
the crowds, the kisses, the bells.
six years of war ended in a day of joy.
but the pacific burned on, and the cold war waited.
victory in europe: the celebration before the reckoning.
the continent was free — and in ruins.
the joy was real. so was the rubble.

the united nations 1945 ce california, usa fifty nations sign the un charter in san francisco in 1945 — the traveler is in the herbst theatre; it wouldn't stop wars, but the paper mattered. fifty nations signed the un charter in san francisco in 1945 —
"never again," on paper.
i was in the herbst theatre, the signatures,
the hope after the league's failure.
the security council, the veto — the great powers' insurance.
it wouldn't stop wars. but it would feed the hungry, shelter the refugees.
the united nations: the league's grandchild, with teeth — sometimes.
never again, on paper. the paper mattered.

the atomic age began in fire.
i stood at the observation point, the countdown,
the flash — brighter than the sun, the mushroom cloud.
oppenheimer quoted the gita: "i am become death."
the scientists cheered, then went quiet.
the first flash: the moment humanity could end itself.
it worked. god forgive us, it worked.

potsdam 1945 ce germany the victors meet at potsdam in 1945 — the traveler is in the cecilienhof palace as the alliance cracks; the crack becomes the iron curtain. the victors met at potsdam in 1945 —
and the alliance started to crack.
i was in the cecilienhof palace, the new faces,
truman, attlee, stalin — the wartime trio, changed.
the bomb was mentioned; stalin already knew.
germany's fate was sealed; the cold war's was drafted.
potsdam: the last summit of the alliance.
the victors divided the spoils — and the world.
the crack became the iron curtain.

the world war was over.
i was in tokyo bay for the signing, the missouri,
the two bombs, the soviet invasion — the end.
six years, 70 million dead, the world remade.
vj day: the celebrations, the kisses, the relief.
the emperor spoke — the first time his people heard his voice.
victory over japan: the war's end, the atomic age's beginning.
the silence after was the loudest sound.

the trial of the century 1945 ce germany the nuremberg trials open in 1945 — the traveler sits in the courtroom as "crimes against humanity" is invented for the occasion; justice, imperfect, necessary. the nuremberg trials opened in 1945 —
the architects of atrocity faced judgment.
i sat in that courtroom, the dock,
goering, hess, the films of the camps.
jackson's opening: the first international war-crimes trial.
"crimes against humanity" — the law, invented for the occasion.
twelve hanged; the precedent lived.
the trial of the century: justice, imperfect, necessary.
the world said: never again — and meant it, this time.

the electronic brain 1945 ce pennsylvania, usa eniac is switched on in 1945 — the first general-purpose electronic computer, and the traveler stands among its 18,000 vacuum tubes; the digital age hasn't slept since. eniac, the first general-purpose electronic computer, was switched on in 1945 —
the digital age stirred.
i stood in the moore school, the room of vacuum tubes,
18,000 of them, the heat, the hum.
it computed artillery tables — the war's last calculator.
then the war ended, and the machine remained.
the electronic brain: thirty tons, and the future.
every computer since descends from that philadelphia room.
the digital age stirred. it hasn't slept since.
end of volume v — continued in volume vi.

the table at yalta february 1945 crimea three leaders split postwar europe over a table in crimea while the war still raged; the traveler watched ordinary people traded like parcels nobody asked about. three old men at a table by the sea,
maps spread like a butcher's cut between them.
i stood behind the curtains and watched them deal —
half a continent traded in a week.
roosevelt dying by inches in his chair,
churchill smoking through his doubts,
stalin smiling at everything they gave.
the war still burned. the ink was still wet.
and nobody asked the people on the map
if they wanted to be bargained.

a charter for the world april 1945 usa fifty nations gathered in san francisco to write the un charter; the traveler heard the old promise "never again" and watched them build hope on paper anyway. san francisco, spring, the bay gone silver —
fifty flags outside the opera house.
i walked the halls where the delegates argued,
every tongue on earth in one long corridor,
and watched them write a promise on paper:
never again, they said, never again.
i had heard men say that before.
but i watched them sign anyway,
because sometimes hope is all you have,
and sometimes you have to build the house
even when you know the storm is coming.

the guns fall silent in europe may 1945 europe nazi germany surrendered and the traveler danced with strangers in a rubble-strewn square, where one night of joy bloomed before anyone asked what came next. the radios crackled and then went quiet,
and a strange sound rose over the rubble —
people laughing.
i was in a square where the buildings stood open
like broken teeth, and strangers danced
in the street among the bricks.
a woman pressed a flower into my hand
though the flower was half ash.
no one knew what came next.
for one night, nobody cared.

the emperor speaks august 1945 japan the emperor's voice reached his people for the first time in history, thin through the wireless; the traveler watched a nation kneel and hear its god sound human. for centuries he had been a god behind walls,
silent as the moon.
then a voice came crackling through the wireless,
thin and formal, reading words about enduring
the unendurable —
and millions knelt beside their radios
hearing their god sound like a tired man.
i stood in a street in tokyo and watched
an old woman cover her mouth with both hands.
the war was over. the silence was broken.
nothing in japan would ever be quiet in the same way again.

the blue flag rises october 1945 usa the un charter took effect with 51 nations under a blue flag showing a borderless world; the traveler remembered the knives of yalta and still honored the paper. a blue flag with the world drawn on it —
every continent, no borders,
as if someone had finally drawn the map right.
fifty-one nations signed their names beneath it.
i watched the flag go up and thought of yalta,
of the table and the knives.
paper, i thought. it is only paper.
but i have learned, walking the long years,
that paper is where everything human begins.

justice at nuremberg november 1945 germany nazi leaders faced the world's first international court in ruined nuremberg; the traveler sat in the gallery and watched power forced to sit still and hear its own crimes. they built a courtroom in the ruins
and sat the architects of murder in a row
to answer for it — all of it — out loud,
before the whole watching world.
i sat in the gallery and listened to the tapes,
the lists, the numbers read like weather reports,
and watched goring puff himself up
in a room that would not puff with him.
it was the first time in all my walking
that power had to sit still and listen
to what it had done.

the melting candy bar december 1945 usa a radar engineer's pocket chocolate melted beside his magnetron, and the microwave age began; the traveler marveled that the atom's fire ended up reheating leftovers. a radar engineer named spencer
stood too close to his magnetron
and the chocolate in his pocket turned to soup.
he didn't curse his luck — he grinned.
he popped some corn with the same strange waves,
cooked an egg till it exploded on his colleague,
and the microwave oven was born.
i love this about humans: the atom's fire,
the radar that hunted bombers,
ends up reheating your leftovers.
the biggest powers always land
in the smallest kitchens.

the assembly convenes january 1946 uk the un general assembly met for the first time in a paint-smelling london hall; the traveler watched small nations speak while big ones listened — the opposite of yalta's table. london, winter, the hall still smelling of paint —
the general assembly took its seats for the first time,
fifty-one nations arguing about seating charts
and the order of the speeches.
it was clumsy. it was slow.
a janitor told me they'd run out of ashtrays by noon.
but i watched the small countries speak
and the big countries have to listen,
and i thought: this clumsy room
is the opposite of yalta's table.
here, at least, the map gets a voice.

the iron curtain march 1946 usa churchill named the iron curtain in a missouri hall; the traveler felt the words fall like a portcullis as half of europe understood the peace was armed. in fulton, missouri, an old lion stood up
and gave the thing its name.
"from stettin in the baltic to trieste in the adriatic,"
he said, "an iron curtain has descended."
i was in the hall. the words fell like a portcullis.
half of europe heard it on the wireless that night
and understood, all at once,
that the war was over but the peace was armed.
churchill didn't build the curtain —
he only pointed at what stalin had hung.
naming it made it real.

fire over bikini july 1946 pacific america tested atomic bombs over bikini atoll after sailing the islanders away; the traveler watched the sky split and saw the islanders never return home. they told the islanders it was for the good of mankind
and sailed them away from their lagoon.
then the sky split open over bikini —
a second sun rising where the palms had been,
the water standing up in a column of fire.
i watched from a ship's deck, the light
burning through my closed eyelids.
the islanders never went home.
their atoll became a word for a swimsuit
and a warning no one heeded.
the bomb had a beautiful face that day,
and it has been lying ever since.

cannes lights up september 1946 france war-weary france launched a film festival on the riviera while rubble still lined the streets; the traveler sat beside a fisherman who wept because the dark was for pleasure again. france was still sweeping up the rubble
when it rolled out a red carpet by the sea.
projectors flickered in the riviera dark
and war-weary people laughed at flickering ghosts.
i sat in the back row with a fisherman
who wept through a comedy — not from the film,
he told me, but because it had been years
since he had sat in the dark for pleasure
instead of hiding.
art came back before the roofs did.
that tells you what humans are.

for every child december 1946 usa the un created unicef to feed and heal the world's children regardless of side; the traveler carried milk crates in naples and watched a boy drink as if the cup might vanish. the war left children like driftwood —
hungry, lost, coughing in the cold.
so they made a fund, plain and simple:
milk, medicine, blankets, for every child,
no questions about whose side their fathers died on.
i carried crates in naples with the volunteers,
powdered milk dust on my coat,
and watched a boy drink as if the cup
might be taken away.
it wasn't. that was the whole point.
it wasn't.

the burping lid 1946 ce usa tupperware's burping airtight seal kept leftovers fresh and turned kitchen parties into a revolution; the traveler heard the future arrive in popping lids, not trumpets. earl tupper had a hunch about plastic,
a paint can's lid, and a perfect seal —
press the middle and it burped,
and the leftovers stayed fresh for days.
housewives held parties to sell the stuff,
neighbors buying bowls over coffee cake.
i went to one in ohio. the laughter,
the clatter of lids popping like applause —
who knew the future would arrive
not with trumpets, but tupperware?

pictures in a minute february 1947 usa edwin land answered his daughter's question with the instant camera; the traveler watched a photograph bloom in sixty seconds and a girl laugh at her own brand-new face. edwin land's little girl asked why
she couldn't see the photo right away —
and her father, being a genius,
took the question seriously.
he held up a camera, clicked,
and pulled out a gray square that bloomed
into a picture while we watched.
sixty seconds. a miracle in a minute.
i watched a sailor photograph his girl
and hand her the still-warm image.
she laughed at her own face, brand new.

the truman doctrine march 1947 usa america vowed to fight communism everywhere; the traveler felt the century's temperature drop as every small war became a big war in disguise. a plain man from missouri stood before congress
and drew a line around the world.
wherever communism pushed, he said,
america would push back — money, guns, all of it.
i listened from the gallery as the applause rolled,
and felt the temperature of the century drop.
it was honest, at least. no more pretending
the two giants could share the playground.
from that day on, every small war
was a big war wearing a mask.

the marshall lifeline june 1947 europe america poured billions into rebuilding shattered europe without humiliation clauses; the traveler watched american wheat unload in hamburg while a dockworker's children stopped asking about supper. america opened its wallet to a ruined continent —
billions for bread, coal, steel, and hope,
no humiliation clauses this time.
they had learned from the last peace.
i walked through a hamburg shipyard
where american wheat was unloading,
and a dockworker told me his children
had stopped asking if there would be supper.
nations are rebuilt the way people are:
someone has to bring the food first.

freedom at midnight august 1947 india india won freedom at midnight, but partition split the land and sent millions fleeing; the traveler cheered in delhi, then walked roads where trains arrived full of the dead. at the stroke of midnight, the flags changed —
india free, the british ships gone from the harbor.
i stood in the cheering crowds in delhi,
and then i walked the roads west and east
where the cheering turned to screaming.
partition: a line drawn through villages,
through families, through kitchens —
millions walking with bundles on their heads,
trains arriving full of the dead.
freedom came at midnight.
by dawn it was bleeding.

faster than sound october 1947 usa chuck yeager blasted past the speed of sound in the bell x-1 and landed asking for a coke; the traveler watched the sky crack open and the old limits tear like paper. chuck yeager climbed into a bullet with wings
over the mojave, lit the rocket,
and punched straight through the sound barrier —
the sky cracking like a whip behind him.
they said the plane might shake apart.
it didn't. he landed, grinning,
and asked for a coca-cola.
i watched the contrail tear the blue open
and thought: the old limits are made of paper.
every wall the world builds,
some farm boy will fly through it.

a line drawn in palestine november 1947 middle east the un voted to split palestine into two states; the traveler walked jerusalem the next morning and watched the news pass like a lit match toward a fire that never went out. the assembly voted, late at night —
thirty-three hands for a line on a map,
a jewish state here, an arab state there,
jerusalem held apart like a disputed jewel.
i walked the streets of jerusalem the next morning
and heard the news pass from mouth to mouth
like a lit match.
by spring the match had found the fuel.
they drew the line with a pencil.
it has been drawn in blood ever since.

the tiny switch december 1947 usa bell labs unveiled the transistor, a pea-sized switch that would shrink room-sized machines into pockets; the traveler held one and felt it outweigh every engine he'd ever seen. in a bell labs room, three men in shirtsleeves
coaxed a sliver of germanium to do
what a whole glowing vacuum tube had done —
switch, amplify, sing.
the transistor: smaller than a pea,
and it would eat the room-sized machines
and shrink them into pockets.
i held one in my palm. it weighed nothing.
it weighed nothing, and it outweighed
every engine i had ever seen.

the mahatma falls january 1948 india gandhi was shot walking to evening prayer in delhi; the traveler heard the wail rise street by street as the man who freed a nation without a fist fell to one. he walked to evening prayer leaning on two girls,
thin as a reed, smiling —
and three shots cracked the garden quiet.
i was in delhi. the news ran ahead of the radio,
a wail rising from street to street
as if the whole city had been struck at once.
the man who freed a nation without raising a fist
fell to a fist raised against him.
they say his last word was ram.
i believe it. he forgave to the end.

a nation reborn may 1948 middle east israel declared independence in a tel aviv museum hall; the traveler danced with the crowds outside, then watched the armies come over every border by morning. on a friday afternoon in tel aviv,
in a museum hall under a portrait of herzl,
ben-gurion read fourteen minutes of words
and a nation was born — israel, at last,
after two thousand years of waiting.
i stood outside in the crowd as the news spread,
people dancing in the street.
by morning the armies were coming
over every border. the dancing stopped.
it has never quite started again —
but the nation stood. it stood.
