to a movement that would change the law,
the culture, the world.
it started because people
were tired of hiding.

helter skelter august 1969 usa the manson cult's murders killed the sixties' innocence; the traveler covered the trial and watched the peace-and-love dream curdle into something feral. the tate house, the labianca house —
nights of ritual murder by a failed musician's
brainwashed "family," apocalypse in their eyes.
i covered the trial, watched manson
carve a swastika into his forehead,
grinning at the cameras.
the sixties' innocence died in those houses.
the peace-and-love dream curdled
into something feral.
after manson, the communes locked their doors,
and the flower children started checking
the locks twice.

three days of mud and music august 1969 usa half a million gathered at woodstock for three days of mud and music; the traveler stood soaked as hendrix played the anthem at dawn to the faithful few. half a million people in a muddy field
in bethel, new york — rain, no food,
no shelter, and the greatest concert ever played.
i was in that mud, soaked to the bone,
when hendrix played the anthem at dawn monday
to the faithful few who remained.
woodstock: the hippie dream's peak,
three days of peace that actually worked.
no violence. just music and mud
and half a million strangers sharing everything.
it never happened again. nothing ever does.

cash from a wall september 1969 usa the first atm dispensed cash from a new york bank wall; the traveler watched suspicious customers turn delighted as banking left the counter forever. chemical bank put a machine in the wall —
the first atm in america —
and it handed out cash after hours.
i watched the first customers approach it
like a wild animal, suspicious,
then delighted.
banking left the counter that day.
the teller's smile, the queue, the hours —
all of it started dissolving into the machine.
now we tap glass and the money moves.
it started with a hole in a new york wall.

lo october 1969 usa the first internet message crashed after two letters — "lo"; the traveler laughed with the ucla engineers before they rebooted and typed it again, and it worked. ucla to stanford, the first arpanet message:
they typed login — and the system crashed
after two letters.
lo. the first word of the internet age
was half a greeting.
i was in the ucla lab that night,
and the engineers laughed till they cried.
then they rebooted, and typed it again,
and it worked.
every email, every video, every everything —
descended from those two letters
and a crash.

sunny days november 1969 usa sesame street premiered with its friendly monsters and eight-foot bird; the traveler visited the set and watched education's greatest trick — making learning feel like play. a street where the monsters are friendly,
a bird eight feet tall teaches the alphabet,
and a green grouch loves his trash.
sesame street premiered —
built by educators, not entertainers,
to give poor kids a head start.
i visited the set in the early years,
watched big bird learn his lines.
it worked. it still works.
generations learned to count
from a count who was a vampire,
and to read from a bird.
education's greatest trick:
making it feel like play.

the jumbo jet january 1970 usa the 747 entered service with its spiral staircase and hump; the traveler climbed to the upper deck as flying went mass-market and the world got coach-class wings. the 747 entered service —
two aisles, four engines, four hundred souls,
a flying building with a hump.
pan am's clipper victor, new york to london.
i was aboard an early flight,
climbing the spiral staircase to the upper deck
like ascending to a private heaven.
flying went mass-market that day.
the jet set became just... the set.
everyone could go now.
the world got its wings, coach class.

the breakup april 1970 uk paul's press release ended the beatles; the traveler read it in a london cafe where the waitress cried into her apron as the sixties ended with a lawyer's letter. paul announced it in a press release
tucked into his solo album:
the beatles were over.
i read the news in a london cafe,
and the waitress cried into her apron.
the sixties ended not with a bang
but a lawyer's letter.
four lads who'd owned the planet
went their separate ways.
the music lived on — it always does —
but the dream of them, together,
died that april.

earth day april 1970 usa twenty million americans rallied for the planet on the first earth day; the traveler marched in new york among accountants with signs and chanting grandmothers. twenty million americans took to the streets —
not for a war or a candidate, but for the planet.
the first earth day: teach-ins, cleanups,
a nation looking at its smog and saying enough.
i marched in new york, and the strangest thing
was the normalcy — accountants with signs,
grandmothers chanting.
the green movement went mainstream that day.
silent spring had warned.
earth day answered.

kent state may 1970 usa guardsmen killed four student protesters at kent state; the traveler stood on the bloodstained asphalt days later as campuses erupted and the war came home. the guard opened fire on unarmed students —
thirteen seconds, sixty-seven shots,
four dead, nine wounded.
i was on that campus days later,
the bloodstains still on the asphalt,
flowers laid where allison krause fell.
"tin soldiers and nixon coming."
campuses erupted nationwide.
a government had shot its own children
for protesting a war —
and the war came home
in the worst way possible.

pride marches june 1970 usa a year after stonewall, gay pride marches filled american streets; the traveler walked up sixth avenue and watched dignity move at the speed of people done asking permission. a year after stonewall, they marched —
new york, los angeles, chicago,
thousands in the streets, no masks, no shame.
the first pride marches.
i walked with the new york marchers
up sixth avenue, and the bystanders
didn't know whether to stare or cheer.
some did both.
from a bar raid to a parade in twelve months —
that's how fast dignity moves
when people stop asking permission.

black september september 1970 jordan jordan's army crushed palestinian fighters and expelled the plo; the traveler heard artillery in amman as arab brotherhood showed its tank-tread limits. king hussein's army turned its guns
on the palestinian fighters in jordan —
ten days of slaughter, thousands dead,
the plo expelled to lebanon.
i was in amman as the artillery spoke,
a civil war inside the arab cause.
black september: the month palestinians
learned that arab brotherhood
had limits, drawn in tank treads.
the plo left. the wound stayed.
the region's griefs, i keep finding,
are mostly family quarrels with armies.

a little coffee shop march 1971 usa starbucks opened as a tiny seattle coffee shop with a mermaid logo; the traveler bought a pound in '72 and smelled an empire starting in one good cup. pike place market, seattle —
three friends, a tiny store,
fresh-roasted beans and a mermaid logo.
starbucks. i bought a pound there in '72,
and the smell followed me down the street.
it was just a coffee shop then.
nobody imagined the green mermaid
would colonize every corner on earth.
but that's how empires start:
one good smell, one good cup,
and a dream bigger than the storefront.

the @ sign march 1971 usa tomlinson sent the first email and gave the @ sign its purpose; the traveler learned even he forgot the first message — but the little curled "a" became the century's hinge. ray tomlinson needed a symbol
to separate the user from the machine —
and picked the @, languishing on keyboards,
meaning "at" the price of.
the first email: forgettable test text,
sent to himself.
i met tomlinson years later; he couldn't remember
what the first message said.
nobody can. but that little curled "a"
became the most important character
of the century — the hinge
between every person and everywhere.

the pentagon papers june 1971 usa leaked pentagon papers revealed years of vietnam lies; the traveler read them in a 2 a.m. newsroom as the press fought nixon's gag order and won. daniel ellsberg photocopied seven thousand pages
of government lies about vietnam —
and the times and the post published them.
nixon tried to stop the presses.
the supreme court said no.
i read them in a newsroom at 2 a.m.,
the coffee cold, the truth hot:
they'd known it was unwinnable for years
and sent the boys anyway.
the press fought back that summer —
and won.

nixon kills gold august 1971 usa nixon cut the dollar from gold on a sunday night broadcast; the traveler watched old-timers shake their heads as money became a shared hallucination floating on faith. on a sunday night, nixon went on tv
and cut the dollar loose from gold —
"temporarily," he said.
fifty years later, still temporary.
i watched it in a bar, and the old-timers
shook their heads: money, unmoored,
floating on nothing but faith.
they were right. money floats free now,
a shared hallucination, rising and falling
on confidence alone.
the gold sat in fort knox, useless.
faith turned out to be the real reserve.

the chip that thinks november 1971 usa intel's 4004 put a computer on a fingernail-sized chip; the traveler held the giddy engineers' speck and watched the computer begin its journey into every pocket. intel's 4004: 2,300 transistors
on a chip the size of a fingernail —
a whole computer's brain, for thirty dollars.
i held one in santa clara,
this speck that could add and subtract
and follow instructions.
the engineers were giddy.
they knew. they absolutely knew.
every laptop, every phone, every rocket —
all of it, squeezed from this speck.
the computer left the room that day
and started its long journey into your pocket.

bangladesh is born december 1971 bangladesh bangladesh broke away in blood after a million dead; the traveler walked calcutta's refugee camps, then watched a scarred nation rise singing in its own language. east pakistan broke away in blood —
a million dead, ten million refugees,
indian tanks rolling in december —
and bangladesh was born, baptized in the worst
birth pangs of the century.
i walked the refugee camps in calcutta,
cholera and monsoon and endless lines.
then the surrender: 93,000 prisoners,
the largest since world war ii.
a nation rose from the killing fields,
scarred and singing.
bengalis finally had a country
that spoke their language.

nixon in china february 1972 china nixon shook mao's hand in beijing, parting the bamboo curtain; the traveler watched him wield chopsticks like a bomb-disposal man as the cold war's geometry changed. the most anti-communist president alive
shook mao's hand in beijing —
a week that shook the world, they said,
and for once the cliche fit.
i watched the banquet toasts on television,
nixon wielding chopsticks like a man
defusing a bomb.
the bamboo curtain parted.
ping-pong opened what diplomacy couldn't.
twenty-five years of silence ended
with a handshake and a toast —
and the cold war's geometry changed forever.

the break-in june 1972 usa burglars were caught at the watergate in a "third-rate burglary"; the traveler watched two young reporters pull the thread until the presidency unraveled. five burglars caught in the watergate,
tape on the door locks, wiretap gear —
a "third-rate burglary," the press secretary said.
i was in washington that summer,
and nobody thought it mattered.
two young reporters did.
woodward, bernstein, a garage source —
they pulled the thread, and the sweater unraveled:
dirty tricks, slush funds, the president's voice
on tape.
it started with tape on a door lock.
it ended with a resignation.

munich september 1972 germany terrorists murdered eleven israeli athletes at the munich olympics; the traveler heard jim mckay say "they're all gone" as terrorism found television and never let go. dawn at the olympic village —
black september terrorists took eleven israelis,
and the world watched the standoff live.
the rescue failed at furstenfeldbruck airfield.
all the hostages died.
i was in the press center when jim mckay said it:
"they're all gone."
the games went on, in shadow.
terrorism had found television —
and never let go.

cable's big bet november 1972 usa hbo launched with uncut movies and no ads; the traveler watched launch night in a manhattan bar as people laughed at paying for tv — then stopped laughing. hbo flickered on — home box office,
movies uncut and commercial-free,
beamed to a few thousand subscribers.
i watched the launch night in a manhattan bar:
a hockey game and a movie, no ads.
people laughed at the idea of paying for tv.
they stopped laughing within a decade.
cable's big bet paid off enormous —
three channels became three hundred,
and television never belonged
to the networks alone again.

pong november 1972 usa atari's pong blipped onto bar screens and the coin box overflowed; the traveler twisted the knob in sunnyvale as a bouncing dot built an industry. a blip, a bloop, two paddles —
atari's pong blinked onto a barroom screen
in sunnyvale, and the coin box overflowed
by closing time.
i played it that first week,
twisting the knob, drunk on simplicity.
the first video game the public ever loved.
nolan bushnell built an industry
out of a bouncing dot.
every billion-dollar game since —
every esports arena, every console war —
started with that blip.

the last footprints december 1972 usa the last moonwalkers left their bootprints in december 1972; the traveler watched the splashdown knowing the plaque still waits on the moon while we stayed home. cernan climbed the ladder last,
paused, and left the final bootprints —
then the lunar module rose,
and the moon went quiet.
apollo 17. the last moonwalkers.
i watched the splashdown on television,
and nobody said what we all felt:
we might not go back.
we haven't. fifty years of footprints
sitting in moondust, waiting.
they left a plaque: "we came in peace
for all mankind."
it's still there. we're still here.

roe v. wade january 1973 usa the court legalized abortion and ignited the culture war; the traveler stood outside as two crowds gathered, already shouting past each other into fifty years of division. seven to two: the court said
the constitution protects a woman's choice.
roe v. wade legalized abortion nationwide —
and the culture war ignited overnight.
i was outside the court that morning,
watching both crowds gather,
already shouting past each other.
fifty years of marching, praying, legislating —
the most contested sentence in american law.
whatever you believe about it,
that january morning split the country
into two americas that never reconciled.

peace with honor? january 1973 vietnam america signed its way out of vietnam with "peace with honor"; the traveler watched the troops fly out as the war ground on without them toward saigon's fall. kissinger shook hands in paris,
the papers were signed, the pows came home —
"peace with honor," they called it.
i watched the last american troops
fly out of saigon, and the honor
felt thin as the paper.
the war ground on without us.
two years later the tanks rolled in anyway.
we signed our way out
and called it peace.
the vietnamese kept dying,
and nobody called it anything.

the dark side march 1973 uk pink floyd's dark side of the moon began its fourteen-year chart run; the traveler dropped the needle and watched white light split into every color of the decade. a heartbeat, a cash register, a prism —
pink floyd's dark side of the moon
began its decades-long play.
i bought it the week it came out,
dropped the needle, and time bent.
it stayed on the charts for fourteen years.
fourteen years.
an album about madness, money, and mortality
became the soundtrack of half the planet.
the prism on the cover says it all:
white light in, every color out —
that's what the seventies did to us.

a house in orbit may 1973 usa skylab hosted america's first space-station crews in a converted rocket stage; the traveler toured the backup module and saw humanity keep an address above the sky. skylab went up — america's first space station,
a converted rocket stage, big as a house,
crews living in orbit for months.
i toured the backup module in houston,
floating through it in my mind:
a shower in zero-g, a window on the world.
the crews fixed it with a parasol —
a sunshade deployed by hand, in space.
ingenuity, orbiting.
it fell in '79, scattered over australia.
but for six years, humanity had an address
above the sky.

the october war october 1973 middle east egypt and syria attacked israel on yom kippur; the traveler heard tel aviv's sirens as the superpowers teetered at defcon 3 and the oil weapon loaded. yom kippur: egypt and syria struck —
tanks across the canal, jets over the golan —
and israel, caught praying, nearly broke.
i was in tel aviv as the sirens wailed,
reservists racing to the front in taxis.
the superpowers teetered: brezhnev threatened,
nixon went to defcon 3.
eighteen days. then the ceasefire.
israel survived. egypt regained its honor.
and the oil weapon was loaded —
the world was about to feel it.

the oil shock october 1973 middle east arab states cut oil shipments and gas lines snaked around the block; the traveler waited in a new jersey line as the world learned the desert held a lever. the arab states turned off the tap —
oil embargo, prices quadrupled,
gas lines snaking around american blocks.
i waited in one in new jersey,
odd-even rationing, tempers flaring,
a nation learning what dependence feels like.
the shock rewrote everything:
small cars, solar panels, speed limits,
the first whisper of energy independence.
the desert had a lever,
and the world learned it could be pulled.

the exorcist december 1973 usa the exorcist terrified audiences worldwide; the traveler stood in a georgetown line wrapping the block as horror grew up and priests debated a film like theology. a little girl's head spun,
pea soup flew, and audiences fainted —
the exorcist terrified the planet
like no film before it.
i saw it opening week in georgetown,
where it was filmed; the line wrapped the block,
people clutching rosaries.
horror grew up that winter.
it wasn't monsters anymore —
it was faith itself, possessed.
priests debated it. the vatican weighed in.
a horror film, discussed like theology.

hello, people march 1974 usa people magazine debuted with mia farrow on the cover; the traveler bought it at a newsstand and watched celebrity culture get the bible that would eat the world. time inc. launched people —
celebrity news, human interest,
mia farrow on the first cover.
i picked it up at a newsstand,
all glossy photos and short paragraphs.
it seemed harmless. it was the seed.
celebrity culture got its bible that march —
and within a generation,
the famous-for-being-famous,
the paparazzi, the whole glittering machine.
we stopped reading about the world
and started reading about the people
pretending to be the world.

the clay army march 1974 china farmers digging a well unearthed china's buried terracotta warriors; the traveler walked the pits at xi'an among thousands of patient stone faces staring east. farmers digging a well struck clay —
not water, but soldiers: thousands of them,
life-size, rank on rank, guarding an emperor
dead two thousand years.
i walked those pits at xi'an,
row after row of terracotta warriors,
each face different, each staring east.
qin shi huang took an army to the grave
and it waited, patient as stone,
for peasants to find it.
the dead, i keep learning,
are never quite done with us.

beep june 1974 usa a pack of gum became the first barcode scan in an ohio supermarket; the traveler heard the beep that rewired checkout, inventory, and modern retail. a pack of wrigley's gum in troy, ohio —
the first barcode scan. beep.
ten cents of gum, and the laser read it.
i was in that marsh supermarket,
and the cashier grinned at the sound.
checkout changed forever that beep:
inventory, prices, the whole humming
machinery of modern retail —
all from ten cents of gum
and a pattern of lines.

nixon resigns august 1974 usa watergate forced nixon's resignation; the traveler watched the farewell v-sign from the white house lawn as evidence, press, and law proved nobody is above it. he gave the v-sign on the white house lawn,
boarded the helicopter, and flew home in disgrace —
the first president to resign.
i watched the speech the night before,
the jowls, the "i am not a crook" echo.
watergate had done it: the tapes, the cover-up,
the saturday night massacre.
the system worked. barely.
a president forced out by evidence
and the press and the law —
proof, for one shining moment,
that nobody is above it.

the lion falls september 1974 ethiopia ethiopia's emperor was deposed by his own army; the traveler walked empty addis ababa halls as three thousand years of kingdom ended with an old man in a volkswagen. haile selassie — the lion of judah,
god to the rastafari, emperor for forty-four years —
deposed by his own army, led away in a volkswagen.
i was in addis ababa that week,
the palace empty, the lions in the zoo
still roaring for a master gone.
famine and war followed, the derg's red terror.
ancient ethiopia, three thousand years a kingdom,
ended with an old man in a beetle.

the cube 1974 ce hungary rubik's cube twisted onto shelves with 43 quintillion combinations; the traveler scrambled one in budapest while the next table solved it — every desk's 2 a.m. tormentor. erno rubik built a twisting puzzle
to teach his architecture students —
and couldn't solve it himself for a month.
the cube: 43 quintillion combinations,
six colors, one maddening click.
i scrambled one in a budapest cafe,
and the table next to me finished it
while i was still on white.
it conquered the planet —
every desk, every backpack,
every frustrated genius at 2 a.m.

two kids and a computer april 1975 usa gates and allen founded microsoft in albuquerque; the traveler met the two kids coding through the night on their bet that software would become king. gates and allen — two kids from seattle,
nineteen and twenty-two —
founded micro-soft to sell a basic
for the altair kit.
i met them in albuquerque that year,
all hair and hurry, coding through the night.
software becomes king, they said.
everyone laughed. they were right.
from a rented office to the biggest company
on earth — built on the bet
that the program matters more
than the machine.

saigon falls april 1975 vietnam helicopters lifted off the saigon embassy roof as tanks crashed the palace gates; the traveler watched from a nearby rooftop as twenty years ended in confusion. the helicopters lifted off the embassy roof,
pushing the last ones out over the sea —
tanks crashed the palace gates by noon.
saigon fell. vietnam united under hanoi.
i watched it from a rooftop nearby,
the thump of rotors, the panic below.
twenty years, 58,000 americans,
millions of vietnamese —
for this morning.
the war ended the way it began:
in confusion, and far from home.

jaws june 1975 usa jaws emptied the beaches on two notes and birthed the summer blockbuster; the traveler sat in a screaming opening-weekend crowd as a 27-year-old spielberg rewrote hollywood. two notes. duh-duh.
a shark emptied the beaches,
and the summer blockbuster was born.
i saw jaws opening weekend,
the audience screaming, the lines for weeks.
spielberg — twenty-seven years old —
invented the modern movie:
big, loud, everywhere at once.
nobody swam that summer.
everybody went to the movies.
hollywood learned the formula
and never forgot it.

the handshake in space july 1975 space american and soviet ships docked and enemies shook hands in orbit; the traveler watched live as detente floated in zero gravity above a twice-nearly-destroyed planet. an american apollo docked with a soviet soyuz —
the hatch opened, and stafford and leonov
shook hands in orbit, 140 miles up.
i watched it live, and the symbolism
was almost too much: enemies, shaking hands,
above a planet they'd nearly destroyed twice.
detente, in zero gravity.
it didn't last — nothing in the cold war did —
but for one orbit, humanity was one crew.

live from new york october 1975 usa saturday night live premiered with its gang of twenty-somethings; the traveler sat in the first-season audience as comedy got dangerous, live, and unforgiving. "live from new york, it's saturday night!"
a gang of twenty-somethings —
belushi, aykroyd, radner —
took over late-night tv and made comedy dangerous.
i was in the studio audience that first season,
and the chaos was the point.
they mocked presidents, priests, and sponsors,
sometimes in the same sketch.
fifty years it's been running.
comedy's boot camp, america's mirror —
live, unedited, unforgiving.

the forgotten invasion december 1975 east timor indonesia seized east timor and the world looked away through twenty-four years of dying; the traveler filed stories nobody printed and learned the world chooses what to notice. indonesia invaded east timor —
tanks, paratroopers, a quarter of the population dead
over twenty-four years —
and the world looked away.
i was one of the few who went,
filing stories nobody printed.
the un condemned. nobody acted.
oil and alliances mattered more.
east timor bled in the dark
while the cameras pointed elsewhere.
remember this when they tell you
the world always notices.
it doesn't. it chooses.

apple is born april 1976 usa two steves started apple in a los altos garage on april fool's day; the traveler breathed the soldering smoke of fifty circuit boards and impossible optimism. two steves in a los altos garage —
wozniak's circuit board, jobs's reality distortion —
apple computer company, founded on april fool's day.
i visited that garage, all soldering smoke
and impossible optimism.
they sold fifty boards to a byte shop.
fifty.
from that garage to the most valuable company
in human history —
built on the belief that computers
should be beautiful.

two hundred candles july 1976 usa america turned two hundred with tall ships and fireworks; the traveler sailed the harbor parade as a wounded nation blew out its candles grinning. america turned two hundred —
tall ships in new york harbor,
fireworks over every town,
a nation throwing itself a birthday party.
i sailed with the parade of ships,
canvas everywhere, horns sounding.
bicentennial fever: everyone suddenly
into colonial costumes and history.
for all its wounds — vietnam fresh,
watergate fresher — the country
blew out the candles grinning.
two hundred years. still standing.
still arguing. still here.

footprints on mars july 1976 usa viking landed and sent the first photos from mars; the traveler cheered at mission control as humanity stood on another planet by robot proxy. viking 1 touched down on chryse planitia —
and the first photo from the surface of mars
came back: rocks, dust, a pink sky.
i was at mission control for the landing,
and the cheer shook the building.
another planet. we were standing on it —
by robot proxy, but standing.
the photos showed a desert waiting.
forty years later we're still staring at it,
still planning the trip.
mars waits. it's good at that.

the earth shakes tangshan july 1976 china an earthquake flattened tangshan, killing hundreds of thousands; the traveler walked ruins where rescuers dug with bare hands and pride refused foreign help. 3:42 a.m.: the earth convulsed —
tangshan flattened in seconds,
an industrial city become a graveyard.
hundreds of thousands dead —
the century's worst quake by toll.
i walked the ruins days later,
rescue teams digging with bare hands,
the dust never settling.
china, in its closed years,
refused most foreign help.
pride, even in rubble.
the dead deserved better
than politics.

mao is gone september 1976 china mao died and china exhaled after decades of campaigns; the traveler filed past the crystal coffin in beijing as a million mourners breathed out. the chairman died — mao zedong,
the peasant's son who remade china
and broke it, both at once.
i was in beijing for the mourning,
a million people filing past the crystal coffin,
some weeping, some just... exhaling.
ten years of cultural revolution,
thirty years of campaigns.
china exhaled that september.
what came next — the opening, the boom —
was built on the silence he left.

rocky november 1976 usa a nobody boxer went the distance and underdogs cheered; the traveler stood with a roaring theater as stallone's three-day script told broke, tired america to get up. a nobody boxer from philadelphia,
a shot at the champ, fifteen rounds —
he loses the decision and wins everything.
i saw rocky in a packed theater,
and when he went the distance,
the audience stood and roared.
stallone wrote it in three days,
shot it in twenty-eight.
the underdog's anthem for all time.
america needed that story in '76 —
broke, tired, post-watergate.
rocky said: get up. go the distance.

roots january 1977 usa the roots miniseries gripped america for eight nights; the traveler watched the finale in atlanta as a grandmother whispered "that's us" and slavery became a family story. for eight nights, america watched —
kunta kinte, the middle passage,
the lash, the generations —
and the nation confronted its past.
i watched the finale with a black family
in atlanta; the grandmother wept quietly,
saying "that's us, that's us."
a hundred million viewers.
roots did what textbooks couldn't:
made slavery a family story,
told around the national television fire.

a galaxy far, far away may 1977 usa star wars premiered and movies became myth; the traveler stood in grauman's opening-day line as a star destroyer rumbled overhead and the audience gasped as one. a farm boy, a princess, a smuggler,
a wizard with a laser sword —
star wars premiered, and movies became myth.
i was in line opening day at grauman's,
the crowd buzzing like a hive.
when the star destroyer rumbled overhead,
the audience gasped as one.
lucas had bottled joseph campbell
and sold it with popcorn.
cinema's campfire story —
told ever since, in every galaxy.

the apple ii june 1977 usa apple's ready-made computer plugged into home tvs; the traveler carried one home like a newborn as living rooms went digital one beige box at a time. a beige box that plugged into your tv —
the apple ii, ready-made, no soldering required.
i bought one of the first,
carried it home like a newborn.
visicalc came later, and the offices fell.
but that june, it was just a beautiful machine
that beeped and blinked in your living room.
homes went digital that summer —
one beige box at a time.

the king of rock'n'roll dies august 1977 usa elvis died at forty-two; the traveler drove to flower-buried graceland gates as the world learned even kings are mortal — and the king never really left. forty-two years old, found on the bathroom floor —
elvis, the king, gone.
i drove to graceland that week,
and the gates were buried in flowers,
fans weeping like family.
he'd been the future in '56 —
by '77 he was a beautiful ruin.
the world got the message:
even kings are mortal.
graceland became a shrine.
the king left the building —
and never really left.

the golden record september 1977 usa voyager launched carrying earth's sounds on a golden record; the traveler watched it ride into the dark — still flying, still carrying our songs to the stars. voyager launched carrying a golden record —
greetings in 55 languages, whale songs,
chuck berry, a baby's laugh —
earth's mixtape for the stars.
i watched the launch at the cape,
that golden disc riding into the dark.
it still flies. it's in interstellar space now,
the farthest human-made thing.
if anyone finds it, they'll hear us:
we were here, we sang, we laughed,
we sent our best.

disco inferno december 1977 usa saturday night fever ignited disco worldwide; the traveler stood in a studio 54 corner watching beautiful people dance like the world was ending beautifully. saturday night fever: white suits,
a light-up dance floor, the bee gees wailing —
and disco inferno'd across the planet.
i went to studio 54 once, stood in the corner,
watched beautiful people dance like the world
was ending beautifully.
it was glorious. it was ridiculous.
it burned out in two years —
but for one shining moment,
everyone in america owned a white suit
and knew the hustle.

grease june 1978 usa grease sang the fifties back with summer nights and thunderbirds; the traveler sang along at a drive-in as nostalgia became rocket fuel with a soundtrack. summer nights, thunderbirds,
travolta's hips and newton-john's transformation —
grease sang the fifties back to life.
i saw it at a drive-in, windows down,
the whole lot singing along.
it was nostalgia as rocket fuel:
the fifties, scrubbed clean and set to music.
a generation that never lived it
fell in love with it anyway.
that's the trick of the past —
it's always better with a soundtrack.

i hate mondays june 1978 usa garfield the cat debuted in the funnies, hating mondays and loving lasagna; the traveler clipped the first strips of the deepest philosophy — a cat nap. a fat orange cat who hates mondays,
loves lasagna, and kicks a dog off the table —
garfield debuted in the funnies.
i clipped the first strips,
this gloriously lazy cat saying
what every office worker felt.
davis drew the perfect anti-hero:
selfish, sleepy, honest.
lasagna sales rose. mondays stayed hated.
forty years of strips —
proof that the deepest philosophy
is a cat nap.

the test-tube baby july 1978 uk louise brown was born through ivf, the first test-tube baby; the traveler stood outside the oldham hospital as infertility met hope in a petri dish. louise brown — the first ivf baby,
conceived in a dish in oldham,
born screaming and perfect.
i was outside the hospital that night,
the press pack buzzing.
the vatican frowned. the scientists glowed.
infertility met hope in a petri dish.
millions of test-tube babies since —
each one a small miracle of persistence.
it started with louise, and a dish,
and two doctors who wouldn't give up.

peace at camp david september 1978 middle east egypt and israel signed peace after thirteen days at camp david; the traveler watched the exhausted leaders emerge like survivors and learned peace costs peacemakers everything. thirteen days in the maryland woods —
carter, sadat, begin, no ties, no sleep —
and two enemies signed a peace.
i was outside the gates when they emerged,
blinking, shaking hands like survivors.
egypt got sinai. israel got peace
with its strongest foe.
sadat would be assassinated for it.
begin would be haunted by it.
peace, i learned at camp david,
costs the peacemakers everything
and the people nothing — which is why
it's always worth it.

the kool-aid november 1978 guyana nine hundred died in jonestown at a cult leader's order; the traveler flew in with recovery teams to the worst thing he'd ever seen — and a phrase for blind obedience. nine hundred and nine people —
men, women, children —
drank the poison in jonestown
at one man's order.
i flew in with the recovery teams,
and the jungle clearing was the worst thing
i've ever seen. the worst.
jim jones preached love and built a graveyard.
a cult's horror shocked the world —
and gave the language a phrase
for blind obedience.
don't drink the kool-aid.
nine hundred people did.

china opens the door december 1978 china deng launched market reforms and china woke up; the traveler stood in shenzhen when it was fishing boats and watched the cranes rise like bamboo. deng xiaoping — purged twice, back again —
cracked the door: markets, zones,
"to get rich is glorious."
i was in shenzhen when it was still fishing boats,
and watched the cranes rise like bamboo.
china woke up that december.
four decades later, the fishing village
is a megacity, and the world runs
on what those cranes built.
one small man's pragmatism
outperformed every ideology.

the shah falls january 1979 iran the shah fled and khomeini returned to a roaring iran; the traveler stood at the airport as 2,500 years of throne ended in weeks and decades of enmity began. the shah fled tehran in tears —
and khomeini flew home from paris
to a roaring million.
i was at the airport for the return,
the old man's black robes,
the crowd like an ocean.
the peacock throne, 2,500 years old,
gone in weeks.
iran traded a king for a theocracy.
the hostages, the war, the decades of enmity —
all of it started on that runway,
with a roar.

the meltdown that wasn't march 1979 usa a pennsylvania reactor half-melted but containment held; the traveler sat in jammed harrisburg evacuation traffic and learned fear is the real fallout, with the longest half-life. three mile island: a valve stuck,
the core half-melted, the nation held its breath —
and the containment held.
the meltdown that wasn't.
i was in harrisburg that week,
the evacuation routes jammed,
a state learning the word "meltdown."
no one died. but nuclear power
died a little that week in america —
no new plants for decades.
fear, i learned, is the real fallout.
it has the longest half-life.

in space no one can hear you may 1979 uk alien stalked the screen and horror went cosmic; the traveler sat in a frozen london audience as ripley became a hero and space became a haunted house. a commercial spaceship, a distress call,
and something with acid for blood
hunting the crew through the dark.
alien stalked the screen —
and horror went cosmic.
i saw it in london, the audience
frozen, ripley the last one standing.
scott made space a haunted house,
and weaver made the final girl
a hero for the ages.
in space no one can hear you scream.
in the cinema, everyone did.

music in your pocket july 1979 japan sony's walkman put stereo on hips worldwide; the traveler walked tokyo in his own soundtrack as public space went private, one headphone at a time. sony's walkman: a cassette player,
headphones, no speaker —
music for one, on your hip.
i bought one in tokyo that summer,
and the city changed around me:
everyone walking in their own soundtrack,
alone together.
the world got headphones that july.
public space became private.
it was the first step toward everyone
staring at their own small screen —
but it started with a song,
just for you.

444 days november 1979 iran militants seized the us embassy in tehran and held hostages 444 days; the traveler covered it from outside the walls as a presidency broke and a nation learned the word hostage. students stormed the us embassy in tehran —
fifty-two americans taken,
blindfolded, paraded, held.
444 days.
i covered it from outside the walls,
the crowds chanting, the hostages' families
on television every night.
it broke carter's presidency.
it taught america a new word: hostage.
and when they finally flew home,
the whole country wept at the runway.
444 days. count them.

the wall november 1979 uk pink floyd's wall rose brick by brick across stadium stages; the traveler watched it built and torn down nightly in london — some walls only fall from inside. pink floyd built a wall —
brick by brick, song by song,
a rock opera about isolation
so massive it needed a stadium.
i saw the tour in london,
the wall rising across the stage,
the plane crashing, the teacher screaming.
"we don't need no education."
rock got its monument that winter:
a wall you could hear.
waters tore it down at the end,
every night.
some walls, the music says,
only fall from inside.

the bear invades december 1979 afghanistan soviet tanks rolled into afghanistan on christmas eve for a ten-year quagmire; the traveler crossed the broken-tooth mountains and watched an empire bleed white. christmas eve: soviet tanks rolled
over the afghan border —
a "limited contingent" that stayed ten years.
i crossed in with the mujahideen later,
the mountains like broken teeth,
stingers in the passes.
moscow's vietnam: 15,000 soviet dead,
a million afghans, an empire bled white.
the quagmire began that christmas.
it ended empires — first the soviet one,
then, decades later, another's illusions.

the mountain blows may 1980 usa mount st. helens erupted sideways, flattening 230 square miles; the traveler watched the sky turn black at noon as ash fell like gray snow on live television. 8:32 a.m.: the whole north face
of mount st. helens slid away,
and the mountain blew sideways —
a lateral blast that flattened 230 square miles.
i was thirty miles out when it went,
the sky turning black at noon,
ash falling like gray snow.
fifty-seven dead. rivers of mud.
the most violent eruption in american history —
and it happened on live television,
a mountain performing its own autopsy.

news never sleeps june 1980 usa cnn launched with twenty-four-hour news; the traveler stood in the nervous atlanta newsroom as the world got faster, louder, and endless — the scroll before the scroll. ted turner launched cnn —
news, twenty-four hours a day,
when the networks did thirty minutes.
everyone laughed. then they watched.
i was in the atlanta newsroom that first night,
the anchors nervous, the phones ringing.
news never sleeps now.
the world got faster, louder, endless —
a crisis in every hour, live.
turner invented the scroll
before the scroll existed.

pac-man july 1980 japan a yellow dot munched ghosts through neon mazes; the traveler fed quarters into a tokyo cabinet, hypnotized, as a pizza-inspired hero taught games to have personality. a yellow dot with a missing slice —
toru iwatani designed him around a pizza —
munching ghosts through a neon maze.
wakawaka. i fed quarters into the cabinet
in a tokyo arcade, hypnotized.
pac-man exploded: the first game character,
the first mascot, arcade fever worldwide.
a pizza-inspired dot ate the decade's quarters
and taught the world that games
could have personality.

the boycotted games july 1980 ussr america skipped the moscow olympics over afghanistan; the traveler watched the half-empty opening ceremony as the cold war played on fields and sport lost to politics. carter said stay home —
and america skipped the moscow olympics
over afghanistan.
sixty-five nations out.
i watched the opening ceremony anyway,
the doves, the misha bear,
half the world missing.
the soviets won everything unopposed —
and it meant nothing.
the cold war played on fields that summer,
and sport lost to politics.
los angeles would return the favor
in four years.

solidarity august 1980 poland polish workers founded solidarity in the gdansk shipyard; the traveler breathed welding smoke and singing as ten million members widened the crack that would split the bloc. the gdansk shipyard struck —
and lech walesa climbed the fence
with a union charter in his pocket.
solidarity: ten million members,
the first free union in the soviet bloc.
i was in the shipyard that august,
the smell of welding, the singing.
the communists signed, then cracked down —
martial law, arrests.
but the crack had widened.
nine years later it split the bloc open.
it started with shipyard workers
who wanted a union.

imagine, silenced december 1980 usa john lennon was shot outside the dakota; the traveler stood in central park at midnight as thousands sang "imagine" in the cold for the dreamer of peace. outside the dakota, new york —
five shots, and john lennon fell.
i was two blocks away when the news broke,
and central park filled by midnight:
thousands singing "imagine" in the cold.
the dreamer of peace, murdered.
the world sang in grief that week —
radios playing nothing but beatles for days.
"imagine all the people."
we did. we stood in the park
and imagined, through tears.

the hostages come home january 1981 iran after 444 days the hostages flew home to yellow ribbons; the traveler watched families sprint across the tarmac as a nation exhaled in pure joy. 444 days — and they flew home
on reagan's inauguration day,
timed to spite carter to the last.
i was at the airbase when the plane landed,
families sprinting across the tarmac,
a nation exhaling at once.
yellow ribbons everywhere.
they'd been blindfolded, beaten, paraded —
and they walked off that plane
with their heads high.
america wept. for once,
the tears were pure joy.

the reusable rocket april 1981 usa columbia flew as the first reusable spaceship; the traveler felt the launch roar like a second heart as humanity got a thirty-year pickup truck to the stars. columbia rose on pillars of fire —
the first reusable spaceship,
a truck to orbit and back.
i watched the launch from the causeway,
the roar in my chest like a second heart.
thirty years of shuttles followed:
stations built, telescopes fixed,
teachers and senators flown.
two were lost — challenger, columbia —
and the grief was national.
but for three decades, humanity
had a pickup truck to the stars.

a new plague june 1981 usa doctors named a mysterious killer that became aids; the traveler walked san francisco's castro as posters multiplied and friends vanished — and the dying taught the living to fight. the cdc's little bulletin noted it first —
five young men, a rare pneumonia,
in los angeles.
then more. then everywhere.
aids: the new plague, and the world
was slow to name it, slower to fight it.
i walked the castro in those years,
the posters multiplying, the friends vanishing.
a generation scarred.
it took activism, fury, and science —
but the dying taught the living
how to fight.

the fairy-tale wedding july 1981 uk charles wed diana before a billion viewers; the traveler stood in the hopeful crowds outside st. paul's on the july morning the world believed in princesses. st. paul's cathedral, a billion watching —
lady diana spencer, twenty years old,
married the prince of wales
in the wedding of the century.
i was in the crowds outside,
the hats, the flags, the hope.
it looked like a fairy tale.
it wasn't. we know that now.
but that july morning, the world
wanted to believe in princesses —
and for one day, it did.

i want my mtv august 1981 usa mtv launched playing videos all day; the traveler watched in a bar as pop went visual and the world started listening to music with its eyes. "video killed the radio star" —
the first video mtv ever played,
and pop went visual.
i watched the launch in a bar,
the vjs grinning, the videos flickering.
music television: all day, all night,
a new language of three-minute dreams.
it made stars overnight
and broke them by lunch.
the image became the music.
we stopped listening with our ears
and started with our eyes.

the blue box august 1981 usa ibm's pc legitimized the personal computer; the traveler watched nervous suits and thrilled hackers as offices digitized by the million and computing grew up. ibm — big blue itself —
blessed the personal computer:
the ibm pc, open architecture,
a beige box that meant business.
i was at the launch; the suits
were nervous, the hackers thrilled.
ibm legitimized the pc overnight —
offices digitized by the million.
the clone wars followed.
microsoft rode it to the stars.
one beige box from the bluest of chips —
and computing grew up.

the falklands april 1982 south atlantic britain and argentina fought over the windswept falklands; the traveler covered it from a press ship in gunmetal seas as the empire fought its last colonial war. argentina seized the windswept islands —
and thatcher sent the fleet
eight thousand miles to take them back.
seventy-four days: ships sunk,
men frozen, goose green, mount tumbledown.
i covered it from a press ship,
the south atlantic gray as gunmetal.
britain won. the junta fell.
the empire's last colonial war —
fought over sheep farms and pride,
eight thousand miles from home.

phone home june 1982 usa e.t. melted hearts worldwide; the traveler wept in a theater of children as bicycles flew across the moon and childhood believed in magic again. a wrinkled alien with a glowing finger,
two kids on bicycles silhouetted
against the moon —
e.t. melted every heart on earth.
i saw it with a theater full of children,
and when he said "home,"
the whole place wept.
spielberg's fairy tale:
the alien just wanted his family.
so did we, it turned out.
bicycles flew across the moon that summer,
and childhood believed in magic again.

rain and neon june 1982 usa blade runner's rainy neon future divided critics and invented cyberpunk; the traveler sat in a half-empty theater watching the most influential sci-fi film ever flop — then not. los angeles, 2019: endless rain,
neon, replicants dreaming of electric sheep —
blade runner divided the critics
and invented cyberpunk.
i saw it opening weekend,
half-empty theater, rain on the marquee.
it flopped. then it didn't —
it became the most influential sci-fi film ever,
every future since wearing its coat.
scott dreamed the future in neon and rain.
we're living in it now.

the future, sponsored october 1982 usa epcot opened with corporate pavilions and a geodesic sphere; the traveler ate around the "world" in an afternoon as the sponsored future turned out to be prophecy. epcot opened — disney's experimental prototype
community of tomorrow, sort of:
a gleaming geodesic sphere,
pavilions sponsored by corporations,
the future with a gift shop.
i walked it opening week,
eating around the "world"
in an afternoon.
it was corporate, corny, wonderful.
the future, sponsored by exxon.
we laughed then.
the joke, it turns out, was prophecy.

thriller november 1982 usa michael jackson's thriller became the best-selling album of all time; the traveler levitated at a new york listening party when the bassline hit. michael jackson — twenty-four years old —
dropped thriller, and the world stopped.
billie jean, beat it, the title track's
graveyard dance: the best-selling album
of all time, forty million and counting.
i was at a listening party in new york,
and when the bassline hit,
the room levitated.
quincy jones's masterpiece,
michael's moonwalk moment.
pop's peak, frozen in vinyl —
the eighties' beating heart.

a heart of plastic december 1982 usa a permanent artificial heart beat inside barney clark's chest for 112 days; the traveler stood outside the hospital as the soul's seat got a warranty. in salt lake city, surgeons replaced
a dying man's heart with a plastic one —
the jarvik-7, whirring in his chest.
barney clark lived 112 days
on a machine heart.
i stood outside the hospital,
reporters everywhere, the ethics debates raging.
a permanent artificial heart beat
inside a man's chest.
it wasn't perfect. it was a beginning.
the heart — the ancient seat of the soul —
now came with a warranty.

the mouse goes mainstream january 1983 usa apple's lisa brought the mouse to offices; the traveler pushed the little gray box around in cupertino as pointing began replacing typing. apple's lisa brought the mouse to offices —
ten thousand dollars, a little gray box
you pushed around to point at things.
i demoed one in cupertino,
moving that cursor like magic.
pointing replaced typing, slowly.
the lisa flopped — too dear —
but the mac was coming.
the mouse won.
your hand, extended into the machine —
that's what it was, all along.

shields in space march 1983 usa reagan proposed space-based missile shields; the traveler watched washington split between thrilled hawks and aghast scientists as the arms race threatened orbit. reagan proposed it on television —
space-based shields to stop soviet missiles,
lasers and mirrors in orbit.
star wars, the critics called it.
i watched the speech in washington,
the hawks thrilled, the scientists aghast.
the arms race went orbital that night —
or threatened to.
it never quite worked.
but it scared moscow into spending
it didn't have —
and some say that spending
ended the cold war.

sally rides june 1983 usa sally ride became america's first woman in space aboard challenger; the traveler heard history's edge in the launch roar as she proved the stars don't check chromosomes. challenger carried sally ride —
physicist, calm, brilliant —
america's first woman in space.
i watched the launch,
the crowd's roar with an edge of history.
twenty years after tereshkova,
america finally sent a woman up.
ride operated the robot arm,
ran the experiments, came home a hero —
and spent her life getting girls
into science.
the stars, she proved again,
don't check chromosomes.

the lost airliner september 1983 ussr the soviets shot down korean air lines flight 007, killing 269; the traveler heard the news in tokyo as disbelief curdled to horror in the cold war's hottest autumn. korean air lines flight 007
drifted into soviet airspace —
and a fighter shot it down.
269 dead, including a us congressman.
i heard the news in tokyo,
the disbelief curdling to horror.
the soviets lied, then admitted.
reagan called it barbarism.
the world gasped as one.
a lost airliner, a trigger-happy empire —
and the cold war's hottest autumn
in twenty years.

the grenada invasion october 1983 caribbean america invaded tiny grenada in the cold war's smallest war; the traveler landed with the press corps as students waved and the island went back to nutmeg and beaches. america invaded grenada —
a island of 100,000 people,
students, a new airport, cuban workers —
operation urgent fury.
i landed with the press corps,
the fighting mostly over,
the students waving.
the cold war's smallest war:
nine days, nineteen americans dead.
reagan called it a rescue.
critics called it a message to moscow.
grenada went back to nutmeg and beaches.
history barely noticed.

the scare november 1983 europe nato's able archer war game nearly triggered real soviet retaliation; the traveler read the declassified files years later with cold hands — the closest call nobody knew. nato ran a war game — able archer —
so realistic the soviets thought
it was the real thing.
missiles readied. bombers fueled.
we were minutes from the end,
and nobody in the west knew.
i learned this years later,
reading the declassified files,
my hands cold.
the world nearly ended in november 1983
because of a rehearsal.
the closest call of the cold war —
and we didn't know for decades.

the hammer throw january 1984 usa apple's "1984" ad aired once during the super bowl; the traveler watched the stadium gasp as a hammer shattered big brother's face and marketing went epic. third quarter, super bowl xviii —
a woman sprints down an aisle,
hurls a hammer at big brother's face,
and the screen explodes.
apple's "1984" ad aired once.
once. i watched it live,
the stadium crowd gasping.
ridley scott directed it;
the macintosh was coming.
marketing went epic that night —
an ad as art, as event, as myth.
ibm never saw it coming.
neither did we.

hello, macintosh january 1984 usa the macintosh's smiling face brought computers to the rest of us; the traveler unboxed one in january as windows, icons, and a mouse won the future if not the market. it smiled at you. literally —
the mac's smiling face on boot,
a computer that said hello.
i unboxed one in january,
this beige miracle with a mouse,
windows, icons — the rest of us
could finally use a computer.
$2,495. worth every penny.
the mac didn't win the market.
it won the future:
every computer since
is just a mac, refined.

purple rain june 1984 usa prince's purple rain peaked and pop got its genius; the traveler watched the detroit tour as five-foot-two of pure voltage bent the laws of physics. prince — five foot two of pure voltage —
released purple rain, the album and the film,
and pop got its genius.
i saw the tour in detroit,
the purple suit, the guitar solos
that bent the laws of physics.
he played everything, wrote everything,
out-funked and out-rocked everyone.
the eighties had michael's crown
and prince's scepter.
purple reigned that summer —
and honestly, ever since.

the games go on july 1984 usa los angeles hosted a sunny, soviet-free olympics; the traveler covered carl lewis's four golds at a party with half the guests missing, dancing anyway. los angeles hosted the olympics —
soviet-free, sun-drenched,
carl lewis winning four golds,
mary lou sticking the vault.
i covered those games,
the smog and the splendor.
the boycott tit-for-tat meant
half the world stayed home —
but la turned a profit,
the first to do it right.
the games went on, sunny and strange —
a party with half the guests missing,
dancing anyway.

the assassination october 1984 india indira gandhi was killed by her own guards; the traveler watched delhi burn in revenge pogroms as the subcontinent's old demons fed again. her sikh bodyguards opened fire
in the garden of her own residence —
indira gandhi, india's iron lady,
cut down by the men sworn to protect her.
i was in delhi that week.
the city burned for days after:
thousands of sikhs murdered in revenge.
the assassination was political.
the pogrom was pure hate.
india's wound, reopened.
the subcontinent's old demons —
still hungry, still fed.

the poison cloud december 1984 india gas leaked in bhopal, killing thousands in their sleep; the traveler walked hospital corridors of the blinded as the world's worst industrial disaster settled for coins. midnight in bhopal: a gas leak,
methyl isocyanate, a cloud
settling over sleeping slums.
thousands died that night,
gasping. thousands more since.
i walked those streets a week later,
the hospital corridors full of the blinded,
the union carbide plant looming.
the world's worst industrial disaster —
and the compensation was coins.
the poison cloud settled.
the company settled cheaper.

we are the world january 1985 usa pop stars sang "we are the world" for famine relief; the traveler stood outside the studio as limos arrived and the simplest song fed thousands. one night, one studio —
forty-five stars, one song for famine relief.
michael and lionel wrote it;
everyone from dylan to diana ross sang it.
i was outside a&m studios that night,
the limos, the secrecy.
"we are the world" sold millions,
fed thousands.
pop's conscience, on vinyl.
cynics scoffed. the hungry ate.
sometimes the simplest song
is the truest one.

gorbachev march 1985 ussr a young reformer took the kremlin with glasnost and perestroika; the traveler watched the un-soviet candor of the man who meant to save the system and ended it. a young reformer took the kremlin —
fifty-four, energetic, with a birthmark
like a map of the future.
gorbachev: glasnost, perestroika,
openness, restructuring.
i watched his first press conferences,
the jokes, the un-soviet candor.
the old guard shifted uneasily.
he meant to save the system.
he ended it instead —
the most consequential accident
in modern history.

the hole in the sky may 1985 antarctica scientists found a hole in the ozone; the traveler read the wound-like graphs as the world actually acted — banning cfcs and proving we can fix what we break. british scientists found it —
a hole in the ozone over antarctica,
cfcs eating the sky's sunscreen.
i read the nature paper in a library,
the graphs like a wound.
the world actually acted:
the montreal protocol, cfcs banned,
the hole slowly healing.
the one environmental crisis
humanity fixed.
proof, filed away and forgotten,
that we can do it —
when we decide to.

back to the future july 1985 usa a delorean hit eighty-eight miles per hour and time travel went mainstream; the traveler roared with the opening-weekend crowd at the clock tower as nostalgia met physics. a delorean, eighty-eight miles per hour,
1.21 gigawatts —
and marty mcfly went back to 1955.
i saw it opening weekend,
the audience roaring at the clock tower.
time travel went mainstream that summer:
every kid wanted a delorean,
every adult wanted a redo.
zemeckis bottled nostalgia and physics
and sold it with a grin.
great scott.

live aid july 1985 uk two stadiums, one cause — live aid fed the hungry; the traveler stood among 72,000 wembley voices as freddie mercury commanded like a general of joy. two stadiums — wembley and philadelphia —
one cause, sixteen hours,
queen stealing the show in twenty minutes.
i was at wembley, 72,000 voices,
freddie commanding like a general of joy.
live aid: rock fed the hungry,
$127 million for famine relief.
the satellite beamed it to a billion.
music's finest hour —
proof that a guitar can be
a bread truck.

it's-a me, mario september 1985 japan super mario bros. revived video games; the traveler played 1-1 in a tokyo arcade as a red-overalled plumber became the most famous fictional character on earth. a plumber in red overalls
jumped over the video game crash —
super mario bros., and nintendo
revived the industry single-handedly.
i played it in a tokyo arcade,
that first 1-1, the mushrooms, the pipes.
mario became king: the most famous
fictional character on earth.
miyamoto's genius: joy as design.
forty years of jumping —
and we're still not tired of it.

the challenger january 1986 usa the shuttle broke apart on live tv, killing seven including a teacher; the traveler watched from the press site as the sky said no and the nation's heart broke with it. seventy-three seconds.
i watched it live from the press site —
the plume, the silence,
the two trails corkscrewing apart.
seven astronauts, including christa mcauliffe,
a teacher, gone on live tv
as schoolchildren watched.
the shuttle broke apart
and the nation's heart with it.
we mourned. we investigated.
we flew again — because they would have wanted it.
but january 28th stays frozen:
the day the sky said no.

people power february 1986 philippines millions ousted marcos in the philippines' people power revolution; the traveler marched on edsa as nuns with rosaries faced tanks and won by showing up. millions filled edsa —
nuns with rosaries facing tanks,
cory aquino's yellow against marcos's guns.
i marched in that sea of people,
the tanks stopping, the soldiers defecting.
people power: the dictator fled
by helicopter, democracy returned.
no shots that mattered.
just bodies, prayers, and refusal.
the world watched a revolution
won by showing up.

chernobyl april 1986 ussr reactor 4 exploded at chernobyl, drifting radiation across europe; the traveler walked the abandoned schoolbooks of pripyat as the lie poisoned the empire. 1:23 a.m.: reactor 4 exploded —
a pillar of fire over pripyat,
radiation drifting across europe.
i reported from the exclusion zone later,
the abandoned schoolbooks,
the ferris wheel never ridden.
the soviets lied for days.
the geiger counters didn't.
chernobyl poisoned the land
and the lie poisoned the empire:
glasnost met its test here,
and the truth got out anyway.

top gun may 1986 usa top gun's fighter jets and volleyball defined the eighties; the traveler cheered the flybys in a packed theater as the navy's recruiting soared on pure adrenaline. fighter jets, volleyball,
"danger zone" —
top gun made the eighties
officially awesome.
i saw it in a packed theater,
the audience cheering the flybys.
tony scott bottled testosterone
and sold it by the bucket.
the navy's recruiting soared.
cinema's purest adrenaline —
all style, all speed, all america,
flying into the danger zone
with a grin.

hello, oprah august 1986 usa oprah's show went national; the traveler watched the first broadcast as a woman who listened like nobody ever had began hosting america's therapy session. a chicago talk show went national —
oprah winfrey, and daytime tv
found its queen.
i watched the first national broadcast,
this woman listening like nobody
had ever listened before.
she'd build an empire on empathy:
books, souls, whole lives changed
between commercials.
from mississippi poverty
to the most influential woman in media —
oprah didn't just host a show.
she hosted america's therapy session.

the almost deal october 1986 iceland reagan and gorbachev nearly ended the arms race in reykjavik; the traveler waited in arctic wind outside hofdi house as the deal died and the trust was born. reykjavik: reagan and gorbachev,
alone but for translators,
nearly abolished nuclear weapons.
i waited outside hofdi house
in the arctic wind, watching history
almost happen.
star wars — the shields — killed it.
reagan wouldn't yield.
they left with nothing signed
and everything changed:
the trust was built that weekend,
and the cold war's end
started in that small white house.

the secret deal november 1986 usa america learned of arms-for-hostages in the iran-contra scandal; the traveler covered the riveting hearings as denials towered and the basement light stayed on. arms for hostages —
america learned its government
sold missiles to iran
to free captives and fund contras.
iran-contra: the scandal brewed,
towers of denials, shredding parties.
i covered the hearings,
north in his uniform, the nation riveted.
reagan survived it.
the truth didn't, quite.
a secret deal in the democracy's basement —
and the basement, as always,
had a light on.

the quilt march 1987 usa the aids memorial quilt unfolded on the national mall; the traveler walked a football field of handmade grief where names became faces, one sewn panel at a time. they unfolded it on the national mall —
panel after panel, name after name,
the aids memorial quilt:
a football field of grief, handmade.
i walked it that first showing,
reading the names, the jokes,
the love stitched in.
names became faces.
statistics became sons.
the quilt did what numbers couldn't:
made a plague personal,
one sewn panel at a time.

tear down this wall june 1987 germany reagan dared gorbachev to tear down the wall at the brandenburg gate; the traveler stood in the cheering crowd as words became hammers two years later. at the brandenburg gate,
reagan faced the concrete and said it:
"mr. gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
i was in the crowd,
the wall looming behind the podium.
the diplomats winced.
the berliners cheered.
two years later, they did —
tore it down with hammers and joy.
words are just words, they say.
tell that to berlin.

black monday october 1987 usa markets crashed worldwide on black monday; the traveler stood on wall street watching the ticker fall like an elevator as paper fortunes vanished in a day. the dow fell 22% in one day —
paper fortunes vanished,
traders wept on the floor.
i was on wall street that monday,
the ticker like a falling elevator.
black monday: the biggest one-day crash
in history, and nobody knew why.
program trading, they said. panic, i said.
by year's end the market recovered.
the lesson didn't stick:
we keep building taller towers
on the same sand.

the missiles come down december 1987 usa the superpowers signed the inf treaty, scrapping a whole class of nuclear missiles; the traveler watched two old enemies sign as history ran in reverse toward peace. reagan and gorbachev signed the inf treaty —
an entire class of nuclear missiles,
scrapped. dismantled. gone.
i watched the signing in washington,
two old enemies with pens,
the world breathing easier.
the first time the superpowers
destroyed weapons instead of building them.
the missiles came down.
the wall would follow.
history, for once, running in reverse —
toward peace.

stones in gaza december 1987 middle east palestinians rose in the first intifada, stones against soldiers; the traveler watched gazan boys with slingshots face rifles as the un-dodgeable question was forced. it started with a traffic accident —
and became an uprising:
the first intifada, stones against soldiers,
gaza and the west bank rising.
i was in gaza that winter,
boys with slingshots facing rifles,
the imbalance obscene.
stones met soldiers for six years.
the world watched, again,
and did little, again.
but the intifada forced the question
no one could dodge anymore:
whose land is this?

the final fantasy december 1987 japan a last-ditch game saved its company and took role-playing games global; the traveler played the tokyo import and learned desperation is a game designer. square was nearly bankrupt —
one last game, they said,
a final fantasy.
i played the import in tokyo,
this sprawling role-playing epic,
and understood: they'd saved the company
and invented a genre's golden age.
final fantasy: the last-ditch game
that became a legend, sequels without end.
desperation, it turns out,
is a game designer.

the calgary games february 1988 canada the winter olympics came to calgary; the traveler cheered the jamaican bobsled team and eddie the eagle as underdogs proved the games are about joy. calgary hosted the winter olympics —
chinook winds, cowboy hats,
the jamaican bobsled team
stealing every heart.
i was there for the whole snowy fortnight,
eddie the eagle soaring (briefly),
the underdogs charming the world.
the games lost money.
nobody cared.
calgary proved the olympics
are about joy, not profit —
a lesson the ioc keeps forgetting.

a brief history of time march 1988 uk hawking's universe in plain words became a bestseller; the traveler heard the robotic voice fill a cambridge hall as mind beat matter, literally. a man in a wheelchair, speaking through a machine,
explained the universe in plain words —
and millions read cosmology.
hawking's brief history of time:
black holes, the big bang, the whole show,
no equations.
i heard him lecture at cambridge,
that robotic voice filling the hall.
the universe, it turns out,
is a bestseller.
mind over matter, literally —
and the matter lost.

the greenhouse warning june 1988 usa a nasa scientist warned congress about climate change; the traveler sat in the hearing room on the hottest june on record as the warning was filed and the planet kept warming. james hansen told congress, plainly:
the greenhouse effect is here,
the planet is warming, it's us.
i sat in that hearing room,
the hottest june on record outside.
climate change entered politics that day —
and then stalled for decades.
hansen was right about everything.
the warning was filed, debated, delayed.
the greenhouse kept warming.
some warnings you only get to give once.
this one we're still ignoring.

yippee-ki-yay july 1988 usa die hard redefined the action hero with a barefoot, bleeding cop; the traveler howled with the opening-weekend crowd as christmas got explosions. a barefoot cop in a los angeles tower,
terrorists, air ducts —
die hard redefined the action hero.
i saw it opening weekend,
the audience howling at every "yippee-ki-yay."
bruce willis bled, limped, wisecracked —
human, for once.
christmas got explosions.
action got a soul.
every action movie since
is just john mcclane
in a different building.

seoul's games september 1988 korea seoul hosted the world for the last cold war olympics; the traveler watched the opening ceremony as a divided land showed the world a korea beyond the dmz. korea hosted the world —
seoul's olympics, the last cold war games,
everyone finally showing up.
i was in the stadium for the opening,
the doves, the drums.
ben johnson's gold turned to shame;
griffith-joyner's speed turned to legend.
a divided land's hopes, on display.
seoul showed the world a korea
beyond the dmz —
and the world applauded.

the earth shakes armenia december 1988 ussr an earthquake buried armenian towns, killing 25,000; the traveler dug with rescue teams as the cold war paused and the world sent help — the earth doesn't care about blocs. 7:58 a.m.: spitak vanished —
a 6.8 quake burying armenian towns,
25,000 dead in minutes.
i flew in with the rescue teams,
the cold, the aftershocks,
a mother digging with her hands.
the world sent help —
even the cold war paused for it.
gorbachev cut short his us trip.
armenia's grief was the empire's grief,
for once shared.
the earth doesn't care about blocs.

the soviets leave february 1989 afghanistan the red army limped out of afghanistan after ten years; the traveler watched the hollow-eyed column cross the friendship bridge home to collapse. the last soviet general walked
across the friendship bridge —
and the red army limped out of afghanistan.
ten years. 15,000 dead.
i watched the column cross,
the soldiers' hollow eyes.
the quagmire ended.
the empire's bleeding stopped —
too late.
afghanistan went back to war with itself.
moscow went home to collapse.
some lessons cost an empire.

the tank man june 1989 china one man faced down tanks on chang'an avenue; the traveler watched the column stop as the bravest photograph ever taken entered history without a name. beijing had crushed the protests —
and then one man, shopping bags in hand,
stepped in front of the tanks.
i was on chang'an avenue.
the column stopped.
he climbed up. he talked.
then he was led away, into history's fog.
the tank man: the bravest photograph
ever taken, and we don't know his name.
china erased him.
the world remembers him anyway.
courage needs no caption.

batman june 1989 usa tim burton's batman darkened the summer; the traveler saw the bat-symbol take over as superheroes grew up and hollywood learned to print money with capes. tim burton's batman —
dark, gothic, prince on the soundtrack —
and superheroes grew up.
i saw it opening weekend,
the bat-symbol everywhere that summer.
keaton's haunted bruce wayne
proved comics could be cinema.
the summer belonged to the bat.
hollywood learned the lesson
it's still milking:
put on the cape, print money.

the pale blue farewell august 1989 usa voyager 2 passed neptune, completing its grand tour; the traveler watched the blue crescent fade as the greatest journey ever taken sailed on into the dark. voyager 2 swept past neptune —
the last planet, the grand tour complete:
jupiter, saturn, uranus, neptune,
twelve years, one spacecraft.
i was at mission control for the flyby,
the blue crescent on the screens.
then the camera turned off,
and voyager sailed on into the dark —
still sailing, still calling home.
the greatest journey ever taken,
by a machine with a golden record
and our best wishes.

the wall comes down november 1989 germany berliners danced atop the wall as the cold war cracked open; the traveler stood on the concrete that night, hugging strangers as hammers rang. a botched press conference —
"effective immediately," the spokesman stammered —
and berliners walked to the wall.
the guards shrugged. the gates opened.
i was there that night, on top of the wall,
strangers hugging, champagne,
hammers ringing on concrete.
twenty-eight years, ended by confusion
and courage.
the cold war cracked open.
i danced on the wall that night.
everyone did.

the velvet revolution december 1989 czechoslovakia czechs jingled keys in wenceslas square and ousted the communists peacefully; the traveler heard the jingling like bells as the gentlest revolution unlocked the future. no shots. just keys —
thousands of czechs jingling keys
in wenceslas square, telling the communists:
your time is up.
i was in that square,
the jingling like bells.
the velvet revolution: the regime folded
in weeks, havel the playwright
became president.
czechoslovakia ousted communism
peacefully — the gentlest revolution ever.
keys, not guns.
the future, unlocked.

springfield, usa december 1989 usa the simpsons got their own show; the traveler watched the christmas premiere as a yellow four-fingered family became america's funhouse mirror for thirty-five years. a yellow family with four fingers each
got its own show —
the simpsons, and television's family
changed forever.
i watched the christmas premiere,
this anarchic cartoon that was smarter
than the live-action shows.
homer, marge, bart, lisa —
america's mirror, funhouse and true.
thirty-five years it's been running.
the longest sitcom in history —
drawn, yellow, eternal.

mandela walks free february 1990 south africa after twenty-seven years, mandela walked free with fist raised; the traveler stood in the singing crowd as a firebrand emerged a statesman, unbroken. twenty-seven years in prison —
and he walked out of victor verster
with winnie, fist raised, unbroken.
i was in the crowd outside,
the singing, the tears.
mandela walks free:
apartheid's end began that day.
he'd gone in a young firebrand;
he came out a statesman.
no bitterness. just the long walk
to freedom, continued on foot.

the baltic break march 1990 lithuania lithuania declared independence, the first soviet republic to break away; the traveler stood in vilnius among barricades of books as a small nation's choir sang the superpower apart. lithuania declared independence —
the first soviet republic to break away,
the anthem sung in parliament.
i was in vilnius that spring,
the barricades of books and bodies,
the soviet tanks looming.
the empire started to split.
moscow fumed, then blinked.
the baltics led; the rest followed.
a small nation with a big choir
sang the superpower apart.

the blurry telescope april 1990 usa hubble launched with flawed vision; the traveler watched nasa's groans turn to glory as astronauts gave it glasses and it became humanity's greatest eye. hubble launched — and couldn't see.
a flawed mirror, images blurred,
the billion-dollar telescope myopic.
i watched the disappointment at nasa,
the jokes, the groans.
then the fix: astronauts gave it glasses,
and hubble saw eternity —
the deep field, the pillars,
the universe in high definition.
the blurry telescope became
humanity's greatest eye.
sometimes you just need
a second chance in orbit.

the invasion of kuwait august 1990 middle east saddam hussein seized kuwait overnight; the traveler watched refugees stream south as the world drew a line and the desert burned on the horizon. saddam's tanks rolled into kuwait city
before dawn — a sovereign nation
swallowed overnight.
i was in the region when it happened,
the disbelief, the refugees streaming south.
the world drew a line:
the un, the coalition, the deadline.
kuwait's oil burned on the horizon.
desert storm was coming.
but that august, the shock was simple —
a country, erased by morning.

the genome quest october 1990 usa scientists launched the human genome project to read our dna; the traveler toured the humming labs as humanity began opening the book of life. scientists launched the human genome project —
thirteen years to read all three billion letters
of our dna.
i toured the early labs,
the sequencing machines humming,
the ambition staggering.
the reading of our dna began that october:
the book of life, opened.
we'd finish it, read ourselves,
and find we barely understood a word.
the quest continues —
we're still learning to read.

one germany october 1990 germany east and west germany reunited less than a year after the wall fell; the traveler watched berlin weep together as forty-five years of division healed. less than a year after the wall fell —
reunification. one germany,
the wound healed, the anthem whole.
i was in berlin for the ceremony,
the flags, the fireworks,
east and west weeping together.
forty-five years divided.
one night of hammers,
one year of paperwork,
and the nation was whole.
the cold war's body, made one again.

desert storm january 1991 middle east allied jets pounded iraq on live television; the traveler watched from a dhahran rooftop as the gulf war became a broadcast and war became a show. the deadline passed — and the sky over baghdad
lit up on live television,
allied jets pounding iraq.
i watched it from a hotel roof in dhahran,
the war as broadcast: green night-vision,
smart bombs down chimneys.
desert storm: forty-two days,
kuwait freed, saddam left in place.
the gulf war began on live tv —
and war became a show,
for better and worse.

hasta la vista july 1991 usa terminator 2's liquid metal wowed audiences; the traveler gasped with the opening-weekend crowd as computer effects grew up and "hasta la vista" entered the language. a robot made of liquid metal
walked through prison bars —
terminator 2, and computer effects grew up.
i saw it opening weekend,
the audience gasping at the t-1000.
cameron spent a fortune;
it looked like the future.
"hasta la vista, baby"
entered the language.
the machines were coming, the film said —
and hollywood's machines
had just arrived.

the world wide web august 1991 europe berners-lee shared the web with the world, patent-free; the traveler saw the little next machine with its "do not power down" sticker — history's most valuable gift, given away. at cern, tim berners-lee
shared his invention with the world —
the web: pages, links, http,
free for everyone, no patent.
i visited his little next machine,
the first web server,
a sticker saying "do not power down."
the internet got its face that august.
he gave it away.
the most valuable gift in history —
and he just... shared it.
