the coup that failed august 1991 ussr hardliners seized gorbachev and yeltsin stood on a tank; the traveler manned the moscow barricades as the three-day coup crumbled and the empire gasped its last. the hardliners seized gorbachev in crimea,
tanks in moscow —
and boris yeltsin climbed on one
and said no.
i was at the white house barricades,
the crowds, the cigarettes, the fear.
three days. the coup crumbled.
the empire's last gasp, televised.
yeltsin on the tank: the image
that ended the soviet union.
it fell not with a bang
but with a drunk on a tank.

smells like teen spirit september 1991 usa nirvana's roar ended the hair-metal era; the traveler heard it in a record store as kids went still then wild — the eighties dying on a power chord. a quiet-loud-quiet roar from seattle —
nirvana's "smells like teen spirit,"
and the hair-metal era died overnight.
i heard it first in a record store,
the kids going still, then wild.
grunge took over: flannel, fury,
cobain's howl.
the eighties ended with a power chord.
a generation's anthem, three minutes long —
and nothing in pop
was polished again.

ukraine's blue and yellow december 1991 ukraine ukraine voted overwhelmingly for independence; the traveler stood in kyiv's determined lines as the empire's breadbasket walked away by ballot. ninety percent voted yes —
ukraine's independence referendum,
the blue and yellow rising over kyiv.
i was there for the vote,
the lines, the quiet determination.
the empire's breadbasket walked away.
moscow's centuries of rule, ended
by a ballot.
no one in that december crowd
imagined what the future held —
but the flag was theirs,
and the choice was made.

the red flag comes down december 1991 ussr the soviet union dissolved as the red flag came down over the kremlin; the traveler stood in falling snow as seventy-four years ended with paperwork, not war. christmas night: the red flag
came down over the kremlin,
the tricolor went up.
the soviet union dissolved —
fifteen nations, alone, free, terrified.
i stood in red square that night,
the snow falling on the cameras.
seventy-four years, ended with paperwork.
no war. no mushroom cloud.
the cold war ended the way it lived:
in moscow, in winter, quietly.
the traveler exhaled.
so did the world.

the euro dream february 1992 europe europe signed the maastricht treaty, shaping the eu and the coming euro; the traveler watched gray suits sign two thousand years of trying to stop fighting. in maastricht, europe signed the dream —
a union, a currency to come,
the euro on the horizon.
i watched the signing,
the gray suits, the grand words.
the european union took shape that february:
open borders, one market,
history's oldest enemies sharing a wallet.
the euro would come.
the dream was older than the treaty —
two thousand years of trying
to stop fighting.

los angeles burns april 1992 usa the rodney king verdict sparked six days of la riots; the traveler walked smoke-filled south central as america watched its reflection burn. the verdict came down — not guilty —
and los angeles exploded:
six days, sixty dead, a billion in damage.
i was in south central that first night,
the smoke, the sirens,
korean shopkeepers on their roofs.
the rodney king verdict lit the fuse;
centuries of tinder did the rest.
the city smoldered for days.
america watched its reflection burn
and looked away, again.

the real world may 1992 usa mtv locked strangers in a loft and reality tv was born; the traveler watched the first season as television stopped telling stories and started filming people. mtv locked seven strangers in a loft,
filmed everything —
and reality television was born.
i watched the first season,
this strange new thing:
real people, real fights, no script.
the real world: it seemed harmless.
it invented the genre that ate television —
confessionals, eliminations, fame
for being filmed.
we started watching each other
instead of stories.
we're still watching.

the earth summit june 1992 brazil nations gathered in rio for the planet's first summit; the traveler sat through thousand-page texts as the world admitted in one room that the house was on fire. rio: 172 nations, the planet's first summit —
climate, forests, the future,
all on the table.
i was in the conference halls,
the translators, the thousand-page texts.
agenda 21. the rio declaration.
the planet got its own summit that june —
and the promises were grand.
the follow-through, less so.
but for the first time, the world
admitted the house was on fire
in the same room, together.

black wednesday september 1992 uk britain crashed out of the erm on black wednesday; the traveler stood in the screaming city as sixteen billion vanished by teatime and markets beat governments. soros broke the bank of england —
black wednesday, britain crashed out of the erm,
the pound in freefall.
i was in the city that day,
the phones screaming, the dealers white.
sixteen billion spent defending the pound.
gone by teatime.
the speculators won.
britain learned that markets
are bigger than governments —
a lesson the world keeps relearning,
expensively.

into somalia december 1992 somalia american troops landed in somalia on a humanitarian mission that turned dark; the traveler stood on mogadishu's beaches as hope met warlords and the lesson haunted a generation. american troops landed on mogadishu's beaches —
operation restore hope,
food for the starving, cameras rolling.
i was on those beaches,
the night-vision green, the hope real.
the mission turned dark:
warlords, black hawk down,
eighteen americans dead.
humanitarianism met reality
in the mogadishu streets.
we came to feed.
we left in coffins.
the lesson haunted a generation.

the first strike february 1993 usa a truck bomb rocked the world trade center in 1993; the traveler evacuated down smoke-filled stairs past terror's first warning — filed away until the towers fell. a truck bomb in the world trade center garage —
six dead, a thousand hurt,
a crater five stories deep.
i was in lower manhattan that day,
the smoke, the evacuation down the stairs.
terror gave its warning in '93:
ramzi yousef, the blind sheikh's men.
we caught them. we moved on.
eight years later, the towers fell —
and everyone remembered the first strike,
the warning we filed away.

mosaic april 1993 usa the mosaic browser painted the web in pictures; the traveler downloaded it that spring as the internet went from text to images and the masses logged on. two students at illinois
painted the web in pictures —
mosaic, the first graphical browser,
images inline, point and click.
i downloaded it that spring,
and the internet changed:
from text to pictures,
from nerds to everyone.
the masses logged on.
mosaic became netscape,
netscape became the boom.
the web got its face —
and the face was friendly.

eritrea's freedom may 1993 eritrea eritrea won independence after thirty years of war with a 99.8% vote; the traveler danced in asmara's highland air as fighters became builders. thirty years of war —
and eritrea voted itself free,
99.8% yes, the most decisive
independence vote ever.
i was in asmara for the celebrations,
the highland air, the dancing.
africa's longest war, ended by ballot.
the fighters became builders.
eritrea's freedom was won the hard way:
a generation in the trenches,
then a single day of voting.

jurassic park june 1993 usa jurassic park's dinosaurs walked again in pixels; the traveler felt the t. rex's footstep shake the theater as computer effects roared into a new era. the dinosaurs walked again —
spielberg's jurassic park,
cgi so real the audience forgot to breathe.
i saw it opening night,
the t. rex's footstep shaking the theater.
computer effects roared that summer:
sixty-five million years, resurrected
in pixels.
"life finds a way."
so did the movies —
a new era, one dinosaur at a time.

the handshake september 1993 middle east rabin and arafat shook hands on the white house lawn; the traveler held his breath in the sun as peace got its chance for one september afternoon. on the white house lawn —
rabin and arafat, clinton between them,
the handshake the world waited decades for.
i was on that lawn,
the sun, the held breath.
oslo: peace got its chance.
mutual recognition, gaza-jericho first.
the handshake was real.
what followed — assassinations, intifadas —
was real too.
but for one september afternoon,
enemies shook hands,
and the future opened.

schindler's list december 1993 usa spielberg filmed the holocaust in black and white; the traveler sat in a silent theater as the girl in the red coat walked through horror and the world wept. spielberg filmed the holocaust
in black and white —
schindler's list, and the world wept.
i saw it in a silent theater,
no one moving, no one coughing.
the girl in the red coat:
the only color, walking through the horror.
cinema's conscience, three hours long.
"whoever saves one life saves the world entire."
we wept in black and white that winter —
and remembered in color.

northridge shakes january 1994 usa an earthquake jolted los angeles, collapsing freeways; the traveler stood in the dust at 4:31 a.m. as california learned again the ground is temporary. 4:31 a.m.: northridge convulsed —
6.7, freeways collapsing,
apartment blocks pancaked.
i was in los angeles that morning,
the aftershocks, the dust,
the 10 freeway broken like a toy.
fifty-seven dead. twenty billion in damage.
california's reminder:
the ground is temporary.
we rebuild. we always rebuild.
the earth shrugs, and we shrug back —
with better building codes.

the lillehammer games february 1994 norway norway hosted a fairy-tale winter olympics at lillehammer; the traveler spent the snowy fortnight at the last innocent games — small, beautiful, human. norway hosted a fairy-tale winter olympics —
lillehammer, snow and candlelight,
the tonya-nancy drama,
dan jansen's golden skate.
i was there for the fortnight,
the cold, the kindness.
the lillehammer games: the last innocent olympics,
before the money took over completely.
norway did it right —
small, beautiful, human.
a fairy tale on ice,
and the world believed it.

rwanda's hundred days april 1994 rwanda hutus slaughtered tutsis for a hundred days while the world did nothing; the traveler was there and carries what he won't describe — humanity's shame, filed under "never again," again. one hundred days.
eight hundred thousand dead —
tutsis slaughtered by hutu militias,
machetes, churches full of bodies.
i was there. i won't describe
what i saw. you know.
the world watched and did nothing —
withdrew the peacekeepers,
debated the word "genocide."
rwanda's hundred days:
humanity's shame, filed under "never again,"
again.

president mandela may 1994 south africa mandela won south africa's first free election; the traveler stood in soweto's miles-long lines as eighty-year-olds voted for the first time and the long walk completed. the lines stretched for miles —
south africa's first free election,
and mandela won it.
i was in soweto that day,
the singing, the old ones voting
for the first time at eighty.
president mandela.
apartheid's end, sealed by ballot.
he'd walked out of prison four years before;
now he walked into the union buildings.
the long walk to freedom —
completed, together.

the lion king june 1994 usa the lion king's roar filled theaters; the traveler wept with the neighbor's kids at mufasa's death as hamlet with lions became animation's crown jewel. a cub's roar filled theaters —
the lion king, hand-drawn,
elton's songs, mufasa's death
making every child cry.
i saw it with my neighbor's kids,
the stampede, the tears.
animation's crown jewel:
the highest-grossing hand-drawn film ever.
hamlet with lions.
shakespeare would have approved —

into thin air told the story:

the mountain's price, itemized.

they caught rudolph years later,

hey, macarena august 1996 spain a spanish dance craze swept the world's weddings; the traveler did the macarena at three weddings as proof joy needs no translation — just a beat and permission. a spanish duo, a dance craze —

the digital pet november 1996 japan tamagotchi's digital pets beeped for feeding in pockets worldwide; the traveler watched osaka kids grieve pixel deaths and learned love doesn't require fur. a plastic egg that beeped for feeding —

to mars december 1996 usa mars pathfinder launched with the sojourner rover; the traveler watched it leave the cape as humanity's first rover rolled onto martian soil and waved back. mars pathfinder launched —

this ordinary-looking sheep
that broke biology open.

ethics, panic, wonder.

woolly, blinking,

the boy who lived
taught a generation to live
in books.

a century and a half of empire,

the promise held, for a while.

diana died in paris;

the subcontinent's bombs:

the unthinkable, thought daily.

around them.

desert fox: the war that wasn't,
before the war that was.

money united a continent:

it held. it holds.
europe's wallet, finally shared.

and... nothing.
the y2k scare: the apocalypse
that didn't happen.
billions spent fixing code —
which is why nothing happened.
the quietest triumph ever:
humanity debugged the future
before it arrived.

and humans have lived off-world
ever since, continuously.

american, russian, together.
a house above earth, orbiting
every ninety minutes.
twenty-five years and counting —
humanity's longest address
beyond the sky.

the night the computers didn't break 2000 ce global the y2k panic spent billions fixing two-digit dates, then the millennium arrived without a glitch — humanity's most expensive scare that never happened. they told us the world would end at midnight —
every banker, every coder, every screen gone dark,
the planes would drop, the lights go out,
because some lazy fool wrote the year with two digits.

the millions spent, the keyboards worn to bone,
and then the clock turned over, clean and clear,

our own small prophecy of doom that year —

sometimes the apocalypse we prepare for, dear,
is just the shadow of the work we've shirked.

reading the human instruction book 2000 ce global the human genome project's working draft printed humanity's three billion dna letters — the instruction book of a species, read for the first time. i watched them read it —
three billion letters,
a working draft
of what makes us us,
printed out and stacked
higher than a man is tall,
all that code that codes
the curve of a thumb,
the color of eyes,
the way we hunger,
the way we fall in love.
not a book you finish,

i held my breath with them.
we had finally read the recipe
and none of us knew how to cook.

with a ghost town, and a few who stayed
to build the real city underneath.

for seventeen days, i believed it.

a hundred million of them sold.

we have spent twenty-five years since
trying to build something that tough,
and we never have, not once.

built a window, and through it
every teenager on earth
could hear everything.

millions of songs, traded hand to hand,
no stores, no money, just music
moving like weather.
the lawyers came with their lawsuits,

but the window had been opened,

the industry never recovered.
the listeners never went back.

everything it ate, everything it saw,

we traded forgetting for keeping,
and we have been scrolling ever since.

the fairy tale didn't die.

with rain on the windshield
and the radio playing your song
while you ran the red lights.

behind the wheel of a stolen car.

to the little corridors again.

a continent woke up with one money in its pocket.

water beneath the red dust 2002 ce space mars odyssey's instruments found vast ice fields beneath the martian soil — water enough for a future, waiting under the red dust. mars odyssey flew over the red desert
with eyes that saw through dust,
and underneath — ice.
vast fields of it, frozen water
hiding inches under the rust,
enough to fill oceans, enough to drink,
enough to make a future there.
i have stood in mission rooms
when the maps came up on the screens,
and grown scientists went quiet
like children on christmas morning.
water. on mars. waiting.
the red planet had been keeping
its most important secret in the dark.

samba kings again 2002 ce global brazil won its fifth world cup across japan and korea — the samba kings reclaimed football's crown and rio poured into the streets. across japan and korea they danced —
ronaldo, rivaldo, ronaldinho,
the yellow shirts moving like music,
and in the final, two goals,
and the fifth star sewn on.
i was in a rio street when the whistle blew —
the whole city poured out of itself,
drums, horns, grandmothers dancing on tables.
brazil had waited eight years.
football's greatest nation was itself again.
some victories are just games.
this one felt like a country remembering its name.

a court for the world's worst crimes 2002 ce europe the international criminal court opened in the hague — a courtroom for genocide and war crimes with no country on its door. in the hague they opened a courtroom
with no country on the door.
genocide. crimes against humanity.
war crimes. the words were carved
into the founding statute like a vow:
never again means a courtroom,
not just a speech.
i watched the first prosecutors walk in,
knowing the great powers would never join,
knowing the dock might stay empty for years.
it was a promise made of paper.
but paper, sometimes, is where justice starts.

a new fever in guangdong 2002 ce asia sars emerged in southern china and rode airplanes around the world — eight thousand cases, a rehearsal for a pandemic nobody knew was coming. it started as a rumor in guangdong —
a strange pneumonia, a fever that wouldn't break,
whispers in hospital corridors,
text messages passed hand to hand.
sars. severe, acute, and new.
i watched it board airplanes
and land in hong kong, toronto, singapore,
watched the masks go on in the subways,
the temperature guns at the airports.
eight thousand cases before it burned out.
a rehearsal, we called it later.
nobody knew we were rehearsing.

forty hours in a moscow theater 2002 ce europe chechen fighters seized a moscow theater; the rescue gas killed 130 hostages along with the captors — a rescue that killed the rescued. eight hundred fifty people
went to see a musical in moscow
and walked into forty hours of hell —
chechen fighters in the aisles,
bombs on the pillars,
a standoff the whole world watched.
then the gas came through the vents,
silent, invisible, and the theater stormed.
the captors died. so did one hundred thirty hostages.
i have never forgiven the arithmetic
of that rescue — the living carried out
past the bodies, the questions no one answered:
who ordered the gas, what was in it,
why the ambulances weren't told.
a rescue that killed the rescued.

fire in paradise 2002 ce asia the 2002 bali bombings killed 202 people, mostly young tourists — fire in paradise, on the island of the gods. bali. the island of the gods,
all frangipani and surf and young backpackers
dancing barefoot in kuta.
then the bombs — two of them,
in the nightclub strip,
and paradise burned.
two hundred two dead, mostly young,
mostly tourists who had come
for the cheapest heaven on earth.
i walked the street a week later.
the flowers were already back,
piled high where the sari club stood.
bali forgave faster than the world did.
but the young ones never came home.

shock and awe 2003 ce middle east the iraq invasion toppled baghdad in weeks on live tv — then came the long insurgency, the missing weapons, and a war with no end. the sky over baghdad bloomed with fire
on live television — shock and awe,
they called the opening act,
and the statues fell in weeks.
i was there for the falling
and stayed for what came after:
the looting, the long insurgency,
the weapons that were never found,
the mission accomplished banner
flapping over a war with no end.
empires have a habit, i have learned —
they win the invasion
and lose everything that follows.

the genome finished 2003 ce global the human genome project declared the full human dna code complete — the reading done, the understanding still barely begun. fifty years after the double helix,
they declared it done —
the whole human code, all three billion letters,
read end to end, the book closed.
i stood among the scientists
who had raced governments and companies
to finish first, and there was champagne,
and there was also a strange quiet.
because finishing the reading
was only the beginning of understanding.
we had the letters. now we needed
the meaning — and meaning,
it turns out, takes longer.

columbia breaks apart 2003 ce space columbia disintegrated over texas during re-entry, killing seven astronauts — a wounded wing, superheated air, and space's unforgiving physics. sixteen days in orbit, a perfect mission,
and then re-entry over texas —
a piece of foam, a wounded wing,
superheated air finding the crack.
i watched the sky that morning
and saw the trails split apart,
saw seven bright streaks
where one shuttle should have been.
seven astronauts. gone in the blue.
the program stood down for two years,
grieving, learning, hardening.
space does not forgive small damage.
it never has. it never will.

two rovers sail to mars 2003 ce space spirit and opportunity launched for mars on a 90-day mission — two small rovers carrying humanity's curiosity across two hundred million kilometers. two golf carts with cameras,
launched a month apart,
aimed at a planet
two hundred million kilometers away —
on a ninety-day warranty.
spirit. opportunity.
i watched them leave earth
on pillars of fire that summer,
two small machines carrying
all our curiosity in their solar wings.
ninety days, they said.
they would outlive that promise
by years, by decades of extra mornings.
but on launch day, all we had was hope
and very good math.

the masks come off 2003 ce asia the who declared sars contained after 8,000 cases — the masks came off, the playbook was filed away, and seventeen years later we'd need it again. the who said the word: contained.
eight thousand cases, seven hundred seventy-four dead,
and the fever that had ridden the airplanes
finally burned itself out.
i watched the masks come off in hong kong,
the temperature checkpoints fold away,
the city exhale for the first time in months.
we told ourselves we had won.
we wrote the playbook — trace, isolate, mask —
and filed it away like a trophy.
seventeen years later we would need it.
we would find the pages stuck together.

fifty million in the dark 2003 ce north america a tree branch in ohio triggered the great northeast blackout — fifty million people dark, and manhattan walked home across the bridges. a sagging power line in ohio
touched a tree branch.
that's all it took.
the cascade ran east like a rumor —
fifty million people, two countries,
dark in the middle of a summer afternoon.
i was in manhattan when the elevators stopped,
when the subways sighed to a halt,
when the whole island walked home
across the bridges in the heat.
no looting. strangers directing traffic.
for one night, the greatest city on earth
remembered how to be a neighborhood.

everybody gets a profile 2003 ce global myspace launched social media's first great boom — profiles, top 8s, glitter backgrounds, and bands discovered in bedrooms. tom was everyone's first friend.
myspace gave the whole world a profile —
a page, a song that played when you visited,
a top 8 that ended friendships.
i watched teenagers learn html
just to glitter their backgrounds,
watched bands get discovered
in bedrooms and basements,
watched the first great boom
of showing your life to strangers.
it was ugly and glorious and free.
then the blue giant came
and the party moved.
but myspace was the first room
where everybody got a page.

a harvard dorm's address book 2004 ce global facebook began as a harvard dorm directory and grew into the social graph — billions eventually living half their social lives inside it. it started as a dorm's address book —
faces, names, who's in what class,
a little harvard-only directory
built by a sophomore in a hurry.
i watched it spill past the campus gates,
college to college, then high schools,
then everyone, everywhere.
the social graph, they called it —
every friendship mapped, every like counted.
two billion people would eventually live
half their social lives inside it.
all from a dorm room directory.
the smallest seeds grow the strangest forests.

the wave that crossed an ocean 2004 ce asia the 2004 indian ocean tsunami killed 230,000 people across fourteen countries — the sea pulled back, then returned as a wall. the sea pulled back first —
a strange low tide, fish flopping on the sand,
tourists walking out to stare.
then it came back as a wall.
i have walked those beaches since,
in aceh, in thailand, in sri lanka,
and the people still point:
the water reached here. here.
two hundred thirty thousand dead
across fourteen countries,
in the time it takes to drink tea.
the wave crossed an ocean.
grief crossed the whole world.

six wheels on mars 2004 ce space spirit and opportunity bounced down on mars in airbags and opened their petals — six wheels in red dust, on a 90-day warranty that lasted years. they wrapped the rovers in airbags
and dropped them at the planet —
bounce, bounce, bounce across the red dust,
then the bags deflated, the petals opened,
and six wheels touched mars.
spirit in the crater. opportunity in the plain.
i watched the first pictures come down:
a salmon sky, a horizon of rust,
tire tracks in another world's dirt.
ninety days, the warranty said.
opportunity would drive for fourteen years.
some machines are built by engineers.
some are built by hope with tools.

orange banners in kyiv 2004 ce europe ukraine's orange revolution filled kyiv's snowy squares with protesters until a rigged election was annulled and rerun — the people refused to go home. the election was stolen — everyone knew it —
so they came out in the snow,
a sea of orange in independence square,
singing, freezing, refusing to go home.
i stood among them, breath fogging,
watching grandmothers hand out tea
to students who wouldn't leave.
weeks of it. peaceful, stubborn, orange.
and it worked — the court annulled the fraud,
the vote was rerun, the people won.
kyiv taught the world that winter:
a rigged election is only final
if the people agree to go home.

saturn up close 2004 ce space cassini orbited saturn for thirteen years — geysers, methane rain, shepherd moons — then burned up in the clouds to protect the moons it revealed. seven years of falling toward saturn,
and then the burn — cassini slipped
into orbit around the ringed giant
and stayed for thirteen years.
i have seen what it sent back:
geysers on enceladus, methane rain on titan,
the rings in such detail you could see
the shepherd moons herding the ice.
thirteen years of wonders,
then a final dive into the clouds,
burning up to protect the moons
it had taught us to love.
the little probe that showed us saturn —
and chose to die rather than risk its children.

the games come home 2004 ce europe the 2004 olympics returned to athens, their ancient birthplace — the torch lit by sunlight at olympia, the games home after 108 years. after a hundred and eight years away,
the olympics came home to athens —
to the marble stadium,
to the birthplace, to the dust
where it all began.
i walked the old track at olympia
where the torch was lit from the sun,
no matches, just a mirror and light,
the way they did it three thousand years ago.
the games were modern, the money was modern,
but for one summer the ancient stones
got to watch their children run again.
home is a powerful word.
athens proved it.

madrid's trains 2004 ce europe coordinated bombs killed 193 on madrid's commuter trains — spain answered terror with candles, dignity, and votes three days later. morning rush hour. four commuter trains.
ten bombs in backpacks, timed to the minute,
and 193 people never made it to work.
i stood at atocha station days later,
among the candles and the handwritten notes,
the whole of spain holding its breath.
an election three days later turned on it —
a government fell, troops came home from iraq.
terror wanted fear. spain answered
with votes, with candles, with the quiet dignity
of a people who refused to be ruled by it.

broadcast yourself 2005 ce global youtube launched with "broadcast yourself" — anyone with a camera became television, and the gatekeepers were walked around, not toppled. three former paypal guys, a garage,
a slogan: broadcast yourself.
i watched the first uploads —
a kid at the zoo, grainy, nineteen seconds —
and thought nothing of it.
then everyone with a camera became television.
bedroom guitarists, makeup teachers,
gamers, preachers, comedians, cooks —
a billion channels, no network, no permission.
the gatekeepers didn't fall.
they were simply walked around,
by teenagers with webcams
and something to say.

katrina drowns a city 2005 ce north america hurricane katrina's broken levees drowned new orleans — the world watched america fail its poorest on live television. the levees broke, and new orleans drowned —
not in the storm, but in the failure after:
the superdome full of the stranded,
the rooftops full of the waiting,
the helicopters that came too late
for the poorest zip codes first.
i was there in the weeks after,
the waterlines on the houses,
the refrigerators on the curbs,
the anger that never quite left.
the world watched america —
the richest nation on earth —
fail its poor on live television.
the water receded. the shame didn't.

live 8's plea 2005 ce global ten simultaneous live 8 concerts demanded an end to africa's debt — billions watched as the planet sang one chorus at the summits. ten concerts. one day. one demand:
cancel the debt strangling africa.
i watched london's hyde park fill —
two hundred thousand voices,
pink floyd reuniting, mccartney and u2,
all of it beamed to billions.
make poverty history, the wristbands said.
the g8 met in scotland days later
and promised — some of it, not enough,
the way summits do.
but for one day the whole planet sang
the same chorus at the same time,
and the powerful had to listen.

kyoto takes effect 2005 ce global the kyoto protocol became international law — the first climate treaty with binding targets, a thin beginning wearing victory's clothes. the first climate treaty with teeth
became law — binding targets,
signed promises, a planet
agreeing, on paper, to cool itself.
i was in the corridors in kyoto years before,
when they argued over commas
that meant gigatons.
america stayed out. the big one.
still, the treaty lived, and carbon markets
learned to price the sky.
it was a beginning wearing
the clothes of a victory —
thin clothes, but better than naked.
the planet noticed. barely.
but barely is where beginnings live.

the whole world from above 2005 ce global google earth put every rooftop on every screen — the whole planet became a thing you could hold, spin, and zoom into. one day the whole world was on your screen —
every rooftop, every dirt road,
your childhood house from five hundred miles up.
i watched people find their homes
and cry, watched them trace
the street where they grew up,
watched dictators realize
their palaces were visible now.
google earth made the planet
a thing you could hold and spin.
borders looked very small from up there.
so did armies. so did we.

a spacecraft punches a comet 2005 ce space deep impact slammed a copper projectile into comet tempel 1 to read its insides — the debris held water and clay, the ingredients of oceans. they flew a spacecraft to comet tempel 1
and shot it — a copper bullet,
a deliberate punch to the face of a snowball
older than the earth itself.
deep impact. the flash was beautiful.
i watched the dust plume rise on the screens,
watched the scientists read the insides
of a four-billion-year-old time capsule:
water, clay, the ingredients of us.
we punched a comet to see what bled.
what bled was the recipe for oceans.

london's darkest morning 2005 ce europe four suicide bombers killed 52 on london's tube and a bus — and the city answered with full pubs, running buses, and refusal to be scared. rush hour on the tube. then the bus.
four young men, four bombs,
fifty-two dead in the tunnels
under the greatest city in europe.
i walked london that evening —
the pubs were full, defiant,
the buses running, the city refusing
to learn the lesson terror was teaching.
two weeks later they tried again.
the bombs failed. the city didn't.
london's darkest morning proved
what london has always known:
you don't beat this city by scaring it.

one hundred forty characters 2006 ce global twitter launched with 140-character updates and became the world's wire service — news by the sentence, revolutions in real time. it began as a side project —
status updates, 140 characters,
what are you doing, in a sentence.
i watched it become the world's wire service:
earthquakes reported before the seismographs,
revolutions organized in real time,
presidents governing by tweet.
news stopped arriving by the hour
and started arriving by the sentence.
the whole planet learned to think
in headlines. we gained the world's pulse
and lost its attention span
in the same small box.

pluto steps down 2006 ce space astronomers voted pluto out of the planet club in prague — the universe didn't attend, but the schoolchildren protested anyway. in prague, the astronomers voted —
a show of hands, and just like that,
pluto was out of the planet club.
too small, they said. hasn't cleared its orbit.
i watched the schoolchildren protest,
the textbooks go stale overnight,
the internet rise in defense
of a little iceball none of them had seen.
pluto didn't change. we did.
nine planets became eight by committee.
the universe, i noted, did not attend the vote.

a dictator hanged 2006 ce middle east saddam hussein was executed in baghdad and the hanging leaked on phone video — justice to some, revenge to others, and a fire that burned for a decade. they hanged saddam hussein in baghdad
before dawn on a holy day,
and filmed it on a phone —
grainy, shaky, the rope, the drop,
the taunts of the guards.
i have seen tyrants fall many ways;
this one fell on a leaked video,
passed phone to phone around the world.
justice, said some. revenge, said others.
the sectarian fire it lit
burned for a decade after.
a hanging meant to end a chapter
only underlined it in blood.

the living room comes alive 2006 ce global the wii got grandparents swinging controllers at televisions — games stopped chasing graphics and started chasing joy, for everybody. nintendo stopped chasing graphics
and handed grandparents a controller —
swing it like a tennis racket,
bowl it like a bowling ball,
and the little white box understood.
i watched living rooms come alive:
families sweating at virtual tennis,
nursing homes running bowling leagues,
kids teaching grandma to serve.
the wii didn't win on power.
it won on joy — the radical idea
that games were for everybody,
even the people who'd never played.

google buys the video age 2006 ce global google bought the money-losing, 18-month-old youtube for $1.65 billion — the bargain of the century, the future of television for a rounding error. a year and a half old, losing money,
bought for 1.65 billion dollars in stock —
and the business world laughed.
i didn't laugh. i had seen the uploads,
the millions of hours, the kids
who would rather watch a bedroom
than a network.
the bargain of the century, they call it now.
google bought the future of television
for the price of a rounding error.
sometimes the smartest deal in history
looks like overpaying for a garage.

microcredit's nobel 2006 ce asia muhammad yunus won the nobel for banking for the poor — tiny loans to bangladeshi basket weavers that were paid back, with interest. he lent twenty-seven dollars to forty-two women —
basket weavers in bangladesh,
too poor for any bank to notice —
and they paid it back.
then he built a bank on the radical idea
that the poor are creditworthy.
i met the borrowers: rickshaw drivers,
seamstresses, fish sellers,
whole villages lifted on loans
smaller than a dinner in new york.
the nobel came in 2006.
muhammad yunus proved what the poor
had always known: given a chance,
they pay it back — with interest.

the longest postcard 2006 ce space new horizons launched for pluto on a nine-year journey — carrying clyde tombaugh's ashes to the world he discovered, demoted before the mail arrived. new horizons left earth on the fastest launch
ever attempted — aimed at pluto,
nine years away, a speck nobody had seen clearly.
i watched it go, a little piano-sized probe
carrying the ashes of pluto's discoverer,
clyde tombaugh, riding along to the world he found.
nine years. four billion miles.
the longest postcard ever sent,
addressed to a planet that would be demoted
before the mail arrived.
it didn't care. it kept flying.

the phone that ate the world 2007 ce global the iphone launched with no keyboard, just glass — and swallowed the camera, the map, and the music player whole, then the whole industry. no keyboard. just glass.
a phone, an ipod, an internet communicator —
he said it three times, and the crowd laughed,
then went silent when they understood.
i held one that june: it swallowed the camera,
the map, the music player, the flashlight,
the alarm clock, the whole junk drawer
of twentieth-century gadgets, whole.
nokia laughed. blackberry laughed.
within five years the laughers were gone.
one device ate the world,
and we have been staring into the glass ever since.

paper light 2007 ce global the kindle made a library weightless — readers resisted, then surrendered, and the strangest thing happened: people started reading more. a library that weighed less than a paperback —
the kindle made ten thousand books weightless,
ink that wasn't ink, pages that weren't pages.
i watched readers resist, then surrender:
the midnight purchase, the enormous font,
the book that never ran out of pages.
bookstores trembled. publishers panicked.
then the strangest thing happened —
people started reading more.
paper light, they called the screen.
it turns out the weight was never the point.
the words were.

the cracks show 2007 ce global the subprime mortgage crisis began — houses bought with unpayable loans, foreclosure signs blooming like weeds, the great boom rotting from inside. it started in the american suburbs —
houses bought with loans
that were never meant to be repaid,
sliced, bundled, sold as gold.
subprime. a ugly little word
for a beautiful lie.
i watched the cracks show first
in the small banks, the mortgage desks,
the foreclosure signs blooming
like weeds across the cul-de-sacs.
the great boom was rotting from inside,
and the rot had a smell: fresh paint
on houses nobody could afford.

the first cyber siege 2007 ce europe hackers hammered wired estonia offline — banks, government, everything — the first cyber siege in history, with no soldiers and no shots fired. estonia — the most wired nation on earth,
voting online, banking online, everything online —
went dark under a hammering
of a million hijacked computers.
banks offline. government offline.
the news sites, the atms, all of it, gone.
i watched a whole country learn
what war looks like with no soldiers:
just traffic, floods of it,
drowning the servers.
the first cyber siege in history.
nobody fired a shot.
everybody felt it.

the saffron monks march 2007 ce asia burmese monks marched in saffron robes against the junta — prayer against rifles — until the guns came and the world watched on shaky phone video. they came in rows of saffron,
barefoot monks with begging bowls turned upside down —
refusing alms from the soldiers,
the deepest shame in their faith.
i watched them march through rangoon,
thousands of robes the color of sunrise,
chanting, peaceful, unstoppable —
until the guns came.
the junta beat them, jailed them,
shot into the crowds.
the world watched on shaky phone video
and did nothing much.
but the image stayed: saffron against rifles,
prayer against power.

humanity moves to town 2007 ce global in 2007 humanity became majority-urban for the first time since farming began — no ceremony, just the slow drift from village to megacity. somewhere in 2007, quietly,
the balance tipped:
more humans in cities than in the countryside,
for the first time since we planted wheat.
no ceremony. no headline that mattered.
just the slow drift — the village emptied,
the megacity swelled, lagos, dhaka, sao paulo
stacking souls toward the sky.
i have walked both worlds:
the field at dawn, the subway at rush hour.
we became an urban species
without ever voting on it.

benazir falls 2007 ce asia benazir bhutto was assassinated at a campaign rally in rawalpindi — the bravest woman in south asian politics, gone in the dust of a december blast. she came home to pakistan after eight years away,
the first woman to lead a muslim nation,
and the crowds were oceans.
i was in rawalpindi that december —
the rally, the wave from the sunroof,
then the blast, the shots,
and the bravest woman in south asian politics
was gone in the dust.
they buried her beside her father.
pakistan wept, then burned for days.
some assassinations kill a person.
this one killed a possibility.

the day the banks froze 2008 ce global lehman brothers collapsed and the world economy seized up — governments wrote unsayable checks while ordinary people lost houses for tower sins. lehman brothers. a hundred fifty-eight years old,
gone in a weekend — and the ice spread:
credit froze, markets fell,
the whole world economy seized up
like an engine run without oil.
i watched the traders' faces that september,
watched governments write checks
with numbers too big to say out loud,
watched ordinary people lose houses, jobs, pensions
for sins committed in glass towers.
the day the banks froze,
capitalism had to be rescued
by the thing it claimed not to need.

one world, one dream 2008 ce asia beijing's olympics opened with the greatest ceremony ever staged — two thousand drummers as one body, five thousand years painted in light. the bird's nest. two thousand drummers
moving as one body. the scroll unrolling
across the stadium floor, five thousand years
of china painted in light.
i have seen a hundred opening ceremonies;
nothing touched beijing.
one world, one dream, they said —
and for one night the dream was real,
the precision, the beauty, the sheer scale
of a civilization showing off.
then the games began, and phelps won eight golds,
and bolt ran like a rumor.
but it was the drummers i remembered.

yes we can 2008 ce north america barack obama's election drew a quarter million to grant park — "yes we can," three syllables carrying four hundred years of waiting. a black man with a strange name,
a community organizer from chicago,
stood in grant park before a quarter million people
and the tears ran down faces
that had waited four hundred years.
yes we can. three syllables
that carried the weight of selma,
of king, of every door that had been closed.
i watched an old woman in atlanta
touch the television screen
like it was a holy thing.
history doesn't always knock.
sometimes it just walks in
and takes the oath.

the machine that sees the beginning 2008 ce europe the large hadron collider fired up beneath the swiss-french border — seventeen miles of tunnel built to rewind the universe to its first trillionth of a second. seventeen miles of tunnel
under the swiss-french border,
colder than deep space,
smashing protons together
at nearly the speed of light —
to see the beginning.
the large hadron collider.
i stood in the cavern when they fired it up,
this cathedral of magnets built
to rewind the universe
to a trillionth of a second
after everything began.
some feared a black hole.
what we got was stranger:
a window into the first light.

nine pages that made money 2008 ce global a mysterious satoshi nakamoto published the nine-page bitcoin paper — money without a bank, without a king, without anyone in charge. nine pages. a pseudonym.
posted to a cryptography mailing list
on halloween, 2008:
"bitcoin: a peer-to-peer electronic cash system."
i read it that week — elegant, strange,
money without a bank, without a king,
without anyone in charge at all.
satoshi nakamoto. nobody knows who.
the paper sat there, quiet, for months.
then someone traded ten thousand coins for a pizza,
and the strangest money in history
began its long, wild life.

mumbai under siege 2008 ce asia terrorists held mumbai for sixty hours of fire — the taj burning on live tv — and the city that never stops refused to stop. ten gunmen came by sea
and held a city of twenty million
for sixty hours —
the taj hotel burning on live tv,
the train station, the cafe,
fire and fear block by block.
i watched mumbai refuse to break:
the dabbawalas delivering lunch
through the cordons, the city
that never stops, not stopping.
when it ended, 164 were dead,
and the sea route was the scandal —
how did they just sail in?
mumbai mourned. then mumbai worked.
that's what mumbai does.

a million pockets, a million apps 2008 ce global the app store opened with 500 apps and turned the smartphone from a phone into a universe — a store in every pocket for everything imaginable. five hundred apps on day one.
a store in your pocket
for things nobody had imagined needing:
a flashlight app, a fart app,
then the real ones — the maps,
the banks, the games, the everything.
i watched developers quit jobs
to build tiny icons,
watched the smartphone stop being a phone
and become a universe.
a million pockets, a million apps —
the iphone had been the stage;
the app store was the play.

money out of thin air 2009 ce global the bitcoin network went live with its genesis block — carrying a bank-bailout headline in its code, money honest about being made of trust. block zero. the genesis block,
mined in january, carrying a headline
about bank bailouts in its code —
a little joke, a little manifesto.
the bitcoin network went live
with no ceremony, no company, no owner.
i watched the first coins move
between strangers who trusted math
more than banks.
money out of thin air, the critics said.
they were right, and they missed the point:
all money is thin air.
this was just honest about it.

the swine flu year 2009 ce global h1n1 swept the globe as the first pandemic of the internet age — milder than feared, a rehearsal with real bodies that we should have studied harder. it started in mexico, rode the airplanes,
and within weeks the who was saying
the word nobody wanted: pandemic.
h1n1 — the swine flu year,
the first pandemic of the internet age,
tracked on maps, argued on forums,
feared in schoolyards.
i watched it sweep the globe
and then, mercifully, spare most of us —
milder than feared, a rehearsal
with real bodies.
we made vaccines in months.
we congratulated ourselves.
we should have taken notes.

a new president's promise 2009 ce north america nearly two million packed the national mall for obama's inauguration — the largest crowd washington ever held, there to witness a door opening. nearly two million people
stood in the january cold on the mall —
the largest crowd washington had ever held —
to watch a hand on a bible
and hear a promise:
hope, change, a new beginning.
i was in that sea of faces,
every color, every age,
breath fogging in the cold air.
the speech was sober, not soaring —
the work ahead, the winter of our hardship.
but the crowd didn't come for the speech.
they came to say: we were here
when the door opened.

kepler's planet hunt 2009 ce space nasa's kepler telescope stared at 150,000 stars to count their planets — and found thousands, proving the galaxy is crowded with worlds. they launched a telescope to count the worlds —
not to photograph them, just to count,
watching 150,000 stars for the tiny dimming
of a planet crossing.
kepler stared at one patch of sky
for four years, unblinking.
i watched the numbers climb:
hundreds, then thousands of worlds —
hot jupiters, super-earths,
planets where it rains glass sideways.
before kepler, we wondered if planets were rare.
after kepler, we knew:
the galaxy is crowded with worlds.

copenhagen's heartbreak 2009 ce europe the copenhagen climate summit collapsed without a binding deal — a hundred leaders, two weeks, and the hollow feeling of firefighters leaving a burning house. a hundred world leaders in one freezing city,
two weeks of talks, the whole planet watching —
and it collapsed.
no binding deal. a weak accord,
noted but not adopted,
the small island nations weeping
in the hallways.
i walked out of the bella center
into the danish winter
with the hollow feeling
you get when the firefighters
leave while the house is burning.
copenhagen's heartbreak taught us:
the planet won't be saved by summits.
it will be saved despite them.

the green wave 2009 ce middle east millions protested iran's disputed election in a peaceful green wave — and the regime crushed it with batons, jails, and motorcycles. the election was a fraud — everyone saw it —
so they poured into the streets of tehran,
millions of them, a green wave,
silent, peaceful, asking only:
where is my vote?
i watched it on shaky video,
the sea of people stretching to the horizon,
the regime's answer arriving
on motorcycles with batons.
they crushed it. jailed it. killed it.
but the green wave had shown the world
what iran really wanted —
and the regime never forgot
how close it came.

nine-point-five-eight 2009 ce global usain bolt ran 100 meters in 9.58 seconds in berlin — smiling mid-race while history chased his shadow, a record still untouched. berlin. a hundred meters.
nine point five eight seconds —
faster than any human being
had ever covered the ground.
i was in the stadium when bolt ran,
and the strangest thing wasn't the speed,
it was the smile — mid-race, pulling away,
grinning like a man out for a jog
while the fastest humans in history
chased his shadow.
9.58. the number sits there still,
untouched, fifteen years later.
the fastest man who ever lived
made it look like play.

the tablet arrives 2010 ce global the ipad turned the computer into a sheet of glass — toddlers swiped before they could read, and the machine dissolved into something held like a magazine. they laughed at first — a giant iphone?
then they held it: a sheet of glass
that was a book, a movie, a newspaper,
a child's drawing pad, a pilot's charts.
i watched the ipad eat the laptop's lunch
in living rooms and cockpits,
watched toddlers swipe before they could read,
watched the computer dissolve
into something you hold like a magazine.
the tablet didn't replace the computer.
it revealed what the computer
had been trying to be all along.

instagram's first photo 2010 ce global instagram launched with a dog photo and quietly rewrote beauty, fame, and self-image — a mirror that taught the world to pose. a photo of a dog. a taco stand.
the first uploads were nothing —
and then the filters came,
and suddenly everyone's breakfast
looked like art.
i watched it quietly rewrite
how beauty is sold, how fame is made,
how a generation learned to see themselves
through a square and a filter.
a photo app, they said.
it was never a photo app.
it was a mirror that charged admission
and taught the world to pose.

a fruit vendor's fire 2010 ce africa a tunisian fruit vendor's self-immolation set the region ablaze — one man's refusal of humiliation lit the arab spring. mohamed bouazizi sold fruit from a cart
in sidi bouzid, tunisia.
the police took his scales, slapped him,
humiliated him — and he walked
to the governor's office, poured fuel
over himself, and struck the match.
i have seen empires fall for less reason
and for more; this one fell
because one tired man
refused one more humiliation.
his fire set a region ablaze —
tunisia, egypt, libya, syria.
one vendor's match lit the arab spring.

haiti shakes 2010 ce latin america a 35-second earthquake leveled port-au-prince — palace, cathedral, hospitals — and the world promised everything haiti is still waiting for. thirty-five seconds. that's all it took —
a 7.0 quake at rush hour,
and port-au-prince folded like paper.
the palace collapsed. the cathedral collapsed.
the hospitals collapsed.
i walked those streets in the weeks after:
the dust, the tent cities, the endless aftershocks,
the world pouring in aid
that mostly never arrived.
hundreds of thousands dead.
a nation already poor made poorer.
haiti shook, and the world promised everything,
and delivered — haiti is still waiting
to tell you how much.

oil in the gulf 2010 ce north america deepwater horizon exploded and bled crude into the gulf for 87 days on live feed — the marshes black, the pelicans dying, our reach exceeding our grip. the rig exploded — eleven men died in the fire —
and then the well wouldn't close.
eighty-seven days. i watched the live feed,
the black plume blooming underwater,
the crude pouring into the gulf
while the whole world watched
and nobody could stop it.
top kill failed. junk shot failed.
finally, a cap held.
the marshes were already black,
the pelicans already dying.
deepwater horizon taught us
what the industry already knew:
the ocean is deep, the oil is deep,
and our reach exceeds our grip.

the world's cup in africa 2010 ce africa south africa hosted the first world cup on african soil — vuvuzelas droning, fan parks dancing, a continent's pride on full display. the vuvuzelas. dear god, the vuvuzelas —
a hundred thousand plastic horns
droning like a hive of angry bees
through every match.
but under the noise: africa's first world cup,
johannesburg singing, cape town shining,
a continent hosting the world
and hosting it well.
i was in soweto when the final whistle blew
on spain's victory — and nobody cared
who won. africa had won.
the world came, the world saw,
the world danced in the fan parks.
the horns never stopped.
neither did the pride.

the cables spill 2010 ce global wikileaks dumped a quarter-million secret diplomatic cables — every embassy's unfiltered gossip, read by the whole planet at once. a quarter-million secret cables —
every embassy's gossip, every diplomat's
unfiltered opinion of every leader —
dumped onto the internet for all to read.
i watched foreign ministries scramble,
watched dictators learn what america
really thought of them,
watched a young soldier's conscience
become the world's biggest leak.
wikileaks didn't invent the truth.
it just removed the lock from the filing cabinet
and let the whole planet read the memos.
diplomacy never whispered the same way again.

the square fills 2011 ce africa tahrir square's eighteen days toppled mubarak — millions refusing to go home, and the arab spring blazed outward from that recipe. tahrir square. eighteen days.
they came with bread and phones and flags,
copts and muslims, old and young,
and they did not leave —
not for the tear gas, not for the camels
charging through the crowds,
not for anything.
i stood in that square when mubarak fell,
thirty years of rule ended by people
who simply refused to go home.
the arab spring blazed outward —
tunisia, egypt, then libya, syria, yemen.
some squares won. some squares burned.
but tahrir showed the recipe:
fill the square, and hold it.

the wave that split atoms 2011 ce asia japan's earthquake and tsunami melted down fukushima's reactors — the wave killed 20,000, the atoms scattered a fear that closed reactors worldwide. the earthquake was the biggest japan had ever felt.
the tsunami was forty meters high.
then the water found fukushima —
and the reactors melted,
one, two, three,
hydrogen explosions on live tv,
a exclusion zone drawn on the map
that may outlive us all.
i walked the empty streets of namie years later:
the vending machines still glowing,
the school clocks stopped at 3:37.
the wave killed twenty thousand.
the atoms scattered a fear
that closed reactors across the world.

the most wanted man falls 2011 ce asia us navy seals killed osama bin laden in abbottabad — a decade of hunting ended in forty minutes, and ten years of grief found release. a decade of hunting ended in abbottabad —
helicopters in the night, a compound
a mile from pakistan's military academy,
and the most wanted man on earth
gone in forty minutes.
i watched obama tell the world at midnight,
watched crowds gather at ground zero
chanting, crying, ten years of grief
finding one sharp release.
justice, they called it.
others called it an execution
in a sovereign country.
both things were true.
that's usually how it goes with history.

goodbye to the showman 2011 ce global steve jobs died and the world mourned a salesman like a saint — shrines of flowers and half-eaten apples outside stores worldwide. he died the day after the new iphone came out —
timing, even at the end, like a product launch.
i watched the shrines bloom
outside apple stores worldwide:
flowers, candles, half-eaten apples,
notes from people who never met him
mourning like he'd been family.
a salesman mourned like a saint —
because he sold us more than gadgets;
he sold us the idea that tools
could be beautiful.
love him or hate him, the showman
changed what we expect from everything we touch.

curiosity leaves earth 2011 ce space a car-sized nuclear rover launched for mars — the most ambitious machine ever aimed at another world, riding fire toward its seven minutes of terror. a car-sized rover, a nuclear heart,
a laser to zap rocks —
the most ambitious machine
ever aimed at another world.
i watched curiosity leave earth
that november, riding fire toward mars,
carrying more instruments
than some whole space programs.
it would land by sky crane,
a maneuver so insane
the engineers called it
seven minutes of terror.
but that november, all we had
was a launch, a trajectory,
and the audacity of the plan.

the world's youngest nation 2011 ce africa south sudan voted itself into existence — dancing in juba's dust on independence day, the world's youngest nation born in joy. they voted — ninety-nine percent for freedom —
and south sudan was born,
the world's youngest nation,
flags sewn overnight, anthems learned by heart.
i was in juba for the independence day:
dancing in the dust, the new flag rising,
fifty years of war finally over.
the joy was real. it was also brief —
within two years the new nation
would turn its guns on itself.
but on that day, in that dust,
freedom tasted exactly like they dreamed.
some birthdays are worth having
even when the childhood is hard.

the tents of wall street 2011 ce global occupy protesters camped in zuccotti park with no leaders and one phrase — "we are the 99%" — and changed the conversation even after the tents were cleared. they pitched tents in zuccotti park —
no leaders, no demands list,
just sleeping bags and signs:
we are the 99%.
i walked among them that autumn:
the drum circles, the people's mic,
the library in a tent,
the quiet fury of a generation
that had done everything right
and gotten nothing.
the tents were cleared.
the phrase stayed.
occupy didn't change the banks.
it changed the conversation —
and conversations, eventually,
change everything.

the god particle found 2012 ce europe the higgs boson turned up at the large hadron collider — fifty years of hunting ended with a bump in the data and tears in the auditorium. fifty years they hunted it —
the particle that gives everything mass,
the reason anything weighs anything.
then the bump in the data,
five sigma, champagne in the cern auditorium,
peter higgs wiping his eyes
at eighty-three.
i was there for the announcement:
the room erupted like a stadium.
the god particle, the papers called it.
the physicists hated the name.
but the universe didn't care what we called it —
it had been holding mass together
for thirteen billion years, waiting to be noticed.

seven minutes of terror 2012 ce space curiosity survived its seven minutes of terror — heat shield, parachute, then a sky crane lowering the rover to mars on cables. entry. descent. landing.
seven minutes when mars
decides whether you live —
a heat shield, a parachute,
then rockets, then a sky crane
lowering a car-sized rover
on cables, like a spider
dropping its young.
i held my breath with the whole control room,
watching telemetry fourteen minutes old,
already history by the time we saw it.
touchdown confirmed.
the room exploded.
curiosity was on mars,
lowered from the sky by a flying crane.

london's summer 2012 ce europe london's olympics opened with the queen apparently parachuting in with bond — wit, rain held off, and bolt defending his crowns. the queen apparently parachuted in
with james bond — and the stadium roared.
danny boyle's opening ceremony
was a love letter to britain:
the nhs, the punks, the queen,
mr. bean on the keyboards.
i watched london do what london does —
take the world's biggest stage
and make it witty.
then bolt defended his crowns,
farah won the double-double,
and for seventeen days
the rain held off and the city glowed.
london's summer. the games
with a sense of humor.

sandy floods new york 2012 ce north america superstorm sandy drowned new york's subways and shore towns — the city improvised kindness in the dark, and started listening to the warning. a superstorm the size of europe
curved into the jersey shore
and drowned the subways —
salt water in the tunnels,
the lights out in lower manhattan,
breezy point burning while it flooded.
i walked the dark streets that week:
neighbors sharing generators,
strangers carrying water up ten flights,
the city improvising kindness.
sandy wasn't the big one.
everyone knew it wasn't the big one.
it was the warning —
and new york, to its credit,
started listening.

gangnam goes global 2012 ce global psy's horse dance became the first billion-view video — a joke with a beat that gave the world one shared dance floor. a chubby korean rapper in sunglasses
did a horse dance —
and the whole planet did it with him.
the first video to a billion views,
breaking youtube's counter,
played at weddings, in parliaments,
by grandmothers and generals.
i watched it happen in real time:
a joke, a beat, a dance so dumb
it circled back to genius,
crossing every border
without a single translated word.
gangnam style proved what the internet
had been whispering: the world
has one dance floor now.

the schoolgirl who would not stop 2012 ce asia malala was shot for going to school and survived to shame the world — the taliban tried to silence a schoolgirl and created its loudest voice. she was fifteen, riding the school bus
in the swat valley, when they stopped it,
asked for her by name,
and shot her in the head —
for going to school.
malala lived. that was the miracle.
then she spoke — at the un, to the world —
and shamed every power that had looked away.
i watched a child become
the conscience of nations.
the taliban tried to silence a schoolgirl.
instead they gave the world
its loudest voice for learning.

a man falls from the edge of space 2012 ce space felix baumgartner skydived from 39 kilometers up — stepping off the edge of space, falling faster than sound, and living to tell it. thirty-nine kilometers up —
a balloon the size of a football stadium,
a capsule the size of a phone booth,
and one man in a spacesuit.
felix baumgartner stepped off the edge
and fell faster than sound,
spinning, tumbling, then steady,
then the chute, then the desert.
i watched the live feed with millions,
holding my breath for four minutes
and nineteen seconds.
he broke the sound barrier
with his body.
sometimes the oldest dream —
to fall from the sky and live —
just needs a better balloon.

a pope named for the poor 2013 ce europe francis became the first latin american pope — asking the crowd's prayers before his blessing, riding in a ford focus, washing prisoners' feet. white smoke. a new name: francis —
the first pope from the americas,
the first jesuit, named for the saint
who married lady poverty.
i watched him on that balcony,
asking the crowd to pray for him
before he blessed them —
a small reversal that said everything.
then the ford focus instead of the limousine,
the washing of prisoners' feet,
the "who am i to judge?"
the vatican's marble halls
had never seen anything like him.
some called him a revolution.
he called himself a priest.

the man who carried the secrets 2013 ce global edward snowden revealed the nsa was watching everyone — every call, every email — and fled to moscow as the debate split the world. a twenty-nine-year-old contractor
walked out of hawaii with a hard drive
full of the nsa's secrets —
and showed the world
that everyone was being watched.
every call. every email.
i watched the revelations land
day after day: the programs had names
like dishes on a menu — prism, xkeyscore —
and the menu was all of us.
snowden fled to moscow.
the debate never ended:
traitor or hero, the question splits rooms still.
but nobody checks their phone
quite the same way anymore.

madiba's long walk ends 2013 ce africa nelson mandela died at 95 — twenty-seven years in prison, one walk to a free presidency, and a world that bowed to proof hatred can be outlived. ninety-five years. twenty-seven in prison.
one walk from a cell on robben island
to the presidency of a free nation —
and then, at the end,
a quiet death at home in houghton.
i stood outside the hospital
with the crowds singing,
then in the long lines
filing past the lying-in-state.
the world bowed — presidents, prisoners,
everyone who had ever needed proof
that hatred can be outlived.
mandela's walk ended.
the road he walked
stays open.

the jade rabbit hops 2013 ce asia china's chang'e-3 landed the jade rabbit rover on the moon — the first soft landing in 37 years, and a message: the moon has new visitors. china landed on the moon —
softly, in the bay of rainbows —
and out rolled yutu, the jade rabbit,
named for the pet of the moon goddess.
i watched the first pictures:
a little rover's tracks in the gray dust,
a nation's flag planted by robot arm.
the first soft landing in thirty-seven years.
america had stopped going;
china had started.
the jade rabbit hopped a short hop —
it broke down within weeks —
but the message landed intact:
the moon has new visitors.

haiyan's fury 2013 ce asia super typhoon haiyan devastated the philippines at record strength — tacloban flattened, a preview of stronger storms where the poorest pay first. the strongest landfalling typhoon
ever recorded — winds at 315 kilometers an hour,
a storm surge like a tsunami
wearing a hurricane's clothes.
it hit the philippines at dawn,
and tacloban simply ceased to exist
as anyone knew it.
i walked that flattened city weeks later:
ships thrown into streets,
the smell, the silence,
then the rebuilding, already starting,
because filipinos rebuild.
haiyan's fury was a preview —
the storms are getting stronger,
and the poorest always pay first.

three words on a facebook post 2013 ce global "black lives matter" was written online for the first time — three words that traveled from a post to a worldwide reckoning. three words, written online
after a verdict in florida:
black lives matter.
i watched them travel —
from a facebook post to a hashtag
to a movement to a reckoning,
carried through ferguson, baltimore,
minneapolis, around the world.
three words that asked the simplest question:
do they? the answer came back
in streets full of marchers,
in statues falling, in a long overdue
examination of the american conscience.
it started with three words on a screen.

terror at the finish line 2013 ce north america the boston marathon bombing killed three at the finish line — and a year later a million lined the route: boston strong, a city that runs toward. the marathon is boston's holy day —
and at the finish line, the bombs.
two pressure cookers, ten seconds apart,
three dead, hundreds maimed,
a city locked down for a manhunt
that ended in a boat in watertown.
i was there for the run a year later:
a million people lining the route,
the chant — boston strong —
not a slogan but a vow.
terror at the finish line
met something stronger at the start line:
a city that runs toward, not away.

ebola's cruel year 2014 ce africa ebola ravaged west africa — 11,000 dead — and health workers in moonsuits became the bravest people on earth, beating it with courage and tracing. it came out of the forest in guinea
and found the cities —
monrovia, freetown, conakry —
and the dying began.
ebola's cruel year: eleven thousand dead,
whole villages emptied,
health workers in moonsuits
becoming the bravest people on earth.
i watched them go in, knowing the odds,
watched them hold the hands
of patients no one else would touch.
the world was slow. then it wasn't.
the virus was beaten — by courage,
mostly, and contact tracing.
the heroes wore rubber gloves
and never took them off.

ice water for a cure 2014 ce global the ice bucket challenge flooded als research with $200 million — the silliest, most successful medical fundraiser in history. dump a bucket of ice water on your head,
post the video, dare three friends —
and somehow, two hundred million dollars
for als research.
i watched the whole planet do it:
celebrities, presidents, grandmothers,
shrieking, laughing, freezing —
for a disease most couldn't pronounce.
the ice bucket challenge was silly.
it was also the most successful fundraiser
in medical history.
sometimes the world doesn't need
a better argument.
it needs a better dare.

landing on a comet 2014 ce space the philae lander touched down on a tumbling comet after ten years of travel — bounced twice, landed anyway, and rode it around the sun. ten years of travel. four billion miles.
then rosetta dropped philae
at a tumbling, duck-shaped snowball
screaming around the sun —
and the little lander bounced.
twice. into a shadow, on its side,
running on fumes and sunlight.
but it landed. on a comet.
i watched the telemetry with the team in darmstadt,
grown engineers crying like children.
humanity had harpooned a snowball in space
and ridden it around the sun.
philae slept. rosetta watched.
the comet kept its appointment with the stars.

the vanished plane 2014 ce asia mh370 disappeared with 239 aboard and was never found — the transponder dark, the ocean keeping its secrets, aviation's greatest mystery. mh370 took off from kuala lumpur
with 239 souls — and vanished.
the transponder went dark.
the plane turned, flew on for hours,
and then — nothing.
the greatest aviation mystery of our age.
i followed the search: the south china sea,
then the indian ocean, the pings,
the debris on reunion years later,
a flaperon, a maybe.
never found. not really.
two hundred thirty-nine people
boarded a plane in 2014
and never landed anywhere.
the ocean keeps its secrets.

crimea taken 2014 ce europe russia seized crimea with unmarked soldiers and a gunpoint referendum — the old map tore, the west frowned, and nobody acted like it was a rehearsal. the little green men came at dawn —
no insignia, no flags,
just soldiers who were definitely not russian
taking the airports, the parliament,
the whole peninsula.
then the referendum at gunpoint,
then the annexation, signed and sealed.
i watched the old map tear
in real time, watched the west
answer with sanctions and frowns
and do nothing that mattered.
crimea was the rehearsal.
everyone said so at the time.
nobody acted like it.
eight years later, the main act began.

the caliphate declared 2014 ce middle east isis proclaimed its brutal caliphate across iraq and syria — black flags spreading like a stain, ancient temples falling, evil gone viral. a man in black climbed the pulpit
of mosul's great mosque and declared
a caliphate — a state of terror
stretching across iraq and syria,
built on beheadings broadcast in hd,
on slavery, on the deliberate
destruction of everything ancient.
i watched the black flags spread
across the map like a stain,
watched palmyra's temples fall,
watched the world slowly, painfully
learn to fight back.
it took five years to erase the stain.
the videos remain.
so does the lesson: evil, too,
learned to go viral.

yellow umbrellas in hong kong 2014 ce asia hong kong students held the streets for 79 days under a sea of yellow umbrellas — the most polite occupation in history, asking only for a real vote. they were students, mostly —
and when the tear gas came,
they opened umbrellas.
yellow umbrellas, a sea of them,
in admiralty, in mong kok,
holding the streets for seventy-nine days.
i walked among them: the study corners,
the supply tents, the art,
the most polite occupation in history.
they asked only for a real vote.
beijing waited them out.
the umbrellas folded. the lesson didn't:
a generation had learned
what it was willing to stand for —
and what stood against it.

paris signs for the planet 2015 ce europe 196 nations adopted the paris climate accord — every country on earth promising to hold the warming line, the gavel falling to tears and cheers. one hundred ninety-six nations.
one agreement. the first time
every country on earth —
every single one —
promised to hold the line on warming.
i was in the hall at le bourget
when the gavel came down:
cheers, tears, hugging diplomats,
the french foreign minister
crying into his hands.
paris didn't solve the climate.
the pledges were voluntary, the math was short.
but for the first time, the whole planet
signed the same page.
the page exists. now we have to live up to it.

the rocket lands standing up 2015 ce space spacex landed an orbital booster upright for the first time — rockets had never come back standing up, and spaceflight got cheap overnight. rockets went up. they didn't come back —
not in one piece, not standing up,
not ever.
then, on a december night in florida,
a falcon 9 booster fell out of the sky,
flipped, burned, and set itself down
on its legs like it had done it a thousand times.
i watched the spacex webcast with the world:
the landing, the cheering,
the quiet realization that spaceflight
had just gotten cheap.
the rocket lands standing up now.
we got used to it fast.
we shouldn't have. it's a miracle, every time.

pluto's heart 2015 ce space new horizons revealed pluto's great icy heart — tombaugh regio, bigger than texas — and the demoted planet had the most beautiful last laugh. nine years. three billion miles.
new horizons swept past pluto
and sent back the picture:
a great pale heart on the ice,
tombaugh regio, bigger than texas,
beating silently in the dark.
i watched the images arrive
pixel by pixel, the team gasping —
mountains of water ice, glaciers of nitrogen,
a world more alive than anyone dreamed.
the demoted planet had the last laugh:
pluto's heart was the most beautiful thing
we'd seen in years.

love wins 2015 ce north america the supreme court legalized same-sex marriage across america 5-4 — couples who waited forty years lined up for licenses as the arc bent. five to four. the supreme court spoke,
and same-sex marriage became the law
in all fifty states.
i was outside the court that morning:
the cheering, the weeping,
couples who had waited forty years
getting in line for licenses.
love wins, the signs said —
two words that had traveled
from a slogan to a statute.
a generation that had grown up
being told no
woke up to yes.
the arc of the moral universe
is long. that morning, it bent.

je suis charlie 2015 ce europe terrorists murdered paris cartoonists, and millions marched in reply — "je suis charlie," four million pencils held up to the sky. they came for the cartoonists —
masked gunmen in a paris newsroom,
twelve dead for drawings.
the next sunday, millions marched:
paris, london, berlin, madrid —
pens held high, the slogan everywhere:
je suis charlie. i am charlie.
i marched in paris that day,
in a river of people so wide
you couldn't see the banks.
they tried to kill satire with bullets.
the reply was four million pencils
held up to the sky.

the long walk to europe 2015 ce europe a million refugees crossed the mediterranean in a year — the largest movement since wwii — as europe argued with itself about its own soul. they walked — from syria, from afghanistan,
from eritrea — across turkey, greece,
the balkans, in columns miles long,
carrying children, carrying nothing.
a million refugees in a single year,
the largest movement of people
since the second world war.
i stood on lesbos as the boats came in,
watched volunteers pull children
from the surf, watched europe argue
with itself about its own soul.
some doors opened. some slammed.
the long walk continues.
it always continues.

nepal shakes 2015 ce asia a 7.8 earthquake killed 9,000 in nepal and toppled ancient temples — centuries of carved wood became dust, and the survivors rebuilt by hand. the earth moved at noon on a saturday —
7.8, shallow, right under kathmandu —
and the ancient temples folded.
dharahara tower fell.
centuries of carved wood and brick
became dust in ninety seconds.
nine thousand dead.
i walked the rubble of basantapur weeks later:
the gods' statues standing headless,
the survivors already rebuilding
with their hands.
nepal shakes often.
it also rises often.
the temples will stand again —
they always do, the nepalis say,
because the gods live there.

the dress that broke the internet 2015 ce global one blurry dress photo split the planet — blue-black or white-gold — the first truly global argument about nothing, proving we see different worlds. blue and black. white and gold.
one blurry photo of a dress,
and the entire planet split in two —
families arguing at dinner,
scientists explaining color constancy,
celebrities weighing in.
i watched it happen in a single day:
the first truly global argument
about nothing, over everything.
it was silly. it was also perfect —
proof that seven billion strangers
could look at the same thing
and see two different worlds.
we never agreed on the dress.
we never will.

britain votes leave 2016 ce europe the brexit referendum shocked the world 52-48 — the pound fell, the pm resigned by lunch, and the arguing never stopped. fifty-two to forty-eight.
nobody believed it, not even the winners —
the polls said remain, the markets said remain,
and then the votes came in from sunderland
and the whole map turned.
i was in london that gray morning:
the stunned faces on the tube,
the pound falling, the prime minister resigning
by lunchtime.
brexit. a word that didn't exist
became the only word for years.
britain voted to leave the club
it had spent forty years half-joining.
the arguing hasn't stopped since.

the outsider wins 2016 ce north america donald trump won the presidency against every poll — the map turned red state by state, and american politics broke in new ways. the polls were wrong. all of them.
a reality-tv businessman
who had never held office
beat the most qualified candidate
in american history —
and half the country celebrated
while the other half couldn't breathe.
i watched the map turn red
state by state that night,
watched the disbelief curdle
into something harder.
the outsider won because the insiders
had stopped listening, or so they said.
american politics broke that night.
it has been breaking, in new ways,
ever since.

zika's shadow 2016 ce global the zika virus spread through the americas — a mosquito bite casting a shadow over every pregnancy, leaving fear and unanswerable questions. a mosquito. a tiny bite.
and for pregnant women, a shadow
over everything — microcephaly,
babies born with too-small heads,
the images no mother could unsee.
i was in recife that winter:
the fear in the clinics,
the travel warnings, the olympics
under a cloud of repellent.
zika's shadow fell across the americas,
then receded, the way viruses do —
leaving behind the children,
and the questions,
and the mothers who never stopped worrying.

catching monsters in the street 2016 ce global pokemon go turned parks into monster-hunting grounds — millions chasing digital creatures, augmented reality's first irresistible proof. one summer, the parks filled —
not with joggers, but with hunters,
phones held high, chasing monsters
only they could see.
pokemon go turned plazas into hunting grounds,
churches into gyms,
and millions of couch potatoes
into walkers.
