i watched a stampede in central park
for a vaporeon — grown adults running,
laughing, alive.
it was silly. it was augmented reality's
first great proof: the real world,
plus a layer of play,
is irresistible.

the machine beats the master 2016 ce global alphago defeated go champion lee sedol 4-1 — move 37 made the master smile at a beauty no human had ever seen. go has more positions than atoms in the universe —
it was supposed to be the last game,
the one machines would never master.
then alphago played lee sedol in seoul,
and won four games to one.
i watched move 37 in game two:
the commentators gasped, the master smiled
a strange smile — a move no human
would ever play, beautiful and alien.
the machine beats the master.
but the real story was the smile:
even in defeat, lee saw something
no human had ever seen.

juno reaches jupiter 2016 ce space juno slipped into orbit around jupiter — first pictures of blue storm-tossed poles, cyclones the size of continents waltzing. five years of falling toward the giant,
and then the burn — thirty-five minutes
that had to be perfect —
and juno slipped into orbit
around jupiter.
i watched the first pictures:
the poles, blue and storm-tossed,
cyclones the size of continents
waltzing at the top of the world.
juno would dive again and again,
threading the radiation belts,
mapping the gravity, listening
to the deep interior.
the king of planets, finally,
seen up close and personal.

rio's games 2016 ce latin america the olympics went to south america for the first time — bolt's triple-triple, the refugee team's march, brazil's football gold in the maracana. the olympics came to south america
for the first time — to rio,
all samba and sunshine and beautiful chaos.
i watched bolt complete the triple-triple,
watched the refugee team march
to the loudest cheer of the night,
watched brazil win football gold
in the maracana and the whole country exhale.
there were worries — the water, the zika,
the unfinished venues.
then the games began,
and rio did what rio does:
it partied through all of it.

water protectors at standing rock 2016 ce north america native-led protesters faced down a pipeline at standing rock — tipis in snow, prayer fires, water cannons — teaching america "water is life." they came to the river —
lakota, then hundreds of tribes,
then thousands of veterans and students —
to stand between a pipeline
and the water.
i was at oceti sakowin that winter:
the tipis in the snow, the prayer fires,
the water cannons in freezing weather,
the dogs, the arrests.
the pipeline was rerouted, then unrereouted.
the camp was cleared.
but standing rock changed something:
the water protectors taught america
a word it had forgotten — mni wiconi.
water is life.

me too's thunder 2017 ce global "me too" became a roar — millions of women speaking at once, powerful men falling one by one, and the end of the silence abuse hid behind. two words. me too.
first a whisper, then a roar —
millions of women speaking at once,
naming what had been unnamed for centuries.
i watched the powerful fall one by one:
the moguls, the anchors, the chefs,
the senators — thunder rolling
through every industry.
it was messy. it was overdue.
some called it a witch hunt;
the witches had receipts.
me too's thunder didn't end abuse.
but it ended the silence —
and silence had been abuse's best friend.

three hurricanes in a row 2017 ce north america harvey, irma, and maria battered the americas in one season — houston drowned, the caribbean flattened, puerto rico left in the dark. harvey drowned houston —
fifty inches of rain,
boats in the streets, the highways as rivers.
irma flattened the caribbean,
then raked florida.
maria killed puerto rico's grid —
and three thousand americans
died in the dark, uncounted for months.
i walked all three aftermaths:
the mold, the blue tarps,
the particular anger of the forgotten.
three hurricanes in a single season.
the ocean was trying to tell us something.
we filed it under weather.

the great american eclipse 2017 ce north america the moon's shadow raced coast to coast — twelve million in its path, the corona's white fire, and a whole country looking up at once. the moon's shadow raced from oregon to carolina —
seventy miles wide, two thousand miles long,
and twelve million people stood in its path.
i was in the totality in tennessee:
the light went strange, the birds went silent,
the temperature dropped,
and then the corona — white fire
around a black sun —
and grown adults wept.
two minutes and forty seconds.
the most-watched eclipse in history.
for one afternoon, the whole country
looked up at the same sky.

the rohingya flee 2017 ce asia myanmar's army drove 700,000 rohingya into bangladesh — the fastest exodus of the century, a million people in bamboo and plastic at cox's bazar. the army came at dawn —
burning villages, the old story,
the one the world keeps promising
never again.
seven hundred thousand rohingya
fled into bangladesh in weeks,
the fastest exodus of our century,
carrying nothing, carrying everything.
i walked the camps at cox's bazar:
the mud, the monsoon,
a million people in bamboo and plastic.
the un called it textbook ethnic cleansing.
the textbooks didn't stop it.
the rohingya fled.
the world watched.
the watching continues.

bitcoin's wild winter 2017 ce global bitcoin hit $20,000 and everyone suddenly knew crypto — taxi drivers day-trading, a mania that crashed but left the idea standing. twenty thousand dollars.
for one imaginary coin.
taxi drivers were day-trading,
grandmothers were asking about wallets,
and every dinner party in america
had a crypto expert.
i watched the mania peak that december —
the wild winter when everyone
suddenly knew crypto,
when the nine-page paper from 2008
became a religion and a casino.
then the crash, the long winter after.
but the idea survived the hype,
the way ideas do:
quieter, harder, still there.

a visitor from another star 2017 ce space the interstellar rock oumuamua streaked through our solar system — cigar-shaped, speeding up mysteriously, gone before we reached the door. it came from somewhere else —
the first object ever seen
that was born around another star,
tumbling through our solar system
at a quarter million kilometers an hour.
oumuamua. the scout, in hawaiian.
cigar-shaped, reddish, speeding up
in a way nobody could explain.
i watched the astronomers argue for years:
comet? asteroid? alien sail?
we'll never know — it's gone,
back into the dark between stars.
a visitor knocked once.
we barely got to the door.

cassini's last dive 2017 ce space cassini burned up in saturn's clouds after thirteen years — its signal fading in mission control, a funeral and love letter sent at once. thirteen years. two hundred ninety orbits.
then the order: dive.
cassini threaded the gap between saturn
and its rings — twenty-two times,
closer than any craft had dared —
and on the final pass, it didn't pull up.
i watched the signal fade in mission control:
the carrier wave thinning, thinning, gone —
the little probe burning up
in the clouds of the giant it loved,
to protect the moons from contamination.
cassini's last dive was a funeral
and a love letter, sent at once.

saudi women take the wheel 2017 ce middle east saudi arabia lifted its ban on women drivers — the first morning brought laughter, tears, and a freedom that had been illegal the day before. for decades, the only country on earth
where women couldn't drive —
then the decree: the ban is lifted.
i watched the first morning:
women sliding into driver's seats,
some laughing, some crying,
all of them free in a way
that had been illegal the day before.
it was a small freedom, some said —
a wheel, a road.
but ask the woman who drove herself
to work that morning what small means.
the kingdom changed that day.
slowly. but it changed.

babies by design 2018 ce asia a chinese scientist announced the first gene-edited babies — the world recoiled, he went to prison, and humanity hadn't decided if it wanted them. a chinese scientist stood up at a conference
and announced the impossible:
twin girls, born from edited embryos —
crispr babies, the first gene-edited humans.
the world recoiled.
i watched the condemnation roll in
from every academy on earth:
too soon, too risky, unethical —
the germline, altered, inheritable.
he jiankui went to prison.
the girls — lulu and nana —
grew up in secrecy.
babies by design had arrived
before humanity had decided
whether it wanted them.

a robot listens to mars's heartbeat 2018 ce space insight landed on mars to feel its quakes — four years of listening to a cooling world's heartbeat, slower and older than ours. not a rover — a listener.
insight landed on the flat red plain
and pressed its ear to the ground:
a seismometer, feeling for marsquakes,
for the heartbeat of a planet.
i watched the first tremors come in:
tiny, faint, the groaning of a cooling world,
meteorites thudding in the dark.
for four years it listened,
and mars told its story —
a big core, a restless crust,
a planet still settling into itself.
a robot listened to mars's heartbeat.
it was slower than ours. older, too.

france's second star 2018 ce europe france won the world cup in russia — mbappe a blur at 19, the champs-elysees a river of joy, a team that was france in miniature. twenty years after the first,
in moscow's luzhniki stadium,
france won it again —
4-2 over croatia, mbappe
a nineteen-year-old blur,
pogba dancing, griezmann cool.
i was in paris when the whistle blew:
the champs-elysees became a river
of blue, white, and red,
a million people singing.
the team was france in miniature —
sons of immigrants, every color —
and the second star went on the shirt.
some victories are about football.
this one was about who france is.

twelve boys in a cave 2018 ce asia twelve thai boys and their coach were rescued from a flooded cave after 18 days — sedated, swum out one by one, all alive: a happy ending on live tv. a soccer team went exploring after practice
and the rains came —
twelve boys and their coach,
trapped two kilometers deep
in a flooded thai cave.
the world held its breath for eighteen days.
i watched the rescue: the divers,
the impossible plan — sedate the boys,
swim them out one by one
through the black water.
it worked. all thirteen, alive.
the world held its breath,
and then it cheered —
the rarest sound of all:
a happy ending, on live tv.

the trillion-dollar fruit 2018 ce global apple became the first trillion-dollar company — the bitten apple worth more than most countries, built on the phones in all our pockets. one trillion dollars.
a company worth more than most countries,
built on phones and the logo
of a bitten apple.
i watched the ticker cross it that august —
the first trillion-dollar company in history,
and the strangest part was how normal it felt.
we had put a computer in every pocket
and called it inevitable.
the fruit was trillion-dollar.
the orchard was all of us,
tending our screens,
paying the tithe of attention.

a journalist murdered 2018 ce middle east jamal khashoggi was killed inside a saudi consulate in istanbul — a columnist lured and murdered for writing, the lies collapsing one by one. he walked into the saudi consulate in istanbul
for a marriage document —
and never walked out.
jamal khashoggi. a columnist,
a critic, a man with a pen —
lured, killed, dismembered,
by a squad that flew in for the job.
i watched the lies collapse one by one:
the fistfight story, the rogue operation —
then the cia's verdict, the tapes,
the world's slow, sickened understanding.
a journalist murdered for writing.
the consulate had cameras.
so did history.

kepler's last light 2018 ce space the kepler telescope retired after finding 2,600 planets — out of fuel, drifting silent, having answered: yes, the galaxy is full of worlds. it ran out of fuel —
nine years, 150,000 stars watched,
2,600 planets found —
and kepler's last light went out
in the dark between the stars.
i thought of the little telescope
drifting now, silent, in its orbit —
the planet-hunter retired,
its fuel spent, its mission complete.
it had answered the ancient question:
are there other worlds?
yes. thousands. more than we can count.
kepler died the way explorers should:
having found what it was looking for.

the kids who marched 2019 ce north america parkland survivors led a million people to washington — teenagers refusing the script, turning grief into the most eloquent lobbying congress ever feared. they were high schoolers —
seventeen dead at parkland,
and the survivors refused
the script of thoughts and prayers.
i marched with them in washington:
a million people, the kids on stage,
clear-eyed, furious, organized —
naming names, registering voters,
the most eloquent lobbyists
congress had ever feared.
march for our lives.
the laws didn't all change.
but the generation did —
they learned that grief
is a kind of power.

the shadow of a black hole 2019 ce global eight telescopes became one planet-sized eye and photographed a black hole — an orange ring of fire around darkness, 55 million light-years away. fifty-five million light-years away,
a darkness with a ring of fire —
and eight telescopes across the earth,
linked into one planet-sized eye,
photographed it.
i watched the image load that april:
the orange ring, the black center,
einstein's prediction made visible,
a shadow cast by gravity itself.
m87's monster, six billion suns heavy.
humanity had photographed a black hole —
the invisible, made visible,
by pointing the whole planet at it at once.

notre-dame burns 2019 ce europe fire gutted notre-dame and the spire fell on live tv — crowds sang hymns to the burning church as paris decided she would rise again. the spire fell on live television —
eight hundred fifty years of stone and faith,
and the roof was a torch,
the lead melting, the bells at risk.
i stood on the left bank that night
with the crowds singing hymns
to a burning church,
parisians weeping openly
for the lady of paris.
the world pledged a billion euros
before the embers cooled.
notre-dame burned.
but paris had already decided:
she would rise again.

how dare you 2019 ce global greta thunberg scolded the un — "how dare you" — a 16-year-old's fury indicting a generation, millions of kids walking out behind her. sixteen years old, alone on a sailboat
across the atlantic, then at the un —
and she looked the powerful in the eye
and said it: how dare you.
greta thunberg. the school strike,
fridays for future, millions of kids
walking out of class for the climate.
i watched the speech go around the world:
the fury, the precision,
the child scolding the emperors
for having no clothes.
how dare you — three words
that indicted a generation.

hong kong's million march 2019 ce asia hong kong rose against beijing's grip — two million in the streets, the bill withdrawn, the grip tightening anyway, one summer of unafraid. a million people. then two million —
a quarter of the city in the streets,
against the extradition bill,
against beijing's tightening grip.
i marched in that river of umbrellas:
the office workers, the grandmothers,
the most massive protest
in hong kong's history.
the bill was withdrawn.
the grip tightened anyway —
the security law came the next year,
and the city changed forever.
but for one summer, hong kong showed
what it was willing to be:
free, loud, unafraid.

a new virus in wuhan 2019 ce asia doctors noticed a strange pneumonia in wuhan and the alarm was silenced — whistleblowers scolded, but the virus didn't read memos. doctors in wuhan noticed a strange pneumonia —
a cluster, then more —
and the alarm was silenced.
whistleblowers scolded.
journalists vanished.
i watched those december weeks
with growing dread:
the wet market, the denied human transmission,
the new year banquet for forty thousand families.
a new virus in wuhan.
the alarm was silenced,
but viruses don't read memos.
by january, it was on every continent.
by march, it was everywhere.

artemis is named 2019 ce space nasa named its moon-return program artemis — apollo's twin sister — promising not flags and footprints this time, but a base, and a woman walking first. apollo's twin sister.
nasa named its moon program artemis —
the goddess, the sister —
and promised what apollo never did:
this time, we stay.
and this time, a woman walks first.
i watched the announcement land:
the old apollo veterans nodding,
the young engineers grinning —
a return to the moon,
not for flags and footprints,
but for a base, a gateway, a future.
artemis is named.
the sister is coming home
to finish what her brother started.

australia ignites 2019 ce oceania australia's black summer burned an area the size of england — red skies over sydney, three billion animals lost, a preview of the century's fire. the black summer —
an area the size of england burned,
three billion animals dead or displaced,
the sky over sydney red at noon,
ash falling like snow on the beaches.
i walked the burn scars in new south wales:
the blackened trunks, the silence,
then the green shoots, already pushing up —
australia's ancient rhythm of fire,
now turned ferocious.
the koalas. everyone remembers the koalas.
australia ignited, and the world watched
a continent burn on live feed —
a preview of the century's fire season.

india's moonshot stumbles 2019 ce asia india's vikram lander crashed into the lunar surface on live tv — a stumble at the moon that was still a reach, rehearsal for the landing to come. vikram was falling to the moon —
india's lander, live on tv,
the prime minister watching —
and then the signal broke.
silence. the lander had crashed
into the lunar dust at full speed.
i watched the control room in bengaluru:
the faces, the held breath,
modi hugging the isro chief
on camera.
india's moonshot stumbled —
but stumbling at the moon
is still reaching the moon.
four years later, they'd land it.
this was the rehearsal.

the world stops 2020 ce global the who declared a pandemic and the world stopped — empty highways, silent cities, chalk rainbows in windows, humanity holding its breath together. the who said the word: pandemic.
and the world stopped —
the planes parked in the desert,
the highways empty, the cities silent,
two billion people told: stay inside.
i walked through locked-down cities
that spring: the chalk rainbows in windows,
the applause for nurses at seven,
the eerie birdsong in the silence.
the world stops rarely.
it stopped for plagues, for wars —
and now for this, the great pause,
when humanity held its breath together.

the vaccine in eleven months 2020 ce global mrna vaccines were approved in eleven months — sequence to shot, the fastest vaccine in history, science running faster than fear. eleven months. from sequence to shot —
a process that usually takes a decade,
done before the year was out.
mrna — a technology decades in the making,
waiting for its moment —
became the fastest vaccine in history.
i watched the first vials ship:
the ultra-cold freezers, the nurses' tears,
the elderly rolling up sleeves
like it was a sacrament.
the vaccine in eleven months.
science, when it runs,
runs faster than fear.

i can't breathe 2020 ce north america george floyd's murder set off the largest protests in american history — "i can't breathe" filmed on a sidewalk, the world marching in masks. eight minutes and forty-six seconds.
a knee on a neck, a man's last words —
i can't breathe —
filmed by a teenager on the sidewalk.
george floyd's murder set the world on fire:
minneapolis, then every american city,
then london, paris, sydney, berlin —
the largest protests in american history.
i marched in the streets that summer:
the masks, the heat, the fury,
the statues coming down.
i can't breathe — three words
that finally made america
look at what it had been doing.

dragon riders 2020 ce space spacex flew astronauts to the space station — america launching its own crews again, on a commercial spaceship with a touchscreen cockpit. for nine years, america hitched rides
to the space station on russian rockets.
then, in may, a crew dragon lifted off
from florida — two astronauts,
a touchscreen cockpit,
and a company logo on the side.
i watched the launch with the old apollo hands:
the tears, the disbelief —
americans flying to orbit
on a commercial spaceship.
dragon riders.
the space age had gone private,
and it wasn't coming back.

the blast in beirut 2020 ce middle east a port warehouse of ammonium nitrate exploded in beirut — the century's biggest non-nuclear blast, half the city leveled by six years of negligence. twenty-seven hundred tons of ammonium nitrate,
sitting in a port warehouse for six years —
then the fire, then the blast,
the biggest non-nuclear explosion
of the century.
i saw the videos: the white dome,
the red cloud, the shockwave
racing across the water.
half of beirut leveled.
two hundred dead, three hundred thousand homeless —
in a country already collapsing.
the blast in beirut wasn't an accident.
it was negligence, stored for six years,
finally going off.

everyone watched the tiger king 2020 ce global lockdown's strangest shared obsession — a tiger breeder, a murder plot, and the whole planet bingeing the same fever dream in two weeks. locked inside, the world needed something —
and found it in oklahoma:
a gay tiger breeder with a mullet,
a murder-for-hire plot,
rivalry, mayhem, big cats.
i watched the whole planet binge it
in the same two weeks —
the strangest shared obsession
in television history.
everyone watched the tiger king
because there was nothing else to do
and because, for seven episodes,
the world outside stopped existing.
lockdown's fever dream,
in a hawaiian shirt.

the arab world's mars shot 2020 ce space the uae's hope probe launched for mars — the arab world's first interplanetary mission, a region deciding its future is in the stars. the uae built a probe, named it hope,
and shot it at mars —
the first interplanetary mission
from the arab world.
i watched the launch from tanegashima:
the rocket rising, the engineers
in dubai holding their breath —
a nation that had never left earth orbit
aiming at another planet.
hope arrived, slipped into orbit,
and started mapping the martian atmosphere.
the arab world's mars shot
wasn't about science alone.
it was about a region
deciding its future is in the stars.

a helicopter bound for mars 2020 ce space perseverance launched carrying ingenuity — a four-pound helicopter bound for mars, aiming for the wright brothers' second flight on another world. a rover the size of a car,
and tucked in its belly —
a helicopter.
ingenuity: four pounds,
twin rotors, a solar panel,
built to fly in air
thinner than a whisper.
i watched it launch with perseverance
that july, this absurd little drone
riding to another world.
nobody knew if it could fly there.
the wright brothers' first flight
was twelve seconds.
ingenuity was aiming
for the second one —
on mars.

the eye that sees first light 2021 ce space the james webb telescope launched on christmas day — a gold origami mirror unfolding a million miles out, built to see the first light. twenty-five years of building.
ten billion dollars.
a mirror of gold, folded like origami,
launched on christmas day —
and then the unfolding,
in the dark, a million miles out,
three hundred ways it could fail.
i held my breath for a month
with the whole world watching:
the sunshield, the mirrors,
each step a small miracle.
the eye that sees first light
opened — and looked back
to the first stars ever born.

shots in arms 2021 ce global billions were vaccinated in the race against the variants — stadiums turned clinics, the largest medical campaign in history, hope in a syringe. the race against the variants —
billions vaccinated in a single year,
the largest medical campaign in history.
i stood in the lines:
the stadiums turned clinics,
the drive-through tents,
the elderly weeping with relief,
the nurses working doubles.
shots in arms, shots in arms —
the rich countries first, too fast,
the poor countries waiting, too long —
the old injustice in a new syringe.
but the needles moved,
and the dying slowed,
and that was everything.

january sixth 2021 ce north america a mob stormed the us capitol — the first breach since 1814 — while congress hid and the world watched american democracy shake. they came with flags and bear spray
and smashed the capitol's windows —
the first breach of the building
since 1814 —
while congress hid under desks
and the world watched in disbelief.
i watched the feed that afternoon:
the gallows on the lawn,
the chanting in the rotunda,
the democracy of two centuries
shaken by a mob in face paint.
january sixth.
america had exported democracy
for seventy years.
that day, it nearly lost its own.

glasgow's last chance 2021 ce europe cop26 in glasgow pleaded for the planet's future — coal phasedown, methane pledges, island nations begging, time bought but not enough. they called it the last chance —
cop26 in glasgow, the summit
where the 1.5-degree dream
would live or die.
i walked the rainy streets with the protesters:
a hundred thousand strong,
greta's "blah blah blah" speech,
the island nations begging for their lives.
the deal: coal phasedown, methane pledges,
promises, promises.
glasgow's last chance bought time —
not enough, but time.
the planet's future, negotiated
in a scottish november rain.

the first flight on another world 2021 ce space ingenuity's helicopter lifted off on mars — twelve seconds, the first powered flight on another world, the wright brothers' dream repeated. forty seconds. twelve seconds first —
then longer, higher, farther.
ingenuity lifted off the red dust,
hovered, and landed —
the first powered flight
